Dianne Barber, sales and marketing manager for the NPD Group, which conducted the poll, said 15,000 on-line users had been asked if they planned to watch the final episode, to be broadcast at 8:45 P.M. About 3,000 users responded. FUTURE CYBERMAGNATES -- Geeks? Smile if you are tempted to mutter the word about any of the 1,200 winners of high-school science competitions who stamped this week into Fort Worth, Tex., for a cerebral showdown at Intel's International Science and Engineering Fair. Competing for more than $2 million in grants and scholarships and two trips to the Nobel Prize ceremony in Sweden, these junior scientists are brainstorming to win. The science fair, which began on Monday and ends tomorrow, began 49 years ago. Among the projects being presented at the fair are "Protecting Our Privacy: New Data Encryption Scheme," "Possible Uses of Computer-Simulated Objects" and "Intercomm: Future of Internetwork Communication." And give one particular student a shiny new apple for "Computerized Public School Attendance Reporting System Utilizing the Internet."  MORE AIR FARES ON LINE -- Joining other air carriers that are posting their least expensive fares on line, United Airlines is offering its new E-Fare program. The program, found on the Internet at www.ual.com, not only lists reduced-fare flights every Wednesday for the upcoming weekend, a spokesman for the airline said, but also includes information for car rentals and hotel bookings. "It has full travel-reservation capability," said Matty Myers, the Web site marketing manager for United. If users find cheaper fares on competing airlines, they may use United's service to make those flight reservations, he said.

title: PC Makers Cool to Microsoft's Push for WebTV
body: One of the few innovations in Microsoft's Windows 98 operating system is the integration of television-viewing software, but many makers of personal computers are giving it the cold shoulder. Microsoft, which has aggressively been trying to gain a foothold in cable and high-definition television, has been offering manufacturers significant discounts on Windows 98 if they agree to install television-tuner cards as standard equipment on their new computers. The cards, which cost roughly between $50 and $130, enable computer users to watch television on their monitors. Microsoft is interested because the company is bundling its Web TV for Windows software with Windows 98. Web TV provides an electronic program guide that shows what's on television and lets computer users watch television in a small window on the computer screen or in full screen. But the program is fully functional only if a television-tuner card is installed. And so far, few, if any, manufacturers say they intend to take Microsoft up on the offer. Some manufacturers say experience has shown that consumers just aren't interested in watching television on their computers. Packard Bell-NEC has the most experience. Two years ago, it offered tuner cards as a standard option on every personal computer it sold. But it turned out that "that was not something consumers used or cared about," said Mal Ransom, senior vice president for marketing at Packard Bell-NEC. "It had no effect on sales. So we discontinued it in early 1997." Today, when many consumers are interested in low-cost PC's, Mr. Ransom said, "I'm not convinced in any way that a TV tuner in a PC is something people want to pay extra for." Lawrence Sennett, a spokesman for the Hewlett-Packard Corporation, said his company had no interest in taking the discount and installing tuner cards. "Everything we do is based on customer demand, not incentives from suppliers, and we don't see any demand for this," he said. If any company intended to take Microsoft up on its offer, it would probably be the Compaq Computer Corporation. Compaq is a member, with Microsoft, of the DTV Team, a small consortium of technology companies that has been trying to move the computer industry into the television business. Unlike Microsoft's bundling of its Web browser into Windows, its integration of television with Windows has not been challenged on antitrust grounds. Jim Finlaw, a spokesman for Compaq, would not say what features Compaq intended to include in its new line of computers, to be offered later this spring. A senior executive for a major PC manufacturer -- among the nation's five largest -- said his company "certainly is looking at adding tuner cards" because "Microsoft is making it quite compelling to offer them in a certain percentage of our PCs." But the executive, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, also noted that the company's experience with offering the cards as an option "was not great; there was not a lot of demand." Executives from several other major manufacturers said they held similar opinions. Ken Plotkin, head of Hauppage Computer Works on Long Island, a manufacturer of tuner cards for computers, is bullish on the market even though, as he noted, "computer manufacturers can't afford to put them in." "We think initially it will be a consumer-installed option," he said.  Steven Guggenheimer, a product manager for the Microsoft Corporation, said manufacturers had expressed "a lot of interest" in WebTV for Windows and tuner cards. But he declined to say which ones. But he and other company executives acknowledged that consumers might be slow to begin using computers as television receivers. "It's like sound cards for PC's," Mr. Guggenheimer said. In the early 1990's, they were expensive and difficult to install, but over time they grew to be standard features on personal computers. "We're at an early stage with this," Mr. Guggenheimer said. "But eventually I would expect tuner cards to be standard features, just like sound cards are."

title: Site Makes Silliness A Science
body: TECHNOLOGY prompts people to ponder many anomalies: for example, if electricity travels at the speed of light, why do electronic mail messages take so long to arrive? Or how does a thermos know whether to keep a liquid hot or cold? Dan Coffey, as Dr. Science, has spent the last 15 years answering such questions, first on stage as a member of the Duck's Breath Mystery Theater, then on the radio and now on the World Wide Web. His page (www.drscience.com) contains a little more than one-tenth of the 3,000 questions he has answered in this time. "There is a thin line between ignorance and arrogance," he writes on the opening page, "and only I have managed to erase that line." In fact, his answers are generally ridiculous, rambling and pompous. The site features a daily question, which is simultaneously sent through a 15,000-member mailing list as it is broadcast daily on about 60 public radio stations. Visitors can also "research" any subject through the on-line archive. For instance, type in "foam" and get questions like "How come every time you see a piece of foam rubber there's always a hair sticking out of it?" and "Shampoo comes in many colors. How come it always foams white when you wash your hair?" Mr. Coffey gets a lot of questions from around the world "from people who don't speak English and don't get the joke," he said. "They ask me something serious about thermodynamics or something. So I just ignore them." This tends to increase as more people use search engines on the Web and enter "science." Rick Alber, a Los Angeles-based developer who manages the site, said it got about 15 questions a day. They are forwarded to Mr. Coffey, who picks 1 in 25 to answer. Mr. Coffey spends about five days every three months working on the questions and answers, followed by a two-hour taping session. Mr. Alber said the Dr. Science persona worked best on line because "he conveys a healthy disdain for authority -- that's a good match for a lot of people who are on the Web."

title: Software and Hardball
body: For all the attention Microsoft's antitrust confrontation with the Justice Department has received, for all the headlines and all the commentary on the subject, it often seems that the Government is stepping into what is essentially an intramural spat within the software industry. To most people, the debate quickly becomes a baffling excursion into the arcane language of computing -- Web browsers, operating systems and Internet programming languages. And it is, after all, a dispute that pits the very rich software mavens from the Netscape Communica tions Corporation against the incomprehensibly rich ones from the Microsoft Corporation. At a time when the nation's economy is surging and its high-technology industries are the envy of the world, many people wonder if this a fight Washington should join. And why, they ask, should anyone outside the software business really care about the Government's escalating battle with Microsoft? The Government and the Attorneys General of more than a dozen states are expected to announce that they are filing broad antitrust suits against Microsoft soon, probably today, on the eve of the company's plan to ship its next-generation operating system, Windows 98. It will then be up to the courts to determine whether the cases amount to an economically wise and legally innovative application of antitrust policy to the information age or unnecessary meddling. But it is already clear that the impact of the Government's policy toward Microsoft could extend well beyond the software business, potentially to all manner of industries from autos and banking to travel and entertainment. "Virtually every discussion we have with companies about their strategy begins with one word: Microsoft -- how do you compete against Microsoft in the future?" said David Nadler, chairman of the Delta Consulting Group, which advises corporations in many fields. In industry after industry, executives share a sentiment expressed last year by Rupert Murdoch, chairman of the News Corporation: "Everybody in the communications business is paranoid of Microsoft, including me." Such worries about Microsoft have little to do with intricacies of computer programming. They center on the perception that Microsoft, through its near-monopoly in personal computer operating systems, has a chokehold on the PC desktop, as the main Windows screen is known. What is more worrisome to many people -- and of great concern to the Justice Department -- is that when the Windows desktop is fused with browser software for viewing sites on the World Wide Web, the operating system becomes a portal to the Internet. This makes the desktop extremely valuable real estate. By determining which icons appear by default on its desktop, Microsoft can steer users of Windows computers to its own sites on the Internet or to the sites of companies that pay Microsoft for a desktop position. The Government, in its suit, is expected to try to break Microsoft's grip on the desktop by allowing PC makers to personalize customers' requests for Internet services and to load those services before shipping the machines. The Government is expected to argue that unless Microsoft's contracts with PC makers are pried open, there is a danger that the company will be able to extend its operating system monopoly into the emerging new markets of Internet commerce and entertainment. In addition, the Government's suit is expected to ask that Microsoft be prohibited from requiring computer makers to install its browser, Internet Explorer, as a condition of licensing Windows. This would enable PC makers, if they chose, to instead install browsing software from rivals, like Netscape. It would also calm nerves in a number of other industries, since Microsoft has its own Web sites for travel reservations, car retailing, city guides and personal finance. Its on-line bill-paying service will start later this year. In Windows 98, the operating system and Internet browsing software are seamlessly integrated with a "channel bar" of featured Web sites, including Microsoft's. "The broad issue is: Does Microsoft control a bottleneck, and what are the limits to that control?" said Carl Shapiro, a professor at the University of California at Berkeley and a former chief economist of the Justice Department's antitrust division. "How much of Internet commerce will Microsoft manipulate, if not capture? The answer is we don't know. But Microsoft's potential control of the Internet bottleneck is at least scary to anyone trying to set up commerce on the Web." The business of Internet commerce, information and entertainment is small today but growing rapidly. Forrester Research Inc. projects that it will increase tenfold, to $350 billion, in the unitedstates by 2001. Increasingly, it is expected, people will venture onto the Internet to shop, find information and be entertained -- especially as televisions shift to the digital technology of PC's. Windows 98 includes software to enable users to view its television-and-Internet service, Web TV, on their PC screens. What businesses from car companies to banks fear is that Microsoft, by controlling the gateway to the Internet, will become an indispensable intermediary between them and their customers. And while the Government suit will also focus on other issues, Microsoft's control of the desktop to direct Internet traffic "was the real trip wire that created this sense of alarm in Washington and in other industries," said David Readerman, a software analyst for Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities. Even so, widespread fears about Microsoft's market power do not make an antitrust case. To win, Microsoft's lawyers contend, the Government would have to show not only that Windows is an indispensable gateway to the Internet but also that its only reason for including certain Internet services or links to featured Web sites was to harm competitors. If Microsoft could show a benefit to consumers or business justification for its practices -- even though those practices harm rivals -- the company insists that the courts should rule in its favor. "The antitrust laws do not dictate a level playing field," said Charles F. Rule, a former director of the Justice Department's antitrust division and a consultant to Microsoft. "The fact is, many PC users and software developers want the Internet features Microsoft has included in its operating system, both in Windows 95 and now in Windows 98. There is a business justification for what Microsoft has done." Besides, some analysts say, worries about Microsoft ruling the Internet are probably wildly exaggerated. Mr. Readerman of Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities estimated that Microsoft lost $500 million last year on its Internet commerce and programming ventures. George F. Colony, president of Forrester Research, asserted: "So far, Microsoft has shown itself to be pretty inept at Internet commerce. I think the idea that Microsoft is going to kill General Motors or Disney someday is nonsense." Graphic   Photo/Chart: "Windows 98: Microsoft's Internet Dashboard" Antitrust allegations against Microsoft could delay the shipment of Windows 98. Here is a look at some of the features of Windows 98 and the antitrust questions they raise.  The Channel Bar -- The Government says it enables Microsoft to steer PC users toward its Internet services and those of preferred partners. This power, the Government believes, could give the company an unfair edge in new markets for Internet commerce, news and entertainment. Microsoft says the channel bar benefits consumers by making it easier to find things on the Net.  Internet Explorer -- The Government is expected to ask a Federal court to stop Microsoft from requiring PC makers to include it as a condition of licensing the Windows operating system. Microsoft says its Web browsing software is an integrated feature of Windows, not a separate product that can be easily lopped off.  Web TV -- Microsoft's Internet-and-television service is not much of an issue yet since PC makers have been reluctant to install TV tuner cards needed to receive and display TV programming on a PC. (pg. D3)

title: The Information Superhighway and Its Back Roads
body: The backbone metaphor is regularly used to describe the huge data pipes that make up the, well, backbone, of the Internet. But the old cliche of the Information Superhighway is probably more accurate. KRIS GOODFELLOW  1. When people speak about the backbone of the Internet, they are usually referring to fiber optic cables that carry large amounts of data. Companies like MCI/Worldcom and Sprint, the biggest carriers have a backbone which can handle 155 megabits of data a second on OC-3 lines and are aiming to upgrade to 2.4 gigabits per second on OC-48 lines between places where there are high amounts of Internet traffic. This is the equivalent of building a superhighway between major commercial centers. 2. People who do not live on that Internet freeway still benefit from it. Just as suburbanites use smaller highways that feed into the superhighway, businesses use T-1 lines (1.5 megabits per second) and T-3 lines (45 Mbps) to connect to the Internet freeway.  3. Companies that do a lot of business with one another on the Internet can even build their own roads. The companies install high-speed line between their businesses to avoid congestion on the superhighway.  4. Home users with a penchant for speed may choose to install a cable modem (100-300 kilobits/second) or an I.S.D.N. (integrated services digital network) line (128 kilobits per second).  5. Anyone with a cable modem knows they can to download a large file quickly, unless the data are coming from an out of the way place. Then it will take longer.  6. Most people use a 28.8 Kbps (kilobits/second) or 56 Kbps modem to connect to the Internet from home. Getting onto the Web can often feel as though you are living in the country and making a trek to the city. But an empty back road can sometimes be as fast as a highway. A new provider who has built a larger road can also speed things up. Graphic   Drawing (Illustration by Gorka Sampedro; Kris Goodfellow/The newyork Times)

title: ANTITRUST ACTION AGAINST MICROSOFT IS CALLED IMMINENT
body: Only three days before it is scheduled to begin shipping Windows 98, the Microsoft Corporation is girding for an escalating round of lawsuits that could block the release of the latest version of its operating system and impose profound limits on the company's freedom to add features to future generations of Windows. The Federal Government and the Attorneys General of at least 12 states plan to file broad new antitrust suits against Microsoft as soon as Thursday. While the Justice Department has not disclosed its precise strategy, the states have come to general agreement on a complaint that "will surprise some people," said a senior official in one Attorney General's office. The official added, "It's going to be more far-reaching than most people expect." State Attorneys General said their suit would ask that Microsoft be prohibited from requiring computer manufacturers to install its Web browser and from requiring them to set up their machines so that Microsoft's default desktop comes up on the screen when the machine is started. They said it would also attack contracts that require computer makers or on-line services to support other Microsoft products or to shun competitors' wares. People with direct knowledge of both lawsuits said that the state and Federal governments were aiming to file their actions on Thursday. But they added that the states were still modifying their suit's language. The Attorney General of Texas dropped out of the group, at least temporarily, because of pressure from two Texas companies that are allies of Microsoft, the Compaq Computer Corporation and the Dell Computer Corporation. Two Attorneys General, who spoke on condition that they not be identified, said their filing would be similar to the Justice Department's suit, which is also likely to be filed on Thursday. They added that it would be flexible enough that more states could join the case later. Late today, Microsoft did get one piece of good news. A Federal appeals court ruled that the restrictions a district court judge placed on the sale of Windows 95 last year could not be extended to Windows 98. Those restrictions bar Microsoft from forcing manufacturers to install the company's Web browser, Internet Explorer, as a condition of their licensing Windows 95. The ruling means that the Federal Government will have to file a new lawsuit if it hopes to persuade a court to impose restrictions on Windows 98, which the Justice Department clearly intends to do. Microsoft called the decision "very significant news." The Justice Department disagreed and called the decision "procedural," adding that "it addresses a narrow aspect of the consent decree." In a related action today, Sun Microsystems, a bitter competitor to Microsoft, asked a Federal court to block the release of Windows 98 until Microsoft alters the program to include a Sun-approved version of Sun's Java programming language. Microsoft said Sun's suit was "without merit." And despite a Microsoft-sponsored rally last week in newyork to demonstrate industry opposition to delaying the release of Windows 98, the nation's leading personal computer manufacturers are not proving to be the zealous allies that Microsoft executives might hope for. In interviews this week, some greeted the possibility of a delay in releasing Windows 98 with a virtual shrug. Microsoft executives have repeatedly warned of severe harm to the nation's economy should Windows 98 be held up. But executives from most of the nation's largest computer companies said this week that they saw no real demand from consumers for an operating system to replace Windows 95. "It would not be a big problem," Mal Ransom, senior vice president for marketing at Packard Bell-NEC, said of a delay in releasing Windows 98. Lawrence Sennett, a spokesman for Hewlett-Packard, said: "I don't think consumers are sitting on their hands deciding whether to buy a PC based on whether it has Windows 95 or Windows 98. Our consumer business is running at record levels." A senior executive with another leading computer manufacturer, who asked not to be identified, said that a delay in the release of Windows 98 "would have a very modest effect on sales -- if there was any effect at all." Even so, Mark Murray, a Microsoft spokesman, said, "We are hearing directly from virtually every major PC manufacturer that they are excited about Windows 98, and they believe their business will suffer if the Government tries to delay the introduction of Windows 98." And while computer makers played down the immediate importance of Windows 98 to their sales, they expressed general concern both in the newyork rally and in the political arena about the threat of Government interference blocking innovation in new technology products. In a statement issued today, the Texas Attorney General, Dan Morales, said that his office was withdrawing, at least for now, because "several officials of Texas' computer industry have expressed concerns that the filing of a lawsuit against Microsoft may negatively impact their companies as well as the consumers of the state." Sun executives insisted today that blocking the release of Windows 98 was not the primary objective of their suit. The company has been battling Microsoft for months over Microsoft's implementation of Java, which Sun says was modified in violation of the marketing license. In a suit filed in San Jose, Calif., today, Sun asked a unitedstates District Court to impose one of three remedies: Windows 98 should be shipped with a Sun-approved version of Java included; a Sun-approved version of Java should be shipped separately along with Windows 98, or Microsoft's version of Java should be removed from Windows 98 entirely. Any of those remedies would delay the release of Windows 98. Todd Nielson, a general manager for Microsoft, called Sun's suit "nothing more than a publicity stunt." At last week's newyork rally, Eckhard Pfeiffer, chief executive of Compaq, the nation's largest personal computer manufacturer, called Windows 98 "the innovation-enabler our customers are asking for." Even so, Jim Finlaw, a company spokesman, acknowledged this week that customers did not appear to be holding back in anticipation, as was the case with Windows 95. "Our consumer business is robust," Mr. Finlaw said. "Things go along very well for us." Greg Golden, a spokesman for I.B.M., said, "We've seen no change in demand in retails sales due to anticipation of Windows 98." All the computer executives interviewed said they hoped Windows 98 would be released on time. And while most of them said a delay would probably not affect their business in any serious way, they expressed concern about a scenario in which the new operating system was released on time only to be pulled from the market because of a court injunction. "It would be a problem, a major financial impact for the industry, if we had to go back after we started shipping Windows 98," Mr. Ransom said. "It would be confusing to the marketplace. I think you'd see a major slowdown in sales."

title: Justice Department Expected To Seek Contract Restraints
body: The Government is expected to sue the Microsoft Corporation to place limits on the contracts the company strikes with personal computer makers, Internet service providers and Web site operators. In doing so, the Justice Department will argue that contracts must be limited to prevent Microsoft from using a monopoly in operating systems, both to unfairly protect its Windows stronghold and to extend its monopolistic reach into the new markets of Internet software and commerce. The use of monopoly power to maintain and expand a monopoly is a violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890. For months, Microsoft has replied that despite the fact that more than 90 percent of new personal computers sold use its Windows operating system, the company is not a monopoly because technology is changing rapidly, posing an ever-present threat to its dominance. Further, it argues that Government meddling would endanger innovation in software development. But the Government says it is precisely to make the information age safe for upstart innovators -- potential challengers to Microsoft -- that the contract curbs are needed. Several contract provisions are likely to be concentrated on in a new antitrust suit by the Justice Department. One is a provision forcing PC makers to take other Microsoft products as a condition of licensing of Windows -- the same issue over which the Government filed a consent-decree case last August. That court challenge, though, focused on Windows 95 and Microsoft's Internet Explorer browsing program. A new suit would seek to have the prohibition apply to Windows 98 as well. Under pressure from the current Federal and state investigations, Microsoft has dropped restrictions it had placed on some Internet access suppliers and Web sites to promote Microsoft's Explorer browser and not the Navigator browser of its main rival, the Netscape Communications Corporation. In a suit, the Justice Department would want to insure that such exclusionary tactics are permanently outlawed. A new restraint the Government will likely demand is that Microsoft not be allowed to give its own on-line products like its Carpoint Web site, an auto retailing service, or its Expedia, a travel reservations site, preferred placement on the operating system's default desktop. The worry among antitrust officials is that Microsoft's Windows dominance could give the company control of the gateway to Internet commerce, which is expected to be a linchpin of the economy of the future. By controlling the first screen that computer users see when they turn on their machines, the Government worries, Microsoft would have an unfair advantage developing on-line businesses. The remedy, antitrust experts say, may be to let PC makers filter requests for Internet services from consumers, then load them before shipping the machines instead of letting Microsoft control the desktop. At a minimum, they say, Microsoft could be prevented from using its Windows dominance by giving favored placement to Microsoft's own on-line offerings or to those of its preferred business partners.

title:
Moscow Journal;
Yeltsin Takes to the Internet for a Half-Hour Chat
body: "Good day, citizens of the Internet," the salutation began. "This is my first live Internet experience." Russians are beginning to discover the Internet. But Moscow has never seen anything like President Boris N. Yeltsin's on-line chat today on the Web site maintained by MSNBC. For 30 minutes Mr. Yeltsin responded to questions ranging from the role of women in politics to the thickness of his hair. Nearly 5,000 people from around the world submitted questions, twice as many as the site received when it interviewed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel in December and the most ever for its live chats. A woman from Ireland asked Mr. Yeltsin if he had any Irish relatives, because he had such a fine head of hair. But Mr. Yeltsin, who is from the Urals, ruled out the possibility of Irish ancestry. "My hair does not deserve so much attention," he explained. "I am taking care of my hair. It is just that the women in my family look after me so well." Mr. Yeltsin told a Dutch questioner that he had never smoked and that tobacco was an evil that needed to be strictly regulated. That, no doubt, came as a surprise to the many Russians who consider smoking in public places to be a veritable birthright. The mercurial Mr. Yeltsin was a most unusual guest. He routinely turns down interviews with the Western press even as he steals the world's spotlight with surprise announcements. Certainly today's chat had the impromptu flavor that characterizes Mr. Yeltsin's unscripted appearances. Mr. Yeltsin allowed MSNBC to pick the questions and dispensed with his overprotective Kremlin minders. The only help he received was provided by two interpreters. That was evident when Mr. Yeltsin volunteered that Russian society would not accept a woman as President. "Our society is not quite mature enough for that," he said. "This applies not only to my daughter, but to the question of a woman President in general." Mr. Yeltsin's unusual chat stirred up a storm of Russian media coverage. Moscow's local television station sniffed that the 67-year-old President seemed to have taken on the pastimes of his 35-year-old Prime Minister, Sergei Kiriyenko, and other youthful aides. The ostensible purpose of today's session was to discuss the coming economic summit meeting in Birmingham, England. But Mr. Yeltsin's underlying motivation appeared to be to quash reports that he lacks the stamina to lead Russia. "Today I've been working since 5 A.M.," he told an American questioner who asked about his health. "I had four hours' sleep. I'm working intensively. I still have a long day ahead of me, and it does not affect either my appearance or my energy." He even challenged a questioner to an athletic contest. Today's live chat was carried in Russia by the Government Internet service, part of the country's recent growing attention to cyberspace. Other Government agencies have also gone on line this year, including Parliament, the Central Bank and the tax service. Boris Y. Nemtsov, a reform-minded Kremlin aide, has set up two sites: an official site and a personal home page, which is intended to burnish his image. Visitors to Mr. Nemtsov's home page can seem him playing tennis and learn about his pride in Nizhny Novgorod, the Volga River region he oversaw as Governor for many years. They can also obtain other vital information, like the fact that Mr. Nemtsov shares a birthday with John Lennon. The Communist Party has also embraced the Internet. Its Web site has had more than 140,000 vistors since it was set up in November. Moscow also has its share of Internet cafes, where students and businessmen guzzle coffee or toss down shots of vodka while they check their email or surf the World Wide Web. At the Internet Bar in downtown Moscow, patrons are given 30 minutes of access to the Internet for every $5 they spend. With cocktails priced at up to $12, that is a lot of time in cyperspace. "Most people come not to drink but to surf the Web," said Mikhail Klyagin, the manager of the bar. "But their interests on the Web are all different." Mr. Yeltsin's session had its origins in an interview request that MSMBC sent several months ago to the President's email address on the Russian Government's Web site, Mr. Yeltsin's press office said. Mr. Yelstin indicated that he was disposed to do the interview just a few days later. To organize the chat, MSNBC asked questioners to send their queries to an email address. Some questions were included in the live chat. MSNBC selected 14 questions from the 4,900 it received, and an interpreter translated them into Russian. Another interpreter translated Mr. Yeltsin's answers into English and dictated them into a microphone hooked up to MSNBC in Redmond, Wash., where they were typed onto the Net. "In newyork it was 5:30 A.M.," recalled Alexei Alesandroff, a producer for MSNBC in Moscow. "So we thought it would be good if we took questions from them, because they made the effort." There were also questions from Venezuela, Sweden, Canada and Russia. Mr. Yeltsin received the queries in the Government studio he uses to tape his weekly radio addresses. Kremlin cameramen captured the moment for Western and Russian television while the interpreters stood by. Aside from dealing with more personal questions, the Russian President expounded on weighty foreign policy issues. He told a worried questioner from Italy that Russia was not selling weapons technology to would-be nuclear powers. A Russian questioner was assured that Moscow deplored India's decision to conduct three nuclear tests. "This nuclear test came as a big surprise to us," Mr. Yeltsin said. He added that he would try to resolve the issue when he visits India this year. Some of the answers may not have been what the questioners were looking for. But Internet surfers may have another chance. Mr. Yeltsin said he enjoyed his experience today so much that he may do another live chat in several months' time. Graphic   Photo: As President Boris N. Yeltsin had his "first live Internet experience" yesterday, Maksim Gusev, 23, a student, typed in questions at the Internet Chevignon cafe in Moscow. Mr. Yeltsin said he might do another live chat. (Associated Press)

title: A New Measure Of Disparities: Poor Sanitation In Internet Era
body: Around the world, more people are getting telephones and access to the Internet while at the same time an increasing number are without basic household sanitation -- toilets, or even simple latrines -- according to a new report. The report, "Vital Signs 1998," was published on Saturday by the independent Worldwatch Institute, a Washington environmental group. It is the latest in a series of annual surveys pulling together a wide range of disparate indicators -- crop yields, climate changes, medical advances and retreats, military expenditures or the production figures for bicycles compared with cars -- to spot new trends. "There are a lot of important trends that never get reported," said Lester Brown, who originated the survey in 1992. It is now published in 21 languages. Looking at sanitation, an important factor in health crises in poor nations, the 1998 "Vital Signs" concluded that the "sanitation gap" has become the greatest risk to public health in some countries. Using the latest available World Health Organization figures, the report says the number without facilities in the developing world increased by 274 million in the first half of the 1990's. "In some countries," the report reads, "less than half the population is adequately covered." These include Afghanistan, Brazil, Cambodia, China, Congo, Egypt, Haiti, India and Senegal. The report notes, however, that some countries, like Brazil, have more exacting definitions of basic sanitation than others, so the statistics are not completely comparable. On telecommunications the numbers are firmer and more recent. They indicate "tumultuous changes," the report said. International Telecommunications Union statistics show that more than 200 million telephone lines were installed worldwide from 1990 to 1996, bringing total telephone lines to 741 million. In 1960 there were 89 million. Some countries have leapfrogged over the use of traditional telephones into the wireless era, the report found. In Cambodia, one of the world's poorest nations, where a national network of telephone cables is considered a long way away, 60 percent of telephone subscribers use cellular phones. Worldwide, cellular phone users have increased an average of 52 percent a year since 1991, with 135 million users by 1996. This trend accentuates the differences between the rich and the poor in many under developed nations with poor communications networks. As for the Internet, its use has grown "exponentially," the report shows. Most of the users are still in industrial countries. Of the estimated 107 million people on line, about 62 million are in the unitedstates and 20 million in Europe. But the Internet has been harnessed to public services in a number of small, poor countries, the report found. It mentions human rights work by the Kuna indigenous people in Panama, agricultural marketing by cooperatives in Peru and shared medical expertise for countries like Uganda and Bhutan. "With 500 million people -- 8 percent of humanity -- projected to be on line by 2001," the report reads, "we can barely guess how the Internet phenomenon will shape the 21st century."

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
Companies Offer a New Service to Back Up Files
body: WITH a couple of keystrokes, you accidentally delete your groundbreaking manuscript about the last days of Amelia Earhart, along with all the research. No problem: You simply grab a handful of backup disks and restore the information. Next day, the hard disk makes noises like a coffee grinder and your monitor displays only a black screen and blinking cursor. No problem: You grab your backup disks and put your data on a different machine. Then the tornado hits. Problem: Your machine and all the backups have vanished just as the aviator did. The story is, of course, fiction. The backup disks are the giveaway. In the real world nobody ever has backup disks. But this cautionary tale does expose real worries. Even if you back up your data consistently, fire, flood and theft could render the backups useless. A precious archive file may turn out to be unreadable when you try to recover it. In your frenzy to restore the information, you may accidentally delete it. Those awful possibilities have led to a crop of new service companies that promise a better way to save your digital bacon. For a monthly fee, they secure your data with the help of software that encrypts your valuable files and sends them over the Internet to a secure, remote storage site (or, more typically, two sites). If you need to retrieve the files, you do it over the Internet. If so much data is involved that piping it through a modem might take half a day, you can have it delivered overnight on a CD-ROM. The backups can be automatic. The system can use your Internet connection to send copies of the files elsewhere late every night or remind you to do it manually whenever you shut the machine down. There are no tapes or disks to shuffle. The result: Backup instead of excuses. The systems can even store successive versions of your files. If you do something unbelievably stupid to that giant spreadsheet today, you can bring back the version you edited last week. There are unexpected benefits: When you forget to transfer that all-important presentation from a PC to a laptop, you can retrieve it over the Internet from the PC's remote backup site. Several companies offer these services under a bewildering variety of labels. To see how they work, I tried two that offer unlimited storage at a fixed price: Atrieva (www.atrieva.com), for $14.95 a month, and Connected Online Backup (www.connected.com), for $19.95. Both work with Windows 95 and NT. Connected also offers a Windows 3.1 version. Before demanding a credit card number, both let you download the software without charge and use it for 30 days; Connected limits you to 100 megabytes of storage. Both have glitches and limitations that become obvious upon close inspection. Installing the software involves bewildering demands for account numbers, passwords, user names and encryption keys. Once up and running, the programs scan your hard drive for relevant files, compress and encrypt them, dial your Internet connection and perform the initial backup. If your disk is full of files, this first transmission can take several hours with a standard 28.8 kilobits per second modem and is best done overnight; subsequent backups are much faster. But since there are many ways the process can fail, particularly when it comes to making the Internet connection, it is worth testing the backup first. These programs can not resurrect a dead machine. That makes them suitable mostly for storing data rather than for system information. And unless you have a high-speed Internet connection, they make more sense for data that does not change much in a given day. Graphic artists with tight deadlines who routinely handle 20-megabyte files are likely to find it unacceptable to have to wait two hours for one of those files to be restored through a modem. The Connected software can save some upload time by doing its best to compute the differences between the last version of a file it backed up and the current one, then transmitting only the changes. This technique works better on some files than on others but it can save a great deal of time during the backup process. However, to restore such files, Connected's software has to stitch all the pieces together again properly, a process that may take some time and could lead to errors. Both systems let you pick your own string of characters to serve as an encryption key to keep your files secure, even from their employees and for now, both use keys of a length that can be broken by the assiduous application of a great deal of computing power. But amnesia is a greater threat. If you forget your encryption key, your backups will remain gibberish unless you can find an expert to track down your key. Write down or print out all passwords, keys and account numbers and put them in a safe place. Atrieva lets you back up two machines for one fee and makes it relatively easy to retrieve individual files over the Web on a different machine. Connected charges extra for more than one machine; you can use a second computer to retrieve information backed up from the first, but figuring out how is almost impossible and the customer service representatives were unaware of the process. After I described a different problem in detail, an Atrieva service representative, reading from a script, asked me to describe my problem. But a knowledgeable technician returned my call in less than half an hour. Connected's software made pretty good guesses about what I might want to include in my first backup, but it also included a huge "hibernation" file of no value and, because of a choice I made at the outset, initially skipped most of the files on my disk. Atrieva's software limits its initial choices severely, forcing you to select the files to be copied. It also manages to use two confusingly different user interfaces for selecting files to back up or restore. Neither product comes with adequate documentation. Although they also offer their services under the brand names of bigger companies, these firms both fall in the start-up category, and what happens to your backups if the companies go out of business is anyone's guess. But the odds of an important file disappearing thanks to accidental deletion are significantly higher than the odds of its backup disappearing because of a bankruptcy filing. For the haplessly unprotected, services like these are definitely worth a try. Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
Eye Catching: How New Media Are Racing to Become the Mass Media;
In Terms of the Audience, Size Matters. But How Big? And by Whose Measure?
body: Call it the case of the five million missing surfers. Last summer, Alta Vista, an Internet search service, was frustrated that competitors like Yahoo and Excite were attracting all the attention in the media. After all, Alta Vista's computers were recording 10 million different visitors a month, a number the company thought should rank it right up there with the other leading World Wide Web search services. So when a new ratings company called Relevant Knowledge announced that it would measure traffic at Web sites by employing a methodology similar to the one that Nielsen Media Research uses to rate television audiences, Alta Vista thought it would finally get some respect. But when Relevant Knowledge published its first monthly ratings last September, Alta Vista was distressed to learn that its site was credited with attracting only five million visitors. Alta Vista dispatched top executives to meet with the upstart rating company at its headquarters in Atlanta to discuss the disparity -- to no avail. It eventually created a new full-time job, director of rating services relationships. But Relevant Knowledge stuck by its numbers. So did Alta Vista. And the standoff continues, with the data gap steadily widening. In March, Relevant Knowledge said that 7.4 million visited Alta Vista. But Alta Vista itself counted 21 million users. The dispute and myriad others like it demonstrate how contentious the Web audience-measurement business has become. And no wonder: big advertisers, like Microsoft and Intel, have already started to funnel most of their money to the handful of Web sites that various ratings services say reach the widest range of users. Jupiter Communications, a research firm in newyork, estimates that the Web sites rated in the top 10 -- which, by Jupiter's reckoning, include Yahoo, Netscape Communications and America Online's AOL.com, -- take in 52 percent of the ad dollars. At the same time, though, many experts say that a prime-time television-style ratings race is misplaced because the Internet should be seen less as a conventional mass medium and more as a way to direct ads to a narrowly defined group of likely buyers. Meanwhile, because no Web ratings service has yet emerged as the industry standard-bearer, disputes about measurement methods give the various services ground for distinguishing themselves from the competitors. The main contenders include companies that extrapolate overall Web usage from the viewing habits of a cross section of people chosen to represent the larger universe of Web users -- a la the television households selected by Nielsen. These contenders include Relevant Knowledge, Media Metrix, Net Ratings and, soon, Nielsen itself. But there are other measuring methods, including the sites' own records of how many pages are being viewed. These records are audited by companies like the Internet Profiles Corporation, known as I/Pro, which was one of the first entrants into the Web measurement race. And then there are surveys that simply ask people to remember their own surfing habits, such as one offered by @Plan. What all these approaches share is their claim that they can break down their ratings by various demographic and life-style categories, allowing purveyors of grunge rock, say, or denture cream, to find the best sites for advertising their products. Many advertisers want to evaluate Web viewership using the same measures they use for other media: "Reach," meaning the number of individuals who visit a site or watch a program, and "frequency," or the number of times they come back in a month. "Once you get reach and frequency you can decide whether to take dollars from print or radio and move it to the Web," said Craig Gugel, the vice president for research at Organic, a leading agency specializing in the creation and placement of Internet ads. Unfortunately, he said, all of the services have their weaknesses. "Relevant Knowledge has a more rigorous method, but Media Metrix has a larger sample," he said. "The jury is still out on which is better." In Alta Vista's view, Relevant Knowledge undercounts people who use the Web from their offices, and it does not even measure use in schools, libraries and -- most important in Alta Vista's view -- by people outside the unitedstates. "We are far larger than where we are perceived in the ratings war, and we have to break through," said Robert E. Hult, the vice president and general manager of Alta Vista, a unit of the Digital Equipment Corporation. "If they say we have 8 million users when we know we have 18 million, that needs a little more than a microscopic footnote." Relevant Knowledge, for its part, says its reports are clear about what the service does and does not measure. "Nielsen doesn't put meters on TV's in sports bars and hotels," Jeff Levy, the company's chief executive, said. "We don't track cybercafes, computer labs and some office computers." In some ways, the plethora of disparate data suits the site purveyors because it gives everyone something to boast about. Two weeks ago, for example, MSNBC, which is owned by Microsoft and the NBC unit of General Electric issued a press release boasting that it was the top-rated news site. And indeed, Media Metrix estimates that 4.8 percent of the Web audience, or 1.9 million people, looked at MSNBC in March, beating CNN's 3.3 percent share, which is equivalent to 1.3 million people. Relevant Knowledge, however, puts CNN ahead with an 8 percent share, which it figures is equivalent to 4.2 million users. MSNBC trails with a 6 percent share for 3.3 million users, according to Relevant Knowledge. The stakes are higher than just advertising revenues because ratings are as important to Wall Street these days as they are to Madison Avenue, and Digital Equipment has considered spinning off Alta Vista as a public company. (Compaq Computer, now in the process of acquiring Digital Equipment, has not said whether it will keep or sell Alta Vista.) "Size does matter," Mr. Hult said. "The value of your enterprise is closely tied to how you are doing in the battle for eyeballs." But counting eyeballs does not tell much about who the users are, what their other interests are or how much money they have to spend on the things that advertisers want to sell. For that information, many in the industry see the best hope in so-called metering programs, which track all the sites that a representative group of users visit. Instead of trying to monitor everyone on the Web, the metered services track the Web activities of a supposedly representative sampling of people who have agreed to participate. Media Metrix, credited as the original developer of Web metering, started publishing its data two years ago and had the field to itself until last fall when two former lawyers at Turner Broadcasting started Relevant Knowledge. Net Ratings, a spinoff from Hitachi, began to publish data this year. And Nielsen itself will start its Web metering system this summer. One difficulty with most of the metering systems is that they require users to install software on their computers, and in some cases to upgrade their Web browsers to more recent versions. Critics say that this requirement might scare off some of the less technically adept survey subjects and thus might skew the ratings. "It's shocking that some services ask people to change their Internet software," said Scott C. McDonald, director of research for Time Warner, which owns CNN. "The first thing you learn about research is that you don't set up a methodology that interferes with what you are supposed to be measuring." Another problem is that currently only Media Metrix can monitor all of a user's activities while logged on to America Online, the nation's largest Internet service provider and the path that millions of home PC users follow onto the Internet. But far and away the biggest gap right now for Internet measurement is how to track use in offices. Since most companies have much faster Internet connections than people have in their homes, many users find that their offices are the best place to surf. For that reason, Media Metrix and Relevant Knowledge want to install their meter programs on office computers, but this is proving to be difficult. Corporations are wary of having unauthorized software on their networks, and they also worry about the privacy of their workers and the security of trade secrets. One way around this problem is not to use meters at all. Another start-up company, @Plan, uses a methodology modeled after the surveys that measure magazine readership by asking people which publications they have read in the last month. Every quarter, it finds 10,000 people to fill out a 45-minute survey about both their Web viewing and their spending habits. People are asked to include Internet sites, whether they use them at home or at work. "We considered building a meter, but we found we could not adequately get a random sample in a work setting," said Mark K. Wright, chief executive of @Plan. "Only one-third of active Web users in the unitedstates exclusively use the Internet at home. You have to measure the whole pie." But others question whether Internet users remember all the places they visit as they click from one site to the next. The @Plan approach, critics say, disproportionately overstates the audience of the biggest, most popular sites with the most well-known names. Mr. Wright counters that such casual surfing is actually minimal. "People have 10 to 15 sites they gravitate toward, and they go to them again and again," he said. Moreover he argues that gross ratings are much less important on the Internet than they are for, say, television, and that @Plan's main value is helping advertisers place ads at sites frequented by their potential customers. "If you want to reach the mass market of people 25 to 44, you are absolutely wasting your money on the Web," he said. "It is a 'targetcast' medium, not a broadcast medium. So you can find people with incomes over $100,000 who are interested in investing in hedge funds." Ultimately, advertisers and Web site promoters say they hope that over time better measurements will emerge. Until then, the case of the five million missing surfers, and many others like it, will probably remain unsolved. Graphic   Chart: "Whose Count Counts?" When it comes to ranking the most popular Web sites, two of the leading audience measurement services see things differently. Here are their top 10 rankings for March. title:
Eye Catching: How New Media Are Racing to Become the Mass Media;
The Search Services Want Your Eyes to Find No Reason to Wander
body: Seek and ye shall find? Of all the searches conducted on the World Wide Web in the last three years, perhaps the most bewildering has been the quest for a profitable business model. But now, a consensus is emerging that the long-elusive money may be found in the search itself. Or at least in building services around Web searching. Led by Yahoo, the top site that people use to find information on the Internet, the search services are among the most popular places on the Web, attracting millions of visitors a day. The precise numbers may be subject to dispute, but the audiences are clearly large enough to stir serious interest in advertisers and on-line retailers. Among the most popular Web sites, in other words, the new media are becoming mass media. And suddenly, counting eyeballs really counts. That is why Excite, the No. 2 search service, went seeking an even larger Web viewership last week by agreeing to pay at least $70 million for the right to sell ads on Netscape Com munications' popular and newly expanded search site. It is why even the on-line network leader, America Online, as well as Microsoft, are overhauling and expanding their Web sites. It is why several big conventional mass media companies -- including Walt Disney and Time Warner -- are said to be looking to buy one of the search sites or build their own. And of course, it is all those consumer eyes that have driven Wall Street to value the stock of Yahoo, Excite and the other two publicly traded search companies -- Infoseek and Lycos -- at a total of $9 billion. But to capitalize on their current popularity, the search companies know they need to be much more than reference librarians. Rather than greeting their customers and then cheerfully sending them off to browse the Web unattended, the search companies want to keep their visitors and their lucrative eyeballs from wandering away -- much as America Online keeps its subscribers primarily confined to its own ad-supported environment. So the search sites have been adding other services, like email, chat rooms, news, sports scores and classified advertising. To build brand loyalty, they offer visitors the opportunity to customize the opening page to present the news topics, sports scores and stock quotes they want to see every day. Rather than "search engines," as Yahoo and the others were originally known, these companies are redefining themselves as audience-aggregating "portals" to the Web. So far, the approach seems to be working. Visitors to Yahoo click on more than 95 million mostly ad-supported pages each day. By some counts, more than 30 million households in the unitedstates surf Yahoo each month, spending a total of 503 million hours at the site. Meanwhile, Excite, Lycos and Infoseek are seen in more than 10 million homes and millions more offices in the unitedstates and abroad. And compared with conventional mass media companies, the potential of these search sites to provide extra service to advertisers is enormous. For one, they accumulate large amounts of data about their users that can enable advertisers to aim messages at the most likely buyers. But even better, the searches that people perform give valuable clues as to what they may be in the market for. An American who looks up information on Paris, say, is a good bet to be in the market for an airline ticket -- which could be bought on line. "This is the first medium that can have an important amount of impact on a whole variety of different consumer purchasing decisions," said Scott Heiferman, the chief executive of I-Traffic, a consulting firm that serves Internet advertisers. "That's big." It is so big, in fact, that besides Disney and Time Warner, the other media giants considering the portal business include General Electric and CBS, Internet executives say. "None of the top 10 Web sites is owned by any of the big media companies," said George Bell, the chief executive of Excite. "They've realized this isn't a fad and they have to be here." Excite is one of the search companies that has held wary discussions about selling part or possibly even all of itself to a big media player. In addition to a huge return for their initial investors, such deals could provide the search companies with additional content, promotion and well-known brand names. A portal service from Disney, for example, could be tightly intertwined with its movies, theme parks, ABC news and ESPN sports coverage. "It's highly likely that we do something with a partner," said Halsey Minor, the chairman of Cnet, a computer news service that introduced a still-small portal service called Snap last fall. "It would allow us to build Snap into a very large brand." Yet the record of the media conglomerates is hardly a reassuring one. One of the oldest of the media Web sites, Time Warner's Pathfinder service -- which draws content from all the company's news and entertainment brands -- trails far behind the ratings leaders. And for companies unaccustomed to the gravity-free environment of the Internet, the probable price tag of any of these money-losing search companies might seem ridiculously high. Yahoo alone has a stock-market value of $6 billion. "There is not enough earnings in any of these companies to get a deal past a committee," said Keith Benjamin, the Internet stock analyst at BancAmerica Robertson Stephens, who predicts that media companies will merely window shop without stopping to buy. A company like General Electric, which is a partner with Microsoft in the MSNBC cable channel and has various Web ventures through its NBC television network and stations, could easily build its own Web portal, of course. (The $10 million that Cnet spent to start Snap would be petty cash to G.E.) But running such operations is deceptively difficult, Mr. Bell of Excite said. "People look at us and say, 'You were put together from dust,' which we were," Mr. Bell said. "But now we're harder to copy than people think." Both Yahoo and Excite, he pointed out, have more than 500 employees. Any big media company, moreover, will have to make a big bet about how much momentum these young companies have in the market -- whether as competitors or potential partners. "The big question is whether people will have one main window to the world or will they use multiple portals?" Mr. Heiferman said. The research so far shows that many surfers use several search services, even though Yahoo is the one that is used most often by the most people. Without clear brand identities, it is unclear whether any of these sites will be sufficiently "sticky," to use the portal companies' term for the ability to retain viewers. Eventually the services will develop different personalities, Mr. Minor predicts. "But now the market is growing so quickly, we are all copying each other and not thinking about differentiation." Graphic   Photos (Dale O'Dell/The Stock Market)(pg. D1)  Chart: "Wider Web Visions" Seeing broader business opportunities, operators of some of the most popular sites on the World Wide Web are expanding the sites into "portals" -- Web entry points that establish audiences large enough to attract advertisers, retailers and other information providers. Because the portals usually do not create their own information, content acquisitions and partnerships are key.  SERVICE: YAHOO VISION: THE LEADER With the most-visited Web site, Yahoo was the first to move beyond a Web-searching service by adding email, news, stock quotes, retailing and the like. "My Yahoo" option, which lets users customize their own opening page, is meant to cultivate a loyal, repeat clientele. MAIN DEALS: Acquired Four11, an email service and provider of on-line telephone and address directories KEY PARTNERS: MCI, which provides network access for Yahoo Online; Geocities, which acts as host to 1.7 million Web sites  SERVICE: EXCITE VISION: CHANNEL SURFING Typically ranked as the No. 2 search company, Excite was an early adopter of the TV-channel metaphor for organizing information that now includes news, bulletin boards and chat rooms. Offers a personalized opening page, like "My Yahoo." MAIN DEALS: Acquired Classified 2000, a classified ad company; Match Logic, a marketing and advertising company, and Netbot, which makes software for finding and buying products on line. KEY PARTNERS: Netscape, for which Excite will provide search services; AT&T, for joint marketing of telephone and Internet access services; Intuit, which holds a stake in Excite and provides on-line financial information.  SERVICE: LYCOS VISION: SOUND SEARCH The first Web-search company to go public, Lycos advertises itself as "Your Personal Internet Guide" and is the only site with a search function for pictures and sounds. MAIN DEALS: Acquired Wise Wire, whose technology organizes and ranks the results of Web searches, and Tripod, a Web community popular with 18-to 34-year-olds. KEY PARTNERS: Globecomm, for email, and Planet All, for keeping track of friends and acquaintances on line.  SERVICE: INFOSEEK VISION: OVERHAULED With an acclaimed search technology but previously no clear strategy, Infoseek has been revamped into a channels-based service by Harry Motro, former head of CNN's popular site. MAIN DEALS: Acquired Web Chat Broadcasting System, a community of home pages and chat rooms. KEY PARTNERS: Offers search on dozens of corporate internal networks and other public Web sites.  SERVICE: SNAP! VISION: LESS IS MORE With Snap, the on-line technology news service Cnet has expanded into a broad-based Web-searching service and content provider. Snap's less-is-more approach to searches promises fewer, more relevant results. MAIN DEALS: Lined up agreements with big information providers for "showcase portal" positions on its 13 channels, including CNN Interactive for news and CBS Sportsline in sports. KEY PARTNERS: Internet service providers seeking to compete more fully with America Online, including AT&T, MCI, Sprint, Bell Atlantic and BellSouth.  SERVICE: NETSCAPE NETCENTER VISION: CROWD CONTROL Netscape is looking to convert its 70 million browser-software users into a portal crowd. MAIN DEALS: Excite agreed to pay $70 million for the privilege of providing search services on Netcenter. KEY PARTNERS: USA.Net for free email service; Bell Canada for integrated email, telephone and fax services. (pg. D5)

title: Support Grows For Faster Modem Speeds
body: Lending international support to an American effort to give consumers high-speed access to cyberspace, the largest foreign telecommunications companies have agreed to join an industry group to work on ways to transmit huge volumes of information over standard telephone wires. The group intends to announce today the membership of British Telecommunications, Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone and Singapore Telecommunications, according to people involved with the organization, known as the Universal ADSL Working Group. ADSL stands for asymmetric digital subscriber line, a technology that the group said could allow consumers to link their personal computers to the Internet at speeds 30 times as fast as those possible with the most advanced modems generally available today. Compaq Computer, the Intel Corporation and the Microsoft Corporation, three titans of the personal computer world, announced the group's formation in January along with the nation's six largest local telephone companies. The group is trying to make modems based on ADSL technology available to the general public by the end of the year. The support of the overseas phone giants promises to strongly increase the group's prospects of developing a global standard for the phone-line technology. Many variants of the system have been invented, but the lack of a single standard has held back deployment by telephone companies, which are reluctant to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in network equipment that could prove incompatible with other companies' systems. For the ADSL group, the foreign carriers' support should make it easier to win the support of the International Telecommunications Union, which coordinates global technical standards. The group is hoping to have the I.T.U.'s approval by the fall. Within the unitedstates, the support of the foreign carriers also gives American telecommunications companies new leverage in their battle with the cable television industry to provide the next generation of technology for connecting consumers to the Internet. Many technology and media executives believe there is a vast market waiting to be tapped by companies that can deliver lightning-quick Internet access to the nation's households. Currently, even the fastest modems commonly available often make browsing the Net a frustratingly slow experience. The nation's local telephone companies predict many consumers would be willing to spend up to $50 a month for an Internet connection that can provide in seconds what takes today's modems minutes to deliver. As a bonus, the version of ADSL technology being developed by the working group could provide a continuous Internet link and normal telephone service over the same line, allowing people to simultaneously talk on the phone and surf the World Wide Web. Dozens of telecommunications equipment companies are involved in the working group, including Aware Inc., a small company based in Massachusetts, which has contributed technology that could enable a consumer to set up an ADSL modem without the help of a trained technician. Last week Lucent Technologies Inc., the giant communications equipment maker spun off from the AT&T Corporation in 1996, announced that it had licensed Aware's technology for use in Lucent's microchips intended for ADSL modems. Deploying such subscriber line systems quickly and in a user-friendly way is imperative for most big local phone companies because the cable industry has taken an early lead in delivering high-capacity, or broadband, access to cyberspace. Analysts estimate that about 200,000 homes in the unitedstates now use modems connected to a cable television network rather than telephone wires. The number of homes now using various ADSL technologies is a mere fraction of that. Helping the deployment of high-speed data systems is also critical to the personal computer industry. Put simply, if most homes remain connected to the Internet by today's relatively thin pipelines, there is less of a reason for consumers to buy faster computers and more powerful software. Microsoft, though, has been covering its bets on network-access technology. The company is one of the main forces behind the ADSL group, but Microsoft has also invested $1 billion in the Comcast Corporation, one of the nation's largest cable television companies.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: DIGITAL COMMERCE;
Customer fears and risks have yet to be worked out with airline electronic tickets.
body: WITH its razor-thin profit margins and endless battles for customer loyalty, the $102 billion commercial airline business is one of the few industries that stand to benefit, or to lose, much from a successful transition to electronic commerce. But commercial air carriers, though much praised for their early embrace of information technology for flight, fare and maintenance schedules, are a few yards short of the gate when it comes to their first big step toward on-line commerce: electronic ticketing, or E-tickets. Most major airlines today issue electronic tickets, which are paperless tickets that exist only in the memory of an airline's computer system. The idea is that instead of having to pick up a paper ticket or wait for it to be delivered, E-ticket travelers simply arrive at the airport with a receipt, picture identification and, when necessary, the credit card with which they purchased the ticket. Since the ticket is stored in the computer system, there is said to be no such thing as losing a ticket, and itinerary changes can be quickly accomplished by telephone without requiring fresh tickets to be delivered. The system has rapidly grown in popularity since it was introduced by United Airlines in the mid-1990's. Continental Airlines says that electronic tickets represent almost 40 percent of the tickets it issues today; at United they account for 52 percent. But despite their growing popularity, business customers, in particular, are wary. The Internet marketing expert Don Peppers, who lives and breathes electronic commerce and travels nearly full time, says that E-tickets are too ethereal for his taste. "I'm worried that I'm going to forget I have E-tickets and just keep buying new ones, and that I won't get a refund," Mr. Peppers said. "And I'm afraid I won't be able to prove that I have a ticket when I want to change my plans. The one time I used an E-ticket, there was a dispute and I almost lost my seat because of it." Mark Benerofe, another Internet consultant who constantly travels between the East and West Coasts, does use E-tickets. But he says he is aware that they eliminate critical freedom for business travelers who fly on unrestricted tickets. "A paper ticket is like holding a title to cash," he said. "If I'm holding a full-fare paper ticket for Delta and something happens and I need to fly United, I can walk right up to the United desk and my Delta ticket is valid. My E-ticket is not cash. My E-ticket receipt is just a glorified confirmation number." Susan Fullman, who as director of distribution planning is in charge of deploying the electronic-ticketing system for United Airlines, agrees that this lack of reciprocity -- she calls it "interlining" -- is one of two big holes in the E-ticket system. "Today, if you wanted to go to another carrier and claim your ticket, you'd have to go to the United desk first and have them generate a paper ticket for you," she said. "We're working on solving that." The other hole, she said, is that customers are not adequately notified about the electronic tickets they may have outstanding in the computer system and for how long those tickets are valid. "We're very aware of the problem, and we're working on a product for the business corporate community that would give them complete disclosure on that," she said. United has no immediate plans to provide such a disclosure service for ordinary customers. And not every airline sees disclosure as a problem. Steve Cossette, staff vice president for distribution planning at Continental, said that his company did not send notifications of outstanding E-tickets to its customers and did not inform them when those tickets were expiring. But he added: "Nor do people who buy theater tickets, or people who don't make it to the football game, expect us to find them and refund their money. If you don't use the tickets, we don't seek you out. We're not in the credit business. We're in the airline business." Such practices may be hostile to customers, but they are not illegal. Although lawyers at the Federal Trade Commission expressed surprise that electronic-ticket refunds were not automatically issued before the tickets expired, they said that the Fair Credit Billing Act required only credit card companies and department stores to refund credit balances automatically. Whatever the legal requirements, it is interesting to contrast Continental's attitude to, for example, that of Amazon.com, the pioneering Internet bookseller. Amazon's on-line account maintenance system provides its customers with secure, password-protected access to everything about their account at any time. Aside from ordering books, they can view their entire purchase history, track orders, customize virtually everything about the system to their own tastes, and reach the bookseller by email at almost every turn, for any reason. Though such information flow to and from customers would paralyze most old-line companies, Ms. Fullman, who uses Amazon as an example of on-line customer service, would be delighted if her biggest problem were how to handle high-volume email. Instead, she says, she faces the arduous task of trying to glue together United's many data base systems in a way that is both useful to customers and secure for transactions. David Risher, Amazon's senior vice president for product development, said: "Good on-line customer service requires thought, and it is hard -- and it's probably easier if you're starting from scratch than if you're retrofitting. Unlike the airlines, we didn't build Amazon for 150 agents or 150 stores; we built it specifically for the individual customer, and that works to our advantage." Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title: TV Listings Stir Windows 98 Dispute
body: Buyers of new personal computers equipped with Windows 98, Microsoft's updated operating system, are to get something thrown in free of charge: an electronic program guide that tells what is on television. Microsoft sees this as an attractive new service -- and, perhaps, a means to broaden its customer base. But a small, privately held Pennsylvania company that sells a similar piece of software already installed on several hundred thousand personal computers is crying foul. "I can make a case, at least, for including Internet Explorer as a part of the operating system," argued Mike Jeffress, a vice president of Electronic TV Host, referring to the Web-browser software also included in Windows 98. "But I am hard pressed to make a case that including a television program guide is integral to the operating system of a personal computer." Mr. Jeffress's concern is this: Why would anyone pay to buy software when Microsoft is offering a similar product free? It is a familiar complaint, heard from smaller companies every time Microsoft issues a new or updated operating system that includes extra features. And while Mr. Jeffress's company is smaller, and the software less well known, in some ways his argument is similar to the one offered by the Netscape Corporation, the leading producer of World Wide Web browsers. Microsoft's inclusion of its own Web browser in the previous version of Windows, Windows 95, is already the subject of Federal antitrust litigation. And many legal experts are now waiting to see if the Justice Department seeks to expand that case to include Windows 98. Hank Vigil, a senior director for Microsoft, contended that an electronic program guide -- Microsoft's, or Electronic TV Host's -- is hardly a unique product. Many companies offer them in a variety of products, and "the ability to make an electronic program guide and offer it is basically something anyone can do," he said. Microsoft got into the program-guide business last year, when the company paid $425 million for WebTV Networks, the manufacturer of a set-top box that allows browsing of the Web on a television set. Sales of the box were slow, though, and one complaint was that the service made no attempt to integrate Web content with television programming. Last fall, WebTV began selling a second-generation set-top box, and it included a TV tuner that enabled the box to actually control the television, rather than simply sending a signal to the television, as the old system did. With that, the company began integrating Web and television services. Some television shows included links to related Web sites, and if viewers clicked on one of those, they would go to the Web site while the television show appeared in a small window. The new box also offered an electronic program guide -- an on-screen grid like those provided by direct-broadcast satellite services and some high-end television sets. The grid, similar in appearance to newspaper TV listings, lists the shows for up to a week. Updated schedules are downloaded weekly from information that is broadcast by another company in an unused portion of television signals called the vertical blanking interval. With the program guide, viewers need only click on the appropriate box to view the show -- or set a videocassette recorder to record it. For Windows 98, Microsoft simply lifted the program guide out of the WebTV package and included it as a free, integrated part of the operating system. The rest of the WebTV package featuring Internet access was left behind because personal computers "already have a complete Internet Explorer environment for the Internet services," explained Craig Mundie, a senior vice president for Microsoft. To use the electronic program guide, however, owners will have to install a tuner card that allows a personal computer to serve as a television receiver. The company chose to bundle the WebTV program guide with Windows 98 "primarily for branding purposes," Mr. Vigil said, adding, "We want to create a common consumer experience associated with our brand, whether it's a PC or a set-top box."
