title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY: CORRESPONDENT'S REPORT;
Web Travel Shopping: The Surf Is Rising
body: TRAVELERS booked $827 million worth of reservations over the Internet last year, a mere pittance for the travel and tourism industries, which measure their size in the hundreds of billions of dollars. But all trends need to start somewhere, and if recent forecasts hold true, the number of people using computers to make travel arrangements will grow quickly. A recent study commissioned by the Travel Industry Association of America estimated that by 2002, on-line bookings of air fares, hotel rooms, rental cars and vacation packages will jump more than tenfold, to $8.9 billion, from $827 million last year. To be sure, five-year predictions can be as reliable as long-term weather forecasts. But in the on-line travel business, forecasts have, if anything, proved to be consistently conservative. "I've underpredicted every time," said John R. Samuel, director of interactive marketing for American Airlines. He offered as an example that he was surprised when American Airlines signed up 20,000 people for fare-sale information sent via electronic mail. The service now has 1.5 million subscribers. Experts said there are a number of reasons on-line travel will grow so quickly. One is obvious: More people will own computers. The Travel Industry Association study predicts that by 2002, 57 million households in the unitedstates will be on line, up from 15.2 million in 1996. Modems and transmission lines will become faster, reducing waiting time for information. But another factor is that travel sites on the World Wide Web do offer things that people cannot get from a brochure, catalogue or phone call. Travel-related Web services, for example, typically allow people to check fares themselves, an attractive feature for those who want to insure that the fares quoted by a travel agent are indeed the lowest available. And for anyone planning a vacation, the Internet holds the promise of virtual tours of a hotel or resort. "This medium can supply consumers with unprecedented amounts of travel information and images, while simultaneously serving as an electronic storefront," said William S. Norman, president of the Travel Industry Association. Many airlines and other travel companies hope that travelers will buy directly from their electronic storefronts, so that they can pocket the money they would otherwise pay out as commissions to travel agents. Many people have doubts about booking a trip on line. Worries about the security of Internet credit card transactions may be generally unfounded, but many users remain reluctant. "Fear of credit-card transactions is still, surprisingly, the No. 1 issue that comes up in focus groups," said Terrell Jones, chief information officer for the Sabre Group, which operates Travelocity, a popular site with more than $100 million in bookings last year (www.travelocity.com). Experts also said that the use of the Internet would grow in tandem with the spread of faster transmission lines. This is crucial for travel sites, they said, because users apparently expect quicker answers from their computers than when they are waiting on the phone for answers from a travel agent. As it is, many travel sites find that their busiest times are during work hours, which suggests people are taking advantage of faster computers and transmission lines at their workplaces. "There's a different expectation with a computer," Mr. Samuel said. "If it doesn't come back right away, it seems slow." Many travelers are still advised that for all the advantages of a Web site, there are clear shortcomings. "The sites are useful and interesting," PC Magazine reported last fall after surveying travel sites. "But a traditional travel agent handles most arrangements more efficiently. Also, an agent won't forget you after finding a fare." Still, given the trajectory of the on-line travel industry so far, its expansion seems likely to continue, particularly if it can provide new services that benefit both travelers and airlines, such as last-minute sales for weekend travel that airlines send out by electronic mail. The idea evolved at American Airlines, which for a time advertised low fares for weekends -- when many planes are flying with a lot of empty seats -- on a local cable station outside Dallas. The airline found that people watched at home, then told colleagues at work about the fares by email. The airline decided it could do the same. Another new service called Priceline (www.priceline.com) has been advertising heavily that it essentially offers travelers the chance to post the fares they want to pay for trips and see if the airlines are willing to issue tickets at those prices. Many large domestic airlines said they have no ties to Priceline, contradicting what the company has said. Nevertheless, by having the customer attempt to dictate terms, Priceline appears to be offering a new twist on traditional ways of buying air fares. Over time, travel services on the Internet will find more fans, particularly among the growing population of retirees whose schedules allow them more spontaneous trips, said Julius Maldutis, an airlines analyst for Salomon Smith Barney. "It is remaking the travel habits of the American people," he said. "I think it's going to have an explosive impact on travel in the years ahead." title:
AUTOS ON FRIDAY/Technology;
Downshift, Download: Commuting as Work
body: CARS used to provide a refuge from the corporate office, a place to unwind on the way home. No one knew just where you were, and no one could reach you. Then came cellular telephones, and you could be tracked down as though you were at your desk. The laptop computer and in-car fax machine made it possible for Type A overachievers to work in traffic jams. Soon, if a few new concept vehicles are any indication, you will be receiving and answering email messages, even surfing the Internet, while commuting. "Our research shows that customers want the time in their vehicles to be productive, entertaining, and most of all safe," Charles W. Szuluk, president of Ford's Visteon auto parts subsidiary, said as he demonstrated his company's Internet-capable multimedia system at the Society of Automotive Engineers International Congress and Exposition here in February. Safety is no small concern, given growing evidence that electronic devices like cellular phones are distracting drivers and increasing their odds of being in an accident. A year ago, when Mercedes-Benz demonstrated the first car with Internet access, it had a computer screen in the center of the dashboard, but did not yet have the voice-recognition technology that is now viewed as necessary from a safety standpoint. The Mercedes also has multimedia screens for the back seat, embedded in the back of the front head restraints. The screens are interactive, providing navigation, entertainment and office applications, like electronic calendars and bookmarks for Internet services. Ford, Nissan and General Motors have also shown vehicles with Internet access, though none have announced when they might have similar systems on the market. The Infiniti division of Nissan has been showing its I30 Executive Luxury Special Edition, or Else, a concept car designed to showcase advanced mobile office technology. It has an in-dash computer called Auto PC, made by the Clarion Corporation of America, the audio manufacturer, and powered by Microsoft's Windows CE software, an operating system for consumer electronics devices. By voice, the driver can change the music, receive email alerts, dial a cell phone, get directions to a destination, find a restaurant or obtain traffic and weather conditions. At Ford, Visteon has demonstrated a multimedia vehicle that it says is "targeted to be the first production-ready personal computer on the road." Called Ices (for information, communication, entertainment and safety/security), it extends to cars the electronics of the home and office. Powered by Intel microprocessors and also using Windows CE, it allows a driver to use voice commands to retrieve and respond to email, voicemail and pages. From the Internet, a driver can obtain sports scores, news headlines, weather reports and up-to-the-minute financial information, including the prices of particular stocks. The climate and stereo controls can also be set by voice. The driver can further customize the system by installing more software. The General Motors Corporation recently showed two vehicles with Internet access at an engineering trade show in Detroit. Its Network Vehicle -- developed by Delphi Automotive Systems, I.B.M., Sun Microsystems and Netscape Communications -- has Internet access that allows the driver to listen to email messages or conduct Web searches using voice commands. Like Ford's system, it can provide the driver with access to sports scores, news headlines, weather information and stock prices. The Network Vehicle is outfitted with other high-tech gadgets including DirecTV and DirecPC from Hughes Electronics, which permit the downloading of television and data signals from satellites through a flat antenna embedded in the car's roof. Passengers can use three terminals in the car to make an Internet connection, watch high-resolution TV or play computer games. G.M. also has a Saab 9-5 called the Personal Productivity Vehicle that is outfitted with similar high-tech features. Developed by Dephi Delco Electronics with Saab, the special 9-5 has Internet capability and advanced mobile office technology. Graphic   Photos: Infiniti's Else concept car has fingertip controls for the voice-activated computer that reads email messages to travelers. At right, buttons on the Else's overhead console provide links to the Infiniti Response Center, which can send assistance in an emergency.

title: 13 States Plan Antitrust Move Over Microsoft
body: Attorneys General from 13 states, apparently intent on blocking the imminent release of the Microsoft Corporation's next version of its Windows software, are in the final stages of preparing a joint antitrust action against the company. "The decision on our action is imminent, and in my opinion some action is likely," said Richard Blumenthal, the Connecticut Attorney General. "I think it will be in the next couple of weeks." While several of the state officials said in interviews that they would rather act in conjunction with the unitedstates Justice Department, which has been pressing its own antitrust suit against Microsoft, they are prepared to proceed without the Justice Department. The states intend to act quickly because Microsoft plans to begin shipping the next version of the software, the Windows 98 operating system, to personal computer makers in mid-May and to release it to the public by late June. The Attorneys General refused to say exactly what their suit would charge because the matter is still under investigation. But interviews with officials in all 13 states, as well as 3 other states that are monitoring the discussions, showed a common interest in preventing Microsoft from using its dominance in personal-computer operating systems to promote the sale of other software products. And the states' concerns go beyond the integration into Windows 98 of Microsoft's Internet Explorer software for navigating the World Wide Web -- which has been one of the issues for the Justice Department. Microsoft's operating system software provides the basic instructions on nearly 9 of every 10 PC's sold. And these days, the PC operating system is not only the control mechanism for an individual computer but also a launching pad into the expanding world of Internet commerce. And the states worry that Microsoft could use its industry dominance to dictate which other companies have access to it. "My concern is that there is, in fact, very active competition, the possibility of entry by other companies, in this very important area," said Charlie Condon, the Attorney General in South Carolina. A senior aide in another Attorney General's office said "the problem we want to address is the exclusionary activities that involve tying and leveraging Microsoft's monopolistic position in operating systems to unreasonably restrain competition in other areas." Word that the states were preparing an antitrust action against Microsoft has emerged in a number of news reports the last few weeks. On Friday, PC Week Online, an on-line industry news service, said a number of states would move to block the shipment of Windows 98. A Microsoft spokesman, Mark Murray, said today: "At this point the states haven't given us any specific information on their concerns. I would hope they would tell us before there is any legal action, so we can respond and try to resolve their concerns." With Windows 98, Microsoft significantly expands its practice of including other software products as part of the program. For example, in addition to Internet Explorer -- which competes head-on with the Netscape Corporation's Navigator Web-browser software -- Microsoft has embedded its Web TV software in Windows 98. Web TV is a Microsoft-owned service that enables people watching television to surf the Web, too. As part of its licensing arrangements for Windows 98, Microsoft is said to be planning to offer PC makers discounts on the software if they agree to install circuitry into the computers that would enable them to receive television signals. Microsoft has long said that its practice of integrating other software products is key to the company's future. After last week's Federal appeals court hearing on the Justice Department suit, William H. Neukom, Microsoft's vice president for law and corporate affairs, said: "This case involves a fundamental principle for us, the freedom of high-technology companies to continue to innovate on behalf of our customers. Part of innovation has to be integration. We are going to continue to integrate products." Several Attorneys General said it was important to act before Windows 98 went on sale because any lawsuit would become significantly more complicated once computer manufacturers began buying the new program and installing it on customers' machines. Some of them suggested they were acting in part because they were afraid Washington would not act soon enough. A joint suit would probably be filed in Federal court, meaning that any judgment or injunction would have force nationwide. "There are significant advantages to coordinating a Federal-state action," said Attorney General Scott Harshbarger of Massachusetts. "But state attorneys general often have different time frames, and I think as attorneys general we are prepared to move on our own. And we're very close." If the states, or Washington, waited to file suit after the release of Windows 98, "the action then would have to include another large set of defendants, the manufacturers," one Attorney General said, speaking on condition that he not to be quoted by name. Mr. Murray, the Microsoft spokesman, said that blocking the release of Windows 98 "would be costly, disruptive to consumers, destructive to the high-technology industry, and it would undermine the strength and health of the U.S. economy." Told of those comments, Mr. Condon, the South Carolina Attorney General, replied: "That's a valid concern. But if you let it be released, speaking hypothetically, then it's so much harder to put the toothpaste back in the tube." Justice Department officials declined to comment today on the plans of the state Attorneys General.  Though all of the Attorneys General interviewed described a suit as quite likely, none said they had made a final decision to act. In several of the states, officials declined to talk about the case. "We're at a critical stage now; we can't discuss it," said an official in the Illinois Attorney General's office. The other involved states are newyork, Ohio, California, Texas, Wisconsin, Minnesota, West Virginia, Florida and Iowa. The Attorneys General are circulating documents and drafts of the proposed suit among themselves and, they say, finding it surprisingly easy to decide how to proceed. "In the Microsoft task force, it's remarkable how well 13 states are working together," said Tom Miller, Attorney General of Iowa. He is chairman of the Anti-Trust Task Force for the National Association of Attorneys General. "It's amazing how the same concerns popped up all over the country, crossing different party lines and different regions of the country," Mr. Condon said. If the states do file suit, the action would continue a trend in recent years of attorneys general banding together to pursue cases in tobacco, product advertising, telemarketing and other initiatives in consumer protection -- a job that Washington has seldom embraced with the enthusiasm it has for other governmental functions. Of course, there can be political benefits for the state officials, too. All the Attorneys General now involved in the case are elected officials, and many are up for re-election this year. Mr. Harshbarger is running for Governor of Massachusetts. newyork, Texas, Massachusetts and California are described as leaders of the group; each of those states serves as home to large concentrations of high-technology companies whose interests the Attorneys General are trying to protect. But other states, like Iowa and South Carolina, have few of these companies. Most states have anti-trust laws patterned after the Federal law, and many Attorneys General say they are acting on behalf of consumers. As Mr. Miller, the Iowa Attorney General, put it: "We enforce the anti-trust laws to protect consumers. If Microsoft can use its monopoly in operating systems to leverage its way into other areas, then consumers will suffer because of price and quality, and the whole system will suffer from loss of innovation." But there are still other reasons. In South Carolina, for example, Mr. Condon seems interested in protecting the state's economy -- and making history. "We just got a report that unemployment in this state is 2.4 percent," he said. "The economy is booming, and I am certain that a large part of that is new technology. I want it to keep going." But, he added: "I suspect before our lives are over we will look back at this as the time when the ground rules are set for these industries. It could get rough; there's lots at stake here. But this could indeed be one of the most important cases of the next century."

title: It Is for You Defective Day Of Hats, No?
body: THE December opening of Alta Vista's nearly instantaneous translation site on the World Wide Web was one giant step toward the golden vision of everyone around the planet chatting nicely together sans language barriers on the Informationen Autobahn. Web surfers can now quickly get the gist of many foreign Web sites just by clicking a Translate button on Alta Vista or by using one of a number of Web-based translation systems or off-the-shelf programs. The easy availability of translations has helped Web bulletin board fans amuse themselves endlessly by lobbing Christmas carols into Spanish and back and has helped language students cheat on their translation homework. It has also meant more orders for companies doing business internationally. But not so fast. If the world has lots to gain from accessible, accurate and affordable computer translation services, there is plenty to lose from anything less. Just as, to quote Robert Frost, poetry is what is lost in the translation, business (and face) can be lost from bad translations. When run through the Alta Vista computer translator from English to French and back again, "I am a reporter for The newyork Times" becomes "I am a journalist during times of newyork." "She is having a bad hair day" becomes, via Italian, "It is having a defective day of hats." But if you want to grasp the major points of a Web page without learning five years' of Portuguese or hiring a 25-cents-a-word translator, it is a great convenience (babelfish.altavista. digital.com/cgi-bin/translate?). Many Web watchers and translation experts scoff, predicting eternal failure for machine translation, which they believe will never score much above 85 percent accuracy. Rainer Schulte, director of the Center for Translation Studies at the University of Texas at Dallas and the editor of Translation Review, said machine translation was very much in its infancy. Machines are unable to operate well contextually, he said, so they do not have a prayer of translating a word like "culture" properly unless they are told that they are talking to humanists or biologists. "Machine translation, certainly in any area of intellectual pursuit, is pretty much useless," Dr. Schulte said. "We'll never get to the point, at least not in the foreseeable future, where machine translation could translate essays, fiction or nonfiction books. That, I think, is an illusion." At the University of Central Florida, however, a professor of German, Finley M. Taylor, said language instructors were using machine translation to help first-year students gain confidence in their ability to recognize errors. "In doing this, we want to make them sharpen their skills," he said. "It builds up their confidence. They can say: 'This is wrong. I can find mistakes.' " For example, he said, "If you're going from English to Spanish, and you have the word 'party,' and if you're talking about a legal party, any fool ought to know it's not a fiesta." Contrary to what one might expect, concerns about the death of translation as a profession and the demise of language study as an academic discipline appear to have been greatly exaggerated. "Not one translator is ever going to lose their job because of machine translation, not in the foreseeable future," said Teri O'Connell, a machine-translation expert at American Management Systems, a computer systems and consulting company. Machine translation is generally used there for triage, to determine if a foreign document has any value and should be translated by a person, she said. Of course, humans have long been capable of producing doomed translations without the help of machines. Consider Frank Perdue, whose motto "It takes a tough man to make a tender chicken" can turn into "It takes a sexually stimulated man to make a chicken affectionate" in some Spanish translations, according to a response to a letter in the magazine American Demographics in 1995. Professor Taylor does not worry that free access to translation services will dampen a student's desire to learn languages. "It should, if used wisely, be used as a kind of bait to say, Let's learn it better, and learn it faster," he said. But some language teachers have complained that students have occasionally taken advantage of the ready availability of machine translation to get their homework done quickly. "We now write essays in class," said Leslie Z. Morgan, a modern-language professor at Loyola College in Baltimore, who grew sick of seeing French homework from her students that had obviously been written in English, then unceremoniously stuffed through software. Without dipping too far into interieur base-ball, there are several levels of translation via computer: machine translation, done solely by the computer, at the sentence level; machine-assisted translation, in which a human translator cleans up a translation done by a computer, and translation memory, stored phrases and sentences, for boilerplate paragraphs in documents. More advanced computer translation systems approach natural language, where new language rules and idioms are added to the translating system; the more documents translated by the program, the more skilled it becomes. For example, by using Globalink technology, human translators have doubled their productivity in translating articles from the Sao Paolo, Brazil, Gazeta Mercantil because the translation system has allowed for the addition of 12,000 frequently used words and phrases. Gregory Roberts, head of Ramworks, a Web architect group, says that anyone who successfully uses computerized translation gets help from human translators. He reached that conclusion after he tried to create a Web site in Spanish for patrons of Blue Cross/Blue Shield of Florida, only to find that the Spanish spoken most often in Miami isn't simpatico with the Spanish spoken in Spain. "I have heard of successful implementations in extremely specific cases, where you train the computer and here's the vocabulary, 10,000 words, and we'll never go outside those 10,000 words," he said. "Then it does it great." Globalink (www.globalink.com), based in Fairfax, Va., uses natural language translation technology called Barcelona; it has helped clients use Barcelona in Internet chat sites for conversations that are translated nearly instantaneously. For about $1,500 a year, Globalink translates a company's Web site into German, French, Italian, Portuguese and various forms of Spanish. James B. Kantor, president of Eastern Avionics International, which sells electronics for small planes, said the company's international business had increased by about 50 percent since the Web site started using Globalink to speak in various tongues. He estimated that it would cost $100,000 a year to have a human translator keep the sites available multilingually. "This may not be perfect," he said, "but for $1,500, it's the best bargain out there." As with most aspects of life, the key to contentment with machine translation is reduced expectations. The Los Angeles Times will soon offer its Calendar Live entertainment section in Spanish, French and Japanese, using translating technology from Alis Technologies (www.alis.com), based in Montreal. But Harry Chandler, the paper's director of new business development, has realistic expectations. "If you're thinking this will be a human translation that's perfect, we're going to disappoint you," he said. Of the paper's 4.9 million readers, 35 percent count Spanish as their dominant language. Mr. Chandler said there were difficulties with a program that translates everything, like the names of Los Angeles streets, many of which are already in Spanish. And movie titles can be jumbled -- "Titanic" can become "Muy Grande." Alis, which uses a variety of translating systems and some human translators, can avoid most of these problems. In a market where such listings are seldom available in other languages, the multilanguage service will be better than nothing, Mr. Chandler said. Readers will receive "big caveats," he said, warning them to verify information before heading out for the evening. And the translation program will use special rules for specific parts of the entertainment listings to make it more accurate. "If you can get into the 90 percent accurate range, compared to not having it at all, we think it's an advantage," Mr. Chandler said. The Babelfish translator on Alta Vista is named for the universal translator in Douglas Adams's "Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy": a fish that slithers into a person's ear. The program, which is still in an early form and can give different results from one day to the next, will translate as much as an entire Web page or any lump of text. It is the first free, widely available service to translate pieces of text, not just words. "It's extremely fast, and it's good enough to get some value from it," said Louis Monier, technical director of Alta Vista, based in California. "It's not perfect. It's pretty good." Using Systran software (www.systransoft.com), the Alta Vista site fields about 400,000 translation requests daily. The translations are most useful from an unfamiliar to a known language so the reader can fill in the gaps. Writing that has gone through an automated translation program should be labeled accordingly, but such translations can be quite useful. Robin Dow, 25, of Atlanta depended upon her grandmother to communicate with relatives in Fiumedinisi, a small village in Sicily, but her grandmother died in January. Ms. Dow could find no one who spoke or wrote Italian, and only one person in the village could translate, so calling was difficult. A friend told her about the Alta Vista translator, so she used it on a letter she wrote in English and sent via snail mail. "It was perfect for me," she said. "I could never have done it on my own, going through the dictionary." Wei-Tai Kwok, president of DAE Interactive Marketing, said that even if the technology was not yet perfect in all cases, or "really not ready for prime time yet," it was improving rapidly. "Most of the Web is in English now, but only 9 percent of the world's population speaks English as a first language," he said. "If we as American companies want to leverage the global communications power of the Web, we'll want to build multilingual Web sites." But it takes more than the lingua franca to make a Web site work cross-culturally. Design elements as well as words need to express the proper sentiment, from one country to another. In France, a home page is a welcome page, so that little house icon is useless. And the thumbs-up sign used occasionally in American marketing? In Iran, that signifies a different raised finger, said Mr. Kwok, whose company, based in San Francisco, helps businesses build culturally appropriate Web sites. "You can imagine some of the innocent mistakes made: 'Welcome to our site! Thumbs up! We love to see you guys! Thumbs up!' " he said, paraphrasing a site that could offend people in some parts of the world. "Just running the site through a translation program isn't enough."  O, Say . . . What?  Poetry, idiomatic expressions and advertisements often do not fare well with translation software. Here are some examples of translations given by Alta Vista's Babelfish.  THE STAR-SPANGLED BANNER  In English "O say can you see, by the dawn's early light what so proudly we hailed at the twilight's last gleaming." In French Becomes "La parole de O peut vous voir, par la premiere lumiere de l'aube ce que tellement fierement nous avons grele a dernier briller du crepuscule." But Ends Up As "The word of O can see you, by the first light of the paddle what so much proudly we hailed with the last to shine of the twilight."  E-MAIL ANNOUNCEMENT  In English "You have mail!" In German Becomes "Sie haben Post!" But Ends Up As "They have post office!"  M&M'S AD In English "Melts in your mouth, not in your hands." In French Becomes "Fontes dans votre bouche, pas dans des vos mains." But Ends Up As "Pig iron and cast iron in your mouth, not in your hands."  DIGITAL TRANSLATORS Sampling of Web sites  ALTA VISTA'S BABELFISH babelfish.altavista.digital.com/cgi-bin/translate? Provides translations of blocks of text and Web pages.  TRANSLATOR'S HOME COMPANION www.lai.com/lai/companion.html Links to on-line dictionaries and global news services.  TRAVLANG'S TRANSLATING DICTIONARIES dictionaries.travlang.com Features dozens of dictionaries, including German-Latin and Esperanto-Portuguese.  GLOBALINK www.globalink.com Translates between English and Spanish, German, French, Italian and Portuguese.  LOGOS www.logos.it/lang/us/refus.html Says it works for all languages, and specializes in technical areas like user manuals, scientific documents and legal documents. Uses native-speaking engineers and computer programmers.  SOFTWARE PACKAGES  UNIVERSAL TRANSLATOR www.languageforce.com/Products/ut.htm Translates between Engligh and 25 languages, including Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian and Latin. $99; (888) 837-8887.  NEOCOR TECH www.neocor.com/products.htm Offers products for translation between Japanese and English. Typhoon translation software, $595; (800) 693-9283.  EASY TRANSLATOR www.transparent.com Translates Web pages and E-mail to and from Spanish, French or German. $129; (603) 465-2230.  JUST FOR FUN  SOUNDS OF THE WORLD'S ANIMALS www.georgetown.edu/cball/animals/swedish.html Provides translations into numerous languages of the noises animals make. In Afrikaans, for example, bees go "zoem-zoem," while in Korean, they go "boong-boong." A must-see for the globetrotting barnyard enthusiast. Taylor, a professor of German in Florida, said he uses machine translators to teach first-year language students. (Joanne Carole for The newyork Times); Robin Dow used a machine translator to write to relatives in a village in Sicily about the death of her grandmother.(Chuck Rogers for The newyork Times)(pg. G7)

title: Modem 'Lite' Offers Fast Web Access at Low Rates
body: IN the race for a simpler and faster way to connect to the Internet over existing phone lines, a new player has emerged. Northern Telecom, the Ottawa-based company best known for large telephone network equipment, has introduced the 1-Meg Modem. As the name implies, the 1-Meg Modem is a technological step backward, the digital version of "lite" beer. The modem, which started shipping this spring, offers always-connected Internet access at 1 megabit per second -- roughly half the speed of current A.D.S.L. (Asymmetrical Digital Subscriber Line) service -- but at a fraction of the cost.  And at 1 megabit per second, the modem is still 17 times as fast as conventional 56-kilobits-per-second units. John Bourne, vice president for broadband network access at Nortel, as the company is commonly known, predicts that the new modem can provide service for as little as $20 a month. The typical cost of A.D.S.L. is $40 to $80 a month, after installation. The price difference is due to the cost of hooking up the systems. Other systems require special wiring, new equipment and expensive service calls. With Northern Telecom's system, by contrast, customers need to buy only a special modem, which the company says will sell for about $200, and a relatively inexpensive network card. The 1-Meg Modem piggybacks onto existing voice lines, eliminating the need for costly rewiring. Back at the central office, the job is even easier. The phone company replaces the line card linking the customer to its switch with a new model that keeps the old voice traffic flowing while diverting the computer data to a separate network. Nortel began testing the new modem at Northern Illinois University in De Kalb, Ill., in 1996. Michael Oswald, an electrical engineering student, was taken aback by the difference between the 1-Meg and his old, conventional dial-up modem: "I was expecting it to be fast but not this quick. Search engines come up immediately." Using a lower speed also seems to help the 1-Meg Modem overcome problems from aging wires that sometimes defeat A.D.S.L. "We've been able to use it in dorm rooms where the wiring is a patch panel under the sink in the women's washroom," said Walter Czerniak, Northern Illinois University's director of computing and telecommunications. So far, Nortel has signed up two customers for the system, Transwire Communications in newyork and Megsinet in Chicago. "We believe that this is the only seamless high-speed network that's ready today," said Debra Niewald, a spokeswoman for Transwire, which began offering 1-Meg service on a trial basis in a small section of Manhattan in late March. "There's incredible pent-up demand for something like this." Transwire, which declines to reveal its number of subscribers, has initially priced 1-Meg service well above Nortel's projected price. It charges $100 a month for simple access, including modem rental, but expects that prices will fall. But the battle for fast and cheap Internet access is going to get even more confusing. Rockwell has also agreed to make 1-Meg Modems. And several other contenders have emerged. Lucent Technologies has announced a system it calls Wild Wire that will feature 1.5-mbps downloads and not require users to have a network card. Testing begins later this year, but no availability date has been set.

title: On-Line Trail to an Off-Line Killing
body: For nearly a year, Elisa DeCarlo had been logging on to the Internet daily to type messages to an on-line support group about her battle against alcohol. It did not matter that Ms. DeCarlo did not know where most of the 200 or so other members of the group lived, or even their names. All that mattered was that they were there for her, and she for them, in a fight that some days sapped all of her strength and sense of humor. But on a Monday morning, March 23, sitting in her usual bathrobe attire, drinking her usual cup of coffee as she scrolled through the previous day's email, Ms. DeCarlo, a 38-year-old comedian in Manhattan, lost faith in her virtual community, she said in an interview. Along with the typical postings from members about their weekends was a message from a man she knew as Larry. In graphic detail, Larry described how in 1995 he killed his 5-year-old daughter, Amanda, here in the southwestern corner of North Dakota. In the message, posted at 12:50 P.M. on March 22, Larry recounted how, distraught at the end of a bitter custody dispute with his ex-wife, he had set fire to his home and trapped his daughter inside. "The conflict was tearing me apart, and the next night I let her watch the videos she loved all evening, and when she was asleep I got wickedly drunk, set our house on fire, went to bed, listened to her scream twice, climbed out the window and set about putting on a show of shock, surprise and grief to remove culpability from myself," Larry wrote, according to archives of the support group's email, available to any member on the Internet. "Dammit, part of that show was climbing in her window and grabbing her pajamas, then hearing her breathe and dropping her where she was so she could die and rid me of her mother's interferences." Ms. DeCarlo said she was horrified by the email message, but she grew further dismayed over the on-line debate that followed. While some members of the group were appalled by Larry's account, others rushed to his defense, trying to assure him that he was experiencing a fantasy driven by guilt over his divorce. Others tried to comfort him by telling him the crime was long past. It seemed to Ms. DeCarlo that the nature of on-line communication -- which creates a psychological as well as physical distance between participants -- was causing her friends to forget their off-line responsibilities to bring a confessed murderer to justice. On March 24, amid an email debate known as a flame war, Ms. DeCarlo was one of three members of the support group to notify the authorities. The police here in Bowman said Larry Froistad, a 29-year-old computer programmer living in San Diego, called them on March 27 and confessed. Mr. Froistad has since been extradited to Bowman, a town of about 1,800 people, and he is scheduled to be arraigned on murder charges on Friday. The courthouse is a few blocks from the slab of concrete and rusted plumbing that is all that remains of the house where his daughter died in a 1995 fire that was ruled accidental. Vincent Ross, Mr. Froistad's lawyer, said his client would plead not guilty. Mr. Ross said Mr. Froistad, who worked for the Sony Corporation, might have been taking antidepressants at the time of the March 22 posting on the Internet. Mr. Ross suggested that he might dispute the validity of the email and challenge its use as evidence. "Any statements that Mr. Froistad allegedly made have to be taken in light of his mental condition," Mr. Ross said, "and certainly there is no evidence that Mr. Froistad killed his daughter." For many of those who knew Mr. Froistad through the ether, his unbidden declaration is testimony to cyberspace's singular capacity to invoke trust among strangers. But the email transcripts in the wake of the confession also provide a glimpse into the interpersonal and moral predicaments raised at a time when an increasing amount of social interaction is taking place in electronic arenas, devoid of cues like tone of voice and facial expression, and structured around their own sets of rules and mores. "My position here is that we, as a list, have two responsibilities here -- to ourselves as members of this list community and to the larger community beyond," read an email on March 26 by Frederick Rotgers, a psychologist who helped found the support group two years ago. "That may sound radical to some, but I believe it is an essential feature of the Internet, and one that we must protect if it is to continue to be a source of great support for people who are in need." Dr. Rotgers said he had not notified the law-enforcement authorities after being informed that someone else in the group already had, because "since the child was already 'dead' no purpose would be served in the form of protecting anyone for rash, emotional and poorly thought-out action."  Self-Help Group For Problem Drinkers Dr. Rotgers administers the group, known as the M.M. List, as a volunteer for Moderation Management, a nonprofit self-help organization based in Woodinville, Wash., for people who consider themselves problem drinkers but not alcoholics. He is director of the program for Addictions, Consultation and Treatment at Rutgers University. Rather than turn Larry over to the police, Dr. Rotgers said he had sent private email to him with referrals to therapists near San Diego. "I had no basis for knowing whether it was true or not," he said in an interview. "Neither did anyone else on the list." Many on the M.M. List said they believed that Larry was simply expressing his desire to be punished for surviving a horrible accident. Perhaps, as he himself suggested in later postings and then discounted, he had unconsciously invented a false memory. Others said he might have done it, but that their role as a support group was not to judge. The few who disagreed became the target of often vicious "flame" attacks. On the evening of March 22, a few hours after Larry's initial posting, one participant wrote: "Oh, man, you are really challenging me. It would be O.K. if you would just go away. This is just repulsive stuff and I just can't deal with you. I personally will not read a post by you again. You do not deserve anything!" Someone else quickly responded: "To me, YOUR post is completely unacceptable, especially in this forum. I am repulsed by YOUR post." Jim Shirk, of Bremerton, Wash., said he had notified the Federal Bureau of Investigation. When news of Larry's arrest reached the group, one member called for the informers to come forward. Mr. Shirk, 59, who said he had been sober for 19 years and is a licensed chemical-dependency counselor, sent the member a private email explaining his desire to remain anonymous. Instead, the member posted the email to the whole list, and sent Mr. Shirk private email back: "Just how big a pervert are you? I bet you really get off talking to the F.B.I. Wow. Did you ask them if you could see their guns?" Others accused Mr. Shirk, a proponent of the Alcoholics Anonymous approach to treating addiction, which calls for total abstinence, of using the incident to tarnish the reputation of Moderation Management. "You get a gut feeling for what's real and what isn't and it struck me as very frightening," Mr. Shirk said in a phone interview. "What really scared me was the part after he described everything he did, where he says he wants another family. I felt both professionally ethically and personally ethically that I had to do something." Some members simply wanted to get back to the purpose of the group. "Can we please talk about drinking? I need your help here," read one posting a week into the exchange.  Illusory Anonymity Is Seen on Internet Some longtime Internet users have been communing in disembodied form for years, with the ups and downs any real-life communities naturally experience. On-line services like Echo Communications in newyork and The WELL in Sausalito, Calif., which serve as gathering places for hundreds of discussion topics have weathered many a flame war, as have Internet news groups. "You do not transform when you log on," said Stacy Horn, author of "Cyberville" (Warner Books, 1998), a book about Echo, which she founded. Ms. Horn recalled that when one veteran member declared that he was a Nazi, and offended many others with his anti-Semitic postings, Ms. Horn required him to start his own topic area. People flocked there, virtually, to argue with him. The Froistad case is not without its off-line version. In 1994, Paul Cox was convicted of manslaughter in the murder of a couple in Larchmont, N.Y. Members of an Alcoholics Anonymous group testified that Mr. Cox had told them that he thought he might have killed the couple in an alcohol-induced blackout in 1988. Experts who study the sociology of cyberspace say the intersection of the confidentiality ethic of self-help groups, and the sometimes illusory anonymity of on-line communion, can make for particularly difficult situations. Among those in the M.M. support group, a frequent source of controversy has been that participants can drink and post simultaneously -- as many believe Larry was doing that Sunday. Spouses have been known to subscribe under a false name to maintain their privacy themselves or, some have said, to keep track of the other. Yet the combination is also what has made the global computer network such a boon to people seeking support on a wide range of issues, from cancer patients to senior citizens to gay teen-agers. "People will reveal more on-line than they might in person," said Sara Kiesler, a professor at the Institute for Human Computer Interaction at Carnegie Mellon University. "Psychologically, economically and in every other way, it's cheap talk, people really enjoy it, and it feels safe too. You're just talking to the screen sometimes people get oblivious to the dangers and they say things they wouldn't have said otherwise." That may or may not help explain the question that still looms in the minds of many of Larry Froistad's on-line and off-line friends. "What I can't get out of the thing is why would a guy up and write something like that on the Internet?" said Rodney Redetzke, 35, a mechanic in Bowman who helped Mr. Froistad tear down the remains of his house after the fire. While Bowman's police chief, Don Huso, reopened the investigation into the fire after hearing from Ms. DeCarlo, he did not issue an arrest warrant until Mr. Froistad called him directly five days after his disturbing Internet posting. "He said, "Don, I set the fire,' " said Mr. Huso, whose only other contact with Mr. Froistad was several years ago when he had to tell him it was against city ordinances to raise rabbits in his backyard. "The memories I have of this is that I did it to destroy Amanda." According to the email transcripts and the criminal case file, Mr. Froistad called Mr. Huso the day after Dr. Rotgers, the psychologist, posted to the email list that someone had gone to the police. If convicted, Mr. Froistad faces life in prison.  Suspect Described As Introspective Residents here remember him as an introspective computer enthusiast smarter than everyone else. In a town where any straying from the norm is regarded with a certain suspicion, neighbors described him as different. "Larry was the kind of guy you could ask him a question and he'd come back and answer you with another question," said Mr. Redetzke, the mechanic. 'My wife would always say, 'Larry, come down to our level!' " The son of a Naval Reserve officer, Mr. Froistad also joined the Reserves after his divorce from his wife, Ann, in 1990. He returned to Bowman two years later and fought and gained custody of Amanda. The thick divorce file contains a report from a psychologist who interviewed Amanda in those years. Reached in Rapid City, S.D., Ann, who has remarried, declined to comment on the case. Among those in the M.M. support group, the furor has largely died down. Its postings are now from people seeking advice on how to get through their 30-day abstinence periods and querying the meaning of alcoholism. Audrey Kishline, the founder of Moderation Management, said the group was considering not maintaining archives of the email conversations, and issuing a more strongly worded notice to new subscribers that their words, once released on to the Internet, can never be considered completely confidential. But Ms. DeCarlo, the comedian, said she now attended only face-to-face meetings of the chapter she leads in newyork. "Ultimately, we are alone," she said. "The closeness is for the most part illusory. If Larry walked into a room, I wouldn't know him. On line, they're just words on a screen. Graphic   Chart: "VERBATIM: The Steps in a Confession"  Excerpts from email between Larry Froistad and fellow members of Moderation Management, a support group for problem drinkers, as obtained from the group's archives. Idiosyncracies of capitalization and spelling are from the originals.  LARRY: 'AMANDA I MURDERED' My God, there's something I haven't mentioned, but it's a very important part of the equation. The people I'm mourning the loss of, I've ejected from my life. Kitty had to endure my going to jail twice and being embarrassed in front of her parents. Amanda I murdered because her mother stood between us. . . .  ELISA: 'What DO YOU MEAN?' Okay, Larry, what do you mean, you murdered your daughter? Is this emotional hyperbole or cold fact? And are you getting professional help? Worriedly, Elisa  LARRY: 'LIstened to her scream' OK, it seems to me that there's a great deal of risk to this; my email can be traced, I've been wide open about my identity. But somehow I've unintentionally left the impression that I'm flailing myself for some sort of weird self-gratification. Maybe I do that to some extent. But when I talk about killing my daughter, there's no imaginative subcomponent.  I suffered for years trying to get custody of her after her mother divorced me. When I did, I still had to deal with her mother's constant attempts to take her back. I had the upper hand; in fact, her mother gave up her summer custody just before I killed Amanda. But I always felt that I was not in complete control. My mother told me that I was too hard on her, that I expected too much from her. When I brought her home from her mother's, I abandoned the rules I had set and let her do whatever she wanted--in fact my mother and grandmother visited the next day and she forgot that she was supposed to get dressed before receiving visitors. :) It really was very cute when she woke up and started to walk into our living room, buck-naked. I loved her for her willingness to be fun in simple ways. I would do anything to have her back; but the conflict was tearing me apart, and the next night I let her watch the videos she loved all evening, and when she was asleep I got wickedly drunk, set our house on fire, went to bed, listened to her scream twice, climbed out the window and set about putting on a show of shock, surprise and grief to remove culpability from myself.  Dammit, part of that show was climbing in her window and grabbing her pajamas, then hearing her breathe and dropping her where she was so she could die and rid me of her mother's interferences. Hearing her wheeze in the smoke which I could barely stand--looking at her bedroom door burning--these are things I can't forget.  Those last two screams that I tell everyone saved my life--they are wounds on my soul that I can't heal and that I'm sure I'm meant to carry with me. I am damaged goods, and as much as I feel I need the comfort of someone in my life that I can be good to, someone I can build a new family with--the simple fact is that I don't deserve those things and I'm meant to suffer a thousand times longer than my little girl did.  I cried like a baby in the emergency room at the hospital; I was very disappointed that I couldn't see her after they pulled her out of our house (where they took her before they carted me off); I was stunned and shocked the whole time they flew me down to Rapid City for observation and such, and I've been destroyed ever since. . . .  KAY: 'what you described does not sound rational'  Whew Larry -- I for one have been thinking about your post just after you wrote it and I happened to be on line. I guess I feel that I should say something -- even though I am not one that has been corresponding much with you recently but because I am a pediatrician and a mother.  I must admit to being a little confused in that I'm not sure, other than numbing the situation, what role that alcohol played in this. What you described does not sound rational -- even in drunkeness and I suspect, from what you said, you don't understand it a well either. -- obviously, you should have been prosecuted and managed not to be -- I would assume your ex-wife does not know this which makes your sharing with this group very very weighty I think. But I think you do need something very specific for what has happened -- and I don't think this group is enough. What a very painful thing, in many many ways. ELISA: 'Do the police know'  Okay, Larry, second question: do the police know you murdered your daughter?  FREDERICK: 'Think about contacting a therapist'  Larry, Several folks have sent me private emails expressing genuine concern over some of the stuff that you've posted very recently. They are concerned, that you might be contemplating suicide or other drastic, harmful and ultimately counterproductive actions aimed at dealing with what seems to have become for you an awful situation. I'm writing for all of the folks who wrote me offlist, and I believe for all of the folks on this list, to urge you to seriously think about contacting a therapist and working things through with yourself in a safe manner. Take care of yourself, my friend. And let us all know how things are going. The people here really care about you. Larry: 'I'm sorry'  I'm sorry to everyone I hurt by my post. I certainly don't want to drive anyone away from the list, but I was hurting and continue to, and it's a BIG part of why I drink as much as I do. (pg. title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Hunting a Bargain at a Web Auction
body: MY biggest problem when I shop for a computer is that I always end up with something far more expensive than I set out to buy. Once I'm in the store, I invariably gravitate toward the fancy, expensive turbocharged boxes with subwoofers as big as pickle barrels. Of course, the same thing happens when I buy shoes. But this time, I was determined to be practical. I was after a 200-megahertz Windows box with relatively modest memory and storage to use as a second computer. And I wouldn't pay more than $800. So I decided to make my purchase where I would presumably encounter fewer temptations to go over budget: at an on-line auction, which generally acts as a liaison for computer makers who want to unload used or slightly out-of-date merchandise. It should be a cinch, I figured, because savvy buyers -- who compare prices before they bid -- can save up to 20 percent off retail prices. Today's on-line auctions grew out of a tradition, pioneered more than a decade ago on services like Compuserve and Prodigy, of offering single items, like cars, for sale. "Back then, the clock was running, and you had to bid before time ran out," said Gary Arlen, president of Arlen Communications, a research company in Bethesda, Md., that studies interactive transactions. "It was a little gimmicky." Today, an on-line auction might offer a number of lots with low-ball starting prices ($99 for a computer, for instance) for a set amount of time. Bidders examine the items' specifications on the Web site, place bids, receive email alerting them to higher bids and monitor the bidding on similar lots. "If you know what you are doing, you can get a bargain," Mr. Arlen said. I decided to go to Onsale, the biggest on-line auction for computer equipment. Starting from the home page, I had to click only twice -- on Computer Products, then Desktop Computers -- to reach a listing of dozens of lots. Each lot was described in a single line of text, enabling me to compare the specs of a whole screenful of computers at once. I could click on any that interested me for more information. An auction scheduled to last 24 hours had been under way since noon the previous day. Skimming the descriptions that promised "200 megahertz or faster," I couldn't find a computer that exactly fit my criteria. One was new but came without a monitor. Another came with a slow modem. A third did not have an easy-to-hide-beneath-the-desk minitower case. If I bought any of these, I would have to invest more time and money to massage it into the system I wanted. Still, the prices looked good. With only two hours left before the bidding closed, I would not have to bid more than $600 to top the current bids. My cursor settled on a Mini Tower 6 x 86-p200, 32 MB RAM, 2.1 GB, 16x CD-ROM + 33.6 kbps. My finger wavered over the mouse. To bid or not to bid? Then my eye idly wandered to a line of text that described a "Micron Pentium II 300 MHZ Tower, w/64MB RAM, 8.4G, DVD, 100 MBzip, 56K, 4MBvideo card, refurbished." Bids on that relatively high-end machine had stalled at $1,549. I felt as if I had just caught a glimpse of a pair of loafers with particularly tempting tassels. I wanted the refurbished Micron computer, but I hadn't done enough homework to know how good the price was. To see how much a similar new Micron system would cost, I phoned the company's toll-free number. (Window shopping is not a crime.) Unlike a real-world auction, where you have to make a split-second decision about bidding, I could return to Onsale anytime in the next two hours. A Micron saleswoman, Linda Lee, listened to my story, then said, "Hmm, that sounds like a returned lease system, something that a business traded in for an upgrade." That same computer would be $2,113 new from Micron. "Ask yourself, are you the type of person who buys a used car?" she said. "Just for the sake of comparison, I could offer you a new computer running at 333 megahertz and configured with everything else you want for $100 more. Now, with that kind of a system, you would have----" "Real speed," I murmured and gave her my credit-card number. A day later, I emerged gingerly from my post-shopping trauma to take stock. I had set out to buy a used system for $800 but ended up with a new one that cost nearly $2,300. Why me? Jerry Kaplan, a founder of Onsale, based in Menlo Park, Calif., sighed when he heard the messy details. "You really aren't the type of person who buys at our auctions," he said, explaining that most are men, repeat buyers who are focused on price. The typical customer, he said, is after a specific item and is not likely to be diverted by other merchandise. "But don't give up," Mr. Kaplan said, displaying the innate sales skills that prompted him to help start the auction house in 1995. "You could bid on a printer to go with that new computer." Well, I did need a printer. And buying on line could be the answer because I didn't really need something state-of-the-art, one of those expensive, superfast color printers that spit out a million pages a minute. No, I just needed something . . . practical.  Site-Seeing: Computers at Auction  There are two kinds of auction houses on line -- those that sell on behalf of established equipment makers and those that will sell anything for individuals (up to and including my old 286 DOS machine, if I care to sell it). Obviously, buying from an individual carries greater risk; if you want a warranty, stick with the auction houses that work on behalf of vendors. Here are some houses that deal with vendors:  ONSALE: www.onsale.com This has by far the biggest selection of computer equipment as well as a comprehensive selection of sporting equipment. USALE AUCTIONS: www.usale-auction.com A site with a much more limited selection. INTERACTIVE AUCTION ONLINE: www.iaoauction.com You can find stereo components, camcorders, VCR's and car stereos in addition to computer equipment. AUCTION DEPOT: www.auctiondepot.com This site offers computer equipment and a wide range of software titles. Graphic   Drawing (Margaret Riegel)

title: Meet Zyshal, Adolescent Avatar of the Chat Rooms
body: SECURING control of the family computer is no easy task on a weekend night in the McLeod household. But Miranda, it is clear, has had lots of practice. By 9 P.M. on a Saturday, her little brother, Kyle, is banished to a friend's house, and Mom is dispatched to the bills stacked on the floor. Then, looking like a cyberpunk Wonder Woman with silver bracelets, metallic nails and dark hair streaked with blond, the 16-year-old assumes her rightful place in front of the computer screen. With a few keystrokes and the shriek of a modem, Miranda morphs into Zyshal, an avatar of multitasking powers. And none too soon. The instant messages -- or I.M.'s, in the relentlessly abbreviated lingo of America Online sophisticates -- are pouring in. Fingers flying at speeds that would be impressive even if she wasn't a typing class dropout, Miranda's electronic persona carries on simultaneous conversations with her best friend down the street, an ex-boyfriend in San Jose and a college guy in New Orleans, all while gallivanting around the World Wide Web and perusing her email. Fortunately for a real life (R.L.) visitor, narration is available via the corporeal husk that is seated barefoot in the cramped study, ignoring proffered cookies but pausing occasionally for sips of water. "I am completely different on line than I am in real life," says Zyshal-Miranda. "In real life, I'm more worried about hurting people's feelings." The offhand explanation cuts to the heart of why this ritual is quickly becoming as central to the social lives of American teen-agers in the late 1990's as going to the mall was for the same age group two decades earlier. Like the mall, the Internet's corridors allow evasion of direct adult supervision in a space that is still relatively safe. But while mall culture seems to reinforce the strictures of adolescent conformity, cyberspace fosters experimentation. Trapped in awkward, changing bodies like every generation of teen-agers, today's wired youth have a legal escape route from the flesh never before accessible on such a mass scale. On line, screen names and personalities are changed at whim, and quick wit and fast typing matter more than the color of eye makeup. "I find it easier not to use caps," Miranda says. "When you're trying to talk to eight people at once you don't have time for formalities." Of course, children of all ages are increasingly partaking of cyberspace's seductive metaphysics. (Lately, Miranda has had to share the keyboard with her mother, a social worker who is divorced and has struck up an email correspondence with several male friends.) But teen-agers are leading the way. The portion of America's 20 million teen-agers who use the Internet has doubled to nearly one-third since 1996, according to Jupiter Communications, a research firm. By 2002, Jupiter estimates that three-quarters of the nation's teen-agers will be on line, a higher proportion than other age groups. These youngsters are using it for schoolwork and to replace television, according to several recent studies. They are using it to cyber, the genteel shorthand for the often- graphic descriptions, fantasies and jokes about one-handed typing that constitute sexual encounters from behind the screen. Mostly, though, they are using it to socialize in a realm that Sherry Turkle, a psychologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has begun to call R.O.L., for rest of life. Professor Turkle's 1995 book, "Life on the Screen," made the case that the on-line world provided the "moratorium space" that the psychologist Erik Erikson deemed essential for identity development in adolescence but that has largely evaporated in the preprofessional off-line world of high school. Professor Turkle says she now sees a fusion of real-life and on-line identity among adolescents that may enable a healthy expansion in how they think of themselves. One of her subjects, for example, hated school but emerged as the brain in an on-line discussion of philosophy and science fiction. "Adults say, 'This is my real life and that's another life there on the Internet,' " Professor Turkle said. "People who grow up with the Internet are learning not to make that kind of distinction. The teen-age years are about a search for a way to think about identity and they're particularly open to the integration of the two realms." Miranda, who counts 41 people on her A.O.L. buddy list, credits Zyshal for improving her off-line social life, although it also helped that some of her friends got their driver's licenses this year and that by junior year the social scene is less rigid. Using a ubiquitous teen-age term of negativity, she described her pre-on-line social life as not terrific. "To have friends you had to be in the really popular group and I just didn't fit the mold," she says. "Then when I came on line, there were all these people who liked me because I was different." For Miranda, the lure of the Net, with its pulsing, instant feedback and its ability to stave off loneliness, was so potent that her grades began to falter. Last year she often logged on after school and didn't log off until 2 A.M. This year, she has cut back, for reasons she explains to the college guy: bsc5: What's your G.P.A.? Zyshal: Like 3.6 or so. bsc5: I had a 2.7 and was happy. Zyshal: But did you apply to Harvard? Not everyone can do it so easily. In a new book, "Caught in the Net," Kimberly Young, a psychologist, describes a syndrome in which adolescents, and adults, engage in an on-line existence to the exclusion of school, work and real-life relationships. But Miranda says the rush wears off. By now, having conducted a debate over creationism, arranged a weekend outing, picked a fight with Katie ("Her on-line persona drives me crazy. In real life, she's completely sarcastic and mean. On line, she just turns into this totally sweet, nice person. Sometimes I want to slap her.") and promised to talk to the ex- later on the phone, Zyshal (whose nom de guerre has since changed) is ready to log off. Which is good, because Kyle is back from his friend's house and anxious to take over. A role-playing game veteran who turned 13 this month, Kyle also admits to a phase that bordered on addiction when he invented Tarquinevermore, an elf best described as "humorous and studly." Now, he wants to confide in a friend he met in his elfin disguise (which has also since changed). Tonight he is burdened by something he has learned about his parents' divorce, and the way he learned it. It's too hard to talk about with school friends, but his on-line friend is helping him sort it out. "She's 16, almost 17, and it's a lot easier to talk to her: one, because she's older; two, she doesn't have links to other people I know, and three, she has problems too," Kyle says. "She's somebody who understands that life isn't always fantastic." Graphic   Photo: Miranda McLeod, booted up and ready for action. On line, she and other young digirati have discovered that quick wit and fast typing matter more than the color of eye makeup. (Mojgan B. Azimi for The newyork Times)

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
For Specialty Users, Browser Price May Be Right
body: NOTHING makes a product more interesting than a really good story. In the normal world, it is the cure for high cholesterol thought up by the female auto mechanic while removing grease from a messy engine. In the computer world, it is the amazing hack, the achievement of half a dozen unkempt guys (they are almost always unkempt guys) working night and day in an unheated garage and emerging a couple of weeks later with hot software half as big and three times as fast as the expensive corporate model, at one-fourth the price. The latest of these tales revolves around a clever Web browser called Opera. It fits on one floppy disk. It runs on older machines some of its competitors cannot begin to contemplate. It has several clever features the big guys never thought of. And although unheated garages do not appear to be part of the tale, the browser does come all the way from Norway. Programmers developed it from scratch in 1994 to run on the internal network of the telecommunications company Telenor AS. At the end of 1995, two of its developers, Jon Stephenson von Tetzchner and Geir Ivarsoy, left with the browser to found Opera Software. In 1996, they began offering Opera to the public over the Internet as try-before-you-buy share ware. Today they preside over a company of 11 employees that sells the program in several languages from its site at www.operasoftware.com. It works only on Windows now, although other versions are in development. But this particular hack gives you a 30-day free trial, after which it goes dead unless you pay $35. In a world where Netscape Navigator and Microsoft Internet Explorer include multiple kitchen sinks and cost not a cent, Opera raises the question "Why should anybody pay for this?" Surprisingly, it makes such a good case for itself that you may want to try it. That should not be hard. The whole thing fits on a standard 1.44-megabyte floppy disk with more than 280 kilobytes to spare, so downloading it from the Net should take 10 minutes, tops. Actual installation takes a whole extra minute on a slow machine, and the code expands only to about 1.8 megabytes. To anyone accustomed to the 13-megabyte download and 56 megabytes of disk space required to install the tiniest configuration of Explorer, Opera may seem a small miracle. But Opera cannot handle certain kinds of content, most prominently Java (although this is promised for the 4.0 version) and ActiveX (which is not). Its mail program is designed mostly to let you respond to addresses embedded in Web sites, and although it accepts Real Audio and several other popular multimedia plug-ins designed for Netscape, it does not come with any. But it does come with most other important features, and, unlike the competitors should be able to run on a machine as lowly as a 386SX with just 8 megabytes of memory. Does smaller translate to faster? In my tests, it did not, despite some reviewers' claims. On my Pentium 90 machine, Opera loaded in about 10 seconds, but so did the latest version of Explorer. Opera's vaunted speed at displaying Web pages was not obvious, either. No browser I tried offered consistent advantages across the wide range of pages I tested over a connection running at about 48 kilobits per second. Sometimes Explorer or Navigator beat Opera; sometimes it was the other way around. Only rarely did the difference amount to more than 25 percent, or a few seconds. But Opera does include a clever button that can improve browsing speed by eliminating graphics. The resulting pages look not at all the way their designers intended but usually load significantly faster; the color and flash are a click and a wait away. Other browsers let you do this only with difficulty, though the Power Toys software at www.microsoft.com/ie/ie40/?/ie/ie40/powertoys adds a similar quick-change feature to Explorer 4.0. As most novices eventually discover, browsers will let you open several windows and surf several sites at once. Unfortunately, the windows behave as if they were separate programs, right down to having to be closed one by one. By corralling a multitude of windows into its world, Opera offers much more control over them. A single click lets you display the windows as tiled panels or overlap them with their title bars peeking out. A special control even lets you separately adjust the size of the information displayed in each window. It all helps make browsing a happier experience. So does Opera's button that restores a site to standard colors and fonts when some artiste sticks you with unreadable type on a background of optical irritation. Opera's downloading progress display gives you a good idea of how many images you will have to wait for before the entire page appears. The program gives you a useful starter set of bookmarks and a handy command that lets you save a file complete with all its links and images. But that feature did not always work, and there were plenty of other inconsistencies and problems. Links sometimes were deaf to clicks, pages with frames refused to print, the URL window sometimes disappeared, and, in part because Opera's programmers apparently adhere more rigorously to the Hypertext Markup Language standard than some Web designers, pages did not always display correctly. The file that remembers where you have been can hold a mere 255 entries. Links to several sites supposedly offering the program seemed dead. The company's Web site admits it gets behind in handling questions from users, but at times Netscape and Microsoft might as well be in Norway for all the good telephoning them does you. I am still trying to figure out why Internet Explorer occasionally insists on disabling my pop-up Start bar. Upgrades within the same version of Opera (for example, 3.1 to 3.2) are free. For versions upgrades (for example, 3.2 to 4.0), paying customers get 50 percent off. Students and educational institutions can also get half-price deals. Opera's story is a Norse saga of smaller size, clever features, reasonable speed and occasional annoyances. In a normal market, it would be a worthy competitor. But unless Federal intervention or some unforeseen factor changes today's giveaway browser bazaar, the only way Opera could beat the competition's price would be to spit out legal tender on your ink-jet printer. Now that would be an amazing hack. Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Mirror Sells Legal Unit To British-Dutch Publisher
body: The Times Mirror Company moved to focus more closely on its newspaper roots yesterday by agreeing to sell its legal publishing business to the British-Dutch publishing giant Reed Elsevier for $1.65 billion in cash. The agreement -- which includes the publisher Matthew Bender & Company and Times Mirror's 50 percent share of Shepard's, a legal citation service -- followed an auction that produced a price well above analysts' estimates. The deal also consolidates the already strong position of Reed Elsevier, which bought the Lexis-Nexis on-line legal and general publishing data base for $1.5 bllion in 1994. But Reed "paid handsomely," said Anthony de Larrinaga, an analyst at Panmure Gordon in London. "Their long-suffering shareholders are going to have to put up with little growth until they can prove themselves next year." Nigel J. Stapleton, co-chief executive of Reed Elsevier, responded, "We are paying what the business is worth." The sale bolsters Reed Elsevier's position in the competitive world of legal publishing, and may salve the bruises left over from the failure of its proposed $9 billion merger with its Dutch rival, Wolters Kluwer N.V. For Times Mirror, the sale of Bender, like the expected sale of the Mosby-Year Book Company, the medical information services company, is bittersweet. Legal publishing "is a higher-margin business" than the company's other interests, said Thomas Unterman, the chief financial officer of Times Mirror. But while it was a business the company had nurtured for years, it was also facing a perilous future as a midsized company in a world grown Gargantuan. Legal publishing is now dominated by Reed Elsevier and two big rivals that have also grown through acquisitions in recent years: the Thomson Company, the Canadian newspaper publisher that bought West Publishing for $3.4 billion in 1996, and Wolters Kluwer, which bought Commerce Clearing House in 1995 for $1.9 billion. Some analysts are betting that that universe will contract futher, giving the surviving players greater pricing power. "Reed Elsevier is willing to take the dilution in earnings because in five years, if you need information on a law case, you'll only have one place to go -- and you'll pay a stiff price," said Louis Ehrenkrantz, president of Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum, who follows the media business. Reed Elsevier, which already owns the other half of Shepard's, distributes far more than legal information; it publishes 1,200 academic and technical journals and its aggressive pricing -- average increases are in the double-digit range -- has made its name a byword among some university librarians. In this new landscape, Mr. Unterman said, "strategically, Bender was not well positioned" within Times Mirror. But it was a business that had done well by its parent company. Along with Jeppesen Sanderson, an aviation-information company, Bender produced the highest profit margins within Times Mirror last year, well above the roughly 18 percent margins in the company's dominant newspaper publishing business, Mr. Unterman said -- although he said the company did not disclose detailed breakdowns of the finances of its various businesses. More than anything else, he said, the sale of Bender, along with the sale of Mosby -- which Times Mirror expects before the end of the second quarter -- reflects the company's commitment to newspapering. "By roots, core and commitment, we are going to be a newspaper business," Mr. Unterman said. According to Times Mirror's annual report, professional information publishing, including Bender, Mosby, Jeppesen and some smaller businesses, brought in $143 million in profits on $853 million in revenue last year. The profits for Bender were $64 million, according to company data and estimates by analysts at Credit Suisse First Boston. When the sale of Mosby is consummated, Times Mirror estimates that about 75 percent of its revenue will come from its newspaper properties, which include The Los Angeles Times, Newsday, The Baltimore Sun and The Hartford Courant.

body: Forecast for Windows 98: Slow Start, Steady Growth Government officials are racing to determine what antitrust action, if any, they should take against Microsoft before it ships Windows 98 to PC makers in May. But while the personal computer industry has been gearing up for Windows 98 for far longer than the antitrust authorities, the software's early impact in the marketplace is expected to be slight, compared with that of Windows 95.
