title: Buyer to Revive 2 Popular On-Line Magazines
body: Two popular on-line magazines shut down by their parent company last month are being revived by an unlikely buyer. The Zapata Corporation, a food processing business based in Houston, will announce today that it is acquiring Word and Charged magazines from the Icon CMT Corporation, as a first step in a "radical transformation," according to Zapata's chief executive, Avram A. Glazer. As part of the refocused business, Zapata, founded by former President George Bush and a partner in 1953 as an oil-drilling business, will also change its name to Zap. Under Mr. Glazer's family, which acquired Zapata in 1994, the company has left the energy business. "Zapata is launching a major strategic initiative to acquire Internet and electronic-commerce companies," Mr. Glazer said. Last month, the initial public offering of a marine protein products business in which Zapata owned a stake, the Omega Protein Corporation, raised $130 million. "We have all these resources, and we're going to dedicate a considerable amount of those resources to acquiring Internet sites," Mr. Glazer said from his office in Rochester. Icon CMT, a network services provider based in Weehawken, N.J., suspended the publication of the two magazines in March and laid off their employees, saying the operations did not fit into the company's core business. Scott A. Baxter, the chairman and chief executive, said at the time that he had unsuccessfully sought a buyer, and was keeping the two sites posted on the World Wide Web in the hope that a buyer would emerge from the publicity about their demise. Enter Mr. Glazer, whose family is known for its seemingly disparate investments. Mr. Glazer's father, Malcolm, bought the Tampa Bay Buccaneers football team in 1995 for $192 million. The Glazer family also owns the Houlihan's restaurant chain. The financial terms of the acquisition of the on-line magazines were not disclosed, but Mr. Glazer said the employees of the magazines would be rehired. For Icon CMT, publishing the magazines despite the losses they accumulated will pay off in a lucrative way. Mr. Baxter said Zap would use his company for network communications and said it had signed a "multimillion-dollar, four-year deal." Mr. Glazer said he saw symmetry in Zapata's decision to refocus itself around a new technology.  "When George Bush founded Zapata 40 years ago, he was in the cutting edge of technology in the oil rig business," Mr. Glazer said. "You can almost relate it to this point in the Internet." The magazine deal was not the only odd Internet partnership that came to light last week. ICC Technologies Inc. in Hatboro, Pa., a maker of climate controls, said it acquired Rare Medium, a two-year-old World Wide Web development firm, for $45 million.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: DIGITAL COMMERCE;
A shift so fundamental that not even Microsoft may know how to respond.
body: THE Microsoft Corporation has a longstanding reputation in the personal computer industry as a schoolyard bully. But recent public scrutiny has propelled the company's swaggering reputation into the mainstream. And predicting the software giant's eventual demise has expanded into something of a national parlor game. Even the venerable Silicon Valley research institute, SRI International, which rarely chimes in on the ideological events of the day, is now "pondering the unthinkable," as it says in its speculative report "After Microsoft" (http://future.sri.com/bip/AM.html). The SRI report, actually a faux newsletter article written by the senior consultant Robert Jacobson from the vantage point of the year 2003, describes a software industry in which Microsoft has "devolved" into five separate Baby Softs. Although the current antitrust investigations do figure in Mr. Jacobson's chronicle of the company's fictional collapse, it also cites other, equally prominent factors: failure of key products to perform as promised; cross-industry competition from large publishers and media companies; unwise investments in risky new industries, and "a decline in Bill Gates's focus and ability to micromanage the company." But whether Microsoft stands or falls, an additional and larger force will be buffeting the company, a force already making an impact not only on Microsoft but almost every other large corporation. That force is technology itself. Consider how the increasing power of technology has contributed to the vast chaos of mergers, acquisitions and strategy shifts in today's business world. Even as giant conglomerates are forming -- as in financial services, where the current fad is toward mammoth providers of "one stop shopping" -- PC's and the global Internet are creating an increasingly favorable economic climate for smaller, more nimble companies, niche markets and customized products and services. Corporations serving mass markets, always at the mercy of their snail-paced bureaucracies and substantial overhead, are square in the path of this inexorable march. For example, desktop publishing, a stunning success for the PC industry in the 1980's, turned the once-monolithic publishing industry upside down, with new magazines, alternative newspapers and small book houses set up by writers and editors who could never afford access to old-line commercial printing presses. A decade later, not only are PC's serving as printing presses but the World Wide Web is providing global distribution for desktop publications. Ditto alternative music and independent film: any of the countless bands or independent studios that have mixed (and sometimes even mastered) their own CD's, or edited film or videos on a desktop computer, can testify that the cost of production has plummeted. Using the Internet these artists can market their work -- and eventually distribute it -- outside the conventional clogged and costly sales channels. And recall that last year a long-distance telephone service reseller named Tel-Save offered America Online's customers what was then the lowest rate in the industry, 9 cents a minute, largely because the on-line service eliminated the need for direct marketing, advertising or billing. A year later, Tel-Save has half a million customers through America Online. Information technology, in short, is creating a shift so fundamental that not even a PC pioneer like Microsoft may know how to respond. The company is so huge, and to date has proved so unwilling to relinquish any control of its markets, that the SRI report suggests the software giant may collapse under its own weight. Mr. Jacobson contends that Microsoft customers are already tiring of bloated software that seems designed to take up the largest possible amount of space on a hard drive, to require the largest possible amount of computer memory and to contain every conceivable feature for the largest possible market of users. (Early indications are that Microsoft's imminent Windows 98 does not reverse the bloatware trend.) Just as in other industries transformed by technology, software buyers are no longer bound to accept what Microsoft chooses for them. Instead, customers may begin reaping benefits from the growing popularity of the "open source code" and component software movements, which encourage programmers and the most motivated users to customize the inner workings of operating systems and application programs. Even consumers who today prefer Microsoft's choices might eventually be swayed by the benefits brought by these movements. Such trends, though, are antithetical to today's Microsoft, whose success is based on controlling its Windows operating system and mass-market sales of general purpose -- not customized -- software. Thus, the emergent leaders may turn out to be niche producers who can quickly form and reform their businesses to respond to individual customers -- a trend already in play on the Web, where software designers create "plug in" modules that provide various types of functions upon request. This clash between mass and niche market seems so primal that the only analogy with sufficient drama is of dying dinosaurs and the darting little mammals that survived them. So far, only one dinosaur -- the former AT&T Corporation, which itself was once the target of the Justice Department's antitrust squad -- saw and embraced mammalian fleet-of-foot tactics as a survival strategy. Having undergone a court-supervised divestiture in 1984, the corporation decided a decade later that it was still too big and could succeed only by voluntarily dismantling itself into three separate companies. So far, all three are not simply surviving, but growing and thriving. Does AT&T provide a model that unwieldy corporations everywhere should emulate? It is far too early to say. And it is highly unlikely that technology will decimate all large companies in its path, not by the year 2003, anyway. But certainly something is afoot -- something much more fundamental than Microsoft's recent mediagenic missteps. Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title: The Hum of Search Engines Is Music to Netscape's Ears
body: The search is on for search engines. A number of companies -- including Netscape Communications and some big traditional media players -- are looking to build or buy their own Internet search services. These services, initially meant only to help Internet users find information from among the millions of pages of on-line material, have now become the primary gateway to cyberspace for many people. Netscape is in the midst of high-stakes negotiations to choose a company to provide the central search function for its ambitious new Internet site. The second tier of search businesses, including Lycos, Infoseek and the Snap service of Cnet, are actively negotiating with Netscape, people involved in the negotiations say. The two larger search services -- Yahoo and Excite -- have talked to Netscape, too, but are said to be less interested. Netscape's hunt for a deal is only one part of its plan to expand its World Wide Web site, called Netcenter, into a full source of communication, information and shopping, to compete with America Online and Yahoo. Now that it is giving away its browser, the company hopes advertising will become a major source of revenue. Last week, for instance, it announced an agreement to offer electronic-mail services. Existing search companies worry about Netscape as a potentially powerful new competitor, simply because millions of people already use Netscape's Web browser software. "They will take market share from all the players," said Steven T. Kirsch, the chairman of Infoseek. "We're not afraid of competition, but that's bad for our business." A deal with Netscape may help a company jump ahead of its competitors. The chairman of Cnet, Halsey Minor, said his company would consider selling a piece of Snap, a service modeled on Yahoo, to Netscape or to a big media company to bring in traffic. "There are a lot of options for us to partner with people who can help us build a brand," he said. Yet it is unclear whether Netscape is interested in building any brand but its own. Mike Homer, general manager of its new Web site division, says Netscape wants a search company to provide it with the information to offer a search service along with a directory of the Internet, similar to the yellow pages, under the Netscape brand name. Netscape had hoped to have a deal set a few weeks ago, but has not reached an agreement, people involved in the talks said. It has asked for large cash payments and stock in the search company, which would earn money from selling advertising. Many companies see such terms as too steep a price for a deal that might last only two or three years. "Would you give away 20 percent of your company for a two-year deal?," a top executive of one search engine company asked. "After that, where do you go?" Mr. Kirsch of Infoseek acknowledged that reaching a deal might be difficult. "We're interested in a deal that expands our reach, if we can do something that makes sense for both parties," he said. "But my past experience with Netscape has led me to believe they are very aggressive negotiators." Mr. Homer said Netscape was also negotiating for sources of other content, like stock quotations and computer industry news. Search services have evolved into popular gateways through which people venture onto the Internet. That makes advertisers interested in these services, which have also collected substantial revenue by selling links to other sites, like those selling books or music. Moreover, these sites have been using their popularity to expand into other services, like email, news chat groups and other activities that keep viewers lingering longer and looking at more advertising. Excitement about the search companies has driven their stock prices to spectacular heights. Yahoo, which is barely profitable, has a market value of more than $5 billion. And competitors are lining up. Microsoft is creating Start.com, a jumping-off point to the Internet that will feed people to Microsoft Web sites. And investment bankers report that many big traditional media companies are considering buying search sites, too, so they are not left out of what could be the next big type of media property. Many Internet experts, however, predict an ultimate shakeout. "There will be three -- four, max -- global, comprehensive Web on-line services," said Jeffrey Mallett, the chief operating officer of Yahoo. He argues that Netscape is not in a position to be one of them. "Netscape's brand conjures up software and browsers, not an on-line service." Mr. Homer of Netscape says it is precisely the company's software that will give it an advantage on line. For example, a prominent link on the Netscape browser (marked "search") now funnels Netscape users to one of several search engines, which pay the company for the traffic. After Netscape reaches its deal, that link will increasingly point users to its own service.

title: Global Trade Show And Conference Set
body: WANT to develop successful international business strategies? Expand your global business instantly through technology and the Internet? Network with hundreds of globally focused business professionals? Visit exhibit booths staffed by international trade service providers? Meet with Federal, state and local export resource specialists? "Technology and Trade: Your Links to Success" is the theme of Globalink '98, Westchester's only full-day international trade exhibition and conference, taking place Wednesday from 8 A.M. to 5 P.M. at the Westchester Marriott Hotel in Tarrytown. The Gobalink conference, sponsored by the Westchester County Association and the World Trade Council of Westchester, will help promote and develop international trade opportunities in the Hudson Valley. The use of technology and the Internet as international business tools is the subject of this year's conference. Globalink was organized by the unitedstates Department of Commerce and the Empire State Development Corporation, and this year's grand sponsor is the unitedstates Postal Service. The daylong program, featuring exhibitors, strategy sessions and speakers who are experts in their fields, will include a continental breakfast, lunch and closing cocktail reception and award ceremony. The keynote address at the lunch will be given by C. Robert Black, senior vice president, office of the chairman of Texaco. He will discuss "Going Global: The Texaco Experience." Strategy sessions in the morning will include a panel that will focus on various marketing and distribution issues in Asia, Europe and Latin America. A second panel will consider the importance of understanding cultural differences in an international business context. The afternoon session, "The Internet as a Successful International Business Tool," will discuss the importance of establishing a presence on the Worldwide Web as a means of generating international revenue. It will also highlight key international Web sites and databases. The Globalink award for International Business Excellence, given to a local company for achievement in its international business performance, will be presented by County Executive Andrew J. Spano to Edward Marwell, chairman of Curtis Instruments, a Mount Kisco manufacturer of instruments and controls. After the award ceremony, a raffle will be held. Among the prizes will be two round-trip tickets to Europe donated by Finnair. The registration fee for the conference is $85 in advance, $95 at the door. Reservations can be made by calling Amy Allen at 948-6444.   PENNY SINGER

title:
MUTUAL FUNDS;
Stepping Up to the Internet Buffet
body: HOW do investors in Internet stocks feel this year? :-) That, for the less technologically attuned, is not a garble but the symbol used by the digerati when they want to crack an on-line grin. Despite a recent pullback in such stocks, these investors have many reasons to smile. To name just a few, the on-line bookseller Amazon.com is up 40.1 percent so far this year, the search engine provider Yahoo has risen 65.7 percent and Doubleclick, an on-line advertising agency, is up 32.2 percent from its public offering on Feb. 20. People committed to mutual fund investing can also benefit from such returns. Unbeknown to most, there are three tiny funds that focus on Internet stocks: the Munder Netnet fund, the WWW Internet fund and the Internet Fund. Each has a track record of more than a year now -- which in the realm of cyberspace passes for a long time. The big question, however, is whether any investor really needs such a fund. After all, it is not as though other funds have been ignoring Internet-related stocks. "Have all these information-technology and communications funds overlooked the Internet?" asked an incredulous Michael Stolper, a financial adviser in San Diego. "Is it very thoughtful of them to create something more specific -- or is this marketing run amok?" he asked about the specialized Internet funds. But Internet fund managers say this is an idiosyncratic business that can benefit from special attention. "The Internet is such a young industry that it's often impossible to use traditional valuation methods," said Paul Cook, co-manager of the Munder fund. "Many of these names are really story-driven." If, in fact, it is only marketing, the funds need a new ad campaign. None has more than $8 million in assets, and they are therefore not listed in the mutual fund tables of The newyork Times or of many other newspapers. The ride in these funds can be wild, too. Despite the 46.4 percent return of the WWW Internet fund over the 12 months ended April 17, for example, the fund was basically flat for all of 1997: a result of double-digit losses in the fourth quarter. (The average technology fund returned 41.1 percent over the 12 months, and 8.4 percent in 1997, according to Morningstar Inc., the financial publisher in Chicago.) But with minimum investment requirements of $1,000, the funds are a cheap way to get exposure to a highflying sector, without betting it all on a single stock. "The most challenging thing in picking Internet stocks is going to be figuring out who is going to be around two years from now," said Michael Stout, senior analyst at Morningstar. Munder Netnet, with $8 million in assets, is the largest of the three funds, and its fund complex, Munder Capital Management, based in Birmingham, Mich., is well known. Most of its other funds are sold through brokers and carry loads, or sales charges, but Netnet is a no-load fund that is marketed directly to investors over the Internet. This also might explain its puny assets. Seven Munder portfolio managers, some of whom work on other funds, run the portfolio. And the fund takes a broad view of its investing universe. "For companies to be considered for inclusion, they have to be directly involved in building out the Internet or be seen as a prime beneficiary of Internet trends," said Paul Cook, one of the managers. An example is Cisco Systems, which makes, among other kinds of computer hardware, switches that allow computers to communicate with one another over the World Wide Web. A big portion of the company's sales, however, is not directly related to the Internet. The fund's other 40 or so stocks include Microsoft, which gets only a tiny fraction of its revenues from the Internet, and N2K Inc. which sells CD's on line. Another big holding is Cendant, whose business includes sales of everything from books to cars over the Internet; its stock fell 46 percent on April 16 after the company disclosed accounting irregularities. Owning relatively established companies like Microsoft and Cisco is intended to lend stability to the portfolio. "We bring a conservative background to investing in a space that seems on the surface to be unconservative," said Steven Appledorn, another manager of the fund. The WWW Internet fund is managed by Lawrence York of WWW Advisors in Lexington, Ky., and is registered for sale in 20 states, including California and newyork. The fund has no load but charges a steep 0.5 percent 12b-1 annual marketing fee. Like Munder Netnet, it owns about 40 stocks and has a broad mandate. "We believe the Internet will cause a convergence of broadcasting, data and telecommunications," Mr. York said, so he invests in these areas. He tries to reduce risk by dividing assets among three tiers of companies, which he refers to as adolescent, midlife or mature, based on factors like their market dominance and the breadth of their business lines. His mature holdings include Cisco Systems and Microsoft. One midlife company is Qualcomm, a maker of communications systems and email software. And an adolescent is Checkfree, which makes software used to process electronic payments; among these four, it is the company most closely tied to the Web. The purest play on hard-core Internet stocks is the Internet Fund. "For a company to be considered for our portfolio, they have to derive a large majority of their revenue on or from the Internet," said Ryan Jacob, the fund's manager who is also director of research for IPO Value Monitor, a research firm in newyork that specializes in initial public offerings. Mr. Jacob was named to run the 18-month-old fund, whose investment adviser is Kinetics Asset Management of North Babylon, N.Y., just last December. Of the 25 stocks in the fund's portfolio, the biggest holding is CMG Information Services, a venture capital company that invests in Internet start-ups. Other big stakes are in Yahoo, the search engine with one of the strongest brand names on the Web, and Egghead.com, formerly Egghead Inc., which has abandoned traditional retailing to sell its goods almost entirely over the Internet. Mr. Jacob said Egghead's Internet sales roughly doubled, to $2 million a week, in the first three months of the year. "Most of the Internet companies have gone public over the last two or three years, and we have followed these companies from the venture capital stage through their I.P.O.'s," he said. "Most are still not profitable, but the underlying fundamentals are exceptionally strong," Mr. Jacob added. "Revenue growth has been 50 percent to 100 percent quarter to quarter; very few industries can boast that kind of growth." Graphic   Chart: "Wired Wonders?" The total returns on three funds that market themselves as Internet offerings: Munder Netnet, WWW Internet, The Internet Fund. (Sources: Morningstar; company reports)

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
Aisle Seat for Movie Buffs
body: When Karen Cooper became director of the Film Forum in 1972, the theater was a two-year-old showcase for independent films but not for old movies. It didn't need to be. The Thalia, the newyorker, the Bleecker Street and the Regency movie theaters did that. Today, those theaters are dark, and the nonprofit Film Forum, which has managed to thrive in a difficult film market, is one of the last revival houses and one of the few theaters regularly to feature independent movies in newyork. Now Film Forum has turned the the Web to reach newyork film buffs and to highlight non-Hollywood films, like "The Farm," opening June 10, a documentary about the country's largest maximum-security prison, and classics. (A 50-film retrospective called "Madcap Manhattan" begins this Friday and includes comedies like Mel Brooks's film "The Producers.") "Movies should be chunks of reality that I would not normally experience living below 14th Street," said Ms. Cooper, 49, who chooses features and documentaries for Film Forum. Bruce Goldstein, 45, who selects the old movies, looks for classic flicks with "good prints that the audience won't boo."  WHAT YOU SEE -- Every year, Film Forum offers more than 40 feature films and documentaries and more than 350 old movies. Until September 1995, when its Web site went up, it relied mainly on printed calendars, scant advertising and word-of-mouth. For technical reasons, Film Forum is not part of the popular 777-FILM telephone and Web page service. But with more than 3,300 dues-paying members, Film Forum can take advantage of the niche marketing that is a specialty of the Web. The Web site gets up to 5,000 page views per month and provides more information than Film Forum's printed calendars, which get Scotch-taped to refrigerator doors and quickly become outdated. The site gives movie schedules as well as information about film distributors. That helps nonprofits like schools and museums obtain acclaimed documentaries, like the recent "A Paralyzing Fear: The Story of Polio in America," which is distributed by the Center for History in the Media at George Washington University. The site also notes special events, like the live musical accompaniment on May 4 by a pianist, Steve Sterner, to the 1928 silent movie "Speedy." The movie stars Harold Lloyd as a baseball-crazy cabdriver who picks up Babe Ruth (the real Yankee, not an actor), and has a climactic chase scene in which the cabby races newyork's last horse-drawn trolley through the Washington Square Arch, which was then a thoroughfare.  LINKS -- Thirty-seven, including such sites as "Indiewire," a news service about and for independent filmmakers (http://www.indiewire.com/index.html).  WHAT YOU GET -- A work in progress. Film Forum's Web master, Richard Hutchins, plans to reformat the schedule as an actual calendar, so a viewer can click on a date to find out what's playing then. Also under consideration: chat rooms for film buffs.  FILM FORUM (http://www.filmforum.com) Graphic   Photo.

title:
Journal;
Hardest Sell on Earth
body: "Yes, I want to support Linda Tripp!" It is a bit of a jolt to come upon this jolly exhortation while surfing the Web. But go to www.lindatripp.com, whip out a credit card and you, too, can contribute to the Linda Tripp Legal Defense Fund. The selling of the most maligned woman in America has at long last begun. Until this week www.lindatripp.com was a Tripp-baiting site; it is still listed in Internet directories as a forum for examining "the betrayal of friendship." But it's now been purchased by Ms. Tripp's handlers, who have replaced its "Ugly Linda" poster with a color portrait of the smiling, re-coiffed Linda. The accompanying text tries to humanize her by noting that she is "an avid collector of 18th-century antiques, porcelain and books," is "fluent in German" and "has served as an officer of the unitedstates Pony Club, a nationally recognized association." In making a pitch for cash, her brother-in-law writes: "People need to realize Linda was not born into the Hollywood fast lane where privilege comes so easy." No Monica she. This tardy effort to rehabilitate Ms. Tripp -- which arrives just as Ken Starr has hired his own new folksy P.R. spokesman -- isn't for laughs. As The Washington Post has observed, "If President Clinton falls, it will be Linda Tripp who largely made it happen." And if Ms. Tripp's evidence is to spur an impeachment proceeding, it wouldn't hurt politically if she were at least somewhat more sympathetic than, say, Nurse Ratched or a finger-pointing harpy out of a dinner-theater production of "The Crucible." But can she be? No P.R. genius has been able to put Leona Helmsley or Mike Tyson back together again. Since the fate of an endless $40 million investigation and a water-treading Presidency may hang on the answer, I queried some of the best and the brightest of American image-builders for help. My experts -- whose problematic clients have included Michael Milken, Barbra Streisand and Geritol -- didn't exactly seem eager to take on Ms. Tripp's case, but they did offer some off-the-cuff tips. Ken Sunshine, who does P.R. for Leonardo DiCaprio, suggested that Ms. Tripp apologize for taping her friend "and then get a life." Failing that, she should "do a long print interview and a long TV interview where she comes off as a victim instead of a whiny tattletale running around bugging everyone." He also advised Ms. Tripp to change her hair -- "yet again" -- and "get a makeup consultant and a clothes consultant" and "rapidly develop a sense of humor" to counter her enemies' snickering. It wouldn't hurt either for Ms. Tripp to dump her own answer to Susan Carpenter-McMillan -- the grasping literary agent Lucianne Goldberg, who does Ms. Tripp "much more harm than good" by being "too over-the-top and too self-righteous." Ken Lerer is president of a firm that handles P.R. crises for Fortune 500 corporations and whose alumni include spinmeisters for both Bill Clinton (Michael McCurry) and Bob Dole (John Buckley). "I wouldn't know where to begin," Mr. Lerer said of Ms. Tripp, then added gravely, "I suppose she could go into the witness protection program." As a lesser alternative, he also proposed a public apology on a "prime-time TV show" -- though "one apology wouldn't fix it" -- and a separation from Ms. Goldberg. "They're like the cast of 'Side Show,' " he said, referring to the recent Broadway show about Siamese twins in a freak show. "They've morphed into one another, and that's hurting Tripp." The ad man Jerry Della Femina, who created Joe Isuzu to sell a Japanese car whose name no American could pronounce, has some sympathy for Ms. Tripp and enthusiastically offered slogans for selling her. "In the fine tradition of John Dean and Sammy the Bull!" he suggested -- as well as "She never ratted on George Bush!" Alas, CNN and The newyorker have reported, despite Ms. Tripp's denials, that while serving in the previous Administration she did spread gossip about Mr. Bush's personal life as well. That still leaves a fallback Della Femina slogan -- "99 percent of the time she doesn't tape what you say!" -- but she might more profitably provoke her ally Ken Starr into martyring her as he has Marcia Lewis and Susan McDougal. For Linda Tripp, shackles, not another new hairdo, might be just what the spin doctor ordered.

title: America Online Libel Suit Dismissed
body: In a decision that was heartening for Internet access providers, a Federal judge today dismissed a libel suit brought against America Online by a high-ranking aide to President Clinton. But the judge let stand a similar suit against Matt Drudge, the cyberspace gossip commentator. The judge, Paul L. Friedman of Federal District Court here, said that he was reluctant to dismiss the suit brought by Sidney Blumenthal against America Online but that the clear intent of Congress -- to protect Internet service providers from liability for material disseminated by them but created by others -- left him no choice. But in allowing the suit against Mr. Drudge to stand, the judge called the commentator "simply a purveyor of gossip" who had no right to the libel protections enjoyed by legitimate journalists. Judge Friedman's ruling, in a suit filed after Mr. Drudge reported old rumors of domestic trouble between Mr. Blumenthal and his wife, Jacqueline, is hardly the last word. The case is almost certain to be appealed to the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, and perhaps to the Supreme Court, which may be called upon to further refine how the First Amendment squares with news gathering and dissemination in the world of computers. The principals reacted to the ruling with caution, with the notable exception of Mr. Drudge. The Blumenthals' lawyer, Jo Bennett Marsh of Baltimore, said his clients were "elated by the court's recognition that Drudge is in no way 'a reporter, a journalist, or a news gatherer,' but is 'simply a purveyor of gossip,' who must answer for his defamation of the Blumenthals." Ms. Marsh said they would seek on appeal to have America Online reinstated as a defendant. George Vradenburg, the general counsel for America Online, said the ruling was consistent with Congress's intent to encourage diversity on the Internet, and with previous court decisions. Mr. Drudge's lawyer, Manuel Klausner of Los Angeles, said he would appeal. "We feel we have a strong case," Mr. Klausner said, adding that the judge had "inaccurately characterized what Mr. Drudge does with 'The Drudge Report.' " Mr. Drudge said by telephone from Los Angeles: "I'm going on the record. I'm not a journalist. I'm a kangaroo! I'll see Mr. Blumenthal in court." What Mr. Drudge does -- news, gossip or both -- has been heatedly debated in recent weeks. On the one hand, he has had some success in breaking news about the President's supposed involvement with other women. On the other hand, critics in the more traditional news organizations complain that he puts rumors and innuendo on his Web site without checking first. Last August, just as Mr. Blumenthal was starting work at the White House, Mr. Drudge publicized what he has since acknowledged as "reports on an old rumor" about troubles in the Blumenthal household. The next day, he ran a retraction and apology on his web site and in The Washington Post. But the Blumenthals were not satisfied and seek $30 million in damages. In dismissing the claim against America Online, Judge Friedman cited language from the Communications Decency Act passed by Congress in 1996 to prohibit the transmission of indecent material over computer networks. The act was overturned by the Supreme Court last year on free speech grounds, but Judge Friedman found its language regarding protection of Internet providers to be applicable, although he did so reluctantly. Because America Online has the right to exercise editorial control, the judge wrote, "it would seem only fair to hold A.O.L. to the liability standards applied to a publisher or, at least, like a bookstore owner or library, to the liability standards applied to a distributor. But Congress has made a different policy choice."

title: Behind Headlines on Study, a Couple Married to Their Work
body: LAST Friday, Donna L. HoffmanDonna L. Hoffman started the day knowing it would be far from routine. The journal Science had just published an article she co-wrote, a groundbreaking report demonstrating that lower-income black Americans are far less likely to have Internet access than whites of similar economic status. News reports about the study had already appeared. Dr. Hoffman is no stranger to sensitive topics. She and her husband and fellow researcher Thomas P. Novak, in their studies of the Internet, have touched on subjects like pornography. So, she expected her phone to start ringing early (most calls were from reporters) at her home in Nashville and at her office at Vanderbilt University, where she is an associate professor. Then she checked her email in box, which was quickly filling up. While some messages were requests for more information, many others were bilious, racist attacks. They not only questioned the study's validity but also expressed anger that such a study would be conducted at all. One man, saying he was "sick of quotas, whining, cultural sensitivity, etc.," remarked, "Why not put a Nike Swoosh on the computer boxes and sell them in Sneaker King?" She was used to strange email, but not to hate. Gary Chapman, director of the 21st Century Project at the University of Texas at Austin, who has worked to bring computer access to low-income communities, said the email was no surprise to him. "The Internet attracts racist speech," he said. "It's unacceptable to say these things in normal public discourse, but on the Internet it can be vented on a system that is essentially anonymous." The import of the Hoffman-Novak study, Mr. Chapman said, was that it pointed not just at who lacked Internet access but also at what was lacking on the Internet. "The results seem to suggest that content on the Internet isn't compelling enough to the African-American community," Mr. Chapman said. "They want to see something that reflects their view of the world, which is often hard to find on the Internet." Dr. Hoffman said few of the people sending racist comments appeared to have read the paper itself, which is available on the Web (www2000.ogsm.vanderbilt.edu/paper list.html), even though they had gone to some lengths to find her email address. "It was stunning," Dr. Hoffman said of such messages. "It points out that there clearly is a problem here, and much of the problem has to do with people's attitudes." The recent study published by Dr. Hoffman and Dr. Novak is not the first of theirs to attract attention. At the forefront of their field -- Internet marketing, an area in which they were pioneers -- the two scholars have a knack for picking topical subjects. For nearly 20 years, Drs. Hoffman and Novak, both 42, have intensely combined work and marriage. Not only do they specialize in the same area -- market segmentation and commercialization of the World Wide Web -- but they also conduct their research together and publish all papers jointly. "Some people might think it's overkill," Dr. Hoffman said. "But we've found it's really efficient to work together and play together." The couple started their careers as statisticians studying behavior. They met in 1978 as graduate students at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. "I thought Tom was too much of an Oberlin hippie, and he thought I was really snotty," Dr. Hoffman said. The frost thawed, however, and one night after a movie date, Dr. Hoffman went to Dr. Novak's apartment and "never left." They married in 1979. After stints at universities in newyork and Texas, they ended up at the Owen Graduate School of Management at Vanderbilt University in 1993. Soon after their arrival at Vanderbilt, they downloaded Mosaic, an early Web browser, for the first time and were immediately captivated by the potential of the Web. IN 1994 they started Project 2000 to study the marketing implications of commercializing the Web, and the program has become a pre-eminent research center for studying electronic commerce. Their recent study is the first to attach numbers to a situation that many people had only suspected. "Donna Hoffman and Tom Novak have brought serious quantitative methods to many of the tough social issues facing the Internet," said Marc Rotenberg, executive director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center in Washington. "They have set themselves apart from the pundits, market analysts and commentators." In 1995, Drs. Hoffman and Novak were the first to discredit the research of Marty Rimm, an undergraduate who asserted that the Internet was awash in pornography. "They put him through a Cuisinart," Gary Chapman said. They drew attention to themselves again later that year when they challenged the methodology underlying a demographic report that led to inflated estimates of the numer of Internet users. Dr. Hoffman, who has become something of a household name in computing circles, has eclipsed Dr. Novak in the limelight. She travels extensively, lecturing and attending conferences. When reporters call, she answers. Less outgoing by nature, Dr. Novak said he preferred to stay home and do research. Dr. Hoffman said she was completely taken aback by the invective that has poured into her computer over the past week. As of Tuesday, she had received close to 50 email messages, about 30 of them negative. Many critics have taken their opinions to the Net itself. More than 170 postings -- many similar in tone to the email Dr. Hoffman received -- have been made to a discussion forum on ZDNet (www.zdnet.com/zdnn/content/msnb/0417/ 307772.html). Given the speed with which things change on the Internet, Dr. Novak said, the data in the paper, collected more than a year ago, are already out of date. New numbers being gathered appear to paint a more optimistic picture. "We would expect that many more African-Americans will be on line when we look at the more recent numbers," he said. It will be interesting, he added, to see what kind of email the researchers receive once they publish the follow-up study, which they plan to do later this year. title:
DOWNTIME;
Musicians Tap Rich Lode of Sheet Music, Sold and Shared
body: DAVID TURNER's PC houses the equivalent of a music store on steroids. Mr. Turner, a retired architect who lives on isolated Marrowstone Island, Wash., regularly logs on to the Seattle-based Sunhawk page, where he scrolls through several popular, jazz and classical selections before selecting a piece of sheet music to download, print and play. Without this service, Mr. Turner would need to order the music by mail or make a 90-minute trek to Seattle. But Sunhawk offers him more than convenience. An amateur pianist, he is not always able to tell whether a certain piece is too complicated or too simple for him. Sunhawk allows him to download the song and preview the first page before he needs to pay anything. And a free utility plays the music, highlighting each note, which makes it easier to learn to perform it yourself. "It's pretty slick," Mr. Turner said. "You can sample it before you buy." A few hundred miles south in Castro Valley, Calif., Emmi Tarr regularly downloads choral and religious music, then sings songs as her PC plays them. Ms. Tarr, who does not play an instrument, finds the computer to be enough of an accompanist for her vocal practice. "I can sing my heart out and not need to get anyone to play the piano," she said. A systems engineer for a local software company, Ms. Tarr certainly has the computer literacy advantage. Still, she said, "anyone with an Internet connection can do this." Sunhawk contains around 2,000 songs, mostly from the Warner and EMI music publishing conglomerates. A similar site from the Hal Leonard Corporation, based in Minneapolis, provides a way for anyone with an Internet connection to download pristine versions of selected songs. The sites offer an immediacy that is exclusive to the Internet. For instance, someone who sees a song performed on a late-night talk show can log on immediately to buy the sheet music, even learning to play it on the spot. Neither Sunhawk nor Hal Leonard wants to antagonize its dealers, so they do not undercut retail prices. Sheets from the Hal Leonard site are priced the same way they are in stores. Sunhawk sheets run a dollar more, but that includes the playback mechanism (which could be a good tool for music education because if you see something spelled out for you, it is easier to play). The on-line sites' offerings can change with news events. Right after Tammy Wynette died earlier this month, Sunhawk's chief executive, Brent Mills, had his Nashville affiliate fax over a copy of her hit "Stand By Your Man." The sheet music, readable in the Sunhawk viewer, was on line within hours. Religious music is also gaining momentum on the Internet. A church can purchase a general license and download sheet music under the terms of that agreement. Craig Dunnagan, senior director of catalogue development for EMI Christian Music Publishing in Brentwood, Tenn., said churches had a voracious appetite for new music and were often looking for songs appropriate for current events or new sermon topics. The songs offered on the Worship Together site range from the traditional to newer selections, like Barbra Streisand's "Higher Ground." Gloria Zeigler, music director for Hebron United Methodist Church in Millersburg, Pa., is using the Worship Together site to develop what she calls "blended worship," a mix between more traditional and contemporary music sources. "I get bored singing the same thing over and over again," she said. "I am constantly looking for new songs. Music carries the service, and this gives me a way to keep the services interesting." Each week, Worship Together offers a free contemporary song. Mrs. Zeigler downloads it and plays the piece on her computer. If it is appropriate, she incorporates the song into the Sunday service. "The congregation loves this kind of music," she said. "There were people literally dancing around the pastor, saying, 'Why didn't we do this before?' " But the music publishers have some less legitimate company on the Web, sites that illegally offer thousands of copyrighted lyrics, chords and the musical notation called guitar tablature. Here, guitarists can log on and print out a version of a popular song that was transcribed by someone without the permission of the composer or publisher. In a sense, the guitar archives, which started out as newsgroups, continue the folk music tradition in which songs are reinterpreted as they are passed from one person to another. A veteran folk singer, Noel Paul Stookey of Peter, Paul and Mary, himself a songwriter, would never begrudge his contemporaries any royalties. But he doesn't find sites like the On-Line Guitar Archive especially threatening. "It's sort of like what you do for friends on a napkin," he said. Graham Nash (of Crosby, Stills and Nash) is even more tolerant of the process. "It's the same as learning it from the record," he said. "If you just want to log on, learn a new tune in the morning and play it on stage in the evening, I don't see why you should be charged for that." Copyright aside, many players will find these sites' egregious inaccuracies annoying. Cal Woods, a co-founder of the Olga , a site for guitar music, acknowledged the problem and said users could submit corrections if they found mistakes. "We have a money-back guarantee," he said irreverently. He added that the audience for Olga was hobbyists who would normally trade songs within the context of a campfire or a garage band, not professional musicians. FOR some, the free flow of songs recalls bygone days. Mr. Stookey said: "The Internet is a little like Greenwich Village in the 1960's. You can do your new song for an audience, and the recording industry would be six months behind. In a sense you were giving it away, but it's part of building a constituency and building an awareness of the material." Mr. Nash said: "Musicians want to communicate with as many people as possible once we've written a song. I agree that we should make money for our art, but this is a gray area. What would they do after they learn the song? If they just play it in their little band, then they shouldn't have to pay for it. If they end up recording it, we get a royalty, so what's the harm?" Musicians do not have to pay royalties on songs in the public domain, like several of the offerings on the new Peter, Paul and Mary collection called "Around the Campfire." (No one receives a royalty from songs like "Kumbaya.") Mr. Stookey said that improvements in electronic commerce would make high-quality music more accessible. "Today, it can be difficult for a patron to support the arts," he said. "Once there is an easy bridge between the payment process and the access to material, the customer will feel more legal and end up with a beautiful piece of work." (Peter DaSilva for The newyork Times)

title: Faking Pain and Suffering In Internet Support Groups
body: A MONK who had taken a vow of poverty could not seek treatment for a rapidly advancing type of cancer and faced death with fear and loneliness. A 23-year-old woman, hospitalized for an eating disorder, suffered a stroke. A teen-age girl mourning the death of one premature baby gave birth to another, tinier and more fragile than the first. Three lost souls with heart-rending stories, they clicked their way to Internet support groups, where they elicited outpourings of sympathy from fellow sufferers. All three were incorrigible fakers. They lied their way into networks of people with real troubles who had come to care about one another and to think of themselves as communities. For months the frauds strung along their on-line audiences, which included many people who were living through genuine crises and tragedies but who had nonetheless extended themselves to comfort others. Eventually, tripped up by their own lies and confronted by their victims, the intruders withdrew. But they had broken the trust of the groups they invaded, leaving members hurt, angry, embarrassed and suspicious of one another. Dr. Marc D. Feldman, a psychiatrist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, said that he had been hearing of more and more people pretending to be sick so they could join Internet support groups. "I've been alerted to about a dozen cases over the past several months, and it seems to be increasing in frequency," said Dr. Feldman, an expert on illnesses that people either feign or actually induce in themselves, which are called factitious disorders. "Lately, whenever I speak on factitious disorders, 100 percent of the time somebody will raise their hand and tell me about such an experience with the Internet," he said. "It's a trend. Virtual factitious disorders." There are no hard numbers on how many people use the Internet in this way, and the Net is certainly a mirror for everything that occurs in the rest of life. But the Internet does lend itself to deception, as people who worry about sexual predators have often noted. In the medical arena, it also offers anonymous access to vast amounts of information on illnesses and support groups for even the rarest diseases, thus opening up a new world of opportunities for people with the urge to pretend they are sick. The medical profession has known about factitious disorders for hundreds of years. The most extreme form is Munchausen syndrome, named in 1951 after Baron Munchausen, a spinner of fantastic tales in 18th-century Germany. People with Munchausen syndrome go to incredible lengths to appear sick or actually make themselves sick: they have been known to bleed themselves to become anemic, fake seizures, take laxatives to induce diarrhea, inject themselves with bacteria to produce fevers or rub chemicals into their skin to cause rashes. In one case, Dr. Feldman said, a woman shaved her head and lost 50 pounds to convince others that she was receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer. People with Munchausen syndrome who have medical training are especially convincing, and others read up on diseases so they can mimic symptoms accurately. Some become so good at it that they fool doctors into ordering needless tests and sometimes even operations. Munchausen syndrome tends to be chronic, and people with it will do these things again and again, wandering from one emergency room to another to find an unsuspecting audience each time. About 20 years ago, psychiatrists recognized an especially dangerous form of the disorder, which they named Munchausen by proxy. It refers to parents who repeatedly seek medical attention for their children, whose symptoms they make up or induce, sometimes causing real harm to the children and subjecting them to operations they do not need. Why would anyone do such terrible things? Dr. Feldman said most people with factitious disorders were "longing for nurturing, sympathy, care and concern that they feel unable to get in appropriate ways." They also like being treated as heroes and admired for their courage in the face of adversity. "But some may have a bit of sadistic motivation in that they get some glee in deceiving others," Dr. Feldman said. "We call it 'duping delight.' " Those who like to fool people are especially fond of deceiving doctors. "I've been scammed a few times myself," Dr. Feldman said. "I'm an expert on lying and deceit, and I think it sometimes becomes a particular challenge to see if they can mislead me." He has a Web site about factitious disorders (ourworld.compuserve.com/ homepages/MarcFeldman2) and a woman who visited the site emailed him to say she had a severe case of the disorder. She asked for a referral to a therapist in another state. He made several calls on her behalf and emailed her a recommendation. Then, he said, "she replied that she had made it all up and since I was a world expert on lying, surely I must have known that." The Internet seems almost to have been made for people with Munchausen syndrome. "It is famous for these virtual support groups which are unabashedly nurturing," Dr. Feldman said. "For someone who feels hungry for attention and sympathy, one is guaranteed to get that promptly by falsely claiming an ailment." The vast resources of the Internet also make it easier to cook up a story. "Medical information is so readily available," Dr. Feldman said. "You can type the most esoteric ailment into a search engine and get back dozens of pages dealing with it." It is, of course, easier to fool people who cannot see you or hear your voice: there is no need to shave your head or lose 50 pounds. "These patients have often injected themselves with bacteria," Dr. Feldman said. "Here, one can sit in one's bathrobe and not have to engage in those grisly things and reap the same benefits." The proliferation of newsgroups and chat rooms also offers a seemingly limitless audience for tales of woe. Instead of wandering from hospital to hospital, people can click from one support group to another. Some, pretending to be ill, have joined more than one, and some sign onto a single group more than once, using different names and acting out different roles. In one case brought to Dr. Feldman's attention, a 23-year-old woman said she had an eating disorder and an abusive boyfriend she was hiding from and told people in a chat room that she was communicating with them via laptop from an intensive care unit. At times she claimed to be in shock and typed garbled messages that alarmed visitors to the chat room, who became quite concerned about her. One night she went so far as to have a stroke on line. Her mother took over the laptop and issued progress reports, but then she, too, had to be admitted to the hospital. Sometimes the father went on line as well. The devil was in the details, and regulars in the chat room eventually began to realize that too much of the story did not make sense. All the characters misspelled the same words in the same way, and a call to the hospital where the mother and daughter had supposedly been admitted revealed that the intensive care unit was not equipped for patients to plug in laptops. Chased out of the eating-disorder chat room, the woman turned up in others, including one for sexual-abuse survivors. She was found out and banished from that one, too, then joined another group. When last heard from, she was dying of AIDS. "I don't need to tell you how much pain this causes others who believe her," one of the people who had been deceived wrote to Dr. Feldman. In the case of the monk with cancer, Dr. Feldman said, people in his support group began to wonder how somebody who was supposed to be so sick could find the energy to send so many messages. Also, he seemed to be hanging on an awfully long time for a man with a lethal illness. When a member finally confronted him in a personal email message, he confessed that he was neither a monk nor a cancer patient. He withdrew from the group and vanished, though he may well have surfaced elsewhere with a new user name and a new set of symptoms. In another scam that dragged on for months last year, a girl who said she was 15 communicated on line with parents of premature infants. The 400 or so members in the virtual support group had babies who were or had been critically ill and had spent months in the hospital. Some of the infants died, and some who survived were expected to suffer lifelong disabilities. The teen-age newcomer, who called herself Kim, claimed to have a tiny preemie. As she detailed the ups and downs of his treatment, members of the group worried along with her,became personally involved with her by email and were devastated when she said her baby had died. Soon after, Kim came back on line, saying she was pregnant again and feared that the second baby would also be born too soon. Sure enough, it was, and the roller-coaster ride began again, narrated at turns by Kim and her aunt, complete with vivid details of brain hemorrhages and heart surgery that rubbed raw the emotions of many parents who had really lived through such desperate hours. By regular mail, Kim sent some members Christmas cards bearing the infant's footprints. Mara Tesler Stein of Chicago, a psychologist and the mother of twins born prematurely, was one of those who became involved with Kim on line. But she gradually became suspicious and confronted the girl. Kim posted a lengthy confession and apology to the group. The second baby had been stillborn, she said; she claimed that she had concealed the death because she could not face it herself. The aunt was a figment of her imagination, she said, but she hastened to add that the footprints in the Christmas cards had been real. But members of the group learned that she had lifted the prints off another family's Web site, and they wondered whether Kim had ever had any children at all. They will probably never know. She withdrew from the group and was taken off the list by its owner. A reporter was unable to get in contact with her. "I have a gut feeling that some things she said were probably true," Dr. Stein said. "People who do this need something. I wonder if it's a metaphor for some other loss she experienced and is playing over and over again in different shapes." Regardless of what drove Kim, her behavior had a chilling effect on a group that had been trusting and closely knit. Some parents expressed feelings of betrayal, and many stopped posting messages. People in the group agreed to provide information so a coordinator could verify that they really were parents of preemies. Some newcomers were put off by the atmosphere of suspicion. In the past few months, the group has bounced back, Dr. Stein said, but those who encountered Kim will never view new postings in quite the same way. "Will anyone believe me when I need support when something odd happens to my baby?" Dr. Stein said. "You don't know if you'll get what you need anymore." Graphic   Photos: NOT EASILY FOOLED -- Dr. Marc D. Feldman, an expert on faked illnesses. (Mike Clemmer for The New York Times)(pg. G7); And excerpt from an email message from someone who called herself Kim and said she had lied to an on-line support group about the extended illness of a premature baby. Later, support group members questioned whether even the confession was true. (pg. G1)

title: Kids, Can You Spell Spy?
body: Abetted by Harry Recon, Ace Photo Recon Pigeon and a bomb-sniffing dog named Bogart, the Central Intelligence Agency has created a children's page on the Internet replete with an option for virtual cloak-and-dagger disguises for curious little nippers. "This is not an effort to recruit," a spokesman for the spy agency emphasizes. "This is an effort to inform in a fun way." With an open smile of welcome from a virtual agent in a virtual trench coat, the "ciakids" page carries the once passionately furtive agency a playful step further into public notice, this time under the prod of a Presidential directive that Government agencies tell citizens, young and old, what they actually do. The Langley, Va., espionage establishment comes across as something other than Mr. Rogers's neighborhood. Describing the tasks of a C.I.A. overseas officer, the kids page does not quite specify the false identities, murderous plots (currently renounced as Government policy), theft of other governments' secrets or inducements of others to treason by way of sex and shakedowns that are part of the officer's job. Rather, young visitors trying to imagine themselves in the trade are informed: "You would like to work with people from all over the world, be able to adapt to any situation (especially dangerous ones!), be well educated, know other languages, be good at working with other kinds of people and be courageous, well disciplined and able to accept anonymity." The children's page is separate from, but accessible to, the C.I.A.'s main web page, which offers reams of adult information on "the ultimate overseas career" in the agency's Clandestine Service, whose requisites include psychiatric tests. Spiced with trivia quizzes on world geography and history, the kids page features Nathan Hale, who had but one life to give for his country, not Aldrich Ames, who sold it out. The spy tales are noble and simple, with never a mention of the lethal treacheries of double agents or such infamous C.I.A. moments as the bungled Bay of Pigs invasion. "Intelligence is information needed by our nation's leaders, also known as policy makers, to keep our country safe," the children are informed. "Policy makers, like the President, do not have time to read all the other countries' newspapers. There are just too many of them." While the "Home Page for Kids," reachable at www.odci.gov/cia/ciakids, hardly invites young ones out into the cold, it does hint at the romantic patriotism to be imagined in the spy's life. "When they say spies come from the most unlikely places, they are right," declares James Armistead Lafayette, a black American spy from the Revolutionary War who is featured on the page's historic figures section. "I crossed enemy lines and Britain's General Cornwallis recruited me to spy! I returned to the Americans, and we planned how to fool him!" Page visitors may not be able to resist taking a clicking shortcut at the question: "Want to try on a disguise?" Alas, the fun of going undercover in appropriate mufti is not to be had without an extra computer program called Shockwave plug-in. "We're starting to get hits," said Tom Crispell, a C.I.A. spokesman, referring to page users. "We've gotten feedback. Kids enjoy it." The spirit of the page and its various tangents is not quite up to the cold war's youthful idealism personified by Pavel Morozov, a 13-year-old Soviet boy who became a hero of the regime in 1932 by taking the game seriously and informing on his father for harboring fugitive landlords. (Angry villagers later killed the cheeky Pavel, but that's a story for another Web page.) Harry Recon, Ace Photo Recon Pigeon, is a smiling cartoon character invented for the page with no allusion apparently intended to U-2 reconnaissance planes. User friendly Harry and his sister, Aerial, reflect the confident eye of President Harry S. Truman, who signed the agency into law 47 years ago. Bogart the dog, on the other hand, is from reality, modeled on the canine corps that helps secure the Langley compound round the clock from intruders. Bogart and a pack of colleague pooches are available as virtual guard dogs to escort young visitors -- authorized with virtual badges -- around the agency's electronic campus. The welcoming C.I.A. officers present a politically correct balance of images, a smiling white man and a waving black woman. Notably, there is a woman still referred to "355," an undercover operative in the Culper Ring, an intelligence net in the newyork and Long Island settlements during the Revolution. "Our ring practiced much of the trade craft that latter-day intelligence gatherers did," notes 355, "corresponding in secret ink, dead drops (leaving information in specified places to be retrieved), and code, all in an effort to get our intelligence product to General Washington." With already close to 1,000 visitors on some days, the ciakids page is open to one and all, said Mr. Crispell, the agency spokesman, implying that there is less to hide than the public might suspect. "We want to get kids on the information superhighway," he said, adding that the C.I.A. intends no more exotic destinations than the net itself in inviting children to stop by and feel at home.
