title:
LIBRARY/ON-LINE BOOKSTORES;
Browsing Books in Cyberspace
body: WILL on-line bookstores someday doom the small, independently owned bookstore? One visit to Readers' Books in Sonoma, Calif., is reminder enough that such an outcome would be one of the sadder byproducts of electronic retailing in the late 20th century. Owned by Andy and Lilla Weinberger, Readers' Books is a homespun maze of book-lined rooms. The store's walls are covered with snapshots of regular customers and authors who have given readings. The building was once a bakery, and the remnants of a large oven in the children's section prompted one little boy to ask, "Is that where they make the books?" Mr. Weinberger, who turns cranky at the mention of on-line bookstores, said he knew more than half the people who entered the store every day. He also knows their literary tastes and routinely calls customers if a book arrives that he thinks will appeal to them. The Weinbergers hold frequent readings at the store and often serve refreshments. "Hah!" Mr. Weinberger said triumphantly. "That's another thing you won't get at Amazon," he added, referring to one of his huge on-line rivals. Readers' Books has just 18,000 titles in stock -- minuscule by the standards of the big on-line stores -- but they are carefully selected. Say you are interested in one of this year's literary milestones, Mark Harman's new translation, based on a restored manuscript, of "The Castle" by Franz Kafka. Die-hard Kafka readers were eager to run their hands over the handsome jacket, to flip randomly among its 328 pages and to ponder the subtle changes from the original translation. Not only did a junior staff member at Readers' Books know about the new "Castle" translation, but he found it on the shelf and took it to the front. Delivery time: 57 seconds. If a book needs to be specially ordered, it often arrives within a few days, which is roughly the time it takes for a book to arrive from cyberspace. There is no discount up front, but customers get $20 off after spending $200. Can an on-line bookstore offer even a close approximation of that experience? No, it cannot. Yet an on-line bookstore can give its customers a very different and, some might argue, equally rewarding experience. Since Amazon.com first went on the Web in 1995, on-line bookstores have sprouted all over cyberspace. According to a recent Prudential Securities report, there are now more than 600 of them worldwide. While none can compete with the ambiance of Readers' Books, they frequently offer superior prices, selection and convenience. What this means, sadly enough, is that people often get a richer experience from the collection of electrons that is Amazon.com, with its many lists, customer reviews and custom-tailored book recommendations, than they would, say, at their local Crown Books.  Amazon: The Web's Pioneer AMAZON.COM FOUR years ago, Jeff Bezos quit his Wall Street job and headed across the country. He ended up in Seattle, where he started Amazon.com from his garage. Now he employs 1,000 people. Though still not profitable, the company has gone public, and among the wired crowd the word Amazon conjures books, not rivers. Amazon has had nearly three years to polish its act. Its search function is simple and powerful. Its catalogue -- 2.5 million titles if you count the out-of-print ones -- is so exhaustive that it doubles as a reliable tool for researching extant literature on any given topic. And Amazon keeps coming up with interesting new features. A search with the word Castle immediately brought up Mark Harman's new translation of Kafka's "Castle" as the top search result. The reader is swiftly treated to a page of reviews and analysis and even the Amazon staff's own evocative synopsis of the book. You can read what others who have already bought the book think of it. You see a photograph of the jacket and are told that if the book is ordered, it will leave Amazon's Seattle warehouse in less than 24 hours. Still better, Amazon's price -- $17.50 -- is 30 percent off the jacket price. Just a few clicks later, your order is in. Within six hours of taking the order, the company sends email reporting that the book was on its way. All this, and you have not even left your desk. Amazon's year-old service for finding out-of-print books is another smart move. Given the rate at which books now disappear from Books in Print, it is very useful. Perhaps the most entertaining feature on Amazon is the page of customer reviews that accompanies many books. Anyone can chime in. If a book is particularly popular or controversial, it is not unusual to see more than 100 customer reviews. "An embarrassment for Grisham and a complete waste of time" was verdict No. 26 on John Grisham's "Street Lawyer" from an dissatisfied customer who wrote in from the Midwest.  Book Giant Has Quirks On Internet BARNESANDNOBLE.COM IN the past year, ever since the debut of Barnesandnoble.com, it has been difficult to open a newspaper or click on a popular Web site without seeing an advertisement for the new on-line bookstore. Still playing catch-up with Amazon.com, the Barnes & Noble site plans to reach $100 million in sales by the end of this year. The site is now the exclusive bookseller on America Online. With more than 1.5 million books in its catalogue -- 600,000 in stock -- the Barnes & Noble site offers one of the largest collections of titles on the Internet. But it's a quirky collection. "Do we know books or what?" is a clever line from an advertisement for the site. Apparently, it does not know all books. A search for "The Castle" came up with the passe 1930 translation, a copy in the original German and, for good measure, in Spanish -- but no trace of the new translation by Mark Harman. On price, Barnesandnoble.com offers no real advantage. According to the Prudential survey, it was comparable to Amazon.com on 80 percent of the books found at both sites. When it comes to delivery, the Barnes & Noble site makes the same promise as Amazon.com: products are shipped within 24 hours, although the book I ordered from the Barnes & Noble site arrived one day later than a similar order placed at the same time with Amazon.com. What's more impressive is the Barnes & Noble site's ability to attract celebrity authors. It was the first to offer real-time chats with authors, who have included Tom Clancy, Anne Rice and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. More than 2,500 people showed up for the Drew Carey chat. All the chats are archived on the site. email interactions with the customer service folks at the Barnes & Noble site are relatively swift, compared with their counterparts at Amazon.com, who are pleasant but slow. But the missives fired off by the Barnesandnoble.com service staff -- with heartfelt sign-offs from "Jeff" and "Victor" -- are obviously form letters. You might think that Barnes & Noble would have turned its geographical ubiquity into an added convenience for customers. But try returning a book you have bought from the on-line bookstore to one of the company's 483 physical bookstores and you will be rebuffed. Quiz Jeff or Victor and in robotic fashion they will explain -- after thanking you profusely for your inquiry -- that the physical bookstores are a separate entity from the on-line service. No wonder the Web site has a cluttered feel to it. It offers a surfeit of choices that tend to afflict visitors with shopping mall space-out, a condition that can lead to impulsive buying. That may be precisely what the site's designers had in mind.  Good on Price and Features but Not on Speed WWW.BOOKS.COM ALSO known as Book Stacks Unlimited, Books.com is great on price but short on finesse. It claims to have an incredible 4 million titles in its database (200,000 of which can be shipped on any given day), and it can beat both its rivals on price most of the time, but it is generally slower getting books into themail. The Books.com site is now one of the few on-line bookstores that feature readings and interviews via Real Audio. A recent makeover included some ambitious technical tricks like creating separate frames for different areas of the store. But the frames seem to slow down the loading of pages on the screen while offering unclear benefits. Books.com got a passing grade on the "Castle" test: the book was available but the presentation was uninspired. A fuzzy photo of the book jacket is the sole adornment to the listing. Books.com beat Amazon.com on price by five cents, but it did not have the book available to ship for two to three days. And not unlike K.'s experience with the elusive inhabitants of the hilltop castle, attempts to communicate with customer service representatives at Books.com were met initially with silence. Once they did respond, they were helpful and personable. The store keeps a running count of the number of "booklovers" visiting the site at any one time, yet the storekeepers seem to have only the vaguest notion of what a passion for books actually means. The site did not waste any time featuring the Pulitzer Prize-winning autobiography by Katharine Graham on its front page after the announcement of the prize, albeit with Mrs. Graham's first name misspelled beneath the book -- a mistake that could have been avoided simply by taking a closer look at the jacket. Had whoever typed the caption actually read the book, he or she would have known that the misspelling of Mrs. Graham's first name is something that she particularly dislikes.  A Focus on Digital Lore COMPUTERLITERACY.COM IN 1996, an on-line bookstore in Silicon Valley called CBooks Express started up, specializing in computer-related books. A year later, in a tail-wags-dog move, the young company acquired a well-established physical store called Computer Literacy Bookshops. The combined result, the Computer Literacy site, is perhaps the most comprehensive collection of computer-specific titles in existence. For people looking for a pure selection of computer and technical books, Computer Literacy should be their first stop. Computer Literacy lists 250,000 titles and stocks 30,000 books are available for shipping on the day orders are placed. Several of the most popular titles are discounted by 40 percent. Computer Literacy is free of frills. Its home page is a simple affair that contains a minimum of exclamation marks and other attention-seeking devices. The site's current best seller is "Samba," and it is not a book about Brazilian dance. It is a book about the marriage of the Unix and Windows computer operating systems. (Neither Amazon.com nor the Barnes & Noble site carries this book.) Do a search for titles related to Java and you will not get distracted by any books about coffee or islands in Indonesia. You will see a list of 503 volumes on the Java programming language. Not all the books are ultratechnical. The site also has a comprehensive collection of books that covering the business and culture of the computer industry. Computer Literacy also has four physical locations. On-line listings are cross-referenced with the physical bookstores, so if you see a book on the Web site, you can look to see if it is in stock at, say, the San Jose store, and go pick it up. And yes, if you buy a book from the Web site, you can return it at any of the physical stores. Are you listening, Barnes & Noble? Graphic   Photos. (Naum Kazhdan/The New York Times)

title:
Q & A;
Who Needs The WWW?
body: Q. I thought all World Wide Web addresses had to have www in them, but I've seen some that don't. How can this be? A. Let's break down the average Web address, known as a Uniform Resource Locator (U.R.L.) into bite-size parts. As an example, we'll use http://www.nytimes.com. You might assume that it is www that tells the computer that this is a Web site, but that is not the case. The first part of the U.R.L. is what points you to the Web. That http:// stands for hypertext transfer protocol, which is the method Web-server computers use to connect to the Web. The last part of the U.R.L., nytimes.com, is the domain name. The www is a common Internet standard indicating that the computer you're trying to reach is a Web server. But it's not mandatory, and it is not part of the domain name. Depending on how the system's administrators chose to set up their site, the www may be a required part of the U.R.L. (as in the case of www.nytimes.com). Some sites have opted to skip the www as part of their addresses (as in netsol.com) and some have set up electronic pointers that will direct those who type www.netsol.com to the right page. And some Web browsers, like the current versions of Netscape Navigator and Microsoft Internet Explorer, will helpfully insert thehttp://www. and the .com for you. If you use one of these, you can type nytimes in the address box and it will take you there.   J. D. BIERSDORFER  Circuits invites questions about computer-based technology to QandA@nytimes.com by email, or by postal mail to Questions, Circuits, The newyork Times, 229 West 43d Street, newyork, N.Y. 10036-3959.

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
I.B.M. Leads Dow Higher As Most Indexes Set Records
body: Major stock market indexes set new highs yesterday, buoyed by quarterly corporate earnings reports that largely exceeded analysts' reduced forecasts. I.B.M. soared 6 13/16, to 118, the leading gainer of the Dow Jones industrial average. I.B.M.'s strength accounted for more than 33 points of the Dow average's 43.1-point gain. So far this week, I.B.M. has gained 10 1/4 points, initially rising on expectations of a strong earnings report. The Dow closed at 9,184.94, beating its record of 9,167.50 set last Friday. Standard & Poor's 500 index rose 3.02 points, to 1,126.67, its third consecutive record. Technology, drugs, banking and energy shares were among the leaders on the S.& P. 500, reflecting the better-than-expected earnings performance of companies in those industries. Despite the further advances into record territory, market action this week has been less than robust. Investors have been selective in deciding which stocks and sectors to move higher. Prior to favorable earnings reports yesterday from Chase Manhattan, Citicorp, Banc One and Mellon, for example, financial services and banking shares had been lagging. "I just think that expectations got overly depressed," Marshall Acuff, an equity strategist at Salomon Smith Barney, said. "The earnings are not that great; they're just not that bad." Mr. Acuff pointed to I.B.M., which rose despite reporting a 13 percent drop in first-quarter profits as a result of price competition in personal computers and weakness in Asia. The stock rose because investors were encouraged that the results, released after the market had closed Monday, showed increases in software and services revenues. Unlike Intel and Compaq Computer, which reported earnings last week that also exceeded analysts' reduced forecasts, I.B.M. did not warn of coming problems. "What companies are saying is maybe the worst is behind us and the wolf is not at the door," Mr. Acuff said. The market was also helped by demand for small, Internet-related shares, which pushed the Nasdaq composite index 16.73 points higher, to 1,903.87, its third consecutive record. Linking its fate to the Internet proved a boon to Market Guide, a company based in Lake Success, N.Y., that compiles financial data and research on public companies. Its stock rose almost 200 percent, or 15 1/16, to 23, after the company signed a deal to make its financial research available to America Online users. Shares of 7th Level, an educational and entertainment software developer, rose 7 7/16, to 9 1/4, after the software maker said its character-animation technology would be distributed by Wavephore, a network and data provider. It was the most active issue yesterday, as more than 29 million shares traded, compared with slightly more than 100,000 on Monday. The company's animation technology helps create interactive animation that can be sent over the Internet and other networked systems. Wavetop, a Wavephore unit, broadcasts graphics, sound and text to personal computers without the delays associated with modems and the Internet. Despite the price gains, 7th Level's stock price remains below the $10-a-share level at which it went public in October 1994. Gains in those shares followed a strong rise in K-tel International on Monday. K-tel closed yesterday at 43 7/8, up 2 1/4 and up from 6 5/8 a week ago, after the music retailer said it planned to sell records through the Internet. But investor interest in Internet-related stocks seems limited to the smaller companies with more opportunities for huge growth, as larger Internet concerns like Yahoo and Excite have lagged in recent days. Yahoo closed at 123 9/32, down 2 15/32. Excite closed at 72 3/4, up 1 1/16. "You can't say they're overvalued because they don't have any multiples because they haven't earned any money," Alfred Goldman, director of market analysis at A. G. Edwards, said of the rising shares. "It's just a love affair." Mr. Acuff of Salomon Smith Barney, however, said that the interest in Internet shares reflected confidence in the market. "That's not usually unhealthy unless it is more pervasive," he said. "If all Nasdaq was taking off it would be something to be concerned about." title: Physics on the Web Is Putting Science Journals on the Line
body: Every day, tens of thousands of physicists in more than 100 countries point their Web browsers to a site maintained by the Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico. There, they peruse research papers that have been posted since their last visit, trolling for new work in, say, quantum cosmology or statistical mechanics, and send email to one another based on the day's postings. Many of them no longer read print journals. They don't need to. The Los Alamos archive -- a vast repository of physics preprints, or E-prints -- is the primary means for today's physicists to exchange information. The archive is the product of nearly seven years of effort on the part of Paul Ginsparg, a 42-year-old physicist who believes that the Internet is ushering in the end of paper-based communication among research scientists. In particular, Dr. Ginsparg's system is a direct challenge to the hallowed 200-year-old practice of peer review, the process by which a scientific paper is evaluated by colleagues before it is published. "Traditional peer review has always been an awkward compromise imposed by the inadequacies of the paper medium," he said. The Los Alamos archive's following has fueled a debate among scientists from a cross-section of disciplines. Some view Dr. Ginsparg's achievement as intellectual history in the making -- a harbinger of what lies in store for all scientific discourse. Others eye it warily, calling it an anomaly in science, well suited to physics perhaps, but not easily adapted to other, larger disciplines like medicine. Peer review upholds a central tenet of scientific publishing: only after careful scrutiny by experts who vouch that a fellow scientist's work is worthy -- that it contains no errors and repeats no earlier work -- should a paper be published. While Dr. Ginsparg's archive has no traditional peer review per se, scientists who post their papers to the Los Alamos site typically revise their submissions in response to direct feedback from others. "Subsequent revisions frequently benefit as much or more from this feedback as from any conventional referee process," said Dr. Ginsparg in an interview that was, at his insistence, conducted entirely by email. The site (http://xxx.lanl.gov) also employs what Dr. Ginsparg calls version control, meaning that any earlier version in a series of revisions can be viewed. Dr. Ginsparg, highly regarded as a high-energy particle theorist, did not set out to build a digital Alexandria. He started it in 1991 to speed the distribution of drafts to other theoretical physicists. He wrote the software for the original system in his spare time, building much of it via a connection between the Los Alamos Lab and his home, 20 miles away "in the middle of nowhere between two Indian pueblos." For years the entire system resided in a computer under a table in Dr. Ginsparg's office. When noise from the fan and disk drive grew too annoying, he moved it down the hall. Since then, Dr. Ginsparg has added 30 subdisciplines to the site and separate sections for mathematics and so-called nonlinear sciences like evolution. Computer scientists will soon join, too. More than 35,000 people visit the site each day. A colorful presence in science, Dr. Ginsparg is known for thinking against the grain. He argues that traditional peer review -- controlled by scientific journals -- will evolve into a system in which refereeing is separated from publishing. He does not disguise his disdain for scientific journals, many of which he believes are unnecessary intermediaries, slow-moving and run by profiteers. Some scientists believe that electronic systems like Dr. Ginsparg's are actually changing the scientific process itself, especially considering the months that usually pass between the time a paper is submitted to a print journal and its publication.  Moreover, say some, the worldwide readership of the archive quickly discovers errors and helps eliminate research duplication. Skeptics of Internet publishing say that its long-term archival ability has not been established. They also worry about having a system dependent on one person or machine. Dr. Ginsparg, who receives funding from the National Science Foundation and the Department of Energy for the archive, has taken steps to allay such fears. The information on the archive is duplicated, on more than a dozen Web sites, and the American Physical Society is planning to incorporate the archive into its publishing operation by way of crosslinks and references. Other scientists have voiced concern about the quality of work published electronically. But the Los Alamos system stands in contrast to freewheeling Internet news groups where anyone can muse on quantum mechanics without so much as freshman calculus. "We try to maintain the ivory tower isolation to protect us from random passers-by interrupting our seminars," Dr. Ginsparg said. In practical terms, that means that submissions from, say, aol.com or hotmail.com get bounced. As a result, the quality of submissions to the archive remains consistently high. "There seems to have been no serious problem of people submitting inappropriate matter, or papers so badly written as to chiefly constitute a waste of the readers' time," said Charles Bennett, a physicist at the International Business Machines Corporation. "I can't say that of themail I get in my mailbox or my email inbox." Another point of contention the archive has brought into sharp focus is prepublication. The journals' practice of restricting dissemination of findings prior to publication can run counter to the authors' interests, said Dr. Ginsparg. Now even the most stalwart journals are making concessions. While editors at the prestigious Nature do not encourage posting a paper to a site like Dr. Ginsparg's, they do not forbid it. "E-print servers to my mind are an extension of an idea," said Philip Campbell, Nature's editor in chief. "It's just a form of intra-scientific communication." But while Dr. Ginsparg's system might work well for physics, its suitability for other fields is open to question. "Physics is a small community of people, and what they put out on their Web site is not going to affect the health of thousands or millions of people," said Jerome Kassirer, editor of the New England Journal of Medicine, which publishes 10 percent of the papers it receives. As for peer review, Dr. Kassirer said, "like democracy it's the only thing we have that really does work." Not surprisingly, Dr. Ginsparg disagreed. "The question is whether we can do without peer review as organized by multinational commercial publishers," he said. "If the answer is yes, the likely benefit is a far more efficient and far more functional system, better adapted to the needs of researchers." Alan Guth, a well-known cosmologist at Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a regular reader of Dr. Ginsparg's archive, said, "The journals are now playing the role of being historical arbiters of truth rather than real disseminators on a day-to-day basis." If Dr. Ginsparg is right, it could spell the demise of the journals themselves, relegating them "decorative paperweights." William Loughlin, physical sciences bibliographer at the University of Georgia, said of Dr. Ginsparg, "He makes the publishers very, very nervous." Other experiments with scientific communication and peer review are beginning to emerge. The Medical Journal of Australia is trying Web-based peer review. Biomedical researchers at the University of Pittsburgh are conducting the first all-electronic peer review under a National Institutes of Health grant. And a group of university administrators has proposed a decoupling system for peer review that would have an independent board of experts certify a paper, free of ties to any journal. Still, some of Dr. Ginsparg's admirers are disappointed that, after seven years, his system remains the exception. Ever concerned about promotion, tenure and their general reputation, even most of the scientists who now read the archive continue to submit their work to journals after posting it to Los Alamos. "Sooner or later someone is going to be shrewd and prophetic enough torealize that Paul has quietly done something absolutely monumental," said Stevan Harnad, director of the Cognitive Sciences Centre at Southampton University in England, who has built an archive modeled after the Los Alamos system. "When the historians write the history of it all, Paul Ginsparg will certainly get the full credit for having shown the way, not just by pointing, but by actually constructing the ultimate solution." Graphic   Photo: In his home between two Indian pueblos, Dr. Paul Ginsparg, 42, built an electronic archive system that is changing the face of scientific discourse. (Douglas Merriam for The New York Times)

title: Small Browser Concession From Microsoft
body: On the eve of a courtroom confrontation with the Justice Department, the Microsoft Corporation said yesterday that it would give personal computer makers an option on the first screen they present to computer users. The issue of Microsoft's control of what people see when they turn on their computers -- through its near-monopoly of the market for personal computer operating system software -- has come under increasing scrutiny recently from the Government and become the subject of increasing criticism within the industry. With the rise of the Internet, the personal computer is a gateway to a widening realm of on-line commerce and entertainment. Through its Windows operating system, which runs more than 85 percent of the world's personal computers, Microsoft, if unchecked, could have a chokehold on the Internet, the company's critics say. The concession Microsoft is making is a modest one. It is giving personal computer makers the option of not displaying on the first screen seen by PC users the collection of entertainment and commerce Web sites hand-picked by Microsoft. The move by Microsoft applies to its next-generation operating system, Windows 98, which the company plans to begin selling to consumers on June 25. The new product's demonstration at a major trade show yesterday proved a bit embarrassing. When William H. Gates, Microsoft's chairman, was putting Windows 98 through its paces at the Comdex Spring Computer Show in Chicago, his computer crashed. "I guess we still have some bugs to work out," Mr. Gates observed. "That must be why we're not shipping Windows 98 yet." The first-screen step represents the third time in the last two months Microsoft has bowed to industry pressure to fine-tune contracts with its business partners. Just before Mr. Gates appeared before the Senate Commerce Committee in March, the company modified its contracts with Internet access suppliers so they would no longer be restricted from promoting the Internet browsing software of rivals, like Netscape Communications. And the day before Microsoft's legal team was to meet with Justice Department lawyers on April 12, the company said it was dropping similar restraints on its Web site partners. The court hearing today in Washington concerns an appeal by Microsoft in the antitrust suit filed last October by the Justice Department. The Government contends that Microsoft violated its 1995 consent decree with the Government by forcing PC makers to take its Internet Explorer browsing software as a condition of licensing its Windows operating system. Though both sides will present arguments, it is unlikely that the court will rule today. Yet by now, the Justice Department's investigation and the public-relations battle between Microsoft and its antagonists has moved well beyond the consent-decree case. The Government is now pursuing the possibility of a broader antitrust case against Microsoft, while a new anti-Microsoft group was announced yesterday. The group, called the Project to Promote Competition and Innovation in the Digital Age, includes Microsoft competitors like Netscape, Oracle and Sun Microsystems. But at the group's news conference in Washington, it was the appearance of Robert H. Bork, the former Solicitor General known as an advocate of a free-market antitrust policy, that caused a stir. Mr. Bork's 1978 book, "The Antitrust Paradox: A Policy at War With Itself," is deemed a classic exposition of the so-called Chicago school of antitrust theory -- a doctrine that strongly influenced the hands-off antitrust stance of the Reagan and Bush Administrations. Yesterday, however, Mr. Bork said that Microsoft had engaged in "practices that exclude competitors without any apparent efficiency gain." Its acts of "predation," he said, do seem to violate the Sherman act, the antitrust law under which the Justice Department could bring a broader case against Microsoft. Mr. Bork, who has been retained by Netscape, defended his position yesterday as consistent with the free-market principles espoused in his book. The first-screen option for PC makers -- reported over the weekend by News.com, an on-line computer news service -- means the manufacturers will not have to display Microsoft's "channel bar" on the screen users see first when they turn on their computers. The sites on the channel bar include ones produced by Walt Disney, Time Warner and Microsoft's on-line offerings, among others. "We made the decision based on feedback" from PC makers, explained Yusuf Mehdi, a Microsoft marketing executive. The company's channel bar, however, will still be part of Windows 98, just one click away from the first screen. PC makers want to be able to tailor Internet offerings to the interests of specific customers, forging closer relations with their customers and collecting a fee on the resulting on-line transactions for themselves instead of being forced to surrender that business to Microsoft. "The real issue is whether Microsoft will allow the PC makers to populate the channel bar with their own selections," said Ken Wasch, president of the Software Publishers Association, a trade group.

title: After Accounting Error, Cendant Reaffirms Rapid Growth Plans
body: Before there was a World Wide Web, before there was America Online, there was Compucard of America, a Stamford, Conn., company with a vision that people would want to shop by computer. That company later became CUC International, which joined last year with the franchising giant HFS to form the Cendant Corporation, praised at its formation as one of a new breed of "virtual corporations" that owned a bundle of brand names but few actual assets. But last week Cendant came under scrutiny of a far more negative kind when it announced that "potential accounting irregularities" in the operations of the former CUC would force it to sharply reduce its 1997 earnings. The announcement caused the company's stock to lose nearly half its value, though it rebounded a bit as Cendant reaffirmed its commitment to its aggressive growth plans. Analysts said it was still not clear, however, what impact the troubles at Cendant would have on the company's on-line businesses, which include the netmarket.com Web site, and the Autovantage and Traveler's Advantage sites on the Web and America Online. Most of the former CUC's revenues still come from more prosaic ventures like Welcome Wagon and Shoppers Advantage, discount clubs that solicit members through telemarketing and inserts in credit card bills. Some analysts said the stock market had overreacted to what could prove an embarrassing, but surmountable, problem in accounting for sales and costs. "They have a huge base of members in these various programs that actually use the services and pay money for them," said Keith Benjamin, an analyst with BancAmerica Robertson Stephens. "There is revenue here, there is value. The only question is, what is the profitability? Some executives appear to have inflated the profitability." But some analysts say the disclosure by Cendant should prompt questions about other numbers cited by CUC executives. "They were claiming $90 million a month in on-line revenue," said Adam Schoenfeld, an analyst with Jupiter Communications. "We put all consumer commerce on the Web last year at $2.6 billion, which means they're claiming more than a third of it. I'd really like to see these on-line revenues broken out month to month to see what the reality is." Cendant says the former CUC's business has 70 million members, who pay an average of $49 as members of clubs like Shoppers Advantage and Travelers Advantage, renewing at a rate of more than 70 percent a year. It said that 375,000 of its members were recruited on line, but analysts note that many of the on-line clubs have offered promotional memberships at very low fees, so they may represent a disproportionately small portion of total revenues. In 1973, when Compucard opened its doors, the vision of selling goods and services on line may have seemed far-fetched, but "starting about three years ago, when the Web really kicked in, it started looking very real," said Gary Arlen, an analyst with Arlen Communications. "There's no question the electronic shopping was a smaller part of the business than the coupon books. Nevertheless, it is starting to become an important part of the Web." And in the last few years, CUC has also become a major player in consumer and educational software, through the acquisitions of Davidson & Associates, Knowledge Adventure, Sierra, and Books That Work. But software was a small part of CUC's total sales, and an even smaller part of the total revenues of Cendant. Robert Davidson, the chief executive of Davidson, who was to run CUC Software, resigned last year. When HFS and CUC agreed to merge, "the software business became extraneous; it's nonstrategic," the former president of one of the acquired companies said. "It's not big enough to spin out on its own, but it's not small enough to forget about." But Jeffrey Tarter, publisher of Softletter, said the software franchise made sense for a company that wanted to make money on the Web. "I don't think they think of themselves as a software company, but software is really the sweet spot of the Web," he said. "Consumer and educational software lends itself perfectly to membership clubs, trusted-brand names. Once you get the Internet truly revved up, they will have a marquee business there."

title: Broadcom First-Day Shares Jump 123%
body: Two guys named Henry took a big step toward becoming billionaires on Friday when the small semiconductor company they founded became one of the hottest initial public stock offerings ever and the latest example of the Wall Street frenzy over Internet-related investments. The Broadcom Corporation, which supplies silicon chips used for high-speed data transmission over cable television or telephone lines, which was priced by underwriters at $24 a share on Thursday but opened for trading at $62 on Friday. The stock touched $70 before falling back to end the day at $53.625, up 123 percent from the offering price. Broadcom's first-day performance in some measures surpassed that of the Internet software pioneer Netscape Communications, whose stock rose 108 percent in its first day. Broadcom, based in Irvine, Calif., ended Friday with a market capitalization of $2.3 billion, compared with Netscape's $2.2 billion after its first day. And the co-founders, Henry T. Nicholas 3d and Henry Samueli -- "the two Henrys," as they are known to employees -- now own stakes in their company worth $600 million each, compared with the $566 million stake that Netscape's founder, James H. Clark, had after one day of trading. This is stratospheric territory for Broadcom, a company founded in 1991 that recorded a net loss of $1.2 million last year on sales of only $37 million. Dr. Samueli, 43, Broadcom's co-chairman and chief technology officer, is also a professor of electrical engineering at the University of California at Los Angeles and was the thesis adviser of Dr. Nicholas, 38, who is Broadcom's president, chief executive and the other co-chairman. The two Henrys have also worked together at TRW and at Pairgain Technologies, another fast-growing Southern California company that makes products to allow high-speed data transmission over copper phone lines and which was co-founded by Dr. Samueli. Many analysts see big futures for Broadcom's chips, which are used in digital cable set-top boxes, cable modems and computer networking equipment made by companies like General Instrument and the 3Com Corporation. General Instrument, Scientific-Atlanta, Intel and Cisco Systems have invested in Broadcom. In addition to benefiting from demand for faster access to the Internet, Broadcom is well positioned for the coming shift to digital television. General Instrument, which is Broadcom's biggest customer and has committed to using its chips, has said it expected to sell as many as 15 million digital set-top boxes in the next few years. The boxes will be used to deliver hundreds of digital channels as well as Web content. Still, the market for digital television is murky. Broadcom's chips were used in Time Warner's 500-channel cable system in Orlando, Fla., which flopped. And Broadcom has many big competitors, like Rockwell International, Philips and LSI Logic. So even though some analysts think Broadcom's sales will triple this year, to $100 million or more, they think the stock is over-valued. "Investors are willing to pay any price for a well-positioned technology company," said Robert Natale, an analyst who follows new issues for the Standard & Poor's Corporation. "It's astounding what price they are willing to pay. Valuation doesn't seem to matter." Broadcom, still in the quiet period that accompanies a stock offering, would not comment much. "There's been a certain amount of celebration," Laura Brandlin, a spokeswoman said on Friday.

title: NBC Offers Video Clips From New Web Service
body: Jay Leno monologues, interviews with "Friends" stars and archival clips from the "Saturday Night Live" vault -- all with a few clicks of the mouse. Those are among the offerings on a new World Wide Web service that NBC plans to announce this week in an effort to capitalize on a growing interest by consumers and advertisers in video on the Web. The service, which is called Videoseeker and will go on line Wednesday at http://www.videoseeker.com, will also include music videos and entertainment news from NBC's syndicated series "Access Hollywood." At the debut, hundreds of clips, each several minutes long and catalogued in a searchable data base, will be available in a variety of formats, with more to be added on a continuing basis, a Videoseeker spokesman said. NBC executives said the new service was meant to demonstrate the ways the Web could be used to enhance the business of broadcasting rather than to obliterate it. "We don't want to replace television," said Martin J. Yudkovitz, president of NBC Interactive, the network's new-media division. "That's not possible. There will always be television, and there will always be an Internet. Neither will ever be the same once they begin to invade each other's space. That's what's happening now as this convergence occurs." Though the service will be free, users will be asked to register when they first visit the Web site, allowing NBC to aim on-line ads at individuals based on their interests and demographic profiles. Doing so would enable the traditional broadcast network, in essence, to narrowcast and to resell existing programming -- same product, different medium. NBC intends to take full advantage of the Web's interactive capabilities. "It supports our transactional philosophy," Mr. Yudkovitz said. "If we wanted to sell a videocassette, this is a perfect way to do that. It's not about making shows available on demand. It's about making our services available on demand." That, analysts said, has broad implications for the way viewers consume television. "Inherent in the concept of a monologue repurposed for a new medium is a different theory for how consumers will get entertainment," said Mark Hardy, a new-media analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. "You really start to stretch the bounds of, 'O.K., how much can I make on an entertainment property?' " The longer-term implication, Mr. Hardy said, is that broadcasters can reach their audiences by parceling out programming. "Since it's self-service," he said, "your audience can come to you at any time, and you can serve it up in any increment that works." Though many cable networks offer video clips on their Web sites, including NBC's MSNBC cable channel, most of it has been news-oriented. And none of the big three broadcast networks has excerpted programming on line in this sort of format. "This is a very compelling consumer proposition," Jeremy Verba, the president of E! Online, which offers video excerpts from the cable channel E! Entertainment Television. "If you believe the Internet as a medium is moving toward a more video-based medium, those that have video assets have a tremendous competitive advantage going forward." title: Old-Line Retailers Resist On-Line Life
body: Executives at Saks Fifth Avenue were a bit dazzled in the fall of 1996 when Time Warner Inc. offered them space on an Internet "mall" for less than $100,000. It seemed like the right partner and the right time to try selling on the World Wide Web. But once on Time Warner's Dreamshop site, Saks sold a $2,000 suit to one man and some candy. By last month, Dreamshop was no more, and Saks has shelved plans for another commerce site. The company will use the Internet to give investors information, but Saks executives have concluded that cyberspace is not conducive to selling the high-priced, high-touch goods they specialize in, like soft, silky scarves and buttery leather purses. As an industry, on-line retailing may be picking up steam, reaching $3.7 billion in sales by the end of last year on the strength of books, music CD's, computers and other goods that buyers do not need to pick up or try on to decide what they want. But for Saks and many other traditional merchants, cyberspace is seeming downright inhospitable, a place without shelves or aisles -- or revenues, in most cases. And maybe most alienating to the old-line merchants, the on-line people do not even speak the language of retail. "They talk in terms of hits," said Sheri Wilson-Gray, Saks's executive vice president of marketing. "But I don't know what that means in terms of the customer. I feel pretty confident in the judgment that there will not be major apparel transactions with a Saks customer in the short term there." For the last two years, an avalanche of press releases, news reports and Zeitgeist buzz has proclaimed the Internet the great electronic bazaar that defines the future of commerce; any merchant left behind would surely perish. But the truth is that American retail stores are struggling mightily to build a path onto the Net from the bricks and mortar that for the last century have defined their selling space. Few if any have made money on the Web, and many are still struggling to decide how to use the medium -- or whether they belong on line at all. At the same time, they are hearing footsteps. Several large retailers -- notably the bookseller Barnes & Noble -- have already seen their turf invaded by Internet start-ups like Amazon.com. The start-ups usually have the advantages of knowing the quirks of electronic commerce, being small and agile enough to turn on a dime as on-line technologies and demographics shift. And they are free of the distractions of simultaneously competing in traditional retail. "The Internet is a new channel, and they are all out there exploring it," said Don Gilbert, the senior vice president of information technology at the National Retail Federation. "But when you look at what people are buying now, in the grand scheme of things, it is not a significant part of their revenue stream." Indeed, despite the seemingly impressive sales figures for electronic commerce so far, only 15 to 20 percent of those revenues went to the on-line sites of conventional retailers, according to Piper Jaffray Inc., a Minneapolis investment company. Most were rung up in the travel and financial services industries and in business-to-business sales. The merchants finding the most success at selling on line tend to be ones -- again, like Amazon.com -- that exist only on line. "Retailers are way back on the prairie, their wagon wheels are covered with mud, and they are not going anywhere," said Laura Berland, an executive vice president at ORB Digital Direct, an on-line commerce consulting firm. "It is very new technology, it is very expensive, and it wrenches at the heart of corporate culture." To be sure, some of the frustrations retailers have encountered on the path to cyberspace are part of the medium's birth pains. But there are also other causes, including the industry's traditional unwillingness to spend money on untried technologies and the failure of many companies to define which managers' roles encompass electronic commerce or to understand the profoundly different ways that people shop on line and in stores. "The Internet scares the pants off of these guys," said Kate Dalhagen, a senior analyst at Forester Research in Boston. Yet retailers who stay on the sidelines, she predicts, will almost certainly lose business to on-line enterprises. Still, retailers' resistance is understandable. The Internet, for all its convenience, is still largely not a pleasant place to go shopping for things that require any sort of inspection, in part because of the low quality of images on the Web. Catalogues offer much better representations of clothing; colors, the textures of fabrics or the stitching details on a sweater are much clearer on glossy paper than they are on most computer screens. What is more, unless a site is exceptionally well designed, clicking around to find items can be frustrating. And when Web traffic is high, as it often is on weekday afternoons and early evenings, on-line shopping can be slower than shopping in a store. But what is trickiest about electronic retailing is learning how consumers shop on line -- almost the polar opposite of how they shop in a store. Many people who would browse in a department store and often buy on impulse go on line with a specific product in mind, find it, buy it and log off. Hence the failure of Dreamshop and other on-line electronic malls that attempted to mimic the shopping patterns of real malls. Nor are many retailers willing to spend the time and money needed to experiment with on-line sales. For example, Sports Authority, the sporting goods superstore chain, has a consumer Web site, but it does little more than list store addresses. "We don't see a reason to make much of an investment in the Internet," said Jack Smith, Sports Authority's chief executive. "I don't really believe the Internet is the wave of the future for sporting goods." Tell that to Brett Allsop, the president of Cedro Group Inc., which runs Sportsite.com, a compilation of dozens of specialized sporting goods catalogues whose merchandise is sold through one site. Since the site was begun in September, its sales have grown an average of 52 percent a month, Mr. Allsop said. Though he declined to disclose total revenue, he said that by the end of the year the site would be generating "seven figures" in sales. Sportsite got its start through a joint venture with Yahoo, but will now finance its growth with venture capital and, eventually, an initial public offering, Mr. Allsop said. Direct merchants like catalogue companies, including Lands' End, have had an easier transition to cyberspace than store-based retailers -- except for chain stores with a history of investing in both technology and sophisticated inventory management. Wal-Mart Stores Inc., for instance, is commended by analysts for having one of the most sophisticated electronic commerce sites among traditional retailers. Unlike most retailers' Web sites, the Wal-Mart site offers even more items on line than it does in its giant stores. In fact, the site's best-selling products are Rolex watches and Nike T-shirts -- items not even found in Wal-Mart stores. "The transition is not simple," said Phil Martz, the director of Wal-Mart Online. "It is a difficult task to track 1,000 orders a day from different homes and very different from shipping one case of something to a store and making sure it arrived." No wonder, then, that some retailers have already given up on the idea of selling goods on the Web, and use it instead as a marketing medium to drive traffic to their stores. Hillel Levin runs a company called Coolsavings.com, which distributes personalized coupons for retail stores and restaurants through the Internet. Clients include J. C. Penney, National Car Rental, Chuck E. Cheese and Blockbuster Video. It is not so much a capitulation, as a gradual realization about which kinds of consumer businesses lend themselves to on-line sales -- and which do not. "In the last year," Mr. Hillel said, "we have seen people who said, 'We believe the Internet has gone beyond the point of us having our own Web sites.' title: Child Abuse On Internet Heightens Vigilance
body: TO educators and parents, the news reports were disquieting: a tenured fourth-grade teacher with more than 25 years in the Yonkers school system was indicted earlier this month for sexually molesting students; another tenured elementary school teacher in Scarsdale was sentenced to more than seven years in Federal prison for sending child pornography over the Internet. In addition, an Ossining educator was arrested during the winter in Paramus, N.J., on charges related to on-line sexually explicit conversations, and in Yonkers last month, a substitute teacher was arrested on similar charges. Because at least two of the teachers were highly respected educators with strong track records, their arrests came as a shock to many. Yet, the handwriting may have long been on the wall, said law-enforcement officials who observed that at least in some respects, they were also risky employees. "Speaking as a mother, I would have been very suspicious of a bachelor man who spent all of his time with young boys and didn't have other friends, although as a Federal prosecutor, I wouldn't have necessarily opened a file on him," Jacqueline Hogan Scola, Assistant unitedstates Attorney in Miami said, referring to the case of Robert Nebens, 37, the Scarsdale teacher, tutor and summer camp counselor. After pleading guilty to two counts of transmitting child pornography over state lines, Mr. Nebens was sentenced last month in Miami by Judge Federico Moreno of Federal District Court to 87 months in prison. Mr. Nebens, a Pound Ridge resident and fifth-grade teacher at the Fox Meadow School in Scarsdale, relinquished his teaching certificates and agreed never to teach or be around children younger than 18 again. Prosecutors said the well-liked teacher met someone he thought was a 13-year-old boy in a chat room on the Internet and arranged to meet him in Miami. But when he arrived, the "boy" was a Federal undercover agent who had been prowling the Internet for pedophiles, and Mr. Nebens was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Ms. Scola said Mr. Nebens carried pictures on a computer disk of prepubescent children and other images of sadomasochistic sexual behavior across state lines to the rendezvous. Reviewing the teacher's background, she said Mr. Nebens adopted a 9-year-old boy about 10 years ago, and the young man recently testified that Mr. Nebens had sexually abused him. The teacher was married briefly, Ms. Scola said, but for the most part, he spent his free time with young male students. There was, however, no cause to arrest him earlier, Ms. Scola said. And therein lies the dilemma that many educators and law enforcement officials are grappling with in the aftermath of the Nebens case and other cases. "Our job as prosecutors is to react to crime," said District Attorney Jeannine Pirro of Westchester. "We can't go in on a hunch and make an arrest." Mrs. Pirro's office is handling the cases of Martin O'Keefe, 52, the Yonkers teacher who was indicted by a Westchester grand jury on April 2 on multiple charges of sexual abuse, and Daniel Romero, 23, the substitute teacher arrested on March 17 for reportedly engaging in a series of on-line exchanges with an undercover agent posing as a 14-year-old girl. The charges facing Mr. O'Keefe carry a prison sentence of up to seven years; Mr. Romero, who was arraigned in Yonkers City Court, faces a maximum of four years in prison if convicted. In the fourth case, Peter Acampora, the Ossining teacher, was arrested on Feb. 24 by the Bergen County, N.J., prosecutor's office and charged with endangering the welfare of a child and luring a child into a motor vehicle. He is free on $25,000 bail pending the presentation of his case to a grand jury. In the case of Mr. O'Keefe, the police received a complaint in December from a student at the Hawthorne Elementary School for gifted children that the teacher had sexually abused him. Further investigation revealed that he had also reportedly molested other children. In an earlier incident about four years ago, Mr. O'Keefe was psychologically evaluated after parents' complaints that he allowed students to sit on his lap in his classroom. Mr. O'Keefe passed the examination and was later warned in writing against continuing the practice with students, the Yonkers Federation of Teachers said. After his indictment on 13 counts of sexual abuse, Mr. O'Keefe, accompanied by his wife, Stephanie, who also teaches at the Hawthorne school, entered a not-guilty plea in County Court in White Plains. Elaine Tsu, president of the Yonkers Board of Education, said her daughter had been a student in Mr. O'Keefe's class six years ago when reports first surfaced that children were sitting on the teacher's lap. "I wanted her out of his class, but the other parents said not to worry," Ms. Tsu said. "They pointed out that he was a really good teacher. I hope that when this case is all over and done with, it will serve as a wake-up call that sexual abuse does happen. Hopefully, it will free kids to talk about these incidents and know that they will be believed." But one educator worried that news of the recent sexual abuse cases could result in overreaction. "In hindsight, people would want to watch teachers carefully for unusual behavior," said Florie Wachtenheim, president of the Parent-Teachers Council of Scarsdale. "But one also cannot start looking in every corner. Yes, we have to pay more careful attention, but, no, we can't start witch hunts." Teachers, too, are worried -- most of all that their best intentions and genuine concern for students will be misinterpreted. "Unfortunately, the climate is becoming one of extreme caution, of nervousness," said Steven Frey, president of the 1,750-member Yonkers Federation of Teachers and a high school social studies teacher for 32 years. Mr. Frey said teachers often hug troubled students or put a reassuring arm around their shoulders but educators increasingly worry about any physical contact with their charges. "We keep our doors open," he said, "and we don't do anything that could be misinterpreted, because the next thing you know, we'd be down in the principal's office, and the newspapers would be all over it. Even if someone is cleared, the stigma remains." A bill, co-sponsored by State Senator Nicholas A. Spano, is pending in Albany to require fingerprinting and background checks for all school employees. A similar bill, covering only teachers, is before the State Assembly. "Every time we see or hear of an incident involving a school employee and a student, it highlights the need for an additional layer of protection for our children," Mr. Spano said. Twenty-seven states and newyork City require fingerprinting and background checks, The Associated Press reported last week. newyork City also has an independent office that investigates all allegations of abuse in the schools. As Reginald F. Marra, Superintendent of the Yonkers schools, said last week, "You still rarely know for certain, even when you check out all of a candidate's credentials." A new teacher in the state now has to sign a statement that he or she has had no prior arrest or conviction of a crime. "What we know is what they tell us," William Hirschen, a spokesman for the State Department of Education, said. The proposed laws pending in the State Legislature would also require school districts to report all allegations of sexual abuse by educators and other school employees to a law-enforcement agency. The bill arose from a recent $2.3 million out-of-court settlement made by the Galway School District in Saratoga County, north of Albany, to settle claims that the district had waited too long to report allegations of sexual abuse -- several days to tell the parents of their child's allegations and almost a week to call the state police. Mr. Hirschen said 29 cases of sexual abuse in the classroom were reported to the Education Department in the 1996-97 school year. In 10 of those cases, teachers were found guilty; other cases are pending. Senator Spano said that even though the proposed bills would not actually prevent cases like those involving Mr. Nebens, Mr. O'Keefe or the others, they would highlight the need for increased awareness of such cases. Ninety-five percent of pedophiles are men with recurrent fantasies or urges that are culturally deviant, said Patricia Singleton, a clinical psychologist from Mount Kisco. Typically, a pedophile is immature, a loner and either not married or experiencing difficulties in establishing close relationships, she said. The object of a pedophile's attentions is often prepubescent children. "Obviously people with those predilections are attracted to careers that put them in contact with their victims," Dr. Singleton said, adding that they are often drawn to teaching, the ministry and Scouting. Because psychologists and psychiatrists have had only limited success controlling the behavior of pedophiles, who often repeat their behavior, Dr. Singleton recommended "tough, stringent standards" when dealing with people who work with children. Recently, the Supreme Court agreed to decide when school districts can be found liable under Federal law for a teacher's sexual abuse of a student. The issue, closely watched by school districts nationwide, has divided the lower courts in the five years since the Supreme Court first ruled that individuals could sue for damages under a law that prohibits sex discrimination in educational institutions that receive Federal aid. The case the Court accepted in December grew out of a yearlong relationship between a teacher in a public high school near Austin, Tex., and one of his students, a 15-year-old girl who, with her mother, eventually brought a suit against the Lago Vista Independent School District. Lawrence W. Thomas, the lawyer for the Yonkers School Board, said the Supreme Court decision would be studied closely by the school district. "These are big issues," he said. title: 3 Charged With Sending Child Pornography on Internet
body: Attorney General Dennis C. Vacco brought his campaign to rid cyberspace of child pornography to newyork City yesterday, charging three Queens residents with using the Internet to send photographs of young children engaged in sexual acts. The three -- Peter Manos, 54, the owner of an air-conditioning company in Long Island City; Salvatore G. Zolla Jr., a 26-year-old restaurant manager from Whitestone, and Chantee Cameron, an 18-year-old student from Jamaica -- have been accused of using email to transmit child pornography to dozens of people across the country over the last year, the authorities said. If convicted, each would face up to seven years in jail and could be registered as a sex offender under the state's "Megan's Law." Mr. Vacco said the photographs depicted children who were clearly minors, some as young as 6. Officials have not been able to identify any of the children. Officials also did not know how the photographs were obtained, but said they did not believe that the suspects were actually involved in producing the pictures. Mr. Vacco said some of the photographs might have been obtained from magazines. "This material is graphic, it's disgusting and it's vile," said the Queens District Attorney, Richard A. Brown, whose office assisted in the investigation. "And we believe that those who traffic in this kind of material are no different than those who physically abuse these children, and they should be prosecuted in the same way." These are the first city residents charged in Mr. Vacco's investigation, which has led to 21 prosecutions in newyork State. Mark Wurzel, a spokesman for Mr. Vacco, said there would very likely be more indictments in the metropolitan area. Lawyers for Ms. Cameron and Mr. Zolla, who were in custody yesterday, said their clients were not guilty of the charges. "As horrific as the charges are, it's just as horrific to be falsely accused," said Mark Gann, a lawyer for Mr. Zolla. "My client is not guilty and these charges came as a big surprise to him and his family." Officials said that Mr. Manos was out of state but planned to turn himself in later this month. His lawyer could not be reached for comment. A man who answered the phone at Mr. Manos's business, Delphi Mechanical, declined to comment. Officials from Mr. Vacco's office said they began to investigate the three Queens residents after they entered an Internet chat room where people were discussing pornography. Over the course of a number of electronic conversations, each of the accused sent the investigators photographs of young girls and boys engaged in sexual acts with adults, the authorities said. "In each instance we never had to pay a nickel for the pictures, so these people were not in it for profit but because they derived some perverse pleasure from it," Mr. Vacco said.  "We're not talking about a dirty picture of a scantily clad child in a sedate pose, but of a very graphic form of child abuse." Investigators obtained the names and addresses of the people sending the photographs after issuing subpoenas to the on-line service providers. Local officials seized the computers of all three individuals, which they said provide a virtual fingerprint showing precisely what was sent from each of the computers. Mr. Vacco, whose office began investigating child pornography on the Internet about two years ago, said the explosive growth of on-line services has made child pornography more pervasive and easily accessible than ever before, particularly because the Internet allows people to obtain child pornography in the privacy of their homes and offices. "In the past, child pornography was generally only available in some out-of-the-way pornographic bookstore, and even then only under the counter because it is so patently illegal," Mr. Vacco said. "Now you can find it in chat rooms that come into your home, on the same computers used by your children." Mr. Vacco's office said it had reviewed more than 2,000 complaints from on-line services like America Online and from on-line subscribers. Those complaints have resulted in charges being filed against more than 200 people in Arizona, California, Pennsylvania, Texas and other states.

title:
COMPANY REPORTS;
New York Times Company Reports 24.7% Rise in Profit
body: The newyork Times Company reported yesterday that earnings rose 24.7 percent in the first quarter. The company cited an 8.25 percent increase in advertising revenue, resulting from both an overall increase in advertising and higher rates, as the main factor in the earnings performance. Some of the increase, however, was offset by a 24 percent rise in newsprint costs, in part because more paper was needed to print the increased volume of advertising and partly because the cost of newsprint rose. Revenue rose 4.3 percent over all, to $722.6 million, from $692.5 million in the quarter a year earlier. For the quarter, the company earned $64.6 million, or 66 cents a diluted share, up from $51.8 million, or 52 cents a share, in the quarter a year earlier. The company said that $4.6 million of its earnings, or 3 cents a share, represented a one-time gain from the sale of equipment. It also took a charge before taxes of $2.5 million, or 1 cent a share, for costs related to buyouts. Before the one-time special items, the company earned 63 cents a share, higher than Wall Street estimates of 61 cents a share, according to First Call, an investment research firm that surveys analysts. The advertising increases in the newspaper group, which comprises The newyork Times, The Boston Globe and 21 regional newspapers, pushed the group's operating profit to $107.6 million from $100 million. The newspaper group accounted for 91 percent of the company's first-quarter revenue. While advertising revenue, particularly in the high-margin sectors of national and classified advertising, remained strong, the overall advertising volume benefited from a quirk in the calendar: Easter weekend, a traditionally slow period for advertising, fell in the first quarter last year. In 1998, Easter fell in the second quarter. The company also told analysts yesterday that circulation in the newspaper group was up over all. For The Times, both weekday and Sunday circulation rose slightly in the six-month period ended March 31, with the gains coming largely from outside the newyork metropolitan area. Advertising revenue also aided the company's broadcast group, which accounted for 5 percent of the company's first-quarter revenue. The group showed an operating profit of $7.3 million on revenue of $33.3 million. In the first quarter of 1997, the group had an operating profit of $5.7 million on revenue of $31.4 million. Profit margins rose most sharply in the magazine group, which divested itself of its golfing tee-time reservation service at the end of 1997. First-quarter revenue in the magazine group declined to $31.9 from $40.1 million, but operating profit rose to $8.3 million from $5.7 million in the quarter a year earlier. title: Racial Divide Found on Information Highway
body: At a time when the Clinton Administration is promoting the Internet as an engine of commerce and a tool of democracy, a new study has found that black Americans are far less likely to use the global computer network than are whites. The sharp racial divide is especially evident among households below the median income. The study, to be published today in the journal Science, found that in households with annual incomes below $40,000, whites were six times as likely as blacks to have used the World Wide Web in the week before the household was called for the survey. Lower-income white households were also twice as likely to own a home computer as were black households. The study documents concerns that the recent exponential growth of the Internet might worsen the nation's existing social and economic gaps. Once a decidedly optional tool for entertainment or the occasional research foray, the Web is seen as fast becoming a crucial mechanism for communication, business and education. And while it is no surprise that Americans with lower incomes are less likely to own a computer, the study highlights for the first time what are the racial disparities in who has access to digital technology. Internet access is hardly the most pressing issue facing the the disadvantaged. Its benefits in the classroom and elsewhere are still the subject of debate. And some black business leaders predict that racial parity on the Web is not far away. But Donna L. Hoffman, a professor of management at the Vanderbilt University and an author of the study, said the schism reflected in the report could have troubling social consequences. "If you want to be a fully functional member of society, you're going to have to have access to the Internet," Ms. Hoffman said. "Anybody poor is in trouble here. But if you're poor and black, you're really in trouble with respect to access." Among blacks with incomes over $40,000, home computer ownership is roughly equal to that of whites of comparable incomes, the study found, and blacks were even more likely than whites to have access to the Internet at work. Among households of all income levels, 44.3 percent of whites own a home computer compared with 29 percent of blacks. But because only about one-third of black households have incomes over $40,000, compared with about two-thirds of white households, the numbers reflect that computer access is in effect restricted to a narrow segment of blacks who are achieving at very high levels relative to whites. For example, Ms. Hoffman and her co-author, Thomas P. Novak, found that blacks at higher income levels have had more education, are younger and are more likely to be working in computer-related jobs than whites with similar incomes. Perhaps the most striking finding of the study is the racial disparity in home computer ownership among high school and college students. The authors found that while 73 percent of white students had access to a computer at home, only 32 percent of black students had access to one. Even after adjusting for household income, the gap remained significant. Moreover, white students without a computer at home were more than twice as likely as black students to have used the Web in the six-month period before they were surveyed and more than three times as likely to have used the Web in the week before they were surveyed. Ms. Hoffman said the report showed the importance of providing Internet access for blacks at places like libraries and community centers. The study's results were based on data provided by Nielsen Media Research in a telephone survey conducted from December 1996 through January 1997. No information was provided on the margin of error in the survey. The quantification of such stark incongruities comes at a time when President Clinton has repeatedly called for the wiring of the nation's schools and libraries and Vice President Al Gore has extolled the virtues of the Internet as a forum for public discourse. This week, Commerce Secretary William M. Daley released a report celebrating the impact of the information revolution on the Unites States economy. But with Internet traffic doubling every 100 days, it appears that for the moment, at least, the majority of blacks are being left behind. At the time of the study, 25 million Americans had used the Web in the previous week, according to a recent survey by Nielsen Media Research. Less than 6 percent of those are black, although blacks account for 12 percent of the population. "Income isn't the only impediment; there's something else going on," said Larry Irving, the Assistant Secretary of Commerce who oversees a $20 million project that finances technology demonstration projects in poor communities. "There is more content by, for and about the African-American community on the Net than there is in probably any other medium, but I don't think that's known. There's still a mythology that this isn't for us, that this is for scientists or upper income people or for geeks." One problem, Mr. Irving said, is that schools and communities with high minority populations are much less likely than predominantly white districts to provide Internet access. "We risk a further widening of the gap between the haves and the have-nots," said B. Keith Fulton, director of technology programs and policy for the National Urban League. As we move into the information age, you need more than reading, writing and arithmetic to participate in our society. You need information literacy, and if African-Americans don't have it, that's a serious problem." But E. David Ellington, a founder of NetNoir, a leading Web site about black culture and issues, predicted that the inequalities would be ironed out in time. "The vast majority of white people aren't on line yet either," Mr. Ellington said. "I'm not panicking that black folks are a little bit slower and haven't found this to be as relevant in their lives yet. I know from my own experience that black people are getting on line in droves." Mr. Ellington said there was evidence that lower-income blacks are also beginning to find their way onto the Net. Computer prices are dropping, and nearly twice as many blacks as whites said they planned to purchase a home computer in the next six months. Still, the survey results indicate that price is not the only barrier to black use of the Internet. "One of the things it looks like we have here are some solid, up-to-date statistics that paint a more comprehensive picture than we've understood in the bast," said Andrew Blau, director of communications policy at the Benton Foundation, a Washington group that studies the social impact of technology. "It's not one that offers anybody easy relief, but having a better understanding of the nature of the problem is the first step toward devising a solution."
