title: Ancient Machines For Making Text - Correction Appended
body: FOR most people, typewriters are beside the point, a relic of a past age. For Richard Polt, however, a typewriter collector who has established one of the Web's most elaborate sites about typewriters, being a relic of the past is the point, like discovering that a sword happens to be Excalibur. A typewriter tells tales, especially a manual one from the instrument's golden age, before World War I, when most technological innovations occurred, said Dr. Polt, 33, an assistant professor of philosophy at Xavier University in Cincinnati. It is a clattering, ringing mass of hardened steel that assaults the senses, he said, in a way that cannot be matched by any computer. Dr. Polt got his first garage-sale Remington when he was 12. "You can imagine," he said, "the police reports, the journalism, the love letters, the novels that all flowed through it." And there is a value to imagination, good and bad. Think of Ian Fleming's gold-plated Royal, sold to the current 007, Pierce Brosnan, for $86,000 in 1995. Or the Remington, appraised at $50,000, that Margaret Mitchell used for "Gone with the Wind." Hitler's Remington, on which he is said to have written "Mein Kampf," sold for $39,000. Dr. Polt and other lovers of the low-tech typewriter have founded a small but growing community of collectors on the Web who buy and sell typewriters, swap repair tips and hunt parts. Dr. Polt's Web site, The Classic Typewriter Page, found at http:// xavier.xu.edu:8000/polt/typewriters.html, went up in December 1995, and now gets 200 hits, or page views, a week. The site contains history, links to other typewriter Web sites, locations of repair and supply shops, and scores of illustrations of bizarre machines. At the top of the Web page is an Oliver, a circa 1890 machine that looked like a brain split in half, with upper-case typebars (which strike the paper to make each letter) on one side and lower-case typebars on the other. Adding wings, Dr. Polt said, "came to me in a daydream." Commercial production of the typewriter began in 1874, when the Sholes & Glidden Type Writer appeared. Principally invented by a Milwaukee newspaperman named Christopher L. Sholes, it popularized the QWERTY keyboard, named after the arrangement of letters.  QWERTY was probably designed to separate the typebars for letters that are frequently used so the typewriter would be less likely to jam. In the 1800's, manufacturers produced a dazzling number of machines, which included keyboards that looked like pincushions and telephone dials. Dr. Polt's collection of 60 typewriters ranges from a pocket typewriter called a Bennett, circa 1910, that weighs less than a pound and is about the size of a Filofax, to a behemoth called a Yetman, circa 1908, that weighs 50 pounds and converted what was typed into Morse code to be sent by telegraph. The seriously afflicted collect what is called ephemera: typewritten manuscripts, such as those typed on a Sholes & Glidden; box art for carbon paper and ribbon tins, the cookie-sized cans for typewriter ribbons. Correction  Because of an editing error, an article in the Circuits section yesterday about typewriter collectors misstated the Web address of the Classic Typewriter Page. It is: xavier.xu.edu/polt/typewriters.html Correction-Date: April 17, 1998, Friday Graphic   Photo: Richard Polt with one of the manual typewriters he collects. (Mark Lyons for The newyork Times)

title: Man Is Convicted of Assaulting Woman He Met on the Internet
body: Oliver Jovanovic, a doctoral student at Columbia University, was convicted yesterday of kidnapping and assaulting a Barnard College student who met him on the Internet and who said he tortured her for more than 20 hours. After the verdict was read, Mr. Jovanovic wept quietly in the Manhattan courtroom. After a three-week trial, the jury found that Mr. Jovanovic had imprisoned the young woman and assaulted her over two days in November 1996. Jurors rejected the defense's claim that the encounter between Mr. Jovanovic and the young woman was consensual. Mr. Jovanovic, 31, who is scheduled to be sentenced on May 6, faces a minimum penalty of 15 years to life in prison and a maximum of 25 years to life. The case drew public attention because Mr. Jovanovic, a doctoral student in microbiology at Columbia, met his accuser in an Internet chat room. The young woman, who was 20 at the time and attended Barnard College, testified that Mr. Jovanovic attracted her interest during an extended email correspondence, and convinced her to accompany him on a date. But the young woman said that after bringing her to his Washington Heights apartment, Mr. Jovanovic tied her to a futon frame and tortured her for more than 20 hours. The young woman, whose testimony lasted several days, said Mr. Jovanovic threatened to kill her, bit her until she bled, burned her with wax and beat her with a stick. The case, a high-profile attack involving the Internet, stirred a debate about the safety of anonymous meetings over computer networks. Prosecutors declined to make any comment after yesterday's verdict. Defense lawyers had claimed that the young woman made up a story about what was a consensual sexual encounter. But the prosecutor in the case, Gail Heatherly, countered that the young woman had given a consistent account of the attack, had suffered physically and emotionally, and had no motive to lie. In Ms. Heatherly's closing statement, she characterized Mr. Jovanovic as "deceptive, deceitful and dishonest." "She doesn't know Oliver's last name," Ms. Heatherly told the jury. "She doesn't know where he lives. She met him one night, and now she has made it her life's goal to ruin his life?" At a press conference after the verdict, Mr. Jovanovic's lawyers and his family expressed their dismay and said they would appeal. "I am totally devastated," said Mr. Jovanovic's mother, Sabina. "Once I fall apart, I will not be able to collect myself. Oliver, we know is innocent." Defense lawyers said that prosecutors had offered a plea bargain before the verdict, but Mr. Jovanovic declined. Fred Sosinsky, one of his lawyers, declined to describe the terms of the offer, but said the proposed sentence was "shockingly, surprisingly low." "The numbers that were proposed were reflective of their view of the case," Mr. Sosinsky said. Mr. Jovanovic's lawyers argued yesterday that the trial judge, Justice William A. Wetzel of State Supreme Court, incorrectly restricted the evidence that defense lawyers could present. They said that Justice Wetzel's decisions had prevented them from making a case that would have established Mr. Jovanovic's innocence. "A travesty of justice has occurred," Jack Litman, Mr. Jovanovic's lead lawyer, said. "An innocent man faces life imprisonment because this American jury has heard only half the evidence." At the heart of the defense's complaint is the judge's interpretation of newyork's rape-shield law. The law, which is intended to protect rape victims, prevents the defense from presenting evidence of the accuser's past sexual history except under narrowly defined circumstances. A bitter argument raged throughout the trial regarding evidence that the judge excluded under the law. Justice Wetzel has sealed the records of the argument, which was carried out in secret. But defense lawyers yesterday described some of the issues they intended to use to appeal the verdict. Without being specific, the defense lawyers said that in an email correspondence with Mr. Jovanovic, the young woman wrote messages that could have helped the defense. Judge Wetzel did not allow the messages to be used as evidence, the defense lawyers said, finding that they were excluded by the shield law. The defense lawyers said that the judge's ruling also prevented the jury from hearing important evidence about Mr. Jovanovic's state of mind before the incident, as well as the young woman's. They said the information could have been used to impeach the young woman's credibility on the witness stand. The lawyers said that courts in other states have held that speech between a criminal defendant and an accuser is not sexual conduct, and therefore should be allowed as evidence. They said that the judge should have allowed the email as evidence under that reasoning. Mr. Sosinsky said the importance of the email was not in what it shows about the previous behavior of the young woman, but in establishing what the two people intended when they met for the date. "Whether it is true or not is irrelevant," he said. "It is certainly relevant to the defendant's state of mind." Graphic   Photo: Oliver Jovanovic, 31, first met his victim in a chat room on the Internet. (Associated Press)

title:
PRODUCTIVITY;
A Free Personal Shopper For Internet News Hounds
body: INFORMATION wants to be free," the old Internet credo proclaims. But if you find yourself asking, "What price freedom?" after wading through advertising-laden search engines or clicking through a twisting stream of hypertext links in search of a decent mix of news, you may find that a Web site with the colorful name Crayon (www.crayon.net) is just the ticket. Crayon, a roundabout acronym for Create Your Own Newspaper, is an on-line service that lets its users compile their own customized Web pages -- 700 free sources are listed. Want to create your own electronic newspaper featuring headlines from CNN, The Los Angeles Times and PC World Online, mixed with links to the audio version of the National Public Radio Newscast, a satellite weather photo, stock quotes and the day's "Dilbert" cartoon? Crayon will let you do all that and more, for the low, low price of "free." With more and more conventional information outlets jumping on line, the Web is proving itself to be a reliable source of breaking news, but the choices can be overwhelming. Pointcast (www.pointcast.com) and Newsbot (www.newsbot.com) will bring specialized information right to your desktop. The AJR Newslink page (www.newslink.org/ mag.html) and the Media Info Links site (www.mediainfo.com/emedia) from Editor & Publisher both offer exhaustive lists of publications on the Net. With Web browsing becoming a popular pastime, bookmark-organizer programs that are shareware (programs that people can download free from the Web but are supposed to pay a nominal fee for if they are satisfied), like Dragnet (www.tikisoft.com/dragnet.html) and Linkman (members.xoom.com/ ultimatum/linkman.htm), can prove quite helpful. And new ones spring up all the time. But for those who favor one-stop shopping for Web links plus organizer functions, Crayon combines the abilities to categorize, customize and manage on-line news, all in the familiar format of a Web page. Unlike utility shareware that stores the retrieved information in your computer, or news-gathering software that presents plenty of advertising along with the headlines, a user's Crayon paper is sort of a self-maintaining superbookmark for current events that does not take up any room on your hard drive. Created in 1995 by Jeff Boulter and Dave Maher when they were Bucknell University students, Crayon has quietly gained a loyal following through a few postings in select Usenet newsgroups and by word-of-mouth. The site now boasts more than 150,000 users. A new user logs onto Crayon's home page, registers his or her email address and selects a Crayon password, then proceeds to a worksheet to put together a personalized (down to handpicked titles and mottos) "newspaper" culled from a lengthy list of links to on-line news sources. The list offers just about every free digital edition of the major American dailies plus dozens of foreign newspapers, including such diverse titles as The South China Morning Post, Vladivostok News, The Jamaican Gleaner and The Times of London. Sites specializing in sports, financial and health coverage are grouped in separate categories on Crayon's master lists of choices. LINKS to information services like C-Span's Congress Today, Air Force Radio News and The Associated Press Newswire are available as well. The list of sources also features easy access to a wide range of other pages, like David Letterman's Top 10 List, the Daily Star Trek Test and something called the Cool Pet Site of the Day. Once a new user has chosen the desired selections, Crayon will create a Web page displaying links to all the sites. Headlines from certain sites pop up throughout the day, and all the links on one's page are automatically updated daily. Crayon newspapers can be easily modified to change the selections, and any desired sites not found on the master lists of choices may be added to an individual's paper, which is stored on the Crayon server. Since the user's paper is stored on a remote server, it can be retrieved from any machine with a Web browser. "Crayon is sort of like a dynamic bookmark manager," said Mr. Boulter, 23, who graduated from Bucknell in 1996 with a bachelor's degree in computer science and engineering. He works as a software developer in Cambridge, Mass. Mr. Maher said, "We strive to keep the selections on the site as high-quality as possible." He is also 23 and graduated from Bucknell with a computer science degree in 1996; he is now an Internet consultant in northern Virginia. While there may be plenty of similar programs and personalized information agents crawling the Web, it is doubtful that any of these other Internet entities were conceived in such a sincere moment of divine inspiration as Crayon. By early 1995, an irregular daily schedule and poor television reception on Bucknell's campus in Lewisburg, Pa., were contributing to Mr. Boulter's growing sense of isolation from "the real world," he said. Although there were some on-line outlets for news, the Web had not yet taken off as a popular forum for mass media. "Jeff had been brainstorming about what to do about the news," Mr. Maher said. "It's always been one of his interests, having on-line access to information." Perhaps Mr. Boulter's muse had sensed his frustration that day. "It was in a really boring class," he recalled. Mr. Maher, who had been friends with Mr. Boulter since their early days on campus, was suffering through the same dry lecture. "I saw him scribbling frantically on a piece of paper," Mr. Maher said, "and I started to get distracted, wondering what he was doing." Mr. Boulter said: "I really wanted to get some news. I was thinking about all these sites that were coming up on the Web: The San Jose Mercury News, The Nando Times and a lot more were jumping on. And I thought, I need to find out what else is out there. "I thought, If I'm going to do this for myself, I might as well do it for other people," Mr. Boulter added. Mr. Maher said: "He started outlining. What if we grouped all of these news services together at a centralized site of customized information?" THE two students got started. In between school labs and classes, Mr. Boulter began gathering his news sources into a database and writing the needed computer scripts (in Perl, a Unix-based programming language) that would generate the daily Crayon papers. It took about a week. Mr. Maher did the debugging work and had the contacts at the university to put the completed Crayon on the school's Web server, where it stayed until the system administrators began to notice an enormous number of daily hits. "Eventually we had to move it," Mr. Maher said. "It was too high a percentage of Bucknell's traffic." Crayon is now living on free, unsponsored Web space, where it continues to thrive, even as its creators start to feel the pull of other projects and the demands of postcollege reality. "We're doing as much as we can with it, but we both have other obligations now," Mr. Boulter said. "So we're thinking about seeing if we can find a good home for the site, maybe with someone who can take it to the next level." They have entertained a few offers from possible corporate partners who might be able to maintain and expand the site. Yet no commitments have been made, and the two buddies continue to work on the site from their respective locations. "It's been a free service for a really long time, and our mandate is that it always be free to the end user," Mr. Maher said. "Maintaining Crayon is a good connection to what the Web used to be. It's noncommercial." Graphic   Photos: Dave Maher, left, and Jeff Boulter, shown as college students in 1995, the year they created Crayon. Top left, the Crayon logo, above a customized page.

title:
Screen Grab;
See the Spiral Spin, See Your Skin Crawl
body: IT'S not difficult to find something on the Internet to make the average person's skin crawl. But a recent email message may be taking that idea a bit literally. An email file attachment making the rounds of the Net invites recipients to experience a disorienting optical illusion by staring for 20 seconds at an animated image of counterrotating spirals. If they do, and then look at, say, a hand on a mouse, their skin will appear to crawl. The illusion exists in many incarnations on the Net. One version can be found at www.sover.net/manx/ spirals.html. (Some sites require a Java-enabled browser, like newer copyversions of Netscape and Microsoft's Internet Explorer.) Al Seckel, a cognitive neuroscientist who is a research associate at the Shimojo Psychophysics Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology, a hotbed of study about sensory perception and motor control, explained that the illusion is based on the concept of "motion aftereffect," which was identified by the ancient Greeks. The first modern scientific account of the phenomenon appeared in the 19th century, offered by the scientist Robert Addams, who noticed the effect after staring intently at a waterfall in Scotland. When Addams averted his eyes to the adjacent cliffs, they appeared to move in a direction opposite to that of the water. As one of the most famous visual illusions, this waterfall effect has even inspired its own site (www.hip.atr.co.jp/departments/Dept5/ MAE.html) where dissertations and articles on motion aftereffect are listed . The wide currency of this illusion on line is a good example of how the Net -- and the Web in particular -- is proving a fertile ground for the sharing, testing and study of sensory illusions of all types. Illusions, Mr. Seckel said, provide "a window into how the brain works by revealing underlying mechanisms in a way that normal perception fails to do." With the help of the Web, he added, static illusions can be made "dynamic and interactive," thus immeasurably aiding researchers. Web pages and freeware programs demonstrating sensory illusions abound. At Illusion Works (www.illusionworks.com), a site that Mr. Seckel created, there are many examples of illusions, as well as some discussion of the cognitive science behind them. Several fascinating auditory illusions can be found at the site of Diana Deutsch, a professor in the department of psychology at the University of California at San Diego (www.philomel.com/oncd.html). In all, there is plenty to make your skin crawl -- and delight the mind. Graphic   Photo: The rotating version of this spiral is one of many optical and auditory illusions that can be found on the Internet.

title: The Sad Ballad Of the Cybercafe
body: HUNCHED over a computer, Mike Rivera pecked at its keyboard, keeping up his end of a conversation in a chat room. "Hey, I think I got a lesbian on here," he said in a stage whisper. Mr. Rivera, who is 19, does not have a computer at home, he said, so he was trading messages with an unseen stranger on a computer at a cybercafe, which sells computer access, light food and coffee. But Mr. Rivera was the only person seated at the neat row of six shiny computers on a recent afternoon at XS newyork, a cybercafe and video game arcade in midtown Manhattan. Worse, Mr. Rivera, who works behind the pizza counter at XS, was not even a paying customer. "Someone left it on so I started messing with it," he said before finally returning to the pizza counter. The deserted computers at XS newyork are not unusual. In city after city, cybercafes have quietly closed or turned into something else. And many of the ones that are still in business are attracting fewer and fewer visitors -- perhaps surprising, given the ballyhoo when cybercafes became popular in the mid-1990's. In a way, the decline of the cybercafe is an indicator of the increasing strength of America's embrace of the computer and the Internet. As people who sampled the World Wide Web in cafes found themselves seduced by it, and as more computers became affordable, many got their own computers and speedy home connections. Along the way, the cybercafes started drying up. The notion of a cybercafe -- a place for Net surfers to socialize on a tide of gourmet coffee -- is at odds with how most people want to use computers, even in their leisure time. Those who Web surf, read email, write or program or do just about anything else on a computer often do so in solitude. Paying $7 to $14 an hour for a seat in a cafe to work or play on a computer is not necessarily logical. "Those two ideas don't mesh well," said Pearl Mitchell, an acting assistant treasurer for a Wall Street bank and trust company and a part-time model. Ms. Mitchell, 21, who was recently in a newyork cybercafe shopping on the Internet for her first computer, said that once she bought her dream desktop machine, she would sharply cut back on her visits to cybercafes. She has been going three to five times a week to check her email and browse her favorite sites, she said. It is precisely that sort of change in computing habits, say many associated with cybercafes in the unitedstates, that have these Internet watering holes dying off like dinosaurs after that really big meteor crash. The IDT Megabite Cafe, for example, which opened two years ago in the shadow of some of Manhattan's biggest computer shops, closed in February. Its owner, Gaddy Haymov, reopened the cafe as a kosher pizza and sushi shop -- without the computers -- called the Original Boychicks. The @Cafe in Greenwich Village, once very popular, stands empty and boarded up. Weathered fliers cling to its bricks, reminding passers-by of the computer cruising that could be had inside not so long ago. Cybercafes have recently closed in cities as different as Washington and Louisville, Ky. Even in San Francisco, ground zero for the current explosion in Internet development and the holy land for worshipers of all things computer, the cybercafe scene is struggling to survive. "It is on the decline in terms of the numbers of people using them," said Craig Phillips, a documentary filmmaker who last year completed a short film about cybercafe culture in San Francisco. "It reached a peak out here before I was doing this film." Mr. Phillips, a 29-year-old administrative assistant for the California Humanities Council, said he had gone from visiting cybercafes in the San Francisco Bay area frequently to visiting them only occasionally. "For being places that provided a way to socialize, to meet a bunch of people, that's not happening as much these days," he said. In fact, he said, while making his 25-minute documentary, "Connected," he discovered that cybercafes, particularly one called the Horseshoe in the Haight-Ashbury section of the city, had severely scaled back computer services. Some computer cafes have become a haven for young people simply looking for a place to hang out more than a place to go on line. "Some tourist would come in and then leave quickly," Mr. Phillips noted. But in many other countries, especially in Central America, Africa and parts of Western Europe, where computer and Internet use has significantly lagged behind that in the unitedstates, the cybercafe scene still sizzles. And in Hawaii, where the rates of computer and Internet use are among the highest in the unitedstates, cybercafes generally remain popular. Some, like the three-year-old Internet Cafe in Honolulu, attract mostly students and tourists who didn't pack their computers along with their bathing suits and suntan lotion. "A lot of people are still coming in just for fun," said Tresy Lorch, manager of the cafe. "We try to keep up and offer people what they want." At the Internet Cafe, that means a friendly atmosphere with reasonable rates and superfast Internet connections. But part of the cybercafes' continuing allure in Hawaii, 5,000 miles from the mainland, is that they provide a way for people to come together and ease the sense of the island state's geographic isolation, some say. "Some people really feel that," said Olin Lagon, who works in Hawaii as a director of special projects for Worldpoint, a maker of language translation software. "Besides being so different and clean, Hawaii is the world's most isolated land mass. Here, cybercafes are like sophisticated nightclubs." FOR different reasons, cybercafes are also flourishing in foreign lands. In Mexico, for instance, Internet directories of cybercafes (www.cybercaptive.com) list 15 in the Mexico City area alone and some 50 nationwide. "We opened 18 months ago with four machines," said Israel Salgado Leyva, manager of the Cyberspace Cafe, a popular spot in Condesa, a neighborhood of leafy parks and Art Deco apartment buildings in Mexico City. "Now we have 14 Pentium computers." He added that he planned to install 10 more soon. In Milan, groups of people routinely visit cybercafes to jointly cruise Internet sites, said Paolo Bardicchia, an Italian-born business consultant who works in England. Any Net sites featuring the actor Leonardo DiCaprio have been especially popular for communal consumption since he starred in the billion-dollar film "Titanic." "It is much different there than here," said Mr. Bardicchia, who stopped in the XS cybercafe recently during a business trip to newyork. "They are not places where people go alone." At the Virtual World Internet Cafe, which is in the Virtual World Electronics Store in Moscow, the scene is decidedly futuristic. Customers, whose ages ranged from 11 to 17 on a recent afternoon, occupy the cafe's nine computer workstations in a well-lighted space where the central decoration is an illuminated photo of two hands reaching across a globe. The Internet access here is free, and no purchases are necessary. But those wishing to surf the Net must get on the waiting list early because vacancies last only long enough for someone to leave a seat and another person to sit down. Yevgeny Alichinikov, a college freshman and self-proclaimed movie addict, was using his hour on the computer to surf the Complete Oscar site. "I can get everything on films on the Web," said Mr. Alichinikov.  "My favorite actor is Rutger Hauer, and this way I can find out all the films that he's been in. Now I am looking for films with Glenn Close." In San Francisco, Jonathan Nelson, chief executive of Organic Online, an interactive design and communications company there, said cybercafes were a logical beginning for people in countries like Russia and China, where the Internet is still a novelty. "They are a first step, and then you move on," said Mr. Nelson, whose work takes him around the world. "That paradigm is happening all over the world. Cybercafes in South Africa are very interesting now." THE key to keeping a cybercafe alive in the unitedstates these days is to offer more to prospective customers than simply snappy computers and superfast T-1 lines to the Internet. At @Alan's, a cybercafe that opened two and a half years ago in Montclair, N.J., its eight computers, juice bar, coffee and light foods are still attracting customers, said its manager, Michael Townsend. As he spoke, a half-dozen preteen-age boys were at the computers, mostly playing games. Nonetheless, Mr. Townsend acknowledged, "it's tough to stay in business." To beef up revenues, he said, the cybercafe also offers, for a fee, of course, computer training and Web site development. The Internet Cafe, which opened three years ago in a former botanica in newyork's East Village, has rooted its appeal in a decidedly low-tech decor and low-key atmosphere. The modest cybercafe is essentially a long, narrow room that has four computers, a color printer and scanner and is filled with comfortable tables and chairs and a small bar and television in the back. The cafe's stereo speakers are partial to vintage Sinatra and midtempo jazz. There is also coffee and an extensive beer list. "This is the kind of place that we hope people would enjoy even if there weren't any computers here," said Arthur Perley, a computer consultant and the cafe's owner. Saying that early cybercafes leaned on the "flash and glitz" of emerging technologies, Mr. Perley concluded: "Once the dazzle wears off, once the hype wears off, then the reality is sitting there. What is it? "Oh, it's a computer sitting in the corner, and you have a cafe." Graphic   Photos: SURVIVING -- The Internet Cafe in the East Village offers computers, coffee, beer and smooth music. (Catrina Genovese for The newyork Times)(pg. G1); CHINA ON LINE -- Two office workers explored the Web at Beijing's Internet Cafe. (Reuters)(pg. G8)

title:
USER'S GUIDE;
Scouting a Path For Home Networks
body: I OPENED the door of my refrigerator the other night and gazed upon a few limp scallions, a cucumber and a forlorn can of tuna. If I had only had a computer -- one that was networked and connected to the Internet -- right next to the refrigerator, I could have conveniently searched the Web for a delicious dish concocted from those foods. As long as I am fantasizing, why stop there? In the tradition of Local Area Networks (L.A.N.'s), why not connect all the computers in my house in a single Home Area Network (H.A.N.)? Like a lot of families, mine has the necessary raw ingredients on hand: a motley assemblage of equipment of assorted ages. In this fantasy, all I would need to live like the Jetsons would be a discreet little black box, intelligent enough to communicate with all the machines and connected by a single plug in an existing wall outlet. My husband and I could be on the Internet simultaneously without tying up both phone lines. Every morning, my daughters could check a master file detailing soccer practices, the weather report and the school cafeteria menu to determine whether to pack a sandwich or sneakers. And I could send universal email: "Family: Couldn't help noticing shoes in foyer. Remove soonest. :-)" Unfortunately, that little black box does not exist yet, although there are 14 million households in the unitedstates that each have more than one computer and might use one. According to research commissioned by Intel last year, most of those families yearn for a home network. For now, the barriers remain high. If everyone owned only Macintoshes, with the Appletalk networking software built in, networking would be a breeze. But multicomputer households are more likely to have idiosyncratic collections. My house contains two Power PC's, an I.B.M. Thinkpad, an old DEC desktop running a 286 microprocessor, a vintage Hewlett-Packard printer, a Laser Writer printer and a machine that ran the old CP/M operating system. Not to mention the Kaypro in the attic. Some households have created order from similar chaos. The Stones of Shaker Heights, Ohio, fall into that category. Martin Stone, a lawyer who works at home, is also a computer consultant. In the last nine years, he and his two sons, Aaron and Robbie, have built a sophisticated network for their family of five, connecting six computers and three printers. They started modestly in 1989, with two 286 boxes that Mr. Stone upgraded to 386's with the help of Aaron and Robbie, then 7 and 4. "We did it instead of building models," Mr. Stone said. "I took the first one and took everything apart and showed the boys what each card was," Mr. Stone recalled. "Then I took the second one, gave the boys a screwdriver to share and said: 'Here. You do it.' They just gradually took it apart, and I supervised after school. It took maybe two months. At that point, my wife was seriously ready to murder me since it was still all over the dining-room table. But we told her it was for a good cause." In 1994, the Stones bought a bigger house. The move inspired them to install a new phone system and wiring for a computer network throughout the three floors of their 75-year-old house. By doing the wiring themselves, they kept their costs low. Mr. Stone designed a star-shaped layout for the network and put the central hub to direct traffic in the basement. Two RJ-11 jacks (for phone and modem use) and one RJ-45 jack (for network access) were installed in each room, bathrooms and closets excluded. Over nine years, the Stones upgraded all their computers so they could communicate, adding network interface cards to each machine. Aside from the computers, the networking costs were relatively low until Robbie, then 12, persuaded his father to buy a server, a gently used Silicon Graphics workstation, for $4,995. It connects the other machines to a central modem. All told, the Stones have spent $25,600 (including hardware) for their home network, an investment they say was well worth it. On top of that, they have budgeted $1,000 for hardware upgrades and $1,000 for software for 1998. Each family member -- including Sarah, 6 -- has a computer in his or her bedroom. The Stones use their network for local email and for editing one another. "I read the boys' assignments and they read my briefs," Mr. Stone said. While the technically savvy Stones may be an anomaly, the desire for home networks has caught the attention of business. "Most families are still trying to get their VCR's to stop flashing," said Michael Gartenberg, research director of the Gartner Group in Stamford, Conn. "The first vendor with a Home-Network-in-a-Box product will make a fortune." Some experts predict that demand could spawn a $1 billion market within five years. "There's going to be an explosion," said Eric Schmidt, the chief executive officer of Novell, a networking giant. "You'll see hundreds of different products in the next couple of years from vendors -- mostly unknown vendors -- to try to solve this problem." If you want to build your own home network before then, you will just have to improvise. The hub, a wire-switching device to route traffic, costs about $100. (The Stones bought one in the early 1990's from Boca Research. Another company that sells hubs is Asante Technologies. Interface cards, which need to be installed in every machine -- every computer, fax, scanner and printer on the network -- typically cost less than $100 each. You will need to buy telephone-type cables and various connectors and wall jacks. These cost the Stones about $500. Because all the computers on your network must be able to communicate with one another, you will need network-server operating systems. The Stones chose Linux (a free version of Unix that can be downloaded from the Net) and Irix, enabling the client machines to run Windows 95. They use the TCP/IP network protocol on each of the machines on the network. With TCP/IP, you can mix PC's, Macs, Unix boxes and many other flavors, including, if you happen to own one, a mainframe. Intel, which commissioned the study on home networks, is studying ways to eliminate the need for cables. Brad Romney, an assistant business unit manager at Intel, said: "We have three approaches: use existing phone lines, use existing electrical lines or else do wireless with radio transmissions. It's not far off." But it did not arrive in time for my family's supper. It was not until I fired up the old modem on my office computer that I found a recipe for dilled tuna salad with cucumbers. I wonder what the Jetsons would have served. Graphic   Illustration. (Margaret Riegel)

title: GTE to Offer Faster Access to Internet
body: The GTE Corporation said today that it planned to offer high-speed Internet access up to 50 times faster than conventional modems to consumers and businesses beginning in June. The company said its unit, GTE Network Services, would offer network-based asymmetric digital subscriber line service in about 300 central offices in 16 states. The plan is subject to regulatory approval, the company said. The company said it planned to expand this service to no less than 30 additional markets in the second half of 1998. This campaign "helps enable GTE to offer end-to-end Internet solutions on a broader scale, and is in keeping with the company's overall goal to become a national provider of integrated telecommunications services," the company said. The new service will provide continuous Internet access in place of traditional dial-up modem connections, the statement said. "Consumers can simultaneously surf the World Wide Web and place telephone calls over the same line," the company said. GTE said it would offer customers monthly and multiyear plans as well as volume discounts. The monthly target price range is $30 to $250, excluding certain charges, such as an installation fee, Internet service charges, and modem leases, the company said.

title:
Bringing Asia on Line;
Hong Kong Tycoon Seeks Internet Success
body: For four years, people here have been asking Richard Li the question he is tired of hearing but knows he cannot escape: What will you do next? hongkong is an impatient place, and this lean, tightly wound 31-year-old has a reputation and a family pedigree to live up to. The reputation was made in the early 1990's, when Mr. Li started Asia's first satellite-delivered cable television service, Star TV, and then sold a controlling stake to Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation for $525 million in 1993. His pedigree is even more formidable: the second son of hongkong's most prominent tycoon, Li Ka-shing, and heir to a fortune estimated near $9 billion. Mr. Li's rarefied background has made him the subject of endless gossip by rivals in hongkong business, who wonder what he might do for an encore. On March 12, they got an answer. Mr. Li announced plans to start a digital media company to provide Internet access and other information services to television sets and personal computers throughout Asia. In a part of the world where firsthand experience with the Internet remains a rarity, Mr. Li's is an audacious undertaking -- all the more so because Asia is limping through the worst economic downturn since the end of World War II. But Mr. Li's company, the Pacific Century Group, has signed Intel as a partner to provide financing and technological expertise for the venture. And Mr. Li says the region's financial turmoil only dramatizes the need for better, faster information. "What separated the countries that did O.K. from those that didn't was the availability of information," said Mr. Li over breakfast at his offices, which had a panoramic view of Victoria harbor until his father began building a 57-story office tower next door. "Which countries are still standing? Singapore, hongkong, Taiwan. Which ones aren't? Korea, Thailand, Indonesia." The difference, he explained, was that when the turmoil began last summer as a currency run in Thailand, business people and policy makers in Singapore, hongkong and Taiwan generally had access to real-time electronic news, while people in other parts of the region did not.  It Won't Be All Serious: Quotes and Karaoke Lest people think Mr. Li aspires to be the Michael Bloomberg of Asia, he still views this latest venture as being in the entertainment tradition of Star TV. So while he plans to distribute Bloomberg-like stock quotes and news in addition to Internet access, Mr. Li also plans to offer video games and a karaoke feature that will allow viewers to warble along with their TV sets. "If you look at our offerings, they will be divided half between work, making money, and half fun," he said. If the plan unfolds as Mr. Li envisions, about two years from now Pacific Century will begin beaming the service by satellite to cable operators throughout the region. They would then deliver it over upgraded cable wires to subscribers, whose homes would be outfitted with modems -- allowing them to receive the service either over their TV's or personal computers. Intel, which owns 40 percent of the venture, is developing the broad-band technology that will enable Mr. Li to deliver information at high speeds over a network of satellites and cable. Typically, satellite services are constrained by the lack of true, two-way communication; they generally require subscribers to send commands back to the Internet by a regular phone line. But Pacific Century plans to beam data to cable operators, who would store it in computers attached to the cable network. Rather than interacting with a satellite, Mr. Li's subscribers would be sending and receiving data over the cable lines. "Think of this as an Asian version of At Home," said Avram Miller, corporate vice president for business development at Intel, referring to the At Home Network, the high-speed Internet service owned by several American cable operators. At Home offers Internet access and an array of information and entertainment services to about 50,000 subscribers in the unitedstates and Canada. But its growth has been slow so far, in part because cable operators have delayed upgrading their systems. Intel holds a small stake in At Home and has a joint venture with Deutsche Telekom, SES Astra and Hughes Electronics to create a similar service in Europe. Intel's investment in Mr. Li's venture is part of its broader strategy of finding ways to stimulate sales of PC's that use its chips. For the moment, the company has limited its investment to $10 million, according to executives familiar with the deal. It may increase that to $50 million -- still a modest wager for a company of its size -- if the market pans out.  Pitching to a Continent That's Largely Unwired And that is a decidedly big "if." While hongkong and other Asian cities have no shortage of Internet service providers, cybertechnology has come to Asia more slowly than in the unitedstates and Europe. Less than six million people in Asia roam the World Wide Web, compared with 19.2 million in the unitedstates, a study by Salomon Smith Barney found. Subtract Japan from the total, and Asia has an Internet population of 1.8 million -- in a region of nearly three billion people. And Internet use here has been hobbled by language barriers, a scarcity of telephone lines and a paucity of personal computers. While 40 percent of households in the unitedstates have a PC, only 15 percent of homes in hongkong have them, and in China, just four-tenths of 1 percent have them. Even lands relatively high PC penetration like South Korea have low Internet use because of a lack of English-speakers. The Web may be worldwide, Mr. Li noted, but its content is still overwhelmingly in English and focused mainly on the unitedstates. "Most of the information on the Internet is of interest to Americans -- face it," he said. But Mr. Li said his service would package and store information aimed at specific audiences in their own languages. It is a strategy he used successfully with entertainment programming at Star TV, when viewers who had subsisted on a diet of Western fare were suddenly offered films in Mandarin and music videos featuring Indian, Chinese and Korean performers. In just three years, Star TV's five channels attracted 50 million households in 38 countries. Two years from now, when Intel completes the development process, Mr. Li will take to the road to sell the service to cable operators from Taiwan to Thailand and from India to Indonesia. They will be mostly the same operators who signed up for Star TV in the early 1990's. He thinks his exuberant marketing will win them over again. "We want to cover at least many countries as Star," he said. In a study Intel prepared for potential technology suppliers, the company projects that the service could sign up 20 million subscribers four years after its beginning. Mr. Li conceded this was probably unrealistic now, but he said the service would break even with less than two million customers. Analysts who follow Pacific Century are skeptical that Mr. Li will have the same quick success as he did with Star TV. "It's easy to be bullish about Asia," said Chia Yew Boon, research director at Santander Investment Securities in Singapore. "But these days, you've got to temper your projections." Then, too, selling a digital information service is a keener marketing challenge than a satellite television service. Although Star TV's culturally specific programming was a breakthrough, it was still plain old television. High-speed Internet access is an exotic concept to many Asians, who have not been weaned on the wonders of the digital age like people in the unitedstates. Kaushik Shridharani, an analyst with Salomon Smith Barney here, said Mr. Li might face an uphill battle gaining distribution -- particularly if he limits himself to cable, which does not have the ubiquitous network of telephone companies. "So far, the phone companies are still in the best position in each market." And for all of Star TV's popularity, Mr. Murdoch continues to lose an estimated $40 million a year on the service. Despite its customized approach, Mr. Shridharani said Star TV still struggled to attract advertising -- often losing to local broadcasters offering purely local programs. Even against long odds, Mr. Li brims with the self-confidence of a young man who has tasted success and has a rich father's backing. The elder Mr. Li invested $125 million in Star TV and allowed his son to plow $400 million in profits from the Murdoch deal into Pacific Century. In addition to the media venture, Pacific owns a life-insurance company and has property investments in Tokyo and Beijing. Despite the plunge in Asian property values, Mr. Li said Pacific Century's real estate investments were relatively conservative bets that allowed him to dabble in the more speculative world of cyberspace. "I want to make money in safe ways; that's the first step," he said. "The second step is doing what you really want to do. But that's not always the best thing for you to do."  To the Manor Born; To the Board Room Bred Fiscal responsibility is deeply ingrained in Mr. Li, who grew up with the privileges and burdens of hongkong's commercial elite. After graduating from Stanford in 1987 with a degree in computer engineering, Mr. Li threw himself into a career as an investment banker in Canada. After four years, his father summoned him home to join the family business. Soon after his return, Mr. Li developed the idea of Star TV -- in large part as a way to carve out an independent role within the family empire. During the frenetic start-up, the 20-something tycoon developed a reputation as an imperious and abrasive boss. But people who know Mr. Li say he has become more relaxed. "As a person, he's mellowed enormously," said Simon Murray, former managing director of the Li family's public company, Hutchison Whampoa Ltd. "He's good fun to be with," added Mr. Murray, who is also on the board of the Pacific Century Group. "He appreciates a good glass of wine." And Mr. Li can always turn to his father for advice. The elder Mr. Li, who came to hongkong as a refugee from mainland China in the 40's, rose from making plastic flowers to controlling an empire that spans real estate, telecommunications, shipping and petroleum. In 1980, his boundless ambition led him to seize control of Hutchison Whampoa, a fabled hongkong trading company, turning him into the city's most prominent Chinese tycoon. While Richard's older brother, Victor, is widely expected to succeed his father at Hutchison Whampoa and the other family businesses, Li Ka-shing takes an interest in his younger son's ventures that goes beyond signing the checks. "Just last night, he was asking me, 'What the hell is this thing?' " said Richard, referring to the Intel joint venture. Richard is a deputy chairman of Hutchison Whampoa, which keeps his hand in the family business. But he has clung stubbornly to his independence. The elder Mr. Li, for example, recently proposed that Richard move into the family's new headquarters, which just happens to be the tower rising outside his window. The son was noncommittal, saying that the two would have to negotiate the rent. "Right now, he just blocks the view," Richard said with a sly grin. title: On Internet, Playing Fair May Mean Paying Up
body: An old adage swirled around the Federal Communications Commission last week as it proposed levying network access fees against some companies that provide telephone service over the Internet. "If it walks like a duck, if it quacks like a duck, it just might be a duck." That was the basic philosophy behind Friday's decision, a person close to the commission said. In other words: If something looks and sounds like long-distance telephone service, the providers should pay the same access fees that conventional long-distance companies must pay. Internet advocates howled. They saw the move as the first of many to come against the freedom of cyberspace. But there is another way to look at the proposed fees -- not so much as a new layer of regulation, but as a realization that there are costs to operating a public communications network and that everyone using the network should help cover those costs. It seems that all the F.C.C. really did in this case was to remove a loophole in the complex web of subsidies that supports basic telephone service in this nation. Phone calls that are routed over the Internet are cheaper than phone calls sent over the conventional telephone network for two reasons. One is that the Internet uses a more economical routing technology than the old-fashioned phone network. The second advantage -- the one the F.C.C. now seeks to remove -- is that because Internet phone service is so new, it is not covered by the federally supervised cost-sharing system of the long-distance industry. Friday's recommendation by the F.C.C. seemed to set the commission against the Clinton Administration, which said the Internet telephone companies should be left alone. But the real difference between the White House's and the F.C.C.'s view of cyberspace reaches much farther. The White House wants to regulate the Internet for what it is. The commission wants to regulate the Internet for what it does. The way the F.C.C. sees it, if a company provides long-distance voice connections between regular telephones it does not really matter whether those links come over the Internet or via a less exotic communications system. Either way, those calls originate and terminate over the local telephone networks. And so, the F.C.C. said, either way the carrier should have to pay into the national cost-sharing pools that help support local telephone networks. In essence, the issue underscores the difference between two basic sorts of networks: "packet switched" networks, like the Internet, and "circuit switched" networks, like the main systems of companies like AT&T and Sprint. The terms may be arcane, but the concepts are fairly simple. If a network is a highway, the lanes of a circuit network are painted solid; each "conversation" travels in its own path, without interference from its neighbors. It is a fast, care-free way to travel but also relatively expensive. In a packet network, the lines between lanes are dashed; if there is room in a neighboring lane, traffic can switch to a faster path. Sharing lanes means sharing costs and everyone travels for a lower fare. Packet networks, originally designed as a way to route computer data, have existed for decades. But only recently has technology emerged that allowed them to show how they can be more efficient than circuit networks for transmitting information like phone calls. Now, though, companies that are building transcontinental communications networks from scratch are building them around packet technologies. These companies include The Qwest Communications unit of the Anschutz Corporation; Level 3 Communications Inc. and IXC Communications Inc. IXC and Qwest each plan to announce this week that they have activated major coast-to-coast portions of their networks. Going forward, the essential regulatory question about the Internet is whether its form of technology merits some sort of special hands-off treatment from regulators, or whether the technology should be forced to prove itself -- and pay for itself -- without any special treatment Eighteen months ago, the Frontier Corporation agreed to pay about $500 million for up to one-third of Qwest's network. In the fall of 1996, the idea of building a national network around packet technology was revolutionary; Frontier's judgment was questioned. These days, most Wall Street investment bankers consider Frontier an attractive acquisition target. The main lure: its one-third stake in Qwest's network. So far, the Internet has been seen as new enough and unique enough that it should be allowed to grow and flourish without Government meddling. And when it comes to new services and the information content of those services, the Clinton Administration so far has advocated a laissez faire approach. But on Friday, the Clinton-appointed F.C.C. chairman, William E. Kennard, and his fellow commissioners seemed to take this stand: When it comes to sharing the costs of maintaining the public network, the ideal of laissez-faire should not get in the way of doing what is fair.

title: Software Designers Share the Code
body: What is the best way to improve the quality of software in the $50 billion software industry? Give it away. Or so say more than a dozen of the nation's best-known software designers, who met last week to promote the idea of freely sharing the underlying code -- known as source code -- for both popular and arcane software. Such sharing, which recalls the "freeware" spirit of the original Internet, could result in better software by giving any programmer the opportunity to modify, add to or otherwise improve existing programs, the group said. Subversive as the idea may sound in the age of stock options and I.P.O.'s, proponents say the point is not to do away with commercial, for-profit selling of software. Instead, the group simply wants to foster more alternatives to the industry-dominant programs created by giants like the Microsoft Corporation and the Oracle Corporation. "There's a fantasy that open source code and capitalism are contradictory; that is false," said Eric Allman, a member of the group and creator of Sendmail, a free program that routes and delivers the majority of the Internet's electronic mail. Until recently Mr. Allman maintained Sendmail as a hobby, while he worked at a variety of programming jobs. But last month, he co-founded Sendmail Inc. to create a commercial version of the program, for which customers would receive technical support. At the same time, the company will continue to maintain a free version of the software. Freeware sentiment seems to be in the air these days. The group's first meeting, last Tuesday evening, came a week after the Netscape Communications Corporation announced that it was making the source code to its Communicator Internet browser freely available to programmers who wished to modify it or add features. Source code is the original programmer's instructions, before the instructions are read by a program called a compiler or an interpreter and converted into a form that can be used by a computer. Netscape executives have said that they are hoping to tap into a ground swell of creativity by the programming community to help the popular program become even more widely adopted and enable the software to evolve in ways that Microsoft's team of in-house programmers might not be able to match with their browser, called Explorer. To compete with Netscape, Microsoft back in 1996 decided to give away the Explorer browser for free. Then last year Microsoft decided to add the browser at no extra charge to the Windows 95 operating system, prompting an antitrust inquiry by the Justice Department. In neither case, though, did Microsoft publicly release the original source code for Explorer. For Netscape, whatever the competing alternatives to Communicator that might result from releasing the source code, the company itself would conceivably benefit by having its program serve as the industry standard. Netscape's goals are similar to those of the ad hoc group of programmers who met last Tuesday: speeding up software innovation by making it a community affair. "This is a second force in the computer industry," said Tim O'Reilly, the meeting's organizer and president of O'Reilly & Associates, a Sebastopol, Calif., publisher of computer software guidebooks. "The open source model is an engine for innovation." The programmers contend that the economic forces that favored Microsoft's market model of selling software in shrink-wrapped packages has been altered by the Internet. The free distribution of software over the network will increasingly favor those who want to freely share their software, they said. Mr. O'Reilly said that much of the software that is integral to the Internet was written by the programmers who attended the meeting. "This is the Internet's dream team," he said. Besides Mr. Allman, the group included Linus Torvalds, creator of Linux, a popular free version of the Unix operating system; Phil Zimmermann, creator of Pretty Good Privacy, an encryption program widely used in both freeware and commercial forms; Larry Wall, creator of Perl, a language used widely by Internet web sites; Brian Behlendor, a software developer who maintains and updates Apache, the Internet's most popular software for Web server computers; Paul Vixie; creator of Bind, the program that translates numeric Internet addresses into names, and John K. Ousterhout, developer of Tcl/Tk, a popular language for special projects and tying together disparate programs. Sendmail and Apache are examples of free programs that dominate markets in which commercial competitors lag badly. In both cases, the free programs were able to quickly establish a foothold because of the ease of distribution via the Internet and were of such high quality that it has been impossible for commercial products to dislodge them.
