title:
TECHNOLOGY;
An on-line tug-of-war over consumers' personal information.
body: Nowhere is the conflict between traditional and electronic commerce more perfectly drawn than in the war between champions of consumer privacy and the companies that sell our personal data. A series of recent events offer a snapshot of the battlefield: * On March 30, in what both parties called "the most widespread initiative undertaken by members of the Internet industry," the Internet Content Coalition (www.icc.org) -- a group of high-powered on-line and traditional media companies, including The newyork Times -- and Trust-E (www.truste.org), an on-line privacy group, announced that they would jointly promote Trust-E's program as the industry standard for disclosing to consumers on the World Wide Web what information is being gathered about them and how it is being used. * One day later, the Federal Trade Commission wrapped up a monthlong survey of privacy policies and practices on commercial and children's Web sites. It will report to Congress in June. The commission had set out to measure what Web vendors were actually doing to protect privacy after listening to consumer concerns and the industry's pleas for self-regulation since 1995. * On that same day, the Metromail Corporation, a consumer-data vendor, agreed to be acquired by Great Universal Stores P.L.C. for about $845 million. Metromail boasts that its National Consumer Data Base contains detailed information on 103 million people, representing 95 percent of American households. * And last week, in a deal that was saluted by some privacy advocates and slammed by others, the Firefly Network (www.firefly.com) -- which over the past couple years has engendered much controversy with its extensive Web-based data collection and consumer profiling capabilities -- was sold to the Microsoft Corporation for $40 million, specifically because of its privacy-protection technology and policies. The exploitation of consumers' personal information as a sales tool has been a very good business for data vendors like Metromail and, more recently, Firefly. But clearly it is the Internet that makes Metromail worth nearly $1 billion. Data vendors believe, as do most modern marketers, that one-on-one sales pitches are the future of commerce -- and because the Internet links so easily to one user at a time, it is their dream machine. But where consumers seem indifferent to junk mail on the front stoop, they are fanatic about guarding their personal information on line -- a fact that, oddly, seems to be lost on Web vendors intent on gathering it. A June 1997 Georgia Tech survey of Web users, for example, showed that 87 percent thought they should have "complete control" over the demographic data captured on sites. More than 71 percent wanted new laws to protect their on-line privacy. In addition, 94 percent of Web users have refused to provide information to a Web site, and 40 percent have given fake information, according to a report by the Vanderbilt University researchers Donna Hoffman, Tom Novak and Marcos Peralta (http://www2000.ogsm.vanderbilt.edu/), who analyzed the Georgia Tech data together with data from a 1997 Nielsen Media Research report. Web vendors can collect oodles of personal data without even telling consumers they are doing so. And once visitors type in an email address, which increasingly they are required to do to gain access to sites, their actions from that moment are directly linked to them as individuals. A Web vendor can track which pages they visit, what they buy, where they have linked from and where they go after they leave, and in certain cases, can tell how long you linger at various sites. The level of detail shocks many consumers. "What the Internet has done is make explicit what used to be implicit -- namely that there are dossiers on you that can be built up with great granularity," says Nat Goldhaber, chairman of Cybergold (www.cybergold.com), a membership site that connects buyers to sellers and posts a strict privacy policy. To allay consumer fears while giving vendors the data to market their products, organizations like the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants and Trust-E now provide audits and reviews of commercial information practices. Trust-E, for example, grants a "trustmark" to companies that post a Trust-E-approved privacy policy on their Web sites. "What we need to see in their posted policies is: What information are you collecting that could personally identify me? What are you doing with it, and who are you sharing it with?" says Susan Scott, executive director of Trust-E. "We don't care whether they sell it; we just care if they disclose it." Ms. Hoffman of Vanderbilt said that many informal surveys consistently suggest that fewer than 30 percent of commercial sites display privacy policies, despite the F.T.C.'s growing involvement in the problem. David Medine, the commission's associate director for credit practices, says that getting the whole industry to practice disclosure might help avoid the need for a Federal privacy law. "We don't have a generalized privacy law today," Mr. Medine said, "but there are deceptive trade practice laws that apply. We are already investigating firms for violating their privacy policies. Once you voluntarily promise, you have to keep your promise." On the flip side, Mr. Medine admits, deceptive trade laws do not force companies to adopt privacy policies. "Consumers want that information, and it's impeding the growth of E-commerce for them not to have it," he said. "The real question is how. Whether we get there by self-regulation or Federal regulation is what we're resolving now." Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
One Site, 14 Ethnic Groups
body: Most start-up Web sites, especially those aimed at ethnic audiences who may have limited access to the Internet, struggle for a few thousand page views a month. By that standard, Asian Avenue, which six young newyorkers run out of an apartment in Manhattan's financial district, is an unusually successful site. It claims more than five million page views a month from more than 50,000 members, a significant increase from the 500,000 page views and 3,000 members it had last September. At least 14 ethnicities are represented among members, including Cambodian, Indonesian, Lao and Malay. Asian Avenue, which was started almost two years ago and developed by a company called Community Connect Inc., has grown mainly by word of mouth, Benjamin Sun, 25, the company president, said "A Web site for car lovers is not really a community," Mr. Sun said. "Age, religion, ethnicity; those are the ties that bind together a community." Many Web surfers are reluctant to reveal such information. But plenty of Asian Avenue visitors, who are typically 16 to 30, have filled out the extensive questionnaire that enables them to become members and use the site's fast search engines to scan profiles of other members. A Filipino doctor in Minneapolis can find other Filipino physicians in the same city, for example. Most of Asian Avenue's content is produced by members themselves. The site offers tool kits to create personal home pages, chat rooms and interactive soap operas. Members, who pay no fees, can see something new almost every time they log on. Four of the founders of Asian Avenue are of Asian descent. Unlike Mr. Sun, who grew up in ethnically diverse Flushing, Queens, Calvin Wong, 25, the vice president of business development, was raised in Tucson, where there were few Asians. Grace Chang, 25, the creative director, immigrated to the unitedstates from Korea at 13 speaking no English. She went to high school and college in Ann Arbor, Mich.  WHAT YOU SEE Among other things, community events prompted by Web site administrators. Cindy Moy, a young woman from the Upper East Side, for example, needed a bone-marrow transplant, and Asian Avenue publicized her search for a donor on its home page. Members took up the cause, exchanging email, and helped find a marrow donor, a young Chinese man in Singapore. Ms. Moy isnow under observation to gauge the success of the transplant. Asian Avenue members also sent a flurry of email complaints to MSNBC during the Winter Olympics, after the Web site owned by Microsoft and NBC ran a headline saying "American Beats Out Kwan" on a story about Tara Lipinksi, who is white, beating Michelle Kwan, who is of Asian descent, for the gold medal for figure skating. (Ms. Kwan won the silver medal.) Edmundo Macedo, MSNBC's executive sports editor, apologized on the MSNBC Web site "for an error that may have been interpreted to state that U.S. figure skater Michelle Kwan was not American."  LINKS A few, mainly to affiliated advertisers.  WHAT YOU GET An intriguing work in progress that Community Connect hopes to extend to black, Hispanic and other "avenues."  ASIAN AVENUE http://www.communityconnect.com/AsianAvenue.html

title: F.C.C. Urges Policy Change In Cyberspace
body: Marking a profound shift in the way the Government views cyberspace, the Federal Communications Commission said yesterday that at least some companies that provide telephone service over the Internet should be regulated in some of the same ways that traditional phone companies like AT&T are regulated. The recommendation could signal the end of the Internet as a wide-open, overwhelmingly unregulated frontier. It is the first time the F.C.C. has proposed that some Internet companies pay the same charges as long-distance phone carriers, and it puts the commission at odds with the Clinton Administration's "hands-off" policy toward cyberspace. The fees proposed yesterday would not apply to all Internet service providers and would not raise the bills of everyday Web surfers. Instead, they would apply to the small group of companies that are infiltrating the highly competitive world of long-distance calling by routing conversations over the Internet. This new generation of Internet long-distance companies provides service between normal telephones but at prices far below those of mainstream carriers like MCI Communications or Sprint. They have been undercutting the long-distance giants because they do not have to pay myriad charges that Federal regulators levy on traditional carriers. That could now begin to change. And Internet advocates fear that the proposal was only the first glance from a Government that is turning its regulatory magnifying glass on the digital world. "To begin regulating any portion of this industry is to me a very bad signal," said Barbara A. Dooley, executive director of the Commercial Internet Exchange, a group based in Herndon, Va., that represents about 130 Internet service providers. "This sets a path down a very bad trail toward regulating an industry that we've grown very quickly and that is critical to the future of our economy." To the commission, however, yesterday's decision was a matter of simple fairness. The recommendation came in a report on the universal service program, which helps subsidize telephone service in rural and poor areas and which helps pay for computer systems for schools and libraries. The basic question before the commission was whether Internet phone companies, like most other sorts of phone companies, should have to contribute to the universal service pool. Almost every phone company in the nation must contribute about 4 percent of the revenue it gets from its customers to the fund. In addition, long-distance phone companies must pay per-minute "access fees" to local phone companies for originating and terminating long-distance calls. Currently, providers of an "information service," like Internet providers, are exempt from most of those charges, while providers of "telecommunications service" must pay them. When Internet telephony meant talking into a computer equipped with a microphone, it could still be considered an information service, people close to the commission said yesterday. But once entrepreneurs starting using the Internet to connect long-distance calls between two standard telephones, the case for a regulatory exemption weakened, they said. Using the abbreviation for Internet Protocol, the computer technology at the heart of cyberspace, William E. Kennard, the commission's chairman, said: "If you look at the characteristics of I. P. telephony and compare them to the characteristics of a traditional long-distance telephone call, functionally they are the same. What this report does is state that very obvious fact, and certain things flow from that." Mr. Kennard said the specific implications of yesterday's decision would not become clear until the F.C.C. held additional hearings. He added that the commission would consider imposing charges on a specific Internet phone company only after receiving a specific complaint against it. But officials close to the commission said it was clear that the F.C.C. would be in favor of imposing the 4 percent universal service contribution and per-minute access fees on some companies that use the Internet to provide phone-to-phone long-distance calls. Yesterday's report put the commission, which consists of three Democrats and two Republicans, at odds with the Clinton Administration. Last year a White House commission led by a Presidential adviser, Ira C. Magaziner, recommended that the Government shy away from regulating cyberspace. The Administration repeated that stance on Thursday in a letter to Mr. Kennard from Larry Irving, Assistant Secretary of Commerce for communications and information. "Any proposal to regulate Internet telephony as a 'telecommunication service' would raise contentious issues, resolution of which would have international, as well as domestic, repercussions," Mr. Irving wrote. "Thus, the Administration urges the commission not to change its current approach." Mr. Kennard was unfazed yesterday by the prospect of contradicting the White House. "Once this decision is fully understood, it will be understood that this is not a fundamental threat to the Internet," he said. "We were looking at a very narrow class of services that resemble telecommunications services." The big winners in yesterday's announcement were the traditional long-distance giants. Most analysts estimate that only about $30 million will be spent on Internet phone service this year -- a minuscule amount of the $80 billion overall long-distance market. But Internet phone carriers like the IDT Corporation, based in Hackensack, N.J., have won the confidence of Wall Street and have raised the hackles of the long-distance traditionalists. In a statement yesterday, AT&T, the No. 1 long-distance company, said: "The success of universal service requires competitive neutrality and a broad contribution base. To that end, the commission must insure that Internet service providers and other carriers who are using new technologies contribute to the universal service fund based on their telecommunications revenues and pay cost-based access charges as well." That made sense to Eli M. Noam, a professor of finance and economics at Columbia University and director of the university's Institute for Tele-Information. "You want neutrality," he said. "You don't want anyone getting a competitive advantage or disadvantage based on the regulatory treatment of the technology they are employing. "The Internet industry would shrink in horror from the idea of industrial policy. But that is exactly what they are advocating. They say they are young, they are new, so treat us preferentially."

title: Microsoft-Intel Television Effort
body: The Microsoft Corporation and the Intel Corporation said this week that they would work jointly on technology for interactive television, as the companies try to increase their roles in home entertainment. Microsoft said it would start the partnership by licensing Intel's Intercast technology, which allows viewers to watch interactive broadcasts, and include it in Windows 98, the computer operating system it plans to offer later this year. Intel and Microsoft are working to get into entertainment markets as the line between television and the Internet blurs, betting that devices that blend traditional television with the World Wide Web will sell well. The companies said they hoped to develop a common framework for putting Internet content into television programming on a variety of devices, including personal computers equipped with TV tuners. They will focus first on traditional analog broadcasts, expanding to digital broadcasting as the new standard develops. Intel's Intercast software lets computer users gain access to Web pages that some broadcasters send along with TV programming. Users now get the Intel software when buying TV tuner cards for their PC's. The licensing agreement with Microsoft means that consumers will get the software automatically in Windows 98. It will be part of the WebTV for Windows package in Windows 98, which puts WebTV capability into personal computers.

title:
Metro Business;
Gateway to Open Office in Manhattan
body: Gateway 2000, themail-order personal computer company in North Sioux City, S.D., announced yesterday that it would open its new Web development headquarters in Manhattan. The office will open within the next few months, and company officials will be scouting locations for the headquarters next week, said Paul G. Roston, Gateway's vice president for global human resources. About 40 jobs will move to newyork with the opening of the office. All except for two senior-level managerial positions will be new hires. Mr. Roston said the company -- known for packaging its computers in boxes that are spotted black and white, like cows -- needed to expand its Internet capabilities. It currently uses its own staff and consultants in South Dakota to run its Web site. Gateway sells about $3 million worth of computers each day from the site. "We wanted the best talent, and we believe that the bulk of that talent is in San Francisco and newyork City, and the best is in newyork," Mr. Roston said. "We wanted to attract them without pulling them out of the life style and environment that they are in." Gateway 2000, a Fortune 500 company, has manufacturing plants in the unitedstates, Ireland and Malaysia and employs more than 13,000 people worldwide. Russell A. Harding, executive vice president of the newyork City Economic Development Corporation, said, "Gateway's decision to open its Web development headquarters here once again shows that newyork City, under Mayor Giuliani, has become the global leader of Internet content and technology."   NICK RAVO

title: Microsoft Joins Debate Over On-Line Privacy by Acquiring Firefly
body: The Microsoft Corporation's purchase of a tiny software developer, Firefly Network Inc., generated barely a ripple on Wall Street when it was announced today. But the deal highlights a debate on privacy over Firefly's technology, which allows computer users to control more of their personal information on the Internet. While some privacy advocates see the Firefly software as greater protection, others warn that if Microsoft integrates the software into its World Wide Web browser, as expected, it will make the gathering of vast quantities of information about individuals part of the fabric of the Internet. At the very least, the Firefly technology represents the potential for businesses to expand significantly the collection of personal information for marketing purposes. Firefly, a spinoff of Nicholas Negroponte's Media Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, designed a form of artificial intelligence that can offer recommendations for items like music and movies based on Internet users' tastes, preferences and behavior when they go to Web sites. But those kinds of data are also hungrily sought by corporations that want to distribute their ads with pinpoint accuracy. Firefly, however, also embraces and champions a new set of Internet privacy standards, which help computer users choose how much personal information is transmitted when they visit a Web site. The debate among privacy advocates stems from the fact that Firefly's standards represent a compromise between those who want to unleash the power of the Internet to transmit individualized advertising in a way never before possible and those who want to curb potential abuses by corporations and government agencies. Today, Microsoft, which dominates the personal computer industry and is a growing force on the Internet, hailed Firefly as a major step forward for personal privacy, calling it a standard that would return control over personal information to the individual. But some privacy advocates, however, questioned whether any system for gathering personal information could ever adequately protect privacy. "The Internet is at a privacy crossroads," said David Sobel, legal counsel for the Electronic Privacy Information Center, an advocacy group in Washington. "Firefly and Microsoft have proposed standards that will make the world safe for data collection, and to that extent we have problems with these technologies." Others disagreed sharply, saying that the safeguards built in to Firefly offer the best opportunity for compromise in a digital world where, increasingly, every mouse click is noted, stored in some vast data base and analyzed somewhere. "We can't be Luddites and put our heads in the sand," said Deirdre Mulligan, staff counsel for the Center for Democracy and Technology, another privacy organization, based in Washington. The dispute revolves around a range of new privacy and data profiling standards now being made final by the World Wide Web Consortium, an Internet standards body based in Cambridge, Mass. Known as the Platform for Privacy Preferences Project, or P3P, the new standard establishes a complicated computerized negotiation that drastically extends the information-gathering potential and the privacy-protection possibilities in each visit to a Web site. In addition to Microsoft and Firefly, the companies and organizations that have been working on the standard include America Online, AT&T Labs, the Center for Democracy and Technology, Doubleclick Inc., I.B.M., MCI Communications, Netscape Communications, Oracle, Sony and the Direct Marketing Association. The P3P standard, which is scheduled to become final in May, foreshadows new Internet technology that will make each visit to a Web site a complicated exchange of information in which a personal computer will have the opportunity to automatically disclose a range of information covering every conceivable category, from birth data to shoe size, depending on rules set by the computer user. At the same time, each Web site will be forced to disclose its policy for using the information it is gathering, hopefully giving the computer user the ability to decline to share data about himself. "This will put users in control of their personal information," said Nick Grouf, Firefly's president and chief executive officer. "Advanced personalized information systems like Firefly are useless unless you can address the information and control issues." Internet users already have to deal with often vexing decisions about technologies like "cookies," digital codes that Web sites deposit on users' computers so that the site can identify them the next time they visit. Cookies are used in a variety of ways, including to personalize ads and other information that are placed on users' screens when they revisit a Web site and to save a returning customer the hassle of having to enter a name and password to log in. Today, most Web browsers allow users either to be notified when a Web site tries to place a cookie or even to reject cookies entirely. Now, however, new Internet technologies with names like "cupcakes" and "BLOB's" (for binary large objects) are emerging that will force Web surfers to grapple with a whole new set of privacy concerns. These new data types represent the growing capability for remote computers to store large amounts of data on the user's computer. Advocates suggest that such changes will enhance privacy protection because personal data will increasingly reside under the user's control rather than on centralized computers. But Mr. Sobel asserted that the new standards were merely attempts to make data collection more palatable to unsuspecting consumers. "If all this technical work is being done in recognition of the fact that users are hesitant to provide personal data, why is the emphasis on collecting data at all?" he asked. Despite contending that information privacy is a basic right of computer users, Microsoft executives were vague today about how they planned to use the Firefly privacy technology. The acquisition was made by Microsoft's Interactive Media Group, rather than by its Internet division, for a reported $40 million. Company officials said that Microsoft had primarily been interested in acquiring Firefly's privacy technology and not its filtering technology. The company, which was founded in 1996, now has 70 employees, all of whom will be moved to Microsoft's headquarters in Redmond, Wash. "Our plans are a little squishy now," said Pete Higgins, the Microsoft executive in charge in the company's interactive media business. "But the driving force is to implement Firefly's privacy technology."

title: Have You Listened to Your Computer Lately?
body: VERY early one recent morning, Rob Gibson was having a hankering for home. For almost a month Mr. Gibson, the executive producer and director of Jazz at Lincoln Center, had been far away from newyork on tour with the center's celebrated jazz orchestra. After a concert, he found himself sitting in his hotel room in Adelaide, a coastal town in southwestern Australia, reading email on his laptop computer. One message snagged Mr. Gibson's attention. A friend who is the general manager of a jazz radio station in Newark urged him to do something he hardly imagined possible: listen to the station, one of his favorites, 10,000 miles away through his computer. "I said to myself, 'Let me try this,' " recalled Mr. Gibson, who described himself as "not a super tech person." He entered the Internet address of WBGO-FM (www.wbgo.org) into his laptop, and it honed in on the station's site on the World Wide Web. A couple of mouse clicks later, to Mr. Gibson's astonishment, jazz sizzled from his computer's tiny speakers. "It was extremely hip," Mr. Gibson said. To be exact, it was Lee Morgan's mellifluous trumpet that mellowed the early morning in Mr. Gibson's Australian hotel room last month before he slipped off to sleep. Mr. Gibson discovered what millions of Web cruisers are learning: the Internet, a computer-generated medium that was dominated first by text, is surprisingly well wired to transmit the great-granddaddy of wireless communications -- radio. After a century of tuning in old-fashioned analog waves that made radio, well, radio, the ever more digital world is translating some of those waves into the 1's and 0's that makes up the language of computers. The result: hundreds of radio stations, from Japan to Johannesburg, from Brazil to Boston and beyond, are being heard on personal computers as well as conventional radios. In fact, Imagine Radio, a new network of more than 20 radio stations (www.imagineradio.com), delivers news, talk and music programs to its listeners exclusively over the Internet. Moreover, the network, by using its own software tuner (available for free download at the site), lets listeners rate what they hear and thus affect the stations' play lists. "The lines are being redrawn about what a device can and cannot do or know," said Brad Porteus, managing director of Imagine Radio, which is based in Brisbane, Calif., near San Francisco. "We thought it was a good time to try to break some new ground in terms of evolution." Quincy Jones, the longtime jazz musician and entertainment magnate, certainly appreciates the potential of Internet radio. Earlier this year, he started Qradio (www.qradio.net). It is a multimedia Web site that carries live connections to four of South Africa's most popular radio stations. Along with background on musicians, many of them heard over South African radio, Qradio uses the Internet to promote and sell their music. Most of their CD's are not generally available in record stores in the unitedstates. Adam Clayton Powell 3d, vice president for technology and programs of the Freedom Forum, an advocacy group for journalistic freedom and education, said the line between what is his radio and what is his computer has so blurred that he actually uses his computer as a radio in his office in Arlington, Va. He said he regularly uses Internet radio to listen to news and music, which he said he "otherwise would be unable to get even in recorded form." "I love it, absolutely love it," he said of Internet radio, which he also uses to make inexpensive broadcasts of Freedom Forum discussions and programs. Much like publishing on the Internet, the relative cost to broadcast on the World Wide Web is modest. Mark Hardie, a senior analyst for Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass., who has closely watched the development of Internet radio, said he expected to see radio on the Web expand and improve. The reasons, he said, are compelling for both the listener and the broadcaster. "When a radio station in the real world chooses to encode and broadcast its signal over the Internet, it expands beyond the geographical boundaries of the station," he said, "including its audience that is now worldwide." The upshot? Broadcast radio will eventually be forced to adapt, much like it was forced to change with the advent of television more than 50 years ago, said Jae Kim, an analyst with Paul Kagan & Associates, a Carmel, Calif.-based research and publishing company that analyzes the communications and entertainment industries. "This will not destroy broadcast radio," he said. "What is probably going to happen more and more is that broadcast radio is going to shoehorn itself into being used in certain capacities." Mr. Kim suggested that radios will be used when people do not have or do not want to have computers: peak drive time or exercise time, when people like joggers want their radios with them. Doubts about Internet radio have generally transmuted into a supportive hum, to a lesser extent than the doubts about Internet television, which suffers because of the relatively poor video quality of its images. Still, no one knows just how many people are listening. One measure is the use of Real Player, the pre-eminent software used to deliver audio and video broadcasts on the Internet; the makers of the program say 40 million of its players have been downloaded to consumers (www.real.com) free over the Internet, while 60,000 consumers have bought a more sophisticated version. Real Networks, which is based in Seattle and makes the industry standard, Real Player 5.0, also provides its users with Timecast (www.timecast.com). It works very much like a typical Internet search engine, except that it primarily searches through more than 600 stations, organized into 20 categories. While Timecast has about 600 stations to search, many more are not in the Timecast engine, and new stations are frequently coming on line. Other stations may be found on other search engines, for example, one run by Audionet. And there is always word of mouth, say, from a friend who has discovered that a hometown radio station can now be enjoyed far away from home. Practically any multimedia computer bought in the last several years -- that is, one equipped with sound -- is able to play radio once the software has been loaded. Only a double click of a mouse on the station's name or icon launches Real Player, making an ordinary multimedia computer sound like a tinny AM radio. Most of the radio stations do not broadcast in stereo. At first blush, however, the thought of listening to the radio on a computer might seem like an idea borrowed from an old Rube Goldberg cartoon in which mind-numbingly complex contraptions are invented to perform very simple tasks. For a generation that has grown up listening to the sterile perfection of music on compact disks, the sound broadcast over the Internet, varying vastly from station to station, is occasionally marred by static breaks, and worse, total drop outs of sound lasting around 3 to 10 seconds. In a random test using a 28.8 baud-modem (the suggested minimum), three stations based in and outside of the unitedstates, played for more than 30 minutes without a drop out of signal. A fourth station, based in St. Petersburg, Russia, had three drop outs in its first 10 minutes. Using much higher-speed Internet connections, predictably, yields much better sound quality. For example, Accent 4 Live, a classical station based in Paris, delivered music in stereo as it streamed data at 80 kilobytes per second. Internet radio more commonly delivers its music at 16 to 20 kbps and the difference shows. Accent 4 Live has to use expensive equipment to create such high-quality sound, which not every station does. Skeptics of Internet radio have also been quick to note that computer users are being asked to push their $2,000 to $4,000 machines to essentially do something a $5 radio could accomplish with a turn of a dial. But not really, said Mark Cuban, 39, the president of Audio Net, the Dallas-based broadcast network that is a major player in putting sound and pictures on the World Wide Web. The analogy raises his hackles. "That's like saying that you are taking a $1,500 big-screen television and making it do what the admission price to the ball park will cost you," said Mr. Cuban, who in 1995 co-founded the company that chiefly raises revenue by selling advertising and charging businesses to broadcast their programs. "That's absolutely crazy." The issue, Mr. Cuban and his supporters say, is access, a magic word in the computer kingdom. By digitizing radio programs and placing them on the Internet, not only has geographic distance been made irrelevant, but so have some of the limitations of time, note proponents of the technology. For example, news, sports, talk radio and some television newscasts on the Internet -- as well as some music radio programs are stored in archives. Adam Zelinka, director of site programming for N2K, a lower Manhattan-based an on-line music entertainment company that operates Jazz Central Station (www.jazzcentralstation.com) that in turn puts Newark's WBGO on the Internet, agrees. Internet radio has made programs, he said, accessible to many listeners. "People all over the country, all around the world, are tuning in to us," Mr. Zelinka said. "We constantly get email responses: 'Thank you for giving us this kind of a radio in Iowa.' " Some of those responses, Mr. Zelinka said, have contained financial pledges to the listener-supported jazz station. Some of the contributions have come from away as New Zealand, he said. "That, more than anything else," he added, "is proof of the concept." title: Horse and Blender, Car and Crockpot
body: IN AMISH communities in Lancaster County, Pa., technological choice is a matter both grand and trivial. The pursuit of simplicity has deep spiritual meaning. And yet the working out of theology in practice can seem contradictory to the larger culture. Some Old-Order Amish households occasionally use washing machines, for instance, but power them with air or hydraulic pressure. They may use telephones and in-line skates, but not zippers. The choices the Amish make collectively may seem odd, but many non-Amish make similar choices as individuals. In a speech at an annual meeting of technologists, scientists and artists earlier this year, Kevin Kelly, the executive editor of Wired magazine, compared the Amish with his own circle of non-Amish acquaintances -- including an avid Web user who eschews email and another on-line regular who will not have a phone in her home. Mr. Kelly himself has a powerful computer but does not watch television. He does, however, use a set to see an occasional videotape. Mr. Kelly's point was this: The distinction between the Amish and many other Americans -- whom he calls the neo-Amish -- is not so stark as it might first appear. Like the Amish, individual consumers set up their own belief systems for accepting some technologies and rejecting others. These choices, which may seem irrational, are often motivated by reasoned yet idiosyncratic personal rules. Mr. Kelly coined the word neo-Amish, but the idea has deep roots in social and technological history. "All of us have a logic we think is reasonable and plausible from our perspective," said Donald Kraybill, provost of Messiah College, a nonsectarian private school in Grantham, Pa., and the author of several books about the Amish. "The Amish are just an extraordinary case of this." A piece of technology is kept out of an Amish settlement if it is seen as a threat to the cohesion of the community or might contaminate the culture's values. Television, video games and Internet connections are just a few examples of banned technology. Anyone caught violating a ban risks excommunication. But if a new item is brought into the community -- like state-of-the-art hay balers (pulled by horses instead of tractors), beepers or electronic typewriters (which run on batteries) -- and no one complains, it may be widely accepted. Telephones are permitted, but the Amish keep them in wooden phone booths that stand a good distance from the house or in barns or shops because they believe that a direct connection from the home to the outside world violates the separation between members of the church and outside society. The same holds for a direct connection to electrical utility lines. "What looks hypocritical or downright silly are in fact negotiated cultural compromises where the Amish are trying to preserve their ethnic identity on the one hand and tap the benefits of modern technology on the other," Dr. Kraybill said. Paul Saffo, a director at the Institute for the Future in Menlo Park, Calif., who has studied how societies and individuals adopt technology, pointed out that the Amish were just one of many cultures that made selective use of technologies. The religious communities of Hutterites, Mennonites and American Shakers have all had rules for making decisions about which technologies to let in. The Shakers have been the most austere. In fact, Mr. Saffo said, "the Shakers made the Amish look like crazed acquisitive yuppies. The Amish get our attention because they're in our backyard, in the middle of suburbs filled with people driving Volvos and using VCR's." The Amish, Mr. Saffo said, are perhaps the most conspicuous example of the process of negotiation between humans and their hardware. If mainstream American consumers have prohibitions, the restrictions tend to be milder, and they make decisions that are more individual. "The Amish stand out because they make their decisions as an entire community," Mr. Saffo said. "The rest of us make similar decisions every day, but we make them as individuals or at most as a single family." THESE days, many mainstream Americans self-consciously mold their identities from the technologies they use -- or from those they reject. Many people who frustrate friends and relatives by refusing to install telephone-answering machines do not want the extra burden of having to return phone calls. "It wouldn't save me time," said Betsy Moses, a high-school teacher in Rohnert Park, Calif., who has turned down friends' offers of an answering machine. "It would create more for me to do." Wittingly or not, people like Ms. Moses -- Americans with disposable income and an overabundance of choices -- are confronting the disadvantages and benefits of modern technologies. "She's made a very sophisticated decision about which technology supports her life and what interferes with it," Mr. Saffo said. Other stands are more conspicuously out of step with modern culture. Cynthia and David Ott, who design computer chips, live in a custom-built house of glass, steel and marble, an aerie high atop the hills of Oakland, Calif. They own dozens of modern conveniences, like an espresso machine, a global positioning system receiver that they use for hiking, a digital camera and six computers -- but not a car. As they were growing up in Los Angeles, they decided against driving, each for a different reason. Mr. Ott, 46, simply rebelled against the car culture of Southern California. Ms. Ott, 44, failed driver's education twice in high school. After she nearly hit two pedestrians during her second license examination, she finally decided that she was too easily distracted when driving and would be a danger to herself and others. What most people would view as a major inconvenience the Otts see as just another aspect of their lives. For the 25 years of their marriage, they have relied on bicycles, taxis, relatives, friends, hitchhiking and the occasional chartered plane. Their daily commute disappeared five years ago when they started working from home. Surprising combinations of high tech and, occasionally, no tech, are more widespread than one might think. According to a recent study conducted by Forrester Research, a market research firm in Cambridge, Mass., 31 percent of American households with no television have a personal computer. Virtually all Amish settlements forbid television in homes. "Television is seen as the den of iniquity," Dr. Kraybill said. Television, he explained, confirms Amish beliefs that the outside world is filled with fraud and frivolous, violent behavior. Computers, by extension, are also taboo in most Amish communities, largely because the screen too closely resembles a television. When traveling away from home, however, the Amish may watch television in, say, a hotel or non-Amish household. Television touches a similarly tender cultural nerve among the neo-Amish. Penelope Finnie, a Web site designer in Berkeley, Calif., banned cable television from her home because, as she said, "it was one more thing that would come into our lives and take up precious time." Ms. Finnie said that if cable television were in the house, her husband, Charlie, would fall prey to channel surfing. Ms. Finnie is also opposed to video games. She has refused to let them into her house, despite the pleadings of her 5-year-old son. She attended the recent conference where Mr. Kelly gave his speech about the neo-Amish, and his words resonated with her. To Ms. Finnie's consternation, she won a Sony Playstation in a raffle on the last day of the conference. There was little she could do but accept the prize. Her son was in the audience, cheering. Choices in technology are often intensely personal. In his home in Basking Ridge, N.J., Steve Crandall, a researcher at AT&T Laboratories, has a panoply of gadgets and appliances: microwave oven, coffee grinder for bulk spices and electric ice cream maker. Dr. Crandall's rule: "If something is clearly superior or even more pleasant to use, I'll choose that route. This can create what appear to be discrepancies." One such discrepancy is his insistence on performing calculations with a slide rule, a tool that slipped into obscurity within a few years of the advent of electronic calculators in the early 1970's. "You can feel the calculations in your fingers, and the experience can be sensual," he said, in a passionate defense of the practice. "There's magic in those things." He uses a calculator only for taxes and expense reports. Two years ago, Dr. Crandall arrived at a brainstorming session with colleagues carrying nothing but his slide rule. "Everyone else walked in with their laptops loaded with spreadsheets," Dr. Crandall said. Afterward, Dr. Crandall's boss asked where he might buy a slide rule. "The mind is not digital; it's very analog," Dr. Crandall said. People who wear analog watches agree with that observation. This reporter's computer-literate father, Everett Hafner, a 77-year-old retired physicist in Williamsburg, Mass., insists on wearing an analog watch because, he said, time travels in circles. He said analog watches gave him a truer sense of the passage of time. The watch-wearing public apparently shares this opinion. According to a survey conducted by Timex, more than two-thirds of all watches purchased each year have an analog face. Neal Stephenson, a science-fiction writer in Seattle whose futuristic books center on such advanced concepts as nanotechnology, has been undergoing something of a technological retrogression in his own life. For years, Mr. Stephenson used cutting-edge software for word processing. Two years ago, his laptop computer crashed, erasing a large chunk of writing. The loss precipitated a rebellion of sorts. Mr. Stephenson is now composing his new novel with a fountain pen. "The computer caused me to spill stuff out as fast as I could type," Mr. Stephenson said. "When I went back and read it later, I found that I was using hackneyed phrases and sometimes writing in kind of a thoughtless way. With the pen, I tend to go a little slower and think a little harder." He is not alone in his nostalgia for a simpler, more elegant tool. Fountain pen sales have surged recently. But technological choice is about more than fountain pens. Mr. Saffo argues that throughout history, societies have made political decisions about technology. Japan in the 16th century rejected the use of firearms. Americans use far less nuclear power than some other countries like Russia. It is extraordinarily important to be aware that choices can be made, Mr. Saffo said. The common fear that technology is an inexorable tide that cannot be stemmed can lead to apathy or a radical rejection of all technologies. "Our worst nightmare is that we will fall victim to our technologies," he said, "when in fact the technologies remain firmly under our control."
