title: It's Confirmed: Web's Size Bogs Down Searches
body: FOR anyone who believes that despite all those search engines, the Internet has grown into an uncontrollable, unwieldy, amorphous mass, computer scientists have a study with one message: You're right. They asked two simple questions: How big is the Internet? And how much of the Internet is covered by search engines? The numbers they came up with suggest that the answers are "huge" and "not much." Steve Lawrence and C. Lee Giles of the NEC Research Institute in Princeton, N.J., found that no single search engine could find more than a third of the documents squirreled away on the Internet and that different search engines found different documents. That means that the best way to find an obscure document is to search with several engines. And, they discovered, the ever-growing Net now contains at least 320 million pages. Those conclusions, Dr. Giles said, came only after "a massive effort." He and Dr. Lawrence gathered 575 Web queries posed by NEC employees last year. Then they tried to answer those queries using six popular search engines: Hotbot, Alta Vista, Northern Light, Excite, Infoseek and Lycos. They downloaded every page that came back, Dr. Giles said, and used a computer program, backed up by some manual checking, to see if those pages contained the search terms. They ended up with 150,000 pages -- and the data to do their analysis. Then they published their study in the current issue of the journal Science. The results, computer scientists say, confirm what they have long suspected. Search engines, said Dr. Haym Hirsch, a computer scientist at Rutgers University, are "in a constant battle to explore all of the Web." But as these engines try to gather the information that is out there, the Web keeps growing, so the search engines end up attempting a modern-day version of shoveling the Aegean stables. "Search engines are struggling under this load," said Eric Grosse, a computer scientist at Lucent Technologies in Murray Hill, N.J. And even if a document is indexed, it is an art to make sure that it contains terms that will signal search engines to provide it to users. For example, Dr. Grosse said, he just discovered that scientists who were looking for a computer program he had put on the Internet were getting an outdated version of it because that version was most likely to pop up in their searches. Even worse is the frustrating effort to find an obscure bit of information that is, in theory, accessible by a search engine. "If it is obscure information, chances are you won't find it," Dr. Hirsh said. But, he added, as you search, the engine "also will inundate you with information that you're not interested in." Part of the secret is knowing all the tricks and quirks of the search engines. Yet even learning this is a never-ending task, experts said. "The information is constantly evolving," Dr. Hirsh said. "The tools we have aren't very good at getting the information we want. And the tools we have are constantly changing." All this is not to say that these computer scientists do not love the Web. But it does lead, inevitably, to the question, Where are we headed? Dr. Hirsh, for one, predicts that the Internet as we know it, and the search engines as we know them, will change. "I'm almost certain that the Web won't persist in its current form 10 years down the line," he said. "But the only prediction I feel comfortable making is that I don't have any idea what it will look like." Meanwhile, there are multiengine search devices like Metacrawler (www.metacrawler.com) and Savvy Search (guaraldi.cs.colostate. edu:2000), which give you results from several individual search engines at once. At least that gives a surfer some edge.

title:
NEWS WATCH;
Tolls Are Increasing For Web On-Ramps
body: after several years of sharply declining prices, connecting to the Internet is getting more expensive again. Last week, America Online, the world's largest Internet service provider, raised its prices by 10 percent for its most active customers, those who formerly paid $19.95 for unlimited access to the Net. The new rate is $21.95 a month. WebTV Networks, a Microsoft subsidiary, announced a 25 percent increase in monthly fees for its WebTV Plus service, effective June 1. The new fee for the premium service will be $24.95 a month. The previous rate, $19.95, will still be offered for a lower level of service that will be called WebTV Classic. Starting next month, AT&T Worldnet Services will redefine "unlimited access" as 150 hours a month. Customers who use more than 150 hours a month will be billed a surcharge of 99 cents for each additional hour. The new fees will affect only the most active users, those who spend an average of nearly five hours on line a day. Earlier, AT&T had considered and rejected a plan to place a three-hour time limit on all on-line sessions to keep some customers from hogging an access port all day. These pricing changes may be the first steps toward tiered pricing and services for the Internet, where customers who use the Internet the most will pay the most. America Online and AT&T Worldnet were the first major services to offer unlimited access for $19.95 a month, and their retreat is significant. Some Internet service providers have explored the idea of charging customers a premium for guaranteed access, free of the busy signals and congestion that have plagued some customers with unlimited-access plans. Others have explored variable pricing, where one hourly rate would apply during peak hours and another during off-peak hours. But not every Internet user will be asked to pay more. Some, in fact, will pay less. AT&T customers who chose the limited-access plan, $9.95 a month for 10 hours with a $2.50 per hour surcharge for additional hours, are getting a price break. Beginning May 1, the surcharge is being reduced to 99 cents. AT&T also promised to install more modems and phone lines to reduce congestion in its busiest markets. And AOL announced that it was beginning trials of a new high-speed Internet service, called a Digital Subscriber Line, in five cities this year. The DSL service would offer connection speeds many times faster than today's fastest dial-up modems for a monthly fee of $49.95 plus a onetime setup fee of $150. The service has been awaited eagerly by Internet users frustrated by long waits for downloading software, video and graphic images, and World Wide Web pages. The initial trials will take place in Birmingham, Ala.; Redmond, Wash.; Phoenix; San Francisco, and the Washington suburbs. GTE Internetworking will provide the service. The $49.95 monthly fee includes access to AOL. While $50 a month for Internet access may seem high to those now paying $20 for conventional modem access, it is less than a third of the cost charged by phone companies for DSL access in many areas of the country.

title: Trial Allowed On Challenge To Software
body: A Federal district judge has decided to allow a trial in a lawsuit filed last by eight Internet authors against Virginia libraries that use software to try to block smut. The judge, Leonie Brinkema, said on Tuesday that the use of the software by public libraries in Loudoun County, Va., raised the possibility of inappropriate government censorship. "The library board may not adopt and enforce content-based restrictions on access to protected Internet speech" unless the county can show the policy is the least onerous means of protecting a compelling government interest, Judge Brinkema wrote. The ruling comes as libraries across the country are considering how to give patrons access to valuable resources on the Internet while not exposing children to inappropriate sites, including some featuring hard-core pornography. Congress is also considering legislation to require all libraries that receive Federal money for Internet connections to install some form of blocking or filtering software to protect children. Last June, the Supreme Court threw out Congress's first effort to bar Internet pornography, the Communications Decency Act, finding that the law was too broad and violated the First Amendment guarantee of free speech. The county library's board of supervisors voted last October to require all library computers connected to the Internet to have software to block material deemed "pornographic" or "harmful to juveniles." The American Civil Liberties Union, which joined the suit against the libraries, argued that the software also blocked Internet sites appropriate for adults, like sites about safe sex, promoting career opportunities for women and opposing Internet censorship.

title: Yahoo's First-Quarter Earnings Exceed Expectations of Analysts
body: Yahoo Inc., the Internet directory service, reported first-quarter earnings today that exceeded Wall Street analysts' expectations. Yahoo said traffic on its World Wide Web pages had increased by nearly 50 percent since the fourth quarter of 1997. Yahoo has become one of the few profitable Internet companies by turning its well-known brand name and popular services into a lure for advertisers. From a simple directory born in a Stanford University dormitory room, Yahoo, based in Santa Clara, Calif., has branched out to offer electronic commerce, financial services and telecommunications. Shares of Yahoo rose $4, or 4.3 percent, today, to $97.25, in Nasdaq trading. Yahoo shares fell along with other Internet issues Tuesday, amid concern that the stocks' prices had risen too high in the last few weeks. Yahoo shares are up 45 percent this year and up nearly sixfold from their 52-week low of $16.62. For the quarter ended March 31, Yahoo earned $4.3 million, or 8 cents a fully diluted share, compared with a loss of $740,000 in the quarter a year earlier. Revenue tripled, to $30.2 million. Analysts had expected Yahoo to report earnings of 4 cents a share, according to First Call, an investment research company. Yahoo said that traffic on the Yahoo global network of sites increased to an average of 95 million page views a day last month, compared with an average of 65 million page views a day in December. A page view is defined as one electronic page of information displayed in response to a user request. Yahoo said it continued to have the largest audience of any Web site or on-line service, with more than 30 million adult users in the unitedstates in March. It also said it had more than 12 million registered users, reflecting the number of people who have submitted personal data for Yahoo's registration process to get access to special services.

title:
SHAPING A COLOSSUS;
Repackaging the Dow 30 as the Dow 29
body: The decision by Travelers Group Inc. and Citicorp to merge will force a change in the composition of the Dow Jones industrial average, but experts said yesterday that the alteration was unlikely to be substantive. Travelers is one of the 30 stocks that make up the Dow industrial average. Citicorp is not. Any decision on changing the average rests with Paul Steiger, managing editor of The Wall Street Journal, published by Dow Jones. Mr. Steiger did not return a telephone call seeking comment. Richard Tofel, a spokesman for Dow Jones, said the company would not speculate on Mr. Steiger's decision. At the very least, Dow Jones would have to replace Travelers and change the divisor -- part of the mathematical equation used to calculate the Dow average. One obvious choice would be to substitute the new company, to be known as Citigroup, for Travelers. Charles Carlson, a money manager and investment expert, said he doubted that Dow Jones would "revisit the components of the industrial average." "They're pretty stingy with the changes," he added, "and they made a fairly aggressive change not that long ago." The last time Dow Jones changed the components of the average was in March 1997, when Travelers was added to the makeup, replacing Westinghouse Electric, which was undergoing a reorganization.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: CONNECTIONS;
In the intricacy of a text game, no object is superfluous, no formulation too strange.
body: XYZZY. That may look like a desperate attempt to finagle a great score in Scrabble. But try entering the nonsense word in an Internet search engine and see how seriously thousands of sites take it. One home page displays a license plate "XYZZY." A Web-zine is called XYZZY News (http://www.xyzzynews.com). The word has even inspired its own site, a "XYZZY page" (http://www.winternet.com/radams/adventure/xyzzy.html). But the unexpected, the quirky and the whimsical are part of the point of XYZZY. According to Eric S. Raymond's "New Hacker's Dictionary," a book plundered all over the World Wide Web, the word XYZZY -- whose pronunciations include "zizzy" and "ik-zizzy" -- came into its own in a 1970's mainframe computer game known as Advent, short for Adventure. That game, which can be downloaded by following links on the XYZZY page, was inspired by an actual network of underground caves in Kentucky. Will Crowther, a programmer, devised textual descriptions for many of its "rooms" and gave the impression that the user could move from place to place in the cave by typing in directions ("east," for example, or "up") and reading the new descriptions. A colleague, Don Woods, then filled that textual cave with odd objects and magical puzzles; the player could pick up objects, use them in other places and disclose new regions of the cave. "XYZZY" was a spell that could instantly transport a spelunking nerd from one part of the cave to another. This imagined universe soon inspired a slew of textual adventure games, notably Zork (http://www.csd.uwo.ca/Infocom/zork1.html), which was commercially released by Infocom, a company later purchased by Activision (http://www.activision.com/games/pub-index.html), which has recently begun rereleasing some of those early text games in their pristine primitive form. In Zork the player came across wizards and trolls, had to figure out how to keep a lantern lighted, how to prevent objects from being stolen, and how to operate odd-looking contraptions -- all by using simple textual commands. Many of these early games were whimsical fantasies. Others were murder mysteries, like Witness, in which the player was a hard-boiled detective reacting to typed descriptions and dialogue. But by the mid-80's, graphics and windows were beginning to thrive on the Macintosh, color monitors began to proliferate, and video game systems started taking off. What power could XYZZY have when a mouse click could send a player careering from one room to another without odd magic spells, and where sword battles didn't require typing commands on a keyboard? Yet somehow, in a world beneath the thriving universe of video game commerce, these text adventures thrived. In fact, they are still being written and are far different from the more precious experiments in participatory fiction that ask the reader to use hyperlinks to create variations in the plot. Now called interactive fiction, these puzzle novels inhabit an intricate network on the Internet, an almost cave-like series of linked sites (see http:// tjwww.stanford.edu/adventure/index-old.html, where the metaphor is taken seriously). There are Usenet news groups for players (rec.games.int-fiction) and creators (rec.arts.int-fiction). Hundreds of new games are available for downloading at the encyclopedic archive found at ftp://ftp.gmd.de/if-archive, along with several in Java form for easy play right off Web sites (http://www.pond.com/russotto/zplet/ifol.html). There is even an annual competition for the best new interactive fiction games (http:// www.afn.org/afn55673/contest). There are advocates who seek ways to use interactive fiction in the classroom (http://k12s.phast. umass.edu/desilets/). There are sites that include reviews of nearly every major game written (http://www.escape.com/baf/if/. There are also links of links (http://www.cs.cmu.edu/wsr/IF/) and two zines devoted to IF: XYZZY News and SPAG (the Society for the Preservation of Adventure Games at http://www.afn.org/afn55673/spag.html). The amount of energy expended in filling those sites is extraordinary. New programming languages are developed; tens of thousands of words are written as guides for creators. And while the numbers of advocates are far from gargantuan -- some sites get just a few hundred hits a month, others a few thousand -- the devotion is palpable, all apparently with no profit sought. Why? To what end? The awkwardness of the form is daunting. In the words of one of the best current practitioners, Graham Nelson, "an adventure game is a crossword at war with a narrative." It isn't really a novel because the plot is broken up with odd demands that the player pick up keys or drink water or turn a dial to get some other mechanized piece of the textual puzzle to fall into place. But read Mr. Nelson's own encomium (ftp://ftp.gmd.de/if-archive/info/Craft.Of.Adventure.txt), and one gets some idea of what is being sought. Mr. Nelson is a British mathematician who played Advent as a child in the 1970's, created his own text game programming language, and in the last few years, has written two acclaimed games -- Curses and Jigsaw (http://www.pond.com/russotto/zpletx/jigsaw.html) -- each freely available on the Internet. He is also one of the more ornately literate creators of interactive fiction. His guide begins with an invocation of Tom Stoppard. The epigram for Jigsaw is from T. S. Eliot. And any player who manages to solve its problems will find untranslated Latin mottos and puzzles involving Proust and Lenin. Mr. Nelson seems to love the intricate machinery of a text game, the way no object is superfluous to its unfolding and nothing required is missing. It is a mathematician's construction, a tightly knit universe of text and symbol. But he also has high ambitions -- that in this weird, stilted form of prose broken by puzzle, there may also be a sense of something more powerful and as-yet rarely realized in interactive fiction, the powers of language to magically transport or transform. Something like XYZZY. Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title:
The View From/Rosebrook Inn;
Comfort Zone Made for the Internet
body: IT'S tea time at Rosebrook Inn, an English country-style retreat "designed to make the most of your fleeting moments." In the drawing room, a fire crackles and a grandfather clock ticks companionably. The antique mahogany table has been set with a Battenberg lace tablecloth. Wine will accompany aged cheddar cheese served with homemade nut bread and pear slices. Soon there will be music, storytelling and lively conversation. It's enough to make you rush to make a reservation. According to the virtual innkeepers -- Bonnie Brooks and Harvey Brooks and Kevin Walsh, partners in Highway Adventure LLC -- people have tried. "I saw your site, but nowhere did the location appear," read a recent email. "Please send information on rates and availability." No need to worry. There will always be a room at this inn. An on-line bed and breakfast, Rosebrook Inn is as accessible as your home computer. Just hop on the Internet and point your web browser to www.highway-adventure.com. "The original concept was to create a comfort zone on the Internet, a cyber-community with Rosebrook Inn as its hub," says Ms. Brooks, a Westport resident who is president and creative director. "Like Main Street, U.S.A., it's a jumping-off place, a stimulating environment where busy people can hang out." Still in its formative stages, Rosebrook Inn with its focus on person-to-person interaction, typifies a new direction in the colonization of cyberspace. The number of travelers on the Internet has exploded to 40 million since 1994, according to Business Week tabulations, doubling in the last year alone. Web communities are the next wave. And forget surfing.  With hundreds of thousands of options available, Americans are gravitating towards web sites where they can meet kindred spirits and feel at ease. "Chat rooms can be incredibly hostile places," says Mr. Walsh, "where the less technically savvy, less hip newbies' are as likely to be flamed as enlightened. At Rosebrook Inn, we're trying to get away from all that harshness." Visitors are invited to start at the inn and then click to its various virtual centers. Well known Connecticut personalities make up the Rosebrook "staff," a diverse group of experts eager to share information and enthusiasm. Via email, guests may chat with Brook Dojny, winner of Newman's Own and Good Housekeeping Recipe Contests, in the inn's kitchen and download seasonal recipes from her many cookbooks. Mary Muryn, author of Simon & Schuster's "Water Magic: Healing Bath Recipes for the Body Spirit and Soul," runs the health spa. Tour the art gallery with the visual artist Barbara Wilk or discuss the restoration of oil paintings with Leeanne Scharf, former curator of art and collections at the Discovery Museum in Bridgeport. The inn's own country doctor, a board certified endocrinologist, is always available to answer general medical questions, as is a family therapist. Knock on the door of Morey Ruza, sports fisherman, to talk about the big one that got away or join Marjolijn Wijsenbeek, gardener, for a tour of the inn's night garden. "It's like stepping into an Henri Rousseau painting," she says. Peruse the Barkham Burroughs Encyclopedia of Astounding Facts and Useful Information, an 1889 tome that has been republished by the author's great-grandson, the Westport artist Miggs Burroughs. See Westport's sister city -- Yangzhou -- through the lens of Larry Silver and learn about Chinese culture, art and cuisine from Rose Wong, a Yangzhou native who is now a Norwalk resident (and the Rose in Rosebrook). (When Ms. Brooks was arranging the September, 1996, cultural exchange between the two cities, she and Rose became friends.) Harvey Brooks offers original guitar compositions and rare sheet music. Larry Merz offers photographs and stories about Chuck Berry, Yoko Ono, Jodie Foster or Martin Scorsese. Are you a talented amateur? A photography contest is in the works. The winning photographs will run on line. The creative spirit behind Rosebrook Inn, Ms. Brooks has chalked up 20 years of experience with video/film and commercial projects for clients ranging from Lifetime Television to corporations. Mr. Brooks, music director of Rosebrook Inn, sees limitless potential for the project.  "In a virtual village, the possibilities are infinite," he says, "like combinations of musical notes. There's input coming from so many different sources. It creates an energy." Mr. Walsh, a Norwalk resident who is the inn's technical director, says, "Bonnie and Harvey have been involved with so many talented people over the years. It's a resource they are eager to share." Professional musician, computer expert and former director of artist relations for Gibson Guitar, Mr. Walsh helped develop the Photon MIDI Converter, one of the first commercially available computer interface systems for music. "The Internet is moving fast in exciting directions," says Mr. Walsh, "and I felt Rosebrook Inn was an intriguing model. It is people getting together for reasons other than just money." At some of the inn's facilities, products are available for visitors who wish to shop, but a percentage of all proceeds is earmarked for the Yale Cancer Center. As opposed to a magazine that has simply been scanned onto the computer screen, Rosebrook Inn is a people-based community which permits direct interaction. "The standard on-line magazine is flat," argues Ms. Brooks. "The writers behind the stories are not easily accessible. Our hosts are our friends and they can become yours as well." "That's why we have made the inn such a visual reality," says Mr. Walsh. "It's like reading a really good book. You are drawn into a dimension that doesn't concretely exist. It exists in your mind. And you can take it one step further. You can interact with the characters on a personal level. At Rosebrook Inn, we are intrigued by your thoughts. If you are a person with a story to tell, we want to hear from you." What began as a community of artists one year ago has broadened its scope. Learn about archeology from Mark J. Meister, executive director of the Archeological Institute of America. Another friend of Ms.  Brooks, Bruce Schlein, is sending digital photographs and first-hand reports from Bosnia where he is working for the Catholic Relief Association. The Web site is the ideal public forum for social issues. "We've involved people who are active and concerned," says Mr. Brooks.  In addition to being artist-in-residence at the Inn's Gilded Rose Gallery, for example, Ms. Wilk is a senior citizen intent on alerting retirees to the danger of scam artists. What better evening adventure than a walk on the beach to search for ghost crabs?  Ms. Brooks will lead the way, pointing her flashlight at the pits near the water's edge where these nocturnal creatures hide. "I become philosophical walking along the shore," she says. "I love to watch the sun set the sky ablaze. Feel free to keep me company anytime." Graphic   Photos: Bonnie Brooks, at the Web site, above, and, left, with Rose Wang, Kevin Walsh and Harvey Brooks. "We're trying to get away from all that harshness," Mr. Walsh says. (Photographs by George Gutierrez for The newyork Times)

title:
THINK TANK;
Covering Their Eyes With Parted Fingers
body: The newyork Times asked a handful of scholars to comment on the apparent ambivalence of much of the country about the sexual accusations against President Clinton. News programs cover the issue constantly and receive higher ratings just when many Americans insist they are no longer interested and think the matter should be private.  Here are excerpts from their answers, compiled by Janny Scott: "People's responses are dominated by a combination of deep absurdity and intense fascination. We feel something unreal and strange is happening. I think Americans feel that they're in a bizarre realm that suggests that there is something wrong with our political culture and something has become unhinged in the structures by which we ordinarily balance personal life, family life, politics, social existence. "Having said that, the same people who have a sense of this absurdity are nonetheless fascinated by it. But fascination can have many sources. Of course, the usual ones are very much there. It is an ongoing narrative; and of course it's got a sexual dimension, which is always fascinating; and it's got dimensions of power. But maybe the deeper fascination is with American political self-destructiveness in playing out this mad game. We're fascinated by the very combination of absurdity and danger. "It reminds one of the way we sometimes speak of technology going berserk, where you introduce certain kinds of technology without being able to imagine what it will do to your way of living or your society. And the technology then takes on a self-generating process; it continues to energize itself into further convolutions of itself. The technology takes on a momentum and it becomes viewed as something absolute and unstoppable." -- Robert Jay Lifton Professor of psychiatry John Jay College of Criminal Justice and the CUNY Graduate Center "I call it 'the vanishing truth paradox.' The public wants to have great leaders, and we use whatever media we have to try to confirm greatness. We've used television now, our dominant medium. The paradox is that greatness only exists at a distance. So the more closely we watch our leaders and the more continuously we watch them, the less great they appear to be. There is a kind of sinking feeling: That person is not good, let's find someone else. "None of our famous leaders -- Washington, Jefferson, Franklin Delano Roosevelt -- could have sustained this level of attention. First, we just thought we had a lot of lousy leaders -- Johnson, Nixon, Ford. But I think some of this ambivalence grows out of the fact that the public is starting to realize that you can't watch people this closely. "I also think there has been a shift in the culture, because of television, that journalists have adapted to -- a shift from 'resume criteria' to 'dating criteria.' We always used to have two sets of criteria for decisions in life: We would not choose a lover or a friend based on a writing sample or a resume; but it was never the case until television that you would consider somebody a viable Presidential candidate because of the twinkle in his eye. "What television has done is taken criteria that make sense in the private realm and extended them into the public realm. Now we use dating criteria to determine whether someone is fit for office. Once the criteria shift, information becomes relevant that wasn't before. We ask: 'What are they like? Do we like them?' Once you're in that intimate realm, it seems as relevant as things on a resume." -- Joshua Meyrowitz Professor of communication University of New Hampshire in Durham "The fact that people might disapprove on the one hand and tune in on the other doesn't automatically make them creeps or hypocrites. Human beings are complex creatures. They may be watching this with one hand over their eyes. They may say, 'this is terrible and I don't like knowing this, but everybody else knows it so I don't want to be out of the loop.' They may regret the invasion of private life while at the same time finding themselves lured in, as we would be by any great drama. So I don't think it's fair to leap to the conclusion that people are two-faced. A more generous view would be to say that they're human." -- Jay Rosen Professor of journalism newyork University "I'll confess I despise Bill Clinton and have for a long time, and I can't get enough of this and my wife is disgusted with me. She doesn't like Bill Clinton, but she thinks it's a weakness of soul, as it undoubtedly is. I have to confess that I want to dance around Bill Clinton's grave. And it's a weakness. "The question is, what should be the proper object of pleasure? Rather than reading about Bill Clinton's difficulties, I ought to take pleasure in, and I do, reading and thinking about Lincoln's Gettysburg address. I ought to look at a beautiful picture, I ought to listen to beautiful music. So, the question really is, in what should we take pleasure?" -- Walter Berns Emeritus professor of government Georgetown University Graphic   Drawing (David Horsey/Seattle Post-Intelligencer/North America Syndicate)

title: Breaking the PC Barrier
body: STEPHEN MOORE, a director of computer services at Georgetown University, likes to log in with his Macintosh from home and run programs built for Windows machines. He runs a program named Virtual PC that makes it simple for Macintosh users to fit in with the dominant culture. Mr. Moore, like all Macintosh devotees, faces continual pressure at work to switch to a PC, but he refuses. An avid guitarist and fan of Frank Zappa and Miles Davis, he says that the best software for musicians is on the Mac and that he has little trouble fitting into a PC world. Even as the Mac portion of the market gets smaller and smaller, the strategies for surviving and prospering with a Mac become better and better. The Internet is a great leveling force, and its open standards have made it easier for Macintoshes, Suns, Unix machines, Amigas and whatnot to exist happily in an office dominated by Microsoft products. Rebels who use Macs cannot do everything, but they can usually do the most important things. For instance, many mail servers now deliver mail using the Post Office Protocol, or P.O.P. email programs like Eudora work the same on the Macintosh and the PC because they both speak the same language. In fact, themail server cannot really tell whether it is delivering mail to a Macintosh or a PC. The same is true for the World Wide Web. Much of the original work on the Web was done in Europe on a Next machine. Since then, all major and many minor machines use Web browsers that download text and images for display. And since some databases now store information in the same programming language, HTML, that Web sites use, Macintosh users can often retrieve information that would once have been inaccessible with a browser. The ubiquity of the Web browsers and HTML data makes it much easier for Macintosh users to fit in at their offices. In the past, most companies stored information about policies, businesses and customers in databases that were accessible by proprietary programs that would run only on one type of machine, usually a PC. Now most database-access tools take requests and spit out their answers in HTML. That makes it easy for an employee to grab information from the database from anywhere through the Internet. But this openness also helps Macintosh users because Macs also run Web browsers that speak HTML. For instance, Mr. Moore says that many of the databases at Georgetown University are accessible with a Macintosh running a Web browser. That approach also helps people who might want to check research results from machines like Web TV or one of the pocket computers on the market. These products also rely upon HTML to get along with the world. Macintosh users can also thank Microsoft, one of the biggest developers of Macintosh software, for Microsoft Office 98. (It was finished for the Mac before the PC.) It makes it possible for Macs to read files built in Microsoft Office on the PC and for Mac fans to argue, quite rationally, that the Mac is functionally the same as a PC. There are still glitches and incompatibilities. Macintoshes can read the data on PC floppy disks, but they can mangle longer names. And exchanging files over a network may not be as easy as it could be. Programs like Virtual PC are wonderful emulators of PC's, but they can be sluggish and slow. Still, the world's embrace of the Internet and its open standards means that in some ways, life will continue to get easier for the people who own Macintoshes. And it is worth noting that new low-cost machines like Web TV and the Oracle NC speak HTML and are even worse at interacting with PC's than Macintoshes.

title:
FUNDAMENTALS: User's Guide;
Cookies May Annoy But They Don't Hurt
body: I FINALLY discovered cookies on my computer after I found their crumbs by accident. It happened while I was completing an innocuous task, helping my 7-year-old daughter, Ella, find a file called "If You Give a Mouse a Cookie," which she had misplaced on my hard drive. When I told my computer to find "cookie," it located a mysterious file in my browser folder. When I opened it, I found dozens of lines of text I had not written -- known as cookies -- that had been sent to my computer without my knowledge while I was innocently browsing the Web. Ella pointed at a line and read, "True/false 2082787201 ubid-main 1772-3565481-758675." "Do you know what that means?" she asked. "Could it hurt our computer?" No, and no, I answered in the same stay-calm voice I use when the cats leave something dead on the stoop. But I was thinking: Actually, those cookies were sent without my permission, and since I cannot decode the little aliens, how can I be sure that they are not whooping it up with one another, exploring my hard drive, sending my secrets back to their leader on some distant planet? (Cookie A: "Hey, Moe, get a look at this file. No wonder she calls it a rough draft!" Cookie B: "Yeah, did you notice she's so cheap that she's played solitaire 749 times without paying the shareware fee?") I know this was not a rational response, given that cookies are not programs that can run amok. They are merely bits of text, a tool created by Netscape in 1994 to enable Web sites to identify repeat visitors. Sent primarily by the biggest commercial Web sites, cookies get stored on your computer. If you return to the site, your browser will send back the cookie, a gesture roughly equivalent to saying, "Hey, it's me again." But forget rational. Cookies provoke a powerful emotional response: they are watching you. Without your consent. One day you open up a file and see dozens and dozens of these critters that you had no idea existed, and then you can't even decipher the gobbledygook, except for the domain name of the Web site that sent it. You cannot even tell what information a particular cookie is trying to gather about you. Tagged with a unique identifying number, a cookie can help a Web site keep track of your movements, for example. Upon your return, you may be served a customized Web page with an advertisement geared toward your interests. Not to sound like George Orwell here, but it is no wonder that cookies have become controversial, with pro-privacy groups lobbying for cookie restrictions and even the recent release of a Department of Energy bulletin (www.ciac.org/ciac/bulletins/ i-034.shtml), known as the Cookie Papers, to reassure people that cookies cannot hurt their computers. "It's like having a video camera posted on your shoulder, watching what you do," said Deirdre Mulligan, staff counsel for the Center for Democracy and Technology in Washington. Actually, cookies gather limited information: the Internet Protocol address of your on-line provider's server and what kind of browser and computer you use. Any other data it gleans comes from you -- if you register at a Web site, for instance. So think of a cookie as a video camera on your shoulder, but one that can see only the back of your head. Still, do you want the world to know you have dandruff? Help is coming, someday. A group called the Internet Engineering Task Force, a loosely knit group of hackers who oversee the Net's evolution, may endorse a technical solution to the problem in the next few months. The goal, said David M. Kristol, a member of the technical staff at Bell Laboratories who is coordinating the effort, is to persuade Web sites to alert computer users about cookie use. "Of course, there's no Internet police," Mr. Kristol said. "But we will try to get everyone on board." Face it, cookies are not going to disappear. A survey of the 100 most heavily trafficked Web sites in 1997 revealed that 20 percent of them used cookies, said David Banisar, staff counsel for the Electronic Privacy Information Center, a nonprofit advocacy group in Washington. "And it's much more prevalent now -- I was just on one site that tried to send me a cookie 20 times while I was reading a news article." While the Net's gurus sort out this issue, you can take a few simple steps on your own. For instance, you can set the preferences on Internet Explorer or Navigator to alert you if a Web site is about to send a cookie. "If you go to a site you trust, you might want to accept the cookie," said Craig Beilinson, a Microsoft product manager for Internet Explorer. "But if you're browsing Dave's Page of Evil and it asks you if you want a cookie, you might want to think twice." Here's how to set the browser preference: If you use Internet Explorer 4.0, look under View at Internet Options. Click on Advanced. Scroll to Cookies, where you have three options: 1. Always accept cookies. 2. Prompt user before accepting. 3. Disable all cookies. Navigator 4.0 offers the same choices, along with the ability to accept only cookies that get sent back to the originating server (as opposed to those designed to be sent to third-party servers to track your movements across the Web). Look under Edit, then at Preferences, then Advanced. (Older versions of either browser will have slightly different steps.) You can also look at the cookies already on your hard drive. For PC users, Navigator stores cookies in a file called cookies.txt in the Netscape directory. With Internet Explorer, cookies are in separate files identified by the domain names of the servers that sent them, in the Windows/cookies folder on the hard drive. Mr. Beilinson of Microsoft said it was fine to edit or delete cookies, but Tom Tsao, product manager for Netscape Communicator, recommends against editing, warning that it could mess up your browser. Informed consent -- that is what I care about. I do not want anybody mucking around in my hard drive without permission. And that goes double for you, Ella. Graphic   Photo. (Margaret Riegel)

title:
Hackers' Bazaar;
On-Line Auction Services Put Haggling Back Into Sales
body: You can usually haggle over the price of a car, or cut a better deal for that rowing machine at a garage sale. But an airline ticket? Imagine walking up to an airline counter, flashing a wad of bills and offering $300 for a ticket to Florida when the lowest available fare is $400. The ticket agent would probably call security. Yet that, in essence, is what consumers will be able to do with an Internet service scheduled to be introduced on Monday. Fares are already all over the map, of course -- but they are dictated by the airlines. Now, though, five of the eight top domestic airlines and several big foreign carriers have agreed to respond electronically to bids for round-trip tickets made by consumers over the Internet, according to Priceline, the company establishing the system. While the tickets have significant restrictions meant to weed out business travelers, industry consultants expect leisure travelers to be able to use the system to buy tickets at well below listed fares, sometimes without advance purchase restrictions. Over the next year, Priceline executives say they plan to extend the concept to the purchase of cars, to interest on home mortgages and even to charges for international phone calls. Technology, in short, is bringing commerce back to the bazaar. Ever since the railroad and the Montgomery Ward catalogue extended the reach of big businesses from coast to coast, companies have largely sold their products at fixed prices. But now more and more goods and services are being sold through auctions or other forms of electronic negotiation. With some 150 World Wide Web sites running auctions of various sorts, the Internet is already loaded with the sort of haggling never seen at the local mall. The acknowledged leader of on-line bidding is Onsale, a Menlo Park, Calif., company that takes bids from 10,000 people a day for surplus computer and electronic goods. And EBay of San Jose, Calif., offers electronic classified advertising in which individuals can auction off their own property. (It has fostered a thriving market in Beanie Babies.) All manner of specialized auctions have popped up, from Bearauction, which sells teddy bears, to Guitarauction, which sells guitars. Businesses, too, are starting to use Internet auctions to buy everything from office equipment to electric power. "The idea that there are fixed prices you have to accept is not actually ingrained in human nature," said Stuart Feldman, director of the Institute for Advanced Commerce at I.B.M.'s labs in Hawthorne, N.Y. Retailers, he said, have imposed fixed prices because they have not been able to bargain individually from the home office with far-flung customers. Nor have they been willing to delegate sales clerks with the authority to set prices in the field. "Now, the Internet allows communication at no cost and infinite speed," Mr. Feldman said. "And you can program computers with rules for what deals they can and can't make, instead of trusting a $5-an-hour clerk." The result, marketing experts say, is likely to be higher prices for goods that are more in demand and more bargains for consumers willing to buy things that are off the beaten path. "If you put out a catalogue with prices good for 90 days," Mr. Feldman said, "some stuff doesn't sell because you priced it too high, while some things fly out the door because you priced it too low." Of course, to judge by the reputation of car buying, the one market in which negotiation has long been common, many American consumers do not like to haggle. But the Internet is radically changing the automobile market, too -- not to eliminate bargaining but to give it clear rules, much the way trading on a stock exchange is regulated to insure that the transaction is fair to both buyers and sellers. And some experts assert that on-line auctions appeal to a certain type of consumer who sees them as a multiplayer computer game in which real dollars are at stake. "Onsale is the perfect shopping experience for men," said Vernon Keenan, an electronic commerce analyst with Zona Research. "Not only do you find a bargain, you have to hunt it and kill it before you take it home." Even before the Internet, computerization began allowing companies to replace fixed prices with prices based on a computerized assessment of supply, demand and type of customer. A prime example can be seen at a rental car counter, where each customer seemingly pays a different rate depending on corporate discount, club affiliation or myriad other deals. Now these systems are evolving into two-way bargaining. Many credit card and long-distance telephone companies, for instance, will cut prices for customers who call and ask for lower rates. The people who really want discounts get them, while everyone else pays full price. The Internet offers a way to connect these central computers, which make ever-finer pricing distinctions, with a mass of customers. "We are moving to an age where businesses will quote a different price to every customer for every product every day," said Jerry Kaplan, chief executive of Onsale. Companies are especially attracted to the Internet as a way to clear out inventory that is either old or, like the unsold plane ticket, will have its value vanish. It is a low-cost way to reach lots of potential customers, yet it is not as public as traditional advertising. That is why big airlines have taken to selling last-minute tickets through email lists and have agreed to participate in the new Priceline auction. "It's plenty easy to fill your airplanes by offering discounts," said Donald S. Garvett, a vice president of SH & E, an airline consulting firm that has done work for Priceline. "But you cannibalize your business with people who would be willing to pay higher fares. Priceline lets you find new demand." On Priceline's Internet site, users enter the price they want to offer to travel to a specified destination on a given date. They agree to accept a ticket on any major airline, anytime of the day, with up to one stopover. The tickets are not refundable and do not earn frequent-flier miles. These restrictions are expected to scare off most business travelers. The offers will be matched against minimum prices that airlines have submitted to Priceline's computers. If any airline is willing to sell the ticket at the offered price, the user's credit card will be automatically charged. These restrictions are so tough, critics say, that Priceline may have a hard time finding customers. "This doesn't seem to be what works for the mainstream consumer, said Kenneth J. Orton, chief executive of Preview Travel, one of the leading Internet-only travel agencies. "People will pay more to fly a nonstop on a major airline rather than changing planes and using a second-tier carrier." He also pointed out that the airlines are operating at the highest capacity in years and thus do not have many surplus seats. Jay Walker, a Connecticut entrepreneur who founded Priceline, said the airlines had committed to providing 100,000 seats a day to the system. By the end of the year, he said he expects Priceline to be able to sell 1,000 to 3,000 tickets a day. But he said participating airlines would not allow their names to be disclosed, just as name-brand manufacturers do not talk about how they liquidate excess stock. "Go to Ralph Lauren and say, 'Where can I buy your clothes?' " Mr. Walker said. "He will say Bloomingdale's and my own stores sell my clothes at great prices. Ask if you can get them at the outlets in Secaucus, N.J. He'll say maybe once in a while." Mr. Walker acknowledges that secrets are hard to keep on the Internet. "There will be all sorts news groups that talk about who is selling tickets on Priceline and at what prices," he said. The airlines did force Priceline to modify its proposed system to give consumers less bargaining room. At first, Mr. Walker proposed allowing customers whose initial offers were too low to raise their bid twice to find a price the airlines would accept. But "the airlines said they were not interested in being pinged every $5 to find our real demand," Mr. Walker said. If consumers offers are turned down, not because the price they offered was too low but because there were no tickets available on the dates they requested, Priceline may give them the opportunity to change the dates and try again. Moreover, as the Priceline system is extended into cars and other markets, it is likely to allow more back-and-forth bidding. One vision of the future of commerce can be seen here in the narrow computer room of Onsale in "going, going, gone" time, the hour between noon and 1 P.M. when most of its 24-hour auctions close. A dozen computer monitors set up on card tables flash as the final bids zip in from all over the world. On a given day, more than 100,000 people will scan Onsale's 1,000 auctions, and between 10,000 and 20,000 of them will submit bids. On one recent afternoon, there was heated bidding to buy 15 long-discontinued personal computers, available without disk drives. With minutes to go before the hammer falls, "RM" from Indiana raised his bid from $249 to $259. He posted a message that all the other bidders could see: "Last time," he wrote hopefully. Indeed, he was the last. Onsale's computers closed the auction and started charging the winner's credit cards and sending them email to say they had won. Meanwhile, another computer, sitting under the card table, prepared new Web pages for the next day's auctions. Mr. Kaplan, Onsale's chief executive, scanned the monitors and tallied up how many Internet users were lingering on the Web site in anticipation of new goods. "There are 500 people outside the doors waiting to get in," he said excitedly. If companies like Onsale and Priceline take hold, though, there could be millions outside those electronic doors. title: Luxury Rentals Adding T-1 To Drmn and Hdwd Flrs
body: LIKE most newyorkers, Michael Baumann had no time to waste, especially on line. As a writer facing deadlines for a German business magazine, he was losing hours a day doing research on the World Wide Web at a snail's speed from his Brooklyn apartment. Investment sites took minutes to download. Graphics files crawled through his phone line. Even reading his company's on-line publication became an excruciating test of patience. "It might have been faster to just have them mail the magazine from Dusseldorf," he said. Finally, last January, Mr. Baumann moved to Manhattan to live life in the fast lane, literally and digitally. He is one of the latest tenants to be wooed into an apartment complex -- in this case, a landmark building at 71 Broadway -- that promises lightning-fast Internet connections. The buzz word among residential real-estate developers is T-1: a high-speed data line that carries information up to 50 times as fast, in theory, as a conventional line connected to an average, 28.8-baud modem. It is the newfangled amenity being pitched to professionals and amateurs on the Web. A promotional announcement for Fulton Plaza, an apartment building downtown, says, "We offer the sophisticated luxury you want with the high-tech convenience you need." Until now, T-1 access has been the exclusive domain of corporations and new-media start-ups that could afford to pay several hundred dollars a month for the service. Hackers have been known to infiltrate T-1-equipped offices (like the Notwork Development Lab in Manhattan) after hours just to get a high-speed fix. These days, on-line rocketry can be had by apartment dwellers for as little as $75 per month in buildings that have been wired with T-1. By offering one shared T-1 line, or a number of them, building developers are able to provide access at a lowered rate T-1's can serve an unlimited number of apartments, though will reduce in speed according to on-line traffic. Residents can plug more than one computer into their T-1 line at a time. "This is the future," said Phillip Gusue, assistant vice president of Crescent Heights, the development company behind the Exchange, one of three converted office buildings that opened recently for residents in the Wall Street area. "It's like having an apartment that's cable-ready. It would be ridiculous to have a new building without a T-1 capacity." Few luxury high-rises offer T-1, but Mr. Gusue believes that it's only a matter of time. T-1 is just one of the ways to speed up the flow of Internet data. Computer users in some parts of the country have access to Integrated Services Digital Network lines or cable hookups. I.S.D.N. lines are four times as fast as 28.8 modems and cost approximately $30 per month, plus an installation fee. Cable modems are available in only a few areas, but they can deliver data even faster than a T-1 at a cost of $40 per month. For the time being, T-1 buildings are the most widely available method offering low-cost speed. Once connected, tenants find T-1's thrills to be indispensable. Dan Turner, a 32-year-old software manager living at 71 Broadway, can now get access to programs over the Internet and test them without slogging through heavy on-line traffic. Since the T-1 line is separate from his phone line, Mr. Turner leaves his computer plugged into the Net all day so it can collect email or simply remain available if he needs to transfer files from work. In fact, his office's Internet connection is slower than the one at his home. "I've had the wacky idea to run my apartment's T-1 line across the street to my office," he said. Unfortunately for Mr. Turner, that is not possible. As developers compete for high-end discerning renters and telecommuters, high-speed connections are becoming as important an offering as a health club or a concierge. The Exchange has even gone a step further by providing a building-wide network through which residents can, say, chat about new restaurants in the area or post advertisements for used furniture. "We're trying to help cultivate a cybercommunity," Mr. Gusue said. In Sunnyvale, Calif., a 709-unit T-1 building recently opened to seduce the troops of Silicon Valley. In newyork, the first opportunity to T off at home came two years ago when an ambitious real estate broker and musician named Greg Salgano erected a building with T-1 on Avenue A at Third Street. Today, Mr. Salgano said, his 28 units are filled with "groovy, fabulous people: mad scientists, Web techies, fashion models, designers of Web pages and assorted Internet gurus." As he prepares to open two similar buildings in the East Village, Mr. Salgano says his mission is not simply to provide speed. He wants to stimulate do-it-yourself on-line publishing, he said. "I want to put the power to contribute content in the hands of the public and not have an inherently hierarchical structure," he said. BUT bringing power to the people is not always what it is cracked up to be. The dream of true T-1 access comes with certain realities. First is the issue of speed. Though a building may be wired with T-1, that line is shared by all the residents. If 200 tenants decide to go on line at the same time, they will each get only a fraction of the potential bandwidth (although their connection will still be considerably faster than through an ordinary dial-up). Bandwidth wars can also ensue when tenants decide to use computers on their T-1 lines as hosts for their own Web sites. Since a T-1 line carries data both in and out of a building, someone who has set up a popular site will be eating up space on the line every time a Net surfer visits the site. Matthew Piscitelli, a 26-year-old Internet entrepreneur who lives at the Exchange, owns sex-toy Web site but does not run it from his apartment for fear of encroaching on his neighbors' virtual space. "I've thought about doing it," he said, "but that would be rude." Actually, it would be against the rules. Tim Ganly, a vice president of Global Center, the Internet service provider for the Exchange, said residents must agree not to operate commercial sites over their shared T-1 line. Usage is monitored by the company. Though an Exchange tenant could buy an individual subscription to another T-1 provider, the tenant would have to pay costly fees for exclusive use of the line. Another potential cramp in the home T-1 user's style is security. A building might provide the connection, but that does not necessarily mean that it provides a a program to protect an individual's data, called a firewall. At the T-1 building on Avenue A, for example, Mr. Salgado said: "As of right now, we don't have security infrastructure built in. Anyone who wants security has to build their own firewall." Although it is unlikely that a resident's data would be broken into, it might be worthwhile for a resident to find out if a competitor lived in the same building. Abhi Chaki, a telecommunications analyst for Jupiter Communications, a computer research firm, advised that people should be not doing critical programming through their apartments unless they had a "firewall or a filtering mechanism that the building has already installed." Mr. Chaki estimated the cost of installing a firewall at at least $6,000 per individual. Still, these are the early years for wired apartments. Many issues need to be sorted out. Some I.S.P.'s and developers -- like Rudin Management, which built the newyork Information Technology Center, a hub of computer-intensive companies near Wall Street, at 55 Broad Street -- are already looking beyond T-1 to technology just over the horizon: digital subscriber loop, or D.S.L., which can run at three times the velocity of a T-1 line and be more easily deployed. As more attention turns to high-speed data lines, there will be no turning back for people like Mr. Baumann. "I'm too used to the speed," he said. "Fortunately, I can't even remember what it was like the old way." title:
Reviews/Fashion;
No Crush: The CD-ROM Runway
body: The most important click-clicks in the fashion world yesterday were not the sounds of editors' heels on the sidewalk as they ran to another show: they were the sounds of computer mice as Helmut Lang introduced his fall collection on the Internet and on CD-ROM's. It was the first time a designer had shown a collection in this way. The grand experiment was not without its drawbacks, but it points the way to the future in a global industry searching for alternatives to runway shows. The computer revolution has been knocking at fashion's door for a few years now, and as in many industries, the fashion professionals are not quite sure how or if to let it in. From computer-assisted design on textiles to using computers for sales to "staging" virtual fashion shows in the way Mr. Lang has done, fashion has been slow on the uptake. It is not hard to see why. The artistry and social elements of fashion do not wear well in the cold, gray world of computers. And computers are only the wave of the future when they work. It is still too early to tell if Mr. Lang's idea was a success. The decision to use multimedia -- he also offered a 15-minute video, a "look book" and the opportunity for editors and buyers to view the collection on racks in his SoHo showroom -- was made at the 11th hour, a week before he was to stage a show. But he said it was an idea he had been toying with for three years. "I said it was now or never," Mr. Lang said of his choice. "This is the first step in the future." The multimedia format is not intended to replace live shows every season, the designer added. It is odd that in an industry that lives by changes every season, the method of presentation has not changed in almost 50 years. Years ago, Norma Kamali broke ground when she presented a collection on video -- and a handful of designers have since continued to do so. In February, the British designer Mark Whittaker showed his line to editors on video. In the last two years, the number of fashion Web sites has grown, but no designer had yet introduced a line there. The images on the Web and in the CD-ROM were photographed on Sunday in a studio. The models were the same ones he would have used had he staged a live show, including the actress Daryl Hannah. The show was posted on the Internet -- at www .helmutlangny.com -- with 81 looks. This approach lets more people -- including editors like Franca Sozzani, the editor of Italian Vogue, who is not attending the shows here -- see the collection quickly. The cost is similar to that of a runway show: for top designers like Mr. Lang, it can hover close to $100,000. "It's exactly the same preparation and we had exactly the same amount of work as if I had had a show," he said. "I never said this would replace shows. But there are too many and it's torture for people." Among the visitors to Mr. Lang's showroom yesterday was Kal Ruttenstein, the fashion director of Bloomingdale's, who applauded the move. "There may be some seasons when we want to see another show from Helmut, but this is the perfect way to see this collection, and it saves time. You're not running around going to a crushed show for three hours. And time is what you want to save." The disadvantages include not seeing the fabric close up. And there are only two dimensions. Video is an improvement because there is movement. But the numbers who can view a site increases the audience exponentially, thereby making a small show a big show -- if people are interested enough to call it up. Always a sought-after ticket, Mr. Lang, who was about to show his first women's line in newyork rather than Paris, infuriated fashion insiders in recent seasons when he slashed the number of guests at his show from about 800 to 150. The Lang Web site and the CD-ROM, which are identical, depict what Mr. Lang calls "casual drama." Pearl-colored parkas with deep, extravagant collars trimmed with light bands of fur. Lemon-colored puckered polyester skirts with the hems turned up so the skirts resemble delicate tulips. Cotton suits with batting layered into the two-button jackets and more relaxed trousers than Mr. Lang has shown in the past. A black jacket is a serious cover over a playful white cotton jersey shirt -- the funnel neck standing away from the body, the sleeves extending like joyful streamers. What browsers or even video watchers will not see is the white satin lining and furry cashmere undercoat beneath the cotton parkas. Nor will they be able to run their fingers again and again through the creamy marabou feathers on an off-white parka over a cashmere tank top and white moleskin cotton pants. They won't be able to see the clever curved seaming in the lemon-yellow puckered polyester dress that goes over the matching skirt. And they will not be able to tell that the sheer lemon scarf-like garment worn with a cummerbund is a brilliant new interpretation of a cardigan. It may turn out to be the big paradox of this experiment that a multidimensional designer has lead the way into a medium that may be best suited to simpler talents. Mr. Lang's creations are so complex that they warrant firsthand viewing. As he carves a trajectory from severity to serenity, Mr. Lang's work is becoming ever more nuanced. There are details that should not be missed. But for spreading the message that put Mr. Lang at the forefront of fashion, the computer is the great democratizer. Manolo, too, showed casual drama.  This prince of evening shades combined nubby heathered sweaters with a long skirt beaded and fringed with jet. A languid fitted gray jersey column stopped just at the calf to reveal the silver stream of skirt swimming below it. In the most artisanal style, he combined hundreds of tiny Ultrasuede squares in aqueous hues in a princess evening gown that he placed over a long-sleeved jersey. And a taupe sweater was the underpinning for a shimmering, floor-sweeping slip dress with a necklace and hem of dangling gunmetal beads. Manolo is another of those designers whose creations yield up more on close inspection. The need to fill a runway may account for the few unremarkable looks -- but Manolo's shows can be counted on for a challenge. Imagine sitting in your seat, waiting. The lights dim, the music swells. A floodlight hits. Out comes the first model: a midget. As festively attired and meticulously made up as the usual six-footers, she walked down the runway with the other models. As no Kate Moss or Emma has ever done, she left the audience to applaud and rethink its expectations. Marc Jacobs was once that challenging, too. He pushed buttons, sending joy down the runway with his Yves Saint Laurent homage, or controversy with his grunge collection. It was exciting and passionate. But it is a course he has abandoned in favor of a safer route. Beaten down by the exigencies of the business, Mr. Jacobs long ago capitulated to the fashion machine that many designers enter as artists and leave as business executives. It has been an emotional experience to see this evolution, so regretful yet so necessary. The line Mr. Jacobs showed on Monday night showed a total acquiescence to formula. There was no heart in this collection, just a few heavy-looking sailor skirts and pants tied with ribbon at the small of the back, long accordion-pleated skirts and uninspired pea jackets. While this sort of outing is all right for a handbag company (Mr. Jacobs designed a group of tight, winning sportswear pieces for his first line for Louis Vuitton), it is woefully inadequate for a fashion house. Perhaps Mr. Jacobs was exhausted by the directional collection he showed last season and by his new work for Vuitton. One wants to be assured that while the designer who created such a stir with grunge may have been bent by the status quo, he has not been broken. title:
Equal Work, Less-Equal Perks;
Microsoft Leads the Way in Filling Jobs With 'Permatemps'
body: They hold high-prestige, high-technology jobs at Microsoft's plush campus. They often do the same work as the Microsoft Corporation's permanent employees, developing CD-ROM's, designing World Wide Web sites and writing software manuals. Yet they do not qualify for Microsoft's coveted stock options, and their health and vacation benefits are pale imitations of those enjoyed by regular Microsoft workers. They are long-term temps -- a seeming oxymoron, but in fact a new and growing phenomenon in the American work force, embraced by many corporations, especially high-tech ones, including Microsoft, AT&T, Intel, Hewlett-Packard and Microsoft's Seattle neighbor, Boeing. Microsoft is perhaps the leading practitioner of the trend, employing about 5,000 temps, including 1,500 long-term ones, meaning they have worked for the software colossus for at least one year. These temps work next to Microsoft's 17,000 domestic employees. Some prefer the flexibility and the higher take-home pay that temp status affords, but many assail temping as a backdoor way to create a two-tier work force. The benefits that the lower tier loses out on, many temps say, far outweigh whatever extra pay they take home. "It's a system of having two classes of people and instilling fear and inferiority and loathing," said Rebecca Hughes, who worked for three years as a temp at Microsoft, helping edit its CD-ROM on health care. With work lives strung together by three-month contracts, some temps have worked at Microsoft for more than five years and have seized on an awkward term to describe their awkward status: permatemps. John Schussler has received a half-dozen promotions since going to work as a tester for Microsoft in 1992, looking for bugs in the endless lines of computer code that make up the company's software products. Now a program manager, he oversees the 18 people who run Cinemania and Music Central On-Line, the company's movie information service and 24-hour music store. But he does not have the one thing he wants most: a permanent Microsoft job and the benefits that go with it. "Why is it that the guy next to me, who does the same work as me, is a permanent employee and can afford to buy a house, and I'm still in an apartment?" he asks. Microsoft insists that Mr. Schussler's temp agency, Rho Tech, is his employer, although he works on the Microsoft campus, is supervised by Microsoft managers and uses Microsoft equipment. He says he has almost no contact with Rho Tech, which deducts his taxes, sends his paycheck and provides a bare-bones health plan. In this era of intense competition and change, management theorists have recommended that corporations stick to their core capabilities and maintain core work forces. The corollary is that companies should hire out for noncore activities. Microsoft's temps may feel their contingent status more keenly than other temps, largely because the software giant's well-known policy of giving stock options to employees has made many of the temps' co-workers millionaires, thanks to Microsoft's soaring stock price. From the start, Mr. Schussler said in a recent interview, he made clear to management that he wanted a permanent job, known as "headcount" in Microsoft jargon. "Everyone knows headcount at Microsoft is the Holy Grail," he said. But his managers repeatedly told him that while they were eager to keep him because of his good work, they wanted to fill the limited number of permanent slots allotted them with the scarcest commodity in high tech: programmers. Sharon L. Decker, director of Microsoft's Contingent Staffing Group, defended the company's use of temps, saying many would rather be temps than permanent employees. "There's a recognition that this kind of free agent approach is growing -- people want to be able to negotiate their own employment," she said. "These workers like the flexibility. They like the ability to work for six months and then go skiing." But Ms. Hughes, the editor, said Microsoft used temps principally to skimp on benefits. "If Microsoft cannot afford to treat all its employees well," she said, "then no company in the history of the world could."  The Math Filling Jobs, Saving Money In 1986, the number of temps employed each day was 800,000, but, according to the National Association of Temporary and Staffing Services, the number soared to 2.5 million last year or about 2 percent of the work force. At least 200,000 of them are long-term temps. By some estimates, temps now represent at least 10 percent of the work force at one-fifth of American corporations. Managers argue that using temps is ideal for the modern market's demands for efficiency and flexibility. Many employees say it dovetails with their desire for independence and for stimulating challenges. Peg Cheirrett, president of the Wasser Group, which supplies temps to Microsoft, said using temps in a volatile industry was humane because they had no false expectations.  "When people know it's a temporary arrangement," she said, "someday when the assignment ends, there's not a sense of a broken trust." Ms. Decker rejected the idea that the company used temps to save money on benefits. Microsoft, she said, is encouraging temp agencies to provide more generous benefits. But even the improved benefits pale next to Microsoft's. Ms. Decker also asserted that many temps earned more an hour than regular workers -- an assertion many temps challenge. Temps may earn $18 an hour as testers and $50 an hour as hot-shot programmers. A technical editor might earn $30 an hour at Microsoft. This means the worker will cost about $70,000 a year -- $60,000 in basic wages and $10,000 in benefits, including Social Security and unemployment taxes and bare-bones health, 401(k) and vacation benefits. If the temp works 200 hours overtime, that could mean $9,000 extra, although workers complain that a new Washington State regulation allows companies to stop paying computer professionals time-and-a-half for overtime. In comparison, a permanent editor might have a $57,000 salary, but could cost Microsoft $94,000 a year -- $17,000 for a richer benefits package, including vacation, holidays and generous 401(k) contributions, plus discount stock purchase plan and stock options that might be worth $20,000 or more. Salaried employees do not receive overtime pay. In this way, Microsoft might save $24 million for every 1,000 temps it uses, excluding overtime. Irene Pasternack, a technical writer at Microsoft, said she preferred temping to a permanent job. "I have two small children at home, and this gives me much more flexibility than a regular worker has," she said. "The other benefit is it's easier to take more time off for vacation." Under the law, corporations are free to use long-term temps, but these workers are increasingly suing companies, asserting that they deserve the same benefits as regular workers. The temps' claims touch on a murky area: whether their employer is a temp agency or the agency's client, that is, the company where they work. The courts and the Internal Revenue Service are wrestling with these issues; the answer hinges on who controls the worker. In interviews with more than three dozen long-term temps -- most insisted on anonymity for fear of being dismissed -- many complained that companies relied on temps to loosen their ties to workers. Employers, for instance, do not have to pay severance to laid-off temps. "It's one more strategy in which companies are seeking to avoid their responsibilities to their workers," said Amy Dean, the A.F.L-C.I.O.'s chief organizer in Silicon Valley.  The History A Ruling Leads To Reclassifying Microsoft and many other companies embraced the use of long-term temps in the early 1990's, after the I.R.S. told the companies that they had erroneously classified thousands of people who were working full time at company facilities as independent contractors. After the I.R.S. found that these workers were common-law employees, it ordered the companies to pay overdue taxes. In response, many companies switched these contractors to temp status, often telling them to sign up with a temp agency, which then sent the workers to their old companies and old jobs. Microsoft is locked in a five-year-old legal battle with hundreds of independent contractors and temps who insist they should be considered regular employees and receive the same benefits as regular employees. Ms. Decker said 30 percent of Microsoft's temps have worked there for more than a year, and 8 percent for more than two years. Microsoft officials suggest that the large number of long-term temps is an accident, noting that the company has dozens of nearly autonomous groups, with many using temps who are expected to leave when a group finishes with them. But many temps hop between groups. John McGowan Jr., a Cleveland lawyer who advises companies on temps, said: "If you're talking about recruiting, on a regular and recurring basis, a whole work force that you're saying are not your employees, you're opening a Pandora's box. If you're doing it as an end run around employment laws, it can come back to haunt you."  The Law Issues: Back Pay, Future Status In January, the Supreme Court dealt Microsoft a major setback by refusing to hear its appeal in a lawsuit that raises daunting questions about high-tech America's widespread use of temps. Stating that Microsoft's contingent workers were regular employees, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco ruled, en banc, last July that Microsoft had wrongly denied millions of dollars in benefits to hundreds of workers who were independent contractors. The plaintiffs' lawyers assert that the court also ruled that Microsoft owed benefits to thousands of temporary employees, too. But Microsoft is challenging this interpretation. The stakes are high, because the circuit court has stated that the plaintiffs -- the former independent contractors, and perhaps the temps, too -- are entitled to participate in Microsoft's discount stock purchase plan, which has provided participants with fabulous returns. Under that plan, regular workers can buy its shares at a discount of 15 percent or more. The plaintiffs argue that if they were treated as regular employees instead of contractors, they each would have bought hundreds of shares when the stock sold for a tenth of today's price. The plaintiffs are seeking an award of hundreds of millions of dollars from Microsoft. The appeals court also ruled that Microsoft was arbitrary in excluding contingent workers from its 401(k) plan, in which Microsoft provides a 50 percent match, up to 6 percent of an employee's income. The court rejected Microsoft's argument that the plaintiffs did not deserve benefits because they had signed agreements stating they had no employer-employee relationship with Microsoft and were not due company benefits. The court ruled that since the workers were common-law employees, they should qualify for benefits because the benefit plans said they covered all common-law employees. Frightened by the implications, companies and industry groups rallied behind Microsoft. "These people are earning more on a per-hour basis than regular employees to help them pay for benefits," said Mark Nebergall, vice president for tax policy at the Software Publishers Association. "They can't complain that they're getting higher salaries and then turn around and say they deserve regular benefits, too." In arguing that long-term temps are due the same benefits as regular Microsoft workers, the plaintiffs say that temp agencies differ little from payroll services that merely send paychecks and deduct taxes. "A payroll agency is not an employer at all," Stephen K. Strong, the plaintiffs' lawyer, said. "They work on Microsoft's campus. They work full time under Microsoft supervisors. They are producing Microsoft products. If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck. They are undeniably Microsoft employees."  A Temp's-Eye View Painful for Some, Fine for Others In Microsoft's corporate directory, temps have an "A--" before their E-mail addresses to designate them as agency employees. In Microsoft parlance, they are called "A dashes," but many dub themselves "alien dashes" and "dash trash." During peak periods, many temps have to work 70- and 80-hour weeks. This has caused some temps to complain that Microsoft cavalierly chews them up because it has scant loyalty to them. "There is such a painful human impact," said Richard Pauli, who spent five years as a temp at Microsoft. "When you know these are temp positions, there's this attitude of really burning people out." Phil Huston, who recently completed two and a half years as a technical writer at AT&T Wireless, likes temping. "I don't have to sweat the office politics the way you do when you're a permanent employee," he said. "And because I've moved from company to company, I've learned a ton of skills." Yet the differences, however petty, are manifest. Permanent workers wear blue badges, temps orange. Temps are not invited to the annual picnic, do not get discounts at the company store and are not supposed to use Microsoft's basketball courts. "You don't get an outside office if you're not a blue badge," Mr. Schussler said. "That means you don't get to see daylight." Graphic   Photos: ON ONE HAND . . .
