title: For $19.95, Slate Sees Who Its Friends Are
body: It is a clear, shining day in Washington, a world away from the Seattle rain. The budding cherry blossoms hint at spring. And Michael Kinsley, the editor and creator of Microsoft's on-line magazine Slate, is pacing the bare parquet floors of a one-bedroom apartment, considering whether to rent it. Mr. Kinsley has been feeling out of touch with the buzz of the Beltway these days and, perhaps to reconnect, he has agreed to occasionally return to his chair on CNN's "Crossfire," where he became a celebrity liberal for butting heads with the conservative Pat Buchanan. An apartment rental? Crossfire redux? Is Michael Kinsley getting cold feet? Has the uncharted boundlessness of cyberspace left him pining for the knowable confines of the capital? On the contrary, Mr. Kinsley, 47, insists. He has become a zealous convert to the Pacific Northwest -- Slate is based in Redmond, Wash. He bought land. He carries one of those wallets that closes with Velcro. He recycles. He has even taken up snowshoeing. Nevertheless, Mr. Kinsley could be forgiven for feeling a little skittish at the moment. Earlier this month, the gate came down on free visitors to Slate; now people who want to read the magazine have to pay for it. It is not a lot of money in the scheme of things: $19.95 for a year's subscription and the magazine still offers a free "front porch," its home page. But paying anything at all is radical stuff for the Internet, and the venture is being watched closely as a test of the potential profitability of the Internet. "The going price on the Internet now is free, and to charge anything more than that you have to have a project that is very unique," said Bill Bass, an analyst at Forrester Research Inc., a technology research company in Cambridge, Mass. "A lot of the stuff that's worked well on line has a financial purpose or is a game or pornography. And Slate doesn't fall into any of these categories." Slate (www.slate.com) is radical in its way -- not just because it is trying to get readers to pay but because it has set out to help define a category that did not exist, a product straddling several worlds. It arguably has the depth and analysis of print, the immediacy of radio and television, the bells and whistles of Web sites. Some articles are carefully conceived, some go out on the Web without editing. Slate calls itself a weekly yet updates its contents daily. Mr. Kinsley says he is learning as he goes along, about things like how to strike the right tone. "There is a voice of the Web that's developing -- I've taken some hits for complaining about its insularity and smugness," he said. "But there is also its casualness and informality, and we certainly have evolved over the last year and a half more in that direction and away from traditional magazine pieces." There are print-oriented people who find Slate too "Webby," cyber-savvy people who find it too mired in old models. "It's still to me very inside the media elite -- it's like they're ricocheting things off each others' computers," said James Wolcott, a media critic who was tough on the magazine in Vanity Fair last year. "One of the things really missing from it, what Salon really has, is a pop sensibility." In going to paid circulation, Slate is largely out there on its own. While a few publications like The Wall Street Journal and the Economist charge for their on-line versions, general interest publications with Web sites are in a wait-and-see mode. The economics seem attractive -- no paper, printing or postage costs -- but there have already been casualties. Recently, the webzines Word and Charged folded before even trying paid subscriptions. And over the last few months, the Microsoft Corporation has scaled back its Internet media efforts, including layoffs at Sidewalk, its on-line city guides. As a result, many people in the publishing world are wary of placing their bets on the future of Slate. "If they pull it off, there are going to be a lot of publishers out there dancing in the streets," Mr. Bass said, "because nobody on the content side is running profitably right now." Mr. Kinsley said navigating such new territory "makes this very interesting but also very hard." "It's as if you were founding a paper magazine and said, O.K., we chopped down the trees, now what?" he said. Slate has planned to go paid since its inception in June 1996. Mr. Kinsley backed away once before -- in February 1997. Finally, the moment felt as right as it ever would. "It seemed to me, we'd been putting it out for over a year and it was time to fish or cut bait," Mr. Kinsley said.  "It's important to us to break even and to be a business, not someone's charity case." To Microsoft, the move is not just philosophically important but financially necessary. Advertisers are proceeding with caution when it comes to Slate because the audience numbers remain relatively low. "It became clear that, on an ad-only basis, it wasn't going to work," said Peter Neupert, Microsoft's vice president of news and publishing. "I didn't see it scaling big enough and the ad marketplace accepting it quick enough to meet our objectives in terms of turning the corner." Slate and Microsoft said they had already received more than 17,000 subscription orders and hoped to reach 20,000 over the next few months. But that number is a far cry from the 95,000 circulation enjoyed by The New Republic, where Mr. Kinsley worked on and off for almost 20 years. Or the 218,000 currently enjoyed by Harper's, where Mr. Kinsley briefly served as editor in 1981. How much readership Slate has lost since the transition on March 9 is difficult to gauge because of the vagaries of Internet measurement. In January, when the Monica Lewinsky story first broke, the site received 270,000 visits, many from repeat readers. The current subscriber response gets the magazine to a mere $340,000 in revenue; Slate's annual operating costs have been estimated at $5 million by analysts. The subscriber response is not a number that gets advertisers excited. Slate would not disclose ad revenue figures. "We're not even talking about critical mass here," Paula Brooks, the media director at the ad agency Margeotes/Fertitta & Partners, said. "A magazine with 100,000 circulation is not truly viable." Slate will now have to spend money to win new readers, just like print publications; it plans to market the magazine with ads on other sites and with targeted email. And given the hurdles ahead, Rogers Weed, Slate's publisher, said he is prepared to ultimately accept defeat. "It's very possible that the Web is just not the place for publications like Slate that have a more limited appeal," he said. Slate's writers, many of whom have left mainstream publications for cyberspace, may be less quick to surrender. It has been hard enough to see Slate's audience drop since going paid, however unavoidable. "This is much more of casting your bread upon the waters," said Jodie T. Allen, Slate's Washington editor, who came to Slate from The Washington Post and covers Congress. "The aides don't know who I am anymore." While Slate has developed a loyal following among many people in the news media and politics, some say the magazine has yet to develop real influence. "Mike Kinsley could make the earth move with his column in The New Republic," said Stephen G. Smith, the editor of National Journal. "He can't do that with Slate." To gain more clout, Mr. Kinsley has to figure out how to make the new medium work for the largest possible audience -- i.e., how to get people to read long pieces in a fast-moving medium that you can not easily curl up with on the couch. "That's our biggest problem," Mr. Kinsley said. "You have to reward people. You have to offer them things they can't get on paper to compensate." That is why Slate offers audio poetry readings along with its featured weekly poem, film clips with some movie reviews. And why, in its printed edition -- which has a circulation in the low hundreds -- Slate often reminds readers what they are missing out on electronically. Slate has also tried to be more Web-specific, offering "hot links" to let readers click on interesting tangents. In an essay on Gertrude Stein, for example, readers were invited to "Click here for an excerpt from 'Lifting Belly,' a witty unpublished love poem she wrote to Alice B. Toklas." "In print, these would have to be footnotes," said Judith Shulevitz, Slate's New York editor. "But on the Web, they come off as a secondary level of discourse." Depending on whom you talk to, Slate's move to paid subscriptions is either brave or foolhardy. "They may make it because they have the deep pocket to wait out the market until it matures," said Stefanie Symon, the co-founder and executive editor of the Web magazine Feed, who also expects to switch to paid subscriptions eventually. While Microsoft and Slate may have been eager to develop a new revenue stream, both said they expect that bringing Slate into the black will take patience. "I have made it clear to them that the experience of the magazine world is that it takes seven or eight years," Mr. Kinsley said. As to whether he will stick around until then, he said: "I could well, I could well not. Have I ever done anything for seven or eight years?" Mr. Kinsley said he began feeling a little bit out out of the loop when the Monica Lewinsky scandal broke. "The average person on the street in Washington can do about eight layers of interpretation on Lewinsky," he said. "So you sort of feel out of it if you can only do five or six. It reinforced the notion that it's important to spend more time here." For the moment, however, Mr. Kinsley said he likes hiking in the mountains and wearing plaid flannel shirts to the office. And despite continuing speculation about whether he will grow restless, the editor's colleagues say his commitment is passionate. "People do not have any idea how much work he has put into this," Ms. Shulevitz said. "And how hard it would be to walk away." Graphic   Photo: Michael Kinsley, the editor and creator of Microsoft's on-line magazine Slate, has tried to integrate the strengths of both traditional and electronic journalism. (Therese Frare for The New York Times)(pg. D1) Chart: "What Kinsley Has Wrought" With Slate, Michael Kinsley is trying to meld traditional publishing forms with the immediacy and special qualities of the Internet. Here are some of the forms he has created.  BRIEFING SECTION  TODAY'S PAPERS -- A summary of what is in the day's Washington Post, New York Times and Los Angeles Times, Wall Street Journal, U.S.A. Today, posted in the wee hours of the morning.  THE WEEK/THE SPIN -- A look at the week's major news events and how the news is being played. May include "The Starrometer" or "The Clintometer" which track the fortunes of Kenneth Starr or President Clinton.  THE GIST -- An intense briefing on some subject in the news, i.e., the tensions in Kosovo, the case against the poet Ted Hughes and Is a lawyer like Robert Bennett allowed to lie for his client?  CHATTERBOX -- Slate's gossip column -- mostly about politics and the media -- by Mickey Kaus.  SUMMARY JUDGMENT -- Reviews of the reviewers: how the critics come down on movies, theater, books, opera.  PUNDIT CENTRAL -- How the TV commentators weighed in on the weekend talk shows like "Meet the Press" and "Inside Washington."  SLATE NEWS QUIZ -- A question of the day. ("Click here by noon to email your answers.")  RECYCLED -- Slate periodically recycles articles from its archives that are given new life by the news.  DISPATCHES AND DIALOGUES  Includes unedited messages from people in places far and near as well as published exchanges about various topics like NATO expansion or the Asian bailout.  UTILITIES  Includes "The Fray," where Slate's readers can communicate with one another. (pg. D7)

title:
TECHNOLOGY: DIGITAL COMMERCE;
On-line sellers learn how to get packages from cyberspace to consumers.
body: Speak the words "electronic commerce" and in most circles, the starry-eyed vision that comes to mind is of a sophisticated new computer system for selling goods to millions of on-line consumers without the costly overhead of a storefront. Win-win, retail revolution, etc. But in their rush to outfit the Internet as a global shopping mall, investors and vendors may have overlooked a practical question that just might be a deal breaker: "How are you going to get me the goods?" Delivery trucks roll during business hours, which is when some 70 percent of Americans are not at home. Coming home to a "delivery attempt" notice is not only annoying and inconvenient for on-line or catalogue shoppers, it is also a major problem for ground carriers, all of which acknowledge they are ill-equipped to handle the onslaught if E-commerce really catches on. "We haven't figured out how to make a profit delivering to homes," says Bram Johnson, senior vice president for marketing and strategic planning for RPS Inc. (www.shiprps.com), a unit of the FDX Corporation and the world's second-largest ground carrier of small packages. "For us, the cost of running a delivery truck is putting on the parking brake -- you take 50 boxes off the truck at Wal-Mart or Kmart. The 'stop cost' is almost zero. But when I stop at your house, the whole cost is absorbed by the package that I leave on your doorstep." That cost becomes even higher when drivers have to redeliver a package. Worse yet, theft and fraud are growing problems in areas where drivers leave packages on doorsteps to save the cost of redelivery: thieves often follow behind trucks, scooping up packages, or customers deliberately do not answer the door to sign for them, then claim they were not delivered. This simply will not do when nearly $12 billion in Internet consumer sales are expected by 2002 -- up from $200 million in 1996, according to the Direct Marketing Association. Assuming an average order of $100, that means 120 million more home-delivered packages -- not counting the 646 million catalogue orders expected that year. "Most E-commerce providers haven't thought about transportation or logistics at all," says Mark Rhoney the marketing vice president for the electronic commerce division of United Parcel Service, the world's largest small-package delivery service. "They've built all this nice software to take credit cards and create invoices that print out someplace and end up on the floor." Only 20 percent of U.P.S.'s business is home delivery, Mr. Rhoney says. It is such a tiny blip on Federal Express's radar that Fedex does not even track home versus business deliveries. Virtually all ground carriers now charge extra to deliver to a residence, and it is still a break-even proposition at best. "Home delivery is definitely the fly in the ointment," says Kenneth Ross, chairman and chief executive of Packagenet (www.packagenet.com). "If carriers can't find ways to deliver more cost-effectively, it will double the cost of residential delivery, and the whole value proposition for E-commerce gets blown." Packagenet, a Fairfield, Iowa, company, provides consumers with U.P.S. shipping and catalogue return services from counters inside some 4,000 supermarkets, including Kroger and Safeway. Until now, its focus has been on outgoing packages. But anticipating a steep increase in home deliveries because of E-commerce, Mr. Ross is developing what he calls a "Depot Network" to give consumers a handy place to pick up packages at convenient times and to help carriers like RPS solve the "stop cost" problem by letting them deliver a neighborhood's packages to a single location. E-commerce customers who choose Depot Delivery from a merchant's site, says Mr. Ross, will pay about a $3 premium over standard shipping charges. The Depot Network, a set of software tools for E-commerce merchants that the company says will be ready for a market trial this year, will link supermarket depots to existing carrier tracking systems and merchant data bases. The software is being developed in conjunction with Packagenet's advisory board, including the Microsoft Corporation, the Netscape Communications Corporation and America Online. Although Packagenet is declaring its intentions early, its competitors are getting their trucks in a row. Home delivery, says Mr. Rhoney, is "definitely a business that U.P.S. embraces," and though he is coy on specifics, he says that U.P.S. is exploring alternatives like night and weekend deliveries three to five years hence, when he expects residential delivery volumes to double. The unitedstates Postal Service anticipates "an explosion" of home deliveries because of E-commerce.  "We'll do whatever the customer needs -- evening deliveries, convenient pick-up hours, tracking, tracing, delivery confirmation," Bill Henderson, the service's chief operating officer, says. Of course, anything is possible. Even Packagenet is considering evening home deliveries. But how much is the customer willing to pay? That is the real issue -- and the deal breaker -- for E-commerce vendors. "It comes down to sales tax versus the cost of shipping and handling," says Packagenet's Mr. Ross. "Consumers have enormous sensitivity to those extra shipping and handling charges. They say, 'You keep raising those and we'll just go back to the department store.' " Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title: U.S. Facing Lightning Technology Shifts in Microsoft Case
body: In its pursuit of the Microsoft Corporation, the Justice Department is breathing hard -- just to keep up, let alone catch the company red-handed with the kind of evidence it needs to bring a broader antitrust case. Under Joel I. Klein, the Assistant Attorney General in charge of the antitrust division, the Justice Department has assembled a formidable team of antitrust litigators and policy experts. But it faces an extraordinary challenge in keeping its investigation in step with the fast-changing Internet software market and Microsoft's quickly shifting tactics. Business practices that seemed questionable, and perhaps even incriminating, to Government investigators a few weeks or months ago can be altered by the company or rendered harmless by the marketplace. In the face of industry criticism, for example, Microsoft recently dropped the contract restrictions it placed on some 40 American and European companies that provide dial-up Internet access to individuals and corporations. Microsoft said it would no longer prohibit these Internet service providers from promoting the Web browsing software of rivals -- a change made just before William H. Gates, Microsoft's chairman, testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee earlier this month. And in his Senate testimony, Mr. Gates seems to have understated the restrictions Microsoft places on some Web site operators, judging from a Microsoft contract recently sent to one of its Web site partners, a copy of which was given to The newyork Times. Microsoft and its rivals argue whether the contract is run of the mill or anticompetitive, but that debate is of little interest to the Web site partners. Their complaint is that being a featured site on Microsoft's desktop did not bring them a sharp rise in on-line viewers. Now, they are looking ahead to Microsoft's next effort to use its desktop software to steer on-line audiences with its next-generation operating system, Windows 98, to be introduced in June. The speed issue extends well beyond the Microsoft case as the Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission struggle to revamp antitrust enforcement so they can deal effectively with fast-moving technology markets. "Will antitrust, though faster than it was in the past, be able to keep up?" said Robert Pitofsky, chairman of F.T.C., which is investigating the Intel Corporation, the leading maker of microchips. "I think it can, but it's going to be quite a challenge." Washington's track record of antitrust enforcement in the computer industry has been anything but fleet-footed. The Justice Department's ill-conceived case against I.B.M., dropped in 1982 after 13 years in court, is regarded as a textbook example of how delay can make antitrust enforcement irrelevant. Yet no high-technology market moves at the pace of the Internet software business, which makes the time pressure on antitrust investigators even greater. Consider Microsoft's deals with the Web sites prominently featured on the company's browser software. The worry is that Microsoft could use its control of personal computer software to give the company an unfair advantage in the Internet software market and to control news, entertainment programming and electronic commerce on the Internet. The Justice Department is investigating Microsoft's contracts with Web site operators, known in the industry as Internet content providers. The Judiciary Committee sharply quizzed Mr. Gates on the contracts. Senator Orrin G. Hatch, the chairman, asked Mr. Gates repeatedly whether Microsoft imposed "any limitation on content providers" restricting them from promoting the Netscape Communications Corporation, Microsoft's main rival in the browser market. The only restriction, Mr. Gates replied, was that Web sites accorded featured billing on Microsoft's Internet browser were not allowed to promote Netscape on their home page, one mouse click away from Microsoft's so-called Active Desktop channel guide. "Except for the specific pages that we link through the channel guide, they are free to promote Netscape and have links to Netscape," Mr. Gates said. But a copy of a Microsoft contract sent to a Web site operator seems to go further. The contract, a copy of which was given to The newyork Times by an industry executive, who asked not to be identified, calls for the Web site partner to promote Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser exclusively on its home page "and any other pages where similar promotions are placed." Under a section titled "Content and Logo Restrictions," the Microsoft contract states that the Web site operator, or Company, "agrees that neither it nor its affiliates will directly or indirectly license or otherwise authorize distribution, transmission, marketing or promotion in the territory of Company content or logos by companies which produce other browsers." But the contract provisions seem less a damaging contradiction of Mr. Gates's testimony than the starting point for a debate about what kinds of exclusive arrangements are permitted for a dominant producer, even a monopolist -- which many industry experts say Microsoft is, given the 85 percent share that its Windows program holds in the market for PC operating system software, which acts as a computer's central nervous system. Microsoft's content and logo restrictions in the contract are exclusionary, said Christine A. Varney, a partner at Hogan & Hartson, a law firm working for Netscape. "I read contracts all the time," Ms. Varney said, "and that says we're not going to give you a place on our desktop if you promote or advertise Netscape." Brad Smith, Microsoft's associate general counsel, said that portion of the contract limited the use of a Web site company's logo only in certain circumstances, like newspaper advertisements for Netscape's browser. Mr. Smith characterized the restriction as a routine marketing agreement similar to that used in many industries. For example, he said, Disney might enter into a cross-marketing deal with Burger King to promote one of its animated movies. The arrangement, he said, would be exclusive only in the sense that Disney would not be promoting its movie at McDonald's restaurants at the same time. Ms. Varney, a former commissioner of the F.T.C., questioned whether the analogy was valid in Microsoft's case. "Disney is not a monopolist," she said, "and Burger King is not a monopolist." Exclusive deals are commonplace.  The antitrust issue arises if a dominant company, like Microsoft, uses exclusive contracts with suppliers or customers to inhibit competition, antitrust experts said. "It is the cumulative effect of these kinds of contracts that is the key," one senior Justice Department official said. The effect of this Microsoft contract has been slight. Industry analysts and some of Microsoft's Web site partners say its Active Desktop approach to steering users to Web sites selected by Microsoft has been a failure. PC users found it confusing to set up, avoided it and used Microsoft's browser in the conventional way -- typing in Web site addresses they select instead of the ones featured by Microsoft. For Web site partners, the hoped-for surge in viewing traffic as a result of being featured on Microsoft's desktop never occurred. More viewers mean more money for Web sites, which charge advertisers based on the size of the audience they attract. "The tactics Microsoft uses with Active Desktop partners have been aggressive for sure," said Kate Delhagen, an analyst for Forrester Research Inc. "But the real problem from an industry standpoint is that it didn't drive traffic." The industry is already looking ahead to Microsoft's next attempt to exploit its prime desktop real estate. Web site companies are closely watching Microsoft's new operating system, Windows 98, which more closely integrates the operating system and Web browser, presenting a unified look to the user. And industry executives expect that a new Microsoft Internet site under development, called Start, will eventually become the start-up screen on the company's browser software unless the user changes the setting. "Microsoft is going to do with Start in Windows 98 what RCA probably should have done -- you turn on your television set and it goes to its network, NBC," said Mike Slade, chairman of the Starwave Corporation, a leading producer of on-line sports and news services. "That's going to be the one to watch," added Mr. Slade of Starwave, which is jointly owned by the Walt Disney Company and Paul Allen, Microsoft's co-founder. "And Microsoft is going to have to be very careful how it exercises its market power there." Microsoft says that plans for Start are still developing; it is being made available first to subscribers of MSN, the company's on-line service.

title: Winners and Losers in Acquisition of Dow Jones Markets
body: For Bridge Information Systems, the laggard in the hotly competitive business of providing Wall Street with desktop financial data, this month's $510 million purchase of Dow Jones Markets was critical. Before it more than doubled its reach by acquiring the troubled financial services arm of Dow Jones, Bridge trailed not only Dow Jones Markets and Bloomberg L.P., but also Reuters, the industry giant. By acquiring Dow Jones Markets, Bridge not only expands its customer base, but as the Bridge chairman, Thomas Wendel, explained it, the company got "a more geographically diverse" customer universe. Dow Jones Markets' customers are divided equally among the unitedstates, Europe and Asia. Assuming the deal goes through, the competitors' reach will be ranked as follows: Reuters, with 386,000 desktops; Bridge would have 169,000, and Bloomberg, with 91,000. In the unitedstates Bloomberg charges $1,200 a month for its service. Reuters charges $800 to $1,200, but discounts the rate depending on the number of boxes a customer uses. Bridge's rate is $150 to $750, depending on how many services one takes. But desktops are only a part of the story -- already Reuters, Bridge and Bloomberg have created personal computer software allowing access to their information over the Internet, a potentially attractive alternative to traders whose desks are cluttered with monitors. For Mr. Wendel, Bridge's key competitor will become Reuters, whose customers are also spread around the world. In Mr. Wendel's view, Reuters has a broader product line than Bloomberg. Bridge desperately wanted the deal. It has been a major provider of data, selling the information primarily to institutional money managers who buy stocks for their portfolios. Dow Jones Markets, formerly known as Telerate, focuses on the fixed-income market with information essential to bond traders. Bloomberg, too, appeals to those who follow the fixed-income market, but its emphasis has always been on analyzing data, rather than simply providing data. And Reuters built its business in foreign exchange -- an area that is still its major strength, though with the advent of the European common market, some argue that the foreign exchange businesses could dwindle. Bob Crooke, a Reuters spokesman, countered that there are emerging market currencies that could counter that consolidation. More recently Bloomberg has been breaking into the equity markets. But it is somewhat easier for investors to get information on stocks from less expensive sources such as ILX Systems, a division of the Thomson Corporation, or from Bridge, and equities traders have shown less need for service that provides detailed and sometimes arcane analyses. But as one data company executive who requested anonymity put it, "Nobody delivers such sophisticated analysis of data as Bloomberg and has the ability to answer as many questions about stocks and bonds as Bloomberg does." That helps differentiate the company from its rivals. Bloomberg's pre-eminence in analysis was evident in January when Reuters said that Federal prosecutors were investigating whether an American subsidiary of Reuters Holdings commissioned computer specialists to steal confidential information in an effort to reconstruct Bloomberg analytic programs. But before Bridge is really ready to compete, it must resolve a myriad of issues, according to several executives close to the negotiations. The thorniest involves the contract that Dow Jones had struck with Cantor Fitzgerald, the company that provides real-time information on government bonds and is still the place to go for information on treasury securities. That data were one of the reasons Bridge was so eager to buy Dow Jones Markets. But transferring the contract to a new owner is a problematic business. A person close to Cantor Fitzgerald said that the original contract with Dow Jones Markets obliged Dow Jones to pay for each screen with "qualifying information," a definition that guaranteed an estimated $50 million annually. People close to Cantor say that after the deal, the contract assures it approximately $30 million in additional payments. Even though Bridge has said publicly that it will not offer its old customers the Cantor Fitzgerald data, Cantor's management apparently believes it should get the same revenue it would earn if Bridge offered its data to all its customers. Ultimately, of course, to get the full value of the deal, Bridge will want to offer all its customers the two services. Mr. Wendel, as well as a Dow Jones spokesman, declined to comment on specifics of the deal. Even if the Cantor contract increases the cost of the deal for Bridge, it can find savings in labor costs, at least two experts have said. Dow Jones markets now has 3,500 employees. Though Mr. Wendel has acknowledged there will be staff reductions, he has declined to say how broad they will be. But several industry experts said they believed the cuts could affect 2,000 or more, a figure that Mr. Wendel denied. Even so, Bridge has already said it will spend about $100 million annually to upgrade Dow Jones Markets. And though Mr. Wendel is adamant that Bridge has strong analytics, several critics point out that they do not match those of Michael Bloomberg. To one financial data expert, the issue for Bridge will be competition from free Internet services. But a Bridge spokesman countered, "In our low-end product, we give far more extensive information, from real-time prices to international equities." Certainly there has been growth: the number of users of financial data has increased at a rate of about 9 percent a year. Overseas, where Bridge now has more of a presence, the potential is greater. Dow Jones itself has made a significant bet on Bridge's chances of success. In the sale, the company receives $360 million in cash and $150 million of preferred stock with a 4 percent dividend, stock that can be converted into 10 percent of Bridge's equity in five years. That 4 percent figure may understate the actual potential returns, since 70 percent of corporate dividends are excluded from taxes. Still, several corporate finance experts said recently that the 4 percent was relatively low. But these experts believe that when Dow Jones swaps its stock, its 10 percent interest in Bridge will be worth more than $150 million. And though they were generally pleased that Dow Jones sold a business that had become a liability, apparently it did not particularly reassure investors about Dow Jones's future. The stock closed down .375, at $52.25, after the deal was announced March 17, though it has since come back slightly, closing Friday at $53.25.

title: Biggest Sender Of Junk Mail On Internet Agrees to Stop
body: In a consent decree that represents a turning point in the escalating war against Internet junk email, or "spam," the company most responsible for stuffing millions of email boxes with unsolicited advertisements has agreed to pay $2 million to settle the last of several lawsuits brought against it by Internet service providers. The judgment against Cyber Promotions Inc. in Los Angeles County Superior Court in effect banishes the company from cyberspace at a time when the cottage industry it helped to spawn and vigorously championed is under sustained attack by legislators and computer software engineers alike. Under the terms of the agreement, the chief executive of Cyber Promotions, Sanford Wallace, will be held personally liable for $1 million if he or any company affiliated with him emails unsolicited advertisements to the customers of Earthlink Network Inc., one of the nation's biggest Internet service providers. Mr. Wallace, who once gleefully embraced his Internet nickname "Spamford" and brashly defended his right to flood the Internet with junk mail, also agreed to write a letter of apology to Earthlink subscribers "for any inconvenience" he may have caused. The draft letter, included in court documents distributed on Friday by Earthlink, says that his company's legal battles have "put Cyber out of the spamming business." "The most important benefit of this judgment is the message we've sent to spammers that illegally tap our resources and clog up the Internet with this trash -- we won't stand for it," said Garry Betty, chief executive of Earthlink, which is based in Pasadena, Calif. "On top of that, now they'll pay a very real penalty." Mr. Wallace, who negotiated the settlement himself, could not be reached for comment. Mr. Wallace is far from the only spammer on the Internet. The ability to send millions of email messages for the price of an Internet account has give rise to a whole industry of electronic hawkers. But Mr. Wallace was among the first and was considered particularly pernicious because he developed and sold programs like "Cyber Bomber" that enabled others to follow more easily in his digital footsteps. More recently, he ceased sending spam himself and sought to build a business as a conduit for other spammers who are typically cut off by their Internet providers as soon as their activities are discovered. Earthlink and virtually every other company that sells Internet access have fielded thousands of customer complaints over the last year about unwelcome email clogging mailboxes with material about get-rich-quick schemes and pornographic Web sites. Such advertising is estimated to account for about 10 percent of all email worldwide and is blamed for slowing other traffic over the global computer network. While the Internet companies most affected by the surge in junk mail pursue its purveyors in court, software programmers are developing technical ways to block bulk email and legislators are writing laws that aim to protect consumers from what is sometimes seen as an invasion of privacy. Last week, Washington became the first state to enact an anti-spamming law. The measure makes it illegal for junk emailers to forge return addresses or misrepresent the point of origin of a message, a common tactic used to circumvent the restrictions Internet service providers place on the distribution of bulk email. On Tuesday, California lawmakers will hold the first hearing on a bill that seeks to keep Internet users from receiving unsolicited commercial email. And several anti-spam bills are pending in Congress. Bulk emailers contend that they are simply pursuing a business opportunity, that many email recipients are glad to be informed of their products and that their right to free speech would be violated by such measures. In the Earthlink case, the court prohibited Cyber Promotions from sending junk email to Earthlink customers based on the same anti-trespass laws that prevent somebody from cutting across a front yard. The case was the last of several judgments against Cyber Promotions, which is based in Dresher, Pa., and has been inactive for several months since its Internet provider refused to continue to provide a connection to the network.The ruling makes it unlikely that it will resume operations. "This is the nail in the coffin that put Cyber Promotions out of business," said Pete Wellborn, a lawyer who argued the case for Earthlink. "But Sanford Wallace is very much an entrepreneurial figure. I would not be surprised to see him back on the Internet in one form or another."

title: At Internet Torture Trial, Defense Builds Case on a Beat Novel
body: Lawyers for a man accused of kidnapping and sexually abusing a woman he met over the Internet used the writings of William S. Burroughs yesterday in an attempt to cast the woman's story as a fantasy drawn in part from the pages of a novel. Clutching a copy of the Burroughs novel "Naked Lunch," a defense lawyer, Jack Litman, repeatedly asked the woman to read passages from the graphically sexual and violent book. He sought to draw parallels between passages in the novel, including grotesque descriptions of murder and rape, and computer messages that the woman wrote to the defendant, Oliver Jovanovic, during the summer and fall of 1996. Mr. Litman also tried to draw parallels between "Naked Lunch" and the story of bondage and torture that the woman told to prosecutors. In her email messages to Mr. Jovanovic, a Columbia University graduate student, the woman referred to Burroughs's writing, often quoting word for word. She testified in State Supreme Court in Manhattan yesterday that she was drawn more to Burroughs's vivid imagery than his philosophy. "You live in a world of metaphor and imagery, don't you?" Mr. Litman asked the woman, a student at Barnard College. "I live in the world of reality," she replied. Burroughs died in August at 83. "Naked Lunch," first published in 1959, is a hallucinatory exploration of American society that is considered one of the foundation works of the Beat Generation. In 1965, it was banned as obscene in Massachusetts, but the ban was lifted a year later by the unitedstates Supreme Court. The woman has testified that she had directly copied parts of the book into her messages, but Mr. Litman said she did not quote exactly, suggesting that she was writing passages that she had memorized. In the first email message that she wrote to Mr. Jovanovic after the alleged assault, the woman paraphrased from "Naked Lunch" to express what she has said was her inability to stop thinking about the incident: "Burroughs best sums my state, saying something about rotten eggs or rotting cheese, the taste is so overpoweringly delicious, and at the same time, quite nauseating, so that one will eat and puke and eat and puke until collapsing from exhaustion."

title: Bringing the Visual World of the Web to the Blind
body: CURTIS CHONG has been using the World Wide Web for three years to look up topics like music, fund-raising and medical research. He also uses it as a way to teach and encourage other blind people to get on the Web. How does someone who cannot see the screen navigate the computer and Web, which is full of glitzy graphics and icons? Mr. Chong communicates all his commands through the keyboard. His printer prints in Braille. He uses the Web browser Internet Explorer 3.02, with a piece of software called a screen reader and a speech synthesizer to turn the written words on the screen into words spoken in a computer-generated voice. "We want to use the Web, and we want to use it like everybody else does," said Mr. Chong, director of technology for the National Federation of the Blind, based in Baltimore. "We don't believe the computer is the great equalizer for the blind, but it's one way to make our lives better." For the more than half-million blind people of working age in the unitedstates, getting on the Web may not only mean being able to research topics of interest but may also be a necessary skill for staying employed. "It certainly affects the jobs of thousands of blind people," said Gary Wunder, a blind man who is a senior computer programmer at the University of Missouri Hospitals and Clinics. He is required to use the Web in his job for project assignments and updates. "It isn't just optional anymore." While current statistics on the use of computers and the Web by blind and visually impaired people are hard to find, technology companies and advocacy organizations say the numbers are rapidly increasing. Tens of thousands of blind people are on computers, and every year more of them are learning to use the Web, Mr. Chong said. A 1991 study published by the American Foundation for the Blind in newyork found that 43 percent of blind and severely visually impaired people were using the computer for writing, said Emilie Schmeidler, senior research associate for the foundation. Her impression is that more visually impaired people are using computers and the Web now, she said, and "more and more jobs require the computer." A screen reader or screen access program like the one Mr. Chong uses is the translator that tells a speech synthesizer what to say when the visual icons are accompanied by a text description. "It's my white cane that helps me know what's on the screen," Mr. Chong said. Henter-Joyce, a company in St. Petersburg, Fla., that manufactures the popular screen reader called JAWS (Job Access With Speech) for Windows, has between 15,000 and 18,000 customers, said the company's president, Ted Henter. He said the customer base had increased four to five times since 1995. At least seven companies make the screen readers. Henter-Joyce's JAWS is one of the top sellers and costs about $795; the company's new version, to be released this spring, will include a speech synthesizer. The National Federation of the Blind Web site includes a computer-resource page (www.nfb.org/computer.htm) that has information on how to get in contact with the companies that sell the readers. But getting the technology right is only one piece of the package. If Web pages do not have text that identifies graphics or if they have moving type, they will not be accessible. The World Wide Web Consortium (www.w3.org), made up of universities, corporations and research organizations and based at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, started a three-year project in 1997 called the Web Accessibility Intiative that is creating guidelines to make technology and Web pages more accessible to blind, deaf and disabled users. The National Federation of the Blind has eight accessibility guidelines for Web pages that can be found on its Web site (www.nfb.org/webacc.htm). The Center for Applied Special Technology, a nonprofit research and development organization in Peabody, Mass., has a free service in which it analyzes Web sites and offer suggestions for their accessibility (www.cast.org/bobby). The change from DOS, a text-based operating sytem, to Windows, a graphics-based operating system, was a setback for the blind. "The world enthusiastically embraced Windows, and we were left out," said Mr. Wunder, who is also president of the Missouri chapter of the National Federation of the Blind. But in the last two and a half years, Microsoft "has shown concern and responsiveness" to the blind, Mr. Wunder said. Version 3.02 of Microsoft's browser, Internet Explorer, includes a component called Microsoft Active Accessibility, a layer of codes that are compatible with accessibility aids like the screen reader. In addition to aiding blind users, these codes also hook into software that helps users who are deaf or have other disabilities. But a newer version, Internet Explorer 4.0, was released on Oct. 1, 1997, without the Active Accessibility component. Angry letters, phone calls and emails let Luanne LaLonde, Microsoft's accessibility product manager, and others at Microsoft know that this was unacceptable. "We got a lot of email," she said. In early November, about 35 days after the release of Explorer 4.0, Microsoft released Explorer 4.01, including Active Accessibility. WEB page design, of course, is an element of accessibility. Vito DeSantis, manager of field operations for the southern regional office of the New Jersey Commission for the Blind, uses the Web to find research on the eye condition that has made it impossible for him to see the computer screen for the past three years. He also likes to read newspapers on the Web. For visually impaired Web users like Mr. DeSantis, the vertical columns on the Web present the biggest problem because screen readers pick up the information horizontally. "You have to really know how to navigate around the screen," Mr. DeSantis said. "I imagine quite a few people might get frustrated. Sometimes it's just not worth the effort." While screen readers help, Mr. Wunder said, "no screen reader has made the Web as easily accessible for the blind as for the sighted." Even with top-of-the-line screen readers, Web pages have to have text explanations for graphics and icons or the visually impaired computer user cannot move. "You get a screen and it says, 'Image, image, image,' " Ms. Schmeidler said, quoting the sound her screen reader makes when the cursor hits an icon without accompanying text. "You have no idea how frustrating it is." In addition to the advice on making a Web page accessible from the National Federation of the Blind and the Center for Applied Special Technology, the World Wide Web Consortium has a group of volunteer computer experts who are leading the Web Accessibility Initiative. The group's goal is to write guidelines for Web page authors who want to make their pages accessible for all disabled users. A rough draft of the recommendations can be found on the consortium's Web site (www.w3.org/wai). "Everything is voluntary, and the documents are called recommendations," said Prof. Gregg Vanderheiden, director of the Trace Research and Development Center at the University of Wisconsin at Madison and a member of the group. But for businesses and government agencies, making sites accessible may not be voluntary, he said. In a policy ruling in September 1996, the Department of Justice said the Americans With Disabilities Act did cover access to Web pages. "A Web site is an electronic front door," Professor Vanderheiden said. "But blind users often have to let individual Web page authors know that they can't understand their pages. "Sometimes people instantly go and fix it, and sometimes people don't care." Blind users say they want basic instruction on how to navigate the Web and get what they want. They do not need long descriptions that are intended to help them see pictures or other graphics. "Don't try to tell me how wonderful the Mona Lisa is," Mr. Wunder said. "You can't do that, but you can tell me how to get the picture and print it out for my daughter."  Carefully Designed Pages Can Make All the Difference HERE are some guidelines for making Web pages accessible, as offered by the National Federation of the Blind. * Keep layout simple. Avoid side-by-side presentations. Unless otherwise instructed to do so, screen-access technology for the blind presents information one entire line at a time, reading across. Columnar information can be very confusing when encountered unexpectedly. * When encoding hypertext links on a Web page, include enough words in the link so that the words can stand alone. People with speech synthesizers or Braille displays can choose to read a Web page in one of two ways: reading all the text on the page, including the hypertext links, or reading only the link text. Since the latter method is often more efficient, it is helpful when the link text can stand on its own. If a blind computer user encounters a page where every link reads "click here," the page will be difficult to comprehend. Users of screen access technology can quickly review the highlighted text representing the links, so the more descriptive the link, the better. * When using an image as a hypertext link, be sure to use a separate "text" file to give a description or transcript of the image. * If an image map (ISMAP) is present on your Web page, provide an alternate means for selecting the items contained within the map, placing them directly above or below the image map. Be sure to include instructions for the user. An image map is a graphic whose different areas represent hypertext links to other documents (selectable with a mouse). Image maps cannot be used with text-only browsers. * Graphically based file formats should be used only as alternatives to ASCII files (standard, unformatted text). If documents must be provided in a specialized format, provide the equivalent text file in HTML or plain text format. * An optional email address should be provided for a user to submit required information as an alternative to using forms. Graphic   Photo: Curtis Chong of the National Federation of the Blind helps Patricia Maurer, a colleague, use voice synthesis and Braille software. (Marty Katz for The newyork Times)

title:
DOWNTIME;
On Line, Universities Link To Alumni and Their Wallets
body: COLLEGE students used to say their goodbyes at graduation and hope to catch up at five-year intervals ever after. But now colleges are offering alumni services like lifelong personal email accounts, home pages for each graduating class and regional alumni newsgroups on the Internet, making it easier than ever for former students to keep in touch -- and for college fund-raisers to find them. The alumni fund-raisers are planning to ride the information superhighway all the way to the bank. Scads of schools are using the Internet to offer graduates on-line classes, mentoring opportunities and career placement for life. Such activities fall under the rubric of "university advancement," and even colleges that do not offer such services are debating proposals to give alumni free permanent email addresses that their mail can be forwarded through, even if they change their Internet service providers. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology offers alumni on-line conferences that allow groups to have discussions over the course of several weeks. That is particularly handy in planning reunions with classmates who live all over the world. "I think it gets alums to have more M.I.T. mindshare," said Maggy Bruzelius, director of alumni network services, "and that helps us in the long term." Farrokh K. Captain, a 1967 M.I.T. graduate who lives in Karachi, Pakistan, said his university email had helped him keep in touch with classmates. "Previously, I was quite disconnected," he said via email. And Tor Jakob Ramsoy, an M.I.T. graduate and strategy consultant in Oslo, took a negotiations course offered on line to alumni last year; it featured live video conferences with 30 students in 10 nations and 6 time zones. He said he has received useful business tips through fellow alumni on the Internet and is glad to avoid international phone charges and time-zone calculations while staying in touch. Some colleges and universities offer email service to only some of their alumni. At the University of Pennsylvania, the service is offered to Wharton School and engineering graduates, but the program might be broadened in the future. "It's certainly something we all want to move toward," said Martha Z. Stachitas, director of alumni relations. An alumni email address is a virtual sheepskin hanging on the wall behind one's laptop and can carry a certain cachet. Polly Whitney, a mystery novelist from Boca Raton, Fla., who said she got 300 email messages a day from readers, relies on her Yale address to keep her from losing messages when her I.S.P. fails her (a common occurrence, she said). Further, she is moving to New Jersey, and the email account will keep her in touch during the move. Another Yale graduate, Travis Stansbury, said of the service (via email): "Given the significantly smaller number of users (compared to most I.S.P.'s), there is a greater chance of getting a 'friendly' user name . . . i.e., 'travis@aya.yale.edu' rather than 'travis756@earthlink.net' or something. Not that big of a deal, but it is a lot easier for people to remember." The only problem is that people sometimes think the owner of a university email address is still an undergraduate, users report. Harvard Business School's alumni join forums on line about acquiring capital, making the transition from entrepreneurial management to professional management, and class reunions. Reunion attendance is expected to rise as classmates keep up with one another electronically. "Last year, the fifth reunion broke attendance records by quite a margin," said Ricardo Chavira, assistant director for information technology at the Association of Yale Alumni. He said attendance had been good largely because the head of the reunion committee had used the alumni email service to publicize the event, arrange carpools and find classmates. Universities are also using computer networks to help graduates find jobs. For alumni who sign up before the end of this month, the University of Pennsylvania is offering free lifetime help with career placement through University Pronet, which has 110,000 members and is run cooperatively by 16 schools. Companies looking for employees pay to search the database of alumni, who usually spend $50 to post their resumes on line. All this computer-based contact will probably strengthen old school ties and loosen alumni purse strings, fund-raisers say. "It keeps people connected to the university, and that's what fund-raising is all about, keeping people connected who want to contribute," said Mary Gresch, a fund-raising official at Washington State University in Pullman. Soon, alumni will be able to donate on line, a service already available at other universities. Colleges are investing in staff and hardware with such hopes in mind. For Yale's on-line alumni services, the university employs two people full time and has spent about $100,000 on extra computers, servers and software. Wake Forest University, in Winston-Salem, N.C., employs 10 people, not counting support staff, for a similar program that serves people with university ties. "It takes people from the time they pay their deposit and become students all the way through their college experience, through life as an alum, till death do we part -- it's seamless," said Bob Mills, associate vice president for fund raising and communications at Wake Forest. "Nothing we've ever done has been able to bring people closer to the university than this technology," said Mr. Mills, who has worked with alumni for 26 years. "It has personalized and extended our communications. "Keeping in touch with Wake Forest people who mean something to them is really what warms their hearts," he said. "If they feel fulfilled in that way, then the money follows." ON-LINE services for alumni can take many forms. The University of Missouri at Columbia schedules chat-room events for alumni, including discussions with the university chancellor, according to CASE Currents, a trade publication for the Council for Advancement and Support of Education. @gocougs.wsu.edu to pay homage to the cougar mascot. Last fall, the Coug-gear section of the alumni Web site opened two days before the football team made it to the Rose Bowl. Income from the site, projected at $10,000 in its first year, jumped to $60,000 in the first six weeks, Ms. Gresch said. Of the 12,000 alumni requests that were sent in for a chance at tickets to the big game, 8,000 came through the Internet. "We think all of it relates to fund-raising," she said.
