title:
FUNDAMENTALS;
Finding Hidden Senders in All That email Gobbledygook
body: BY now, most of America has enough experience with electronic mail to realize that it is often not what it seems. Spoofs and pranks are easy to pull off. Most email programs make it as easy to claim a false name as it is to write a false return address on a paper envelope. Still, the system has some protections against fraud, developed precisely because people sending junk email have abused the system and used fake addresses to avoid being tracked down. These protections make it possible for anyone to trace an email and find out whether it is likely to be false. This approach is not guaranteed because there are many more sophisticated approaches to faking email, but it does expose some of the simpler schemes. In other words, if your friends are ribbing you, you can find out. If it is serious spam, see the User's Guide column below. The accompanying illustration includes a message from monica@whitehouse.gov that appeared in my email box. It was not really sent by anyone named Monica or anyone at the White House. In fact, I made it up and then proceeded to route it through several computers that I own just to give it a history that could be parsed. The best place to start explaining how to read not the email itself but the routing information that accompanies it is to look at how computers exchange pieces of email. Everywhere on the Internet wheremail is sent or received by any computer and any software, there is a set of instructions that tells computers what to do when mail arrives. That process for moving mail through the Internet goes by the name Standard Mail Transfer Protocol. The S.M.T.P. is naive and trusting. The receiving computer asks a few questions (like "Who is the message to?" and "Who is the message from?") and believes whatever it is told. If the sending computer says that the message is from monica@whitehouse.gov, the receiving computer dutifully takes this on faith. I use Eudora to send and receive email, and it, like all other email programs, uses S.M.T.P. My version of the program lets me type in whatever I want on the From line. Most versions of Netscape and Internet Explorer, and some Eudora versions, let the user do the same thing by changing some settings. In this case, I could have easily typed elvis@cool.com just for fun. While the email system is trusting, on the surface, it does keep some records that can reveal fraud or deceit. The header of a message contains many details about the route taken by a message. Many email programs do not show this header because it is virtually unreadable to most people and it is rarely important to anyone. Eudora users can expose the headers by clicking on the Blah Blah Blah icon at the top of an opened message. Microsoft Access users, on the other hand, must dig deeper and look in their menus for the Property of a message. Each email program is different. Once you get to the header, examining it reveals the path that the message has taken. The header looks the way it does because each computer that handles the message has added a line to the top of the message. Often, several computers have handled a message. The message ostensibly from Monica had five stops. It began with me, of course, sitting at my computer -- *1 newray.digex.net -- writing it on my Eudora program and sending it off to myself at pcw@flyzone.com. The next stop was the computer that handles mail at my Internet Service Provider, *2 pony-2.mail.digex.net. That machine passed the message to a second computer in my office: *3 flyzone.com. I have that computer programmed to take all the email it gets for pcw@flyzone.com and forward it to another address of mine: pcw@access.digex.net. To do that, the flyzone computer sent themail back to *4 pony-2.mail.digex.net for a second stop. That machine finally sent the message to me, at the computer at which I composed it. There is no *5 in the message because the header does not include the final hop. The easiest way to reveal that this message is a fake is to compare the From line with the first Received line. The From line says that the message is from someone at whitehouse.gov, but the Received line says the message began at some machine with the name newray.digex.net. While it is possible that someone at the real White House might have a machine with this weird name, it is highly unlikely. That machine, newray.digex.net, is the name of the first computer on my desk. The number 199.125.128.5 is the I.P. (Internet Protocol) address of that machine. There is a one-to-one correspondence between I.P. addresses and computers connected to the Internet. Some names, like www.nytimes.com, actually refer to multiple machines because one machine is not large enough to handle the traffic. If the received line said the message had come from a machine like westwing.whitehouse.gov, then it might be accurate. Of course, it might just be a better fake. It could be coming from someone inside the White House or even someone with access to the network. Just getting a computer name isn't necessarily much help. Machine names are often assigned at random as people dial into pools of modems. Sometimes the I.S.P. maintains records that in concert with phone records could identify someone, but these are often incomplete. There are solutions on the horizon. Good cryptography can scramble the message so only the right person can read it and can also create digital versions of signatures that are very difficult to fake. But cryptography runs into a lot of political resistance because of the question of whether it would block authorized police surveillance. For now, most people should put only a moderate amount of trust in the email system. Most messages are not faked, and the faked ones usually stick out. Analyzing the header will reveal the simplest fakes. For instance, one from robots asking you to report to a human-slave-processing center is almost certainly a fake. If only the stories from Washington were so obvious. Graphic   Photos/Chart: "The Bits And Pieces" Beyond the familiar message, the jumble of letters and numbers at the top of an email, especially one that has been passed from one computer to another, are an indecipherable code. Here is a brief explanation of some email shorthand. The smaller email examples listed below were culled from this fake message, too.  S.M.T.P. is the standard way of moving email through the Internet.  Blah, Blah, Blah icon reveals the path of a message.  The names in the From and Received: from lines match if the email is legitimate.  I.P. addresses that match indicate email from the same machine.  The -0500 is the difference from Greenwich Mean Time.  Message-Id, which includes the I.P. address corresponding to the sender's computer, is a unique number created to track messages.  The message.

title: Guess Who's Going On Line
body: THE email was brief, but for the loose group of Webheads who subscribe to a list where it was posted recently, no further explanation was required. They could identify. To: obvious@list.sirius.com From: David Hudson Subject: The Dawn of a New Age My parents came on line today. I'm still trying to absorb this. Mr. Hudson's message touched off a chorus of generational commiseration on the Obvious List, where several dozen 20- and 30-somethings typically share observations about the wide world of Web technology and culture. Michael Sippey, for instance, reported that his father had recently signed up for America Online, the leading Internet service provider: "He still has a tendency to call it 'Americans Online,' " wrote Mr. Sippey, a 28-year-old business school student at the University of California at Berkeley. "Even though he sends a good amount of email, tracks his investments on line and his primary source of news is the Reuters feed on Yahoo." Beyond a certain studied horror at this latest intrusion by bumbling elders, however, such accounts signal a demographic shift that may herald one of the Internet's more provocative effects yet on social relations. Whether the Gen-X'ers are ready or not, people middle-aged and even older are now hoisting themselves on line in droves. As a result, the Internet, often touted for its capacity to bring strangers together, is increasingly becoming a conduit for communication among the closest of kin. The newfound infatuation with email among the more mature is prodding scattered families to reconvene in cyberspace, where they can once again exchange the banalities, support and incessant guilt trips at which blood relations so excel. And the Net's proven propensity for lowering inhibitions and sanctioning intimacy seems to take on a particular power when the correspondents have had whole childhoods to repress. "I communicate with my dad now more than I ever have in my whole life," said Cynthia Joyce, 28, of San Francisco, who recently set up an Internet account for her parents in Charlotte, N.C.. "He's not the type to emote much. He hated talking on the phone, and he still does. But he's much more comfortable expressing himself in writing. This has opened up a whole dialogue between us." It is not that older people have never been on line before. Grown-up scientists and unitedstates military employees were the first to populate cyberspace, in the late 1960's and early 70's, quickly followed by geeks of all ages. But an apparent genetic predisposition of youth to grasp digital technology, combined with the widespread distribution of free email accounts to students by universities, beginning in the late 1980's, has led to a distinct sense that the kids have the run of the place. Now comes the next big shift. Since 1994, surveys have shown an upward trend in the percentage of Internet users in the unitedstates who are at least 50 years old, to 16 percent in 1997 from 13 percent in 1994. The average age of all users is 38, below the national average of 44, according to "State of the Net," by Peter C. Clemente (McGraw-Hill, 1997), but that number is rising. A survey in December 1997 by Cyber Dialogue, a market research firm in newyork, found an even larger increase in the number of people 50 or older on line. Cyber Dialogue gauges the total number of adult Americans on the Net at around 40 million. Like those who have ventured on line before them, the middle-aged are using the technology to make purchases and proffer their opinions on pressing social questions like whether to bomb Iraq or to watch "Ally McBeal." They compare notes and commune with their peers in on-line discussions devoted to grandchildren, retirement plans and other issues of import to people at their stage in life. BUT as parents, often with grown children and living parents of their own, they have seized on the Internet not only to form such virtual communities but also to knit together very real, if sometimes fraying, family ties. "I can't tell you how much I've learned about my son that I never knew," said Morris Powazek, a 50-year-old psychologist in Los Angeles who often exchanges several email notes a day with his son, Derek, in San Francisco since he bought his Apple Macintosh a year ago. ("Derek said he wouldn't speak to me if I got a PC.") It was on Derek's Web site (www.fray.com), for example, that the senior Powazek learned how his son stole his first cigarette from him when he was 15 years old. "I told him, 'Hey, you know the first time I smoked a cigarette, I stole it from my father, just like you," Mr. Powazek said. "We talk about very personal, emotional things in email. When I call him, I just get his answering machine." Nan Aitel-Thompson, 51, credits email with saving her relationship with her daughter, Talibah Thompson, a student at Cornell University who stopped speaking to her soon after Talibah's father died of cancer a few years ago. "She felt that if I loved him more, he wouldn't have died," said Ms. Aitel-Thompson, who took comfort from on-line discussion groups of single parents. For her part, Talibah says she moved out of the house after her mother entered her locked room and read her diary. But slowly, through email, they began to sort things out. "I had no intent of talking to her, really -- it was just business stuff," said Talibah, 20. "We still can't talk face to face very well, but we can talk over email. I felt like I was being listened to more over email, and I think it made me put my thoughts in words before I said them. There's that second before you hit Send where you can always delete." Talibah's grandparents, Grace and Moe Aitel, said they stayed in touch with all their children and grandchildren over the Internet. So important is email communication to the Aitel family that one of Ms. Aitel-Thompson's sisters prints out the weekly correspondence and sends it by express mail to her brother, a dairy farmer in Vermont, the one remaining off-line sibling. Whether this new mechanism for family intimacy has some sort of therapeutic effect on those who take advantage of it is unclear. But at a time when technology often seems to be straining traditional family relations, sending children off to various corners of the world in pursuit of careers and requiring them to build their own social ties, the global computer network, icon of the fragmented post-modern age, is being pressed into service reinforcing age-old kinship networks. It almost seems instinctual. For even as some of them express dismay about the fogeys' intrusion into their on-line hangout, many children are conspiring to get Internet accounts for their parents. And while little data is available on how many families stay in touch on line, a reporter asking sociologists and psychologists for such information was invariably plied with personal anecdotes. "The real key was when my parents finally got the email," mused Daniel T. Lichter, 44, director of population research at Pennsylvania State University, whose daily family correspondence spans three generations and eight states. "Once they got it, they networked everybody in. Parents are the hub. Even if they're less computer literate, they're still the focal point." One advantage of email over the telephone is the ability to send copies to the entire extended family with a few keystrokes. "It creates a cohesion that you wouldn't get by making isolated telephone calls," said Mr. Lichter, who grew up in Mitchell, S.D., with 10 siblings, all of whom followed his father's recent surgery via his mother's Internet updates. THOUSANDS of family home pages festoon the Web. Many babies now get their own sites in lieu of birth announcements, often mere hours after they are born. With a password provided by their daughter, the grandparents of a newborn named T. J. Herring have been viewing updated pictures of him since his delivery in a San Francisco hospital room earlier this month. Great-Aunt Barb from St. Louis and Uncle Charles from Alexandria, Va., among others, have weighed in with congratulations and advice in the on-line guest book. "I think the reason people are doing so much of this fishing around for relatives and lost connections is that there's a felt need, a loneliness, a feeling that 'there must be a community of people who care about me in other than a passing way,' " said Armond Aserinsky, a family psychologist in North Wales, Pa. "And the family automatically has been vetted. There's a safety in that.' " Still, virtual family life is not without its actual traumas. Many parents go on line in the first place only because their children drag them -- a precipitous inversion of authority making this particular rite of passage about as tension-free as the average bar mitzvah. And then there is the ongoing melodrama of technical support. In a recent column in the Web magazine Salon, Ms. Joyce, who helped her parents go on line, compiled a list of suggestions based on her experience, including: "Do teach one parent at a time -- it'll be easier for all of you" and "When your mother refers to the 'typewriter' when what she really means is 'keyboard,' go with it. Don't act like you don't know what she's talking about -- it didn't work when you were 12, and it won't work now." Many of the young say parents tend not to grasp the finer points of email etiquette. "Mom sends these long messages that detail the entire lineage and projected progeny of the entirety of eastern and midcoast Maine, recent family events, long-term weather forecasts, reports on my dog's health and sometimes a schedule of her week or upcoming weekend," complained Steven Champeon, 27, a Web site designer in Raleigh, N.C., whose typical email with friends and business associates is limited to a few paragraphs at most. The sins of his mother, Elizabeth, include using the same subject line header, "Family Matters," over and over again and forwarding personal email that referred in unflattering terms to her ex-husband's branch of the family to other family members, including Steven, who cringed. ("Yes, Steven got real mad at me about that," Mrs. Champeon recalled. "I never did it again.") FOR those who have designed their own home pages in the self-revelatory spirit of much of the Web, a parental audience can be something of a dilemma. Consider Drue Miller, 31, whose confessions on line include a picture of herself on a boyfriend's lap with her skirt hiked up to show a lizard tattoo her parents did not know she had. She set up a Web page for her father after he broke the Internet barrier (www.drue.com/coredump/dad.html). The page was a tongue-in-cheek way to acknowledge her own anxiety. "Hi Dad! Welcome to the Internet!" she said with enthusiasm, providing hypertext links to the Federal budget and mutual fund reports rather than to her own home page. "No, the car is fine. Yes, I'm changing the oil regularly. Yes, I'm using my Club. . . . Hey, look -- here's a photo of us! Isn't digital technology neat?" Only on her separate Web page did Ms. Miller drop her guard. "I mean, he doesn't even know I have a motorcycle -- do I want him to know that I rode it down Market Street with 999 other women during the Pride Parade?" (www.drue.com/writings/ culture.html) As for Mr. Hudson, 38, who lives in Berlin, he is still coping with what is now a regular barrage of email from his parents in Dallas. As he reported to the Obvious List: "I was egging them on, O.K., click AOL, click MSN, click something, and let's get going. You're going to love it. We can talk endlessly for pennies, and the whole spiel I'd been giving them forever. Then the actual email. That's when it hit me. They're heeere." Graphic   Photo. (Peter Zeray for The newyork Times)(pg. G1)  Charts: "As the Older Log On . . ." With an estimated 40 million American adults now on line, the percentage who are 50 or older is growing -- reported at 15 percent or more last year.  ". . . The Younger Move Over" And the percentage of on-line adults who are 18 to 29 years old is a shrinking slice of a growing pie -- reported at 30 percent last year, down from 42 percent in 1994. (Sources: Cyber Dialogue; "State of the Net" by Peter C. Clemente) (pg. G1)  Chart/Photos: "Family Connections" Until recently, the Internet was a home away from inquisitive parents for many 20-somethings like Steven Champeon, below, who must now contend with Mom and Dad venturing on line to find out what their offspring are up to. On the other hand, computer scientists the age of Mr. Champeon's parents were sending data (and bad jokes) to one another on the Arpanet before there was an Internet -- before there was a Steven Champeon, in fact. Steven Crocker, right, was one of these early Internet explorers and has since brought both younger and older family members on line. Here are Mr. Champeon's and Mr. Crocker's on-line family trees.  ON LINE 1991 STEVEN CHAMPEON, 27 First hooked up to the Internet in 1991 when he was a student at Syracuse University. Since then, he has moved to Raleigh, N.C., and works for a company called Hesketh.com building large Web sites.  ON LINE 1996 LIZ CHAMPEON, 53 Steve's mother, Liz, persuaded her boss to get an America Online account at the office. The next year, she signed up for one at home, in Orrington, Me. Now she exchanges email with her family several times a week.  ON LINE 1997 SUSAN HOWARD, 47 Liz's youngest sister, who lives in Florida, recently got an email account through her job.  ON LINE 1997 PEGGY NEAL, 50 Liz's other sister, who lives in Kenne- bunkport, Me., keeps up on family happenings through email.  ON LINE 1969 STEVE CROCKER, 53 Chief technology officer at Cybercash in Reston, Va. Mr. Crocker helped set up U.C.L.A.'s first connection for the Arpanet, the Internet's predecessor, so he could trade data with researchers at universities. These days, he uses email to keep in touch with his family.  ON LINE 1993 ANDREW CROCKER, 13 He got his own email account through his father, Steve, about three years ago. He taught himself how to build a Web site during spring break last year. The site features sounds he has collected from movies like Star Wars.  ON LINE 1995 NORMAN CROCKER, 79 Steve's father, Norman, had been using an an- cient I.B.M. PC in his job as an insurance broker. On his birthday about two and a half years ago, Steve and his brother, David, bought him a machine with Windows 95 software. Norman then got an account at a Los Angeles Internet service provider and now keeps his sons abreast of his travels through email. (pg. G7)  Graph: "The Internet Matures" As the on-line population starts to reflect a broader cross section of society, the Internet crowd is growing older. Graph tracks percentage of Internet users age 18 to 29 and those 30+, from 1994 through 1997. It also shows the average age of Internet users during each year. (Source: Find/S.V.P. via The State of the Net,by Peter Clemente McGraw-Hill, 1997 )(pg. G7)

title: Guess Who Was There First
body: FOR nearly two decades, the Internet was mainly the province of computer scientists, physicists, biologists and other researchers at a few dozen universities around the country. By all rights, these first settlers should be incensed at the influx of 20- and 30-somethings. They should look in horror upon the parvenus and interlopers who have moved in and made themselves at home. But the Internet's inventors and earliest users, now in their middle and late years and still going strong on the Net, have for the most part greeted the influx of the rest of civilization with surprising magnanimity. Many of them are more amused than offended by the proprietary claims of the young fry. "It's like teen-agers who think they invented sex," said Steve Crocker, 53, chief technology officer of Cybercash, a Reston, Va., firm that builds payment systems for the Internet. "They have no clue that some parents actually understand all this." Nearly 30 years ago, as a graduate student, Dr. Crocker worked on setting up U.C.L.A.'s first connection for the Arpanet, the Internet's predecessor. Begun in 1969 as an experiment in computer networking financed by the Pentagon's Advanced Research Projects Agency, the Arpanet connected just a handful of research universities and Government sites. Well into the 1980's, to be on the growing Net was to be among an elite. The Net was a private playground -- and an expensive one. Only those institutions with agency financing could join the club, and maintaining a university's annual connection cost upward of $100,000. Another hurdle was technical. Navigating one's way around the Net in the early days required more than a rudimentary command of Tenex, the operating system of choice for serious programmers. Back then, people logged on by using acoustic couplers attached to telephone receivers and teletype terminals connected to large mainframes -- the network's "host" computers. Words were not displayed on monitors; they were spewed out on teletype printers. Computer screens were a later innovation. The scientists used the Net mostly to collaborate on research into computer networks. But they also used it to socialize, plan parties and carry on flirtations. When the Arpanet's population was just a few thousand, everyone knew, or knew of, everyone else. Of course, that cozy network of old has long been replaced by something at once more sophisticated and more unwieldy. Inexpensive, easy-to-use personal computers, coupled with the point-and-click interface of the Web, made a ubiquitous Internet possible. By 1995, America Online disks were showing up in airline snack boxes. THE old guard, by and large, is resigned to the changes. "This happens to all resorts," said Brian Reid, a computer scientist with the Digital Equipment Corporation in Palo Alto, Calif. "It happened to Fire Island, and it happened to Santa Barbara," he said. "The Net is no different from a beach or anything else that gets discovered." Mr. Reid, 48, wandered onto the Arpanet for the first time in 1972. He said he had first noticed the intrusion on his world in the early 1990's, when he began to see email addresses ending in aol.com. Still, Mr. Reid said, the population explosion has had little real effect on him. "The great thing about the Net," he said, "is I don't have to pay any attention to any part of it that I don't want to." Mr. Reid and others point out that complaining about the growth of the Net would be like the Wright brothers objecting to the masses' flocking to the skies. Dr. Peter Salus, 59, an author and consultant in Boston who has been on the Net since 1974, agrees with Mr. Reid. "It was a wondrous thing when it was just people in computer science departments, or in biology at Columbia," he said. "But I really believe in the democracy of it." These democrats reared their children as good Net citizens and set their parents up with Internet accounts when America Online was still a glimmer in its founders' eyes. It was way back in 1982 that Mr. Reid got his mother, Betty, a high-school teacher in Connecticut, connected to the Arpanet. She used a Zenith Z19 terminal with a 1,200-baud modem. Her address then: breid@choate. It was not until 1984 that the Net had grown to the point where extensions to addresses became necessary -- .com for commercial organizations, for example, or .edu for educational institutions -- to make sure that the networked world would not quickly run out of the words, called domain names, that could be used as addresses. In 1984, Mrs. Reid started using breid@choate.edu. The popularity of the Internet has made minor celebrities out of some of the pioneers who would otherwise have spent their professional lives in relative obscurity. "I always thought the Net was rather dull in the old days," said David Farber, 64, a telecommunications professor at the University of Pennsylvania who has been on the Net since 1971, when he was a young computer scientist at the University of California at Irvine. Professor Farber is now such a fixture of the wired world that he has even been the subject of a People magazine profile. "People sat around talking about technical things," he said. "Now they talk about everything." Professor Farber's two children, now in their 20's, have been on line since they were old enough to reach a keyboard. The old-timers like to cite Metcalfe's Law, named for their contemporary Robert Metcalfe, the co-inventor of Ethernet, a popular technology used for creating office networks of PC's. The law holds that the value of networks grows as more people use them. "Every influx of newcomers increases everyone's possibilities on line," said John Quarterman, the 43-year-old president of Matrix Information and Directory Services, an Internet research firm in Austin, Tex. He began using the Arpanet before any of his four employees were born. Dr. Crocker is another believer in Metcalfe's Law. "Now you have to put up with get-rich-quick schemes, junk mail and all the hassles that come with growth," he said. "But at the same time, you get unbelievable benefits." Like several of the other pioneers, Dr. Metcalfe has become wealthy from his invention; he was traveling but weighed in via email from London. He had this to say about the Internet's earliest users: "I think we should hold a BIG PARTY. Invite the Internet Intelligentsia -- those who built the Internet, 1969-1993. "At the party, we should thank them profusely. And celebrate wildly. Give medals. Take videos. Do TV interviews. "Then we should ask the Internetgentsia to GO HOME. The Internet has outgrown them." NOT everyone agrees. Paul Ginsparg, a physicist at the Los Alamos National Laboratory who runs a Web site for the distribution of scientific manuscripts, has been on the Net since 1973, his freshman year of college. Dr. Ginsparg said that while he had no objection to letting the general population use electronic resources, he believed that high-level academic communication should take place in a restricted environment. "Jeffersonian democracy and all that is well and good, but we also need the electronic analog of ivory towers and to keep them clean of graffiti," Dr. Ginsparg said. "In other words, the problem with the global village is all the global village idiots." For those people who do believe that they need a Net of their own, there is always Internet 2, a plan to add high-speed connections to the Internet. More than 100 universities are working on the next-generation Internet as an alternative to today's congested and outdated network. The idea behind Internet 2 is to support cutting-edge research into new technologies -- the reason the first Internet started three decades ago. title:
Q & A;
Keeping Bookmarks In a Place That's Safe
body: Q. How can I permanently save the bookmarks that I use with my Netscape browser? I want to back them up so the site-address part (and not just the title of the site) is retained if they get corrupted. I have been a victim of corrupted bookmarks too often. A. The Bookmarks feature, offered by most Web browsers -- it is called Favorites in Microsoft Internet Explorer -- allows a user to slap the electronic equivalent of a Post-it note on a Web page. It allows the program to remember and save the exact address of the page and to provide a shortcut back to the site when you wish to return. To make a backup, open your Netscape browser and open your Bookmarks file, under Window on the menu bar. If you use Explorer, select Open Favorites from the Favorites menu. Then, with that file up, go to the File menu and select the Save As option. Give the new file a name and save it as an HTML document, either in another folder on your hard drive or on a floppy disk. That's your backup file. To keep the backup file up to date, repeat the process each time you have added sites that you want to keep. Netscape automatically saves your bookmarks into a file called bookmarks.htm -- or, if you are using a Macintosh, bookmarks.html -- in the Netscape program folder on your computer. Internet Explorer does the same with its favorites.htm document. If this Bookmarks file becomes corrupted in a crash or some other sort of system error, the browser may either freeze when it is opened or when you try to go anywhere on the Web. Removing the Bookmarks file and replacing it with the copy that you have made as a backup will save your sanity, time and most likely, the delicate ears of those around you. And remember to make a copy of the new file.  Q. What is the difference, if any, between recordable CD's and rewritable CD's?  A. The quick answer is that a recordable CD (known in the tech trade as a CD-R) can be written to -- meaning recorded on -- only once, while a rewritable CD (CD-RW) can be erased and written to repeatedly. That makes them seem much like floppy disks, except that a CD-RW can hold about 650 megabytes of data, about 250,000 pages of text. CD-R's can store the same amount of material. At about $5, blank CD-R's are much cheaper than their CD-RW cousins, which cost about $30. The drives that can produce CD-RW media are also more expensive than those that just create CD-R's, but many CD-RW drives are quite versatile, as they can write to both CD-RW and CD-R discs and play CD-ROM's.   J. title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Net's a Natural for Fantasy Baseball
body: FOR baseball fans, spring is a season of seduction. The siren song of off-season trades and Grapefruit League statistics stirs irresistible hope for championship glory. And then there's the bandwidth drain. As ball parks fill up for the opening of the Major League Baseball season on Tuesday, a virtual sellout crowd of hundreds of thousands will begin to track player statistics on the Web. For the last month, fans have been using Web-based baseball simulations to play virtual ball games that pit would-be general managers against one another in leagues where the major league stats are real, the money is phony, and the real trophy is bragging rights around the water cooler (or these days, on the corporate intranet). On Tuesday, the flag drops. Statistics will begin to flood the databases of Web sites like ESPN's Sports Zone (espn.com), CBS Sportsline (sports line.com) and the free and increasingly popular Small World Sports (baseball.smallworld.com). Complex corporate computer networks and high-speed Net connections will be used to track the progress of teams like Jimbo's Bombers and the Amazin' Jakes as executives sweat the decision to drop $11 million in funny money on Mark McGwire while leaving the bullpen to the likes of Turk Wendell. Among fantasy sports players, Small World -- a newyork company founded by a trio of enthusiasts in their living room four years ago -- has developed something of a cult following. While the ESPN and Sportsline games are high-end on-line versions of the popular Rotisserie-style fantasy leagues and cost $19.95 per team to play, Small World is free and uses a stock market system for assigning player values and a point system to reward home runs, wins, saves and the like. The mode of play is simple and players can draft a full team in about 30 minutes. The game has seen a huge increase is users. Last year, 26,000 players ran teams. This year, 150,000 Small World managers will check their stats on Opening Day. (Licensed versions of the game are also available at Cox New Media's Fastball.com, CNNSi.com and Time Warner's Pathfinder.com). Small World followers are so devoted that a group of them met at Yankee Stadium for a real game last season. "Believe it or not, it helps you not to be myopic about baseball," said one of the Stadium day-trippers, Colin Samuel, a 23-year-old engineering graduate student from Manhattan who describes himself as a Red Sox fan. Few things move smoothly from the real world to cyberspace, but fantasy gaming is a notable success. A recent survey by Cyber Dialogue, a research firm, showed that 34 percent of adults who use the Net regularly played some type of game on line. Web sites now use the real-world results of professional baseball, basketball, football, hockey and golf to generate fantasy results for Mitty-esque "owners" who draft and trade players, using digital funny money to pay their salaries. Of course, Rotisserie-type leagues have been popular among hard-core sports fans for many years. But it seems that the Web has completed the evolution of card games like Strat-o-matic Baseball and in-person Rotisserie drafting contests, allowing more fans than ever the joys and heartbreak of fantasy team ownership. The on-line games solve two major problems that kept more casual fans away: they keep stats and allow players access from anywhere. Those who scoff at the notion that a Web baseball game might be a drain on corporate productivity should consider the case of Dave Hall. A successful investment portfolio manager from West Hartford, Conn., he drafted his first Small World team on the Web last season. Mr. Hall, 44, quit his job to follow fantasy sports full time, founded a Web site for Web gamers and may pursue his own gaming company. "I realized," he said, "that I was spending more time thinking about my next baseball strategy than my next investment strategy." title: Show Me the Mummy! Internet Offers a Home to Archeology
body: THE archeologist Heinrich Schliemann used Homer as his guide when he excavated Troy, and he published his findings in books. When Howard Carter unearthed the tomb of Tutankhamen in 1922, the world learned of his discovery through a spectacular scoop by The Times of London in a dispatch sent "by runner from the Valley of the Kings." The paleontologist Richard E. Leakey drew widespread attention to humankind's African origins with a series of popular television documentaries. Runners are no longer needed to carry the latest news from the Valley of the Kings. Archeologists are turning to the Internet to announce their finds and findings, with many of their postings geared more toward the generalist than the specialist. Journal articles follow later for colleagues and the historical record. So with only a modicum of digging, the armchair archeologist can uncover a wealth of archeological sites. Web sites, that is. A few clicks of the mouse will transport a Web surfer to the Valley of the Kings, the great necropolis on the west bank of the Nile where archeologists are busy excavating one of the largest tombs ever found in Egypt. They are combing through what they call Tomb Five, believed to be the tomb of the many sons of Ramses II, who dominated the known world in the 13th century B.C. and, in his spare time, fathered more than a hundred children. Visitors to the Theban Mapping Project's Web site (www.kv5.com) can, with the aid of a plug-in or two, watch that excavation through a montage of color photographs. One by one the layers are peeled away on screen: first, discolored reddish dirt, which suggests the presence of mummified tissue to the practiced eye; 20 centimeters lower, the mummified thigh bone of a calf, which was once a prized food offering; below that, three skulls, some with vertebrae still attached, and beneath them, a fully articulated skeleton lying amid bits of wrapping and burned fragments of wood. Thanks to the nature of interactive sites, the Web surfer can watch these skeletons unearthed in slow motion or at double speed or, should the desire strike, go backward to bury the bones all over again. Archeological Web sites are proliferating and come from all corners of the world. You can visit a dig of Mayan ruins in Belize (alishaw.sscf.ucsb.edu/ford), check out the excavation of a Maltese tomb from 2500 B.C. and see computer renderings of what it might have looked like (www.bris.ac.uk/ Depts/Archaeology/html/research/ comvis/insite.htm) and (www.apva.org) learn about the excavation of Jamestown, Va. Field workers no longer have to wait as their manuscripts languish on the shelves of understaffed, underfinanced university presses. They can go on line almost instantly. Scholarly publishing and peer review can come later. More immediately, the Web connects archeologists to their far-flung colleagues (for consultation, or information on where to buy a centimeter scale or a good hieroglyphic pattern for needlework). But many sites are aimed at the general public, for education and entertainment and sometimes a little fund-raising. Many find the medium uniquely suited to the message. "One of the wonderful things about the electronic media is the pace at which you can continue to change and update things," said Angela M. H. Schuster, an associate editor at Archaeology, the publication of the Archaeological Institute of America. "One fragment or one glyph can suddenly readjust your entire understanding of a site. The Web allows you to revise very quickly." Archaeology magazine now has its own Web site (www.he.net/archaeol), and its editors have compiled a useful directory of favorite sites (www.he.net/archaeol/ wwwarky/wwwarky.html). Its parent organization, the Archaeological Institute of America, put its own directory of favorite sites on the Web this month, graded by appropriate audience (csaws.brynmawr. edu:443/web2/AIAWebSites.html). Nigel Strudwick, an Egyptologist at the University of Cambridge, set up Egyptology Resources (www.newton.cam.ac.uk/egypt), one of the first such Web pages, in 1994. "I was thinking of, to use a posh English term, the educated lay public," Dr. Strudwick said. "Egyptologists are very bad about publicizing their work, and it is difficult to interest the media except in the most spectacular finds. Books are expensive -- 120 pounds sterling for a two-volume set with a lot of black-and-white photos and a few color plates -- and reach a small audience." Dr. Strudwick's site takes an in-depth look at his excavation of the tomb of Senneferi in Luxor. There are Quick Time Virtual Reality panoramas that place visitors in the shrine of the tomb, enabling them to examine the hieroglyphics and paintings on the walls ("My apologies for the various items of expedition equipment visible in the photographs"), a Coffins page and some very detailed explanations of how excavations are done, from digging techniques to staffing rotations to the forms that must be filled out for each artifact recovered. BACK in Thebes, the mapping project maintains a mixture of useful and enjoyable information on its site: timelines of 3,500 years of Egyptian dynasties, 365-degree color panoramas taken from various spots in the Valley of the Kings, the names and hieroglyphics of the known sons of Ramses II, blueprint-like plans of the tombs and pictures and biographies of the major players on the dig. The director of the mapping project and dig, Kent R. Weeks of the American University in Cairo, keeps Web visitors apprised of the latest developments through occasional progress reports. His letter of March 15 tells of sailing the Nile from Aswan to Abu Simbel to photograph scenes of Ramses II and his sons on the walls of temples, of the engineering problems involved in shoring up the walls of the ancient tomb to guard against collapse and, most important, the news that he and his colleagues have identified 108 chambers and corridors in the tomb so far and expect to find a total of 150. At its best, the sites give visitors an Indiana Jones, you-are-there sense. "On some walls, traces of finely carved raised relief scenes can still be seen," Dr. Weeks wrote. "In many chambers, pieces of carved limestone or painted plaster lie on the floor where they fell after floodborne debris knocked them from the walls." Graphic   Photo: The Theban Mapping Project's site allows viewers to watch the excavation of skeletons in slow motion, double speed or reverse.

title:
Taking In the Sites;
Finding Business Ethics on and About the Internet
body: The World Wide Web is not exactly a haven for good business ethics. It can be a lawless place filled with unscrupulous operators pushing get-rich-quick schemes and other scams. Naturally, those who study business ethics worry about the Web. "Every possible abuse of integrity and decency takes place on the Web," said Laura Pincus Hartman, director of the Institute for Business and Professional Ethics at DePaul University in Chicago. Randy Pennington, an ethics consultant based in Dallas, said there was "a sense that moral and ethical values are not important" on the Web. But that does not surprise him. "There is no standardization in technology on the Web, so why do we expect standardization in behavior?" he said. Mr. Pennington said that to avoid an attempt at "regulation of ethical behavior in the future, the on-line community must regulate itself." "This country has a history of regulating those industries that do not control themselves," he added. Despite the global nature of the Web, he sees the possibility of Government intervention. The Netcheck Commerce Bureau is one attempt at self-regulation. The agency, which has 700 corporate members in about 80 countries, maintains a list of companies involved in electronic commerce. Visitors to Netcheck's site can register consumer complaints about anything from unsolicited email to copyright disputes. There is even a place to compliment a company. The site's philosophy is that "public pressure is the only real deterrent in this new frontier." The Web is also a great place to learn about and research the issues of business ethics, both within the Internet and beyond. An excellent starting place is the site of the institute at DePaul that Ms. Hartman heads. The site provides an introduction to business ethics but goes well beyond that. It is home to the Online Journal of Ethics and has comprehensive links to other sites that deal with the topic. The business of domain names and how they are registered involves some of the worst breaches of ethics on the Internet. Corporations and nonprofit groups are being forced to spend a lot of time, money and energy to fight piracy of high-profile .com and .org addresses. Even in the world of business ethics, names can be less than clear. For example, Business-ethics.org is the home of the International Business Ethics Institute, and Businessethics.org belongs to the Council for Ethics in Economics. The institute, which has a truly global background, has a site that contains a sparse brochure. The council -- which is trying to "strengthen the ethical fabric of business and economic life" -- has a more substantial site with articles from the quarterly publication Ethics in Economics, and texts of speeches on ethics organized by the institute, based in Columbus, Ohio. The Ethics Resource Center is a leading nonprofit ethics consultancy. The site offers information about the center's work with large corporations in developing ethics programs. The Center for Business Ethics, at Bentley College in Waltham, Mass., is home to the Ethics Officer Association. This group represents the executives that help police many of the nation's large corporations. Few industries have been mired in as many questions about ethics, both real and perceived, as the military industry. One attempt to address its problems is the Defense Industry Initiative on Business Ethics and Conduct, a group of large military contractors, which has an in-depth site about the organization and aspects of Government contracting. Much of the information is applicable to other industries. Unlike many other sites, the Better Business Bureau site, which is run by the Council of Better Business Bureaus, is aimed at consumers in addition to the corporate world. It provides tips on various consumer frauds. It also has a guide to "establishing an ethical business" and a detailed code of advertising that explains common abuses and misleading claims. Establishing an ethics code is an important step for any company or industry, and a growing number of sites carry such codes. The DePaul site has compiled a list of direct links to a variety of codes, including Johnson & Johnson, Northern Telecom and the National Association of the Remodeling Industry. Also included is the code of ethics of the International Ethical Business Registry, a Canadian organization that promotes ethics codes. Among the aims of the registry: donating at least 10 percent of its gross income "toward the betterment of mankind." Its site has pointers about setting up a first-time code and answers a common question: "Is a code of ethics like a mission statement?" (Answer: "No. A mission statement states what you do. A code of ethics states how you do it.") At first glance, a site that promises "business ethics from an Islamic perspective," as the Islamic Training Foundation does, seems to be far removed from most of what is available on the Web. But in a closer look at some of the material, readers learn that Allah describes successful people as those who are "inviting to all that is good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong." What non-Islamic business ethicist would not endorse such a view?
