title:
TECHNOLOGY: CONNECTIONS;
A rather benign declaration on the Internet is treated as a revolutionary manifesto.
body: HOW neurotic is the Internet? Put aside for a moment its seeming hospitality for marginal characters, for hysterics and obsessives. After all, there are plenty of ordinary people plying their wares and interests there. What happens instead when the Internet thinks about itself and tries to imagine its place in the world? Can one trust the Internet's sense of proportion and purpose? Or, when it comes to the Internet, do its advocates and participants see anything clearly? The evidence has not been overly encouraging. And during the last two weeks, a group of high-profile, youngish Internet advocates began to say as much. The group decided that views of technology and the Internet had been skewed toward extremes. On the one hand, the Internet is treated as the electronic frontier, the hope of humankind, the harbinger of a coming utopia. On the other hand, this high-technology nexus has seemed to be a home for pornography and perversion populated by sexual predators, a fitting example of the evils and dangers of unfettered technology. In response to these views, the dissidents wrote a manifesto calling for "techno-realism" and calling themselves techno-realists. This manifesto -- instantly given its own World Wide Web site at www.technorealism.org -- rejects the "louder voices at the extremes" in favor of a more balanced consensus, a "fertile middle ground between techno-utopianism and neo-Luddism." The eight principles of techno-realism generally seem as if they should be obvious to anyone. "The Internet is revolutionary," the writers declare, "but not utopian." It is, they say, a communications tool that will not bring paradise. "The thrill of acquiring or distributing information quickly," they add, should not be confused with wisdom. Freedom is important, but some government intervention is necessary. Wiring schools to the Internet will not save the schools, but can augment education. This middle ground seems both commonsensical and very nearly trite. Who could object? And judging from the manifesto's signers, who has? Its supporters range from commentators like Steven Johnson, the editor of Feed (www.feedmag.com), to hip-hop Internet advocates like Douglas Rushkoff, a self-described youth-culture enthusiast who likes to "poke holes in the system" and has always seemed a bit of a techno-utopian himself. It is supported by David Shenk, the author of "Data Smog" and a techno-skeptic, as well as by Mark Stahlman, a founder of the newyork New Media Association, who more than a year ago wrote an intriguing critical analysis of the utopian ideology of Wired magazine for the 'zine Rewired (www.rewired.com/96/Fall/ 1118.html). Even Kevin Kelly, one of the cyber-gurus behind Wired, has joined the ranks of supporters. But the triteness appears only when viewed through the scrim of real life. On the Internet, this mild-mannered declaration is being treated like a truly revolutionary document, with signatures still accumulating http://www.technorealism.org/list-html). Techno-realism has inspired flames and counterflames at forums run by Feed (http://www.feedmag.com/html/dialog/98.03dialog/intro.html) and even more hostile commentary on the Well. Sarcasm and insider allusions are the rule at another site that mocks the manifesto and its signers (www.technorealist.org): "SEE The TECHNOREALISTS Go Against The Wired LIBERTARIANS" as they "FIGHT For The Digital FUTURE!" The techno-realism "movement," barely a week old, even inspired a conference at the Berkman Center for Internet and Society at the Harvard Law School on Thursday (http://cyber.harvard.edu/technorealism.html). At the conference, techno-realism was called "a more nuanced and useful way to think" about technology. But it is only in the slightly neurotic world of the Internet and its insider commentators that this kind of statement would cause this kind of controversy or inspire such hyperbolic advocacy. Outside the Internet, most of its points seem obvious or facile. In the Feed-sponsored dialogue on techno-realism, David Hudson, a founder of Rewired, points out that taking the techno-realist middle ground is a "bit like establishing a political party for those who breathe air or put their pants on one leg at a time." There seems to be a fun-house quality to the fuss, as if the manifesto writers were pointing out that perhaps the emperor was not wearing pants at all, not realizing that neither were they. The statement is opposed to the distortions of the Internet's utopian thinkers, but its promotion and style can seem right at home. Wired magazine bears its utopian message with neon colors and high-concept color ads that seem custom designed for the Internet set; it gains stature with its links to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Media Lab through Nicholas Negroponte. Techno-realism preaches humility but has been just as earnestly promoted and pumped up, sprouting links on the Web and finding a Harvard connection in one of its creators, Andrew L. Shapiro, a fellow of the Berkman Center and a contributing editor at The Nation. In both cases, too little is carefully analyzed; too much depends on appearing to be progressive and ahead of the curve. But in a conversation, Mr. Shapiro noted out that the techno-realist statement was just a first step, one needed for attention. He argued that the kind of support now being given to techno-realism might be a sign that "Internet thinking is coming of age." He suggested that the "laissez-faire extremism" of Internet utopianism might be coming to an end with a new kind of "political maturity." In the meantime, the fact that techno-realism is being considered a revolutionary step is a sign of how undeveloped and off kilter most Internet thinking is.

title: World Medical Community Frets Over Unregulated Medicine Sales on Web
body: The unregulated atmosphere of the World Wide Web may be a boon to the First Amendment, but the international medical community might argue that freedom has its limits. The on-line promotion and sale of medicines and dietary supplements have health and consumer groups scrambling for regulation. International drug sales have never been simple, and the Web further complicates the situation. A prescription drug in one country may be a nutritional supplement in another, for example. And while the unitedstates permits drug advertising to consumers, most of Europe does not. Disclaimers and disclosure information vary from country to country, as does sales licensing. Meanwhile, the Web has increased the potential for medical fraud. "In the old days, it was the snake oil salesman at the county fair. Now there's a tool where he can hit all the county fairs all the time," said Richard Barnes, director of Federal-state relations at the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Regulatory Affairs. Although difficult to quantify -- no agency or organization tracks on-line drug sales -- much of the trade is in experimental and unproven substances. For example, dozens of sites sell nootropics, also called "smart drugs," like Piracetam, Vasopressin and Hydergine, which are substances said to improve cognitive abilities. Many of these are hormones and amino acids, and if they were made in the unitedstates, the F.D.A. might classify them as dietary supplements -- meaning there could be no claim of curing diseases nor could they be administered as drugs -- and would require disclaimers to that effect. But that is not the case in other countries, where the classification and availability of drugs vary. For example, manufactured L-tryptophan, an amino acid, was taken off the market in the unitedstates in the early 1990's after it was associated with eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, a potentially fatal blood cell disease. Yet it is easily available from the Web site of Quality Health Inc. of London, as are Retin-A, Deprenyl and Proscar, all prescription drugs in the unitedstates. More than the sale of risky substances on the Web, however, health agencies fear the lack of protocol for administering them. "The smaller firms send these things out without any counseling or control, so if you order this stuff by fax you cannot be sure if it meets quality requirements," said Dr. Martijn ten Ham, the head of drug safety for the World Health Organization. "It may say a dosage is 200 milligrams, but how can you be sure? And you cannot be sure of drug-combination problems without a doctor or pharmacist." There have been no reported cases of death from a medical product bought over the Internet, although the F.D.A. says drug reaction cases are underreported. If a patient was already suffering from a fatal disease, for instance, that disease would be listed as the cause of death. Many sites sell controlled substances, but out of self-interest, most are careful about where they ship their products. Amazing Nature of Nijmehen, the Netherlands, deals in marijuana seeds and hallucinogenic mushrooms, both legal in the Netherlands if sold in small quantities. Henk van Velthooven, the company's owner, said, "We try to keep strictly to the rules, because I think if I sold illegal things to the unitedstates, I would soon be out of business." Those with rare or incurable illnesses may find a world of new or experimental drugs on the Web. Yet if they are not approved in the unitedstates, the world's most profitable market, there is usually a good reason, said Abbey Meyers, president of the National Organization for Rare Disorders. "You may find a great epilepsy drug in Europe, but it's so toxic that its makers know the F.D.A. would never approve it," Ms. Meyers said. Rumors of miracle cures spread more quickly on the Web, Ms. Meyers said, adding: "There was lots of rumor on the Internet about vitamins that could help with Lou Gehrig's disease, so people were taking huge doses. Well, you can overdose on vitamins." Still, the organization uses the Web, maintaining an on-line data base about rare diseases that receives a million visits a year. "People are desperate for medical information," Ms. Meyers said. "They don't want to take the doctor's word for it and go home and say, 'I've put my life in someone else's hands.' " The volume of commercially sponsored information on the Web, though, can make it difficult to find facts, said Lisa Hayes, a spokeswoman for Health Action International, a nonprofit consumer rights group based in Amsterdam. While consumers "think they're getting objective information, what they're actually getting is promotion," she said. "There might not be information on other treatments," she said, "or that person might not even need a drug solution. Sometimes you can't even see who is sponsoring the Web site." unitedstates pharmaceutical sites that promote drugs use technicalities to meet international laws, disclaimers such as, "This site is intended for U.S. residents only" -- a Web oxymoron -- or separate links for unitedstates and non-unitedstates residents. The F.D.A. steps in when it can if it discovers sales infractions. Last June it forced a company called Contraceptive Technologies Inc., in Bogota, Colombia, to stop selling do-it-yourself abortion and sterilization kits on line on the grounds that the products were dangerous when used without a physician's direction. The company's Internet service provider, Rapidsite Inc. of Boca Raton, Fla., voluntarily removed the ads after the F.D.A. notified it of its concerns. Rapidsite said that Contraceptive Technologies violated unitedstates laws and, therefore, its contract with Rapidsite. According to Dwight Rawls, a special agent and operations manager of the F.D.A.'s Office of Criminal Investigations, if an offending site's service provider is outside the unitedstates, the F.D.A. will notify the country of origin or try to stop incoming shipments of the drugs. The F.D.A. has also blocked on-line sales of two unapproved drugs: gamma hydroxybutyric acid, a drug producing the same effects as a steroid, and laetrile, a cancer treatment. Border controls can also be effective. unitedstates residents may import up to a three-month supply of drugs for personal use unless they are illegal, known to be dangerous or are foreign versions of a drug produced in the unitedstates. According to Brad Stone, an F.D.A. spokesman, the agency recently detained about 800 packages of unapproved substances, all from one overseas company, over five months. The problem is "substantial," Mr. Stone said, although the F.D.A. does not have exact statistics. For its part, the World Health Organization is urging countries and organizations to increase monitoring, self-regulation and consumer education and is planning to develop full-scale guidelines for Internet drug sales and promotions. "We are not a police agency," Dr. ten Ham said. "But we're afraid that if this goes on and proves to be a lucrative activity, then that will undermine all kinds of drug policies that are currently in place." Graphic   Drawing (Scott Menchin)

title: New & Noteworthy Paperbacks
body: STENDHAL By Jonathan Keates. Carroll & Graf, $15.95. In his youth, Henri Beyle (1783-1842) appeared destined for a career as a scientist. But circumstances intervened, and he became a Napoleonic soldier and, eventually, the novelist we know as Stendhal. Keates's "prose twirls through Stendhal's peripatetic career like a gentleman's stick, striking sparks when it taps a point home," Frederick Brown said here in 1997.  DOWN BY THE RIVER By Edna O'Brien. Plume, $12.95. Set in the author's native Ireland, this novel focuses on Mary McNamara, a pregnant country girl whose situation is even more desperate than that of other expectant teen-age mothers: she is to bear her father's child. After a neighbor learns of Mary's plight and takes her to England for a legal abortion, Mary becomes a pawn in an Irish political battle that is as much about self-righteousness and spite as it is about morality. Last year our reviewer, Hilary Mantel, called this a "forlorn, unsparing and consciously exquisite novel of rural despair."  DEEPER: Adventures on the Net By John Seabrook. Touchstone/Simon & Schuster, $13. The author chronicles his two-year odyssey in cyberspace, a journey that transformed him from an idealistic enthusiast to an educated skeptic. "He is an elegant and lucid writer," David S. Bennahum said in these pages in 1997. The same publisher has also reissued LIFE ON THE SCREEN: Identity in the Age of the Internet, by Sherry Turkle ($14), and WHERE WIZARDS STAY UP LATE: The Origins of the Internet, by Katie Hafner and Matthew Lyon ($13). Turkle, a psychologist and sociologist, explores the ways in which the virtual world both expands and constricts the user's sense of self. "The result is almost an archeology of changing cultural responses to the computer," Bernard Sharratt wrote in the Book Review in 1995. The history of computers is examined further by Hafner and Lyon, who describe how the Internet ultimately grew out of Arpanet, a network that originated with the Eisenhower Administration's Advanced Research Projects Agency. "The book compiles a great deal of much-needed information," Stephen Manes said here in 1996. The future of technology is the subject of WHAT WILL BE: How the New World of Information Will Change Our Lives, by Michael L. Dertouzos (Harper Edge/HarperSanFrancisco, $14). Here, the founder of M.I.T.'s Laboratory for Computer Science sees the Internet as the 21st-century equivalent of the village marketplace. He "refreshingly attempts a return to basics, eschewing hype," Rick Prelinger said in these pages last year.  THE MANIKIN By Joanna Scott. Owl/Holt, $12. The title refers to the false skeletons taxidermists use when stuffing dead creatures, which are everywhere in this novel. They fill an old house that was once owned by a natural historian and is the scene for a Gothic tale, set in 1927, involving the housekeeper and her daughter. In 1996, our reviewer, Peter S. Prescott, wrote of one of the author's passages, "We haven't heard a voice like that since Ovid wrote his 'Metamorphoses.' "  I'M LOSING YOU By Bruce Wagner. Plume, $12.95. Screenwriters, actors, casting directors and numerous other Hollywood types populate this satiric novel, which deals with the vicissitudes of life in the film industry. "The author's achievement is that almost every character is fascinating, no matter how hideous," Anita Gates said in the Book Review in 1996. The reality of the business is examined just as acidly in HELLO, HE LIED: And Other Truths From the Hollywood Trenches, by Lynda Obst (Broadway, $13). The author, a film producer, counsels other women while recalling her own experiences. The result is a "smart, amusing new memoir," David McClintick wrote here in 1996.  THE LIFE OF GOD: As Told by Himself By Franco Ferrucci. Translated by Raymond Rosenthal and Franco Ferrucci. University of Chicago, $11.95. This elegiac novel is a kind of travelogue through the human universe, executed by the mind that created it but ultimately cannot control it. In 1996 our reviewer, Jack Miles, called the novel "the synthesis of a charming writer's Italy-centered education and the expression of his boundless hopes for, and poignant disappointment in, his own human kind."  A FACE AT THE WINDOW By Dennis McFarland. Broadway, $13. Cookson Selway, the narrator, is haunted, both literally and figuratively. Although he has given up drugs and alcohol, he feels the tugs of his unhappy childhood and of the three disgruntled spirits who inhabit his London hotel. This ghost story is "thoroughly satisfying," Isabel Colegate wrote in these pages last year.  FROM BONDAGE: Volume 3 of "Mercy of a Rude Stream" By Henry Roth. Picador USA, $15. This posthumously published novel by the author of "Call It Sleep" continues the autobiographical story of Ira Stigman, the young son of immigrant Jewish parents who becomes a celebrated writer. This volume "is clearly indispensable to the appreciation of Roth's unique life and work," Frank Kermode said in the Book Review in 1996.   Laurel Graeber Graphic   Photo: (THE newyork TIMES)

title: Export Laws Challenged by Sale Of Encryption Software Abroad
body: An American maker of data-scrambling software said today that it would circumvent unitedstates export policies by allowing its Dutch subsidiary to begin selling an international version of Pretty Good Privacy, a strong encryption program that does not provide a back door for law enforcement surveillance. Because the company, Network Associates, is the nation's largest independent maker of computer security software, its action could have a serious effect on unitedstates export policies on software. Network Associates' decision to sell a program specifically prohibited by the Commerce Department comes at a time when the Clinton Administration is already fighting Congressional attempts to end export controls on encryption software for fear that such restrictions will hurt the ability of American industry to compete internationally. "This is the biggest challenge yet to the U.S. policy," Ted Julian, an analyst at the Forrester Group in Cambridge, Mass., said. "It potentially has a tremendous consumer base." The battle over data scrambling -- software that hides everything from love letters to passwords to credit card numbers from prying eyes -- has become a bitter struggle in recent years between the American software industry and privacy advocates on one side and national security and law enforcement officials on the other. The Clinton Administration, in the name of fighting crime and terrorism, has been trying to force the industry to build back doors into encryption software to make it possible for law enforcement officials to secretly decode private messages. Opponents argue that the keys to the proposed back doors could be too easily stolen, compromising not only privacy but also the security of credit card numbers and other highly personal information. The Government does not restrict powerful encryption software domestically but, with very few exceptions, it limits export licenses to codes that can be easily cracked. Earlier this week, Justice Department officials testified before Congress that they had no plans to introduce domestic controls on strong encryption technology. Government officials said yesterday that they had not yet determined whether Network Associates would be violating unitedstates laws in selling P.G.P internationally. "We'll be looking at this very closely," William A. Reinsch, the Under Secretary for export administration, said. "The question of whether or not this product is based on legal or illegal export of U.S. technology is a question to be investigated. If the Government determines that it was illegal, then we'll take appropriate action." In part, that decision will hinge on whether the entire software package was developed independently from the unitedstates company, Mr. Reinsch said. Network Associates executives said that in developing the international version of P.G.P. they took care not to violate unitedstates laws. The international version was developed by Network Associates in Europe in partnership with a small group of cryptographers at Cnlab Software in Switzerland. Network Associates said that the international version would be marketed by its European subsidiary, Networks Associates International B.V., based in the Netherlands. "We're not sure what the impact of this will be," Peter Watkins, general manager of the company's Net Tools Secure Division, said. "This is the first time that a U.S. company has taken this approach, but there are no prohibitions against this." While unitedstates laws restrict the export of strong encryption products, there are no restrictions on exporting the text of the original source code. This loophole allows programmers in other countries to translate the source code into new software programs. P.G.P was written in the early 1990's by a privacy activist and computer programmer, Philip Zimmerman, and was freely distributed in the unitedstates. Mr. Zimmerman also made his source code available internationally in text form. As a result, versions of the program have long been widely available in many countries. Network Associates' executives said they had met with Commerce Department officials earlier this year to explain their plan but the department had not responded. Mr. Reinsch said that his staff had been briefed by the company. Richard Hornstein, vice president of legal affairs for Network Associates, said the Justice Department was notified because "we wanted to make sure they felt comfortable about this, but there was no way the Commerce Department should have a role." Network Associates is not the first unitedstates company to attempt to use an international partnership to circumvent export restrictions. Currently C2net Software Inc., an Oakland, Calif., security software concern, sells an international version of its Web server which has powerful, built-in cryptography. The company said that the international version of the product was developed overseas independently from the unitedstates product. Sun Microsystems has run into Government opposition to a similar project which was based on a cooperative development project with Elvis+, a company formed by scientists from the former Soviet space program.

title:
DOWNTIME;
For Fanatics, Sports Webcasts
body: IT'S not quite like being there. It does not even approximate television. But if you are in Fresno, Calif., or Chippewa Falls, Wis., and your favorite team is in Chicago or Denver, it's the next best thing. And for some sports junkies, that is a great leap forward. Meet the Internet simulcast, the newest medium for live sports, and its fan: the Web potato. "It's obviously not TV, where you can get all excited, but for my options, it's as good as it gets," said Chris Grusz, a Seattle software salesman who uses the browser in his cubicle at work to tune into Chicago Bulls basketball games. To some, the idea of "watching" games unfold in simple text is a likely sign of lunacy. But Mr. Grusz is among thousands of point-and-click fans who are happily tuning into ESPN Sportszone, CBS Sportsline and a handful of smaller operations that seek to simulate games as they happen, using animation or text updates fed from the sidelines. ESPN is set to begin its first full season of Web-based baseball coverage, while CBS is embarking on a second full season. Each offered football games last season, and ESPN recently started Gamecast for the National Basketball Association. Last season, CBS Sportsline's Baseball Live was its most popular on-line offering, attracting hundreds of thousands of viewers each game, the company said. Perhaps more impressive, the Total College Sports Network, a division of Total Sports, based in Raleigh, N.C., was viewed by at least several hundred thousand viewers during the first weekend of the NCAA tournament. The 10-month-old network has provided real-time play-by-play, charts and digital photos for hundreds of college basketball, football and baseball games in the last year. Make no mistake, the experiences are not even a distant cousin of television. CBS provides animation based on Java, an Internet language for interactive and multimedia programs. For football, an image of a football helmet moves across the field as a team marches on a drive; for baseball, animated figures round the bases as a running box score keeps a tally. The network promises an elaborate upgrade for this baseball season. CBS is using a program called Shockwave, a multimedia application for a browser, to make the action look like an arcade baseball game. ESPN focuses more on statistics, providing running play-by-play text, rosters, box scores and shot charts. These Webcasts may be a harbinger of what is called convergence, the melding of television hardware and content with home computer hardware and content. In the case of sports, that means fans will be able to use one screen to get access not only to broadcasts but also to mountains of statistics -- chocolate and peanut butter for fans. The signs of convergence are already evident in radio, where technology that permits broadcasts to be carried over the Internet makes hundreds of games and events available to anyone with a connection, speakers and a copy of audio-streaming software like Microsoft's Netshow or Real Network's Real Player. In baseball, at least 13 major league baseball teams, two dozen college teams and a handful of minor league teams were set up for doing audio feeds as of February. And you thought you had to be at the park to follow the Winston-Salem Warthogs or Durham Bulls. The Internet now provides audio access to many other sports: hockey, soccer, golf, auto racing, college basketball, horse racing and rodeo, among others. Audio Net, a Dallas-based Internet broadcaster, even offers play-by-play for contests broadcast exclusively for the Internet, like events at some small universities. There is even access to sports talk radio, which is where sports fans can go after they have seen the game and the highlights (twice) and they need to find the deeper meaning. Eventually, Web simulcasts should begin to incorporate not just audio but also video streaming and still shots to create a much richer experience, said Ross Levinsohn, vice president for programming and executive producer at CBS Sportsline. "We've just built the Edsel," Mr. Levinsohn said. "This is the forebear to the Rolls-Royce, which is still three to six years away." The early incarnation is apparently welcomed by displaced fans like Louis Crandall, an economist with R. H. Wrightson & Associates in newyork, who cannot wait for the baseball season. During the summer, two of the computers on Mr. Crandall's desk are devoted to work and one to the Pittsburgh Pirates. A native of Pittsburgh, Mr. Crandall said he loved to keep the Webcast on in the background; he said it was less intrusive than radio. Last season, he used his browser to watch a no-hitter that Pittsburgh won in extra innings. "It was great when Mark Smith's home run came across" the Internet, said Mr. Crandall, his voice rising as if he had actually been there. The Webcasts are also attractive to gamblers, their creators admit. "We have no idea how many, but a pretty significant number of people are looking at this because they have an interest in gambling," said Geoff Reiss, senior vice president for sports at ESPN Interactive. Other competitors may soon get into the Cybercast game, too, said Rick Alessandri, vice president and general manager of Sports Ticker Enterprises, an ESPN-backed venture that provides real-time statistics to more than 100 on-line services. Mr. Alessandri said Yahoo, Fox and America Online were among the companies considering more elaborate real-time coverage. CNN/SI, the Web site representing CNN and Sports Illustrated, already carries live video of sports-related press conferences. There is just one catch: it runs at 10 frames per second, pokey slow. Indeed, Web-based live sports are primitive enough to be the domain of die-hard fans. Basketball may be the ultimate example. It is a game that is so fast-paced, it sometimes does not even lend itself to television commentary, let alone to text-based updates. To wit, from a recent ESPN Gamecast of a contest between the Houston Rockets and Minnesota Timberwolves: "Hou: Charles Barkley defensive rebound "Hou: Clyde Drexler 3-pointer (Hou 55, Min 43) "Time remaining, 3:33 "Min: Kevin Garnett layup, assist Stephon Marbury (Hou 55, Min 45) "Time remaining, 3:17 "Hou: Charles Barkley 3 second violation "Hou: Mario Elie for Clyde Drexler "Min: Stephon Marbury miss" Even David Stern, the Commissioner of the N.B.A., would have trouble selling the experience as Fan-tastic. ESPN gurus do not dispute that. "This medium cannot and does not replace visual satisfaction in terms of covering Kobe Bryant taking an alley-oop pass and dunking it," said Mr. Reiss, of ESPN Interactive. "What we can do is provide a far greater level of understanding of what is happening in that event. For the hardest-core fans, it's the greatest augmentation that they've ever seen." Technology aside, the Webcasts will probably face some opposition from other media in the not too distant future, legal experts say. The courts may have to decide whether the Internet functions more like a newspaper or like a broadcast medium, which would put it into direct conflict with television licensing. But the Webcasts are a godsend to a self-admitted sports junkie like Joseph Pilar, a retired courier in Baltimore. Rather than watch games from his couch, as he used to, Mr. Pilar sits at his desk. That way, he can still watch games on the 21-inch television, then swivel to the 17-inch monitor to get text-based play-by-play updates on the Internet for other games. "This way, I don't have to wait for the CBS announcer to say, 'Let's go to newyork for an update of other scores,' " Mr. Pilar said. "I know everything as it happens."  Site-Seeing: Sports  Here are sites for sports Webcasts and audio feeds:  www.audionet.com www.cbssportsline.com www.cnnsi.com www.finalfour.net www.sportsticker.com espn.sportzone.com www.totalsports.com Graphic   Photo: Chris Grusz, stuck in his Seattle office, tunes in to Chicago Bulls games on the Internet. (Therese Frare for The newyork Times)

title: Lawyer Questions Woman In a Sexual Attack Trial
body: A woman who said she was tortured and kidnapped by a Columbia University graduate student she met through the Internet came under withering cross-examination yesterday as a defense lawyer questioned how she managed to free herself, get dressed and fight off her attacker simultaneously. Prosecutors have charged Oliver Jovanovic, a doctoral student in microbiology, with kidnapping and sexually abusing the woman, a Barnard College student, in his Washington Heights apartment in Manhattan. The young woman, who testified for the prosecution earlier this week, gave a detailed account in State Supreme Court, describing how she fought her way to freedom after 20 hours of torture. She said she was naked when she freed herself, and managed to dress and fight off Mr. Jovanovic before running from the apartment. But the defense lawyer, Jack Litman, repeatedly tried to punch holes in her account. Striding about the courtroom, he questioned how the woman could battle Mr. Jovanovic, a martial arts expert while also finding her scattered clothing and dressing in the small studio apartment. "You get off the bed; you run for your pants?" Mr. Litman asked. "That is correct," the young woman said. "Was Oliver asleep?" he asked. "No, he was in shock, looking at me," the woman answered. "Did Oliver grab any part of your leg, or any part of your pants?" the lawyer asked. "I remember him getting up," she answered. Mr. Litman then questioned how she was able to put on her sweater, pants, socks and a pair of boots while Mr. Jovanovic chased her around the apartment. The woman did not provide an explanation, other than to say she was "like a deer in the headlights, very frantic." Mr. Litman returned to the questioning, asking about how she managed to put on her sweater. "In order to get a sweater on, you have to put one arm in and then another and then you have to put your head in?" he said. "Three things you have to put through, and Oliver is right there, right behind you, trying to prevent you from leaving the apartment?" "That is correct," the woman said. He then wound up the questioning. "Isn't it a fact that you didn't have this running routine at all, but you put on your clothes and walked out of the apartment?" he asked. "No, that is not correct," she said. The prosecution has charged that Mr. Jovanovic, 31 at the time, met the 20-year-old woman in an Internet chat room. Prosecutors have said that he used his formidable intellect to dominate the young woman emotionally and entice her into meeting him for a date on the night of Nov. 22, 1996. After meeting to see a movie, prosecutors have said, the couple returned to Mr. Jovanovich's apartment. Once there, prosecutors have charged, Mr. Jovanovic used his dominance to persuade the woman to undress and then bound her to a futon frame. They charge that he hit her with a police nightstick, burned her with candle wax, bit her until she bled and sodomized her. The defense has asserted that Mr. Jovanovic never coerced or injured her. During her testimony, she said she undressed and allowed Mr. Jovanovic to tie her to the futon after he insisted that she do so. She did not say in her testimony that he threatened her or used physical force. The defense has also attacked the prosecution's version of events. In his opening statement, Mr. Litman referred to an email message that the woman wrote to Mr. Jovanovic, claiming that she expressed an interest in sadomasochism and "the pleasure of hell's pain." Testimony is to resume on Monday with continued cross-examination. Graphic   Photo: Oliver Jovanovic, accused in a sexual attack case, outside court. (Associated Press)

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
For All the Matador Types Out There
body: STANLEY CONRAD admits that bullfighting is not a subject near and dear to the average American. But he thinks that this is exactly why his three-year-old Web site, Mundo Taurino (mundo-taurino.org), has become so popular. "You get spit on if you bring bullfighting up," said Mr. Conrad, a 49-year-old graduate student in library science at Long Island University. "That's one of the great things about the Internet. It allows you to finesse all that." The Internet has become important to the ancient spectacle of bullfighting, and the most important Web site devoted to it is actually American. Mundo Taurino, which means "the world of bulls," has little original content and almost no graphics, but it is a sort of international clubhouse for aficionados. The start page has 20 subject categories that contain more than 190 links. You can go to the newsgroup alt.culture.bullfight, where, in English or Spanish, you can argue the merits of bulls and bullfighters -- or insert yourself into a running debate on the morality of the spectacle. For those who wish to avoid argument, there is the Web site of the Madrid magazine 6 Toros 6 (www.6toros6.com). Click on little matador-hat icons to read the schedules for the major rings worldwide, in-depth articles on bull breeders or interviews with star matadors. If this offends you, Mundo Taurino also has a link to the anti-bullfighting page of the World Society for the Protection of Animals (way.net/ wspa/wsbull.html). Mr. Conrad said that Mundo Taurino receives about 100 visits a day, but the site's reach is wider because hemails daily news items to 3,000 international subscribers. Many in the bullfight world say that the Internet has helped promote bullfighting, especially in places like the unitedstates, where you cannot see it or read much about it anywhere else. "Aficionados look upon Stanley as a guiding light," said Lyn Sherwood, a writer in San Juan Capistrano, Calif. "Because of his Web site, many people who have only seen one bullfight are learning about bullfighting through the Internet." So if you are dreaming of the drama of the bullring, you might go to Mundo Taurino and click on "music" to find the lyrics of the Tom Lehrer song "In Old Mexico." As Mr. Lehrer wrote: "Best of all we went to the Plaza de Toros. Now whenever I start feeling morose, I revive by recalling that scene." Graphic   Photo

title:
User's Guide;
Hunting the Elusive Spammer
body: APPARENTLY no one informed the sparrow.mooncrater.net postmaster that there are only two kinds of "personal" email I really like to get: a short note from my literary agent promising to send a check right away or a quick line from my husband announcing his intent to come home early to cook dinner. Try as I might, I just could not fit the junk email I got the other day from sparrow.mooncrater.net into one of those categories: "Subject: A Personal Message . . . Find out the secrets that some of the wealthiest Internet marketers are using to propel their sales through the cyberspace roof." This particular bit of spam went on (and on and on) about how I could become fabulously rich if I were the kind of person willing to pay $34.95 for an Internet marketing guide. But I am not that sort of person. In fact, I would happily settle for a lean-to on the sand in Acapulco and a job selling ice-cream cones to tourists if I never had to endure spam again. Spam is a betrayal of all that mail once stood for. Remember when you were a kid and your mom said there was mail for you, and that meant your favorite aunt had written you a letter and maybe enclosed a pressed violet she had picked from her yard? Now, that was mail. There once was a quiet satisfaction in knowing that someone out there had something personal and interesting to say to you. When I got old enough to read Jane Austen, I discovered that in early-19th-century England, themail carrier came to your house repeatedly in a single day. And he delivered gossipy messages from friends or invitations to dinner at the vicarage. Sealed with wax. Of course, paper mail lost its allure long ago. As an adult, I accepted the fact that most of what the unitedstates Postal Service delivers to me consists of unwanted bills, garbage from my Congressman and glossy catalogues with a vaguely Southwestern theme. I was willing to put up with that when I still had my email to look forward to. But the on-line world has gradually gone dark in the past couple of years as direct mailers have capitalized on the Internet's growing population, clogging all our in boxes. Junk email is worse than junk paper mail for a very simple reason: the recipient bears a portion of the cost. No matter how trivial the charge, there is a philosophical issue here. When spammers complain that attempts to curb their behavior violate their right to free speech, I respond, Say whatever you want, as long as I do not have to pay a single penny for it. For me, it was time to take a stand. Maybe I could just phone a spammer to explain my position? If I told that touching story about my aunt and the dead violet, the postmaster at sparrow.mooncrater.net might have an epiphany about the sanctity of email. Of course, first I had to find the culprit. I tried to reply, but my email bounced. Then I looked up the computer's registration at www.internic. net/wp/whois.html, but the phone number on the form had been disconnected. This task should become easier over the next few months, as the computers that route email over the Internet begin to use new tools to prevent spammers from faking return addresses, available on the latest version of the popular Sendmail mail-delivery program. But in the meantime, the spammers have the upper hand. I figured I needed help from an experienced spam fighter, so I called Matt Korn. As America Online's senior vice president in charge of network operations, he has to sort 26 million email messages a day, culling them for spam. Although spam is a universal problem for on-line services, America Online's huge population has made it a particularly ripe target. In fact, spammers unleash software programs that interrogate AOL's system to collect lists of screen names, Mr. Korn said. Customers can protect themselves by not publishing their names in the member directory. "I recommended, for instance, that my own kids not publish their names in the directory," Mr. Korn said. America Online estimates that on a given day, as much as 30 percent of the email that arrives from the Internet consists of spam -- clogging computers, annoying customers and prompting Mr. Korn to assign an anti-spam team to stanch the flow. "It's my No. 1 challenge," Mr. Korn said. For now, America Online uses software filters to block email that originates from addresses of known spammers and also tells customers how to restrict incoming mail to a list of approved addresses (for help, type keyword junk mail). Doesn't the phrase "restrict incoming mail" say something sad about the state of the Internet? In less than a decade, we have managed to discover the most revolutionary communications medium of the century, populate it, commercialize it -- and rob it of much of its ability to convey useful information. You need not be on America Online to use common sense when confronting spam. Don't be fooled by email that claims you can get your name removed from futuremailing lists by sending a reply message to a specific address. "In general, they actually use this as a validation attempt, to get a new list of email addresses that are active," Mr. Korn said. I knew my attempt to track down the spammer was probably drawing more attention to my own email address. But I could not stop myself. I found out that the address to which one could mail $34.95 belonged to a rent-a-mailbox outfit in Fort Collins, Colo. A woman named Cindy answered the phone there, at Mailboxes Etc., and confirmed that the spammer was a customer. "But I can't give you any more information," she said. "It would violate the customer's privacy." Next: Interview with the spammer.  email address: Slatalla@nytimes.com Graphic   Photo (Margaret Riegel)

title: Bridge to Pay $510 Million For Dow Jones Data Business
body: Capping weeks of negotiations, Dow Jones & Company said yesterday that it had agreed to sell its troubled financial information business to Bridge Information Systems for $360 million in cash and $150 million in Bridge preferred stock. The sale to Bridge, a competitor of the data business, Dow Jones Markets, would be for far less than the $1.6 billion that Dow Jones invested in the operation when it bought it in the 1980's. "The value is not bad, especially since everybody has been considering the worst -- prices as low as $350 million," said Peter Appert, who follows the company for BT Alex. Brown. "But even $510 million is extraordinarily low compared to the $1 billion the company was thought to be worth just a few years ago. Still, it gets Dow Jones out of a difficult situation and gives them some upside with the preferred stock." The preferred stock has a 4 percent dividend and is convertible in five years to 10 percent of Bridge's equity. Perhaps more important for Dow Jones, the deal allows it to focus on its core publishing operations, which include The Wall Street Journal. Dow Jones Markets, formerly known as Telerate, has faced seemingly insurmountable competition from its two biggest rivals, Reuters Holdings P.L.C. and Bloomberg. It lacked the more complex historical pricing information and other analytical software that investors needed. But Dow Jones, in an effort to make the business more competitive, said last year that it would invest $650 million in it. But the company later dropped that plan and chose to take a roughly $900 million charge against earnings last year, reducing the carrying value of the unit to $550 million. The operation is still carried on Dow Jones's books at $550 million, and the company said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission yesterday that it would take an additional write-off. There has been great pressure from some members of the Bancroft family, which controls Dow Jones -- principally Elizabeth Goth and William Cox 3d -- to sell the troubled operation. Their position had reportedly gained the support of some new outside board members. The deal immediately makes Bridge, which has trailed Reuters, Bloomberg and Dow Jones, the second largest company in the field of providing analytical, historical and trading data for financial experts. Reuters currently has 272,000 customers, compared with 90,000 each for Bloomberg and Dow Jones and 75,000 for Bridge, a Bridge spokesperson said last night. With the Dow Jones unit, Bridge will have annual revenue of about $1.1 billion, analysts said. The combined business will be named Bridge/Telerate. Bridge had been seen as the leading candidate to buy Dow Jones Markets, but the securities firm of Cantor Fitzgerald L.P., with which Dow Jones Markets has a lucrative contract, had also been interested. Cantor Fitzgerald had put together a group that included a Dow Jones Markets executive, Gregory Smith, and the Texas Pacific Group, an investment concern. That group, however, apparently dropped out of the process late last week, according to a person close to the talks, before resurfacing with a new offer yesterday. Apparently, the board of Dow Jones selected the Bridge offer during a board meeting conducted by telephone yesterday. Under Cantor's contract with Dow Jones, it provides information on the Treasury market to subscribers of Dow Jones Markets. Bridge Information Systems' chairman, Tom Wendel, said last night that after the sale of Dow Jones Markets, Bridge's existing customers would not receive that data, though existing Dow Jones Markets customers will continue to do so. But another offering that Dow Jones customers have received, Capital Market Services, which provides data on fixed-income markets, will be available to original Bridge customers as well as to any other customer. Additionally, Dow Jones Markets has had the exclusive rights to the Dow Jones news wire services overseas. Those will become available to any customer. Bridge's equity data will be available to existing Dow Jones Markets customers.

title: Attack That Began on Internet Is Described
body: Opening the kidnapping and sexual assault case against a Columbia University graduate student yesterday, the prosecution described the defendant as a kind of folk monster of the information highway, a sophisticated man who used the anonymity of computer communications to entrap an unsuspecting victim. Hours later, as the first day of trial came to a close, the man's accuser briefly took the stand, saying that when she first communicated with the man, Oliver Jovanovic, she thought he was offbeat and interesting. "Oliver was not like most of the people" on the Internet, she said. "Oliver was imaginative, he was quite interesting." Speaking before the jury in Manhattan Supreme Court, the prosecutor, Gail Heatherly, had said it was just those attributes that Mr. Jovanovic, a Ph.D. candidate in microbiology, used to dominate the young Barnard College student, who is from a small town near Buffalo. Ms. Heatherly said that Mr. Jovanovic used his formidable intelligence and dominance to bring the young woman to his studio apartment, undress her, and bind her to a futon. Then, Ms. Heatherly said, he taunted her, tortured her for 20 hours on Nov. 22 and Nov. 23 of 1996 and repeatedly threatened to kill her. "Before the night was over, she would wonder whether she would ever leave that apartment alive," Ms. Heatherly said, adding that Mr. Jovanovic told the woman: "I'll never be arrested for this." Mr. Jovanovic, small and bespectacled, sat motionless at the defense table during Ms. Heatherly's opening argument, looking more like a junior clerk than a defendant. He barely shifted his position as Jack Litman, his lawyer, rose repeatedly to attack the prosecution's story. Using examples from Ms. Heatherly's opening and from email between the young woman and Mr. Jovanovic, Mr. Litman described the events as consensual. He said the woman repeatedly expressed an interest in sadomasochism during her email conversations and told of her interest in films of murder and violence. At one point before the incident, the woman wrote Mr. Jovanovic about her interest, Mr. Litman said. He said she wrote him, saying that she was "drawn to the pleasure of hell's pain." Reading from a message that he said was sent two days after the incident, Mr. Litman said the woman specifically described what she thought of that night. "The taste is so overpoweringly delicious and at the same time quite nauseating," the message said, according to Mr. Litman. He said the young woman was "scared and repulsed by what was inside of herself, repulsed by her own desires." Mr. Litman repeatedly stressed that there is almost no medical evidence of assault, despite allegations that Mr. Jovanovic burned the young woman, bit her until he drew blood, beat her with a club and sodomized her with a baton. Prosecutors argued that the lack of evidence was due to a lapse of several days between the attack and the time the young woman went to a doctor. Mr. Heatherly said her roommate and her boyfriend would testify that they saw livid bruises on her body.

title: Internet Is Expanding Arms Race With Junk email
body: The Internet's most popular software for routing and delivering email on the Internet is being armed with a powerful set of tools to fight the unsolicited junk electronic mail known as spam, which is increasingly bedeviling cyberspace. The war over spam has pitted computer users, privacy-rights advocates and Internet service providers against companies like Cyber Promotions and Quantum Communications, which fire off millions of advertisements each day in the form of email messages. Not only are most spam messages unwelcome, but their sheer volume -- now estimated to account for about 10 percent of all email worldwide -- frequently clogs the electronic pipes through which all data on the global computer network must pass, slowing the entire system. Now, Sendmail, the electronic post office used on about 75 percent of the computers that route email messages to their proper recipients on the Internet, is being fitted for battle with the spammers. On Tuesday, Sendmail's author, Eric Allman, is to announce the addition of anti-spam tools to version 8.9 of the software as part of his plan to create a company that will continue to develop new features for the free version of the program and sell software and support services to business users. Mr. Allman created Sendmail while he was working as a Unix programmer at the University of California at Berkeley in 1981 and made it freely available to the thousands of administrators and computer researchers who have built and maintain the Internet. In recent years, the program, which has been developed based on the Internet's tradition of cooperation, has been used by spammers to stuff themailboxes of Internet users with messages promoting get-rich-quick schemes, weight-loss plans and advertisements for pornography, among other unwanted come-ons. The new version of Sendmail includes a variety of anti-spam features, including the ability to reject mail from known spam addresses and a mechanism that will force spammers to disclose their real Internet addresses. Today most spammers hide their email addresses to make it more difficult for irate computer users to retaliate. Version 8.9 also offers the ability to check automatically a continuosly changing list of spammer's addresses called the Realtime Blackhole List and to reject messages coming from such addresses before they are stored on themail computer's hard drive. Internet experts said that by arming administrators with these new anti-spam weapons, Mr. Allman's software would make the first serious dent in the rising deluge of junk email. The problem is becoming serious for some of the nation's largest Internet service providers. For example, officials at UUNET, the big Internet provider that is now part of Worldcom Inc., said that at the end of 1998 they had seen their mail volume double, and they estimated that at certain times, as much as 50 percent of that traffic was spam. "It's a real war," said Kyle Jones, a senior systems analyst at UUNET. While he asserted that the systems engineers who maintain the Internet were slowly gaining the upper hand against the spammers, he also said that progress was being made at the expense of the openness and sharing that marked the early days of the Internet. Deploying the new version of Sendmail to Internet service providers will mean that the companies that suffer the burden of unwillingly carrying the most spam will be able to modify their systems to fight back quickly. "Spam is an arms race," Mr. Allman said. "When we get better, they get better." On the other hand, he added, many spammers are using inexpensive, off-the-shelf programs and lack the technical skill to circumvent Sendmail's new spam blockers. Randall Winchester, a computer systems administrator at the University of Maryland at College Park who helped Mr. Allman test the new tools, called them a real big victory. "As more people use this version, it will make a huge difference," Mr. Winchester said. His records show that the new software frequently deflects thousands of email messages an hour from the university's more than 40,000 student email accounts. Mr. Allman said that it generally takes about a year for his entire customer base to adopt each new version of his software. But as major Internet service providers begin to deploy the new technology, he said, it will be increasingly difficult for commercial spammers to avoid detection. Spammers are also under attack in Federal and state legislatures and in the courts, where major Internet service providers like America Online are suing them for harassing customers and stealing resources. On Tuesday, Mr. Allman is to announced plans to start a company, Sendmail Inc., to continue development of both the free version of the program and a new commercial product line. The company, to be based in Emeryville, Calif., has $1.25 million in initial capital from investors including the co-founders of Sun Microsystems, Andreas Bechtolscheim and William Joy. Currently Sendmail's only significant competition is the Microsoft Corporation, which offers a similar program that handles electronic post office functions for corporate computer sites. Microsoft currently has only a 1.3 percent market share, said Greg Olson, Sendmail's chief executive. Graphic   Chart: "Screening for Spam" Programmers and computer system administrators have tried many strategies to automatically filter out spam -- unsolicited junk email -- from other electronic messages. Here are four of the measures that will be built in to the latest version of Sendmail, the delivery program most widely used on Internet servers.  AN END TO PROMISCUOUS RELAY-- Larger servers are usually set up to help smaller servers and individual computers by doing most of the work of routing email for them in a process called relay. Right now most servers will relay for any computer that asks them to, making big computers at major companies and universities unwitting accomplices in spreading spam. The new software will turn down relay requests unless they come from users or servers approved by the system administrator.  MOST-WANTED LIST -- New versions of Sendmail will instruct servers to reject automatically messages sent by sources appearing on a widely circulated list of known spam originators.  REALITY CHECK -- Spammers often put a fictitious return address on their messages, partly to slip past filters like the most wanted listand partly to duck replies. The new version of Sendmail will look up return addresses on an Internet registry and will only deliver mail if the domain name in the return address is registered.  VERIFYING THE SENDER -- Sendmail will also send a short verifying query back to the sending host for every message and wait for an answer before making delivery. This will slow down legitimate email sent in small batches only trivially but may swamp the servers of those who send large batches of mail -- legitimate bulk mailers as well as spammers -- with tens of thousands of queries. The hope is that the cost of the powerful servers needed to cope with such a flood of queries will deter spammers more than legitimate bulk mailers.(pg. D6)

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
User Challenge: Getting Modems Up to Speed
body: HOORAY! A new international standard for so-called 56K modems will eventually eliminate much confusion. Hooray? In the short run, users are likely to be more bewildered than ever. Some history: Last year some vendors began offering 56K modems with the promise of faster performance than 28.8- and 33.6-kilobits-per-second predecessors. But the 56K label was a misnomer. These modems send information no faster than older ones. Performance gains come only when they are receiving data from a source like an Internet provider's digital servers (but not directly from a similar modem). Even then, power restrictions imposed by the Federal Communications Commission limit their theoretical top speed to 53 kilobits, but with imperfect lines, they rarely achieve a speed higher than 50. The modems, from many manufacturers, come in two similar but incompatible flavors: X2, championed by the 3Com Corporation, and K56flex, supported by the Rockwell International Corporation and Lucent Technologies. To see the speed improvements, users need to make sure their Internet service providers use equipment designed for the same protocol as their modems. On Feb. 6, the International Telecommunication Union, a United Nations agency, announced that it had agreed on the technical specifications for a single international 56K standard, to be known as V.90. The formal approval process should be completed in September, and Burk Murray, 3Com's product line manager for desktop modems, said approval was simply a formality. Modem makers quickly jockeyed to demonstrate their support for the new standard. In recent weeks, Rockwell, Lucent and 3Com announced that modems based on their V.90 technology would work with each other's server hardware. Several vendors began shipping modems labeled with the V.90 rubric. 3Com began offering free software upgrades to V.90 for many of the company's X2 modems, and other manufacturers have announced similar offerings. So can we put the situation to rest with a "happily ever after?" Not quite. Internet service providers are only beginning to upgrade their systems to the new standard, so the rule remains: If you want 56K service, you still need to be sure your provider's 56K standard matches your modem's. But now there are extra gotchas. 3Com's software upgrades, for example, are meant to allow desktop modems to handle either the new model V.90 connections or the older X2 ones. But as PC World Online reported, some users have had problems with their connections after upgrading. Mr. Murray said that the problem was limited to the few customers whose providers had not upgraded their server software, which 3Com is now offering free. And he offered a solution for those people having the problem. But I personally got bit, and not on an Internet site. Some modems from other companies have a different problem. Because they have less flash memory, they lack the room to hold enough software code to handle two 56K standards at once. If you upgrade one of these modems to V.90 and then discover that your Internet provider has stuck with an older standard, you will not get 56K service back until your provider upgrades its service or you pour the old code back into your modem, assuming you can get the manufacturer to supply it. At least the modem should fall back to one of the older, slower speeds. In the last year, many 56K modems have come with new computers. Most should be upgradable to V.90, but getting the upgrade from a computer maker may be difficult. In looking through the Web sites of several manufacturers, I was unable to find a single mention of an upgrade, let alone an offer of one. If you can figure out what kind of modem you have, the modem maker's Web site is probably a better place to look. In the interest of research, I tried upgrading my 3Com U.S. Robotics modem. At the Web site, www.3com.com/56k/usr/upgrade/, I was asked to find a product code on the bottom of the unit and click it in an on-screen list. Two clicks later, the site confirmed that I was entitled to a free upgrade and invited me to click on the Upgrade Now button. A 1.2-megabyte file downloaded in about 3 minutes and 45 seconds. Installing and running it took a few minutes more and would have been quicker had I not stopped to ponder the meaning of messages about possibly having to pay for the improvement. Those messages, it turned out, were actually meant only for people upgrading from some of the company's pre-56K models. The software's three-minute long-distance call to a Chicago area code at my expense finished the job. But the next time I booted the machine, the Windows 95 plug-and-play system saw my modem as a different model from the one it knew about yet apparently failed to install the proper driver software for it, which could cause several annoying problems down the road. Moreover, no documentation mentioned the need to switch several software settings from the "old" modem to the "new." But everything seemed to work fine until I tried to file this column by modem. Then, the only way I could solve the problem and connect was adding the command "S32=66" to the connection string in a hard-to-find place to turn off the V.90 code. The lessons: When buying a 56K modem or getting one with a computer, you still need to make sure it will be compatible with the Internet provider's service. Since most modems on the shelves and in new machines are not V.90 yet, make sure whatever you buy can be upgraded easily at no cost. And look for deals letting you trade in older, slower models for new ones. If you already own a 56K modem and new software is available to upgrade it to V.90, wait until you are absolutely sure your Internet provider has done its own upgrading, probably sometime before the end of the year. Then, knowing that V.90 software should result in more robust and faster connections, and expecting some additional tweaking to be necessary, fearlessly do the deed. Still, after all that, you are likely to discover that no matter which standard you use, 56K is merely a pleasant improvement, not a synonym for "blazing." If you use the Web a lot, you will soon start wishing for another standard entirely, like the cable or the digital subscriber line, commonly known as D.S.L., phone modems that are slowly beginning to rewrite the definition of "fast." body: Buffett Says Cheap Stocks Were Tough to Find in '97 Warren Buffett, who built his reputation by buying stocks that were destined to soar, says he is having a hard time finding new investments that look cheap. So last year, he began selling some of the stocks his company, Berkshire Hathaway, had acquired over the decades. In Berkshire Hathaway's annual report, Mr. Buffett wrote that the company cut back on three of its largest holdings: Walt Disney, Wells Fargo and Freddie Mac. Floyd Norris: Market Place.  Page D2. title: Filtering the Internet
body: Less than a year after the Supreme Court struck down the 1996 Communications Decency Act, which banned distribution of indecent material to minors on the Internet, Congress is again considering legislation that would harm free speech in the name of protecting children. A bill sponsored by Senator John McCain, Republican of Arizona, would require schools and libraries to install anti-pornography filters on their computers in order to receive Federal funds for Internet hook-ups. But recognizing potential opposition from educators and librarians, Mr. McCain kept open the possibility that a compromise would be offered when the bill reached the Senate floor. The desire to protect children from pornography is understandable. Many parents have used filtering software at home. But such filters often miss some of the smut and block material that is not pornographic. The hazards posed by the McCain bill are playing out in a lawsuit in Loudoun County, Va. The library board installed on every terminal the X-Stop software filter, which blocked access to scores of non-sex-related Web sites, including those sponsored by the Quakers and the American Association of University Women. The library system is being sued by library users and publishers of Web pages for violating their First Amendment rights. The McCain bill could inflict the same problems on schools and libraries across the country. All school computers would have to use filters, and public libraries would have to have at least one machine with a filter. Senator Conrad Burns of Montana has offered a more sensible approach. His substitute bill would require schools and libraries that want the Federal Internet subsidies to adopt appropriate Internet use policies for children as they see fit. Many public institutions have already done so, without denying students or adults access to huge swaths of information. Given the limitations of filtering technology, the best way to protect children is to teach them how to use the Internet. A software program simply cannot do that.

title:
Taking In the Sites;
Tuning Into the Music of Developing Nations
body: Once upon a time, before the Internet had pictures and was all the rage, Quincy Jones, the music impresario, sat with William H. Gates, the computer magnate, at a technology conference, talking about the future. The year was 1992, and the conversation was a melding of the two titans' respective passions: the preservation of musical cultures and the nascent on-line universe that would become cyberspace. It took six years to realize a complete fusion of the vision that emerged that night. On Wednesday, Mr. Jones will introduce Qradio, a venture that marries the Internet to his advocacy of the rich, varied and largely unknown music of developing nations. "Web radio," a technology that transmits audio programming to Internet-connected personal computers, offers the potential to reach a wide audience at a fraction of the cost of traditional broadcasting. "It's a different sort of landscape, a 21st-century language," Mr. Jones said of the Internet. But while his site is devoted to music, unlike broadcast radio, it is not limited to sound. Rather, it is a multimedia product of which actual radio is only a part. Though it is being formally introduced this week, Qradio began in February with an initial focus on South Africa. It offers a data base of South African musicians, including biographies, discographies and sample clips, a multimedia history of musical evolution in the region and continuous feeds of three of the South African Broadcasting Corporation's 16 radio stations. Qradio, which was started with $5 million in private investments, plans to sell advertising, but it hopes to derive revenue from the sale of CD's and audio tapes marketed by means of on-line music samples. Mr. Jones and his partners in the venture say they hope eventually to broaden the site to embrace music from other parts of Africa, as well as from the Americas. Ultimately, it could serve as a medium for breeding new species of music, but for now, Mr. Jones suggests that the goal is to build bridges between cultures and technological classes. "Here we are, entering the next century," he said. "That number with three zeroes behind it is very heavy. It's ironic -- here we are dealing with the Internet and some of these people in South Africa don't have electricity." Adam Clayton Powell 3d, a lifelong friend and former employee of Mr. Jones, said the seed that germinated into Qradio was a 1991 trip that the two of them took to South Africa just as that nation's legacy of apartheid was collapsing. At the time, Mr. Powell said, the two men discussed the feasibility of a cable channel to promote the various indigenous musical cultures of the region, but the costs for such a venture were prohibitive. Even then, Mr. Powell said, the notion of using on-line technologies as a delivery mechanism piqued Mr. Jones's interest. "We have got to come back," to South Africa, Mr. Powell, now the vice president for technology and programs of the Freedom Forum in Arlington, Va., recalls his friend saying. It would take the development of the World Wide Web and the technology known as streaming audio before the possibility of on-line radio transmission would be realized. But the technology alone cannot insure that anyone will be listening, and industry analysts question whether a medium born in the 1920's will ever find an acceptable fit in the medium of the millennium. "To put radio on the Internet is not what it's all about," said Alan Brody, an independent media analyst in Scarsdale, N.Y. "It's like using TV to broadcast shipbuilding information. It's a cute idea but that's not where the future is. The future is in personalizing what we hear on the radio." Mr. Powell disagreed. Now that virtually all new personal computers are equipped with audio capability, more people than ever will use the Web as a platform for radio-like programming. "Radio is the most ubiquitous medium we have," Mr. Powell said. "It's a form familiar to us as a species. We have a long tradition of oral history, and this fits that tradition." What is more, Qradio starts at a time when music is among the few real success stories in the on-line marketing efforts lumped together under the term electronic commerce. At-Plan, a marketing research firm, says its latest data show that CD's and tapes are the fifth- most-popular product sold on the Web, bought by 1.3 million people in the last quarter of 1997 and that more than 12 million people visit music-oriented Web sites in a typical 30-day period. The question with Qradio, as it is with many new on-line ventures, is whether enough visitors will frequent and shop at a niche Web site to make it financially viable. Distinguishing oneself in new media, experts in on-line broadcasting say, demands a delicate balancing act -- a product that is narrowly focused enough that an audience cannot get it elsewhere yet of broad enough appeal to support advertising and direct on-line sales. Many other players in the medium are embracing a more horizontal strategy. The print publishing group Imagine Media of Brisbane, Calif., which specializes in computer-oriented magazines, last week started a new Internet service called Imagine Radio, a group of 20 original radio stations created just for the Web. Audio Net, a Dallas-based company that has been in the streaming audio business for two and a half years, offers 260 radio and television stations from around the country, plus some 400 special events each day. "When you're in your car you've got 30 radio stations," said Audio Net's president, Mark Cuban. "On TV, there are 20 to 100 stations. On the Net, you have millions. That's why the economics of the stand-alone radio doesn't work. It's expensive to be successful. It's really easy to get in the door. It's difficult to make money." Vern Fotheringham, a founding partner of Qradio, said: "The more people who denigrate Internet opportunities, the better I like it. It means there are fewer people out there trying to build fallow content. We're about marrying the capture of content while everyone is looking at it as a substandard, living today but prospering in the future. But after 50 years in the music business, Mr. Jones says that what is most important is encouraging the development of a medium that speaks to people across cultures and economic levels. "It's very important that the urban voice gets in there," he said. "You know -- a PC in every pot."
