title: Taxing Sales on the Internet: Many Governors vs. Congressional Legislation
body: Buoyed by White House support and facing only tepid opposition from the nation's governors, Silicon Valley has state and local tax collectors on the defensive: Congress is on the verge of passing legislation that would effectively bar sales taxes on Internet transactions until 2004. "The outcome is not in doubt," said Representative Christopher Cox, Republican of California, who is sponsoring the Internet Tax Freedom Act in the House. The bill responds to fears that a thicket of conflicting taxes will choke off the growth of Internet commerce, in particular inhibiting its use by small businesses that could not cope with the burden of the paperwork. But some analysts -- and many governors -- worry that a Federal moratorium would set a precedent that would permanently deprive state and local governments of a huge potential revenue source. "If we don't tax Internet commerce now, it will never be taxed," said William Gale, an economist at the Brookings Institution, the research group in Washington. With a few exceptions, states have made little effort to tax Internet service providers like America Online. Retail sales through the Internet are, in theory, covered by "use" taxes that require consumers to pay taxes in their home states no matter where they buy. But under Supreme Court rulings, one state cannot compel a merchant in another to collect use taxes unless the merchant has a substantial business presence in the state where the buyer lives. That has not prevented businesses from imagining a day when states try to tax Internet use. In a survey of executives from large retailers and media corporations conducted by KPMG Peat Marwick in 1996, half said that tax ambiguities had already tempered plans for Internet commerce. And Senator Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, along with Representative Cox, has been leading the charge for a legislative remedy. The Senate and House bills that have emerged from committee would bar taxes on monthly Internet access charges until January 2002. State and local governments would remain free to tax purchases made on the Internet, but the Cox-Wyden bill would bar attempts to go beyond the limits on out-of-state collection set by the Supreme Court. "The states would be no less able to collect sales taxes than they are today," Mr. Cox said. Many tax specialists sympathize with efforts to avoid discriminatory taxes on Internet service providers. "States are notorious for their inconsistencies, taxing services on a hit-or-miss basis," said Joel Slemrod, an economist at the University of Michigan's business school. By the same token, many sympathize with the problems that businesses -- particularly "mom and pop" stores expanding onto the Internet -- potentially face in selling to customers in thousands of different tax districts. But they are wary of precedents that effectively put Internet sales out of bounds to state and local tax collectors. "Internet commerce is small today," Mr. Gale said, "but what happens to local tax bases when the Net becomes a major presence in retailing?" With flat-out opposition to the Internet legislation no longer a realistic option now that the President and the Governors of newyork, California and Virginia have taken a stance in favor of the Cox-Wyden bill, the National Governors' Association is pressing an alternative. Led by Gov. Michael O. Leavitt of Utah and Gov. Roy Romer of Colorado, the association is willing to accept a permanent prohibition on taxing access to the Internet. But in return, it wants Washington to give individual states a powerful incentive to create a single consolidated tax on out-of-state purchases, both electronic and mail order. The association's proposal would override the Supreme Court ruling by requiring large vendors to collect use taxes on behalf of states as long as the states conformed to a single tax structure. "Now is the time for a system that creates a level playing filed for all sellers," Governor Leavitt said. But the governors' approach faces strong opposition. Although their bill would meet the primary objective of Internet service providers, it would also open Internet commerce to taxation. "We see this as a new tax that would generate $16 billion in revenue by the year 2000," Senator Wyden said. Probably more important, it would tie Internet tax legislation to the fate of the states' attempts to forcemail-order vendors to collect taxes from out-of-state customers. And because there is hardly a ground swell for such a move in Congress, there might be no legislation at all -- a result that would not unduly disturb most opponents of the Internet Tax Freedom Act. The governors, it is generally conceded, are playing a weak political hand. House leaders are promising a floor vote on the Cox-Wyden bill this month. And last week, Senator Trent Lott, the majority leader, predicted that the bill would come to a vote in the Senate by May. The real question, then, is whether the governors can salvage a compromise with the bill's Congressional sponsors. "I'm persuaded there is still a lot of common ground here," Governor Leavitt said.

title:
The Law Where There Is No Land;
A Legal System Built on Precedents Has Few of Them in the Digital World - Correction Appended
body: Cyberspace, only yesterday the proud Wild West of the information age, is rapidly being settled and tamed. The best evidence is a sudden -- and some might say alarming -- infestation by a new species, the cyberlawyers. They seem to be everywhere. Last month, at the Computers, Freedom and Privacy conference -- an annual gathering once dominated by hackers and security agents -- they clogged panels with subjects like "Government jurisdiction over cyberspace transactions." Each week, they post hundreds of messages to their own "Cyberia" email list, pondering matters like "Usenet Death Penalty -- Legal?" And a pack of cyberlawyers are petitioning the White House for access to its planned conference on Internet privacy. The nation's top law schools are vying to dominate an area of jurisprudence called cyberlaw, while law firms promoting such practices are becoming as ubiquitous as spam email. And court dockets are swelling with digital-age disputes of "first impression." Whatever happened to the electronic frontier? Perhaps, as they like to say in the legal trade, res ipsa loquitur -- the thing speaks for itself. The Internet has changed from a playground for like-minded libertarians to a workplace and social space for millions. The latest wave of settlers has little interest in the cyberstate of nature or the utopian manifestoes of pioneers, like John Perry Barlow's oft-cited "A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace," which defied any state's assertion of having control over the Internet. That is where the lawyers come in. "It's like when you start a colony," said Mike Godwin, chief counsel for the Electronic Frontier Foundation, an advocacy group that only a few years ago was practically alone in the field. "The first thing you do is you find out where the water is. The next thing you do is form couples, start families. The notion of having law, which is a way to order social interactions, only happens after you have a lot of social interactions such that they become problematic." But in a legal system that reveres precedent and relies on analogy, even defining the nature of an Internet-related dispute can be a source of contention. Consider just a few of the pending cases and the questions they raise across a range of legal doctrines: *The unitedstates Government sues the Microsoft Corporation, charging it with antitrust violations. How is monopoly measured in an information age? *A White House aide, Sidney Blumenthal, sues an Internet gossip columnist, Matt Drudge, for libel. What is the burden of proof and what are the remedies for libel on the Internet, where everyone can be a publisher? Moreover, can Mr. Drudge be sued in the District of Columbia for an item that he posted on his World Wide Web site in Los Angeles? *America Online sues for an injunction against multiple distributors of junk email. Is such "spam" mail a violation of privacy? Would attempts to block it violate the First Amendment? *A mathematics professor is suing the unitedstates Government for denying his application to send an encryption program over the Internet. Should the Government be able to prevent him on national security grounds, or would that violate his free-speech rights? Cindy Cohn, the lawyer representing the math professor, said it was in part the lure of the unknown that made cyberspace law so appealing. "It's a chance to think about first-level questions," said Ms. Cohn, a partner in the McGlashan & Sarrail firm in San Mateo, Calif. "With nine-tenths of my other cases, the same issue has already been decided. With this, you can say maybe you need to think in a new way about it." Ms. Cohn is scheduled to testify tomorrow before a Senate Judiciary Committee subcommittee on proposed encryption legislation. Not everyone is as sanguine about the prospect of a clean legal slate. What is at stake, legal experts say, is whether the values that evolved over two centuries of case law will apply in cyberspace -- and what those decisions will teach us about the law in real space. "There is anxiety, yes," said Judge Stewart Dalzell, a Federal circuit court judge. Alluding to his role last year in overturning the Communications Decency Act, a landmark decision for cyberspace law that was later upheld by the Supreme Court, Judge Dalzell recalled: "I know going in that when I started to hear the testimony I went, 'Oh my God! Oh my God! I have to learn about packet switching?' And had we gone down the wrong path, it could have done immense mischief to the medium." As judges and lawyers search for metaphors, elite law schools are scurrying to stake their claims as the center of legal theory that will make sense of it all -- and to lure cutting-edge law professors and attract students eager to enter what looks to be a lucrative new field of practice. Earlier this month, Harvard Law School said it had received a $5.4 million donation from the estate of Jack N. Berkman, an alumnus, and his wife, Lillian R. Berkman to support its Center for Internet and Society, which was established last year and is overseen by Jonathan Zittrain, the executive director. Professor Charles Nesson, the center's director, said the money would be used in part to experiment with opening up the gates of the august institution to the general public. More than 1,000 people have enrolled in Privacy in Cyberspace, the center's first free no-credit course offered over the Internet. The gift will also endow a professorship. First to be named to the Berkman chair was Lawrence Lessig, whose appointment by a Federal district judge as special master in the Government's antitrust case against Microsoft did much to raise the profile of the nascent field of cyberspace legal theory. (Mr. Lessig's investigation has been suspended pending an appeals court decision on the propriety of his appointment.) Not to be outdone, Harvard's longtime rival, Yale Law School, made Mr. Lessig a standing job offer as part of its effort to jump-start its Information Society Project. The school has offered visiting professorships to two intellectual property experts: James A. Boyle from American University and Robert Mergess, the co-director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Technology at the University of California. "Yale is going to be the place to be for cyberlaw," said Jack Balkin, director of the school's program. "What happened at Yale is, nobody came to us and said, 'Here's some money. Go found a technology center.' This was something we identified as a priority." Yale's stance is making other schools nervous. "The competition has definitely heated up," said Pam Samuelson, who helped found Berkeley's center two years ago and hopes that Mr. Mergess will stay put. Ms. Samuelson, a leading critic of the Clinton Administration's proposal to adapt copyright law to cyberspace, said Berkeley's advantage was being in the midst of the industry that is creating so many of today's legal challenges. Ms. Samuelson said that centers like Berkeley's would teach different skills and values than the traditional law school curriculum has taught. "Rather than trying to develop fixed sets of black-letter law rules that you can memorize and then apply, this requires that students learn to be supple and adaptable," Ms. Samuelson said. Although by most accounts Harvard, Yale and Berkeley have the strongest offerings, expertise in the field has spread. Michael Froomkin at the University of Miami has published several articles on law and cryptography, for example; Dan L. Burk at Seton Hall University is an expert on jurisdictional issues in cyberspace. David Post, co-founder of the Cyberspace Law Institute and now a professor at Temple University Law School, is at the center of an active debate among lawyers about whether the emergence of cyberspace requires a whole new legal model. "There is a division between the incrementalists and the radicals," Mr. Post said. "To me it makes more sense to think of this as a separate domain of interaction that's going to have its own rules." The stress that the new technology places on existing law has provoked some scholars to argue that cyberspace needs laws of its own in areas like copyright and privacy. Others wonder whether at a time when private companies wield power over on-line behavior by computer code, constitutional principles should regulate private as well as state action. But many legal scholars scoff at the notion that cyberspace presents the need for a new discipline. Among them is Judge Frank Easterbrook of the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit and a professor at the University of Chicago. In an article for the University of Chicago Law Review titled "Cyberspace and the Law of the Horse," Judge Easterbrook warned of "multidisciplinary dilettantism." A law of cyberspace makes about as much sense as a law of horses, he said. Still, even critics agree that the emergence of cyberspace is forcing the deepest and most critical consideration in years of law in general. "Maybe dividing the world up into real space and cyberspace is artificial," said Brian Dally, 26, a student in Mr. Lessig's cyberspace law class.  "What really came rushing to the fore for me in this class is that this should give us pause to examine some of our basic understandings about the purpose of government and the purpose of law." Correction  An article in Business Day last Monday about the emerging field of cyberspace law misidentified the publication that carried an article titled "Cyberspace and the Law of the Horse," by Judge Frank Esterbrook of the unitedstates Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, in which he argues against the idea that the Internet creates a need for a new legal discipline. The publication was the University of Chicago Legal Forum, not the University of Chicago Law Review. Lawrence Lessing, left, Charles Nesson and Jonathon Zittrain are seeking to make Harvard Law School a leading authority in the new area. (Photograph by Peter DaSilva for The New York Times top and Evan Richman for The New York Times)  Chart: "Digital Docket" Increasingly, the spread of computers and on-line interactions and transactions is creating new case law. Here is a sampling of the new kinds of cases and the legal fields affected.  CRIMINAL LAW U.S. v. Thomas, 1996 U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit Federal criminal obscenity case. A California couple used email and a modem to market and sell pornography. One customer was an undercover U.S. Postal Inspector in Tennessee. The court upheld defendants' convictions in Tennessee for violating Federal obscenity laws through their operation of an electronic bulletin board from California.  CIVIL PROCEDURE/TRADEMARK Panavision Int'l, L.P. v. Toeppen, 1996 unitedstates District Court, Central District of California An Illinois resident reserved Internet domain names, like Panavision, that were trademarks of well-known companies, then attempted to resell or license the domain names back to the trademark holders. The court held he could be sued in California for trademark infringement.  TORTS Cubby, Inc. v. CompuServe Inc., 1991 U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York Cubby claimed that it was defamed by a newsletter published by a third-party but carried on CompuServe and that CompuServe was liable because it had republished the work. The court found that CompuServe had little editorial control over the publication and was more like a book store or public library and thus was not liable for damages.  CONSTITUTIONAL LAW Reno v. American Civil Liberties Union, 1997 unitedstates Supreme Court The Supreme Court struck down as unconstitutional, on First Amendment grounds, provisions of the Communications Decency Act that criminalized the knowing transmission of indecent messages to minors. The court found the provisions prohibiting such transmissions were in violation of the First Amendment protection of freedom of speech.

title: With Goto.com's Search Engine, the Highest Bidder Shall Be Ranked First
body: In the world of Internet search services, finding just the right business model is proving as elusive as finding an entirely relevant list of search results. But the effort can be seen on the Web sites of all the industry's most familiar names. Yahoo, the biggest of the dozens of sites devoted to navigating the Web, is looking more like a commercial on-line service every day, with "channels" that organize information into categories. Likewise, Excite and Lycos have also added chat rooms, electronic mail and a wide range of original content like news, financial services, shopping and local entertainment guides. And earlier this month, Infoseek announced its entry into electronic commerce, adding travel-booking and home-buying services. "The function of searching has become a commodity," said Alan Braverman, Internet analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston. "So search engine companies are making a transition into Internet media companies." And as they do, consumers are changing the way they use them. Search engines were originally developed to help Internet users find what they were looking for among the millions of pages on the World Wide Web, and as such they were judged solely by how well -- and how quickly -- they matched key words to results. Today, however, searching is only one small reason people go to sites like Yahoo, Lycos, Infoseek and Excite. On Yahoo, for example, only one out of three users goes there to search, said Jerry Yang, co-founder of the company, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif. The rest of the time, they go there to use other Yahoo features like email or chat services or Yahoo Finance, which has become one of the most popular financial sites on the Web. "We certainly are becoming more on-line service-like," he said. "But that doesn't make our navigation service any less important." It does, however, mean visitors to sites like Yahoo and Excite tend to stay longer -- and potentially do more -- than if the site offered only searching. And that has translated into more advertising. Last year, Yahoo was the top ad-supported Web site for the second consecutive year, generating $53.2 million in advertising, according to the Electronic Advertising and Marketplace Report. That is up 180 percent from $19.0 million in 1996. Excite ranked second of all Web sites, generating $40.2 million in advertising in 1997. Despite a huge growth in advertising, profits have been elusive for all but Yahoo and Lycos, which had its first profitable quarter in 1997. Infoseek stumbled as it struggled with management changes, and has since refocused itself toward consumers rather than businesses. Excite lost money last year, though analysts appear bullish on its prospects. But while Yahoo and others are trying to turn their sites into destinations in themselves, an ambitious start-up is taking an entirely different approach. Goto.com, a spinoff of Idealab, a self-described business incubator based in Los Angeles, says it will focus entirely on searching and on making money by encouraging Web sites to pay for more prominent placement in the search results. Rather than ranking search results according to where and how often certain key words appear, as conventional search engines do, Goto.com actually ranks results according to how much sites are willing to pay. The service posts the per-word pricing in an open auction, allowing Web sites to continually bid for higher placement on a given topic. Goto.com then requests that visitors vote on the quality and relevance of search results -- information that is later used to improve future searches. Bill Gross, president of Idealab, said an important difference between his approach and that of other search sites was that Goto.com was not trying to become a media company. "They make money when you stay -- I make money when you leave," Mr. Gross said, comparing his service to the Yellow Pages. "We're changing the alignment of the proposition. We really are a true search engine." By letting a combination of market forces and user feedback determine the results of searches, Goto.com will actually provide better results, he said. "We're not letting a blind algorithm decide," Mr. Gross said. Mr. Gross said the Web had simply become too large for the conventional search approach of matching key words. But, his critics say, a true search engine is exactly what Goto.com is not. Its "pay for placement" approach leads to skewed results, they argue, particularly when the information being sought is not readily available on a commercial site. Yet Mr. Gross insists that nonprofit groups, universities and even medical organizations will find it in their interests to pay for placement. "There's almost always a way that someone will make money by having you come to a site," he said. "Even if it's philanthropic, it wants your attention." And if some sites do not care to pay, they will still appear in the search result -- at the bottom of the list of paid sites. That way, at least, users will know where to find the smallest sites, rather than having them mixed in with larger, typically commercial sites. Perhaps one reason for industry skepticism is that "pay for placement" has already been tested. Two years ago, the Open Text Corporation, then a search service, allowed advertisers to pay for premium placement in search results. But the practice was quickly abandoned when consumers complained. "We got a pretty strong emotional response," said Abe Kleinfield, a vice president at Open Text, based in Waterloo, Ontario. "People thought it was immoral." But the difference in approach is important: Open Text did not tell users that it was allowing companies to pay for higher placement; Goto.com is open about the practice. But regardless of the approach, Goto.com may not succeed simply because it is so late to the market, analysts say. "I wouldn't be bullish on any newcomer," Mr. Braverman said. Success today comes from branding and distribution, and Yahoo and a few others are going to be tough competitors on both counts. "The main reason people go to Yahoo is habit," he said. Rather than embrace new entries, he said, the market is likely to favor more consolidation. Mr. Gross is confident that his strategy will work. "What these guys have is traffic, but they don't have a good business model," he said. title: Maker of Software That Pinpoints Problems
body: LESS than a year ago, when America Online, one of the largest internet service providers, crashed, making it impossible for subscribers on the Eastern Seaboard to gain access to the Internet, chaos reigned for eight hours. In another systems scenario, when a customer trying to withdraw money from an A.T.M., was told the system was down, his reaction was apoplectic. "Besides the inconvenience and possible harm to customers, the cost of downtime to business is astronomical," said Shaula Alexander Yemini, president of Smarts, formally known as System Management Arts, a high-tech company in White Plains engaged in the development of software products to pinpoint the cause of network failures so they can quickly be corrected. "As for the example of the A.T.M., what it indicates is that there is a network failure somewhere in the bank's national computer network," Ms. Yemini said. "Is the problem with leased telephone lines or with its data center 2,000 miles away? Or perhaps the hardware or software is causing the trouble. And it is trouble that impacts on all functions of the bank. Tellers can't make deposits or withdrawals. End-of-the-day records can't be compiled, which leads to fines. It's a bad state of affairs." The cost of downtime to business is staggering, she said. "In the brokerage industry it is estimated at $100,000 a minute. For service companies, the loss is $100,000 for 15 minutes of downtime, and in the manufacturing sector the cost is estimated at $100,000 for every 30 minutes of downtime. The cost to corporations of network downtime has increased 600 percent since 1994." An industry consulting concern, Northeast Consulting, based in Boston, estimates that trouble-shooting, trying to find the root of the problem, contributes to more than 80 percent of the downtime. "In a network system when one thing fails, there's usually an avalanche of other events that fail," Ms. Yemini said. "Since each problem causes a cascade of alarms, network operators would try manually to figure out the root cause of problems on their network. That kind of trouble-shooting is a complex, long, tedious process, prone to errors. And if a misdiagnosis is made, applying the wrong fixes can exacerbate the problem." Developing a software product that would automatically identify the source of failure in a network had long been a goal for Ms. Yemini. Fulfilling the goal meant she had to leave a prestigious research management position at the Thomas Watson Research Center of International Business Machines in Yorktown Heights to embark on a start- up venture of her own. "Frankly, I was scared to death," she said about going out on her own. "Although I was one of the few women in management at I.B.M.'s research center, I was in charge of some remarkable projects. I built a software prototype for I.B.M., which I took on the road for two years, visiting every I.B.M. facility to get concurrence for it. And it almost got to be a product, until the last minute, when one person shot it down." The experience proved so frustrating that Ms. Yemini, who had spent almost her entire career with I.B.M. and won awards for her design work, said she felt at that point it was doubtful she would ever have an impact on the corporation. "I.B.M. was ideal for research," she said. "I had helped pioneer the development of a distribution system in 1988 that touched upon every part of the computer industry, but by 1993 I was interested in harnessing years of scientific research to develop software products I could bring to market." And so Ms. Yemini left I.B.M. and in March 1993 she and her co- founder, her former husband, Yechiam Yemini -- a scientific adviser and board member of the company and a professor of computer science at Columbia University -- rented an office at 199 Main Street in White Plains for their new company. "We financed the start-up from savings, and with my brother's help," Ms. Yemini recalled. "We needed a lot of capital to buy equipment. But early on we got a multimillion contract from Motorola Communications to develop products for them. We also received a small-business innovative grant and in April 1997 a private equity placement of $5 million from the Soros Group, led by the financier George Soros. Their participation confirms our faith in future prospects for Smarts and gives us the resources to achieve our goals of becoming the market leader in automated management solutions, a huge and rapidly growing market." Smarts' breakthrough product, In Charge, took more than three years to develop. It is the first in a family of products shipped to customers a year ago and is the industry's first software product that automatically identifies the root cause of network system problems and determines their impact. Ms. Yemini said the root-cause-analysis process "can tell you what broke even if the thing that's broken isn't being monitored." She added: "It reduces trouble-shooting time from hours to seconds and downtime up to 80 percent. The most important property is that the system self-adjusts when you change the configuration of the network. There's never any reprogramming to be done once the system is installed." But setting up In Charge can take anywhere from several days to two months, depending on the complexity of the network models, she said. In Charge, which costs $25,000 a copy and anywhere from $30,000 to $1 million a site, has already been installed at 20 sites, with 20 additional sites under review. Initial users include telecommunications and enterprise networks of several Fortune 100 companies. Smarts has moved to larger quarters at 14 Mamaroneck Avenue, and its work force now numbers 35. "Most of them are highly trained technical people, creative types who enjoy working on cutting-edge projects," Ms. Yemini said. "And so do I. My work is also my hobby." A native of Israel, Ms. Yemini attributes her unaccented English to the years she spent as a child in the unitedstates. "We lived in newyork from the time I was 5 until I was 9, while my father was buying communications equipment for the Israeli Army," she said. "I went to P.S. 6 on the East Side, and I remember those days fondly." Later on, after the family returned to Israel, Ms. Yemini, who had a liking for math and science, became one of seven women to major in math and physics at Hebrew University in Jerusalem. "Four dropped out, so only three of us graduated." she said. "The university is known for its math department, considered to be one of the best in the world." She came back to the unitedstates to earn a doctorate in computer science at the University of California at Los Angeles. "And I never went home again, that is with the exception of a one-year assignment from I.B.M. to manage a scientific center in Haifa," she said. "I visit Israel, but I've lived in Briarcliff Manor for years, and I love it." title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
A Voice for the Irish
body: No shamrocks or leprechauns here. "Traditional musicians and their year-round fans view St. Patrick's Day in the same jaundiced light that seasoned drinkers see New Year's Eve: it's amateur night," said Don Meade in his column On the Fiddle, a regular feature of a Web site called Irish Voice Online. Music events on "Paddy's Day," he continues, "tend to attract a lot of once-a-year, 'Kiss-me-I'm-Irish' types who can't tell a hornpipe from a gaspipe." Behold Ireland for the Irish (and the Irish in America). Mr. Meade, who is Irish-American, also writes for the Manhattan weekly newspaper Irish Voice. It was founded some 10 years ago as a forum for Irish immigrants, who were flocking, legally and illegally, to the Northeast when Ireland's economy took a nasty spill in the 1980's. A rudimentary version of the paper went up on the Web in summer 1996. The latest site, with many of the articles in the newsstand version, went up last August. "We are still writing for the Irish newly arrived," said Darina Molloy, 27, a former reporter for The Connaught Telepgraph in County mayo who came to newyork in 1994. Besides writing and reporting for the Irish Voice, she also organizes stories for the Web. "But we've also tride to expand the audience to Irish-Americans and to anyone interested in Ireland and Irish affairs," she said. The number of visitors to the site, while still small, is growing quickly. Weekly hits, or page views, are averaging 3,000, up from 800 hits a week last fall. The Irish Voice says the newspaper's circulation is 65,000. WHAT YOU SEE Irish Voice Online covers news about the Republic of Ireland, Northern Ireland and Irish communities in America, especially those in the newyork region. An article on Feb. 11 by Ms. Molloy, for example, reported that recent Irish immigrants were returning to a newyork institution where their numbers had been dwindling: the newyork City Police Department. An article on March 4 bearing the headline " 'I Owe Nothing,' Says gertie Byrne," brings readers up to date on a complex lawsuit pitting two Irishmen in County Mayo against an Irish-American woman in newyork over a festival held at Yonkers Raceway in 1994. OUTSIDE LINKS Scores, including news groups and chat rooms in Scottish Gaelic, Irish Gaelic and Manx, a nearly extinct language spoken on the Isle of Man. WHAT YOU GET A work in progress. Ms. Molloy says the newspaper's first priority is to establish digital archives so more than one issue at a time can be displayed on the Web. title: Battle Cry of the Technorealists
body: ANDREW SHAPIRO, a 29-year-old writer, was commiserating over lunch in Greenwich Village one day last summer with a fellow author, David Shenk. Their problem: in writing and speaking, they spend a lot of time in linguistic contortions, trying to explain that they neither love nor hate technology. Unlike previous generations, they have grown up with technology. They don't expect it to bring about utopia, nor do they demonize it. So they gathered a half-dozen like-minded friends -- and friends of friends -- and dubbed themselves the technorealists. Their goal, Mr. Shapiro said, is to infuse shades of gray into a debate that has until now been black and white, and to bring a more realistic dialogue to the topic of technology. "We're trying to find a more nuanced, balanced and accurate way to discuss these things," Mr. Shapiro said. The technorealists have taken as their adversaries the older commentators who tend to divide themselves into camps for or against technology. Most prominent is a cadre of self-appointed guides to the information age: Esther Dyson, computer cognoscente; John Perry Barlow, co-founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and George Gilder, libertarian writer. As Mr. Shapiro sees it, these so-called cyberlibertarians tend to romanticize technology, particularly the Internet. They have long argued for a hands-off approach by government in most matters related to cyberspace. All of this would be little more than an intellectual exercise if it were not that the reigning experts can have a hand in guiding public policy on Internet-related issues. Mr. Shapiro said Ms. Dyson and others had helped influence a laissez-faire approach toward electronic commerce that the Clinton Administration outlined last summer, the idea that business conducted over the rapidly growing Internet should be allowed to flourish without government regulation. Technorealism is codified in a 1,100-word announcement and manifesto that the group published on the World Wide Web for release today. Although painfully obvious in parts ("information is not knowledge"), the document argues pointedly against complete freedom from government control of cyberspace. Government, the group states, has an important role to play on the electronic frontier. Copyright needs protection, but not at the expense of fair use. And privacy protection is too important to be left completely to the private sector. Mr. Shenk, 31, is known for his book "Data Smog." Mr. Shapiro, a fellow at Harvard Law School's Center for Internet and Society, has written widely on the topic of technology and politics. Steven Johnson, 29, the group's third founder, is the editor in chief of Feed, an on-line magazine. Their chosen opponents argue that the difference in opinions is largely in the minds of the technorealists. Mr. Barlow said: "They think I'm a techno-utopian. I'm not that big a fool." Ms. Dyson said that while she might be more optimistic than most people about technology's potential, she agreed with many of the techno realists' principles. Moreover, she said, the very formation of the group, which crystallized through email exchanges and the group's Web site, bolsters her own position. "I say that solutions come not just from the market, or the government," she said, "but from individual action, and the Web gives you much more of a way to do that." To have one's views aired, Ms. Dyson said, "you used to have to bribe a politician or buy a newspaper. Now you put up a Web site." In this case, that site can be found at www.technorealism.org.

title:
DOWNTIME;
Every Day's a Music Festival on the Web
body: THE Web is alive with the sound of music. International record labels and unsigned songsmiths alike offer Internet audio samples of their newest releases. Fans of Pearl Jam, U2 and other major bands get advance copies of their idols' latest albums from industry sources and illicitly post them on the Net before they reach the stores. "Cybercasters" transmit on-line programs, like the Allman Brothers Band concerts in newyork, scheduled for Friday and Saturday, that will be heard live on the Rocktropolis site (www.rocktropolis.com). And on-line CD retailers offer catalogues with try-before-you-buy song clips attached. "I've discovered bands that I'm totally into now because I heard them on the Web," said Nicolle Neulist, a 15-year-old in Raleigh, N.C. Music distribution on the Web seems to make sense. Companies that sell music on line have recognized that a single, universally accessible on-line record shop can be less costly and more efficient to operate than a national chain of bricks-and-mortar stores and can be more convenient for consumers. It is an approach that booksellers like Amazon.com have already demonstrated. But music retailers are better able to capitalize on the multimedia capabilities of the Web, constructing huge on-line databases of recordings that are searchable by artist, title and genre. Many of the entries offer cover art, track listings and, most important, audio samples. A shopper can listen to snatches of thousands of titles, a capability that no record store can easily match. While the sheer diversity can spur exploration, there are still limitations. Half-minute excerpts are rarely sufficient to assess the merits of longer works. And, as in real stores, obscure artists and composers tend to be overlooked. Browsing through the CDnow site, for example, one can find samples for almost every Rolling Stones album, but a search for the minimalist composer Charlemagne Palestine will return citations only for Palestrina, the 16th-century classical composer. While the sites have made on-line credit-card payments an automated snap, software designed to recommend additional recordings can produce quirky results, like the CDnow suggestion that buyers of the "Sound of Music" soundtrack might also enjoy the Chemical Brothers' "Dig Your Own Hole." Of course, anyone expecting music over the Web to match the sound quality of a home stereo system may be disappointed, especially if the music is being squeezed through a telephone line and modem and played on the tiny, tinny speakers found with most personal computers. Even on fast modems rated at speeds up to 56,000 bits per second, audio transmitted over the Internet needs to be highly compressed, a software task that in some cases involves chopping out bits that the listener is least likely to miss. In "streaming audio," which can be used to transmit either live performances or recorded sound, the audio information tends to get compressed even further. Streaming audio is listened to as an incoming flow of sound instead of being downloaded and then played back. The need for compression and factors like Internet traffic jams can result in sound that is muffled, distorted or even subject to annoying gaps. Downloading a file completely before playing it back can, in some cases, lead to CD-quality sound. But that route is reserved for the patient because it can take an hour or more to capture a four-minute track. Storage is also a concern. That four-minute track can easily occupy 6.5 megabytes of hard-drive space. At that rate, an album-length work would use up 3 percent or more of a 2-gigabyte hard drive. High-capacity recording devices for PC's -- like recordable CD drives, now selling for less than $300, or the coming generation of high-density digital versatile disk, or DVD, recorders -- must become much more common before consumers will purchase entire albums over the Internet. Regardless of the type of audio format, your computer will need to have a playback program installed -- and frequently more than one. A number of these programs, called players, are available free on the Web. The instructions for them are generally good, although repeated downloading and installation efforts can be needed. Real Audio is the most prevalent player for streaming sound. For downloading recordings, Liquid Audio and a2b Music are battling to become the dominant format. People willing to wait out the lengthy downloading times may find their patience rewarded with surprisingly clear playback sound and stereo separation. But Ken Pohlmann, a music engineering professor at the University of Miami, challenges the industry's claims of CD-quality audio. "Just because they sound darn good doesn't mean they have the same fidelity as a CD," Professor Pohlmann said. For all the current drawbacks of Web music, though, many techies seem willing to endure less-than-perfect sound from the Internet. "We're all guilty of this," Professor Pohlmann conceded. "I'm sitting here in Florida listening on my computer to a live classical-music radio station from Seattle with Real Audio. It sounds pretty terrible. I can tune in the radio on a local classical-music station from Miami and hear excellent fidelity. But I listen to Seattle -- just because I can."  Some Sour Notes Along the Way A FEW intrepid companies have started to make entire pieces of music available via downloading. During my own recent test drives, these systems performed well, if not flawlessly. I had already downloaded and installed the Liquid Audio player and sent my name, address and credit-card information to Music Boulevard. Now I was ready to preview "Time Just Flew," an unreleased track by Peter Himmelman, a folk-rock artist. I agreed to have 99 cents charged to my credit card, then proceeded to pull down the song. Suddenly, time crawled. Although Music Boulevard estimated that it would take 30 minutes to download the tune, it took closer to 45. Then the player stalled a little more than two-thirds of the way through the 3-minute-28-second track. I tried three times to make it go past that, then called Music Boulevard's customer-support line and was instantly credited with another download. The file transfer took 52 minutes this time, but it was completed. Andrew Milne, senior developer for N2K Entertainment, the site's Manhattan-based producer, was puzzled by the flaw in my first download. "To the best of my knowledge," he said, "this is a rare occurrence."   MATTHEW MIRAPAUL  Site-Seeing: Music on the Web THE following sites are good starting points for finding the free software you are most likely to need to listen to music on the Web, listen to "cybercasts" and other free music and buy CD's or downloadable music on line.  Software  Real Networks: www.real.com Download Real Player, which includes Real Audio, the leading player software for listening to cybercasts and other streaming audio.  Liquid Audio: www.liquidaudio.com One of the two most common players for downloading music to store on your computer or other recording medium. (Requires a computer with at least 16 MB of RAM and a 100-MHz Pentium chip or 100-MHz PowerPC chip.)  a2b Music: www.a2bmusic.com The other most common player for downloading music. (Requires at least 16 MB of RAM and a 100-MHz Pentium chip.)  Cybercasts and Archives  Audio Net: www.audionet.com Cybercast directory, with links to concerts, radio broadcasts and talk shows, plus a streaming audio jukebox with 2,000 albums.  The DJ.com: www.theDJ.com More than 60 channels of continuously streaming music, divided into genres including ballads, classical, classic metal, jazz, big band and psychedelic.  Internet Underground Music Archive: www.iuma.com Sound clips for more than 1,000 independent musicians, searchable by genre.  Music Retailers  CDnow: www.cdnow.com CD retailer with sound clips attached to thousands of album entries in a searchable database. Similar sites include CD Universe, Tunes.Com and Soundstone.com: www.cduniverse.com www.tunes.com www.soundstone.com  Music Boulevard: www.musicblvd.com CD retailer with searchable database, sound samples and audio-enhanced discographies and music news. Offers more than 30 tracks to purchase via download at 99 cents each.  Muzic.com: www.muzic.com News and features on rock, and 250 tracks for sale at prices ranging from 50 cents to $2. title:
Turf;
When Banks Step Back, Middlemen Rush In
body: WHEN Lorraine Altman arrived for her first meeting with a mortgage broker, she came armed. From her perusal of the Internet the night before, she knew the current interest rates. From discussions with her real estate agent, she knew what type of loan she wanted. And from talking with her accountant, she knew exactly how much she wanted to spend on the monthly mortgage payment for the new $165,000 Upper East Side one-bedroom apartment she had picked out. The only thing this savvy 52-year-old Long Islander didn't know -- and was relying on the mortgage broker to tell her -- was where her mortgage would be coming from: a bank, a small investment group, an insurance company or a giant mortgage conglomerate. Ms. Altman, a job-training executive in Manhattan, found that getting a mortgage these days is a lot different from the way it was 17 years ago, when she bought a co-op in Great Neck, N.Y. "I never even heard of a mortgage broker when I bought my last co-op," she said. "I just walked into the Dime Savings around the corner." Times have changed. Real estate agents, brokers and bankers say that these days, home buyers are more inquiring, the old-line banks are more reluctant to lend and the mortgage brokers are a lot more reputable. In a decade, the number of mortgage brokers has tripled; the use of mortgage brokers has soared, from less than 20 percent to 52 percent. In Manhattan, the percentage is probably higher; experts estimate that mortgage brokers handle as much as 75 percent of all co-op loans. "Ten years ago, all top 10 lenders in the country were banks," said Neil Bader, the chief executive of Skyscraper Mortgage, one of the largest mortgage brokerage companies in newyork City. "Now, there's only two or three." Not only that, but customers are also more technologically plugged in. "Consumers are more adept at using the Internet, and bankers and mortgage brokers are, too," said Barbara Kent, a lawyer at the newyork State Banking Department. In response to dozens of requests from buyers, lawyers and brokers, she said, the state has proposed a new rule to allow mortgage applications to be filed over the World Wide Web. "newyork is the first state to address using the Internet to get a mortgage," she said. The Banking Department is currently gathering comments on the rule -- which contains the same protections for consumers as the old-fashioned transactions -- and said it might release the new rule sometime in April or May. It used to be a lot simpler. In the early 1980's, when Ms. Altman was getting her first mortgage, the prospective home buyer would stroll into a bank, brandishing a contract to buy a house. The banker might even know the place. There wouldn't be too much discussion about rates -- the percentage the bank charges to make the loan. There would be lots of forms, lots of hand-shaking, an appraisal and, finally, at the closing, the bank officer would appear with a check. The idea of a mortgage broker -- a middleman who would scout the market, find the best rate (even if it was from a lender in San Diego or Dallas), counsel and advise, and then do all the paperwork -- was almost unheard of. In the past, mortgage brokers often took their fees from the customer -- occasionally opening themselves to criticism that they were gouging the home buyer. Now, they increasingly take their commissions from the lender. In effect, the lender offers the broker a discount to do what the bank officers once did: things like filling out applications, scanning credit reports and arranging appraisals. For his fee, the broker takes the difference between the discount rate for the loan and the retail rate. (Regardless of how the fee is figured, reputable brokers say a customer should never pay more than if he walked into a bank.) Most of these changes have occurred since the mid-80's, when the states started registering mortgage brokers and many banks switched their focus away from residential mortgage lending. Now, customers complain that the banks have abandoned the off-the-street mortgage customer. The change, newyork Banking Department officials say, may be most noticeable in the savings banks. "Savings and loans did a tremendous mortgage business, and that definitely has lessened after the S.& L. crisis of the 80's," Mrs. Kent said. "They were encouraged to diversify, and the business that has left the savings banks has gone to mortgage brokers." (In 1987, those banks did 41 percent of the country's mortgage business; two years ago, they were down to 19 percent.) Banks still give mortgages, but many would rather let the mortgage broker stand between them and the customer. Even if a loyal bank customer gets a mortgage through his bank, he may find that his mortgage is sold shortly afterward to a different bank or a large consolidator. The March 2 issue of The National Mortgage News lists the top 50 mortgage lenders; only a handful can be considered old-fashioned banks in the sense that they have branches. Norwest Mortgage, based in Des Moines, is first, followed by Countrywide Home Loans of Pasadena, Calif. Chase Manhattan Mortgage of Edison, N.J., is third. In the newyork region, the only old-fashioned banks listed are Marine Midland (No. 29), in Depew, N.Y., and the Long Island Savings Bank (No. 45). To tie in to the big, out-of-state lenders, a customer probably needs a broker. "You can usually get a better deal from the mortgage brokers than from the banks; they'll generally write the business faster because they'll draw on all those sources," said R. Marshall Kneeland, a building contractor from Winsted, Conn., who used to be a real estate agent. Five years ago, when he was selling houses, he said, many people thought of mortgage brokers as "kind of slimy specimens who took out small ads in the classifieds, like: 'Refused by your bank? Come see us.' " Now, he said, mortgage brokers are "taking out giant billboards on I-91." Mr. Kneeland, who is currently using a mortgage broker to help him shop for his own mortgage, pointed out that many borrowers don't keep track of who holds their mortgages. "It might be the bank you signed up with -- or it might be the ABC Finance Company in Albuquerque," he said. "You might as well go for the best deal." Getting the best deal has become an obsession for many of today's home buyers, some of whom are comparison shopping on the Internet, a tool that wasn't even available 10 years ago. Refinancing, which allows borrowers to better the interest rates they got in the past, now makes up 55 percent of today's mortgage business. All of this points to an increasingly investigative shopper. Yet, even the best informed home buyer may need help with the paperwork involved in applying. That's where a broker -- or even the Internet -- can help. Richard Hodos, a commercial real estate broker, figured there would be no snags in applying for a $300,000 loan to buy a huge 1,000-square-foot one-bedroom apartment in an elegant prewar co-op building in Greenwich Village. After all, he was putting up 40 percent of the $499,000 price. But despite Mr. Hodos's sterling credit report, Bruce G. Maasbach, the broker at Skyscraper Mortgage, was concerned about two recent credit inquiries from banks. "They want to make sure you're not taking out any other mortgages on different properties," he explained. So Mr. Hodos, an enthusiastic and affable man of 37, gave reasons for the credit inquiries, including his request to one credit card company for an increased limit this past Christmas. AT their first face-to-face meeting, Mr. Maasbach -- who had drafted a pile of forms after a brief telephone interview -- laid out for Mr. Hodos what he would be charged, above and beyond the monthly payment and the up-front money that would be required, including an application fee of $290, a credit check for $10 and the appraisal fee of $275. By the end of the session, Mr. Hodos had filled out all the paperwork and had a tentative rate -- 7 3/8 percent, from the Astoria Federal Savings and Loan Association in Lake Success, N.Y. -- and a tentative monthly payment: $2,072. These days, the banks rely on brokers like Mr. Maasbach and Elise Leve Wittenberg at Manhattan Mortgage, who met with Ms. Altman, to funnel clients and paperwork to them. But it wasn't always that way. In fact, before the mid-1980's, the banks didn't usually deal with mortgage brokers at all. When the business of mortgage brokering began, "we were the lender of the last resort," said Tuck Marshall, who will become the president of the National Association of Mortgage Brokers in June. He continued: "The mortgage broker helped you clean up your credit and found you a loan -- but not through a bank. It was seen as slightly shady business." From 1990 to the present, there was an even greater shift, away from commercial and savings banks to mega-lenders like Countrywide, which last year lent $45 billion. "No one knows these big mortgage conglomerates' names -- they don't even have branches," Mr. Bader said. "They're using the mortgage brokers as conduits." This all gets a bit heady for a consumer who wants to research the rates on his own, and confusing for those who are not yet ready to spend their spare time hunkered down over a computer keyboard, trying to surf the Web. L. Daniel Rawitch is the chief executive of Finet, the parent company of I Qualify, a mortgage brokerage company on the Internet. Mr. Rawitch says his company (at www.iqualify.com) will give a preliminary approval in six minutes, based on a quick, fill-in-the blanks application, to prospective homeowners for only $39. If the applicant gets the preliminary approval, he or she can take the results to any lender, the company says, or use Monument Mortgage, the mortgage company Finet also owns. The Web site may be helpful in spotting weak areas; applicants may be told to explain late payments on credit cards, for instance. After a client pays a fee, I Qualify will also mail him the current percentage rate for a mortgage and the monthly payment. But Manhattanites beware: the company does not handle loans on co-ops. And, as it states in bold type, "This is not a commitment to lend." To Mr. Rawitch and his competitors, the Internet is the wave of the future. Others are not so sure. "The Internet isn't there yet," said Mark E. Zimmerman, a real estate lawyer in Manhattan. "People want personal service, plain and simple. The banks are really missing the boat." Mr. Bader, whose mortgage brokerage company has three Web sites, grumbled, "The Internet will be there for my children." Still, there are plenty of people already betting that Mr. Zimmerman and Mr. Bader are wrong.  Defining the Terms FOR the novice searching for a mortgage, here are a few terms to throw around so you can sound like a pro. ADJUSTABLE RATE MORTGAGE -- Often called an ARM in the ads, it means that the interest rate changes at specified intervals; for example, "10/1" means the rate will stay fixed for 10 years, then will change each year for the duration of the mortgage. LIFE CAP -- The limit on the interest rate on an adjustable rate loan. POINTS -- A one-time charge by a lender: each point equals 1 percent of the loan amount. CLOSING COSTS -- Costs incurred in buying real estate, which can include points, attorney's fees, the cost of a lien search, filing fees and more. LOAN COMMITMENT -- An agreement to lend. Synonym: Loan approval. REFINANCE, OR REFI -- Money borrowed by the owner of real estate to replace an existing loan on the same real estate.   TRACIE ROZHON  Proceed With Caution ALTHOUGH a lot of the uncertainty when dealing with a mortgage broker is gone -- newyork State and the surrounding states have some of the toughest rules around -- the smart home buyer always comes to the first meeting well prepared. Get a recommendation from a friend or colleague who has used a good broker in the past. Failing that, get several names from your real estate broker. Check newspapers or the Internet to learn the most current rates for the kind of mortgage you want. Last month, the newyork State Banking Department began posting the latest interest rates for mortgages on the World Wide Web, at www.banking.state.ny.us. (Look under the section called Interest Rate Surveys.) For the Web-challenged, hard copies of the reports can be obtained from (800) 518-8866. Remember to ask the mortgage broker to go over every one of the charges you will have to pay. You shouldn't pay more for a mortgage through a broker -- including all preparation costs -- than you would pay if you walked in to a bank. (Brokers say you will often pay less, because of their ability to comparison shop.)   TRACIE ROZHON Graphic   Illustrations (Illustrations by Leslie Cober-Gentry)(pgs. F1 & F8)

title: Microsoft Adding to Java and to Sun Rift
body: The Microsoft Corporation plans to announce new capabilities Wednesday for its version of the Java programming language that are certain to deepen a bitter rift with Sun Microsystems Inc., Java's inventor. Microsoft executives said today that they were departing further from the standard that Sun refers to as "100 percent pure Java" in an effort to give software programmers better performance and increased compatibility with Microsoft's Windows operating systems features. The move, underscored by Microsoft's decision for the first time to add several new keywords to the Java language that will run only on Windows, emphasizes the company's strategy of trying to wrest control of the Java standard from Sun. Sun introduced Java in 1996 as part of an effort to develop software better suited than existing programming languages for the new style of computing that was developing with the rise of the Internet and the World Wide Web. Java was intended to provide better computer security and enable a programmer to write a program once and have it run on any computer that had the ability to support Java applications. But Sun's version of the Java language, which is licensed by companies such as Netscape Communications, Oracle and I.B.M., has collided with Microsoft's "embrace and extend" philosophy of trying to influence Internet standards. Wednesday, Microsoft will announce the availability of an early trial version of its Visual J++ 6.0 programmer's environment. The company said the new programmer's tool kit would have the ability to support special software libraries known as Windows Foundation Classes, which are intended to link Java programs directly to Windows operating system features. Microsoft executives said press reports saying they were trying to create an entirely new language were "exaggerated," but they acknowledged that they were chafing under Sun's control of the Java standard. "There's been a concerted effort to keep Microsoft from innovating in the Java space," said Charles Fitzgerald, Microsoft's group product manager for platform marketing. "The keywords are pretty trivial. If you don't want to use them, you don't have to." He acknowledged, however, that programs written to include the new keywords would not run correctly on computers that do not use Windows. Sun executives said the two areas that Microsoft had been stressing -- performance and compatibility with Windows -- were nonissues. "The thing that Microsoft doesn't seem to agree with us about is, Java technology is all about being able to run on multiple platforms," said Jon Kannegaard, Sun's vice president for software products. Several industry executives said Microsoft would get limited endorsement from Apple Computer, which is trying to walk a middle ground between the warring camps. Sun and I.B.M. executives argued that the new features, to be announced at the Internet World trade show that begins Wednesday in Los Angeles, were a significant departure from Sun's Java standard. "Microsoft has been trying for the past two years to extend and bury Java," said David Gee, an executive in I.B.M.'s Java development business. He said the strongest feature of the Java language was the efficiency offered to programmers to write a program once and then run it on many different types of computers. That capability requires a single, strictly enforced language standard. Microsoft, in contrast, has been arguing that Java is merely a programmer's tool that has several desirable features not available in Microsoft's two most popular languages: Visual Basic and C++. Microsoft executives discount the ability to share programs widely, saying most programmers work on the Windows platform, where performance and compatibility issues take precedence. Last October, Sun sued Microsoft in Federal District Court in San Jose, Calif., accusing it of trying to steal Sun's Java standard by shipping a conflicting version of the programming language. No trial date has been set. But last month the judge in the case heard and took under advisement Sun arguments for an order to temporarily restrain Microsoft from using the Java trademark. Microsoft officials said they had not seen significant growth in interest in Java. But a recent study by the International Data Corporation offers a contrasting view. The study found an 11 percent increase in large corporations adopting or using Java in the last three months of 1997. The interest by large corporate users in Java because of its portability features could defeat Microsoft's strategy, analysts said. "This is all about being able to manage heterogeneous computing environments," said Amy Wohl, a corporate computing consultant and president of Wohl Associates in Narberth, Pa. "How is Microsoft going to fit into that? Sometimes I think there's a basic misunderstanding at Microsoft on how large enterprises manage their computers."  Oracle in British Coup By Dow Jones The Oracle Corporation's Network Computer Inc. unit scored a tactical victory over the Microsoft Corporation yesterday, announcing a contract from a British cable company to supply key software for Internet-ready television set-top boxes. Going head-to-head with Microsoft, Network Computer won a contract to provide the so-called middleware for Cable and Wireless Communications P.L.C.'s digital set-top boxes. Cable and Wireless will use the Network Computer technology to expand its channel offerings, provide an electronic programming guide and offer email.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Icon Shuts 2 On-Line Magazines And Dismisses 12 Staff Members
body: After failing to find a buyer for its two electronic magazines, Word and Charged, Icon CMT shut down both publications on Monday and dismissed their 12 full-time editorial staff members. Word, an off-beat daily multimedia publication, was a pioneer among the electronic magazines published in the hyperlinked text of the World Wide Web, and an anchor of the newyork new-media community dubbed Silicon Alley. It had long been held up as an example of the medium's potential as a platform for a new genre of publication. Scott Baxter, the founder of Icon, a network services provider based Weehawken, N.J., that went public on Feb. 12, financed Word's start-up in the spring of 1995 as a way of building his company's image with Internet-savvy customers. Word's artful irreverence created a buzz in the nascent new-media industry, then eager to break out of the "Internet as nerd media" mold. And though Icon's core business was the development of corporate products -- extranets, intranets and industrial-strength bandwidth -- Mr. Baxter said yesterday that the cachet of the product proved useful as a marketing tool. But Word never made money, and after he took Icon public, Mr. Baxter said he was forced to make a decision strictly on financial merits. "Real business, real profit -- I didn't derive that from Word like I did historically," he said. "It was a good thing for us, but it's not any longer." Icon's stock closed at $10.75 a share yesterday, down 25 cents. It went public at $10. He also closed Charged, a two-year-old publication devoted to extreme sports. Critics said the decision was a result of treating the publications as a marketing tool for other products rather than as a publishing business. Dan Pelson, a creator of Word who first interested Mr. Baxter in the property, faulted Icon yesterday for failing to invest in the publications. One former editorial employee said neither publication had had an advertising staff for more than a year and that sales terms had made the properties unattractive. Mr. Baxter declined to discuss the publications' financial details because he is still seeking a buyer. For that reason, both publications will remain visible on line in the near future. Just last week, another Silicon Alley publication, Total newyork, was shut down by America Online's Digital Cities, which acquired it in January 1997. But Mr. Pelson cautioned that neither closing signaled trouble for the new media industry. "This will be reported as 'Oh look, new media doesn't make sense,' " he said. "But what it is, you have to adapt and you grow." While both sites were popular by Web standards -- Word reportedly served about 120,000 page views a month -- Mr. Pelson said they would have had a better chance if they had been owned by a media company that understood how to attract targeted audiences.

title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Newspapers End Network For Web Sites
body: The New Century Network, a consortium of newspaper sites on the World Wide Web that was created less than three years ago by the newspaper industry as a bulwark against potential on-line competitors like Microsoft, America Online and the phone companies, was dissolved on Monday, The network went out of business because the feared competition never developed and because the partners could not agree on a new role for the service. The network was intended to help small newspapers create their own Web sites. It later began a service called Newsworks, which organized articles from the New Century Network's approximately 140 newspaper sites and started an advertising sales service for its affiliates. "We were unable to agree on a business plan going forward that received the support of enough owners to enable N.C.N. to continue," the board said yesterday in a statement. The life and death of the network could stand as an object lesson on the uncertainty of the Internet. When it was founded by nine companies, including The newyork Times Company, the Times Mirror Company, the Gannett Company and Knight-Ridder Inc., newspapers were consumed with worry that their traditional franchises in delivering news, advertising and going-out guides -- all content that translates easily to the Web -- was under siege. But even the smallest papers quickly showed that they did not need help to put their own advertising-supported material on line. Newspaper Web sites have proved both durable and dominant because Web users extended their allegiances to newspapers to the papers' Web sites. The New Century Network had some success as an advertising sales broker but not enough to satisfy the partners, network officials said. At the same time, to hedge their bets, the founding members began investing money and lending their content to competing on-line services. These included Zip2, in which several of the the network's founding members are involved; Citysearch, in which Times Mirror has a stake, and Real Cities, a service of Knight-Ridder. The other founding partners were the Hearst Corporation, the Washington Post Company, Advance Publications Inc. and Cox Enterprises.

title: Get Inside Data On Any Broker
body: The National Association of Securities Dealers will put brokers' employment histories on line starting on March 26, as the first step in a $50 million project to make it easier for investors to find out about the backgrounds and disciplinary histories of unitedstates brokers. Initially, the expanded N.A.S.D. public-disclosure system will offer access through the Internet to such basic information as a broker's work and registration history, said a spokeswoman for the association, Nancy Condon. By October, the N.A.S.D., which polices unitedstates brokers and runs the Nasdaq stock market, expects to begin making disciplinary histories -- such as information about fines, suspensions, or other actions against a broker or firm -- available over the Internet. Until then, investors will be able to request disciplinary information from the association through an electronic message, fax or mail. The association hopes to make all disciplinary data available on its World Wide Web site by mid-1999. The system will give investors, state regulators and other users speedier and more convenient access to brokers' disciplinary files. The N.A.S.D. operates a 17-year-old disciplinary data base called the Central Registration Depository.

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
2 European Publishing Giants Cancel Their Plans for Merger
body: Reed Elsevier P.L.C., the British-Dutch publishing giant, and Wolters Kluwer N.V., a Dutch rival, said today that they had canceled plans to merge after they were unable to renegotiate their agreement, which had encountered regulatory objections. The European Commission and regulators in the unitedstates apparently would have required the companies to divest themselves of more assets than originally planned in their $9 billion deal, which would have formed the world's largest publisher of professional and trade journals. Wolters Kluwer had wanted a larger stake in the merged company, to be named Elsevier Wolters Kluwer, after the companies realized that they would have had to sell assets.  The original deal called for Wolters Kluwer shareholders to control 27.5 percent of the new company. "In light of the projected divestitures by the antitrust regulators, we recalculated the effect and unfortunately couldn't move forward without a different arrangement," said Caroline Vogelzang, spokeswoman for Wolters Kluwer. "Obviously, we are very disappointed." According to Reed Elsevier's co-chief executive, Nigel Stapleton, the objection to the deal from antitrust authorities was unexpected. "We had not factored into our thinking that Brussels was going to block the deal," Mr. Stapleton said, referring to the headquarters of the European Commission, whose officials could not be reached for comment. "The divestitures would have been disproportionate and would have made the deal significantly less attractive." Today's announcement surprised many analysts, because both companies had denied speculation last week that the deal was unraveling. The shares of Reed International P.L.C. and Elsevier N.V. -- Reed Elsevier's parent companies -- and of Wolters Kluwer fell sharply. Reed International's stock fell 57 pence (93 cents), to 620 pence ($10.12), in heavy trading in London. The stock had traded as highly as 739.5 pence less than a month ago. Elsevier's stock fell 3.1 guilders ($1.50), to 34.5 guilders (16.67), in Amsterdam. And Wolters Kluwer's stock slipped 3.9 guilders ($1.89), to 303.1 guilders ($146). "It came as a surprise and is such a missed opportunity," said Anthony de Larrinaga, an analyst at Panmure Gordon in London. Reed Elsevier is the world's largest publisher of academic and trade journals and owns the Lexis-Nexis data base company. Reed Elsevier had gone on a shopping spree in the last year, buying Chilton Company, a publisher of trade magazines, and also acquiring MDL Information Systems, a software company. Asked whether other mergers or acquisitions were on the horizon, Mr. Stapleton said, "There are no other merger partners around." Analysts question that contention. "Reed is always looking to buy," Mr. de Larrinaga said. "The big question is whether this signals a broader problem in terms of regulation for Reed."

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Technology Earning Reports Finally Drive Down Markets
body: The stock market was haunted yesterday by warnings of disappointing earnings from some of the largest technology companies late last week. Major stock market indexes finished lower, with technology shares suffering the brunt of the declines. Investors turned away from technology issues in favor of such market sectors as retailers and multinational consumer products companies. Analysts said that the possibility of weaker sales and slowing demand for personal computers and semiconductor equipment had finally sunk in for investors. There had been earnings warnings on three consecutive days last week from Intel, Motorola and Compaq Computer. Stocks finished strongly higher Friday, as investors seemed to brush aside the first two companies' statements that first-quarter earnings would not meet expectations. But Compaq's announcement after the close of trading on Friday led to selling yesterday. "It was kind of silly to have the market up 50 to 100 points like it never happened," one trader said. "You've got a clear Compaq-driven signal," said Alan Bond, chief investment officer at Bond Procope Capital Management in newyork. Bond Procope recently sold its entire Compaq holding at 35 because Mr. Bond was concerned about possible inventory buildups. Compaq, yesterday's most actively traded issue, closed at 25 7/16, down 2 3/16 on the Big Board. The Nasdaq composite index, which is heavily weighted with other technology issues, fell 28.33 points, or 1.62 percent, in a retreat led by such bellwether technology issues as Microsoft, Intel, Dell, Cisco Systems and Sun Microsystems. But as investors fled from those computer-related issues, one of the places where they sought refuge was in Internet company stocks. Internet-related shares like Amazon.com, Yahoo, Excite, America Online and Lycos soared, with many of the companies reaching new highs amid expectations that falling personal computer prices would lead to more sales and increased Internet use. Announcements of mergers and acquisitions helped stem broader market declines, analysts said. Alcoa's plans to purchase Alumax for $2.8 billion and Qwest Communications International's deal to buy LCI International for $4.4 billion indicated that companies would continue to consolidate to buoy market share and stock prices, said Richard E. Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. After trading higher during most of the day, the Dow Jones industrial average slipped 2.25 points, closing at 8,567.14. Standard & Poor's 500 stock index fell 3.38 points, to 1,052.31. Two of the Dow's technology issues, I.B.M. and Hewlett-Packard, contributed to a large portion of the declines. Sears, Roebuck, Coca-Cola and Procter & Gamble, which had been leading the Dow higher, managed to hold onto their gains. Those increases were a sign of a more defensive stance among investors, as they pushed cash into retailers and consumer nondurables on the reasoning that demand for their products would be aided by a strengthening economy. The Labor Department reported Friday that unemployment had fallen to 4.6 percent, a 24-year low. Mr. Bond, who became more defensive during the fourth quarter, has recently bought shares of CVS and Walgreen. He has also added to holdings in AMR, the parent of American Airlines, and Carnival, which owns Carnival Cruise Lines. Both will benefit from falling oil prices, he said.
