At right, Jesse Jackson is seen on the group's Web site in its Kenya campaign. (Photographs by G. Paul Burnett)

title: Bloomberg to Supply AOL With On-Line Business Data
body: Bloomberg L.P. will announce today that it has signed on as America Online's featured provider of business information, giving another vote of confidence to on-line consumer markets that have yet to show a profit. The position at America Online was vacated at year's end by Dow Jones after a contract dispute. In a sign of how on-line business strategies are changing, America Online paid Dow Jones for its business information; Bloomberg is reportedly paying America Online an undisclosed sum to be a featured part of the on-line service, which claims 11 million subscribers and is based in Dulles, Va. Financial news and information will begin appearing on America Online later this week. Terms of the partnership were not disclosed, but America Online typically charges millions of dollars for "anchor tenancies," deals that feature news or entertainment services on its opening screen. For example, Intuit, a maker of tax and financial software, paid America Online $16 million up front this month and is guaranteeing a total of $30 million over the next three years for an anchor tenancy. "A few years ago, you wouldn't think of Bloomberg content as something that would appeal to the kind of market we have," Barry Schuler, America Online's president of interactive services, said. Today, however, the market for personal finance information is booming. America Online reports that its users look up 60 million stock quotes each day and track six million portfolios, a growth of 70 percent in the last year. In addition, America Online's position as the largest Internet service provider -- it delivers an estimated 56 percent of all Internet users -- proved irresistible to Bloomberg, which is looking to broaden its consumer reach. "The bottom line is there's a large interest in financial and business news," said Michael Bloomberg, the former Salomon Brothers trader who parlayed a $10 million buyout in 1981 into the upstart financial news business that bears his name. It now employs 700 reporters in 80 bureaus worldwide and includes a news service, radio and television networks and book publishing. Its core business, however, remains the Bloomberg terminal, a proprietary news box that delivers immediate stock quotations and analysis to the desks of 90,000 financial professionals who pay $1,200 a month. Of the $1.3 billion in reported revenue for the privately held company, 99 percent comes from the terminal service, a spokeswoman said. Mr. Bloomberg said the America Online deal would not "cannibalize" the professional part of his business, because it would not include the analysis and deep financial data available to terminal subscribers. Despite a dearth of revenue in the consumer portion of his business, Mr. Bloomberg has continued to make deals to provide on-line news and information. In the last six weeks alone, he has announced agreements with CNet, an Internet news service, and its fledgling on-line service, Snap; with the Women's Wire service on the World Wide Web, and with the cable-modem Internet service At-Home. Bloomberg's two-year-old Web site says it delivers 17 million page views a month. "We think it will be lucrative for us," he said, "because if we can deliver for advertisers the eyeballs and minds that they're trying to have pay attention to their message, AOL will make some money and the customers will be well served." In a report to be released tomorrow, the on-line analysis group At-Plan says that its survey of 40,000 Internet users in the last quarter of 1997 showed 12.1 million were actively using on-line finance sites. The survey also showed that sales of stocks and mutual funds on line grew 291 percent in the last nine months. "This is the future of investing," said Mark Wright, the chief executive of At-Plan, which is based in Stamford, Conn. "A vast new industry is being created overnight. If you look at the profile of the typical user, you can see why the Bloombergs of the world have such great interest.  Our research found that 8.4 million Internet users have self-directed portfolios of over $100,000." Bloomberg is not the only provider of professional financial information that is gambling on the consumer market. Edgar Online, for example, provides Securities and Exchange Commission filings on its Web site and to a variety of other Web resources, including Yahoo. "It's an interesting bridge between two very different organizations," said an Edgar spokesman, Jay Sears. "It shows the incredible demand for financial information from a mass market that didn't exist until a few years ago. Bloomberg is high end, and on the other end, there's AOL. It's a very interesting match. It'll be interesting to see how they do. The devil's in the details."

title: Clinton Talk to Oppose Internet Tax
body: President Clinton will speak against taxing Internet commerce when he addresses a technology investors' conference here on Thursday, an Administration official said today. The President's position, in support of a bill recently introduced in Congress that would bar state and local governments from enacting taxes on the Internet until 2004, places the Administration directly in opposition to state Governors. On Tuesday, the National Governors' Association called on Congress to enact legislation creating a uniform system to collect state taxes on sales conducted over the Internet. Meeting in Washington, the governors said that as Internet purchases increased, states would lose a valuable source of revenue unless they could collect sales taxes on transactions conducted over the Internet. But Mr. Clinton believes that the Internet is spurring the growth of new industries and that new taxes imposed by thousands of local jurisdictions would undermine that economic impact, said an Administration official, who spoke on condition that he not be further identified. The President will support a moratorium on taxing Internet commerce, the official said, during which time he hopes for a long-term discussion about how to allow the Internet to keep growing without hampering the ability of state and local governments to pay for programs in areas like education and law enforcement. The President's decision to appear before the investors' conference, sponsored by BancAmerica Robertson Stephens, was a surprise, and White House officials said he hoped to use the forum to make his case for the concept of a new economy based on high-technology industries. He will also announce expansion of a network of universities connected to a Next Generation Internet, adding 29 schools for a total of 90. The project is developing a much higher-speed version of the Internet.

title:
SCREEN GRAB;
Can You Spare a Dime? Click Yes.
body: RICH SCHMIDT did not see much point in posting a personal Web page that listed, say, the contents of his CD collection. "No one would care," he said. But then he hit on an idea that might get attention and address a rather persistent lack of disposable income: ask strangers for money. The result, the Amazing "Send Me a Dollar" Website (tt.net/send-me-a-dollar/), is an example of a very old profession updated for the Web. The virtual beggar has arrived. For indisputable proof, check the Net's most popular directory, Yahoo, which has created a spot in its taxonomy called Begging for Money under "Humor, Jokes and Fun." That may seem unkind, but Yahoo has put its finger on the central paradox of on-line begging. In real life, panhandling depends on personal contact; on the Web, mendicant sites are quite easy to avoid. They must, therefore, entertain to attract visitors. Sure, there are some digital beggars who play it straight, like the unemployed computer technician with a heap of debt, including a $10,000 loan for a 1995 Ford Thunderbird (lonestar.texas.netblessing). But they are generally no fun. Too needy. For that matter, anyone with a couple of grand for a PC, a modem, an Internet account and access to a Web-server computer should probably not try to keep a straight face while claiming to be destitute. The Amazing site is entertaining and even endearing (a subliminal advertisement flashes, "Do It!"). And Mr. Schmidt was among the first on-line beggars to offer an interactive incentive. In return for a dollar -- "cash only!" -- mailed to a post office box, he will put donors' messages on his site's bulletin board. With its mix of personals, jokes and commercial messages, it is worth visiting as an example of Internet culture and commerce. Mr. Schmidt's pitch has proved effective, relatively speaking. He has received alms from Australia, Brazil, France, Finland, England, Germany, Italy and Japan. His virtual tin cup now contains about $300, which is by far the most sent to any on-line beggar turned up by searching the Web. Still, themail-in approach seems a tad archaic, given the medium. Some beggars, embracing the Internet ideal of electronic transactions, now offer to accept handouts via Visa, Mastercard and, yes, even the various forms of digital scrip known as "virtual cash." Even with such conveniences, however, it seems that few other on-line beggars have been able to match Mr. Schmidt's meager returns. Most are like Jim Denison, who publishes the Make Me Richer Than Bill Gates page (web2.airmail.net/gandolf/ you.htm) and who cheerfully takes payment by "cash, checks, gold bullion, bearer bonds, loose jewels" and credit card. Mr. Denison said he had brought in "roughly $30 over nine months." He added, "That would put me about $165 short of paying my Web bills." Graphic   Photo: Rich Schmidt's virtual cup is on his Send Me a Dollar Web site. (Chris Pizzello for The newyork Times)

title: WebTV Offers Cheap Web Access, but Consumers Are Wary
body: WHEN Microsoft bought WebTV Networks for $425 million last August, speculation began about how quickly pumped-up televisions would replace home computers as the electronic road to the Internet's super information highway. Why not? Television sets are a little like elbows and navels, went some of the thinking: just about everyone has them, but only 4 out of 10 American households have computers. A complete WebTV system can be bought for less than $200 -- one-fifth the price of a bargain personal computer -- and that is encouraging to supporters of this emerging technology. They hope that the little black set-top boxes will prove to be a popular way for millions, especially the budget-conscious, to find their way to the Internet. But sales of WebTV, the most established player in the Internet-television industry, have proved modest. They appear particularly disappointing, retailers say, when compared with the rapid adoption of video-cassette recorders. Even with recent improvements in how WebTV operates, and with Microsoft's deep pockets to herald the set-top boxes' features, doubts persist about whether there are enough bargain hunters to support the much-vaunted notion of convergence, the term used in the industry to describe the melding of technologies, like televisions and computers. Yet some people, like Matthew York, believe that lots of people will want easy access to the Internet through their television sets. Last August he began Smart TV, a glossy magazine published six times a year that covers the dissolving edges that have for decades separated TV's and computers. "I think the days of TV as we know them are numbered," said Mr. York, the magazine's editor and publisher. "A major paradigm shift is taking place." WebTV tends to be no larger than a VCR and plugs into a television and a telephone jack. Some units, however, like those being offered by budding WebTV competitors like World Gate, @Home and Media One, depend more on cable to bring Internet services to standard television sets. In either case, the Internet comes to television with a fee. WebTV charges $19.99 per month, much like on-line services like America Online, for unlimited use. Neither fish nor fowl, these set-top boxes do blend, with varying degrees of success, some of the best functions of computers and televisions. The user can use a specially designed remote control to move a highlight box around a television screen arranged with icons, clicking on the images to select WebTV functions. Despite the apparent convenience and cost advantages of WebTV, consumers generally do not understand what Internet-television really is, suggested Aharn Schachter, vice president and general manager of Datavision, a Fifth Avenue electronics superstore in midtown Manhattan. "This is not something that can be thrown into the superstore to be bought like bread or milk," Mr. Schachter said of WebTV. "That can be done when everyone understands what it does." Some consumers wonder aloud whether Internet-television systems -- or, as some call them, Net-top boxes -- will be the eight-track cassette players of the 1990's, a transitory technology whose time may come and go faster than last year's fashions. At least for now, WebTV could change television habits. Someone watching television with an Internet Net-top box could, for instance, tune in to "Baywatch" on the television, then click to the Web and check weekend weather forecasts for Malibu, read the history of lifeguarding or order autographed posters of David Hasselhoff and Pamela Anderson Lee, and send email to the studio with plot suggestions for new episodes. "We've taken this very complex hacker world that you need to be very savvy about, and we've tamed it to the point where it's ready for an average consumer,' said Steve Perlman, the 36-year-old chief executive of WebTV, which he co-founded in 1995. So far, WebTV has 250,000 subscribers, Mr. Perlman said. That is surprisingly modest, many media experts agree, when compared with the 11 million subscribers to America Online, the biggest on-line service in the unitedstates. WebTV has been hard at work trying to entice more buyers, Mr. Perlman said. WebTV Plus, the company's latest and more expensive version, released in December, creates a Web-in-picture window on television screens so TV viewing does not have to be interrupted if a viewer wants to cruise the Internet. Unlike the "Classic" models, WebTV Plus has a hard drive. This means that the box can receive and store frequently requested information, like weather reports, movie listings and incoming email, even before you ask for it. The information is sent by the WebTV system of computers, or servers, in the middle of the night, when most viewers are asleep. The effect for the user is that those kinds of information appear almost instantaneously. Yet WebTV, with or without a hard drive, cannot run computer software, like Quicken or Quake II, that is sold on diskettes or CD-ROM's. WebTV has no disk or CD-ROM players or means to attach them, but printers can be connected. Users also cannot store information they find on the Internet. In addition, very few things on the Internet are designed to take full advantage of WebTV's capabilities. Those shortcomings have led some to wonder how much allure these devices will ultimately have in the home electronics marketplace. "It is enhanced television now as opposed to being the wide open world of the Internet coming into the living room," Peter Clemente, a vice president at Cyber Dialogue, a research group on computer use, said of Internet-television's Net-top boxes. Despite WebTV's generally acknowledged success in resizing and rendering Internet sites onto common television screens, some WebTV users complain that some of the type is too small to read comfortably from an average television viewing distance of six to eight feet. That, too, may be a problem, Mr. Clemente said, because the Internet is primarily text-based and geared toward delivering information rather than entertainment. "The ability to broaden the audience for the Internet by bringing the Internet to people on a different device is interesting," said David B. Wertheimer, president of Viacom's Paramount Digital Entertainment, which develops original on-line entertainment. "But I don't think it's revolutionary." What Internet-television convergence needs, Mr. Wertheimer said, is a killer application, something equivalent to what Milton Berle was to early television. "That is what kicked the television industry into high gear," he said. Surveys of WebTV users indicate that the technology is not attracting high-end personal computer users. In fact, Mr. Clemente said, 65 percent of WebTV subscribers do not have personal computers. Moreover, he said, a recent survey found that 44 percent of WebTV users were 50 years old or older and that 14 percent of the users were between the ages of 10 and 18, suggesting that people intimidated or unable to afford personal computers were buying WebTV. "I was not going to go into debt to buy a computer," declared Jay Holtzman, a 38-year-old case analyst for a Maryland security-clearance service whose wife, Patricia, also 38, works as a part-time secretary in a law office. So the Holtzmans, of suburban Baltimore, bought a WebTV system. Using a television-like remote control, Mr. Holtzman's 4-year-old son, Jonathan, recently navigated an Internet site that explains to children the explosive workings of an active volcano. Jonathan's 2-year-old sister, Alison, looked on. Weeks earlier, Mr. Holtzman found the volcano site in an Internet guide that came with his WebTV. He simply typed the site address into a blank on his screen, and the Web site appeared. By using Excite, an Internet search engine that runs on WebTV whenever anyone clicks on the word Search on the screen, Mr. Holtzman found dozens of sites of interest. He typed only general themes, like "music" and "radio," into Excite and got scores of sites to visit, including a radio station that broadcast its music over the Internet. Mr. Holtzman, who regularly surfs the ESPN Web site for its sports coverage and statistics and listens to foreign radio stations, said he enjoyed his WebTV and was especially fond of using it for email. "I was able to find a friend of mine who I had gone to high school with," he recalled, noting that he had not talked to his former classmate in 25 years. Using WebTV, he did an Internet search for his friend's email address. He found three listings under that name and sent a brief email message to each one. To his surprise, one of them turned out to be his friend, who sent an email message back, saying he was now a weekend news anchor in San Francisco. "That," Mr. Holtzman said, "was really cool."  Wireless Systems Take a New Approach So you are ready for the next wave, the convergence of your television and personal computer. Yet you are unsure about embracing a new technology, like Microsoft's WebTV, that weds some of the best features of both. There is an alternative: RF-Link Technology, a small start-up electronics company in Torrance, Calif., is offering a kind of shotgun marriage that joins a TV and PC in a way different from the WebTV method. Called Wireless PC@TV, the RF-Link system uses transmitters, receivers and an infrared keyboard to do the trick. RF-Link's technology is similar to radio frequency links that commonly connect wireless speakers and headphones to home stereo systems. In fact, RF-Link, whose parent company is the Chia-Heir Group, based in Taiwan, has been making wireless links between video-cassette recorders and TV satellite dishes to televisions in different rooms. "You can virtually do anything on your television in your living room -- print, download, save, surf the Web -- that you would do on your computer," said Melanie L. Cohen, RF-Link's sales manager and spokeswoman. She added that PC@TV had a range of about 300 feet and could send its signal shorter distances through three to five walls. Jim Mikles, associate editor of Smart TV magazine, said that along with Wireless PC@TV, a company called AI Tech is a leader in a wireless PC-TV industry so new that few people at his magazine know what to call it. He added that the Laral Group's Wireless PC Hub and X10's Big Picture also provide similar PC-to-TV links. Some drawbacks persist, Ms. Cohen conceded. PC@TV has considerable trouble pushing its signal through heavy brick walls, glass and steel. So perhaps PC@TV is not a great gift idea for someone living in Windsor Castle. But Ms. Cohen added, "Generally, in most normal homes, it works really well." A complete Wireless PC@TV setup costs about $400, she said; that is twice as much as WebTV Plus, the best that WebTV has to offer. Ms. Cohen noted that WebTV required that you use its Internet service, at about $19.99 a month, while PC@TV required nothing more than the service already providing Internet access to the home computer.   M. Four-year-old Jonathan held the controlling keypad as the family recently explored Internet offerings. title: Young Editors Speak Up and Out
body: NET surfers have been riding waves of dirt since the White House scandal broke, but are they ready for "All the Principal's Men?" Bolt Reporter is banking on it. Bolt Reporter, a high-school journalism site, hopes to do for teen-agers what Matt Drudge, the Internet columnist, has done for politicians: create an on-line forum for all the news that's unfit to print. Started by a creator of the on-line literary magazine Word, Bolt Reporter (www.boltreporter.com) seems inspired by equal parts USA Today, "60 Minutes" and MTV. Its national team of high-school editors adds at least one new article a day, either original reporting or a reprint from a school paper. Bolt Reporter encourages readers to type their responses in message boards that accompany each story. The site is produced by Concrete Media of newyork. One notable part is the Banned section, which runs features that had been killed by school administrations. Adrian Holovaty, an editor from Naperville North High School in Illinois, wrote a story for the site about a teacher accused of sexual harassment.  After officials deemed his original story too sensitive to run in the school paper, Mr. Holovaty beamed it to students worldwide through Bolt Reporter. "Don't let administrators intimidate you -- you have a right to your own opinion, too," he wrote. "If the administration refuses to change its mind, let the public know." According to Parker Stanzione of Concrete Media, who oversees the site, "kids need the opportunity to speak out against everyone who's infringing on their rights." Targets range from principals (an article about a Connecticut high school that banned T-shirts inspired by the cartoon "South Park") to Mom and Dad (a group of California students will write about a classmate whose parents shipped him to a behavioral-treatment center in Jamaica). While on-line services like Reuters Teen Magnet and the Youth Outlook site are playing the teen-age news game, Bolt Reporter's investigative mission is the most ambitious, encouraging students to explore controversial stories. That is, of course, assuming they can find the time. "This depends on midterms, soccer matches and college application deadlines," Ms. Stanzione said, "but we try to work around all that."

title: Prostitutes on Wane In New York Streets But Take to Internet
body: The old prostitution haunts now crawl with nearly as many police officers as streetwalkers, part of newyork City's continuing assault on "quality of life" crimes. Once-seedy areas where the sex business flourished, like Times Square, have given way to Disney-style family entertainment. And the combined forces of AIDS and drug addiction have further thinned the ranks of prostitutes on neighborhood streets. But while prostitution may be less visible in the city, it is no less prevalent. The Internet, pagers, cellular phones and subterfuges like escort services have enabled more discreet forms of prostitution to thrive beyond the reach of the street-level crackdown, the authorities and prostitutes themselves say. "You have some people who have no alternative but the street," said Capt. John Costello, commander of the Manhattan South police vice squad. "But there are a whole lot of people that we never deal with, working out of offices, apartments and the Internet. And if they are acting behind closed doors and are discreet, we will never hear about them." As the police have forced prostitutes to change tactics, the city's resurgence as a destination for conventioneers and tourists has expanded the demand for prostitution, said Ronald Moglia, a professor of human sexuality at newyork University. And the business is adjusting. Prostitutes cruise the Internet nightly looking to arrange liaisons in newyork, the computer and modem having replaced the sidewalk and street lamp as the means by which many prostitutes and customers meet, size one another up and negotiate transactions. Ads for sexual services flourish on Web sites and in mainstream publications. And the current Manhattan Yellow Pages now has 52 pages devoted to escort services -- legal businesses that the police say frequently front as prostitution rings. That is 17 more pages than two years ago. Long-established escort services are feeling the competitive squeeze. "This business is growing like crazy," said Nerissa Braimbridge, whose International Escort service in Manhattan has brought together young women and wealthy men for more than two decades -- for companionship only, she said, adding that her service receives many queries over the Internet. "It's grown from something small to something degenerate. Everyone is getting into the business and operating as an escort." Prostitutes have certainly not been driven off the streets, and many still shiver nightly on the sidewalks in desolate stretches of the city. But they are an increasingly beleaguered, often desperate group. "It's not like it used to be," said Candace, a 41-year-old prostitute who has worked in Hell's Kitchen and other Manhattan neighborhoods for more than a decade. Referring to Ninth Avenue, she said: "There used to be 15 girls working here; now it's only me. You've got to move around a lot more and work more secluded places to get by, and you can't take as much time sizing up your customer. Things are tough on the street." But another prostitute, a 26-year-old man who gave only his professional name, Steve, has managed to do brisk business while keeping far away from the hazards of the street corner. On a recent evening he worked at his computer making dates for Valentine's Day. He said he had found steady work since he began selling sex on the Internet, through an on-line account that cost him $10 to set up. A posted profile describes Steve as a "head-turning escort for evenings or travel" whose hobbies include "making wealthy men very happy." On-line prostitutes say the Internet is a natural medium for selling sex: it is anonymous and connects them to a vast array of potential clients. It is safer than the streets, where vice officers and predatory strangers are constant threats. And it is cheap. An escort company can buy an ad on a Web site for $50 a month, compared with thousands of dollars for half a page in the Yellow Pages. Prostitutes also say the Internet enables them to avoid sharing their profits with a pimp or an escort agency. One beneficiary of the evolution of newyork prostitution has been Redlightnet.com, a clearinghouse for the on-line sex trade that has been run for a year and a half out of a small apartment in Chelsea. Redlightnet's page on the World Wide Web is supported by more than 10 regular advertisers in the escort business and more than 400 personal ads. "It doesn't take a rocket scientist to do this job, it just takes looks," said Alan M., a 26-year-old former Navy sailor who said he started selling sex out of his home in Chicago several months ago and averages $1,500 a week for about 10 hours' work. His costs are mainly for clothes and keeping his computer in good repair. Clients pick up most other expenses, including taxi and plane fares when he travels to newyork and other cities. In these and other ways, off-street sex workers are sharply different from those who walk the streets, experts say. They usually do not refer to themselves as prostitutes, sociologists say, noting that it is easier for them to escape the industry's stigma because they are unlikely to develop a criminal record and are more often in business for themselves. "You have a more open attitude toward sexuality on the part of young people," said Ira Reiss, professor emeritus of sociology at the University of Minnesota. "Now we have a variety of new communication devices, there is a much easier moral code and a willingness to experiment and try new things by both men and women. And it's much easier to say, 'I'm just making extra money.' " There are no authoritative figures on the prostitute population in newyork City. But evidence from a variety of sources suggests that the industry is growing, even as fewer prostitutes work the street. And electronic technology appears to be central to the industry's success, both in attracting business and avoiding the authorities.  Discreet Operations Are Rarely Targets The police say prostitutes who work on line or for escort services are unlikely ever to be arrested, since law enforcement agencies rarely go after discreet indoor operations. In fact, the only way such businesses get into trouble, escorts and police officials say, is by employing under-age prostitutes, annoying neighbors with too much foot traffic, or failing to pay taxes. One newyork State law enforcement official who spoke on condition of anonymity said his office had made several attempts to reel in on-line sex workers over the last year but had failed each time because the prostitutes became suspicious before a deal was brokered. According to the city police, only 30 establishments were closed during the first eight months of last year, and only 44 were closed the year before. While the Police Department could not give complete statistics for prostitution arrests in 1997, vice squad officers arrested fewer than 2,000 prostitutes and clients in 1996, fewer than a third of whom were prostitutes working inside buildings. From January to October 1997, the department's vice enforcement division arrested only 1,380 prostitutes and their customers, fewer than half from inside establishments. The police say there is no evidence that a significant number of street prostitutes have gone into the booming escort business. But many have adopted more modest technological means to stay ahead of the police. They try to build client lists so that they can arrange work by phone rather than on the street. Others work out of bars or dance clubs, giving out pager numbers to clients. Pimps sometimes set women up in roving vans and limousines, beeping them whenever the police are spotted.  Using Technology To Evade Prosecution Escort services, which are often fronts for prostitution, are notoriously ingenious at evading prosecution. Police officials said attempts to find and infiltrate such services required a great deal of luck. The telephone numbers they use are often in locations where no prostitutes have ever set foot, instead housing only a receptionist with a bank of phones. Donna, a 26-year-old escort who has worked for several services in the city, including one on line, said she had never met the madam of a service that calls her regularly. Its phone number, which turned out to be a beeper, was given to her by another escort she knew. When she first called looking for a job, she left her number and was quickly called back by a woman who asked her who she was and what she wanted, then told her to go to a bar in SoHo and wait. Donna was met there by a man who asked her questions about her background and took her phone number. He gave her a key to a hotel room in mid-Manhattan and explained the rules. She was to report when available, for periods ranging from all day to one hour. The key was for a hotel room that contained a locked closet, where the money that she and other escorts made would be left. Now, she is paged occasionally and told to go to a certain client's hotel room. Or she is told to go to the service's hotel room and wait five minutes for a man to come calling. One always does, she said. Undercover officers say that when they do make contact with a real bordello, its operators usually tell them to call back from a pay phone before giving out their address. Someone from the operation then looks out the window to see if the client is a recognized officer. If he is, the receptionist just hangs up. Should an officer get in the front door, he will be questioned by a worker and asked for several forms of identification before he is allowed to pass. "They have closed-circuit cameras, lookouts and sometimes vastly superior technology," said Captain Costello, the Manhattan South vice squad officer, adding that officers often show up at an establishment to find that their cover has already been blown. "They say they're sorry, we're closed," he said. "Then, you're just standing there looking like a jerk."  After Crackdowns, A Changing Market Although prostitutes have thrived behind closed doors, their counterparts on the street have had far less luck in evading the law. The city's police crackdown on streetwalking began in 1994, when more than 9,500 prostitutes and clients were arrested. Clients found their names being published and vehicles taken away, while judges proved less likely to allow prostitutes back on the street without jail sentences. Experts say the crackdown has cut the number of streetwalkers in half in some parts of the city, and repeat offenders are fewer. The number of convictions per prostitute has also declined, with 50 percent of the prostitutes now seen by the court having no more than one prior conviction, said Michele Svirdoff, research director at the Midtown Community Court's Center for Court Innovation. "When the court first opened, it was not unusual to see defendants who had 100 prior arrests on their sheet," she said. "Now, a majority of those we are seeing are novices. What that tells is that the market is changing."  Upturn in Consumerism Is Increasing Prostitution Like any service industry, prostitution is affected by the economy, and both sociologists and prostitutes can cite numerous economic reasons that it flourishes in newyork City. For one, in a city where well-paying, low-skill jobs are scarce and the unemployment rate, nearly 9 percent, is well above the national average, the lure of prostitution can be high. At the same time, experts say, demand for prostitutes has been increasing sharply now that clients have more disposable income and tourism and convention business is booming. "Prostitution is a market-related economy, so if there is a lot of consumerism, then it grows," said Professor Moglia of newyork University. "And an increase in tourism obviously increases prostitution because it is an increase in consumerism." The operator of Redlightnet, the on-line prostitution clearinghouse, who spoke on condition that his name not be given, said more ads were coming in and more prostitutes were going on line every week. Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani's campaign for safer streets, he said, had unwittingly helped his businesses. "He has generally made the streets safer for all newyorkers and tourists, and more tourists means more hookers here to take care of them." title:
Staying With the Pitch;
Stalwarts of Face-to-Face Sales Reluctant to Peddle on Line
body: At a virtual Tupperware party, no coffee is served and there are no demonstrations of the product's notorious "burp" when properly sealed or how the cheese plane doubles as an eggplant peeler. But Regina Baker thinks her modern interpretation of the fabled American sales gathering is an effective substitute. "Not everybody has time to go to a party," Ms. Baker said. Which is why she built a site on the World Wide Web two years ago to sell her plastic products. She said that the site now accounted for 60 percent of her revenue and 80 percent of her customer base, which has grown to include Tupperware buyers in Japan, Singapore, the Netherlands and Germany -- markets far beyond the reach of a living-room gathering near her home in Houston. But by selling over the Internet, Ms. Baker is violating the policies of the Tupperware Corporation. The company, based in Orlando, Fla., forbids its self-employed sales consultants -- about one million of them worldwide -- from building Web sites to sell its products, and a year ago, it amended the contracts of its new consultants to reflect the prohibition. Since then, warning letters have been sent to site operators, and the number of Tupperware sites has reportedly dropped from 100 to a renegade handful. "The Internet is an information source, not a sales source," said Lawrie Hall, a spokeswoman for Tupperware. "We see it as a wonderful way to educate people. The Internet doesn't provide the kind of service we see as beneficial to the consumer." The traditional Tupperware party, Ms. Hall says, connects the customer to the product in an essential way: "At a party, you see more, feel it, understand it." Though electronic commerce is widely promoted as the Holy Grail of the Internet and the next wave of retailing, Tupperware is not alone in swimming against the tide. Other direct-sales businesses, including Amway, Mary Kay, the cosmetics company, and Electrolux, the vacuum cleaner company, have all shunned the notion of selling directly to consumers on line, though each company has built a Web presence for educating customers, enhancing brands and recruiting salespeople. Several others, including Avon Products and Fuller Brush, a unit of CPAC Inc., are offering their products for sale on line but say that is a sign they wish to appeal to the wired generation -- not that they are dropping the notion of face-to-face selling. Mary Kay has developed a compromise approach: For a small fee, it helps its sales force by building individual Web pages on its central computer. To date, 10,000 sales associates in the unitedstates have signed up for the program. But sales are not allowed. "We wanted to maintain a consistent branding of Mary Kay on the Internet, but this allows them to publicize their independent businesses," said Karen Dodge, a spokeswoman for the company, based in Dallas. Of the main national direct sellers, only Encyclopaedia Britannica has completely abandoned the notion of direct sales, shifting 18 months ago to phone and on-line sales bolstered by advertising. Even in a harried, increasingly digital age, face-to-face selling outside a retail environment with product demonstrations has experienced slow but steady growth. According to the Direct Selling Association, an industry group in Washington, sales of products sold in this manner, ranging from baskets to vitamins to small appliances, added up to $20.84 billion in 1996, up 6 percent since 1992. Those numbers reflect the need for customer education and personal service in selling some products, association officials said. "The classic example is Tupperware," said Liz Doherty, an association spokeswoman. "It was originally sold in stores. But people looked at it and said, 'Plastic is smelly, and the lids don't seem to close.' Demonstrations were needed to show the value of the product." And as for vacuum cleaners, Ms. Doherty said, "Before they came out, people used to beat their carpets with a stick. People were skeptical, until a salesman showed up at their door and demonstrated how they worked." Yet proponents of electronic commerce insist that the Internet, especially the media-rich World Wide Web, is well suited for demonstration and targeted marketing -- the next generation of old-fashioned door-to-door sales. They suggest that direct sellers may in fact be holding on to their old way of doing business for a different reason. For one thing, the Internet could wreak havoc with companies that are built on a pyramid of salespeople. "In many cases, the goods and services facilitate what multilevel marketing companies are really selling, which is distributorships," said Don Peppers, co-author of "Enterprise 1 to 1: Tools for Competing in the Interactive Age." "If you're in the business of selling distributorships, you don't want your end users to go around the channels to obtain that stuff," he said. "Amway recognized that right away. What they say is, 'We're selling dreams.' They're selling the chance that anyone can make a business for themselves." That dream, Ms. Doherty said, is the reason that the number of people engaged in direct sales has grown to 8.5 million from 3 million the last four years. That number can be very misleading, however. "Most people who sell it don't last 60 days," said Ken Voght, a Tupperware salesman who runs the Modern Shopping Web site. "They have two parties." Even so, Ms. Doherty said: "It appeals to people for the 90's catchwords: own your own business; work from home; set your own hours and compensation. With downsizing and corporate impersonality, it is appealing to people." Tupperware and other direct sellers say they see the Web as an excellent way to recruit new salespeople but most feel strongly that using it to sell their goods would undermine the shoe-leather efforts of their human sales force. "It would be destructive of morale if they saw us competing for sales with them," said Steven Cooper, a spokesman for Electrolux, based in Atlanta. "Besides, if someone goes on the Web in newyork City and sells a vacuum cleaner to someone in San Francisco, and they want to get it serviced, it's not good for customer service to do that." But Mr. Peppers counters that improved customer service is exactly what the Web offers. "The power of the old way of doing business is not just that I can look you in the eye," he said. "What's personal is that I remember what you like from the last time." Paradoxically, he suggested, impersonal technology, especially large data bases that link products and consumer behavior, allows more efficient management of customer preferences. "It's inefficient for the neighborhood bookseller to remember his best 100 customers' preferences," Mr. Peppers said. "On the other hand, Amazon.com does just that with every customer. Is Amazon an insidious encroachment on the way we do business? No, they're a rejuvenation, a technologically enhanced form of doing business. It's back to the future, in a sense." The Tupperwares and Amways could borrow from the Amazon model to better focus on their customers' needs, Mr. Peppers said. To be sure, the Direct Selling Association and its 140 members recognize the Web as a force that must be addressed and have formed an Internet council, which will meet this week to address issues raised by electronic commerce. While standards are created and refined, a handful of renegade Tupperware salespeople like Ms. Baker continue their efforts, committed to the notion of extending their sales -- and in turn, the company's revenue. They maintain that on the Internet, they reach an entirely different audience, one that is seeking products the way they might in the Yellow Pages. Indeed, most direct-sales businesses have traditionally done little formal advertising beyond listing distributorships in local white pages and have forbidden their salespeople from doing so. The vagaries of the Internet as a medium -- more public than a phone number, more private than a billboard -- are inspiring companies and salespeople to rethink the way they reach customers. And while great unknowns loom, there is one certainty, Mr. Peppers said: The Internet is only going to become more pervasive. "Every time someone predicts the technology isn't there yet," he said, "I think about the turn of the century, when people said that the horseless carriage wasn't going to catch on because you've got to learn how to drive and you've got to be a mechanic." Ms. Baker, the renegade operator of a Tupperware site, asserted that she was not generally one for breaking rules, and she said she understood Tupperware's position. Yet, she wants to be able to run her business the way she sees fit. "I just feel we should be able to sell the way we want to," she said. "People are busier now. This is the way things are going to go." Graphic   Chart:  ENCYCLOPAEDIA BRITANNICA  FOUNDED: 1768 HOW IT STARTED: Was initially sold section by section. Began door-to-door sales in the 1930's. title:
Taking In the Sites;
The Internet Gears Up For Conflict With Iraq
body: It has become fashionable recently to say the Internet has come of age as a news vehicle. As O. J. Simpson made his second run through the limelight, the Internet came of age. When robots landed on Mars, the Internet came of age. One could believe that the experts, having repeatedly heralded the Internet's maturity, would now allow cyberspace to age gracefully. But that probably would be wrong. As President Clinton attempts to build support for a possible attack on Iraq, the Internet is getting ready to grow up all over again. Whatever it would be called -- war? surgical strike? -- an attack on Iraq would be the first major American action of its kind since the emergence of the World Wide Web. It is unlikely that the Internet would gain as much attention from another unitedstates-Iraq conflict as Cable News Network did from the first; videos of bombs falling down chimneys do not look as compelling in jerky little computer windows as they do on television. But the sheer volume of information about Iraq's military systems that is available on line could make Americans more informed than they have been leading up to any previous military engagement. The most sensitive military information is not available on line. For instance, the Defense Intelligence Agency, which surely must be tracking Iraq's Republican Guard, runs a relentlessly uninformative Web site. And it would appear next to impossible to independently verify much of the information that is available on the Web. But that should not bother experienced Web surfers. The unitedstates Government provides many Web pages about Iraq, but not much information. The unitedstates Information Agency, which functions in part as the Government's overseas public relations operation, runs a page that outlines what seems to be the Administration's official posture toward Iraq. The site also includes links to large maps of Iraq maintained at the University of Texas. But the agency's fact sheet on Iraq's "Program of Weapons of Mass Destruction" is fairly thin. Far more illuminating is the text of a background briefing given by Pentagon officials last November on Iraq's chemical and biological weapons program, including a discussion of anthrax, that is found on Defenselink, the armed forces' site. On Defenselink, there is also a big picture of a Scud missile launcher, but it can only be viewed if the user states an organizational affiliation and a purpose in obtaining the photo. Defenselink is more forthcoming on American weaponry, with files on many different systems available. The unitedstates Central Command, which is responsible for the American armed forces in the Middle East, includes in its Web site a cursory political analysis of the nations under its scrutiny. There is far more detailed information about Iraqi forces available outside of the Government. The Federation of American Scientists runs perhaps the most complete site, with pictures of Iraqi military installations and information on Iraq's missile capabilities. That site is complemented by a site run by the Center for Defense and International Security Studies at Britain's Lancaster University. That organization takes a serious interest in missile proliferation and maintains detailed country-by-country tables detailing missile forces. People with a serious interest in chemical warfare may be interested in a site run by Mario Profaca, a freelance journalist. On his site, Mr. Profaca includes what he describes as a declassified report from the Central Intelligence Agency that includes information on various chemical and biological weapons, Iraqi production facilities and delivery systems (planes and missiles). The Jane's line of publications from Britain includes an overview of Iraq's military, but most of the company's resources, including "Jane's Missiles and Rockets" are accessible only for a fee. There are also more overtly political sites run by groups debating the American stance toward Iraq. A group called the Iraq Action Coalition uses its site to advocate an end to sanctions. One of the coalition's mirror opposites is the Center for Security Policy, a Washington think tank. The center uses its site largely to excoriate President Clinton for not being tough enough on Saddam Hussein, issuing papers like "Accept No Substitutes: Clinton Address on Iraq Signals Continuing Failure to Grasp Need for Toppling Saddam." title:
INVESTING IT;
Belle of the New-Issue Ball, But Will Its Charm Last?
body: IN an otherwise dreary season for initial public offerings, the stock of Verisign Inc. has been a glamorous debutante. At the stock's introduction in late January, the company set an offering price of $14 -- well above the expected range of $9 to $11. Then the stock raced to $25 in its first day, settled at nearly $28 a week later and closed on Friday at $31.875, for a market capitalization of $642 million. That performance has made something of a digital Cinderella out of the company, which provides the workaday security services needed to unlock the Internet's commercial potential. Behind the scenes, however, doubters worry that the stroke of midnight will soon sound for Verisign. "I think there's something here, but I don't think it justifies a $600 million market cap at this point," said David Jones, an analyst for the California Technology Stock Letter. Internet stocks are often high-priced, but even among them Verisign is expensive, Mr. Jones said. For instance, Verisign stock trades at 68.5 times its sales per share, by Mr. Jones's calculation, while Yahoo, Cybercash and Amazon.com trade at 41, 29.1 and 10.2, respectively. True, Verisign's revenues have grown steadily, from $382,000 in 1995 to $9.4 million in 1997. But because of high costs, the company's losses have also increased during that time, from $2 million to $19.2 million. Verisign has big bills because it is trying to develop and market a large number of security-related products. There is also the great cost of keeping the security business unimpeachably secure, said Mark Brown, president of Market Analytics, an I.P.O. research firm in Los Angeles. "In this early stage, when sales are failing to match expenses, they have to spend resources keeping the computers humming and the security high and maintaining a staff of specially selected employees with pristine backgrounds," Mr. Brown said. Nevertheless, on several levels, it is far from certain that these outlays will pay off. The first question: How much Internet commerce will there be to secure? Although the International Data Corporation, a market research firm in Framingham, Mass., predicts that Internet business will balloon to $237 billion by 2001, the total in 1997 was just $12.4 billion. That leaves a far piece to go, and a great deal can happen along the way. And even if Internet commerce expands, it is unclear which security processes will be used. Verisign's basic approach is to provide digital identity certificates -- which serve as both a driver's license and a transaction record -- to companies and individuals, thus reducing the chance of fraud and theft. Verisign, which is based in Mountain View, Calif., then functions in many cases as the "certificate authority" -- the keeper of these on-line verifications. The company has been very successful and creative in promoting its certificates. It has already issued two million of the digital ID's to individuals, and conducts various promotion efforts, like giveaways for limited periods. "What they are trying to do is similar to what Yahoo is trying to do in the sense of establishing a brand and awareness," said Mr. Jones, referring to the Internet browser company. But Verisign's approach to Internet security is not the only one. One competitor, Entrust Technologies, a unit of Nortel, the Canadian telecommunications company, never serves as the certificate authority itself, according to Shauna White, an Entrust spokeswoman. It only provides the technology to others. Indeed, some observers say the Entrust approach may prevail. "Internet security has to be done in such a way that it mirrors commercial practice," said Jay M. Tenenbaum, chairman of Commercenet, an industry consortium. Mr. Tenenbaum then points to Blockbuster Video, which issues its own I.D.'s rather than relying on an outside firm. Even if Verisign's basic approach does not fall by the wayside, the company will not have a clear field. As Verisign acknowledges in its registration statement, its technology is not unique. And while Verisign does have its own copyrighted code, its competitors have their own, too. Verisign's chief executive, Stratton Sclavos, said he could not discuss these and other issues because of a Securities and Exchange Commission rule against company comment for 30 days after an initial public offering. Verisign does have an impressive roster of backers and customers, including Intel, Microsoft, Netscape, Cisco Systems and Hewlett-Packard. Ken Fleming, an analyst at Renaissance Capital Corp. in Greenwich, Conn., said that such respected names was "a sign for the rest of market" that Verisign had a promising future. Indeed, such affiliations greatly influence investors. "It's difficult for investors to gauge who has the best technology, so one factor is whom does the company have partnerships with," Mr. Fleming said. But these enterprises may in many ways be rivals, not allies, of Verisign. In fact, the company's registration statement lists I.B.M., a prized customer, as one of its competitors. It also notes that Netscape, which carried Verisign software on its browser, has begun to develop its own products for Internet security. Of all these many rivals, Entrust and GTE Cybertrust, a subsidiary of GTE, may provide Verisign with its biggest challenges. Not only are they backed by multibillion-dollar businesses, but they have their eyes on the spectrum of Internet-security markets and they are already full-fledged operating units. And Nortel plans to bring Entrust public later this year. Also, the odds are good that yet more heavyweights will crowd in on tiny Verisign, according to Mr. Brown. "The area they are in is important -- Internet security -- and because it is big it will attract big players," he said. "Verisign won't be a big player; it will be a tier-three player. Some people thought they'd be leading the charge in this area and it's not true. If it doesn't find a niche, it will go through a lot of money and not have a lot to show." But Mr. Jones observed that the stock's lofty valuation made far different assumptions. "On its face," he said, "the stock is priced as if Verisign will always be the only and best-known player in the field." title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
Reconstructing Central Park's Black History
body: To Cynthia R. Copeland, Central Park is filled with ghosts -- and this month, those ghosts went on the Internet. Ms. Copeland is the co-curator of "Before Central Park: The Life and Death of Seneca Village," a New-York Historical Society exhibition that opened in January 1997 and, after being extended three times, is now set to close on March 8. With technical help from the newyork Public Library and Columbia University, much of the exhibition can now be viewed on the Web. The exhibition takes viewers back to a time before the Civil War, when most of urban Manhattan was south of 14th Street and the rest of the island was forest. It tells the story of what became known as Seneca Village, a squatter camp of free blacks and some Irish who had fled the potato famine. The village, which was once home to nearly 300, showed signs of becoming an established settlement but was torn down by 1857 to make way for Central Park. The site now faces the apartments of Central Park West between 82d and 86th Streets. In part because the surrounding area contained foul-smelling soap and candle factories (including a bone-boiling plant where Tavern on the Green is now) and in part because of who lived there, the area took on a reputation as a shantytown, despite the presence of three churches, a school and a number of two- and three-story frame houses. When Ms. Copeland worked with seventh- and eighth-graders exploring the exhibition, she began to realize that children thought that history was far more certain than it is. "Our philosophy on the Web site is to force the children to become historical detectives," she said. Indeed, the site tells visitors, "you will have the opportunity to become a historical detective who will reconstruct the story of a 19th-century community based on clues recovered from the past." WHAT YOU SEE -- A rich trove of primary sources, including a state census, from which viewers can draw conclusions. Viewers can learn the contingent nature of historical evidence, like whether the site was called Seneca Village at all. There was only one contemporary published reference to Seneca Village, the 1847 parish records of All Angels, a white church at the site, and a second reference long after the site was razed, in a newyork Herald article in 1914. Most published references of the time used either Yorkville or racist references to blacks. LINKS -- Dozens, including one to the Great Hunger, about the Irish potato famine in the 1840's. It notes that a variant of the fungus that killed the potatos appeared briefly in Idaho last year (http://www.aoh.com/index/hunger.html). WHAT YOU GET -- A sophisticated introduction to historiography for both young students and adults. The New-York Historical Society plans to add up to 300 more documents, as well as a "virtual" archeological dig.  SENECA VILLAGE (http://projects.ilt.columbia.edu/seneca/start.html) Graphic   Photo.

title: New York's Starving Libraries
body: Beleaguered libraries throughout the state took heart last month when Gov. George Pataki included $88.5 million in this year's budget to aid libraries, which run mainly on inadequate local tax revenues. If the Legislature approves the plan, the state will finally deliver aid that it has been promising since the library funding law was passed in 1990. The money is badly needed to acquire new books and computer equipment to access the Internet and electronic library catalogues. One assumption of the information age was that libraries would become less necessary as home computers and Internet services became plentiful. But with almost 70 percent of the state's households lacking computers, libraries have been swamped with requests for Internet searches from students, job seekers and people trying to start small businesses. The libraries have been unable to keep pace, particularly in rural areas. Less than 60 percent of the state's 1,100 public libraries have Internet connections. Of the 4,000 public school libraries, less than 20 percent have a connection. Governor Pataki's aid proposal will help libraries keep the lights on and pay basic infrastructure costs. The newyork Library Association has proposed that the state allocate an additional $11 million a year for its Electronic Doorway Program, which would help libraries throughout the state get on line. This is a small price to pay, given the need and the benefits that would result.

title: Press Freedom at Issue in Use of 'Sealed' File by Paper and Reporter
body: Should a reporter be jailed or fined, or both, if she reads a sealed court document mistakenly given to her by a court clerk? And should her newspaper pay damages for printing some details from the document? These are among the questions raised in a contempt proceeding here in Federal District Court that has evolved into a clash between judicial power and freedom of the press. The reporter, Kirsten B. Mitchell of The Wilmington Morning Star, has already been found guilty of criminal contempt by the judge who originally sealed the document, W. Earl Britt. Judge Britt held that even if his clerk erred in handing over the document, which included sensitive details about a $36 million out-of-court settlement in a pollution lawsuit, Ms. Mitchell nevertheless knew that it was sealed from public view and that its contents therefore should not be disclosed. Ms. Mitchell, 32, contends that she was only doing her constitutionally protected journalistic duty when she read the document and that she did not know it was sealed. She is scheduled to be sentenced on Feb. 24 and could be given up to six months in jail and fined up to $5,000. Judge Britt appointed a special counsel to prosecute the case when the office of Attorney General Janet Reno refused to allow the local unitedstates Attorney to take part. The judge has also found Ms. Mitchell liable for civil contempt, along with her newspaper. He has ordered them to pay damages of $500,000. The Star is owned by The newyork Times Company, which plans appeals. Nearly three decades ago, in perhaps the most celebrated of all legal fights involving publication of confidential documents and information, The newyork Times prevailed in court in the Pentagon Papers case. "At its core," Judge Britt said in ruling on the Wilmington case on Jan. 21, "this matter is not about the freedom of the press but about the respect that any citizen, individual or corporate, should have for an order of the court." The Times Company contends that even if the document given Ms. Mitchell was sealed by court order, under long-established journalistic principles Ms. Mitchell and The Star had a right to view and use its contents once it had been handed over by the clerk, even though mistakenly. The company argues that if the judge's findings are allowed to stand, there will be a chilling effect on the news-gathering process all over the country and accepted journalistic tenets will be turned on their head. "Kirsten Mitchell was handed a document by a court clerk, and that she could be held in criminal and civil contempt for then reading that lawfully obtained document is simply unprecedented," said George Freeman, assistant general counsel for The Times Company. "Neither reporters nor Joe Citizen have an obligation to return or ignore materials that a Government employee, either purposely or inadvertently, gives them." Hugh Stevens, the legal counsel for the North Carolina Press Association, offered this assessment: "There are a lot of troubling things in this case, from whether the details of the settlement of a major environmental lawsuit should be sealed by a judge to whether the judge should become his own prosecutor and jury when things go wrong in his office. But most disturbing of all, in this case a reporter and her newspaper are being punished for doing their job, for printing the truth." The dispute traces back to Oct. 14, when Ms. Mitchell, the state capital correspondent for The Star, went to the Federal courthouse in downtown Raleigh and asked to see the file in the case of Ashcraft, et al. v. Conoco Inc. The Conoco oil company, a division of E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Company and 178 residents of a trailer park near Wilmington had just settled a lawsuit in which the trailer owners charged that Conoco had permitted leaking gasoline to contaminate the park's water supply. A jury had already found that Conoco stored its gasoline negligently and then fraudulently tried to cover up its negligence. The jury was deliberating how much compensation the company should pay the trailer residents when lawyers for both sides reached an out-of-court settlement that provided for Conoco to pay the residents $36 million. The judge accepted the settlement, sealed its details at the request of both parties and dismissed the jurors, telling them not to reveal details. According to undisputed testimony at Ms. Mitchell's hearing before Judge Britt, this is what happened after she asked to see the file: The court clerk, Anne Caviness, handed Ms. Mitchell a six-inch stack of documents but removed one, saying it had been "sealed" by Judge Britt and was not available to the public or news organizations. Flipping over the remaining stack of documents so as to get to the latest ones first, Ms. Mitchell began reading, working her way through a stack in which the documents were all now face-down. When she got to one, "opened" was printed on the rear flap. She lifted the flap, pulled out a document and found the full story of the settlement and its amount, $36 million in restitution. After reading the document, Ms. Mitchell said she returned it to the envelope and, for the first time, saw a warning on the front. In capital letters, it said: "Confidential settlement agreement. Filed under seal. To be opened only by the court." Ms. Caviness had somehow failed to remove the most sensitive document in the stack. "I simply forgot," she later testified before Judge Britt. A Federal employee for 27 years, Ms. Caviness left Government service the day after testifying about her mistake, giving no explanation. Ms. Mitchell told Judge Britt at the contempt hearing that she did not believe that she had to keep secret what she had read because she had been given the document by the court's clerk, who had pointedly removed sealed matter from the stack of documents. Besides, Ms. Mitchell added, the writing on the back of the envelope said it had already been opened. "I assumed everything given to me by the clerk was public document," she said. "It was never my intention to violate any court order." After reading through the rest of the court file, Ms. Mitchell called her editor, who told her that another Star reporter had obtained the same information from various other sources but that the court file was useful as confirmation. The article about the pollution settlement that was published by The Star the next day said "sources" had provided most of the details, including the size of the settlement, noting that court papers confirmed the $36 million figure. Two weeks later, Conoco went back to court and asked Judge Britt to find The Star and its reporters in contempt. The company also asked for compensatory damages, contending that its ability to negotiate future lawsuit settlements -- it is involved in more than 50 lawsuits involving toxic substances -- had been hampered by the disclosure of its handling of the Wilmington settlement. "In any kind of civil case you can only be compensated," Jonathan Staffer, a Conoco lawyer, said in explaining why the company returned to court. "If you lose your arm, you can't get your arm back, you can only try to be compensated for it. That's what we're trying to do."

title:
THE MARKETS: STOCKS;
Markets Rally After Trading Lower for Most of the Day
body: The stock market staged a comeback yesterday, with the Dow Jones industrial average returning to positive territory after a decline Thursday snapped a six-day streak of consecutive records. Although it was lower throughout most of the day, the blue-chip average rallied, closing at 8,413.94, up 38.36 points, with companies like Merck, American Express and McDonald's among the leading gainers. Because of the expiration of stock options and futures, known as "double witching," traders and analysts had anticipated a volatile session. While the Dow did rebound from early losses, which pushed it down as much as 57 points, the average failed to beat the high of 8,451.06 reached Wednesday. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index, however, did reach a new record, closing at 1,034.21, up 5.93 points. "People knew that they wanted to buy," said Alan Bond, chief investment officer at Bond Procope Capital Management in newyork. "It was just a question of how long they wanted to wait. They really want to own them," he said of investors' stance toward stocks. After strong gains among technology shares helped to push the Nasdaq composite index closer to its October 1997 record high of 1,745.85 on Thursday, the technology-laden index rose just 1.12 points yesterday, to 1,728.13. The modest gain, however, belied the strength of one of the Nasdaq's newest members, Doubleclick Inc. After trading as high as 31 3/4, Doubleclick closed at 26 3/4, up 9 3/4, or 57 percent, on its first day of trading. The newyork-based company, which provides Internet advertising, sold 3.5 million shares at 17 in an initial public offering on Thursday. The size of the offering and original price range were increased based on expected strong demand. The success of the deal illustrated the keen interest of investors in Internet-related companies, said Mark Basham, a research analyst at Standard & Poor's. In an offering in late January, another Internet-related initial offering, Verisign Inc., a data security company, rose 11 1/4 from its 14 offering price during its first day of trading. Those stocks also benefited from the record highs logged by broader market indexes, which have made some investors less nervous about investing in riskier smaller-company shares, analysts said. Doubleclick also illustrates a pickup in the pace of initial public offerings, which got off to a slow start in January, said Linda Killian, a research analyst with the Renaissance Capital Corporation, a firm that specializes in such deals and is based in Greenwich, Conn. So far this year, 53 offerings, each exceeding $5 million, have raised about $2.7 billion, according to the Securities Data Company, a research firm in Newark. Over all the offerings have gained about 10.2 percent. That rise eclipses the 10.05 percent gain of the Nasdaq, and far outdistances the Dow's 6.4 percent rise this year and the S.& P.'s 6.6 percent increase. Although some analysts do not expect initial public offerings this year to exceed last year's issuance of about $43 billion, a continued increase in the number of such offerings could signal trouble for the market, said Richard E. Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. If the continued strong demand for equities causes the pace of initial public offerings and secondary stock offerings to outstrip demand, the stock market could falter, Mr. Cripps warned investors in a recent research report. title:
THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Two Are Nominated for Board Of New York Times Company
body: The board of The newyork Times Company has nominated two executives for election as directors at its annual shareholder meeting on April 16. Those nominated were Brenda C. Barnes, a former president and chief executive of Pepsi-Cola North America, and Ellen R. Marram, the president and chief executive of Tropicana Beverage Group and executive vice president of its parent, the Seagram Company. The nominees would replace two directors, Ruth S. Holmberg and George B. Monroe, who are retiring. Mrs. Barnes, 44, led Pepsi-Cola North America from 1996 until she stepped down last year. During her more than 22 years with Pepsi-Cola and its parent company, Pepsico, Mrs. Barnes held senior executive positions in general management, manufacturing, sales, marketing and corporate operations. She is a director of Avon Products Inc. and Sears, Roebuck & Company. She earned a bachelor's degree in economics at Augustana College in Rock Island, Ill., and a master's degree in business administration at Loyola University in Chicago. Ms. Marram, 50, was named chief executive of Tropicana Beverage in July after serving as its president since 1993, when she joined Seagram. She was previously president of the Nabisco Biscuit Company. Before joining Standard Brands Inc. in 1977, which later merged with Nabisco, Ms. Marram worked with Johnson & Johnson and Lever Brothers. Ms. Marram is on the boards of the Ford Motor Company, the newyork and Presbyterian Hospitals Inc., Lincoln Center Theater, the Conference Board, the Advertising Council and the Associates of the Harvard Business School. A graduate of Wellesley College, she earned a master's degree in business administration at Harvard University. In addition to The newyork Times, the company publishes The Boston Globe, 21 regional newspapers and 3 magazines; it operates television and radio stations and news, photo and graphic services as well as electronic publishing and new-media businesses.
