title:
Business Travel;
Microsoft is moving into the business of supplying fast Internet access for hotel guests.
body: AT last, Seattle -- a city in Microsoft's backyard -- has a hotel with a bit of dazzling computer technology. It's the Vintage Park, which in a deal with the Redmond, Wash., software giant has outfitted 30 of its rooms and suites with computers, Microsoft Office Suite software and digital T-1 lines that can provide access to email and the Internet at speeds up to 100 times faster than a dial-up modem. The hotel, managed by San Francisco-based Kimpton Hotels and Restaurant Group, is not charging extra for the service. But Microsoft, never one to miss a sale, has additional software for purchase through the concierge. "Corporate travelers are doing less wining, dining and partying these days and using their rooms more for quality things," said Stephen Pinetti, Kimpton's vice president of sales and marketing. "We've found that about 30 percent of guests in our high-tech rooms are accessing the Net -- half of them for the first time." With its partner in the Vintage Park deal -- the San Diego-based Atcom/Info, which has installed many Internet-access kiosks at airports -- Microsoft has an even bigger game plan afoot for business travelers. On March 2, the computer team -- together with a third company, CGX Communications -- will begin testing a new jack called Iport at 10 to 15 hotels nationwide. The sophisticated device will make it easy for laptop users, long frustrated by slow or busy hotel lines, to plug in and call up email and World Wide Web addresses swiftly. "The truth is, the hotel industry has been thinking about Net access in rooms for more than a year," said Neil Senturia, a former real estate developer who is the chief executive of Atcom/Info. "We're going to supply it. An estimated 70 percent of business travelers today carry laptops. We think it's a big market." Microsoft thinks so, too. "We believe that providing high-speed Internet access will quickly become an essential service for hotels wishing to remain competitive," said Stan Julien, Microsoft's hospitality industry marketing manager.  Checking for Explosives Kennedy International Airport's new Terminal 1, which opens for business on May 22 with Air France, Japan Airlines, Korean Airlines and Lufthansa as tenants, will have the first security system in the unitedstates for automatically detecting explosives in all baggage. The $1.7 million system, equipped with machines developed by Vivid Technologies and Invision Technologies, will inspect checked and oversized bags in four stages and carry-on bags at security barriers near gate areas. A similar system is already in use at London's Heathrow Airport, Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris and other airports in Europe as well as in Asia. "About 25 percent of bags will end up going to stage two and only a fraction to stage three, where the slower Invision machines will scan them," said Alain Content, chief property officer for Terminal 1. "If there's still some doubt, they'll be shunted to a small room to be opened with the passenger present."  Upping the Ante In Rome, where prices can be stratospheric, the Eden Hotel near the Via Veneto now claims to be the city's most expensive hotel -- and proud of it -- with deluxe rooms costing about $500 a night. "We charge $75 more than the Hassler," said the hotel's general manager, Paolo Biscioni, invoking the name of its stylish rival situated at the top of the Spanish Steps. Who's paying these prices? "Salomon, Merrill Lynch and other financial houses have been coming in -- for two or three nights -- because of the privatization of Government holdings, Mr. Biscioni said during a visit to newyork to drum up business. "Some 38 percent of guests are American -- our largest contingent -- with 45 percent from newyork." What do you get for your money at the Eden? "We have all the technology -- dual phones, CD players, fax machines -- in every one of our 112 rooms," he said. "Our La Terrazza is a one-star Michelin restaurant -- not easy to find in Italy. The chef cooked for Princess Di and Prince Charles for three years."  Future Shock The travel consultant Runzheimer International's crystal ball predicts that sometime in the near future, business travelers will pay for services by electronic funds transfers -- with built-in controls. For example, if a traveler should spend $200 for dinner for two and corporate policy calls for a maximum of $125, the electronic funds transfer system will debit the company account for $125 and the traveler's personal account for $75.  Gleneagles Upgrade Gleneagles, the Scottish golfing resort favored by Americans for corporate meetings, will replace its not-so-great pool and other tired workout facilities with an elaborate $4 million fitness center, due to open in April. It will be a match for the hotel's estimable equestrian center and shooting and falconry schools.

title: Prospect of U.S. Raids on Iraq Stirs a Protest in Times Square
body: Hundreds of soaked and shivering protesters picketed the unitedstates armed forces recruiting station in Times Square in drizzling rain last night, in what organizers vowed was part of an intensifying campaign of demonstrations against the prospect of military action against Iraq. While the setting and stakes mirrored largely ineffective antiwar rallies on the eve of the 1991 Persian Gulf war, organizers said the Internet and email have aided their movement and eroded public support for going to war. Protesters said the poor treatment of American gulf war veterans and the lack of a compelling reason for military action were also undermining public support. The Clinton Administration says bombing may be necessary to limit Iraq's ability to build weapons of mass destruction. While organizers said 750 people turned out for the protest, the police estimated the crowd at 250. No arrests were made during the rally, which began at 4:30 P.M. and ended two hours later across the street from the Port Authority Bus Terminal on Eighth Avenue and 42d Street. Gallup polls in mid-January and early February showed Americans divided over whether to use military action against Iraq, but the surveys indicated that support for an armed attack has been growing recently. But leaders of the newyork-based International Action Center, the group that organized last night's picketing and helped plan protests nationwide in 1991, said that this time, the Internet is allowing them to spread information quickly and better organize demonstrations. "We've utilized the Internet very, very extensively to organize," Deirdre A. Sinnott, 37, one of the group's coordinators, said, adding that the group receives about 150 email messages a day. "We get requests for information like, 'Do you know what's going on in Columbus?' 'Do you know what's going on in Tucson?' " The group's Web site last night listed more than 70 recent or planned demonstrations in dozens of American cities and in London, Scandinavia, Japan and Australia. Ms. Sinnott said interest in the site has swelled as tensions between the unitedstates and Iraq have intensified. She said the site recorded 6,000 visits in one 24-hour period last week. But several waterlogged commuters shuffling past last night's protest seemed more ambivalent than impassioned about it. Chris Hughes, a 26-year-old construction site manager, said after the rally that he felt people were less concerned about bombing Iraq today than they were in 1991. "I think it's a bad idea," he said. "But generally, on a whole, I don't think people are focused on it." title: An On-Line Lesson in Thin Mints and Lemon Pastry Cremes
body: It's time again for that annual celebration of grass-roots entrepreneurship, the Girl Scout cookie sale, when Scouts fan out across America, striking fear in the hearts of the Keebler elves and earning their cookies and dough badges. But even this seemingly low-tech ritual is being changed by the Internet. Driven by the lure of the new technology badge, some Scout councils are selling cookies on line. More than a third of the country's 319 Girl Scout councils have gone on line in the last two years. And two New England councils -- the Swift Water council in Manchester, N.H., and Patriots' Trail in Boston -- have been among the leaders in moving cookie sales onto the World Wide Web. Both have secure servers, allowing them to take credit card orders. The council in San Francisco is adding an encryption program, too. In Boston, Prosoft, which provides information technology training, volunteered to teach Web design to the girls. Patrice Buckley, 15, a Scout for nine years, said, "Prosoft taught us Microsoft Front Page 98 and I was part of designing the site." Amanda Michienzi, 17, a Girl Scout for 12 years, said, "We did the links, learned some HTML coding, and we put our own voices on the site with hyperlinks." To buy cookies on the Web, one fills out an email form that links to credit card processing services. Scouts working on Web sites track the orders, send email acknowledgments and ship the cookies. A minimum order of three boxes plus shipping comes to about $13. Each council takes guidance from national headquarters in newyork but makes many business decisions itself. Although the New Hampshire Scouts accept orders only within their designated territory, Boston Scouts fill orders from anywhere in the country, as do San Francisco Scouts. Boston-area girls forward names of out-of-area cookie buyers to local councils for follow-up sales, but in San Francisco the Scouts have not made a decision on that. Janine Carlson, communications director in San Francisco, said: "Territory is still a gray area. Hawaii went on line last year and got inquiries from all over the globe." What does the future hold? Will thousands of freebooting Girl Scout troops hoist the Jolly Roger on the Internet high seas, pirating away one another's cookie sales? The organization's guidelines on cookie sales speak of "honor" when addressing Internet sales to insure that "competition is fair," and that "sales are made locally." Even before the Internet, Scouts had begun promoting their cookies using the media, creating press releases or taking public service announcements to radio stations. "The cookie sales teach entrepreneurship," said Beverly Cheuvront, director of public relations for the Girl Scout Council of Greater newyork, which does not have a Web site. "The girls set up a business plan and figure out how many cookies they need to sell to meet a specific goal, which may be renting a bus or going to summer camp." This year, the San Francisco-area girls are trying to finance a trip to summer camp in England, and the Patriots' Trail Scouts are hoping to pay for a trip to Ireland. Nationally, income from cookie sales also goes toward scholarships for economically deprived girls, programs for the elderly, recycling efforts and the girls' educational and civic outings. To be sure, the vast majority of the almost 200 million boxes of thin mints, trefoils and other cookies sold each year are sold door to door. The country's 2.6 million Girl Scouts ring up more than $500 million; in three months, they sell almost as many cookies as Nabisco sells all year of its Oreos, America's best-selling cookie brand. In Boston, both Patrice and Amanda continue to sell door to door. "I've been selling cookies for 12 years," Amanda said. "I've known my customers since I was a Brownie." title:
Patents;
Could a new chip in your electricity meter become the brains of a household computer?
body: WHAT if someone patented an idea so revolutionary that it could give every American home a powerful computer, with an Internet connection -- free. And what if this same idea serendipitously turned out to be the David that slew the Microsoft Goliath? Charles Roos, a professor emeritus of physics from Vanderbilt University, makes such a claim for his newly issued patent. The core of Professor Roos's new technology is not a new computer chip or operating system. Rather, it is a new type of electricity meter. Yes, an electricity meter. "This would make electric utilities major players in the telecommunication industry," Professor Roos said. Professor Roos would get rid of traditional meter readers, who walk from house to house checking monthly electricity use on mechanical meters. He would replace them with computer chips inside the meter. These chips would "read" electricity usage continuously. "With the price of computers dropping so fast, the utility can afford a few hundred dollars to put in a sophisticated computer chip," Professor Roos said. Once the chip is in place, he reasons, it could serve as the brains for a household computer. "It would be a full-fledged computer, not just a minimal toy," he said. "It could do word processing, spreadsheets, games." Professor Roos's patent covers what he calls a "data junction box," which serves as a digital gateway for the home and which transmits signals through electrical wiring or video coaxial cables that allow a television set to function as a monitor for a computer and also establishes a high-speed modem. "A more sophisticated householder can use his own computer equipment and simply use this as a fast modem to the Internet," Professor Roos said. "But at the basic level, the householder wouldn't have to do anything. We'll make your TV set function like WebTV." Professor Roos said the computers could use alternate types of operating-system software. "This could crack Microsoft's monopoly and open competition," he said. "It would put everyone on a level playing field." For Web access, his plan requires that the utilities strike a deal with cable television companies to share their video cable. If a cable company resists, Professor Roos says, the utility should "remind that cable company that it owns the right of way to all the poles and it can run its own fiber optic cables." But what is the incentive for utilities to pay for such an ambitious plan? Professor Roos said the utilities that distribute electricity could profit in part by being able to charge customers higher rates when they consume electricity at peak periods. And, of course, they would save on the cost of paying meter readers. Professor Roos's patent, No. 5,699,276, has been licensed to Datapump L.L.C., in Summit, N.J.  Taking the Sting Out of Skin Care Cosmederm Technologies, a skin-care company in La Jolla, Calif., has patented what it says is a way to take the sting out of everything from chemical facial peels to men's after-shave. The key ingredient? A substance found in lettuce and other green, leafy vegetables. The active ingredient in its newly patented formulation is strontium, a soft, yellowish metallic element that is chemically similar to calcium. (Company officials hasten to point out that the substance is completely safe and should not be confused with strontium 90, the radioactive isotope that occurs during nuclear fallout.) "What we've got here is a highly effective method for reducing skin irritation and inflammation," said Dr. Mark G. Rubin, a Beverly Hills, Calif., dermatologist who presented clinical data on the substance recently at a dermatological conference in Hawaii. Cosmederm has licensed patent 5,716,625 to the Collagen Corporation of Palo Alto, Calif.  A Paper Clip For Laptops Christapher Adams, a motivational speaker in newyork, and Paul Adams Reaux, an engineer in Delcambre, La., are brothers who were separated at an early age when they became orphans. But the brothers remained in close touch, and over the last two years collaborated cross-country on a patent that has just been issued. They have invented a new type of clip that attaches papers to a laptop computer. It is essentially two plastic clips hinged together. One clip attaches to the computer, the other to whatever material the user wants to refer to while typing. Christapher Adams contended that the clip was superior to others on the market because it could easily be stashed into a coat pocket, could attach to any part of the computer and was robust enough to grip an entire magazine rather than just a single page. The brothers are looking for seed money to begin producing the clip. "We've got all the pieces lined up, except for the capital," Mr. Adams said. They received patent 5,697,594. Patents are available by number for $3 from the Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C. 20231.

title: Push, the Hot Technology of '97, Gets a Cold Shoulder in '98
body: As new technologies go, the promise was enormous: With a new category of software known as "push" technology, the World Wide Web would finally take its rightful place among moneymaking commercial media. That was last year. Today, many of the nearly two dozen start-ups that hoped to hit pay dirt in the push market are gone, the few companies that have survived have done so by reinventing themselves, and the flood of venture capital pouring into companies developing push software has been reduced to a trickle. "Push has gone from the most popular buzzword of 1997 and late 1996 to something verboten on business plans," said Ross Rubin, an analyst at Jupiter Communications in newyork. It is not necessarily that the thinking behind push was flawed. In simplest terms, push refers to software that delivers Web information to consumers, rather than forcing consumers to forage through the Web to find it. The concept attracted considerable attention because many people thought it was a solution to the most nagging problem of the Net: information overload. Perhaps even more significant was that push offered advertisers a familiar metaphor: It delivers information via regularly updated "channels" that appeal to specific audiences. In some cases, the push software sends a message to the user's screen saying the information they requested has been downloaded automatically for them, while in others it displays news headlines and other information on a predetermined schedule throughout the day. "This was an area that was seriously hyped," said David Dorman, who recently became the chief executive of Pointcast Inc., perhaps the best known company still standing behind push. "People were heralding it like it was a cure for world hunger." But despite all the noise, push has made little headway in its battle for the hearts and minds of the average Internet user. Some early users complained that having their computer automatically log onto the Net and retrieve data on a predetermined schedule was obtrusive; others complained that the filters employed by these programs were not smart enough to sift the truly relevant information from the unnecessary. Rather than helping to solve the problem of information overload, some say push exacerbated it. And many others simply see a basic contradiction between the concept of push and the interactivity of the Web: Push renders the user passive, as with television. "Push was a solution in search of a problem," said Kim Polese, chief executive of Marimba Inc., which after an early period of trial and error with push technology is now positioning itself as the provider of a software distribution mechanism. "It was never clear consumers wanted it." In a recent poll of readers of PC World Online, an on-line magazine, only 8 percent of respondents said they preferred to get information pushed to them; the rest said they would rather use bookmarks or other place-saving features of their Web browser programs. While some analysts, and certainly some push companies, have criticized the survey as lacking a broad representation of push users, the message is clear. Yet many analysts say that at least in theory, the idea of aggregating Web content and then delivering it to users makes sense -- if only for a very small number of companies. "Lots of push companies are out of business," said David Coursey, editor of Coursey.com, a newsletter that covers the computer industry. "And not just because people don't want it but because if it's all you do you're not going to have a business." But luckily for the few remaining developers, corporate customers may be a better bet than individual users, who were initially seen as a major target of push technology. Scores of companies, including FDX, Fidelity and Nationsbank, are paying substantial sums to the likes of Marimba, Backweb and Pointcast to enable them to distribute company data, rather than simply news headlines. In some of these cases, corporations are distributing company information via intranets, or internal corporate networks; in others, they are using channels to communicate with outside sales forces and major customers. With this shift in focus has come a shift in jargon. Suddenly push has become "knowledge management." That the business market is where push is most likely to gain a foothold is a point not lost on Pointcast, still the most successful of the companies that have been given the push label. Preferring to describe itself as a broadcast information service, Pointcast made an early decision to sell its products to corporate information technology departments seeking a better and cheaper way to distribute company news and business information to employees. With Pointcast software, users can receive regular updated transmissions of stock quotes, news and company data, like financial results. The company has cut deals with newspapers and other information providers, enabling the software to deliver only the specific information the user wants. As for the complaint that having information "pushed" to a screen can seem as much a cause of information overload as a solution to it, Jusuf Mehdi, director of marketing for Microsoft's Internet division, suggests the answer lies in improved filters. "That's a problem that's not going to go away." "It's a function of using the Internet," he said. "The opportunity for companies like Microsoft is to better filter out what you don't want."

title:
Taking In the Sites;
Forecast for the Internet: More El Nino Web Pages
body: Jeff Cohen has grown to appreciate the Internet immensely over the last couple of weeks. As an information officer at a state flood emergency operations center in Sacramento, Calif., he relies on the World Wide Web to help provide accurate, timely information to concerned homeowners and the news media. The center deals with the catastrophic damage caused by the floods, mud slides and storms that have hit California. Mr. Cohen knows what to blame for the unusual weather: El Nino, the warm body of water in the Pacific Ocean that causes global "weather events." And he uses the Web to gain access to the latest data and articles while he operates a phone line. "The Web is a great tool for responding to emergencies," said Mr. Cohen, an employee of the state's Department of Water Resources. By constantly updating his bookmarks, he is able to "create a solid base of information," he said. "This is different from previous emergencies because even though we had a lot of information on our desks, it was buried in a file two inches thick. With the Web, it's fresh and easier to access." Mr. Cohen is right about sites concerning El Nino: there are plenty of them. But unless you navigate carefully, much of your time could be spent staring at satellite images that are indecipherable to all but meteorologists. The site of The Old Farmer's Almanac explains the basics of the phenomenon, starting with the name (which is the Spanish word for "little boy" that is used to refer to the baby Jesus, and was applied many years ago to the weather condition because it was first noticed by Peruvian fisherman around Christmas). The Almanac has a link to a section of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration that goes into technical detail, but it still has some easy-to-understand areas including a handy set of links to El Nino-related news pages. El Nino.com would seem to be an obvious place to visit. It is a site from The San Diego Daily Transcript, a local business newspaper, and its information is heavily San Diego-centric. That makes it of little use outside California, since much more than just that state has been affected by El Nino. Everything from tornadoes in Miami to the warm winter in parts of the Northeast to fires in Indonesia to drought in Africa has been traced to it. To grasp the world-wide impact, see the Cable News Network's maps that allow you to click and learn about specific parts of the unitedstates and the world. A visit to Australia's Bureau of Meteorology provides a look at El Nino from outside the unitedstates and is one of many sites that explains La Nina (little girl) or the anti-El Nino, which is the abnormal cooling of parts of the Pacific. Two news sites that offer useful perspectives are the Environmental News Network and Nova Online. E.N.N.'s site uses photographs and Real Audio software to tell the story of El Nino events through the years. Nova Online, the companion site of the science television series on PBS, has a wide range of features on tracking El Nino, including field reports, frequently asked questions and Web cameras in various cities. The Web provides practical information about handling the effects of El Nino. Mr. Cohen's Water Resources Department offers weather forecasts, flood warnings and even "how to fight flooding at home." The Federal Emergency Management Agency's site has a special area about the current situation. Businesses of all sizes are also keeping track of El Nino. Some insurance companies have put up sections about it on their sites. For instance, Factory Mutual, a property-loss engineering company that is owned by three insurance companies -- Allendale Mutual Insurance, Arkwright Mutual Insurance and Protection Mutual Insurance -- tells visitors how to prepare their businesses for El Nino's "possible effects." Among the topics covered: historical El Nino loss data and how to deal with such problems as flooding, freeze-ups and roof collapses. A small-company site that has gotten into the act is Rochester Tent City, a camping store in Rochester. It has an El Nino Preparation Center filled with terrible warnings of "billions in damage expected on West Coast," and quotes Government officials, including Vice President Al Gore and Senator Barbara Boxer from California. The goal is to encourage visitors to buy such emergency supplies as life boats and water purifiers through its on-line store. On the Web, there is always someone who will find some humor in any situation, and El Nino is no exception. The "El Nino Hotline of Doom," has a "hype gauge" and a collection of more than 300 dire predictions from media outlets nationwide. Unfortunately for the dozens of people who call the operations center where Mr. Cohen works, many of those predictions have turned out to be true. title:
TECHNOLOGY: DIGITAL COMMERCE;
It seems there's no fail-safe way of protecting children on the Internet.
body: ONE of the most striking paradoxes of Internet culture is that children are the most computer literate among us, but their vulnerability to on-line predators prevents their being able to enjoy or explore freely what is likely to be the defining medium of their lives. The problem, to date, is intractable. On one hand, how do on-line services create a safe place for children to meet and play together while at the same time protecting them from pedophiles and unscrupulous marketers who often pose as children? On the other, how can we keep children away from pornographic adult sites, which are accessible at the click of a mouse button? Today's solutions to the pornography problem, at least, are not working very well. For example, "filtering" programs like Cybersitter, Net Nanny and Cyberpatrol are supposed to block access to a constantly updated list of "adult" World Wide Web sites. But an article in last September's issue of Consumer Reports noted that all were relatively easy to circumvent. Even if blocking programs worked, they do not begin to address the problem of how to keep adults from masking their identities in on-line settings like chat rooms, where children can be lured unwittingly into sexual conversations or even meetings, or coerced into commercial transactions. Thomas Morgan, a longtime on-line executive and the president of Nvolve Inc. (www.nvolve.com), a company that develops on-line communities, has devised a solution he calls the Safe Playgrounds Initiative. He has been discussing it privately for several months with various organizations, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a civil liberties group, and the Children's Advertising Review Unit of the Better Business Bureau. Mr. Morgan is now going public with the initiative, which he developed after deciding to build an on-line community for children and realizing that all the security measures were too complex or constricting. For example, America Online's "Kids Only" site displays many warnings and safety tips, but its "pager" system, which allows children to summon a monitor if they feel threatened on line, is hopelessly backed up. Many users report waiting half an hour or longer for a monitor to respond. And to protect both its young users and its reputation as a family company, the popular Disney Web site (www.disney.com) allows children to communicate only inside its Disney Blast area, which not only requires registration but asks parents to specify with whom their children are allowed to communicate. "Parents can drop the restriction if they want," said Jake Winebaum, president of Disney Online. "But if they do, we educate them about the consequences of their decision." Mr. Morgan is hoping to change the rules of engagement, and thus the consequences as well. "We wanted children to be able to go to places on the Web where they can feel safe to explore and play," Mr. Morgan said. "We also wanted something that doesn't require every consumer to be a Web genius -- something simple, clean and easily applied." The result was Safe Playgrounds, which Mr. Morgan is now asking industry executives and politicians to support. Its tenets are: *To develop a "kid's browser" that includes an unbreakable bit of software code that Mr. Morgan is calling a G-bit, for general audience. This identifies the user as someone who is either under 18 years old or who does not want to see adult material. Web publishers then rate and code their own sites, and anyone who shows up at an adult site with this G-bit will be denied access. *To stop sexual and commercial predators who seek out children on line, by means of what Mr. Morgan calls the Safe Playground Law, which would make it a Federal crime for an adult to impersonate a child on line in any site declared a Safe Playground. Adults on children's sites would be required to identify themselves as adults. Mr. Morgan said this tenet dealt with the issue of intent. "If you impersonate a child, you intend to defraud a child," he said, "and we won't deal with that. What happens between consenting adults is one thing, but children require special circumstances, and it's incumbent upon adults to behave accordingly." *To develop Safe Playground qualification criteria, including trained monitors in chat rooms to keep an eye peeled for predators; a guarantee that no child's full name, physical address or personal email address will ever be revealed; an agreement to inform parents when sites are collecting data about youngsters, and an agreement to display only clearly identified, age-appropriate, noncoercive advertising messages. "The Safe Playground criteria are very closely in sync and may even surpass what we're trying to get the industry to do," said Elizabeth La Scoutx, vice president of the Council of Better Business Bureaus and the director of its Children's Advertising Review Unit. Beleaguered executives like Disney's Mr. Winebaum predict that enacting an initiative like Safe Playgrounds will be difficult, but he is also adamant that an industrywide, mandatory solution is "the only way to solve the problem on the scale that's required." Lori Fena, the chairman of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, agreed. "No one wants to pay to babyproof the Net, but everybody is willing to support creating child-safe areas like playgrounds in the real world," she said. "This initiative is the most sane thing I've seen yet -- socially, legally and economically. If the goal is to go after predatory behavior by adults, then let's go for it." title: Echoids
body: CYBERVILLE Clicks, Culture, and the Creation of an Online Town. By Stacy Horn. 340 pp. newyork: Warner Books. $23. Nearly a decade ago, Stacy Horn, a 33-year-old Internet aficionado, created East Coast Hangout (Echo) in her downtown Manhattan apartment. Echo, an interactive bulletin board service, was among the earliest Internet communities, one with a distinctly newyork City attitude. In "Cyberville," Horn's own analysis of the virtual community that began with a $20,000 nest egg, she explores, in a breathless mixture of essays and rants that are rife with sagacity and introspection, the fractious, neurotic democracy she nurtured. In 12 chapters that are peppered with the populist wit and perspicacity of dozens of "Echoids," Horn embarks on a frank, down-to-earth and sometimes bawdy explanation of what an on-line community means to those who populate its innards. Sometimes whining like teen-agers, sometimes as erudite as ancient scribes, Echoids frantically seek to communicate, debate and argue by sending notes and letters about events of the moment. They descend on news like vultures. Horn likens this feeding frenzy to the cable television program "Mystery Science Theater 3000," in which quick commentary about a movie is more important than the movie. In an on-line rapture that at best is literary and at worst sophomoric, Echoids live to gossip about culture and sex, in phrases that on the surface are overridingly condescending, even mean. But Horn demonstrates how the language reveals a kind of concerned worldview that is often lost in this city, where manipulative power and success become substitutes for love. In Horn's detailed characterizations, dozens of Echoids appear like colorful characters in a popular novel. There's Miss Outer Boro, a joking yet woeful Brooklynite who places hilarious one-liners in the self-deprecating folder "I Hate Myself." Vivian and Jack flirt in cyberspace and then date in real life. With abandon that makes most pornography appear tame, they engage in extreme sadomasochistic sex and fall in love to have a lasting relationship. Now and then, the appalling realities of socializing on line threaten to pulverize what Horn has fought with such determination to maintain. There are Nazi interlopers, sexual harassers, even an incessant stalker with whom Horn has to do battle, and she points out that the off-line world never quite understands her endeavors. At every turn, it seems, she is frustrated in her efforts to justify her community to the dunces who populate the Luddite planet outside. Especially annoying is that the traditional media just don't get it. Although "Cyberville" is all about the way people relate to one another, surely it could have used more facts about the business that is Echo. What business decision led Horn to move Echo from her cramped apartment to a fancy office in TriBeCa? When the competition offered a buyout, what sum was she offered? How does the text-based Echo expect to compete in a world where every day the Internet becomes more graphic and video-and audio-oriented? Readers are never clearly told. THE Echoids' sometimes onerous cynicism can alienate the reader of this book, and so might Horn's confession that she started Echo "to meet guys." But "Cyberville" resonates because, beyond helping us get inside the technology that separates us as much as it brings us together, the words of the author and of the Echoids are about the souls of people, about how they live together over time. (If they ever do choose to leave the fold, Horn sends them an uplifting Robert Penn Warren poem.) Horn proves that Echoids have built up a lasting municipality that is flawed, mistake-ridden, sin-filled, but entirely their own. Yes, sometimes Echo is too like a closed-minded clique or a snobbish private club. More often it shines with the hip, flashing neon of youngish inhabitants who are always ready to speak their minds with unbridled openness and turbulent emotion.

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
For Children, an Olympic Computer Event
body: When Elina Teplinsky, an 11th grader at Polytechnic Preparatory Country Day School in Brooklyn, watched the opening ceremonies of the Winter Olympics last week, she noticed an odd detail. Instead of releasing doves near the Olympic torches, as is the tradition, the International Olympic Committee released biodegradable, dove-shaped balloons. Her curiosity piqued, Miss Teplinsky, a 16-year-old resident of Bensonhurst, did some research and shared her findings on the Internet. "The balloon dove idea came to life for reasons of safety and in deference to animal lovers," she wrote, "after some doves were roasted to death by the Olympic flames" during the Seoul games of 1988. As part of a school project devised by Poly Prep, which is in Bay Ridge, and Alfred Doyle, the head of the school's computer department who also works with the Public Broadcasting Service, Poly Prep students are filing stories about the Winter Olympics in Nagano, Japan until its close on Feb. 22. They are also editing similar contributions by students from around the nation and the world. The stories are displayed, with the help of WNET-TV in newyork, on "Cyber School," a PBS Web site. Unlike similar sites, like that of Scholastic magazine, Poly Prep is perhaps the only site put together by students and teachers themselves.  WHAT YOU SEE -- The commentary ranges from the surprisingly polished to the unrestrained. Eric Shoikhetman, a 16-year-old 10th grader at Poly Prep, wrote that one of the odd consequences of the Olympic hockey competition is that teammates from National Hockey League clubs who will represent their respective countries will end up on opposing teams. "For example," he wrote, "instead of the Rangers' Wayne Gretzky passing the puck to Brian Leetch in the slot for a power play goal, the Great One will have to maneuver his way around Leetch in his attempts to score." Students in Japan were surprisingly blunt. Tomoaki N, a 16-year-old student from Hyougo, wrote: "I was surprised to watch the opening ceremony. Because it reminds us of old Japanese culture, which we can seldom find these days. However, in fact not many Japanese people are interested in this Olympic. I think we ought to be proud of this festival in Japan."  LINKS -- About a dozen, including one to an English-language version of coverage from Shinano Mainichi Shimbun, a local newspaper in Nagano (http://www.shinmai.co.jp/oly-eng/).  WHAT YOU GET -- Kids say the darnedest things on the Internet.   ANTHONY RAMIREZ  PBS Cyber School http://ibm.pbscyberschool.org/news/index.html  Polytechnic Preparatory Country Day School http://www.polyprep.brooklyn.ny.us/ Graphic   Photos

title: 'The Web Made Me Do It'
body: Velocity was the key word in the outraged debate over the media's coverage of the sexual allegations against President Bill Clinton. Critics complained that reporters, driven by the competitive backdraft of the new media -- meaning the Internet, of course, but also the three cable-news channels -- shattered the ethics barrier in their manic pursuit of the story. The press moved "too fast from the bullet to the atom bomb," said Joan Konner, publisher of The Columbia Journalism Review. "The digital age does not respect contemplation," said James M. Naughton, former executive editor of The Philadelphia Inquirer. Michael Isikoff, the Newsweek reporter whose scoop was pre-empted when Matt Drudge reported it on his Web site, the Drudge Report, weighed in, too, saying that Drudge "disposes of all the journalistic conventions and simply recycles the most sensational gossip that's going around." The critics were right on some points. A journalistic echo effect did take over, as many reporters blindly reported what other reporters had dug up -- never mind whether they had checked the details themselves. And the Internet and television's constant need to be fed did speed up the news cycle, with reporters churning out stories at a furious pace that created cycles within cycles. For instance, The Dallas Morning News published on its Web site and in its paper editions an article about the President and Monica Lewinsky that it retracted in a matter of hours. The next day, The Morning News republished its article -- with modifications -- after its source changed his statements. Several days later, The Wall Street Journal's interactive edition blared the news that Bayani Nelvis, a White House steward, had told a grand jury he caught Clinton and Lewinsky alone together. As controversy erupted -- Nelvis's lawyer called the report "absolutely false and irresponsible" -- the paper's print edition backpedaled. The turbulence made everyone a little woozy, but critics overstated the case when they heaped blame on the new media. After all, the biggest miscues, like The Morning News's yo-yo and a similar goof by ABC News, involved "old media" that went with a story too soon. Matt Drudge's contribution was straightforward and defensible: he reported, accurately, that Newsweek's editors, worried about the explosive nature of Isikoff's original article on the sex charges, had decided to delay it. So why was the criticism so intense? Perhaps because the new media exposed a wound. The real sin was that they laid bare, for all to see, how news is made. Like the preparation of sausage and legislation, the process can be ugly. Facts, rumors and hunches are collected and set down in the jigsaw puzzle of narrative. Editors and reporters move the pieces around to see if they form a pattern. Meanwhile, the competition is doing the same. The first organization to complete the puzzle wins the scoops and the readers. When the deadline whistle howls, things get messy. But the critics seem to think the Internet has an especially demonic power to distort; Tom Shales of The Washington Post called it "the new electronic Tower of Babel." But technology is neutral. It makes as much sense to blame modems and the Internet for distorting the spread of news as it does to blame telephones. In reality, the Internet is a technological tool with the same good and bad aspects as any other. Among its positive uses, for reporters and readers alike, is its role as a tip sheet and rapid-transmission medium. In the hectic days after the scandal broke, reporters at every newsroom in the country surfed Web sites, as did droves of readers. Drudge himself maintains an email list that allows him to zap his stories directly to subscribers, many of whom are journalists who don't always disdain what he has to say. Among news consumers, details of the scandal spread like an algae bloom, as devotees of the story emailed breaking news stories to their comrades and posted their own messages on newsgroups like alt.current-events.clinton.whitewater. The MSNBC News Web site recorded a nearly 300 percent increase in daily hits. Thanks to the Web, regional papers like The Dallas Morning News were in a position to compete in real time with print journalism's front four: The newyork Times, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal and The Los Angeles Times. The forces that compel journalists to break news at hyperspeed may sound futuristic, but actually they hark back to the speediest time in American journalism: the turn of the century. In newyork in 1900, there were at least 65 daily newspapers (counting the vital ethnic press), whose reporters scrambled to match and beat the competition. The new technology of the telephone, which many reporters disparaged when it was introduced (because it de-emphasized legwork), became as indispensable as the shorthand pad. Whenever the news cycle demanded it, dailies would publish "extra" editions (similar to the instant "extras" that some news organizations now publish on the Web). The variety offered by the newsstand in those times almost approached that of the Web today. Back then, newyorkers could choose the demagogic fulminations of William Randolph Hearst's newyork Journal, the prim institutional voice of Adolph Ochs's Times and papers representing all points in between. Determining the truth value of stories was left up to readers and editors. Somehow the Republic survived that info-glut. The ethics of early journalists were often shaky, but the hurly-burly also brought vigor to reporting. H. L. Mencken, worshiped by many as a newspaper god, writes with glee in his memoirs of how he and a reporter for a competing Baltimore paper made up stories out of whole cloth. Their target was a reporter who covered their beat for the city's third leading daily and who refused to pool his reporting. The recalcitrant reporter finally joined the pool after his editors bawled him out for missing the malarkey that Mencken and his pal were publishing. To be sure, the old days are overromanticized in plays like "The Front Page," but damned if Matt Drudge's jumping the gun on Isikoff's scoop didn't sound like Hildy Johnson pulling a fast one on Walter Burns. In the world of electronic commerce, you hear a lot about "disintermediation" -- the elbowing out of middlemen and distributors by the Web, which directly connects manufacturers with consumers. It is premature to herald the disintermediation of the news business by Web independents who leapfrog editors, libel attorneys and conventional journalistic standards. But the example of Drudge shows that anybody who has an Internet connection and something original to say can reach a global audience. Sensing this disintermediation in the works, the old media have expanded their profile on the Web. In addition to the Newsweek extra, practically every big daily, newsmagazine and TV network added a "Clinton Crisis" page to their Web sites. Disintermediation might sound like a prescription for an orgy of libel, but so far most of the alleged libel in the on-line world has centered on financial advice. The Web -- like old media -- appears to be self-policing: the very velocity that spreads untruths on the Web also brings instant accountability. As anyone who works on the Web knows, readers spank you via email the moment you make an error. The success of Matt Drudge also indicates that readers hunger for reporting that hasn't had the life pecked out of it by editors and lawyers who identify too strongly with the bow-tie-and-braces brigade that runs the Government and corporate America. As Drudge has repeatedly said, the sexcapade scandal was right under the noses of the Washington news establishment for months and months. Why was Isikoff the only reporter chasing it? Ethical standards are important, but we should never ignore the price we pay for them. Listen to the muckraker Lincoln Steffens, who rebelled at the stylistic straitjacket that The newyork Evening Post forced him to wear in 1892. "Reporters were to report the news . . . without prejudice, color and without style," he complained. "Humor or any sign of personality in our reports was caught, rebuked and, in time, suppressed." Instead of bemoaning the rise of cheeky Web characters, we should welcome them for what they are -- new voices that enliven journalism. No endorsement of new media should be unqualified. Drudge does play things fast and loose. He now faces a libel suit filed by the White House aide Sidney Blumenthal, stemming from Drudge's report that "court records" said that Blumenthal beat his wife. No such court records exist. Although Drudge withdrew the column and apologized, Blumenthal is continuing the suit against Drudge and his distributor, America Online. Already, electronic commerce mavens are talking about "reintermediation," in which a new breed of Web middleman will rise to make sense out of the chaos wrought by disintermediation. As the technology of the Web evolves, Internet devices will become as ubiquitous as telephones. Every newspaper will have the potential to break news as fast as a television station. Every television station will have the potential to become a newspaper. But people will still only have 24 hours a day to consume news. After the novelty wears off, most readers of the news on the Web will depend on Web reintermediators to dispense journalism of dependable accuracy, just the way they turn to dependable newspapers and networks today for scrupulous reporting. That's not to say that reckless journalists will vanish from the Web. Just like the supermarket tabloids, they'll find their markets. But if we're half as sophisticated as were big-city newspaper readers early in this century, we'll quickly figure out the difference, velocity and all, between excess and excellence. title:
TRAVEL ADVISORY;
CYBERSCOUT
body: There are no reliable figures on how many millions of people surf the Web for information about travel destinations and services. But there are recommended ways to get started, as I have learned from my own and others' experience, and, if you are already started, ways to improve the passage. And it can be useful to review the basics, even for experienced Web travelers. HARDWARE -- First, you need a computer. On the Windows 95 side, you can get by with an older PC using the 486 microprocessor if you already have one or can find a used one, but you will be far happier with a Pentium or Pentium II machine. On the Macintosh side, you can get by with the older 68040 chip, which you can't buy new, either, but you will be far happier with a Power Macintosh. Speeds are expressed with numbers like 66, 133, 166, 200, 300, 333; the bigger numbers represent faster computers; 133 used to be fast, and is now just adequate; 333 is extraordinarily swift, today. Prices for a new minimal machine start at about $1,000 (more for Macintosh), although $2,000 or so will buy a speedier vehicle. If you have an antediluvian Kaypro or Commodore or Apple II, put a "Computer Museum" sign on your front door. The more working memory, or RAM, the better; 16 megabytes is the minimum these days. The bigger the hard disk the better, too: a gigabyte or more. MODEM -- The computer must have a modem, the device that connects it to other computers through the telephone line. The speed of the modem determines how quickly a Web page will appear on the screen; and such travel-related pages as hotel and airline sites often depend on space- and time-eating graphics for their appeal. The minimum acceptable speed here is expressed as 28.8; 36.6 is better and 56 is still better. Surfers with that elderly 486 might squeeze by with a 14.4 modem if they are very patient. Modems cost $100 to $200. BROWSER -- There are two major software programs for browsing in cyberspace, Internet Explorer and Netscape Navigator. At any given moment, Internet Explorer is better than Netscape Navigator. At the next given moment, it is the other way around. You don't have to spend a lot of money on them -- they are free, or close to free, and the service that supplies you with access to the Internet ordinarily will provide them. SERVICES -- Yes, service. With a computer, modem, phone line and browser, you still can't connect directly to the Internet (the vast World Wide Web is part of that vaster network). You have to connect to a service that is itself connected to the Internet. The service might be America Online, Compuserve or the Microsoft Network, which have their own proprietary sections, forums and chat rooms, as well as connections to the Internet and Web. The other choice is an internet service provider, a company set up to provide a connection and offering little or nothing else. Prices range from $10 to $30 a month, plus telephone charges if the service does not have a local or an 800 number. Absolute beginners do best with one of the big services, which have a reasonably user-friendly home base as well as access to the Internet labyrinth. After a few weeks, or months, you can reassess the situation and decide if plain Internet access is all you need. Compuserve, my home base (lrshan@compuserve.com), has scores of its own travel facilities divided into such categories as Tools, Reservations, and Research, and forums divided both geographically and thematically, where members can seek and exchange information. The other services have similar offerings. One advantage of these proprietary categories over the Web is that they look and operate pretty much the same, so when you learn one you have gone a long way toward learning them all. WEB -- The Web is less uniform and can be confusing. For a start, search for your travel interests through one of the search engines that "index" the Web; Yahoo, Altavista and Lycos spring to mind, but there are many others. And you can collect addresses from newspapers, magazines and even books. The last step is experimentation. Whether your interest is skiing or kayaking, the Caribbean or the Arctic, the sources of information never come to an end. Even if they do, by the time you get to the end the first ones you looked at will have changed. Only dead Web sites are ever finished. Both Internet Explorer and Netscape Navigator will save addresses of Web sites that are worth a return visit. The last technical tip is to avoid contracts with short connection times (usually five or six hours) at a lower price. Five hours can slip by between dinner and bedtime, and the rates for hours beyond the minimum are steep; unlimited access is the way to go.   L. R. SHANNON Graphic   Illustration (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: America Online to Raise Fee For Unlimited Use to $21.95
body: In a major defection from the standard monthly price of $19.95 for Internet access, America Online, whose 11 million members make up more than half the home Internet market in the unitedstates, announced yesterday that it was increasing its charge for unlimited access to $21.95. America Online introduced its $19.95 flat-rate plan at the end of 1996. It announced its new pricing at the same time that it disclosed a broad management reorganization that elevated Robert W. Pittman, currently the president of America Online's network division, to the newly created position of president and chief operation officer of the entire company. In a separate announcement, the company said it was laying off half the remaining employees of Compuserve, the onetime rival that it purchased last week. Mr. Pittman, the founder of MTV, joined America Online in 1996 and was widely credited with curing the busy signals that had earned the service the nickname America Onhold and with increasing the company's profitability. America Online's shares surged $11.9375 yesterday to an all-time high of $110.4375 on the announcement. It is scheduled to release its earnings after the market's close today. "The Internet industry needs to raise prices," said Michael Parekh, an analyst at Goldman, Sachs. "None of the 4,000 Internet service providers that want to grow their subscriber base can make money at $19.95." Stephen M. Case, America Online's chairman, said the price increase was not expected to add to the company's profits this year. "The primary reason is to absorb higher network costs and to fund innovations like new content," he said of the price increase. International Business Machines recently replaced the unlimited pricing plan for its Global Network service with 100 hours a month for $19.95 and an additional fee for more time on line. Telephone companies, on the other hand, have been lowering prices. Bell Atlantic is offering unlimited Internet access at $17.95 a month, and MCI Communications recently dropped its rate to $14.95 a month. Mr. Pittman said yesterday in a telephone interview that the price increase might slow the company's rapid growth by prompting some customers to cancel their memberships. But he predicted that it would be "a one-time blip" and that "we will go right back to the growth curve, albeit more slowly." Customers, he said, would still be willing to pay extra for America Online's content, service and reputation. America Online also offers a plan that costs $4.95 a month for the first three hours and $2.50 an hour after that. Three-quarters of its customers, however, are on the unlimited plan. The company announced that it would lay off 500 of the 1,000 employees of Compuserve, mostly from customer service, which will be contracted to outside companies. In addition, the company said it would halt development of a planned new service that would have offered Compuserve's on-line forums on a wide range of topics to users of the Internet's World Wide Web. Instead, America Online said it would concentrate on improving the main service, which has more than two million paying customers. As for the appointment of Mr. Pittman as the No. 2 executive in the company, Paul W. Noglows, an analyst with Hambrecht and Quist, said: "This is a real positive for AOL. He has the energy to build the AOL brand going forward." As expected, the heretofore independent America Online Studios division run by Ted Leonsis, who was once America Online's president, will be folded into Mr. Pittman's oversight, and its advertising and marketing functions will be combined with a unified, companywide sales operation.

title:
COMPANY REPORTS: THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Write-Offs Result in a Loss At Dow Jones in 4th Quarter - Correction Appended
body: Dow Jones & Company reported a big net loss yesterday for the fourth quarter, mostly because of a write-off connected to the reorganization of its financial information business. The company, which also owns The Wall Street Journal and other publications, had a net loss of $889.3 million, or $9.22 a diluted share, compared with a 1996 fourth-quarter profit of $59.6 million, or 62 cents a share. The loss this year included a charge of $922.5 million for the financial data business, Dow Jones Markets, which was formerly known as Telerate and which the company has put up for sale. Excluding one-time items, Dow Jones profits fell 24 percent, to $38.7 million, or 40 cents a share. Investors barely reacted to the report, sending the stock up 37.5 cents, to $51. Peter Appert, a media analyst at BT Alex. Brown, said that the earnings were in line with expectations but that the write-off was larger than expected. Still, he said, "they are letting go of Telerate and going forward, so they are much better off." Dow Jones had indicated that it would have a loss in the quarter, figures for which are generally released during the last week of January. This year, however, the company said it was pushing back release of the earnings report because the write-offs were complex and took more time to prepare. Several analysts who follow the company said, however, that they believed that Dow Jones had been waiting to evaluate the range of bids for potential buyers of the financial information business. According to one person involved in the discussions, the company has received an offer of $500 million for Dow Jones Markets from Bridge News, which is owned by the investment company Welsh Carson, Anderson & Stowe. Other offers, from Cantor, Fitzgerald Securities; ILX Systems, a unit of the Thomson Corporation, and the Primark Corporation, are said to be lower. However, the bidding is not yet officially over. Bids could be raised -- or dropped -- in subsequent rounds, and a final decision is not expected for several weeks. Dow Jones acquired Telerate in a series of transactions for a total of $1.6 billion between 1985 and 1989. It had already written off $200 million and is carrying the business on its books at $1.4 billion. Several of the younger members of the Bancroft family, which controls Dow Jones, have been pushing for a sale of the unit, but the decision to put it on the block has apparently not assuaged their dissatisfaction. Two cousins -- William C. Cox 3d and Elisabeth Goth -- are still said to be unhappy with the overall performance of the company, according to a person close to the family. In addition, this person said that Mr. Cox and Ms. Goth had learned that the chairman of Dow Jones, Peter R. Kann, had been attributing the stock's increase in recent months to his management team in talks with some investment groups; Mr. Cox and Ms. Goth are said to be upset because they believe the increase in the stock price is attributable to pressure from them and outside investors to improve the operations of the company. In the last year, the stock has risen roughly 25 percent, from less than $40 a share. A Dow Jones spokesman said yesterday that stock prices were always the result of a large number of factors. Still, the Bancroft family is hardly unified in its approach, because older family members have generally been more supportive of the management. Indeed, at a regularly scheduled family meeting in Boston several weeks ago with Roy Hammer, the influential lawyer who is a trustee of many family trusts that own Dow Jones stock, the older family members still appeared quite supportive of the management, according to a person who attended the meeting. As for the most recent quarter's results, there were other one-time items, in addition to the cost of the Dow Jones Markets restructuring. The company also took charges to restructure its television operations and IDD Enterprises L.P., a financial publishing subsidiary; it also recorded a gain on the sale of a newsprint mill and related timberlands. The company said that revenues in the fourth quarter rose 2.7 percent, to $689.5 million. Though the company said The Wall Street Journal had a strong year, The Journal is part of its business publishing segment, which also includes some TV businesses and the interactive publishing group. Because of write-offs in those businesses, the business publishing unit reported fourth-quarter operating income of $52.6 million, down from $66.6 million in the period a year earlier. The company said that advertising linage at The Wall Street Journal rose 8.6 percent for the quarter. The financial information services segment includes the results of Dow Jones Markets, Dow Jones Newswires and the Dow Jones Indexes group. For the quarter, those businesses had a loss of $1 billion, compared with income last year of $36.9 million. Correction  Because of an editing error, an article in Business Day yesterday about the fourth-quarter results of Dow Jones & Company misstated the name of a possible suitor for its financial information business, and described that company's ownership incorrectly. It is Bridge Information Systems, not Bridge News, and it is owned in part, not entirely, by Welsh Carson, Anderson & Stowe. Correction-Date: February 11, 1998, Wednesday Graphic

title: 2 Internet Access Services Discuss Joining Forces
body: The At Home Corporation is in talks with Road Runner, a unit of Time Warner Inc., about combining their high-speed Internet access services to strengthen their competition with local phone companies in the race to link millions of homes to the Internet. "We've been talking to them for a while," an At Home spokesman, Matt Wolfrom, said Friday. But, he added, "no deal is imminent." At Home's talks with Road Runner, first reported in Broadcasting and Cable magazine, come as cable television operators rush to improve their existing lines and roll out digital set-top boxes to offer home Internet service. The cable companies must compete with phone companies, like the regional Bells, which also are working to deliver faster on-line access to consumers. At Home's majority shareholder is Tele-Communications Inc., the nation's largest cable operator. Road Runner provides Internet access over Time Warner's cable lines. Time Warner declined to comment on the talks. Industry analysts estimate that the market for Internet access in homes could reach $10 billion a year. Last month, Compaq Computer, Intel, Microsoft and the nation's six largest local phone companies teamed to establish standards for digital subscriber lines to send information at higher speeds over existing phone lines. Digital lines give computer users faster data services like Internet access and faxing, while leaving the lines open for regular phone calls. The Compaq-led group wants to offer the service by year's end. At Home provides Internet access over cable lines in Baltimore, Chicago and elsewhere. The company said that it expected to spend up to $40 million a year in the next several years to bring its service to new cities in the unitedstates and abroad.

title: More Join Challenge to Library Over Blocking of Internet Sites
body: A newspaper columnist and a champion of banned books are among eight plaintiffs who are challenging restrictions on Internet sites at the Loudoun County Library as unconstitutional. Rob Morse, a San Francisco Examiner columnist; John Ockerbloom, who publishes the text of banned books on his World Wide Web site, and the American Civil Liberties Union are among those who intervened Friday in a Federal lawsuit against a library policy that blocks some mainstream sites as well as pornography. Sites that the filtering software blocks include those belonging to The Examiner and The San Francisco Chronicle, a Methodist church in San Francisco and a University of Maryland women's association, the complaint contends. Blocking the sites violates the right to free speech, the A.C.L.U. contends. The library installed the special X-Stop software in November on computers that library patrons use for access to the Internet. X-Stop filters the Internet by screening material for obscene or sexually explicit language. A group of residents sued in Federal District Court in December, claiming that using the software was a form of government censorship and was arbitrary. Ann Beeson, an A.C.L.U. lawyer in newyork, said of the filter: "It's similar to banning books. Library patrons should be able to decide for themselves what to read and what not to read." In 1997, the Supreme Court ruled that material on the Internet should be given at least as much free speech protection as books enjoy. Libraries, Ms. Beeson said, should be held to the higher standard of the First Amendment. "You simply can't block books that are constitutionally protected," she said. The Library Board's lawyer, Ken Bass, denied that the policy violates free speech. He said the board, which approved the policy on a 5-to-4 vote in October, based its decision on two goals -- protecting children from pornography and avoiding Web sites that would create a hostile workplace for library workers. X-Stop was designed by the Log-On Data Corporation of Anaheim, Calif. Calls to Michael Bradshaw, the company chairman, were not returned Friday. The library director, Douglas Henderson, said last month that he knew that X-Stop would have flaws. He said his test found that the software allowed 9 pornographic sites to get through and blocked 57 sites that contained no objectionable content. But Mr. Henderson said that X-Stop performed better than other software he tested.

title:
Taking In the Sites;
Focusing On Heritage Of Blacks
body: Black History Month need not be confined to a four-week period anymore. Thanks to the World Wide Web, it is possible to study the history of the African-American experience year round. But February, when it is officially observed, is a good time to seek out information, as many sites have highlighted special sections for visitors. "Over the last couple of years, the visibility of sites about the month has greatly increased," said Joel Dreyfuss, former editor of Our World News, an on-line newspaper that offers "news from a black perspective." Mr. Dreyfuss, who is now a senior editor at Fortune magazine, said that the increased presence went hand-in-hand with the growth of general sites owned and operated by African-Americans. One starting point is San Francisco-based Netnoir, which bills itself as the "soul of cyberspace." Its spotlight on Black History Month features a background essay about the origins of the celebration, as well as profiles of important figures, including Rosa Parks -- whose refusal to move to the back of the bus helped start the civil rights movement -- and the actor Paul Robeson. There is also a trivia section that tests and educates at the same time. Among the questions: Who was the first black to win the Nobel Peace Prize? No, it was not the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Ralph J. Bunche, the United Nations Under Secretary, won the Nobel in 1950 for his mediation of the 1948 Arab-Israeli dispute. Naturally, Dr. King and his legacy are highly visible on sites that deal with African-American history. The definitive site is the Martin Luther King Jr. Papers Project, based at Stanford University. It has an extensive collection of documents by and about Dr. King, as well as a link to the King Center for Nonviolent Social Change in Atlanta. Afro-Americ@, the site of Baltimore-based Afro-American Newspapers, has several exhibits in its on-line Black History Museum, which has links, photographs and documents. The site deals with aspects of black history that are well known, like slavery and the Black Panthers, as well as some that are not, such as the black reporters who covered battlefronts in World War II. The Encyclopaedia Brittanica site has a guide to black history that is free until the end of this month. The encyclopedia's vast print resources have been combined with video and audio to make the section useful to students and adults alike. The entry on Malcolm X, whose death anniversary is on Feb. 21, is an effective example of its multimedia approach. A handy timeline takes you through the ages, beginning with the early 16th century (the start of the slave trade) and ending with 1997 (Michael Jordan and the Chicago Bulls win their fifth N.B.A. championship). There are several sites that deal with the man who is widely considered the father of the study of black history. To learn about Carter G. Woodson, who established Negro History Week in 1926, visit the Association for the Study of Afro-American Life and History. In 1976, 26 years after his death, the week was turned into Black History Month. Two sites that do not prominently feature Black History Month per se but are worth a visit are the site of the N.A.A.C.P. and the W.E.B. Du Bois Institute for Afro-American Research. N.A.A.C.P. Online is a good introduction to the oldest and most famous civil rights group in the unitedstates. And the Harvard-based Du Bois Institute, which is named for the co-founder of the N.A.A.C.P., has information about its programs, fellowships and faculty. The on-line resources of the newyork Public Library's Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture provide insight into the extent of the contribution of blacks to the shaping of American culture. They include exhibits about the Harlem Renaissance in the early part of this century and key figures in it, like the writer Langston Hughes. A site that is unusually creative in its approach to African-American movies and music is Black Voices. It includes a "Blaxploitation" section, which lists movies in this genre, like "Shaft" and "Blacula," and a "Jukebox" section, with sound clips from a variety of recordings, like Scott Joplin's "Maple Leaf Rag," Charlie Parker's "Bird" and the Supremes' "Where Did Our Love Go." Black Voices has also teamed up with the on-line retailer Music Boulevard to offer a selection of albums and articles to accompany observations of Black History Month (all conveniently for sale, of course).
