title:
INVESTING IT;
Netscape Battles Takeover Talk and Shrinking Sales
body: THE Netscape Communications Corporation has suffered through a humbling month. Once the highest flier of the Internet, Netscape said in January that it would report a loss for 1997 of $115.5 million and lay off 400 of its 3,200 workers. Yet the crowning indignity came last week, as it seemed that Netscape had moved from a turnaround situation to takeover bait -- a speculative stock. On Wednesday, Reuters reported that the company's long-falling stock had jumped that day because of rumors that Sun Microsystems might acquire Netscape. Then, The Wall Street Journal reported the next morning that Netscape was in talks with several companies -- Sun, Oracle, I.B.M. and America Online -- about selling all or part of itself. On Thursday, Netscape shares rose sharply again, closing up $2.6875 a share, at $21.9375. Netscape refused to comment publicly on the reports. But in an email message to Netscape employees on Thursday, James Barksdale, the president and chief executive, said, "These rumors are damaging to us and extremely distracting." On Friday, Mr. Barksdale again did not seem eager to auction off Netscape, people who attended a company meeting said. Speaking to more than 2,000 employees, Mr. Barksdale urged them to stay focused on their jobs. "We've defied the odds before and we can do it again," he said. The takeover speculation cooled somewhat on Friday, as Netscape shares slipped to $21.625. Despite its recent losses, Netscape "has viable business opportunities without selling out," said David Readerman, a software analyst at Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities. And Mr. Readerman is not a Netscape enthusiast, having pulled his buy recommendation off the company more than a year ago, when the stock was trading at $40. But clearly, Netscape faces a slow, difficult transition, analysts say. Mary McCaffrey, an analyst at BT Alex. Brown, estimates that the company will not return to profitability until the third quarter. She expects Netscape to lose $3 million over all this year on sales of $573 million. Even in 1999, she anticipates slender profits of $30 million on sales of $718 million. Netscape, an Internet pioneer with the first commercial World Wide Web browser, is under intense pressure from the Microsoft Corporation. Netscape still has an estimated 60 percent share of the browser market, compared with 35 percent for Microsoft. But Microsoft is gaining fast and it gives away its Internet Explorer browser. Netscape was really hit in the fourth quarter, when its revenues from so-called client software, which includes its Navigator browser, dropped to $12 million, down from $52 million a year earlier. The company's other businesses -- advertising and electronic-commerce revenues from its popular Web site, and sales of Internet software used on computer hubs, or servers -- grew, but not enough to offset the drop in its client software sales. To cope, Netscape announced two steps on Jan. 22. It would match Microsoft by giving away its Navigator browser, and it would freely distribute the source code -- the basic programming language -- for its popular Communicator suite of Internet software products, including the browser. Both moves are intended to spread Netscape's technology and brand -- attracting people and advertising dollars to its Web site, and bringing in corporate customers for its server software. What signs of life should prospective Netscape investors look for? Analysts point to four: a stabilization or an uptick in Netscape's share of the browser market; declarations by personal-computer makers or Internet service providers that they will use Navigator as their preferred browser; strong growth in the company's mainstay business of selling server software to large corporations, and, of course, a return to profitability. More than anything else, says Kathey Hale, an analyst for Dataquest, they should watch Netscape's core business of selling software to companies. That business is growing sharply, but Netscape needs to convince many more corporations to choose its technology over that of rivals like Microsoft. Ms. Hale estimates that Netscape's software sales to corporations more than doubled last year, to $276 million, though that figure included sizable revenues from browser software that it will now give away. "The challenge for Netscape is to get that kind of growth again this year in its core business," Ms. Hale said. "And that's going to be very difficult."

title: F.C.C. Rule Review Assailed By a New Republican Member
body: A major rift on the Federal Communications Commission opened yesterday as a new member of the its Republican minority sharply criticized the commission as failing to review its myriad telecommunications regulations adequately. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 directs the commission to evaluate all of its telecommunications regulations every two years, beginning this year. Yesterday the F.C.C. said it had completed an internal review and it proposed initiatives aimed at altering or eliminating 31 rules deemed unnecessary or overly burdensome. But a new member, Harold Furchtgott-Roth, a former chief economist for the House Commerce Committee, called the commission's effort inadequate, saying in an interview, "I find it very difficult to believe that this notice is going to be sufficient." Referring to the section of the act that mandates the review, he said: "I don't think it's there just to do a paper shuffle. It's there for a purpose. Aside from simply following the law because that's what we have to do, I think there's a real public policy reason for that section to be there. And I'm afraid that if there's just a selective review of a few regulations we're not following the letter or the spirit of the law." "The issue there is read the law," he added. "Don't try to get around it. Follow it. Do what it says." Mr. Furchtgott-Roth said he was undecided what official action -- if any -- he would take if the commission's chairman, William E. Kennard, a Democrat, refused to broaden the review significantly. Four of the five members of the commission, which consists of three Democrats and two Republicans, joined the F.C.C. last fall. The sole holdover is Susan Ness, a Democrat. Mr. Kennard, himself a new member, has described the group's relations as cordial. Last month Michael K. Powell, the other Republican on the commission, publicly criticized the panel for making it too difficult for the Bell local telephone companies to win approval to offer long-distance service. Mr. Kennard agreed with parts of Mr. Powell's assessment and said the F.C.C. would try to work more closely with the Bells as they drafted their long-distance petitions. But yesterday Mr. Kennard seemed to find no common ground with Mr. Furchtgott-Roth. "This is the most comprehensive review ever conducted by the F.C.C.," Mr. Kennard said in an interview. The proposed revisions include altering the rules on the amount of electric power that can be fed into the public telephone network. Increasing the amount could allow consumers to use computer modems that transmit data at higher speeds than are now generally possible. Mr. Kennard said that the review met the requirements of the law and that a focused approach would be more effective than an open-ended evaluation of the commission's regulations. "The suggestion that we would take all of the rules that govern the agency and put them on a table and invite the public in to tell us which ones to do away with would be a very unproductive process," he said, adding that the F.C.C. had tried to do just that while he was the commission's general counsel in the mid-1990's. "You get a pile of comments, and it's not shaped and it's not targeted and it's useless." Mr. Furchtgott-Roth said that neither he nor members of his staff had been invited to participate in the commission's review. Mr. Kennard said that Mr. Furchtgott-Roth had in fact been invited, and that a meeting between Mr. Furchtgott-Roth and David Solomon, the commission's deputy general counsel, had been scheduled for today to discuss the review.

title: Microsoft Shifts Web Unit to Windows Group
body: In a quiet reorganization that is certain to raise eyebrows in light of the Microsoft Corporation's antitrust battle with the unitedstates Government, the software giant today moved the group that develops its Internet Explorer World Wide Web browser into the business unit that develops and markets its Windows operating system. The issue of whether Internet Explorer is a separate application or an integrated part of Windows 95 is at the heart of a lawsuit filed by the Justice Department charging that Microsoft violated a 1994 antitrust agreement. Today's move will shift the Internet Explorer group headed by David Cole, who testified as a Microsoft witness last month, into the company's Personal and Business Systems Group, which is headed by James E. Allchin. Microsoft insists that it has the right under the terms of the 1994 agreement to add any new features it likes to its operating systems. But the Justice Department asserts that browsers are distinct applications and that Microsoft is using its dominance of the operating system market to build a monopoly in the browser market. In December, Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson of unitedstates District Court in Washington sided with the Justice Department and issued a temporary restraining order that blocked Microsoft from forcing computer makers to include Internet Explorer as a condition of installing Windows 95 on their products. Analysts said today that irrespective of antitrust arguments, the move made sense from a business standpoint. "Internet Explorer is an integrated product," David Readerman, a financial analyst at Nationsbanc Montgomery Securities Inc., said. "You better integrate the reporting responsibilities." Under the new organizational structure, three of Microsoft's product groups will report to Paul A. Maritz, the company's group vice president for platforms and applications. The three are the Personal and Business Systems Group run by Mr. Allchin, the Consumer Platforms Group led by Craig Mundie, and a new Applications and Tools Group, which is the responsibility of Bob Muglia. A separate division, the Interactive Media Group, which is led by Frank M. Higgins, does not report to Mr. Maritz. In the past, Brad A. Silverberg headed the Applications and Internet Client Group, which also reported to Mr. Maritz and which included Mr. Cole's Internet Explorer group. The Applications and Internet Client Group has been disbanded and replaced by Mr. Muglia's new Applications and Tools Group. The reorganization affected several key Microsoft executives. Brad Chase, who was a key member of the company's Internet marketing effort, will move to Mr. Allchin's Windows group to become vice president of marketing. And John Ludwig, who had been heading some of the company's Internet and home products groups, will move to Mr. Higgins's Interactive Media Group to run a business called Web Essentials. Conspicuous in his absence today was Mr. Silverberg, the veteran Microsoft executive behind Windows 95 development. Mr. Silverberg has been on leave since last summer, leading to speculation that he might leave the company. However he sent email to various Microsoft employees today saying that he was still on leave and was waiting for the right job before returning. "At that level, there aren't many chairs to fill," one Microsoft employee said. "And the egos are very large."

title: Reuters Consultant Seen Taking Large Amounts of Data
body: A Manhattan computer consultant linked to a suspected scheme with a subsidiary of Reuters Holdings P.L.C. to steal information from Bloomberg L.P. was monitored downloading hundreds of screens of proprietary Bloomberg data during one-day periods, people briefed on the case said yesterday. The amount of information said to have been obtained from the Bloomberg terminal used by the consultant, Cyberspace Research Associates Inc., was so large that it significantly exceeded the amount downloaded by other Bloomberg customers. Indeed, at one point Bloomberg executives were said to have debated shutting down the consultant's terminal, but were persuaded to keep it active by law enforcement officials in order to allow the investigation to continue. The Government is investigating whether the subsidiary, Reuters Analytics, commissioned Cyberspace Research to steal the information from Bloomberg. The investigation, which has been under way for about a year, is examining whether the data were incorporated into products of Reuters, and whether officials used it to reconstruct analysis programs used by Bloomberg through a process known as "reverse engineering," Reuters said in a statement this week. Michael Bloomberg, the chairman and chief executive of the company, did not return a telephone call seeking comment. Robert Crooke, a Reuters spokesman, also declined comment. Telephone calls to Cyberspace Research have gone unanswered for several days, and the line was disconnected yesterday. A telephone number for David Schwartz, the president of Cyberspace Research, could not be obtained. The investigation, which is being handled by prosecutors in the unitedstates Attorney's office in Manhattan, is said to be examining a number of possible charges, including violation of the Economic Espionage Act of 1996, which made theft of trade secrets a Federal crime. People who have been briefed on the case said prosecutors believe that Cyberspace Research obtained thousands of screens of Bloomberg data, the fundamental product of the computer system. Prosecutors believe that the information was then turned over to Reuters executives, these people said. The inquiry is examining whether that information was used in Reuters products. Cyberspace Research, a customer of Bloomberg, obtained the data directly from its authorized terminal. But, if it did so in order to turn the information over to Reuters, those acts would violate its agreement with Bloomberg and could well constitute a criminal fraud, lawyers said. Reuters was not a customer of Bloomberg, and indeed, companies in this industry do not allow competitors to have access to their computer systems. The most valuable data to obtain from a Bloomberg system, industry experts said, involve historical information about an investment, as well as related facts, such as payment dates for bonds. Bloomberg established a lead in such data early on, although Reuters maintained its strength in pricing data fed from exchanges and information known as "contributed data," which is provided by financial institutions reporting in such areas as foreign exchange. In the week since Reuters first disclosed the grand jury investigation, Cyberspace Research has rapidly emerged as the linchpin of the inquiry. Federal prosecutors were said to have obtained more than 100 written communications between Reuters Analytics, which is based in Stamford, Conn., and Cyberspace Research. Moreover, law enforcement officials were said to have confronted an executive with the consulting company months before Reuters was told of the inquiry -- a sign that the consulting company may have been cooperating with the investigation.

title:
TESTING OF A PRESIDENT: MEDIA NOTEBOOK;
Internet Story Revives Questions on Standards
body: The first story hit the Internet around 4 P.M. Wednesday. The Wall Street Journal reported on its Web site that a longtime White House steward had told a Federal grand jury that he had seen President Clinton and Monica S. Lewinsky alone together in a study next to the Oval Office. The story also included other details about evidence The Journal said he had provided to the grand jury. The article went on to say that the steward, Bayani Nelvis, had recounted what he had seen to the Secret Service because he was "personally offended" by it. The Journal attributed the information to anonymous sources. Before long, the steward's lawyer had strenuously denied the account. During the evening and the next morning, The Journal amended its initial version of the story, but not before it had been picked up by other news organizations across the country. The episode provides another cautionary tale in the reporting of a story as fast-paced as the one that broke two weeks ago centering on accusations that the President had sex with an intern in the White House and encouraged her to lie about it under oath. The speed with which news travels has been accelerated in recent years by the rise of the Internet and 24-hour cable television news. Within minutes after the first story was posted on the Internet, The Journal's Washington bureau chief, Alan Murray, was on CNBC, a cable television news channel, talking about The Journal's scoop. His remarks were later picked up by MSNBC and posted on the MSNBC Web site. Then at 6:40 P.M., The Journal posted a revised version of the story. It quoted the steward's lawyer calling the first story "absolutely false and irresponsible." The steward was now said in The Journal article to have spoken to the Secret Service, not necessarily the grand jury, about what he had seen. Then yesterday morning, yet another version appeared in the printed edition of The Journal, incorporating a number of small changes from the original. It ran, on page A24, under the headline, "Controversy Erupts Over Testimony to Grand Jury by White House Steward." Precisely what happened with The Journal's story remained a subject of heated disagreement yesterday. Joe Lockhart, a White House spokesman, accused The Journal of lowering its standards to beat its competition by getting its story out first, an accusation that has been repeatedly leveled against news organizations in the two weeks since the scandal against Mr. Clinton broke. But Richard Tofel, a spokesman for The Journal, said the newspaper had done nothing other than update a breaking story, a standard journalistic practice. He called the White House accusation of declining journalistic standards a red herring. "We stand by our account of what Mr. Nelvis told the Secret Service," The Journal's managing editor, Paul Steiger, said in a prepared statement. Ever since the media began covering the accusations against Mr. Clinton, critics inside and outside news organizations have suggested that the rise of the Internet and 24-hour cable television news have badly eroded standards. They say that news now breaks 24 hours a day, round the clock, instead of on the more leisurely news cycles that once prevailed. As competitors have proliferated on line and on cable, they say, news organizations have relaxed their rules on procedures like sourcing in the race to break news first. "I understand the competitive pressure that everybody is under," Mr. Lockhart said. "But I do think it's a significant lowering of standards when getting it first supersedes getting it right." According to Mr. Steiger's statement, The Journal posted its story on its Web site when the editors "felt it was ready." The Journal did not wait for a White House response because it felt the White House had made clear it would not answer questions or provide information about the case. Mr. Lockhart said a Journal reporter approached him shortly before 4 P.M. on Wednesday for a reaction to the accusations about the steward's testimony. The reporter said he needed the information quickly because The Journal intended to post the article on the Web site, Mr. Lockhart said. "I said, 'How much time does that give me?' " Mr. Lockhart recalled. "He said, 'I don't know, I haven't done this before.' " Mr. Lockhart said he and the reporter agreed that he would get back to the reporter within 30 minutes unless the reporter paged him to say he had less time. Within a few minutes, Mr. Lockhart said, the reporter paged him to say the story had already been posted. Meanwhile, Mr. Tofel said, the lawyer for Mr. Nelvis, Joseph Small, had declined to discuss the report with The Journal before it was posted on the Web site. After it was posted, he said it was false. But he declined to give details about Mr. Nelvis's testimony, yesterday's article said. At a briefing yesterday, Michael D. McCurry, the White House spokesman, acknowledged that lawyers for Mr. Clinton contacted Mr. Small "to see if there was some willingness to address what was believed to be here at the White House a false and misleading and irresponsible story." Mr. Small could not be reached yesterday for comment. Mr. Tofel, a vice president for corporate communications for Dow Jones & Company, which publishes The Journal, said there were no "substantive differences" between the first and subsequent stories. The principal difference, he said, was the denial from Mr. Small. "In the wire service business, this happens all the time," Mr. Tofel said. Several wire services filed their own stories about The Journal's story after it appeared on the Web site. But the Associated Press did not. Darrell Christian, the managing editor, said, "We went to our own sources and tried to check it out and were pretty much convinced that there were enough doubts about the accuracy of the report that we would not go with it."

title:
COMPANY REPORTS: THE MEDIA BUSINESS;
Times Company Profit Rose For Year and 4th Quarter
body: The newyork Times Company said yesterday that operating earnings rose 18 percent in the fourth quarter. For the year, operating earnings rose 34 percent from a year earlier. The company cited higher advertising revenues and the continued strong performance of two television stations acquired in 1996. For the fourth quarter, the operating earnings, which exclude a number of special items, were $82.7 million, or 84 cents a share, up from $70.1 million, or 72 cents a share, a year earlier. Revenues rose 6.8 percent, to $768.4 million. Over all, including the special items, net income rose to $79.3 million, or 81 cents a share, from $52.7 million, or 54 cents a share. All earnings per-share figures are for diluted earnings. Earnings for the year rose to $262.3 million, or $2.66 a share, from $84.5 million, or 86 cents a share, in 1996, but that figure was depressed by an accounting charge. Excluding such one-time items, annual profits were $249 million, or $2.53 a share, up from $185.9 million, or $1.89 a share. Revenue rose 9.1 percent, to $2.9 billion. Advertising revenue for the company's newspaper group, which comprises The newyork Times, The Boston Globe and 21 regional newspapers, rose 10.1 percent in the year because of higher ad rates and more advertising volume. Circulation revenue rose 2.2 percent. The company said that operating earnings of its newspaper group, excluding the cost of employee buyouts and other special factors, rose from $337.2 million in 1996, to $441.6 million in 1997. It said strength in national and classified advertising helped the results as did a lower cost of newsprint. But it said newsprint costs in the fourth quarter were higher than they were a year earlier, depressing results. Operating profits of the company's magazine group for the year were $28.3 million, up from $25.8 million, helped by higher advertising revenue at its golf publications. The company sold its tennis, skiing and sailing magazines in the fourth quarter, and profits from them were included in the first 11 months of the year. It reported a gain of $10.4 million before taxes, or 6 cents a share, on the sale. Operating profits for the company's broadcast group rose to $39.4 million, from $30.9 million in 1996. The increases were largely attributed to the July 1996 acquisition of television stations in Oklahoma City and Des Moines. Other special items that affected profits in the fourth quarter included a charge of $10.1 million, or 6 cents a share, for corporate expenses that need to be charged off under a new accounting rule related to costs of some technology-related projects and a charge of $6 million, or 3 cents a share, for employee buyouts.
