title: Investigators in Reuters Case Met With Computer Consultant Months Ago
body: An executive with a Manhattan computer company was confronted several months ago by Federal law enforcement officials investigating whether the company was commissioned by a subsidiary of Reuters Holdings P.L.C. to steal information electronically from a rival, Bloomberg L.P., people briefed on the case said yesterday. The contact between the Government and the executive of Cyberspace Research suggests that at least some people working with the small company could have been cooperating with the Federal investigation of the subsidiary, Reuters Analytics Inc., before it was disclosed last week. Telephone calls to Cyberspace Research have gone unanswered for several days. A number for David Schwartz, a former Bloomberg employee who runs Cyberspace Research, could not be obtained. Prosecutors have been investigating for as long as a year to determine whether Reuters took part in a scheme to steal proprietary information maintained in Bloomberg's central computers. They are examining whether that information was later improperly incorporated into products like the Reuters 3000, which has been widely viewed in the financial data industry as the product most likely to compete with the Bloomberg terminal. In the week since Reuters announced that a Manhattan grand jury was investigating whether it improperly obtained and used Bloomberg's information, the company has said little about the nature and scope of the inquiry. But yesterday, Reuters released its first comprehensive statement on the case, describing information that it has learned since first being made aware of the Federal inquiry earlier this month. In the statement, Reuters said that investigators were examining whether the company induced a consultant it did not identify to gain access to proprietary data maintained in Bloomberg's central computers. That consultant is Cyberspace Research, according to people briefed on the case. But, Reuters said, the access under investigation did not involve hacking, in which Bloomberg's central systems would be penetrated by an outside computer. Rather, Reuters said, the activities under investigation involve direct access to the information in the computer systems through a Bloomberg terminal. Cyberspace Research subscribed to Bloomberg's service. Reuters did not, and indeed, companies in this industry do not allow competitors to have access to their computer systems. People who have been briefed on the case said prosecutors thought that Cyberspace Research had obtained thousands of screens of Bloomberg data, the fundamental product of the computer system. Prosecutors think that the information was then turned over to Reuters executives, these people said. The investigation is examining whether that information was then used directly in some Reuters products. The prosecutors are also examining whether the company used such information to reconstruct analysis programs used by Bloomberg through a process known as reverse engineering, in which a final product is broken down to find out how it works. While this would give Reuters the ability to duplicate some Bloomberg analytical functions, it did not require or involve access to the system's operating code, people who have been briefed on the case said. In its statement, Reuters said that the investigation was examining "whether Bloomberg data obtained by the consultant was improperly incorporated into Reuters products and whether Bloomberg information was used by Reuters Analytics for any improper 'reverse engineering' of certain analytics," the statement said. The investigation involves information relating to fixed-income investments, the statement said, and "to some extent" to equity investments, too. Reuters said that it did not think the company would have to withdraw any products because of the investigation. But it said that if it discovered proprietary information belonging to Bloomberg in its products, "it intends to take remedial action." At this point, Reuters said, the principal focus of the investigation is on Reuters Analytics and employees with that unit. But the investigation also involves "an examination of the activities of other individuals and entities outside of Reuters Analytics," the company said. Investors reacted positively. In London, Reuters shares rose 40.5 pence, to 560.5 pence. The stock remains down about 5 percent from its level before the market learned about the investigation. The company's American depository receipts -- each representing six shares -- also rose, closing up $4.4375 yesterday, to $55.125. Reuters did not identify any of the employees whose activities might be under investigation. To date, it has placed three executives on paid leave, including Hubert Holmes, the unit's director. Mr. Holmes, who has declined to comment, reported directly to senior executives at the parent company in London. Michael Bloomberg, the chairman and chief executive of Bloomberg, declined to comment on the unfolding investigation at a press conference yesterday announcing a strategic partnership with CNET, an Internet publisher and television production company in San Francisco. "It's between the Justice Department and Reuters," he told reporters.

title: A New Competitor in 5-Cent Phone Calls
body: Talk is cheap these days, at least in newyork and Chicago. Those are the two cities where consumers can make long-distance telephone calls to anywhere in the unitedstates for 5 cents a minute using calling cards released yesterday by the IDT Corporation. The MCI Communications Corporation and the Sprint Corporation offer a 5-cent rate at some times. IDT's rate, which is one-third that of the AT&T Corporation's common flat-rate plan, is valid at all times. IDT, a small company based in Hackensack, N.J., is able to undercut the long-distance giants by sending conversations over the Internet rather than over traditional networks. The catch is that conversations over IDT's system, while quite intelligible, do not match the sound quality of calls over standard networks. Still, the low end of the long-distance market is booming. In December, the Qwest Communications unit of the Anschutz Corporation announced a service for 7.5 cents a minute that uses the Internet, and AT&T said last week that it intended to enter low-price Internet calling. IDT says it will offer its 5-cent service in Boston, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Washington by the middle of next month and in 19 more markets by the end of the year.

title:
GOLF;
Pebble Beach Final Postponed
body: This year's AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am will be remembered as the wettest, the longest and the most bizarre. The final round, put off until today because of bad weather over the weekend, was postponed again this morning, until March 2, because of heavy rain that has made all three golf courses unplayable. It all continued a wet history for one of the PGA Tour's most popular events, one played in a picturesque setting on one of the world's most famous courses, but one that has been plagued by bad weather in recent years. The event was canceled in 1996, and some players have suggested that the tournament date should be permanently moved. Tournament officials selected March 2 as the new final-round date, because that is the Monday after the Nissan Open in Valencia, Calif., and many players will be on the West Coast. Only 36 holes have been completed, and a PGA Tour event is not official unless 54 holes are completed. No decision has been made on what will happen if it rains again on March 2. "It appears we will have some unusual circumstances on the West Coast this year because of El Nino, and we must be prepared to take unusual measures in order to complete our events," Tim Finchem, commissioner of the PGA Tour, said in a statement. "We want to do everything that is necessary for fans, our players and our sponsor to complete our competitions." The PGA Tour has not moved an event to a different month since 1991, when the Houston Open, scheduled for April, was postponed by rain until October. But with heavy rain falling again today, and with more precipitation expected Tuesday on the Monterey Peninsula, tournament officials believed March 2 was the best choice. A decision had been made Saturday to shorten the tournament to 54 holes, after a four-hour rain delay last Thursday. "After consulting with the commissioner, the players, others involved, and to make this an official PGA tournament, this is the best scenario we could come up with," Arvin Ginn, PGA Tour tournament director, said in a media room news conference today. Final-round play on March 2 will start from the beginning. Some players completed as many as seven holes Sunday, but those scores will be wiped out. The tour felt conditions were so bad Sunday that starting the third round from scratch would be the fairest way. "You want to start everyone with the same conditions," Ginn said. When play resumes, Tim Herron and Tom Watson will be tied for the lead at 10 under par, with Tom Lehman, Phil Mickelson and Jay Haas all one stroke back at nine under par. When play was halted Sunday, Herron had moved into a two-shot lead over Watson, Mickelson, Lehman and Davis Love 3d. Both Herron and Watson completed three holes Sunday, with Herron making a birdie on his second hole, while Watson made a bogey on his second hole. Those scores will be erased, and Watson was pleased. But reaction among the players was mixed when they were told of the decision at a meeting this morning. Players who are not in contention may elect not to come back. But the leaders were happy they still had a chance to win the $450,000 first-place check. "It's good for me," Watson said. "I'll be back to 10 under par and tied for the lead. "It think it's a creative decision to come back here. Obviously, it won't be fair to everyone. I'm sure there will be some no-shows. But whatever date you pick, there will be some conflict." Jerry Pate, who stood at two under par, and said he would probably return, added: "There is no right decision that can be made, but I think they made the best decision due to all the factors. Whatever decision they made was going to make somebody unhappy. A lot of guys already have commitments for that Monday, but your first commitment should be to the tour. And it's unfortunate for the fans. "I've come out here 23 years, and the tour should really consider changing the date, either make it the last tournament on the West Coast swing, or maybe in the fall. "I'd say 30 percent of the guys won't come back March 2. I'd say the bottom 30 guys won't be here. The top 30 guys will do everything in their power to make it back. But you can't control the weather, so what do you do if it's raining March 2? I guess we'll just see what happens." Graphic   Photo: A groundskeeper, Miguel Rosado, working on a flooded bunker at the 18th green yesterday at Pebble Beach. (Associated Press)

title: Inquiry Said to Focus on Ties Of Reuters Unit to Company
body: Federal prosecutors are investigating the relationship between an American subsidiary of Reuters Holdings P.L.C. and a Manhattan company that they believe was commissioned to steal information electronically from a big competitor, Bloomberg L.P., people briefed on the case said yesterday. The newyork company, Cyberspace Research Associates Inc., has been described in trade publications as being in the business of developing customized computer applications.  Prosecutors are said to believe that it was working with the subsidiary, Reuters Analytics Inc., to assist it in obtaining information about Bloomberg's operating code, which governs how the company's proprietary financial software works. Cyberspace Research, which has a small staff, was set up several years ago by David Schwartz, who formerly worked for Bloomberg. Telephone calls to Cyberspace Research were not answered late yesterday; a home telephone number for Mr. Schwartz, who worked at Bloomberg at least seven years ago, could not be obtained. The precise legal relationship between Reuters Analytics and Cyberspace Research -- for example, if it served as an independent contractor or had a closer affiliation with the subsidiary -- could not be immediately determined. It also could not be determined if Cyberspace Research or any of its executives or employees are subjects of the investigation, or are cooperating with it. Robert Crooke, a spokesman for Reuters America, declined to comment, as did Chris Taylor, a spokeswoman for Bloomberg. The Government has obtained more than 100 written communications between Reuters Analytics and Cyberspace Research, people who have been briefed on the case have said. The communications, including memos and other records, requested Cyberspace Research to obtain detailed information about technical programs for analyzing investments, these people said. The company was then said to have electronically obtained the information. Afterward, it was passed to Reuters, at times directly to the parent company's London headquarters, they said. Prosecutors were said to have also obtained those responses. In response to the investigation of possible corporate espionage, Reuters Holdings has sent a senior executive from its London offices to oversee the operations of the American subsidiary, an executive with the financial data services company said yesterday. Geoffrey Weetman, managing director for media and new business ventures, was assigned to oversee Reuters Analytics, after the company learned that a Federal grand jury in Manhattan was investigating the possible scheme. Until late 1996, Mr. Weetman was managing director of Reuters Asia region. The assignment of Mr. Weetman to the subsidiary came even as the company placed three executives with the unit on leave. Those executives include Hubert Holmes, the head of Reuters Analytics, which is based in Stamford, Conn. "He is there looking over the interests of the company in this situation," Mr.  Crooke, the spokesman, said. As the head of Reuters Analytics, Mr. Holmes, who has declined comment, reported directly to executives at the parent company in London. For several years, he reported to David Ure, an executive director responsible for marketing and technical policy. Since late 1996, he has reported to John Parcell, an executive director responsible for the financial information product line. More than $6.5 billion is spent annually to keep computer terminals providing up-to-the-second bond and equity prices, currency valuations and offering complex analytical tools that combine years of historical and contemporary data to predict current trends. Reuters Holdings, the largest and oldest competitor in the business, had more than a century's head start when Michael Bloomberg founded Bloomberg L.P. in 1981. But the brash competitor to Reuters developed new analytic tools that Wall Street professionals regard as well suited to their needs in an era of derivatives and other increasingly complex securities transactions. The unfolding scandal involving the two companies has taken a toll on Reuters stock since the company announced the existence of the investigation last Thursday. Yesterday, shares of Reuters dropped 2 pence in London, to 548 pence. In newyork, the Reuters American depository receipts fell $1.1875, to $52.4375, in Nasdaq trading. Analysts have begun putting out cautionary reports on the company in light of the scandal. "Uncertainty is likely to dog the shares for some time," David Forster, an analyst with Salomon Smith Barney in London, wrote in a research report released yesterday.

title:
PERSONAL COMPUTERS;
WebTV: Easy, Cheap and Limited Internet Access
body: BEFORE I first tried WebTV a year ago, I was positive that not even the comforts of my favorite recliner could make surfing the Web on television anything but a headache fraught with eyestrain. Wrong: Even on my ancient tube, the original WebTV unit delivered clear text without noticeable flicker. Some tiny type was hard or impossible to read, but most text and graphics looked fine, even if only a couple of paragraphs could fit on the screen at once. The user interface was easy to master, though navigation was occasionally tricky. email worked well, and the system offered five extra addresses free. On a line with call waiting, the unit could disconnect itself, let the call ring through, and, when you reconnected, pick up where you left off. In hours of surfing, the unit never crashed, which is more than you can say about most computers. Except for having to put up with a telephone cable running across the room, starting up was a snap. When you first turn it on, the system dials an 800 number, figures out where you are, installs a local access number, takes your credit card information and even customizes the on-screen display for your locality. At a reduced price of about $150 (counting the wireless keyboard that is sold separately but ought to be mandatory), plus about $20 a month to link up, WebTV Classic remains one of the simplest, cheapest ways to take advantage of sizable portions of the Net. For about $100 more, new WebTV Plus models add a few clever wrinkles and promises for the future. I tried a Sony unit; models with virtually identical functions but different designs are available with Mitsubishi and Philips Magnavox labels. The WebTV network can upgrade the unit's internal software automatically, and it has slowly been improved to understand more types of information, including standards like Realaudio and MPEG-1. But WebTV still cannot work with many forms of data common on the Web, including Java, Activex, Quicktime, streaming video and most plug-in software, so surf potatoes see messages like "You are unsupported" or nothing at all instead of some of the most advanced visual experiences the Web has to offer. For example, even though the Microsoft Corporation now owns WebTV Networks Inc., WebTV units display an apology instead of the 360-degree views of automotive interiors found on Microsoft's CarPoint site. The Plus models' new features include a built-in printer port that is compatible with several popular Hewlett-Packard and Canon models and a one-gigabyte hard disk that does not yet do much of anything. For now the most interesting improvements involve a built-in TV tuner that lets you watch television while you surf the Web. That feature is not quite as clever as it might be, because the little television window appears over Web pages in a fixed position near the lower right corner of the screen. You can change the channel, but you cannot move the window; when it hides Web information, you must close it to see what is underneath. A better solution would let you move it or at least eliminate the picture temporarily while listening to the sound. The Plus units provide an interactive television program guide customized for your local cable system. Alas, the on-screen point-and-click program grid is too interactive; when you search the listings for coming shows, the channel changes whether you want it to or not. The guide sometimes offers Web links relevant to the program on the screen. They typically lead either to the show's shameless promotional site or the Internet Movie Database. But the device can also superimpose a clickable letter "i" over television shows, linking them to special pages related to precisely what is happening at the moment. A company spokesman said that so far the technique had been used only in conjunction with a single commercial. The Plus devices offer several other intriguing glimpses of the future. The hard disk now holds only the television schedules that the system downloads daily; someday it might gather and instantly deliver volumes of data broadcast earlier on special channels or in portions of the television channels that are normally invisible. A smart-card slot is useless now but may eventually let you pick up your mail from a friend's machine or waste buckets of electronic cash. The printed documentation abandons you once you finish installing the hardware. To figure out the rest of what you need to know, you must surf through slow-moving pages of on-screen instructions. And there is still no way to save data that interests you except by printing it out or recording it on a VCR. The service agreement amounts to 54 screens of legalese and an "enough" button that encourages you to quit reading before knowing what you are being asked to agree to. It includes clauses giving the company the right "at its sole discretion" to "share certain information with third parties" about things like "user-selected options and preferences." The spokesman said that language is meant to cover "aggregated" information about groups rather than personal information about you. If so, somebody should tell the lawyers to say what they mean. Computers are getting cheaper and cheaper. Web access is likely to begin appearing this year in devices like cable boxes that may offer faster connections. Microsoft has announced that the next generation of WebTV will use a different operating system, eventually rendering these units less desirable. But since $20 a month for Internet service is the going rate and you can quit anytime, think of the current WebTV units as the Volkswagen Beetles of the Net. Their cheap, dependable, cramped transportation lets you tilt back and relax while they take you almost everywhere that is really important but not necessarily everywhere you want to go. When the money rolls in, you can abandon them for unreliable roadsters that go fast, require lots of attention and make you sit up straight. Graphic   Drawing (Stuart Goldenberg)

title: Building 'Internet 2'
body: A handful of researchers scattered across the country are rushing to develop a video conferencing computer program so sophisticated that it will allow executives in four locations to "sit" around a table together, "handing" documents back and forth while they talk. The virtual meeting is perhaps the most ambitious of many programs now being designed for the next generation of the Internet, an endeavor President Clinton championed in his State of the Union address. Researchers at more than 100 universities, with the backing of a few companies, are taking the lead in the effort, and their quarterback is Douglas E. Van Houweling. One of the creators of the original Internet, Mr. Van Houweling (pronounced HOWL-ing) is chief executive and president of the University Corporation for Advanced Internet Development, a nonprofit group that is trying to harness academia, government and industry to put together Internet 2, as the project is called, as well as the programs needed to operate it. Mr. Van Houweling's plan is to add high-speed lanes to the clogged electronic highway that today's Internet has become. After the universities develop and debug these new lanes over the next two to five years, commercial interests will probably take over, imposing charges on those using Internet 2's premium services. Mr. Van Houweling envisions Internet 2 as a way for high-end users to quickly and reliably move huge amounts of data across phone, cable, satellite or other yet-to-be-invented networks. The virtual meeting is just one advance that would be light-years ahead of current technologies. "Today's Internet is like a single-lane highway with unlimited access points and no traffic control," said Mr. Van Houweling, who is based in Ann Arbor, Mich., home of the University of Michigan, where he is on leave as a professor in the School of Information. "There will never be a red light that will come on and say you can't use it -- when the traffic gets heavy, things slow down." Internet 2 will add toll lanes to speed things up. "What we're trying to do is build a multilane highway," Mr. Van Houweling said. One lane might be designated for moving mountains of data between companies or researchers. Another might be dedicated to the virtual-reality video conferencing, and a third for transmitting television shows. "On each of these special lanes, we can regulate the amount of traffic to guarantee performance," Mr. Van Houweling said. Referring to the current Internet, he added, "We'll still have the far-right lane, where everybody can get on." The Internet was set up in the 1960's and 1970's by the Federal Government as an all-but-private club for researchers and academics. Of course, it has since mushroomed into a sort of electronic public park and market, used by computer literate people around the world and the multitude of companies seeking to do business with them. But the strength of the Internet -- its accessibility -- has become a weakness for those who need to move large amounts of data quickly. There is now no way for them to separate themselves from the rest of the pack, who typically use the Internet for sending email. Mr. Van Houweling's long history with the Internet makes him the right leader for the next phase, those who have worked with him say. "Since he was involved in the first generation so closely, he knows a lot of the pitfalls," said Allan H. Weis, chief executive of Advanced Network and Services, a nonprofit organization based in Armonk, N.Y., that is in the midst of a $10 million, three-year program to develop virtual video conferencing capabilities. Mr. Weis said he hoped the technology would be up and running by 2000 and commercially available by 2003. Companies that want to commercialize the service will most likely need to license the intellectual property rights from the various universities that developed it, he said. Mr. Van Houweling's organization consists of 117 universities, including newyork University and Columbia in the newyork area. Each contributes from $500,000 to more than $1 million a year to upgrade its campus computers and to help develop programs for Internet 2. On the business side, about 25 companies have pledged to pay $10,000 each in annual dues and to provide services. Participants include Cisco Systems and 3Com, which will be involved in designing advanced switches and routers for the system; I.B.M., which plans to give $3.5 million in grants; the telecommunications giants MCI, AT&T and Sprint, and Starburst, an independent software vendor. Public and private research centers like the National Institutes of Health and the International Business Machines Corporation's Watson Laboratory may become members of the University Corporation, which is also holding talks with the Microsoft Corporation about joining. The main Government component in developing Internet 2 is the Very-High-Performance Backbone Network Service. The network links supercomputers and other computer banks across the nation and is managed by MCI and financed by the National Science Foundation. "This is a good example of the kind of partnership between industry, universities and government," said Vinton G. Cerf, senior vice president of Internet architecture and engineering at MCI. By working closely on developing the new technology, the thinking goes, the corporate participants can help to insure that it will have commercial applications. That is one difference between the development of Internet 2 and the current Internet, which evolved slowly from its specialized military and research roots. "We're starting off this time with an even more determined effort to work with the major companies in the industry," Mr. Van Houweling said. "The applications are the focus of what we do -- we don't want to build a highway for some kind of vehicles that will never arrive." Mr. Cerf concedes that it is impossible to know how many of the projects of Mr. Van Houweling's group will make it to commercial use. Still, he is optimistic. "The more people who are out there exploring the technology, the faster we will discover the good stuff," he said. Internet 2 is already expected to be capable of advanced data mining -- combining information in several data bases around the country to analyze files and find patterns. This might help insurers or drug makers, which could sift the records of the nation's major medical centers to search out disease patterns. Manufacturing companies could use Internet 2 to securely transfer technical data on the design of cars and car parts, say, between offices and even suppliers. Auto companies are beginning to do that now, but must buy expensive software and send the data over internal networks installed at certain locations. In the future, any computers that could reach Internet 2 would have the potential for access to the information. The broad commercial use of Internet 2 is at least four years away, those involved in the project say. And after Internet 2 is up and running, the next task is clear. "Five years from now, we'll be talking about Internet 3," Mr. Van Houweling said. Graphic   Photo: Douglas E. Van Houweling, who helped create the Internet, is leading a project to add high-speed lanes to today's clogged electronic highway. (Peter Yates for The newyork Times)

title:
GOLF;
The Rains Keep Coming, Threatening Tournament
body: For the second time in three years, heavy rain has caused huge problems for the AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am. Today's final round was suspended and rescheduled for Monday morning after steady rain made the grounds unplayable. But with more rain predicted for Monday, play may be extended until Tuesday, or the event could be canceled, as it was in 1996. Tournament officials decided Saturday to shorten the tournament to 54 holes, the minimum required for an official event. Today, the amateur portion of the event was canceled. If play resumes, only the professionals will compete. But the outlook is not bright. "A lot of work has to be done on the golf course," said Lou Russo, the tournament's executive director. "The main concern of ours and the PGA Tour is to get a 54-hole tournament in. We will try everything to make it work. It looks real bad, but we will give it every chance in the world." After the limited golf played today, Tim Herron (11 under par) held a two-stroke lead. Four players were tied for second place at nine under par -- Tom Lehman, Davis Love 3d, Phil Mickelson and Tom Watson. Herron completed just three holes at Spyglass Hill, Watson completed three holes at Poppy Hills and Love played four holes at Poppy Hills. Mickelson and Lehman never teed off. Herron started the day tied with Watson at 10 under par, but Herron birdied his second hole to take the lead, while Watson bogeyed his second hole to fall two strokes back. Most of the attention, however, was on the weather. After spending a week in the Monterey Peninsula, and with a first-place check of $450,000 at stake, none of the players wanted to see the tournament washed out. "I just hope we play," said Mickelson, who is trying to win his second tournament this year after his victory at last month's Mercedes Championships. "Two years ago, I was a shot back going into what would have been the third round, and we didn't get a chance to play. I have been looking forward to the opportunity to get back in the same position." Russo said it was unlikely that the tournament would be moved to a different date to avoid bad weather. "There are not that many open dates, especially with some new tournaments coming in," Russo said. "This time of year on the West Coast, that's one of the dangers you get into. I guess we have to go to church more often."  CHIP SHOTS Five players were tied three strokes back at eight under par -- PAUL AZINGER, JIM FURYK, JAY HAAS, TOM PERNICE JR. and CHRIS SMITH. Haas played two holes Sunday, Smith and Pernice played one, while Azinger and Furyk never teed off. . . . TIGER WOODS, who has struggled this week (four over par) will compete this weekend at the Buick Invitational in La Jolla, Calif. Graphic   Photo: Tom Watson, right, and his caddie walking off the 13th green at Poppy Hills yesterday. Watson bogeyed one of the three holes he played. (Jamie Squire/Allsport)

title: Memos Said to Detail Reuters Effort to Obtain Bloomberg Data
body: Federal prosecutors have obtained more than 100 written communications between an American subsidiary of Reuters Holdings P.L.C. and a consulting company that investigators believe was hired to steal information from the computers of a competitor, Bloomberg L.P., people in touch with the investigation said yesterday. The communications from the subsidiary, Reuters Analytics Inc., include memos and other records requesting detailed information about technical programs for analyzing investments, these people said. The consultant was then said to have electronically broken into Bloomberg's corporate computers and obtained the information. Afterwards, it was passed to Reuters, at times directly to the parent company's London headquarters, they said. Prosecutors were said to have also obtained the consultant's responses. The computer consulting company, whose name could not be immediately determined, was said by people in touch with the investigation to have been founded by a former employee of Bloomberg. They said that the company is based near the Stamford, Conn., headquarters of Reuters Analytics. Prosecutors obtained the documents during an undercover investigation of Reuters Analytics that has lasted about a year. In the investigation, at least one confidential informant helped the Government obtain an array of evidence, including tapes. Robert Crooke, a spokesman for Reuters America, declined to comment. The written communications are the first documentary evidence known to have been obtained by prosecutors in the case. Such written communications, including messages sent by email, would be potentially critical evidence, because they could be used to establish which executives were connected to the purported scheme. Already, Reuters has placed three executives in the subsidiary on paid leave in the wake of the scandal. According to people with ties to Reuters, they include Hubert Holmes, the unit's head, as well as Jeff Walker and James Feingold, two executives in the unit. In telephone calls, Mr. Holmes and Mr. Feingold declined to comment. A home telephone number for Mr. Walker could not be obtained. More than $6.5 billion is spent annually to keep computer terminals on the desks of Wall Street spewing out up-to-the-second bond and equity prices and currency values and offering complex analytical tools that combine years of historical and contemporary data to predict current trends. Reuters Holdings, the largest and oldest competitor in the financial information services business, had more than a century's head start when Michael R. Bloomberg founded Bloomberg L.P. in 1981. But Reuters's brash competitor developed new analytic tools that Wall Street professionals regarded as well suited to their needs in an era of derivatives and other increasingly complex securities transactions. According to people in touch with the investigation, prosecutors have obtained evidence that Reuters was stealing information from Bloomberg's operating code, the underlying software that governs the functioning of Bloomberg's data terminals. As the head of Reuters Analytics, Mr. Holmes reported directly to senior executives at the parent company in London. For several years, he reported to David Ure, an executive director responsible for marketing and technical policy. Since late 1996, he has reported to John Parcell, who is executive director responsible for the financial information product line. Executives in London maintained direct contact with the analytics division, occasionally traveling to Stamford to meet with Mr. Holmes and other executives. In recent months, investigators have been examining the travel of London executives to the subsidiary and their contacts with its American executives as part of an effort to determine if they knew of the purported scheme, people in touch with the investigation said. Since announcing the grand jury investigation on Thursday, Reuters has declined comment on the extent of the inquiry. Reached by email in Davos, Switzerland, where he was attending the annual World Economic Forum, Mr. Bloomberg, who is the chairman and chief executive of Bloomberg L.P., also declined comment. "Sorry, have nothing to add to obvious story," he wrote. From its earliest days, Reuters Analytics has been faced with accusations that it used unsavory business practices to obtain other companies' technologies. The subsidiary was originally an independent company with a mission to develop technology to compete with Bloomberg. It was acquired by Reuters after the settlement of a bitter 1993 lawsuit, in which the founders of the predecessor company, Capital Markets Decisions Inc., accused Reuters of secretly hiring its programmers and using their proprietary knowledge to build a clone of Capital Markets' software. Mr. Holmes, Mr. Walker and Mr. Ure, the London executive, all played roles in that earlier dispute. Mr. Crooke, the Reuters spokesman, said that the court records had to speak for themselves. Many of Reuters's documents are missing from the public record. However, in the records that do exist and in interviews at the time of the suit, Reuters executives denied all of the allegations made by Capital Markets Decisions, saying that no effort had been made to obtain any confidential information from the small company. In 1989, Reuters, in its efforts to move further into the business of analytics, turned to J. Stephen Levkoff, a senior vice president at Smith Barney who had previously developed analytics systems. Reuters asked Mr. Levkoff to develop a product equivalent to the Bloomberg terminal, and he agreed to join Reuters as a consultant through his own independent company, Capital Markets Decisions, according to the court documents. Bloomberg had made rapid inroads into Reuters's business by offering fund managers and other institutions a data terminal that allowed traders to aggressively analyze purchases and sales of investments. Reuters had no such product, known as an analytics system, and did not have the programming expertise to develop one. After his discussions with Reuters, Mr. Levkoff left Smith Barney to run Capital Markets Decisions, which would create a new analytics system for Reuters to sell. According to the contract, Capital Markets Decisions would receive royalty payments on each terminal installed, and Reuters would supply its data for the system. By 1991, Capital Markets Decisions had developed and released its system, known as Decision 2000 and nicknamed the "Bloomberg Killer." That year, Reuters began installing the new units on customers' desks. Relations between the two sides began to break down in early 1993. According to court records, after repeated disputes about the contract between Reuters and Capital Markets Decisions, Mr. Levkoff and Mr. Ure renegotiated it, with handwritten revisions. But, when pressed for a final draft of that agreement, Mr. Holmes refused to provide it, according to an affidavit by Mr. Levkoff. In 1993, Reuters declared Capital Markets Decisions in breach of contract for what it said were a variety of failures. But Mr. Levkoff believed the declaration was made in bad faith, as "an effort to break the contract or wear us down into selling the business to Reuters," according to court records he filed in the case. That would give Reuters ownership of the system, eliminating the need for royalty payments. Employees of Capital Markets Decisions began hearing from Reuters employees that their company faced imminent demise. According to the court papers, employees began leaving Capital Markets Decisions without telling their colleagues where they would be working. According to Mr. Levkoff's affidavit, a showdown occurred during a dinner with Mr. Holmes on Sept. 18, 1993, at the Homestead Inn in Greenwich, Conn. Mr. Holmes produced a draft letter, declaring Reuters's intent to terminate the contract immediately, despite a negotiated term that required six months' notice. Mr. Holmes informed Mr. Levkoff that Reuters had been working on Capital Markets Decisions' termination for a year, and had already paid a law firm $500,000 as part of the effort, the affidavit says. During the meeting, according to Mr. Levkoff's affidavit, Mr. Holmes told him that several Capital Markets Decisions employees who had disappeared were working for Reuters. A number of employees with Capital Markets Decisions signed affidavits saying that Mr. Walker was personally involved in the effort to hire them. One Capital Markets Decisions programmer, Tom Kokoska, had secretly joined Reuters after leaving Capital Markets Decisions for Bloomberg. To conceal Mr. Kokoska's work, he had taken the job under a pseudonym, Joe Pope. Memorandums written by Reuters executives at the time show the name Joe Pope was even used on internal communications. And an affidavit by another Capital Markets Decisions executive describes how a friend of Mr. Kokoska could reach him only at Reuters by knowing to ask for Joe Pope. Why the subterfuge? According to Mr. Levkoff's affidavit, Mr. Holmes told him it was because Mr. Kokoska was working for almost a year on a secret project to make a clone of Decision 2000. Once it had used the knowledge of former Capital Markets Decisions programmers to make its own system, Reuters could take over the business, Mr. Levkoff said. Mr. Kokoska did not return a telephone call to his home seeking comment. But, as described in Capital Markets Decisions records filed in the United States District Court in Manhattan, Reuters, whose needs had spurred the creation of Capital Markets Decisions and its flagship product, was secretly hiring away some employees who understood its software. In turn, according to an affidavit by Mr. Levkoff, they were using that knowledge to develop a similar product. Mr. Levkoff said in his affidavit that he was told of the effort by a Reuters executive. As a result, Mr. Levkoff said, the value of Capital Markets Decisions would be reduced, allowing Reuters to buy the company at a low price. That would give Reuters use of the Decision 2000 product without paying royalties. Before the Homestead dinner was over, Mr. Holmes presented a copy of an agreement for Reuters to buy Capital Markets Decisions. Mr. Levkoff said in court papers that Mr. Holmes told him that with the clone project under way, Decision 2000 was no longer considered a valuable asset. "Every day that goes by, Decision 2000 is worth less to Reuters," Mr. Levkoff quoted him as saying. Mr. Levkoff said in his affidavit that he refused the deal because Reuters was offering a lowball bid; Mr. Holmes stated in an affidavit that a deal was agreed upon. On Oct. 19, three weeks after the Homestead Inn dinner, and after Mr. Levkoff rebuffed a second offer to buy his company, Reuters severed all communications links, including real-time data feeds, that Capital Markets Decisions needed to get access to the operational Decision 2000 product to update the data used by customers. It also changed the number for the Decision 2000 help desk, which had been at Capital Markets Decisions. Mr. Levkoff brought suit, seeking $30 million in damages. After much battling, he won the right to depose many of the principals in the case. But Reuters reversed course. It reached a confidential settlement, in which it purchased Capital Markets Decisions for an undisclosed sum that was acceptable to Mr. Levkoff. He then left the company. Under the supervision of Mr. Ure, Mr. Holmes, along with Mr. Walker, began working with Reuters latest subsidiary, the newly named Reuters Analytics.

title:
TECHNOLOGY: DIGITAL COMMERCE;
Netscape's decision to give away code could alter the software industry.
body: RATHER than escalating a dead man's curve race against its archenemy, the Microsoft Corporation, the Netscape Communications Corporation has made a course correction that may profoundly affect the commercial software industry. On Jan. 23, Netscape announced that by the end of the first quarter of this year, it would begin giving away the source code of its popular Communicator suite of Internet software products, including its Navigator World Wide Web browser. The company also announced that it would give away the retail version of its Communicator products and would allow other companies to customize and distribute them free as well. But it was its decision to publish Communicator's source code that stunned the industry. In the commercial software world, source code is a company's most valuable property. A combination of digital alchemy and architecture, source code is not only the blueprint of a program's underlying design and structure; its prose also exposes how its programmers thought about and built its inner workings, right down to the digital equivalent of its plaster, plumbing and wires. Commercial source code is copyrighted, sometimes patented and always jealously shielded from competitors who might use it to create clones or to match its functions in other programs. It is shared cautiously at best, and usually under legal strictures. Thus it is understandable that many people in the software industry think that Netscape has lost its corporate mind for posting a crown jewel on the Internet for anyone to scrutinize, copy and modify. But Marc L. Andreessen, one of Netscape's founders and its executive vice president for products, said that given the company's death race with Microsoft, it had little choice. "We'd much rather be able to charge for it," he said, but he added that Microsoft had triple-whammied them -- first, by giving away its Internet Explorer browser, making it impossible for Netscape to keep charging for its browsers, and, second, by pressing hardware vendors into shipping Explorer instead of Navigator on their new computers. Third, he said: "Microsoft has a ton more developers and programmers. Source code is the only way we could tap the energy of all the people who wanted us to modify it or port to other computers or create new features. So overnight, we got 10 to 100 times more programmers to work on it with us." And while Netscape will continue to charge for its server software -- the programs that corporations and publishers buy so they can set up Web sites -- it turned its back on commercial software for the consumer market to join a longstanding programmer tradition -- free software. The proponents of free software say that freedom is about liberty, not price -- free speech, as they say, not free beer. They believe that people who buy and use software should be free to run, copy, distribute, study, change and improve the software in any way they like. Free software is especially popular with programmers who are proficient with Unix, an operating system used to run midsize to large businesses and the majority of commercial Internet sites. And perhaps because it is so easy to acquire over the Internet, free software is becoming increasingly popular to a broader base of customers. Though source code is freely distributed and copying is encouraged, free-software companies do sell their versions of the software, as well as applications, service contracts, manuals and other accouterments. Hundreds of businesses have sprung up around free software -- especially around a flavor of Unix called Linux (http://www.linux.org), originally created by Linus Torvalds, a Finnish programmer. Linux source code is freely available over the Internet. As a result, it is gaining popularity; it is already a strong competitor in the Unix market and is emerging as a viable competitor to Microsoft's Windows NT, which now commands more than 35 percent of the sub-$25,000 network server market, according to Kimball Brown, a senior analyst for the market research firm Dataquest. Because the products can be freely copied and distributed, the number of computers running Linux is impossible to know for sure; most estimates range from 5 million to 10 million. And some believe that Linux is winning many of NT's potential customers, even though it obviously does not come with Microsoft's extensive customer support and wide variety of applications. Marc Ewing, 28, a co-founder of a leading Linux company, Red Hat Software Inc. (http://www.redhat.com), says that his company's sales of Linux are doubling every year. Red Hat sells its customers 500 megabytes of software, including Linux and source code, software compilers, Web servers, email clients, Web browsers and more, for $49.95. Certainly no one is going to make their fortune at those prices, but those who start free-software companies have reasons for choosing the noncommercial model. "The most visible people in the free-software world are good, and everyone knows it and wants what they do," Mr. Ewing said. "It's a meritocracy, so you end up with great software and highly talented people." And, he added, making source code freely available means that problems get fixed more quickly "and innovation happens a lot faster." Many people, including Netscape's Mr. Andreessen, believe that the growing popularity of free software like Linux may signal a shift in how the software industry conducts business. "If I'm the chief information officer in my company, I don't want programmers mucking around in the source code," Mr. Brown said. "You never know what else breaks when they fix something." On the other hand, he said, the quality of Linux and its steady market growth is "fascinating." Given its success, added Mr. Brown, and the obvious interest in free software, it seems possible that "the next iteration of Internet standards will not be governed by people who want to make money." Graphic   Drawing (Randy Jones)

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
For a Bank in Latvia, Typos Spell Opportunity
body: All the recent attention being paid to Matt Drudge, publisher of the Drudge Report, an on-line gossip sheet, has meant that his Web site (www.drudgereport.com) has become one of the most popular information destinations on the Internet, often making it difficult to get on to the site. But if users seeking the latest gossip on Monica Lewinsky, the White House intern, and her tape-recorded confidences about President Clinton, type the Web address as drudge-report.com (note the hyphen) or drugereport.com (note the missing letter "d"), they will end up in a site that has little to do with Mr. Drudge or Washington. They will be transported to the cyberhome of a bank in the Baltic nation of Latvia, which is capitalizing on Mr. Drudge's notoriety to drive Web traffic its way. Paritate Bank, which is based in the city of Riga, and bills itself as an offshore, on-line bank, uses the Internet aggressively to draw new business. Not satisfied with the usual tools of the trade -- banner ad placements, link exchange programs and search engine registrations -- the six-year-old bank has registered a variety of domain names. In addition to the obvious addresses, like www.paritate.lv and www.paritate.com, it has laid claim to www.anonymousbanking.com and www.offshore-account.com. The bank has also registered dozens of marquee brand names, or variations thereof. The variations run the gamut from businessweekonline.com to bloombergs.com, ny-time.com and warnerbrother.com. Most of these sites have been registered since the beginning of this year, with the help of a company based in Dublin named Martinside Marketing. "We believe these sites help drive general traffic to our site, and even if a visitor was not looking for bank facilities in Latvia, he might remember us and come back," said Alexander Ruchkovsky, Internet project manager for Paritate, who estimated that 30 percent of new accounts come through the bank's Web site. In the freewheeling world of the Internet, playing fast and loose with domain names is nothing new. As a result, many giant corporations register variations on their names. Larry Chase, publisher of Web Digest for Marketers (www.wdfm.com), thinks Paritate's tactics are a waste of time. "What are the chances someone interested in Matt Drudge is also looking for an offshore bank in Latvia?" he asked. For his part, Mr. Drudge considers the Latvian bank's use of his name in its site bizarre. "Perhaps they know something I don't about my popularity," he said.   SREENATH SREENIVASAN

title:
Updates/Media and Technology;
Microsoft Will Soon Offer Peek at New-Media Strategy
body: The Microsoft Corporation is about to give an invitation-only crowd of 40,000 a glimpse of the company's new-media strategy. This week, the company will begin sending out invitations to on-line samplers of a new World Wide Web site called Microsoft Start, according to industry analysts who have been briefed by the company. The new site, scheduled to open this summer, will feature Web-searching technology, email and special software for personalized data collection. Microsoft Start is the company's effort to create a preferred "portal" to the Internet by using Microsoft's strength in software to offer users personalized data bases in special-interest areas, from travel to cooking. A user, for example, could be sent the cheapest air fares for favorite travel destinations, or recipes could be retrieved, after typing in the contents of one's refrigerator. All the major companies in the on-line business -- America Online, Yahoo, Netscape and Microsoft -- are scrambling to assemble full-service Internet portal sites, seeking to lure millions of regular users and thus attract advertising dollars. The new Microsoft site, analysts say, is a further step in the evolution of the company's new-media strategy of pulling back from on-line entertainment offerings while concentrating on using its software expertise to deliver personalized information over the Internet. Microsoft Start is where the company will use some of the technology it has spent aggressively to acquire recently. The email on the new site, for example, will come from the Hotmail Corporation, a free email service that Microsoft acquired last month. The purchase price was not disclosed, but the stock deal was estimated to be worth $300 million or more. The Web-search technology will come from the Inktomi Corporation, which signed a contract with Microsoft last year. Microsoft Start will be a stand-alone site on the Web, available free to anyone with Internet access. The company, analysts say, also expects most subscribers to MSN, Microsoft's on-line service, to use Microsoft Start as the first page that appears on their screens when they sign on.   STEVE LOHR

title: U.S. Plan on Internet Names Lacks Support From All Users
body: The Clinton Administration released its proposal to relinquish Government control of the Internet's centralized address system to a competitive market on Friday, seeking to privatize a crucial function of the sprawling network and formalize a system that rests largely on the technical community's personal loyalty to one of its founders. The plan recommends the creation of a nonprofit corporation based in the unitedstates to direct the expansion of the Internet's domain scheme, which sorts World Wide Web sites and email addresses by a handful of suffixes like ".com" and ".org." The new organization, to be run by a representative group of the Internet's users, would also oversee the core computers that keep track of who lives where in cyberspace. The goal, which has widespread support, is to lower costs and broaden consumer choice as thousands of businesses and individuals seek to stake out an identity within the fast-growing medium. But the long-anticipated plan -- developed by the Administration's top Internet adviser, Ira C. Magaziner, after months of lobbying by rival Internet stakeholders -- met with a mixed response. Corporations, fearing it will make protecting their trademarks more difficult, are critical of the Government recommendation to add five new domains relatively quickly. But some entrepreneurs, hoping to build a business by creating domain registries, are calling for a more open and competitive system sooner rather than later. Other factions contend that the Government is providing little protection for consumers by advocating an open market for registries. Jon Postel, the father of the Internet's address system, has expressed dissatisfaction with parts of the Government proposal. Mr. Postel, who has been assigning addresses since the network's early days, is the sole member of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, which handles its technical underpinnings. Mr. Postel has endorsed the proposal of an international group organized by leaders of the Internet's technical community to add more domain names and a swifter end to Government involvement than the Clinton Administration's proposal recommends. Last week, as the Commerce Department prepared to publish the Administration report, Mr. Postel alarmed some Government officials by directing several of the 12 computers that handle address queries to circumvent the Government-controlled machine in Herndon, Va., which has traditionally served as the hub for such traffic. A researcher at the University of Southern California, Mr. Postel works under a contract from the Defense Department. But his authority, emblematic of the haphazard organizational structure of the Internet -- a structure that the Government would like to see formalized -- stems from more than two decades of arbitrating disputes and building consensus among the network's engineers. Mr. Magaziner called Mr. Postel a tremendous asset, but added that "having one guy who is basically operating" the domain name system under an old contract from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency "makes a lot of people uncomfortable." Mr. Postel said Friday that the timing of his rerouting experiment "may have been unfortunate" but that it was only a test and that he would return the "root server" computers to their previous configuration. He said he fully supported the transfer of his duties to a nonprofit corporation like that described in the Government report. The report said the transition should take place by Sept. 30. The Government would retain oversight for two more years. "It's always been one of these things where you can call up somebody and say, 'Paul, we really need to change the address on this server,' and he knows it's you because he can recognize your voice," Mr. Postel said. "But the scale has become so large, you can't go on depending on particular individuals just because they're that individual and they play a critical role. "My main concern," he added, "is that the Internet technical community started this effort more than a year ago and people followed it in good faith, and that doesn't seem to be spoken to at all in what the Government is saying." The independent group, called the Internet Council of Registrars, had recommended the addition of seven domain names, and its 88 members had organized an international oversight board not unlike the one proposed by the Government. The Government's draft proposal will be open for public comments for a short period. A Commerce Department official, J. Beckwith Burr, said the Government hoped to have a plan approved by April. Network Solutions Inc. of Herndon, Va., which has an exclusive contract with the National Science Foundation to administer the key ".com" ".net" and ".org" domains, applauded the proposal for moving toward competition without sacrificing stability. Under the plan, the company would open its data base to competing registrars "as soon as possible." Network Solutions, a subsidiary of the Science Applications International Corporation, is also expected to drop its price for an initial two-year registration to $70 from $100 on April 1, when the Government proposes to eliminate a 30 percent surcharge on registrations that now goes into an Internet infrastructure fund. Some entrepreneurs who have already laid claim to new domain registries were also enthusiastic about the Administration's proposal. "Isn't it wonderful?" asked Christopher Ambler, founder of Image Online Design, a company in San Luis Obispo, Calif., that has registered several thousand applicants under the ".web" domain, which is not currently accessible by Internet users. "It opens the domain name registration arena for fair competition." Trademark holders criticized the lack of a unified system for hammering out trademark disputes. "It's a disappointment," said Sally M. Abel, the chairwoman of the International Trademark Association's Internet subcommittee. "We are concerned about consumer confusion and increased costs of policing trademark rights and we plan to submit a formal response." And some international groups raised questions about insuring representation on the board that would oversee the address system. "My concern is there is no mechanism to provide proportional representation," said John Wood, a London-based Internet consultant whose company, Prince P.L.C., was sued by the American tennis equipment company Prince Sports Group Inc. for using the Prince.com domain name. Well aware that the report would probably not please everyone -- or indeed, anyone -- the Government cautioned that its paper "does not propose a monolithic structure for Internet governance." "We doubt the Internet should be governed by one plan or one body or even a series of plans and bodies," the statement continued. "Rather, we seek to create mechanisms to solve a few, primarily technical (albeit critical) questions about administration of Internet names and numbers." Many people view the creation of a new address system as a critical first step toward a new governance structure for a medium that is increasingly global and difficult for traditional governments to control. "This is a first draft," Mr. Magaziner said. "If it gets completely torn to shreds, we'll go back to the drawing board."

title:
ATLANTIC CITY;
Coastal Webmaster
body: URBAN LeJEUNE has loved Atlantic City since he was 6, although that's not why he created the "I Love Atlantic City" World Wide Web site (http:// www.IloveAC.com), which he says is among the busiest sites in the state. A former professor of computer science at Stockton State College in Pomona, Mr. LeJeune still remembers the summer when his father took the family from North Jersey to the Boardwalk. "I was mesmerized," he said. "This was like nothing I'd ever seen anywhere. We'd be in the car, driving south for hours, and then he'd take that turn east, and all of a sudden, rising up from the marshes, were all these hotels connected by a big, wide Boardwalk. I was overwhelmed by it all." The web site he designed, with more than 500 virtual pages and links to 6,000 other sites, is just as mesmerizing and overwhelming as the city of his youth. "I'm 65, and quite a bit has happened to me between that first visit to Atlantic City and spring of 1997, when I set up the page," he said. "I've been on the Internet for 12 years, back before there was a Web. I've written three books about the Internet. I've designed close to 100 web sites. Most importantly, I've connected with the culture of the Internet, so I know what people tend to be looking for on the Internet and how people who want to be found on the Internet can get their message out." But he added: "I wanted the web site to appeal to me first. I like being dazzled. I like vitality. I like learning something new. I like history. I like interesting stuff. I like activity, and I like interacting. I like getting something for nothing. All those things happen in the real Atlantic City. It follows that a web site should at least approximate those experiences." To be sure, he has his competitors, on and off the Web. In a town whose technological achievements peaked in 1891 with William J. Somers's invention of the "observation roundabout," a precursor of the Ferris wheel, Atlantic City has become a boom town for Web-spinners. They have fashioned distinct sites for City Hall, the Miss America pageant, the Public Library, Atlantic County, the Atlantic City Visitors and Convention Authority, a few restaurants and eight of the city's dozen casino hotels. (All of those sites are linked to Mr. LeJeune's Atlantic City web site.) But Mr. LeJeune, who had worked for Bell Labs in Murray Hill before teaching at Stockton, is among the lucky few with track records. He previously created tourism-oriented web sites for Bucks County, Pa., and for Long Beach Island in Ocean County, which, on a lark, he decided to call "I Love LBI." Mr. LeJeune, who lives in Little Egg Harbor Township, said he modeled his Atlantic City page on Long Beach Island's. "I got into this because I wanted a business in which I could work while on vacation," he said. "The beauty of the Internet for the entrepreneur is that aside from the occasional need to meet clients face to face, it really doesn't matter where you live, how you dress or what hours you keep. It's perfect for someone like me, who has never really enjoyed working for anyone but himself. My kids are all grown and on their own. For the last four years it's been me, my wife and my laptop. If there's a power failure, I just sit in the dark and whine until the lights come back on." Local restaurants, room reservation services and classified advertisements helped the page pay for itself by last summer, but Mr. LeJeune has received no sponsorship from the casinos themselves. He said "I Love Atlantic City," the busiest web site he has created, is visited about 1,200 times a day, with half the visitors looking for tourism-related information like weather, casino news, restaurant reviews, entertainment listings, hotel room availability and discounts from local merchants. Mr. LeJeune has also used the site to raise money for the Atlantic City Boys and Girls Club and the Jersey Shore Big Brothers and Big Sisters. The site's visitors, who Mr. LeJeune said have hailed from as far away as Japan and Indonesia, are part of what he calls the "interactive community." "They're surfing around and something in the site has caught their eye," he said, "and now they want to have some fun, get something for free or watch something do tricks. "They get that in the real Atlantic City. They should get something similar from me." Graphic   Photo: Urban LeJeune was captivated by Atlantic City when he was 6. Now his web site spreads information about the city around the world. (Frank C. Dougherty for The newyork Times)

title:
INVESTING IT;
Is Yahoo Flying High With a Bull's-Eye on Its Back?
body: EVER since the Internet launched Netscape Communications, a tiny start-up with a good idea, into the stock market stratosphere, investors have been searching lists of new public companies to find the next Netscape. But now that the browser company has fallen to $16, from its high of $72 a share, investors are also trying to identify the next Internet Icarus before it crashes. Closest to the sun these days may be Yahoo, the leading "search engine" for Internet users. Yahoo is the prototypical Internet start-up, founded by David Filo and Jerry Yang, two Stanford University graduate students who built a directory of "cool sites" on the very new World Wide Web in 1994. The two 20-somethings quickly brought in the requisite venture capitalists, professional managers, advertising sellers and stock underwriters. Those, and 30 million users a month, have built the hottest investment in cyberspace. In fact, Yahoo! (the company uses the exclamation point in its name) was the exclamation of anyone lucky enough to have owned the stock last year, when it shot up 511 percent. At a peak of $71 a share on Dec. 31, Yahoo was worth $3.9 billion, making it the world's most valuable Internet-only company. Now that it has dropped back to $63.375 a share, for a $2.8 billion market capitalization, most analysts who follow the stock are calling it a bargain. "The search services have emerged as the most heavily trafficked sites on the Internet," said Paul N. Noglows, an analyst with Hambrecht & Quist. "If you want to invest in the Internet area, this is one of the stocks you need to own." But any investor who remembers the visions of Netscape nirvana may want to think harder. The case against Yahoo is not that management is doing anything wrong or that there isn't a potentially large market for advertising on a service that helps people to use the Internet. It is just that even $2.8 billion is an awfully high value to place on a company that barely breaks even in an industry where trends live as long as fruit flies. The Yahoo bulls back their predictions with forecasts of meteoric sales and profit growth. But if anything goes wrong -- or if things just go right more slowly than expected -- the stock could dive, leaving investors to shout "Yikes!" instead of "Yahoo!" No one said that investing in high technology was for the faint-hearted. And there certainly are the Microsofts and Cisco Systems that handsomely rewarded investors who saw their promise before it was proved. Still, there is a price that is too much even for a well positioned start-up. One of investors' most vexing questions is figuring out how much to pay for shares of the dozens of Internet-related companies that have gone public in the last few years. Traditional valuation methods do not seem to apply. Yahoo has started to make money, putting it ahead of many of these companies. But its price-to-earnings ratio hardly indicates value. It is now selling for 181 times estimated 1998 earnings and 90 times very optimistic estimates for 1999 earnings. (As a reality check, Microsoft, hardly a cheap stock, is selling at 41 times its more predictable 1999 earnings.) Of course, Internet companies are not supposed to earn much now, Yahoo's proponents say. "The strategy is to build your brand as fast as you can," said Bruce Smith, an analyst with Merrill Lynch. "This isn't a marathon anymore; it's a 100-yard dash." So how can investors pick the winners in this sprint? Rather than study price-to-earnings ratios, some analysts look at the stock price as a multiple of revenues. But here, too, Yahoo soars, with a multiple of 42 times revenue, far above even other Internet companies. Straining further for a measure to justify their buy recommendations, enthusiastic analysts cite the novel price-to-eyeball ratio. Eyeballs, in Internet slang, represent the Web surfers who look at advertisements or buy items from on-line stores. The conventional wisdom is that whoever gets the most eyeballs wins the race. Keith E. Benjamin of BancAmerica Robertson Stephens calculates that with 33 million users a month, Yahoo is selling at roughly $100 per pair of eyeballs. To many investors, that might seem a bit pricey, given the company's 1997 revenue of $3.65 per eyeball pair. By 2000, however, Mr. Benjamin estimates that Yahoo's audience will quadruple to 140 million people a month; if so, Yahoo is selling at what he argues is a reasonable $24 per set of projected eyeballs. What's more, since the company doesn't have to pay for paper or other distribution costs, as print publications do, its audience can rise with very little additional expense. As a result, Mr. Benjamin estimates that in 2000, Yahoo will take in $327 million in revenue, producing $144 million of profit. "The stock is so expensive because people realize that the business model is so inherently profitable and the brand is so well recognized they don't seem to have to spend that much to market it," Mr. Benjamin said. He predicts that the stock will rise to $80 by year-end. What could go wrong with this picture? Almost anything. First, even if Yahoo's sales growth is explosive, but just slightly less so than predicted, the models all collapse. Some analysts, for example, project that over time, the use of search engines will decline. "In the long run, we'll all find the five or six Web sites we regularly visit," said Brian C. Oakes of Lehman Brothers, one of the minority of analysts who rate Yahoo a hold. "And we won't need to search as much." Some wonder how sure Yahoo's advertising revenue will be. The company will not comment, but competitors say at least 20 percent of Yahoo's ad revenue comes from ads for pornographic Web sites. Yahoo says it is not at risk from any puritanical backlash, because the pornographic ads are displayed only to people who search for X-rated sites. But the next time a senator's daughter tries to research a report on "Little Women" and finds ads for a very different kind of literature, the company may be forced to rethink its policies. Another assumption that is hardly certain is Yahoo's ability to remain the pre-eminent search-engine brand, drawing in those eyeballs. Unlike, say, cable TV, with its limited number of channels, Yahoo depends on users' choosing its site over an ever-expanding range of choices. America Online, which dominates the home market and serves as a competing guide to the Internet, is pressing into offices, where Yahoo is ahead. And competitors like Excite and CNET are making deals with Internet service providers -- the companies that sell phone links to the Web -- to make their search pages the first thing users see. (Some investors see these companies, despite their trailing audiences, as better stocks, simply because their multiples are in a much lower level of the stratosphere.) Yahoo is fighting back, building and buying more services to keep those eyeballs lingering longer as it emulates America Online with news, chat rooms, stock quotes and email, all plastered with advertisements. And it is going after home users with its own brand of Internet service, in a joint venture with MCI. But it is too soon to know how much impact this will have. Waiting in the wings, moreover, is William H. Gates. Microsoft has made the Internet its top priority, with an investment of hundreds of millions of dollars a year in various sites. It is planning its own Internet search service, to be tied into Hotmail, the free email service it bought recently for a reported $400 million. Microsoft, as you may remember, caused a little trouble for that other hot Internet company, Netscape Communications.
