title:
MUTUAL FUNDS;
Hopping On the Dow Bus
body: THE name Dow Jones resonates with investors, so now that Dow Jones & Company is licensing the use of the Dow Jones industrial average, two mutual fund sponsors are among the financial services firms offering new products based on the benchmark. "The Dow Jones industrial average is one of the most widely recognized stock market indicators in the world," said Larry Waterhouse, founder and chairman of Waterhouse Securities, a discount broker in newyork, which in March will begin selling a mutual fund that mimics the Dow average. The first such fund, ASM Index 30, was started in 1991 but has flown under many investors' radar because, "We haven't had the advantage of using the Dow name," said Steven H. Adler, the fund's manager. A new fund, Strong Dow 30 Value, which started on Jan. 5, mimics the average with half its assets and invests the rest using Dow-linked strategies. Also, the Diamonds Trust, a unit investment trust that began trading on the Amex on Jan. 20, mimics the average, and a number of houses including Merrill Lynch, Bankers Trust and Credit Suisse Financial Products offer options, warrants and other products. Some other fund companies offer funds based on the "Dow dog" strategy. That involves investing in the 10 highest-yielding stocks of the average, which are considered depressed because their prices are low in relation to their dividends. These funds started before Dow Jones licensed its name and hence have other noms de guerre. Just as well, perhaps. After years of outperforming the Dow industrials, the dogs have lost their bite recently. For that matter, why should investors buy any fund linked to the Dow average? The S.& P. 500 and the Dow have only once diverged more than one full percentage point in return over the trailing 3, 5, 10 or 25 years ended Dec. 31. People who want index-linked investments would probably do as well in an S.& P. 500 fund. And investors can choose from 66 of those, at last count by Morningstar, the fund-tracking firm. An important factor in the choice is the funds' expenses. A Waterhouse Securities spokeswoman said her company could not yet disclose its fund's expenses but that it expected them to be "competitive with other passively managed index funds." That could be a tough standard to meet. The granddaddy of all S.& P. 500 index funds -- the Vanguard Index Trust 500, with $48 billion in assets, is run on a razor-thin margin of just 0.19 percent a year, which lets investors reap almost the entire index return, and ASM runs on a margin of just 0.18 percent a year. Strong Dow 30 Value hopes to improve its return by overweighting certain Dow stocks in half its portfolio. It uses both the Dow-dogs strategy, and the "Dow theory," an idea originated by Charles Dow, a founder of Dow Jones, who held that a bull market was in place only if the Dow industrial and transportation averages were both hitting new highs. If the Dow theory indicates a bear market, the fund can move as much as 20 percent of its assets into cash. The "Dow dogs" strategy -- trading annually to hold the previous year's 10 top-yielding Dow stocks -- has been a winner over the last 25 years, beating both the Dow and the S.& P. 500 by more than three percentage points a year, on average, according to Merrill Lynch, which sells a unit investment trust based on the strategy. But last year, the Dow dogs were, well, dogs. The 10 stocks rose 19.6 percent, compared with 24.8 percent for the Dow 30, after dividend reinvestment. In fact, the Dow dogs' outstanding gains in the last quarter century resulted largely from their strong performance in the early years. From 1973 through 1977, the dogs beat the Dow average by 10 or 20 percentage points a year. After that, the spread grew smaller and the Dow dogs lagged behind the Dow 30 in more years than not. They last beat the average in 1993. The results of the other three funds that use the Dow-dog strategy have been decidedly mixed -- as are their portfolios. Hennessy Balanced, which holds an equal mix of the dogs and short-term Treasuries, returned just 12.3 percent a year, on average, from its March 1996 inception, compared with 16 percent for all domestic hybrid funds, Morningstar said. O'Shaughnessy Dogs of the Market, which devotes roughly one-third of its portfolio to the dogs and the balance to about 30 to 40 other high-yielding stocks, returned 21.9 percent a year on average from its November 1996 inception, just ahead of the average of 20.4 percent for all large value funds. Payden & Rygel Growth and Income, with equal amounts of dog stocks and S.& P. 500 stock futures, rose 27.3 percent a year on average from its November 1996 inception, exceeding the 25.7 percent average gain for all large value funds. Graphic   Graph: "An Average Par Excellence" Over a quarter century, the Dow "dogs" -- the 10 highest-yielding stocks in the average -- outperformed both the average and the broader market. But in the last decade, a plain vanilla Dow portfolio won the race. Hypothetical $10,000 portfolios show results over last 10 and 25 years. (Source: Merrill Lynch)

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
Hip-Hop Culture Out of a Williamsburg Warehouse
body: In Williamsburg, Brooklyn, in a dark, drafty warehouse where snack food wrappers are scattered on the stairwells and the most prominent sign on the building reads, "Space Available," an unusual idea for a Web site is thriving. Ben White, 28, who once mixed music for the animated series "X-Men," and Tina Imm, 23, who briefly researched video games for the talent agency International Creative Management, joined last year with Stephen Greco, 47, a former editor with the magazines 7 Days and Interview. They formed Platform, a cooperative of 12 Web-based and printed magazines and 7 retailers with products like Wu-Tang Clan skateboards. Their common themes are hip-hop, skateboarding, disk jockeys and street-wise fashion. Other sites, like Geocities, can be large consortiums of Web sites, but are rarely focused on common themes. "Connecting communities of interest is what the Internet is for," said Mr. White, who said youngsters who could not get hip-hop clothes in a suburban mall, whether in Minneapolis or Tokyo, jump at the chance to order street fashion over the Web. "Ninety-eight percent of our kids have, or have access to, credit cards." In December, the site had 400,000 hits, or perhaps 150,000 actual viewers, the equivalent of a small, thriving fashion magazine. WHAT YOU SEE The site is a digital cornucopia. Click on the magazine selector and you can connect to the British hip-hop magazine Trace, with its visually striking closeups of models and hip-hop performers. Its articles are striking, too, including one on the singer Finley Quaye, whom Trace describes as an Afro-Celt griot, or storyteller. "Balls," a collection of profiles of athletes, has an eclectic view of sports, including an interview with a champion bodybuilder, Monique Distasi, who complains that "Guys are constantly saying, 'Flex for me!' " The magazine Strength offers an international perspective on snowboarding, including a profile of a rising competitor, Jennie Waara of Sweden. Answering a question about differences between Sweden and the unitedstates, she said: "I think that Swedish people are little bit more into nature maybe. They are more natural acting maybe. Maybe they sometimes can be hard. They are not that polite to people, but they say what they mean always. I think it's harder to grow up in the States because it's a lot more violent. It can be a fantasy world over there almost." To avoid simply recycling material from printed magazines, Mr. Greco attempts to find leading-edge artists and perfomers with exclusive articles for the Web. A future article, for example, will focus on Brian Kaws, a newyork graffiti artist known professionally simply as Kaws who purloins advertisements from telephone booths and other venues, covers them with his own art, and then returns them to their original spots. LINKS None. WHAT YOU GET A bracing introduction to the worlds of hip-hop, skateboarding and snowboarding. Graphic   Photo: PLATFORM (http://www.platform.net)

title:
INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS;
Reuters Unit Puts 3 Executives on Paid Leave
body: Three executives with an American subsidiary of Reuters Holdings P.L.C. were placed on paid leave by the company following the disclosure of an investigation into the possible theft of confidential information from the corporate computers of a big competitor, Bloomberg L.P., Reuters executives said yesterday. The decision to place the executives on leave was directly related to the unfolding scandal at the subsidiary, said Robert Crooke, a spokesman for Reuters America. Mr. Crooke said that the three executives continued to work with the unit, Reuters Analytics Inc., which is based in Stamford, Conn., but would do so from their homes. Mr. Crooke declined to identify the executives. In addition, people close to the company said yesterday that Reuters had hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, the prominent Manhattan law firm, to conduct an independent investigation for Reuters. Reuters shares fell 7 percent in London trading yesterday following a report that the subsidiary had commissioned computer experts to electronically steal information from Bloomberg, and that an undercover investigation had been under way for more than a year. The shares fell 42 pence, to 550 pence in London, bringing its two-day decline to more than 11 percent. Its American depository receipts fell $4.25, or 7.3 percent, to $53.625 yesterday. The stock drop began Thursday after Reuters disclosed that the subsidiary was being investigated by Federal authorities. Reuters had been notified of the inquiry eight days earlier, but delayed its announcement until rumors swept the marketplace. The delay raised questions for some shareholders about whether the announcement had been improperly delayed. But Government officials and lawyers said yesterday that unless it was in the process of selling new securities a company was not required to immediately disclose knowledge of a criminal investigation.

title:
The Neediest Cases;
This Year, a Record-Setting Sum Is Within Reach
body: As The newyork Times Neediest Cases Fund enters the final month of its annual appeal, the tally of donations points to what could be the most successful drive ever. By yesterday, the fund had received $4,830,466, compared with $4,171,567 at the same time last year. That puts this year's donations about $660,000 ahead of last year's. With 28 days until the end of the appeal, at least $253,086 more must be received to surpass the record total of $5,083,551 that was collected during the 1991-92 drive. "The seven charitable agencies receiving funds for the neediest cases all over the city have asked me to express their gratitude to Times readers for making the campaign so far this year such an extraordinary success," said Arthur Gelb, president of The newyork Times Company Foundation, which administers the fund. "The agencies point out that thousands of impoverished newyorkers -- especially the working poor -- have been sinking into hopelessness, and contributions from readers have been helping them stay above the poverty line," Mr. Gelb said. "Our wish now is that the contributions will come in at the same pace so that we can make this a banner year." This is the 86th year in which readers of The Times have contributed in response to daily articles about orphaned children, homeless immigrants and hungry newyorkers who have nowhere else to turn. It was an encounter with a homeless immigrant at Christmas in 1911 that convinced Adolph S. Ochs, then the publisher of The Times, that people would give money to help ease the suffering of others if they knew about their struggles. When the man, an unemployed Dane, told Mr. Ochs his story, the publisher handed him a few dollars for lodging, and his card. A few days later, the man showed up at The Times and Mr. Ochs gave him a job in the circulation department. "I would like to say he became an executive," Iphigene Ochs Sulzberger, Mr. Ochs's daughter, said in a 1986 interview, "but unfortunately he died young." The publisher never told anyone the man's name, but from then on, he became known as "the Christmas Night man." Inspired by the experience, Mr. Ochs asked a reporter to delve into the files of the city's largest charities and write unsentimentalized accounts of the 100 most compelling cases. On Christmas Day in 1912, The Times published "The 100 Neediest Cases"; in response, 117 donors gave a total of $3,630. Last year, 12,518 donors gave $4,921,909, and because The Times pays all administrative costs for the fund, every dollar reached those in need. Many of those who have responded are first-time contributors like Margaret Sedilis of East End Avenue in Manhattan, who sent $100 to honor her mother, Cynthia. "I do not remember a time that my mother did not send a check to the Neediest Cases," she wrote. Others are like Kathy Porder of the Upper West Side, who sent $150 that would otherwise have been spent on Christmas presents. Gregory Simon of Chappaqua, N.Y., decided to send in $550 -- one-tenth of the jackpot he won in an office football pool. Werner and Erika Bloomfield of Kew Gardens, Queens, were moved by the accounts of people not so different from themselves. "As immigrants who came here more than 50 years ago, we would appreciate if you could use this money to help struggling immigrants," wrote Mrs. Bloomfield, who sent $100. title:
A New Era Of Wheeling And Dealing;
Rising Competition Squeezes Car Sellers
body: When James Bordoshuk shopped for a Ford Explorer seven years ago, he lugged his young children to one showroom after another over several weekends and haggled for hours. He finally bought the sport utility vehicle from a dealership three miles away from his home -- one of 42 Ford dealers in metropolitan Chicago. Last August, when Mr. Bordoshuk decided he wanted another Explorer, he took a different approach. He went on the Internet to check wholesale prices. Then he turned to an Internet buying service and ordered the vehicle from a dealer 18 miles away, bypassing a dealership only a mile from his home. In fact, he made his only trip to a showroom when he drove the Explorer home. "I wouldn't do it any other way," Mr. Bordoshuk said. After nearly a century of making comfortable livings selling cars in their immediate areas, car dealers now face one of the most difficult environments in years. Despite buoyant sales of cars and trucks, 850 dealerships have closed since 1992. Pretax profit margins are now wafer thin, and many experts predict that hundreds of dealerships will close within the next five years. Thanks to the Internet, almost anyone selling the same product is a potential competitor whether the showroom is in the next town or the next state. The used-car lot and the service department, long big moneymakers, are facing fresh competition from superstore used-car chains and specialized repair stores. And in an unexpected turn, the improvement in car quality and longer-lived components are producing a dark side for dealers: lucrative warranty repairs have declined and tuneups are few and far between. Dealers are also being squeezed by big players entering the business. Publicly traded companies with wads of Wall Street capital are buying dozens of dealerships, hoping to operate chains with money-saving efficiencies. Even the manufacturers have gotten into the act. They are buying out some dealerships and shutting them down. Strong auto sales for the last four years have helped even the weakest dealers. But given the high rate of attrition among dealerships during recent recessions, the next sales slump could drive far more dealers out of business. When auto dealers from across the country gather in New Orleans this weekend for their annual convention, competition will be Topic A; not whether it will continue to increase, but how quickly. A few experts, like Mark Rikess, a Los Angeles-based consultant to 400 dealerships, predict that up to half the nation's dealerships will disappear within five years, even without a recession. "Margins are continuing to tumble across the board, and will tumble severely in the next two to three years," Mr. Rikess said. "It's just going to be too difficult to make a return on investment." Many dealers say that such predictions are too gloomy. Dealers are learning to use the Internet themselves, while constantly re-evaluating ways to stay competitive, said John P. Peterson, a Pontiac and GMC dealer in Bloomington, Minn. Car dealers have overcome difficulties before, such as rising gas prices in the 1970's and high interest rates in the 1980's, he said, adding, "Not many of us run and hide and not many of us get out of the business." But many dealers are clearly concerned, particularly about the Internet. A survey released earlier this month by J. D. Power & Associates, a consulting firm, found that only 10 percent of dealers viewed the Internet as a help, while 48 percent saw it as a threat. Traditionally, dealers tried to stay out of each other's way to avoid needless competition. Auto makers have long assigned territories to dealers, although several of them can share an area in large cities. Though nothing prevents car buyers from traveling across these imaginary lines to check prices, time-consuming haggling has discouraged most buyers from doing so. But the Internet now allows some dealers to market their low-cost cars to anyone with a computer and a modem. There has also been a rapid proliferation of car buying services on the Internet that take orders from buyers and forward them to dealers willing to sell at close to invoice prices. These buying services charge up to $3,500 a month to dealers in exchange for referring buyers. The services have generally concluded that there are far more dealerships in the unitedstates than are really necessary, because Americans are willing to drive greater distances to buy cars. Auto-by-Tel, which arranged for Mr. Bordoshuk to buy his Ford Explorer, has stopped recruiting new dealers now that it has a network of 2,700 dealers around the country. But that is still only an eighth of the dealers in the unitedstates. All told, roughly 1 in 5 auto purchases is made by buyers who consult the Internet or a traditional car buying service that for a fee helps buyers locate the car and price they want. Only a few years ago, just about 1 in 10 buyers consulted an intermediary. About a third of those who consult the Internet or a buying service actually buy cars through them, while many of the other buyers use the prices they obtain to wrangle better bargains from nearby dealers. Either way, the result is that showroom profits are being squeezed and on-line services are growing. Executives at on-line buying services acknowledge that they are making life more difficult for many dealers. "We allow a dealer to reach other dealers' customers, and get their customers," said Frank Zamani, the chief executive of Autoweb.com. The typical buyer who uses the Internet winds up driving twice as far to purchase a vehicle as a traditional buyer, Mr. Zamani added. Auto makers are encouraging the consolidation of dealerships, concluding that many dealers are needlessly competing with others selling the same brands. But auto executives are trying to avoid panicking dealers by suggesting that there will be widespread closings. "I don't see it as being a fast process," said John F. Smith Jr., the chairman and chief executive of the General Motors Corporation. "I see it as a slow process." An extreme example of long-distance auto marketing has been unfolding in Kellogg, Idaho, a rural town of 2,600 people where a Dodge dealership, Dave Smith Motors, has been selling nearly 4,000 cars and light trucks a year. Using low prices and traditional marketing methods -- giving solid gold coins to people who refer buyers -- as well as the Internet, the dealership has drawn customers from as far as Seattle, some 300 miles to the west. It even provides a shuttle service from the airport in Spokane, Wash., for buyers who fly in and drive their purchases home. Rival dealers in the region are furious, and they have complained bitterly to the Chrysler Corporation that Dave Smith Motors should not be allowed to buy so many vehicles from the manufacturer, particularly popular full-size Dodge Ram pickups. But Chrysler has continued to ship ever more vehicles to the dealership in northern Idaho, while trying to reassure smaller dealers that they, too, can increase sales if they improve customer service and attract more buyers by word of mouth. General Motors and the Ford Motor Company have been more cautious than Chrysler in shipping lots of high-profit vehicles to successful dealers, but they are consolidating dealerships. Ford agreed this winter to set up a joint venture with its dealers in Tulsa, Okla., for example. The company's plan is to buy all eight Ford and Lincoln-Mercury dealerships in Tulsa and close at least half of them. It will also open several shops that service cars but do not sell them. G.M. is acquiring a dozen of its dealerships in the San Fernando Valley, north of downtown Los Angeles, with the goal of closing many of them and consolidating the rest under a single owner. But factory takeovers of showrooms are few compared with acquisitions by publicly traded companies. Until late 1996, auto makers resisted the idea of publicly held companies controlling dealers, fearing that the manufacturers would lose control of their distribution systems. But they now say that corporate management and deep pockets could prove useful in transforming the business. Republic Industries, run by H. Wayne Huizenga, who has already made a fortune consolidating the nation's waste disposal business and the video rental business, has been the busiest acquirer of dealerships. Mr. Huizenga has amassed 52 dealer groups with a total of 268 franchises, mostly clustered in big cities in the South. With competition eroding showroom profits, some experts suggest that the next area of trouble could come in service and parts departments. Most service business comes from new-car customers. But as quality has improved, repairs are more likely to come to light later, when the vehicles are in the hands of second owners, who tend to use independent garages. Auto service and parts chains, owned by companies like the Penske Corporation, have also taken away from dealerships much of the high-profit oil and lube business. Now they are moving into more complicated repairs. With all these changes happening simultaneously, profit margins are under pressure in every area of a dealership, said George E. Hoffer, an economics professor at Virginia Commonwealth University who specializes in the business. "Consolidation in auto industry retailing," he said, "is inevitable." title:
GOLF: ROUNDUP -- PEBBLE BEACH NATIONAL PRO-AM;
A Lot of Rain Limits First Day to Nine Holes
body: As usual, people left Pebble Beach today talking more about weather than about golf. First-round action at the AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am was limited to nine holes, after morning rains delayed play for four hours, and dumped even more water on the already soggy Monterey Peninsula. With the weekend forecast calling for more precipitation, tournament officials were hoping to avoid a scenario like that of 1996, when wet conditions forced the event to be called off after two rounds. Tournament officials have already decided that Friday's play will be limited to nine holes. A full 18-hole second round has been scheduled for Saturday, but no decision had been made on whether the tournament will end on Sunday, as a 54-hole event, or if players will return Monday in an attempt to play 72 holes. "Our goal is still to play 72 holes," said Arvin Ginn, the PGA Tour tournament director. "Our next goal is to play 54 holes. Because we're dealing with three courses, it is not an official win unless we play 54 holes." Three players were at four under par when today's play was halted: Tom Lehman, Phil Mickelson and Tom Pernice Jr. The sun broke through around noon and play continued under clear skies from that point. But the ground was already saturated. All three courses in the event -- Pebble Beach, Poppy Hills and Spyglass Hill -- are soggy, with standing water in places. But players who played the front nine at Pebble Beach today had an advantage because the holes played downwind, and players were able to reach the greens of the two par-five holes in two shots. Pernice and Lehman both played the front nine at Pebble Beach; Mickelson shot his impressive four under par on the back nine at Poppy Hills. Lehman, who had momentum, wished he could have continued, but he understood why everyone was stopped at nine holes. "If we had tried to play until dark, you would've had guys having to come back tomorrow at eight, and it probably wouldn't have gotten you anywhere," said Lehman. Some players managed to play well under the conditions, others struggled. Mark O'Meara, the five-time champion and last year's winner, shot a six-over-par 42 on the back nine at Poppy Hills. O'Meara had a double bogey on his first hole, followed by a bogey on his second hole and he never recovered. Tiger Woods, playing with O'Meara, stood at one over par after nine holes. While everyone hoped for better weather, fog was predicted for Friday morning, and the players were bracing for more testing conditions. "It was pretty unplayable out there," said Neal Lancaster, who finished his nine holes at two under par. "We are hitting out of mud puddles. I say if they want us to play, let us play. The man who muds the best wins."  HEINEKEN CLASSIC Ian Woosnam, the defending champion, was as cool as the ice he had applied to a pinched nerve in his left arm yesterday before shooting a 66 for the opening-round lead in the Heineken Classic in Perth, Australia. "I iced the arm down overnight because it was still twinging a little bit," Woosnam said after the six-under-par round gave him a one-stroke lead over Jose Maria Olazabal of Spain. "I had some treatment this morning and I'm going to go back now." Olazabal, making his first appearance in Australia, birdied the final two holes on the Vines Resort course. "I think from 15 onwards I put it very close to the stick," Olazabal said. "I hit it close on 16, to a foot on 17 and I think it was that stretch of holes that gave me confidence."   (AP)

title: Reuters Unit Is Investigated Over Theft of a Rival's Data
body: Federal prosecutors are investigating whether an American subsidiary of Reuters Holdings P.L.C., the news and financial data giant, commissioned computer specialists to steal confidential information from the corporate computers of a major competitor, Bloomberg L.P. The inquiry, under way for close to a year, has included an undercover investigation of the subsidiary, Reuters Analytics Inc., people who have been briefed on the case said. At least one confidential informant was said to have helped the Government obtain an array of evidence during the investigation, including audio recordings of executives. In the apparent scheme, Reuters was said to have obtained information from Bloomberg's operating code, which governs how the company's data terminals work. The case has emerged at a time of increasingly heated competition in the financial data industry. The two companies -- far and away the largest in the business -- have been battling to increase the number of investment institutions that use their services to help decide which stocks, bonds and other investments to trade. Already, the investigation has begun to reach the London headquarters of Reuters. During the summer, investigators were said to have begun examining the role of certain executives in London to determine whether they knew about the apparent scheme. Indeed, without the knowledge of those executives, investigators in recent months have examined their travel to the American subsidiary and their contacts with its executives, people who have been briefed on the case said. Investigators have evidence that some of the data obtained from the Bloomberg corporate computers may have wound up on the desks of some executives in London, people who have been briefed on the inquiry said. It was not immediately clear whether such data could be recognized as coming from Bloomberg or whether the executives knew about its origins. The evidence in the investigation indicates that some executives with Reuters Analytics were responsible specifically for overseeing the apparent scheme, people briefed on the case said. Indeed, industry executives said, a large part of the division's purpose was to develop a product intended to take over much of Bloomberg's business. But that effort was unsuccessful. According to people who have been briefed on the inquiry, investigators have developed evidence that the scheme worked like this: The Reuters subsidiary commissioned another company, whose identity could not immediately be determined, to conduct electronic break-ins of Bloomberg's computers. They would then obtain confidential data and later turn it over to Reuters executives. The investigation, which was said to have been touched off by a former employee of one of the companies involved, is part of a new Government effort to crack down on industrial espionage by foreign companies. That effort began in 1996 with the passage of the Economic Espionage Act, which made theft of trade secrets a Federal crime. Despite that law, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said earlier this month that such espionage against American companies had increased, with the potential damage reaching $300 billion in 1997 alone. In the Reuters investigation, prosecutors were said to have developed evidence that the analytics division, based in Stamford, Conn., used the scheme to obtain the operating code of Bloomberg's market data system, which one person briefed on the case described as "the Holy Grail" of Bloomberg's product. In essence, the operating system represents the central nervous system of the software on which Bloomberg built its business. Bloomberg was made aware of the inquiry several months ago, people who have been briefed on the inquiry said, and has been secretly cooperating with the Federal inquiry. Federal agents were said to have been permitted to monitor Bloomberg's corporate computers, tracking at least some of the break-ins as they occurred. In a statement, Michael Bloomberg, the company's chairman and chief executive, declined to comment. The existence of a grand jury investigation was disclosed yesterday in a news release by Reuters Holdings. In the short statement, Reuters said the analytics subsidiary was the subject of a grand jury investigation in newyork and added that Reuters was cooperating with the inquiry. Reuters said the investigation was focused on whether the subsidiary "improperly obtained access to, and used information from, Bloomberg L.P.'s product." The company also said it had hired an outside lawyer to conduct an internal investigation. It declined to comment further. People involved in the case said that Reuters was notified of the criminal investigation on Jan. 21. American companies are required to disclose such information immediately. It was not immediately clear why Reuters delayed its announcement for eight days. The disclosure sent shares of Reuters Holdings down 28 pence, or 4.5 percent, to 592 pence in London trading. American depository receipts for the company, which trade on the Nasdaq exchange, fell 5.8 percent, or $3.625, to $57.875. Marvin Smilon, a spokesman for the unitedstates Attorney's office in Manhattan, declined to comment. The investigation could shake up the highly competitive world of the nearly $6 billion financial information industry. Some 15 years ago, Bloomberg was little more than an idea; the industry largely belonged to Reuters and the company now known as Dow Jones Markets. But both companies failed to notice the phenomenal growth of Bloomberg, which built its foundation on a squat terminal that sits on more than 75,000 desks worldwide. As the years passed, Reuters remained the undisputed leader, offering a breadth of market information that remains unsurpassed. But Bloomberg, focusing on the needs of institutional investors and investment analysts, homed in on the business of providing historical data packaged with analytical software. That made the company's equipment almost a requirement on Wall Street, for bankers, traders and others who rely on that analysis. "What Bloomberg did was come to the market and appeal to a new set of users who had been underserved," said Andrew Delaney, senior vice president with Inside Market Data, an industry publication. "Reuters noticed several years ago that Bloomberg was growing at an alarming rate, not only in North America but globally. It also noticed it wasn't growing at those same rates." In response, Reuters decided to take on Bloomberg at its own business. It contracted with Capital Markets Decisions Inc., an American company, to develop Reuters Decision 2000, its own data and analytics service. Within the industry, Decision 2000 was nicknamed the "Bloomberg killer," because it was thought that the purpose of developing it was to capture Bloomberg's market and put the company out of business. But relations between Reuters and Capital Markets Decisions broke down, and Reuters eventually bought the small company. After its purchase, the company was renamed Reuters Analytics, the subsidiary at the heart of the current investigation. Decision 2000 never took off. But Reuters came back with a new product, Reuters 3000, which supplies historical data and analytical software that allows users to accomplish much of what they could do with a Bloomberg terminal. By the end of last March, Reuters had received orders for nearly 18,000 installations. Now, prosecutors are keenly interested in Reuters 3000 and are said to be examining whether lines of code from the Bloomberg operating system were used in its development. Federal prosecutors suspect the unit of stealing a competitor's confidential information. (Tom McDonald for The newyork Times)(pg. D18)

title:
GOLF;
O'Meara and Woods on Center Stage
body: When Mark O'Meara thinks about Pebble Beach, he thinks about winning. Last year, O'Meara won the AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am for the fifth time, more than any player in the tournament's history. So when Tiger Woods was looking for a playing partner this week, no wonder he asked to play the first three rounds with O'Meara. "Actually, it's funny," said O'Meara, who will join a foursome that includes Woods and his father, Earl Woods, when first-round play begins on Thursday. "Tiger said, 'You won five times, how many times do you need to win? I just need to play with you, see what's going on, so I can win.' I know he would like to win this tournament." So would O'Meara. Watching the competition between O'Meara and Woods, close friends and neighbors in Orlando, Fla., will be one of the highlights of this year's tournament, an event that is one of the world's most popular because of its picturesque setting and the star-studded amateur field. Despite his easygoing manner, O'Meara is a fierce competitor who is one of the game's great putters, especially on familiar courses. Last year at Pebble Beach, O'Meara captured one the most impressive victories of his outstanding career, when he held off a late charge by Woods to win by one stroke. Starting the final round seven strokes off the lead, Woods shot a brilliant eight-under-par 64, and he came to the par-5, 548-yard 18th hole needing an eagle to tie O'Meara. Woods thrilled the gallery by reaching the 18th green on his second shot, a 267-yard 3-wood. But his 35-foot putt for eagle slid past the hole, and O'Meara's birdies on No. 16 and No. 17 gave him a one-stroke margin over Woods and David Duval. Because he plays regularly with Woods when they are home in Florida, O'Meara is unfazed when he sees Woods make one of his miraculous runs. "When he was going crazy down the stretch last year, I expected him to do that," O'Meara said. "I expected him to eagle the last hole. For me, it was a big win, because I held off Tiger." Woods enters this week with momentum, having won the Johnnie Walker Classic in Thailand on Sunday in spectacular fashion, coming from eight strokes behind on Sunday to defeat Ernie Els on the second hole of a playoff. And no matter how well he plays, Woods will enjoy playing with his father in a tournament for the first time since Earl Woods underwent heart surgery last year. "It will be great," Woods said. "To have him here is pretty special." Many top players are entered this week, including Davis Love 3d, Steve Elkington, Justin Leonard, Duval and Phil Mickelson. The tournament is held on three courses -- Pebble Beach, Poppy Hills and Spyglass -- with players rotating the first three rounds before Sunday's final round at Pebble Beach. Rain and wind are often factors, and Thursday's forecast called for rain in the morning, with the wind expected to pick up in the afternoon. "I seem to play better the worse the weather is here, so I kind of like it," Love said. "These courses are going to play very, very long. You've just got to be real patient." But confidence is also important, and O'Meara has plenty at Pebble Beach. "To sit here and tell you why I won five times, I can't really explain it," said O'Meara, who also won in 1985, '89, '90 and '92. "This place doesn't owe Mark O'Meara anything. I go out there with the attitude I have done it five times. There is no reason I can't do it again."  CHIP SHOTS Among the celebrities competing in this year's tournament are MICHAEL DOUGLAS, JOE PESCI, KEVIN COSTNER, DONALD TRUMP, HUEY LEWIS, BRYANT GUMBEL, VINCE GILL, JERRY RICE, OREL HERSHISER, CHRIS O'DONNELL, MARK GRACE and JIMMY CONNORS. Meanwhile, the tournament mainstay BILL MURRAY will once again look to amuse the gallery. "I just hope he doesn't yell at me," MARK O'MEARA said of Murray. "He brings a lot of fans to come watch him who are die-hard 'Caddyshack' fans." Graphic   Photo: Mark O'Meara plays his best golf at Pebble Beach, where last year he won for a fifth time. (Craig Jones/Allsport)

title: Netscape Registers Big Loss for Quarter
body: The Netscape Communications Corporation, bruised by its Internet rival, the Microsoft Corporation, said today that it had lost an unexpectedly steep $88.3 million in the fourth quarter amid sagging revenues from selling browser software. Netscape said its loss came to 92 cents a diluted share in the three months that ended on Dec. 31. That compared with a profit of $8.2 million, or 9 cents a share, in the comparable quarter a year earlier. Excluding various one-time charges, Netscape lost $20.77 million, or 22 cents a share, in the quarter. Wall Street analysts had expected a loss of 16 cents a share. Netscape had warned Wall Street of a loss exceeding $80 million. Overall revenue grew 9 percent, to $125.3 million, but software sales slipped in the latest evidence of damage from Microsoft in the browser wars. While Netscape's Navigator software for browsing the Internet is used by a majority of Web surfers, Microsoft's aggressive marketing tactics have sharply cut into sales. By giving away its browser and cutting deals with PC makers and Internet service providers, Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser came from nowhere two years ago to capture nearly half of the market. Last week, Netscape said it would also give away its browser. For the full year, Netscape said it lost $115.5 million, or $1.23 a share on a diluted basis. In 1996, Netscape earned $19.5 million, or 21 cents a share. Revenue last year was $533.9 million, up from $346.3 million.

title: 'Gay' Sailor's Dismissal Is Blocked
body: In a decision hailed by gay rights groups and advocates of electronic privacy, a Federal judge ordered the Navy today to halt its efforts to dismiss a highly decorated sailor because he posted a message on an on-line computer service that described his marital status as gay. The judge, Stanley Sporkin of Federal District Court in Washington, accused the Navy of conducting a "search and 'outing' mission" against the sailor, Senior Chief Petty Officer Timothy R. McVeigh, and said that the Navy's investigation of his sexual orientation probably violated Federal electronic privacy laws. "This court finds that the Navy has gone too far," Judge Sporkin said in issuing a preliminary injunction to block the Navy from dismissing Mr. McVeigh, a 17-year Navy veteran who was described in his most recent performance evaluation as "the embodiment of Navy core values." Mr. McVeigh is no relation to the man convicted of the Oklahoma City bombing. "Although Officer McVeigh did not publicly announce his sexual orientation, the Navy nonetheless impermissibly embarked on a search and 'outing' mission," the judge said, adding that he "cannot understand why the Navy would seek to discharge an officer who has served his country in a distinguished manner just because he might be gay." In a statement issued in response to the judge's ruling, the Navy said that "it would be inappropriate to comment further since this case is in the process of litigation." Judge Sporkin concluded that Mr. McVeigh would probably win if his lawsuit against the Navy went to trial later this year and said that the Navy's inquiry into his sexual orientation was a clear violation of the Defense Department's "don't ask, don't tell" policy. The five-year-old policy is intended to allow gay members of the services to remain in the military as long as they are discreet about their private lives. The judge's decision reached beyond the facts of Mr. McVeigh's case and offered a broad defense of the privacy rights both of homosexuals in the military and of anonymous users of cyberspace. Judge Sporkin appeared to side with lawyers who have suggested that the Navy and Mr. McVeigh's on-line service, America Online, violated a 1986 Federal law that bars computer service companies from releasing confidential customer information without a court order or the customer's permission. "In these days of Big Brother, where through technology and otherwise the privacy interests of individuals from all walks of life are being ignored or marginalized, it is imperative that statutes explicitly protecting these rights be strictly observed," Judge Sporkin said. Of homosexuals in the military, he said: "It is self-evident that a person's sexual orientation does not affect that individual's performance in the workplace. At this point in history, our society should not be deprived of the many accomplishments provided by people who happen to be gay." Mr. McVeigh's lawyer, Christopher Wolf, said that Judge Sporkin's condemnation of the Navy's tactics meant that homosexuals in uniform "can take some comfort from the fact that their rights are being protected," while Internet users "can find solace that the electronic privacy laws mean what they say and should be enforced." In recent interviews, Mr. McVeigh, who had been the senior enlisted sailor aboard the nuclear-powered submarine Chicago, would not discuss his sexual orientation, saying it was irrelevant to a court case that should be focused instead on the possibility of misconduct by the Navy. The case dates back to the first week of September, when Mr. McVeigh sent an email message to the wife of a fellow crewman aboard the submarine discussing a Christmas toy drive for the crew's children. Navy officials say the woman was disturbed by the return address on his email -- "Boysrch," which presumably meant "boy search" -- and she consulted the customer profile listed under the return address on American Online. The profile identified the user as Tim of Honolulu whose hobbies included "collecting pictures of other young studs." The information was passed on to a Navy investigator who contacted America Online and, without identifying his ties to the Navy, asked for the full name of Tim. America Online, the nation's largest on-line service, acknowledged last week that one of its customer-service representatives had violated the company's in-house rules and confirmed to the Navy investigator that Tim was Senior Chief Petty Officer McVeigh.

title: BUSINESS DIGEST
body: White House Prepares Plan On Internet Domain Names The White House is expected to release a plan this week that could change the way Internet domain names are created and assigned. The move follows months of intense lobbying from corporations anxious to limit the number of domains to protect their trademarks, entrepreneurs demanding the right to start their own domains and the technical community urging Internet "self governance." The plan is not expected to endorse a proposal by a coalition known as the Council of Registrars, or CORE, to start a shared data base to register sites in seven new domains such as ".firm" and ".store."
