title: 'Don't Ask, Don't Tell' Online
body: The Navy's move to dismiss a highly decorated sailor, Senior Chief Petty Officer Timothy R. McVeigh, for homosexuality shows the senselessness of the military's "don't ask, don't tell" policy and the vulnerability of private information on the Internet. Mr. McVeigh, no relation to the man convicted of the Oklahoma City bombing, is a 17-year Navy veteran with an exemplary record. Recent performance reviews have called him "inspiring," an "outstanding role model" and the "embodiment of Navy core values." Yet Mr. McVeigh is being drummed out on the suspicion that he is gay. The case began when Mr. McVeigh, who is a subscriber to America Online, sent an email message to the wife of a fellow crewman about a Christmas toy drive with a return address of "boysrch." She looked up the user profile under that address and found the name "Tim," a marital status of "gay" and a hobby of "boy watching." This information was given to a commanding officer who believed that there was no basis for further inquiry. A superior officer overruled that decision and turned the case over for investigation. A Navy investigator obtained Mr. McVeigh's full name and address from AOL. The company admits that disclosure violated its own confidentiality rules, but says the investigator failed to identify himself or the purpose of the request. Federal law prohibits the Government from getting customer information without a subpoena or court order, which the investigator did not have. Now the Navy is using that information against Mr. McVeigh. The guidelines on "don't ask, don't tell" allow military personnel to attend gay rights parades, go to gay bars and read gay literature without having evidence of those activities used against them. The policy supposedly allows associational freedom and a zone of privacy. The idea is to protect individuals from inquiries spurred by rumor and suspicion. The fact that the Navy had to pry away, by improper means, an essentially anonymous email address shows how far it went beyond the "don't ask, don't tell" policy. Mr. McVeigh has asked a Federal court to enjoin his discharge. That request should be granted when the judge rules this week. Otherwise the "don't ask, don't tell" policy affords no privacy protection at all. This is another grievous instance of the military destroying an honorable career solely for homophobic reasons.

title: Enter Geekdom's Diaper Dandy. Can You Explain This, Sigmund?
body: He's no bigger than a computer screen, and no more than two years old, judging by appearances. His features are minimal, his hair even more so, and it is not even completely clear that he's a he. But the precocious, boogaloo dancing antics of a creature who is now known as the Dancing Baby are all the rage on the Internet. For two years, the 10-second video clip of the infant with the smooth moves has been forwarded from one computer to another, turned into a screen saver, and otherwise mesmerized growing numbers of computer users. The little diapered dynamo, the three-dimensional animated creation of software designers in California, has already become one of the first virtual characters to make the leap from the World Wide Web to prime-time television. His big break came a few weeks ago, when "Ally McBeal," the popular Fox Television show, featured the Dancing Baby in a segment that posed him as a hallucinatory reminder to Ms. McBeal that her biological clock was tick, tick, ticking away. Since then, the Dancing Baby has vaulted into the national consciousness as the newest pop icon. "Our Web bulletin board has exploded with talk of the baby," said Jeffrey Kramer, an executive producer of "Ally McBeal." "I think this is the first time the Internet -- which is a baby itself -- has influenced the larger medium." Already there is talk about a Dancing Baby doll, endorsements and even a television show. Of course, no one knows why this free-spirited, perversely sexy, footloose infant is poised to become the pet rock of his time, but, inevitably, greater significance is being attached to the phenomenon. Some believe the Dancing Baby (a.k.a. Baby Cha Cha) offers telling signs, not only about the future of technology but about deeper aspects of American culture and the human psyche. On request, Camille Paglia, the enfant terrible of academia, weighed in with a commentary on how fascination with the baby was really a sign of how infantile American youth have become. "For people to identify with a dancing baby indicates some deep, deep trauma," she said in a telephone interview. "Young people want care-taking. They want someone to make rules, to monitor their sex life; they want daddies. The Dancing Baby is a self-portrait of American youth." What would Freud have made of the appeal of a diapered cyberkid with provocative gyrations? "Clearly this has an appeal," said Maryam Razavi, a professor at the newyork School for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis, navigating her computer and clicking her mouse on the baby's tummy to see it dance. "The baby clicks into something in our unconscious. A Freudian would see this as a person's wish to exhibit, to exhibit your freedom and your sexuality." The Dancing Baby was actually born about two years ago, by animators working for Kinetix, a software publisher in San Francisco, which said at least three animators designed the baby as a demo for an animation program. Michael Girard, an animator at Kinetix, a unit of Autodesk Inc., said designers superimposed the baby's image over the digital skeleton of an adult -- thus the adult-like movements. The dance was enhanced by another animator and that version was released sometime in mid-1996.  "It was passed from geek to geek," says Lev Grossman, a producer at Pathfinder, the Web site owned by Time Inc. "It was an amazingly good piece of animation." Because the video dance clip could be easily altered, it spawned a generation of permutations: Psycho Baby, Rasta Baby, Car Crash Baby and even Drunken Baby, which shows the corrupted digital infant smoking, drinking beer and urinating. There was even a version called Madonna Baby, which purported to be a digital clone of the pop singer's real child, which she had vowed to keep out of the public eye. And its dance motions, which include stroking an air guitar and dipping its head, were said to be imitations of one of Madonna's early pop incarnations -- another appealing Internet legend without foundation. But even if Madonna wasn't the inspiration, the baby still inspires. "The thing about the Internet is you find something and you can pass it around to 50 of your friends in no time," said Janelle Brown, a reporter at Wired News. Graphic   Photo: Dancing Baby in his television debut on the "Ally McBeal" show. (Liquid Light Studios/Encore Visual Effects)

title: In Africa, Reality of Technology Falls Short
body: When Jean-Marc Angoran began setting up an Internet cafe here in late summer, he had the giddy feeling of catching a wave at just the right time. Indeed, for a while almost everything seemed to be going his way. The owner of a popular video rental boutique gave him space to run his business in one of the most affluent neighborhoods of the city. An advertising war had broken out between two local Internet service providers, and that, he assumed, would do wonders to introduce the World Wide Web to legions of uninitiated consumers. And a boom in high-technology gadgetry, from beepers and cellular phones to electronic voicemail, he thought, would make a Web-surfing cafe a natural among the prestige-conscious elite in West Africa's most modern city. Five months later, his cafe is devoid of customers for most of the day, and Mr. Angoran has taken to using other attractions, from rentals of Nintendo and Sony video games to an old-fashioned chess set, to draw people into his desolate shop to help recover the $20,000 in start-up costs. "It was pure euphoria when we started out," said Mr. Angoran, who is 23. "We were convinced that we would take off, just like the boom in cellular phones. Unfortunately, Ivoirians don't have the Internet culture, and there just hasn't been an Internet boom here yet." Conventional wisdom in the West held that as new technologies like cellular telephones and the Internet spread around the world, they would set off a great leap forward in Africa, offering this continent's collection of predominantly poor countries a prime opportunity to overcome one of the most crippling legacies of underdevelopment: unreliable and prohibitively expensive communications. Through the Internet, African schools would be able to supplement tiny or nonexistent libraries with on-line access to collections all over the world. Scientific researchers and doctors who lack the money to subscribe to leading journals would be able to keep abreast of the latest work in their fields. And businesses large and small would be able to market their goods or hunt for foreign partners cheaply. The new telephone technology, meanwhile, would supposedly provide a reliable and affordable way to overcome hopelessly outdated copper-wired phone networks, with their noisy lines and overloaded switching systems. But just as surely as Mr. Angoran has been left wondering whether his Internet cafe will ever take off, the reality on the ground of these vaunted new technologies has so far lagged far behind their promise for most of Africa. In a few places, like Congo, formerly known as Zaire, the near-total collapse of the conventional telephone network has made cellular telephones an indispensable and even popular fallback. And in countries like Ghana and Senegal, a small but fast-growing Web culture is sprouting up as competition drives the price of Internet access steadily downward. But in most of the continent, the new technologies, instead of ushering in a communications revolution, are still hobbled by the same stubborn facts of life as predecessors from the automobile to the telephone: on the world's poorest continent, the have-nots outnumber the haves so greatly that many modernizing innovations simply pass millions by. At the moment, Manhattan has more telephone lines than exist in more than three dozen countries of sub-Saharan Africa. In the Ivory Coast, getting a new telephone line can take two to three months. And there has been fierce competition between the three cellular telephone operators that have been in service here for about a year. But for all of their advertising and promotion, the companies have signed up only about 30,000 customers out of a population of nearly 15 million. The Internet, which has been available here for about the same length of time, has proved to be even rougher going for local marketers, and the underlying statistics make it clear that until some things change radically, use of the Web here, and in much of Africa, will remain limited to a minuscule elite. People in the computer industry say that only 3,000 to 4,000 computers are sold each year in the Ivory Coast, and that 80 percent of those are bought by the Government or private businesses. Given such low access to computers, Africa Online, a Kenyan start-up and now a subsidiary of the American on-line service Prodigy Inc., has so far been able to sign up only about 2,000 customers in the Ivory Coast. "People are very interested when you explain the Internet to them," said Alain Ahounou, the commercial director of Globe Access, a more recent entry into the Ivory Coast's Internet market, with 200 subscribers. "But then they tell you that they are still waiting for a telephone line, or that the computer they want to buy is too expensive. In the end you realize that what we really have here is a lack of equipment." Whether for equipment or the services themselves, price stands out as the major inhibiting factor throughout Africa, and the continent's difficult economic straits present a cruel barrier to the very technologies that many expected would help create an economic takeoff. Annual per-capita income in the Ivory Coast is relatively high by African standards, but at about $650 is tiny compared with that of the developed world. Therefore, very few can afford the $3,000 to $4,000 that even a modest computer setup here would cost. Much the same is true for the cellular telephone market, where start-up fees, including a portable phone, begin around $400. Because so few can afford the basic equipment needed to take advantage of technologies like these, providers must charge exorbitant fees to make up their investment costs. That is true up and down the chain of services, from Mr. Angoran, who charges $7.50 an hour to surf the Web in his Cybercafe, to Africa Online, which at $127 a month for unlimited access, charges more than twice the average per-capita income -- and far more than comparable services in the unitedstates. "The nearest Internet node is 4,200 miles away, and we are importing foreign know-how, so the cost to us is very high," said Martial Nogbou, the commercial director of Africa Online, who defended his company's pricing policies. "I compare it to wanting to eat a typically Finnish diet in the middle of West Africa. Of course it is going to be expensive." An American aid program known as the Leyland Initiative is trying to reduce those price hurdles by giving away the technology needed to run national Internet nodes and training local personnel in their upkeep. Over the next three years, at a total cost of $15 million, the program expects to provide 20 or so African countries with their own high-speed Internet access lines. While this is happening, Internet and telecommunications experts say, expected advances in technology will drive down equipment costs, making broader Internet access a reality. "The Internet in Africa is going to be limited to a fairly thin slice of the population for a little while," said Lane Smith, an official at the unitedstates Agency for International Development who is coordinator of the Leyland Initiative. But, he added, "it won't be too long before everybody on the continent lives within five miles of an Internet access point." Graphic   Photo: A billboard advertises Africa Online, an Internet service for the Ivory Coast, along a highway in Abidjan. For a lettuce farmer, access to the service must seem a distant future. (Robert Grossman for The newyork Times)

title: Internet Group Challenges U.S. Over Web Addresses
body: One of the more remarkable features of the computer network on which much of the world has come to rely for communication is that nobody owns it. That does not mean, however, that no one controls it. And over the weekend, as a working group of the Clinton Administration prepared to release recommendations trying to balance competing proposals about the Internet's future, a group of technical experts decided that they had had enough of the lobbying battle and would move to put their own proposal into effect. The Federal Government, one expert said, should not have the sole voice on the crucial issue of naming addresses. "If the Government tries to dictate without the will of the Internet agreeing, it will not function," warned Don Heath, president of the Internet Society, a nonprofit organization whose members are drawn largely from the technical community. "The Internet works by cooperation. When there ceases to be cooperation, there ceases to be an Internet." At stake is who can assign Internet domain names -- the addresses ending in ".com" and other suffixes that define identity in cyberspace. Pitted against each other are the Federal Government, which has financed the critical administrative task for two decades, and an international group calling itself the Council of Registrars, which is led by many of the engineers who have written the code that makes it work. Also in the fray are two rival groups of businesses. On one side are those who have already staked out territory on the World Wide Web and do not want to see new Web sites confusing consumers who are already familiar with existing sites -- a site called "amazon.book" instead of "amazon.com," for example. On the other are entrepreneurs demanding the right to start their own domains -- ".sex," say, or ".web." The Administration's plan, scheduled for release this week, is unlikely to endorse a proposal assembled by the council to start a shared data base to register sites in seven new domains like ".firm" and ".store." Getting wind of this, the group resolved over the weekend to go forward without the Government's involvement. The council has argued that seven new domains are necessary so that organizations that did not happen to be quick enough or rich enough to register the domain identity of their choice could have more options. But the group has opposed exclusively owned registries like ".web," which, it argues, could lure customers with inexpensive registration fees and then raise prices after their investment in a particular Internet identity became difficult to relinquish. But whatever the engineers say, the Government retains nominal control over the machine known as root server A, which distributes new address information to the other root servers worldwide. It is the linchpin in the system that allows Web users to type "www.whitehouse.gov" to view the White House home page, for instance, no matter where they are. Just who else has authority is unclear. Five years ago, the National Science Foundation awarded a contract to Network Solutions Inc. of Reston, Va., to administer the server and register the most popular domains, including ".com," ".org" and ".net." In 1995, the company began charging a $100 registration fee for the first two years and $50 a year after that. That contract, which became extremely lucrative as domain name registrations soared from 7,000 in 1993 to more than one million today, is scheduled to expire at the end of March. Much of the current turmoil comes from widespread indignation that the egalitarian Internet would be the source of such a profitable monopoly for Network Solutions. There is also a consensus, embraced by the Clinton Administration, that it is time for the Government to extract itself from its quasi-colonial rule over the network. At the same time, Administration officials say, they want to insure a smooth transition. An abrupt withdrawal could lead to a situation where electronic mail would not be delivered and browsers would not work. "As the Internet grows bigger and more international, it is not appropriate for it to be an appendage of the U.S. Government," Ira Magaziner, the Clinton Administration's chief Internet adviser, said in an interview last week. "But we have a prime directive, and that is to preserve the stability of the Internet. That's why we can't say, 'O.K., we're getting out of it next month.' " Mr. Magaziner, who received 1,500 pages of email on the subject last fall, is likely to endorse only one new domain name. He is expected to favor extending Network Solutions' contract -- and the Government's oversight of domain names -- for two years, while moving to establish a nonprofit organization to oversee a new competitive system for domain registrars. Network Solutions would turn over control of the root server to the nonprofit organization. Mr. Magaziner has been more sympathetic to the idea of an open market for registries and to the concerns of trademark holders who complain that more domain names make it more difficult to prevent infringement. A meeting has been scheduled this week between the council and Mr. Magaziner, a member of the group said yesterday. What will happen if there is a showdown between the group, whose 80 or so members have already paid $10,000 each toward building the software for a shared registry data base, and the Government is unclear. The Council of Registrars, whose oversight committee includes international standards-making organizations like the World Intellectual Property Organization and the International Telecommunications Union, also has the backing of Jon Postel, who has been administering the domain-name system since the Internet was born. Mr. Postel's work, known as the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, is financed by the Government. He assigns the registrars for country domains and makes technical decisions by gauging the consensus among the Internet's key players. Although he has been reticent in recent weeks to openly oppose Mr. Magaziner's plan, Mr. Postel -- who is well regarded by those who control the Internet's technical underpinnings -- over the weekend added his weight to the council's resolution to move ahead. His support is particularly significant because he exercises considerable control over the domain name infrastructure -- including the crucial root server A. "The details of who asks whom to do what when to get new names into the root domain are still being discussed, and there may be further options," Mr. Postel said. "I very much want to keep the options open and the discussion going. I don't want a confrontation."

title: New Wave of Screen Phones Is Ready to Hit the Market
body: By some estimates, nearly half the households in the unitedstates have a personal computer capable of connecting to the Internet. Now a handful of telephone makers would like to sell a phone to the other half. In coming months, Cidco Inc., Philips Consumer Communications -- a joint venture of Philips Electronics and Lucent Technologies -- and the Mitsui Comtek Corporation plan to start selling souped-up screen phones that can perform many data-communications functions that personal computers do, including surfing the Internet and sending faxes. Cidco, already the largest maker of caller identification devices, is hoping its new iPhone, with built-in keyboard, data modem and notebook PC-style monitor, will appeal to customers who do not plan to buy a home computer. The company plans to start selling the device this week. "We want to tap into a whole section of society that is afraid of PC's, or just not interested in using a PC," said Edward M. Cluss, chief executive and president of Info Gear, a Cidco business partner that provides iPhone's software and World Wide Web browser. "The challenge with PC's is they've become so complex." Cidco's chief executive, Daniel Eilers, called the iPhone the ideal device for grandparents who would like to keep in touch with their families. And in homes that already have a personal computer, he said, the iPhone could provide a method of checking email that is as easy as operating an answering machine. The concept of using the phone to connect to the Internet is not entirely new. And because it coincides with a separate effort by some phone makers and telecommunications companies to develop Webphones -- devices that enable callers to place phone calls over the Internet rather than on the telephone network -- the notion of merging phone functions with PC functions is becoming familiar. Two phone makers, Uniden America and Intelidata Technologies, have been selling screen phones that connect to the Internet, but so far those models have been limited to displaying plain text like email, stock quotes and news headlines. Nokia sells a wireless phone that lets customers check email and download bits of data from the Web, while Philips Consumer provides similar functions in an attachment for its Trapeze digital wireless phone. But Cidco and its competitors are taking the notion a step further. The iPhone, along with phones under development by Philips Consumer and Mitsui Comtek, will be far closer to providing computer functionality, allowing, for example, the user to view entire Web pages with graphics. The user taps the device's screen to perform operations or uses the built-in keyboard to insert text. The iPhone screen is black and white; Philips Consumer and Mitsui Comtek models will display color. There is a catch. While a conventional phone costs as little as $20 and a basic Internet-capable phone perhaps $199, the iPhone is $500. A Philips Consumer IS-2630 screen phone will cost $650, and Mitsui Comtek's Interactive Phone will sell for $599. Analysts say the high prices will be a barrier to consumers, who have seen the prices of some home computers fall below $1,000. Sean Kaldor of the market research firm IDC said that until the prices come way down, makers of these hybrid devices will have little luck selling to consumers, though they may have some early success appealing to businesses in markets like banking. In such a business, these sophisticated screen phones could give employees quick access to customer data or market statistics. To attract high-end customers, makers of the phones are angling for deals with Internet service providers and phone companies to help get the products into more people's hands. Once that happens, and as the price of the screen technology comes down, these devices will be cheaper as well, analysts say. At that point, most phone manufacturers will be developing Internet devices. "If they can get down to the $199 price point, there's a different kind of consumer," Mr. Kaldor said. "Then it costs less than a bread maker." Eventually, Mr. Kaldor said, that will happen. IDC expects sales of all Internet phone devices in the unitedstates to grow from about 333,000 units last year to 1.5 million units in 1999. In 2001, unit sales will reach 4.5 million, the company predicts. Yet it is doubtful that screen phones will ever replace personal computers for full-scale Web browsing, analysts say. For Web surfing, each of the phone devices has disadvantages. None, for example, supports industry-standard Web browsers from Netscape or Microsoft, nor are they able to take advantage of many Web enhancements. The Cidco phone, for example, uses a proprietary Web browser developed by Info Gear and requires that customers subscribe to an Internet service plan from the Concentric Corporation, which acts as a sort of translator between the Web and the phone. Likewise, Mitsui Comtek's Interactive Phone uses a Web browser from Planet Web. Even with their graphics-oriented screens, the iPhone and its competitors may always be best suited for performing on-line transactions and retrieving small bits of information, said Christopher Mines, an analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass. And for many consumers, that may be enough. It is always there and is easy to use, Mr. Mines said, adding that there will be a niche for that kind of product as a kitchen command center.

title: No Frills, Just Service With a Screen
body: On the face of it, the idea seemed preposterous: Who would pay hundreds of dollars a month to subscribe to an Internet chat room? Over the years, on-line chat has earned a reputation as the seamy underbelly of cyberspace -- a magnet for misfits who live out their role-playing fantasies under the cloak of Internet anonymity. But none of that bothered Oliver L. Velez when he set up an Internet-based subscription service for small stock market investors. The way he saw it, chat, which allows participants to exchange typed messages in real time, was the right medium for feeding timely buy and sell instructions to so-called swing traders, who try to capitalize on moment-by-moment fluctuations in stock prices. Last June, Mr. Velez and his partner, Greg Capra, both experienced traders and newsletter editors, started the Pristine Real Time Trading Room (www.pristine.com), at a subscription price of $525 a month. So far, the service has attracted more than 400 subscribers in 32 countries. "What chat has allowed us to do is to put slightly better than 400 people directly in our trading room, giving them direct access to just about our every thought and idea on trading opportunities that present themselves on the spot," Mr. Velez said. But Pristine is just one take on what seems to be a flurry of interest in chat as a business tool. Even huge companies like Merrill Lynch & Company and I.B.M. are experimenting with chat as a way to interact more intimately with customers over the Internet. On the day after the stock market plunge of last October, for example, Merrill Lynch, which is now regularly host to chat seminars, trotted out its brokerage chief, John Steffens, to calm ruffled investors in a chat session attended by more than 500 people. I.B.M. used chat sessions with top company executives last fall to help promote the introduction of its Internet commerce-ready line of AS/400e mid-range computers. More than 2,000 customers took part in the sessions, which were repeated three times to cover time zones in Europe and Asia. The software maker Symantec this month added chat to its World Wide Web site to offer live help to customers with technical problems, and the software retailer Egghead's on-line store lets customers chat with a "sales egg" while they are shopping, or with other customers in a virtual lounge. Mail Boxes Etc., the chain of business service centers, is installing chat as a training and advice forum for its 3,000 franchisees, and DuPont is looking at chat as an aid for its corporate customers. As a business tool, chat holds out the promise of reducing a company's dependence on the telephone as a means of conducting customer service, sales and support, as well as the costly call centers and toll-free lines that go with it. Symantec, a software company with about $500 million in annual sales, employs about 500 people to handle thousands of phone calls a week at its customer service center in Eugene, Ore. The company, which provides free phone support for its software for 90 days, has been encouraging customers to solve their own problems by going to its Web site and using a self-help data base. Now, they can also get live help by clicking a button on the Web page. "Chat should reduce costs from the telephone, but at this point it's hard to say how much specifically," said Michael Gelardi, a manager in the service marketing department. A recent study by Jupiter Communications, a newyork-based consulting and market-research firm, suggests servicing customers with chat could cost as little as 25 cents a transaction, compared with $1.25 for each phone transaction. But keeping customers happy may be just as important. Chase Manhattan Bank is looking at chat as a way to assist retail customers who run into difficulty while using its Web site. "Rather than have that customer walk away unsatisfied, we want to provide a safety valve where somebody from Chase can help that customer right away," said William Graham, Chase's manager of Internet services. Others see chat as a promising new tool for training and education. Marshall Industries, a distributor of electronic components, chips and test equipment, began Internet seminars in 1995 to educate customers and its sales force about the company's new products. Robert Edelman, a Marshall vice president, said he saw seminars on the Internet as a substitute for the costly road shows the company had been doing. The Internet seminars follow the typical business presentation format: a slide show with voice-over narration -- but delivered live over the Web. At the end of the presentation, chat is used to handle a question-and-answer session with the audience. The seminars turned out to be so effective that Mr. Edelman has since spun off a company called the Education News and Entertainment Network, which last year produced more than 100 such seminars for companies like Advanced Micro Devices, Texas Instruments and others. For the software industry, the emergence of chat as a business tool is not expected to have a major impact, at least in the short term: Forrester Research estimates revenues for the sector were less than $10 million last year. But chat start-ups like iChat, eShare and E-Pub, which make chat software for Web sites like Yahoo and Geo Cities, see business chat as a much bigger opportunity. "The majority of the companies that we are talking to see the need to interact with customers on the Web," said Dean Cruse, director of marketing at iChat. Another company, Business Evolution Inc., based in Princeton, N.J., predicts that business customers will want a stronger and more capable kind of chat software than that which is used for socializing. The company, which specializes in business software for collaborative work, has created a software program called Interact.Service, which is designed to provide one-click access to a live customer service representative. "You are not running a chat room, you are running a customer service center on the Web and you have to project the kind of professional image you project in the real world," said Business Evolution's chief executive, P. V. Kannan. The company's customers include Symantec, Chase Manhattan and DuPont. The cost of installing a chat service on a Web site is quite modest. Symantec, for example, paid $30,000 for the basic software from Business Evolution and now has 50 customer service representatives using it. Pristine got its on-line trading room up and running for just $15,000 and pays about $1,000 a month to iChat to be host of the service on its server. So far, however, few of the early experiments with chat as a customer service medium seem to have found the right formula. For example, on several recent visits to Egghead's on-line store, not one "sales egg" responded to numerous requests for assistance. (Several other shoppers periodically drifted through the virtual lounge area, but none of them seemed very talkative, either.) Nevertheless, Amy Bruckman, an assistant professor at Georgia Tech and a former researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Media Lab, predicts that chat will eventually become almost as popular for business as it is for users of on-line services. "I don't think it will ever be as widely used as email," she said. "But I think it already is and will continue to be used in serious business contexts." Graphic   Drawing (Scott Menchin)

title:
Taking In the Sites;
A Virtual Trip to World Fairs Past
body: It has been more than a quarter-century since the last newyork World's Fair closed up shop on a former ash heap in Queens. Precious little of it remains in Flushing Meadows -- just the Unisphere and a few other structures in varying states of decay. But the 1964-65 fair lives on on the World Wide Web, as does its precursor, the 1939-40 newyork World's Fair, and other grand expositions. And the fairs' poorer cousins, amusement parks, are well represented too, with sites devoted to defunct parks like Coney Island in Brooklyn, Freedomland in the Bronx, Palisades Amusement Park in New Jersey and Boblo Island near Detroit. These sites are lovingly created and maintained by aficionados, and largely devoid of commercialism. To tour them is to rekindle memories of sheer wonder (in the case of world's fairs) and sheer terror (in the case of amusement parks). In the vernacular of Disney, they are definitely "E" tickets. There are two good sites dedicated to the 1964-65 newyork fair. Both offer extensive information about the fair's 140 pavilions, which ranged from an elaborate re-creation of a Belgian village to a house built of Formica. One site, by Jeffrey Stanton, an amateur historian and author in Venice, Calif., features clickable maps of the fair grounds, plenty of photographs, and articles on the construction of the fair and the technology it showcased. (The latter offers the delicious tidbit that the fair organizers asked the Atomic Energy Commission to build a mobile nuclear reactor for the event. The commission declined.) The Web is a generational thing, of course, so perhaps it is not surprising that people with memories of the 1939-40 newyork fair have fewer options. The best site consists largely of a personal essay in which the author points out that he created the site after finding nothing about the fair on the Web. The site has links to other articles, book reviews and photographs, and serves as a kind of gathering place for others who fondly remember the Trylon and Perisphere, the fair's symbols. The granddaddy of world's fairs, at least in the unitedstates, was the World's Columbian Exposition, held in Chicago in 1893 to celebrate the 400th anniversary of Columbus's voyage to the New World. It is represented by two sites, one of which details everything from the number of tickets sold (21.5 million) to the cost of various forms of transportation (a sedan chair, borne by native Turks, was 75 cents an hour). There is extensive information about the fair's great innovations, including the Ferris wheel (invented for the event by George Ferris) and the Midway Plaisance, the central group of paying attractions that helped make the fair a financial success. The midway concept was so successful that it became the basis for most American amusement parks until the Disneyland era, after World War II. And some of those now-silent parks can be found on the Web. The site for Boblo Island, which closed in 1993 after 95 years of entertaining Michigan and Ontario residents, consists solely of a long essay. But the history is fascinating and detailed, describing, among other things, the origin of the name (it is a corruption of Bois Blanc) and several unfortunate incidents, including the time in 1941 when 3,000 women and children were stranded on the island for most of a night because of a lack of ferry boats. There are references to Coney Island, once the grandest of America's amusement areas (it was actually three separate parks), all over the Web. The most elaborate site is one created by Mr. Stanton, who has made something of a specialty in researching old fairs and parks (he has sites for Expo '67 and the Venice, Calif., amusement piers as well). As Mr. Stanton's site painfully details, Coney Island is just a shell of its former self: aside from the Cyclone coaster, there is little left. Two other parks in the newyork area -- Palisades, on the cliffs overlooking the Hudson, and Freedomland U.S.A. in the Bronx -- have disappeared completely, except on the Web. Palisades has its own historical society, which maintains a Web site that, while still under construction, features a history of the park and some sound files, including the famous radio jingle ("Palisades has the rides, Palisades has the fun, come on over"). Freedomland's site is more extensive, with plenty of photographs and maps of the park, which was laid out in the shape of the unitedstates. There is also a listing of where some of Freedomland's rides are today (the Tornado ride, for example, migrated to a park in Lake George, N.Y.) and even a link to Co-op City, the vast housing project that rose from the park's ashes. Even Disneyland, while obviously not defunct, has a retro site of sorts. Cleverly titled Yesterland, it features descriptions of attractions that have been phased out at the California park over the years. It also includes a discussion of Disneyland's old coupon policy, in which a separate ticket was required for each ride or attraction, an "A" ticket for the simplest ride to an "E" ticket for the most elaborate or thrilling. Disneyland, of course, begat Disney World in Florida, the crown jewel of what have come to be known as theme parks. But as one other site shows, not all Florida entertainment ventures turned to gold. "Florida's Forgotten Tourist Attractions" describes many that came and went, like the Honey Bee Factory, a glorified observation hive in Fort Myers, and the Anirama near Miami, a museum of animated figures that was soon eclipsed by Disney. Perhaps the weirdest was Weapons of the World, near Cypress Gardens, where in the 1950's visitors could use modern copies of old weapons "on ranges designed to simulate actual historic and native conditions." It went out of business in the 1960's, a victim, it appears, of the peace movement. title:
THE PRESIDENT UNDER FIRE: THE INTERNET;
Cyberspace Is on Alert For More Scandal News
body: No self-respecting scandal gets by these days without a frenzied following in cyberspace, and the Monica S. Lewinsky episode has not disappointed. President Clinton's previous troubles -- including Whitewater and the stories of Gennifer Flowers and Paula Corbin Jones -- have drawn attention on line. But that coverage seems like a flickering candle beside the Internet floodlight shining on the recent accusations that Mr. Clinton had an affair with Ms. Lewinsky when she was a 21-year-old White House intern. The clamor has not quite reached the level it did during the O. J. Simpson trials -- the high-water mark for Internet hype. The Internet has already played a bigger role in the Lewinsky scandal than it has in any major news event since Pierre Salinger, the White House aide turned journalist, signed on to the popular Internet theory that T.W.A. Flight 800 was shot down by the Navy. The Lewinsky story first appeared on Jan. 17 when Matt Drudge, a gossip writer, reported on his Web site that senior editors at Newsweek had killed an article on the accusations. By now almost every major news organization in the nation, including The newyork Times, has set up special Web pages for their coverage of the story. Some major sites, such as that of ABC News, include video clips of Mr. Clinton hugging a woman identified as Ms. Lewinsky at a rally just after his re-election in 1996. ABC News also includes portions of the notes reported to have been used by Linda R. Tripp, Ms. Lewinsky's confidant who gave tapes to Kenneth W. Starr, the Whitewater independent counsel, of Ms. Lewinsky reportedly describing a sexual relationship with Mr. Clinton. But a result of the essential democracy, or anarchy, of the Internet is that established news organs have no more claim to screen space than basement efforts. There are at least six Monica Lewinsky fan pages on the Web, and they run the gamut from pages detailing her resume to prurient shrines ("This is the place for all of us smitten by this Capitol Hill cutie to talk about all things Monica"). Experts in Internet commerce have said that the only thing that sells reliably on line is sex. A Web page that claimed to be run by Ms. Lewinsky herself was on America Online until last week. But America Online took it down, saying it was a hoax. But on the Internet, where truth often seems relative, it hardly matters whether the page really belonged to Ms. Lewinsky or not. The meaning of its contents are being debated heatedly on Internet bulletin boards Electronic chat rooms are devoted to the subject. "The fact that Clinton isn't talking this time when he responded so fast before should say at least that he's in trouble," one participant said in a Yahoo chat room. "The American voting public has already indicated that it does not care about his sex life," commented another.

title: Three Giants Of PC World Turn Focus To Speed
body: On the first Monday of last month, Compaq, Intel and Microsoft summoned representatives of the nation's largest local telephone companies to a hotel in San Francisco. There, the three giants of personal computing told the telephone carriers that unless they joined the companies' new consortium for providing faster links to the Internet over normal phone lines, they would be left in the tracks of the digital revolution, according to executives at the meeting. The meeting was the technology companies' effort to insure that they would control access to the newest avenue to fast connections to the Internet. Their aim was to enlist allies in what is expected to be a long and bloody war of attrition between two technologies in their infancies -- cable modems and digital subscriber lines. This struggle -- akin to the mid-20th century war between railroads and highways for control of the long-haul freight market -- will determine which technology brings the World Wide Web, or digital movies or any other informational freight into people's homes. But for the telephone companies to compete with the existing, and spreading, cable modem technology, they would have to agree on technical standards. That was what Compaq, Intel and Microsoft wanted them to agree to do in that early December meeting. All but one of the phone companies signed on, and that one, Bell Atlantic, is expected to join in the near future. Perhaps the most revealing element of the emerging high-speed Internet coalition is how desperate most of its members have been to join it. The gravitational force and hardball negotiating tactics of the group's three principals have only exacerbated those familiar business pressures: greed and fear. By the time the new coalition is officially announced this afternoon, it will include dozens of technology companies of almost every size. Many of them will have joined the bandwagon only in the last few weeks. That is a far cry from the situation late last summer, when Compaq, the world's largest maker of personal computers; Intel, the world's largest maker of microprocessors, and Microsoft, the world's largest maker of PC software, decided that today's modems were too slow and that they would band together to do something about it to guarantee a viable competitor to cable modems. But there are some problems unique to telephone-based connection to the Internet. The Federal Communications Commission does not limit how fast data moves over telephone lines, but it does regulate how much electrical power may be fed into those lines. Surpassing the current limit, which keeps most modems from operating faster than 52,000 bits a second, is one of the many technical hurdles the consortium must overcome. At the moment, about 100,000 households, less than 1 percent of Internet users, are hooked up to cable modems. A few thousand are hooked up to the new digital subscriber lines, the technology whose development the consortium wants to shape and accelerate. The remainder of those connected to the Internet at home -- about 15 million -- have connections through phone lines at speeds averaging perhaps 28,800 bits a second, about 1 percent of the speed of the other technologies. The technology companies' need to increase that speed is directly tied to their need to expand their markets. One of the main strategic questions computer companies face is how to persuade people who already own computers to buy new ones. That was easier when a computer's main function was to process data. Programs became more complicated and needed more powerful -- and expensive -- machines; computers needed to be replaced or upgraded to run the newest programs. But the most important function most computers now perform is to communicate with other machines. And as long as the speed of connections to the Internet remains constant, people have less of a reason to buy new machines than they would if the links became faster. Essentially, Compaq, Intel and Microsoft want the computers to be able to talk faster. In the short run, users will be encouraged to buy faster computers. In the long run, the companies will also determine how the computers talk to one another, giving them control over standards that in turn could give them significant leverage over future markets. The new technology, which could allow consumers to link to the Internet up to 30 times faster than they can now, is known as digital subscriber line. Compaq in particular had been discussing subscriber line with other big technology companies at least since the summer of 1996. But the three did not come together as a group until last summer. They staged their first big "cattle call" in September at the Networld conference in Atlanta, executives involved with the coalition said. The three invited dozens of companies to present their versions of subscriber-line technology. The computer companies' chief concern was that average consumers be able to use the new technology without requiring the installation of special equipment by trained technicians. An earlier high-speed protocol, known as I.S.D.N., has floundered in part because it requires local telephone companies to dispatch an engineer to each place where it is to be used. The companies were adamant that everyday computer users be able to buy a subscriber-line modem and plug it in just as easily as they install existing modems. The computer companies' concern with subscriber line came at an ideal time for the nation's big local telephone companies. The regional Bells and large independent local phone companies like the GTE Corporation have been experimenting with subscriber line at least since the late 1980's. But they had not deployed it widely for at least four reasons: They had no pressing reason to make the investment; there was no agreement on standards; there was little sense of cooperation from computer manufacturers, and perhaps most important, there was little confidence that the technology could be deployed quickly and easily enough to avoid a catastrophic backlog of orders. With the emergence of the Compaq-Intel-Microsoft alliance, all four conditions were changed. For the last few years, cable television companies have been saying that their networks are going to pave the information highway of the future, posing a direct threat to local telephone companies. The new group was promising to standardize the technology and fully cooperate with the telephone companies. And perhaps most important, the computer companies said they would take responsibility for most marketing and retail distribution. The phone companies would still have to spend up to $1,000 a line upgrading their equipment to handle the faster flow of data. But with retail prices for the service expected to be at least $40 a month, those costs could be recovered fairly quickly. U S West was an early convert, having already deployed subscriber-line technology in the Phoenix area earlier that year. Bell Atlantic was the only holdout, having made a bet on a rival subscriber-line technology. However, that company will probably join the group soon. Negotiations have been more difficult on the hardware side of the coalition. Although it appears that some of the main technology for the group will come from Alcatel of France and Aware Inc., many other companies had to be given a role for fear that they would turn their market power against the group. Lucent Technologies Inc., for instance, will play a big part, not least because of the simple fact that its equipment is in about 70 percent of the local switching offices in the unitedstates. The group wanted to announce its existence last month, according to executives who deal with it, but delayed to help insure that disagreements -- especially over patents -- would be dealt with inside the coalition rather than in courtrooms. Besides the cable television operators, the most important company that could suffer because of the coalition is the 3Com Corporation, which will surely be part of the group. But 3Com's U.S. Robotics unit is a leading maker of modems, and Compaq and Intel are looking to make much of the subscriber-line equipment. Many of the other companies that will be a part of the coalition will have jumped in for a simple reason. As one data networking executive said, "If you are going to have three enemies, they really shouldn't be Microsoft, Intel and Compaq." title:
INVESTING IT;
Choosing Between Phone and Cable for Internet Access
body: WHEN Wall Street learned last week that most of the Baby Bells were joining with three computer giants to offer consumers superfast access to the Internet, there were some short-term stock gyrations and some long-term speculation about the meaning of it all. The biggest question: Will the telephone companies or the cable companies win the battle to offer this service? The new consortium, which is scheduled to announce its venture this week, so far includes GTE and U S West Communications, BellSouth, SBC Communications and Ameritech, together with the technology giants Microsoft, Intel and Compaq Computer. The companies hope to develop new modems and software that will be up to 30 times faster than today's telephone modems. The alliance wants these products on store shelves by Christmas, although some experts suggest mid-1999 as a more realistic target. Whenever the sales start, the group, like others that aspire to this market, is eyeing in particular those people who work at home, telecommuters who need quick access to their employers' computer networks and heavy surfers of the Internet. One company happy about the initiative is Aware Inc., based in Bedford, Mass. The new alliance has partly embraced Aware's technology for a "digital subscriber line," or D.S.L., which would allow for high-speed data transmission over normal telephone wires without the installation of special wall jacks by trained technicians. Shares of Aware rose about 27 percent last week, to $14.25 at Friday's close. "Aware is a small company, and they happen to have a key component to make the wishes of the consortium come true," said Michael B. Neiberg, a stock analyst for Furman Selz, which helped Aware go public in 1996. "They are a big winner. Pairgain could be another winner." The stock of Pairgain Technologies, which has a D.S.L. technology that differs slightly from Aware's, rose about 10 percent last week, closing on Friday at $19.1875. Other possible D.S.L. players include Texas Instruments and Westell Technologies, although their relationships with the consortium, along with Pairgain's, remain unclear. Some stocks sank on news of the telephone-based alliance. They include mostly companies that have spent heavily to provide high-speed Internet connections through the major alternative to phone wires -- television cables. Shares of the At Home Corporation, which sells such cable connections, slipped about 16 percent last week, closing on Friday at $22.3125. Scientific-Atlanta, which makes cable boxes, suffered about a 12 percent decline and now trades at $14.9375. Do these short-term reactions tell the long-term story? Michael Murphy, portfolio manager for the Murphy New World Technology funds and author of "Every Investor's Guide to High-Tech Stocks and Mutual Funds" (Broadway Books), thinks so. "In the big bet between cable and telephone companies, the likely winner is the phone companies" because their technology is designed to carry two-way traffic, Mr. Murphy said. By contrast, "television cables were designed as one-way systems to broadcast to the home," he said. "In order to have two-way communication, you have to rebuild the whole thing." Many analysts disagree, saying it is too early to write off cable. So far, about 100,000 people have signed up for cable modems, and service is available to about 10 percent of the nation's homes. That is just a toehold, of course, but the cable industry has big investments at stake and will therefore fight aggressively to increase its market share and fend off the phone companies. Moreover, Daniel H. Rimer, an analyst with Hambrecht & Quist, which took At Home public in July, said: "At Home's advantage is that they've been thinking about this a long time and they've got common agreements with all of their partners. You should invest in what seems to be the solution with the most traction behind it." Other analysts stake out a middle ground. "As the market develops," said Beth Gage, a consultant for Tele Choice, a telecommunications consulting firm, "the cable-versus-phone battle is going to be fought in each local market, depending on how quickly the different players roll out services and their pricing packages." Whoever is right, the stakes may be large. Nobody knows exactly how many consumers will switch to superspeed connections to make it easier to watch videos, listen to audio and download large data files. One consulting outfit, the International Data Corporation, projects about 2.5 million digital subscriber lines by the end of 2001. And projections for the growth in cable modems range from three million to seven million. Besides considering the obvious stocks involved, like Aware and At Home, how can investors think about this potentially huge market? One strategy involves the trickle-down effect: look for companies that are suppliers to the companies that you expect will profit from high-speed Internet access. If the new consortium looks like the winner to you, for example, consider Analog Devices, which makes the computer chips for Aware, and National Semiconductor, which makes similar chips. "These chips are going to be turned out like jelly beans," Mr. Murphy said. Companies that supply Internet-related equipment to Baby Bells may also see business surge if the alliance prevails. Analysts mentioned Lucent, Northern Telecom, Motorola, Newbridge Networks and Bay Networks as some big potential beneficiaries. A SECOND, safer strategy is to hedge: seek companies that will prosper no matter which industry wins. Microsoft, for example, has bet on both the telephone and the cable technologies. It is part of the new telephone-based consortium and it has invested $1 billion in the cable company Comcast, which owns part of At Home. Cox Communications has also invested in both sides of the question, analysts said. No matter which system dominates the market, high-speed Internet access should be a boon for companies like America Online that provide the graphical interface and data packaging for users of the Internet. On-line publishers, particularly those that are constrained by the speed of today's modems, could also benefit either way. "Speed just makes them more accessible and opens up programming options," said Paul W. Noglows, digital media analyst for Hambrecht & Quist. title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: ASTORIA;
Web Surfing Amid the Suds
body: Monica Serrano could have been watching cartoons or playing with friends on a recent Saturday morning. But she insisted on going to a new Laundromat in her neighborhood. The fourth grader, whose favorite subjects are science and math, was not interested in sorting and folding clothes. She wanted to surf the World Wide Web. "This is the specific reason we went to the laundry, because she said she wanted to go to the Internet thing," her stepfather, Nick Naclerio, said in the Super Internet Laundromat, at 31st Street and 30th Avenue. Monica found a Web site devoted to Picasso and, after looking at several paintings, added an electronic bookmark so she could find her way back. By the time the rinse cycle started on her laundry, she was playing solitaire on screen. If the coffeehouse-cinema-Laundromat was the coin-laundry industry's marketing gimmick for the early 90's, perhaps the cyber Laundromat is the one for the turn of the century. Victor Tiganila and Nicky Borcea think so. Mr. Tiganila said he and Mr. Borcea had come up with the idea two years ago over beers at Tony's Souvlaki, across the street from a Saab dealership that gave way to the Laundromat. They were searching for ways to go into business together. Mr. Borcea owned a Laundromat, and Mr. Tiganila, a computer specialist at a Queens company, had earned a master's degree in computer science in Romania, their native country. The cyber Laundromat was born two months ago, next to a Bangledeshi grocery and a Greek employment and immigration agency. An industry expert, Brian Wallace, said he knew of a few other cyber Laundromats around the country. "The first I heard of this was about two years ago," said Mr. Wallace, director of communications for the Coin Laundry Association.   WILLIAM MAXWELL Graphic   Photo: Monica Serrano, left, and Joy Laurel surf the Web as the laundry spins. (Andrea Mohin/The newyork Times)

title:
NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: NEW YORK ON LINE;
A Museum for Digital Art
body: Even before it had a Web site, the Museum of Modern Art was on the Web. As long ago as 1995, decades away in Internet time, MOMA curators would put on other institutions' Web sites such exhibitions as "Mutant Materials in Contemporary Design," a look at artists working in materials like carbon-fiber-reinforced plastic. That May 1995 exhibit, with Paola Antonelli as curator, was on the Web site of the School of Visual Arts, another Manhattan art institution. But eventually, in April 1996, the museum established its own site, which the staff has taken care to use for the Web's audiovisual and interactive features. The museum now buys art expressly for the Web, much as it would any other art object, except that instead of photographing a painting or sculpture and then posting it on the Web, the art exists solely on a computer disk and in cyberspace. MOMA's Web site has 1.5 million visitors a year, about the same number of physical visits per year to the actual museum, said Patterson Sims, who oversees the site. "We want to avoid bells and whistles in the Web site, things that are just gimmicks, and provide a legible, comprehensible experience of art," he said. WHAT YOU SEE -- Peter Halley's "Exploding Cell" is a digital work of art that the museum has purchased. It is part of a current exhibition, ending on Feb. 8, called "New Concepts in Printmaking 1." The Web project consists of digital files that Mr. Halley used to produce images for the wallpaper in the printmaking exhibition. Web visitors select one of Mr. Halley's nine images, then choose colors to illuminate areas of the image and print the composition. The finished image carries the visitor's and Mr. Halley's signature. In "Stir-Fry: A Video Curator's Dispatches From China," Barbara London, an associate MOMA curator, filed daily diary entries, as well as audio and video clips, from a monthlong trip to China in September 1997. Looking for contemporary art, she was surprised to find interesting pieces, which she posted on the Web, in a Guangzhou university devoted mainly to science, which did not appear to have "art police" monitoring students' activities. But the school, she wrote, "was out of the loop, a backwater for art." "Engineering, physics, mathematics," she said, "these are the faculties that counted, and they ran the school. They had no time for the political intrigues of the art establishment." Even in MOMA's more conventional section called "The Collection," the museum has taken advantage of the Web by providing audio clips -- the same commentary on the museum's Acoustigude headphones -- for works like Edward Hopper's 1925 painting "House by the Railroad," whose use of light influenced cinematographers. "There is no sign of human presence," comments Kirk Varnedoe, chief curator for MOMA's department of painting and sculpture, in the Web site audio commentary, "but if you look closely at the window, some with shades half drawn, other closed, it's not clear if the house is totally abandoned." title:
POSTINGS: A Site That Crunches Numbers;
Refinancing On the Web
body: With mortgage rates low, many homeowners are wondering whether they should refinance. To help provide answers, Intuit Inc., the Mountain View, Calif., company that markets Quicken financial software, opened an electronic Refinance Center last week on its Quicken Mortgage Web site -- a cybershopping center for mortgages that the company started last November. The center (www.quicken.com/mortgage) allows mortgage shoppers to provide information about their mortgage, such as the interest rate they are paying, the amount of the mortgage and the number of years and months remaining on it, and then quickly receive an assessment of the costs and benefits of refinancing. The assessment includes the size of the new monthly payment at current rates, and the number of years and months it would take before refinancing, net of the costs of taking out a new loan, would be profitable for the homeowner. "The object is to get a quick feel for whether it makes sense to refinance," said Carl Reese, vice president of Intuit's Quicken Mortgage. He said the assessment was based on interest rates charged by the company's six participating lenders. Homeowners can obtain more information and determine whether they qualify for a particular mortgage by providing more data. Those who find an offer they like, Mr. Reese said, can instantly transfer their data to a participating lender, who will then contact the customer. "Information in our database is only sent to a lender at the customer's request," he said.

title: Browser War: A Concession And a Push
body: Microsoft blinked yesterday in a pragmatic, if belated, gesture that concedes one tactical skirmish to the Government in its high-stakes antitrust battle with the software giant. But by giving personal computer makers the option of erasing its Internet browser icon from the face of its Windows operating system, the Microsoft Corporation gave not an inch on any of the larger issues in the case. Whether Microsoft is violating its 1995 consent decree by tying one product to another is something the courts must decide in the months ahead, while the Justice Department is also weighing a broader antitrust suit against the software giant. Yesterday's settlement, by itself, will have little effect on the competitive landscape in the computer industry. Because of its dominance of the crucial operating sys tem market, Microsoft is already a powerhouse in the new market for Internet software. The more significant announcement for the software business, industry analysts agree, came a few hours later from the Netscape Communications Corporation, Microsoft's main rival in the browser market. An Internet pioneer, Netscape has been battered lately in the browser war with Microsoft. The company announced two weeks ago that it would report a loss for 1997 and planned to lay off 400 of its 3,200 workers. Its stock price plunged, and its future seemed bleak. Netscape's future, to be sure, is still uncertain, but the company struck back at Microsoft yesterday with an innovative shift in strategy. First, the company said it would begin distributing its browser products free -- the same tactic Microsoft has used since 1995 to catch up to Netscape in the browser market. But the more surprising move by Netscape was that it would freely license the basic computer code for its browser products to outsiders and let them tailor the Netscape technology for their own use. This means that software developers -- from professional programmers in big companies to 14-year-old hobbyists -- can fine-tune Netscape's programs, giving it their own look and feel. The free licensing -- far more than the Washington settlement -- could open the door for Netscape's technology being the preferred browser used by personal computer makers. The new strategy will allow, say, Compaq, Dell or Gateway 2000 to modify the Netscape browser and even put their own brand on it. If the PC makers decided to do that, it could break Microsoft's lock on the desktop brand that users see when they turn on their computers -- Windows and Internet Explorer. "This could open up the desktop to competition, and that could be a huge opportunity for Netscape," said Bruce D. Smith, a software analyst with Merrill Lynch & Company. The two steps by Netscape amount to a bet-the-company gamble to try to stop an erosion of its share of the browser market in the face of Microsoft's vast wealth, market power and armies of skilled programmers. By freely licensing its intellectual property -- the so-called source code for its browser -- Netscape hopes to rally a community of software developers around its technology standard, and push that standard forward. The practice of free distribution of software code is a step back to origins of Netscape, which grew out of a team of young programmers at the University of Illinois supercomputer center. The early ethos of the Internet embraced the free distribution of software, as did the pioneer computer hackers of the 1970's. And as a start-up company, Netscape built a following for its Navigator browser and Communicator software with a strategy of free sampling. "This is a very powerful play by Netscape," said James F. Moore, president of Geopartners Research Inc., a consulting company in Cambridge, Mass. "The company is going back to its roots. Netscape grew so rapidly because it first created a community and that community became a force." Given the public debate surrounding the Government's antitrust case against Microsoft, Mr. Moore added, "This move also puts Netscape firmly into the pro-innovation camp, which plays to the larger issues." Microsoft's opponents contend that its firm grip on personal computer software stifles innovation in the industry. For its part, Microsoft says the real threat to innovation would come from Government intervention to stop it from bundling products, like a browser, into its Windows operating system -- thus giving computer users more for less. But the strategic shift by Netscape is a gamble. It will lose revenue from giving away its browser, typically sold for $39 in retail stores. But the company believes that the top goal is to retain browser market share, and that should increase sales of its server software, which acts as the hub of corporate computer networks. In addition, Netscape has one of the most heavily trafficked World Wide Web sites on the Internet thanks largely to its 58 percent share of the browser market. Advertising and electronic commerce revenues from the Netscape Web site have been rising rapidly. Browser revenue accounted for 13 percent of the company's revenue in the fourth quarter of 1997, compared with 45 percent in the quarter a year earlier. "Netscape is no longer a browser-only company," said James Barksdale, the president. "But the browser market share is the seed corn that feeds the other businesses."

title: Microsoft Gives In To a Federal Order On Internet Browser
body: After insisting for weeks that its World Wide Web browser software could not be separated from its Windows 95 operating system, the Microsoft Corporation agreed today to do just that to avoid being found in contempt of court. In another display of the legal brinkmanship that has marked its antitrust battle with the Justice Department, Microsoft agreed to a last-minute settlement under which it will sell the latest version of its Windows 95 operating system to computer manufacturers with the company's Internet browser hidden or partly removed. The agreement settled only a part of the Government's antitrust case against the software giant. The larger issues are now before a Federal appeals court, where a hearing is scheduled for April 21.  Page D1. In a sign of how tough competition in the browser market has become, the Netscape Communications Corporation, maker of the industry-leading Navigator, announced today that it would begin giving away its browser, just as Microsoft does. The Microsoft settlement, accepted at a brief hearing this morning by the Justice Department and Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson of unitedstates District Court, brings Microsoft into compliance with the judge's order last month that it stop forcing computer makers to install its browser, Internet Explorer, as a condition of licensing Windows 95. By definition, a browser is a program that translates data coming into a computer from the World Wide Web into type and graphics. But Microsoft has stated its intention to merge the browser with its operating system so that the Web blends seamlessly with the Windows desktop. Until today, Microsoft had insisted that its merging of the browser and operating system was already so advanced that it could not remove Internet Explorer without disabling Windows 95. "We are extremely pleased; Microsoft has agreed to immediately make available the most up-to-date, fully functional version of Windows 95 without forcing computer makers to take its browser as well," Assistant Attorney General Joel I. Klein said immediately after the hearing. "Competitors and innovators should know that their products can compete on their own merits and not be snuffed out by Microsoft's use of monopoly power." Microsoft said it would continue to make Internet Explorer available to computer companies that license Windows 95, "and we expect it to be popular," said William H. Neukom, the senior vice president for legal affairs. Still, Robert Herbold, Microsoft's chief operating officer, said: "We are pleased to put this compliance issue behind us. Now we can proceed to the merits of the case." Last month, Microsoft tried to comply with the judge's order by offering computer makers two alternatives to the combined browser and operating system: an outdated version of Windows 95 or a current version that did not work. No manufacturer accepted either alternative, the company said. The Justice Department argued that Microsoft's response was a mockery of Judge Jackson's order and moved to have the company held in contempt. At a sometimes contentious hearing last week, the judge hinted strongly that he would find that Microsoft was not complying with his order. Under today's agreement, Microsoft offered computer manufacturers two additional options. Under the first, they can buy Windows 95 with the browser fully installed but hidden. No Internet Explorer icon will appear on the desktop. In this case, a moderately knowledgable user could easily install the icon on the desktop. Under the second option, computer companies could buy Windows 95 with more than 90 percent of the Internet Explorer files included but some key files removed -- the same ones that would be deleted if someone used the Windows "add/delete program" function. Today Mr. Herbold and Mr. Neukom both said that users would not be able to install Internet Explorer under the second option without first obtaining the missing files, and Mr. Herbold said that this option "will still disable Windows 95 to some extent." Mr. Neukom said that several Internet-related program offerings would not function. At the same time, however, Microsoft insisted that "under either approach, nearly all third-party software programs that rely upon Internet Explorer platform services will continue to function." For example, a word processer would still be able to display Internet files. As is the case now, Netscape Navigator or other competing Internet browser software could be loaded under either option. "This remedy shows that they could have been in compliance with the court order, and they are in compliance now," Mr. Klein said. "This will increase consumer choice and will also send precisely the right message to the market." When Netscape announced this afternoon that it would begin giving away its browser, the company also said that it would release the program's source code. That will allow other software companies to manufacture directly compatible products. It will also allow computer manufacturers to create customized versions of Navigator that bear their own brand names or are optimized for their machines. Netscape, while still claiming about 60 percent of the market, has been losing share steadily to Internet Explorer. It recently attributed the slide to Microsoft's policy of bundling its browser with Windows 95. But at the same time, Microsoft, which got off to a slow start in creating a Web browser, recently released a version of Internet Explorer that has been widely praised as technologically equivalent, and in some ways superior, to Navigator. The Justice Department sued Microsoft in October, charging that the company was trying to use its overwhelming dominance in computer operating systems to compete unfairly in the browser market. That charge still stands and will be heard by the appeals court starting in April. And while Microsoft did a turnabout today on the judge's order, the company said it was planning a full and vigorous fight for what it insisted was a matter of principle -- that the Government has no right to determine what it adds or how it develops its operating system. To that end, it has challenged many aspects of the Justice Department's case and virtually every action by Judge Jackson, including the judge's appointment of a Harvard law professor, Lawrence Lessig, as a court consultant known as a "special master" to help sort out the legal and technical issues in the case.
